3.5 stars 
 In Under Rose-Tainted Skies the main character (Norah) has agoraphobia and OCD. 
 I'm so happy this book exists. 
 We need books that deal with invisible disabilities without ableist plot twists (Yes, I'm talking about Everything, Everything. I loved that book, but it was definitely written for abled people and I would never recommend it for its representation ). 
 The representation of mental illness in Under Rose-Tainted Skies was perfect. As a teen with phobias, I related to Norah. 
 At the same time, I felt Norah was underdeveloped. Phobias like agoraphobia change the way you see the world and your life, I know. But I'm not my illness. 
 I'm not sure I can say the same about Norah. Maybe the book was too short. 
 I wanted to love Under Rose-Tainted Skies, but I couldn't. While I was reading it, I thought yes, I feel that way too, but I never really cared for the romance. The only thing I liked about it was that it didn't cure her illnesses (another common and harmful trope). 
 The day I find a book about phobias (or about a phobia that is not agoraphobia or arachnophobia, that would be great) without romance I will be happy.

Wade Mitchell and his second wife Ann live an isolated life on a mountain in rural Idaho. Because Wade is suffering from early onset dementia, his memories of life before he and Ann married are disappearing so Ann tries to "keep" those memories intact for him. 
 However, as the story moves forward, the reader discovers in fits and starts what happened to Wade's first wife and their two daughters and since Wade has rarely spoken to Ann about those events, all she really knows is what was reported on local media. So she makes suppositions from the clues she is able to gather. If Idaho were only about Ann's love for her husband who can't remember a tragic event but still suffers from the repercussions of it, it would be a beautiful (and shorter) book. But the author goes beyond Ann and Wade's perspective (at one point there is even the perspective of a bloodhound bizarrely enough) and muddies the story too much for my liking. 
 I am becoming weary of reading books with pretty writing but weak plotting and/or characterization. Jenny's motivation is never explained which would have been fine had the reader never had any narration from her point of view. But we do and her thoughts and behavior (IMO) are inconsistent with that of a woman who would kill her child or cover up for her child. And had just been an accident, surely at some point she or her husband would recognize this? And why and how did June go missing? That just doesn't make sense to me with the information given in the novel .

This book is awful. There, I said it. There isn't much plot to the book, just a bunch of setup for the rest of the series. I only finished it because my boyfriend insisted that I get through the first one. I promised to finish this one and read the second one, because he swore up and down it gets better. To be fair, he's right. I'm on Book 8 right now (Kings of Clonmel), and the series does improve markedly starting in the second book. But for this one, you will probably struggle through it, for a couple of reasons: 
 1. There's no plot. Seriously. I waited for the whole book to watch the plot develop. Never happens. Just a series of unconnected events in the training of the apprentice ranger. There's a lot of setup for the following books. 
 2. The writing style of Flanagan. He flips from one point of view to the next, and it's hard to see whose PoV he's writing in from one sentence to another. Sometimes I have to read something a couple of times before I get what he's trying to say for that reason. 
 3. There are NO surprises in this book. It's quite fairytale-ish in that nothing bad ever happens to the major characters. 
 4. Will doesn't act his age. He's supposed to be fifteen, but he talks more like he's ten, and people treat him like he's ten. I kept getting this image of a ten-year-old in my head, only to be reminded every once in a while that he's really fifteen. 
 5. This has a medieval feel to it, but the characters talk like they're from our time. He can get away with it because it's fantasy, I guess, but the story world is largely based on Earth, so I sort of expect to get talk that's a little less modern. I don't expect period perfect speech, but he goes a little too modern for my tastes. 
 6. Too many positive coincidences and too many things he only mentions as he needs them. For example, Tug, Will's horse, is constantly showing new abilities that we only learn about just when Will needs them. This happens throughout the whole series, not just in this book. They always have a lot of equipment they need as well. Flanagan would do well to set these things up in advance so they don't seem so contrived. 
 7. On a note for the whole series, I find it obnoxious that he starts out using semi-mystical things in his first two books, but then that whole fantasy element completely disappears starting in the third book. You have the kalkara and the wargals in the first two books, but then you don't ever encounter any other mystical creatures after that. I feel like Flanagan just gave up on that aspect part way through the series. 
 All of those things said, the story really does improve drastically beginning in the second book. If you can make it through the first book, it's worth it to get to the second and move on with the series.

Solomon looks in incredible detail at what he terms "horizontal identities". Vertical identities are identities that parents share with their children i.e. race would be a vertical identity. Horizontal identities are ones where the characteristics are not necessarily shared with the parents i.e. transgender or autism or sometimes deafness. Solomon writes extensively on each of these various differences. 
 He writes with incredible empathy, but really tries to show all sides of every issue. There are sides? Yes, there really are. If you are deaf, should you or should you not get a cochlear implant and at what age? What types of interventions are best for a child with autism? Forced medications or not for someone with Schizophrenia? There are actually an amazing number of issues and disagreements with how to proceed when a child manifests any of these issues. Limb lengthening for dwarfs? Parents disagree on all of these issues and more, but throughout Solomon shows respect for all the viewpoints while providing medical arguments and whatever evidence is available for the reader. And he also shows how parents often love these children as they are and don't wish them to necessarily be different. Just a very, very compelling read. I think they should excerpt some of this for use in schools to foster better understanding of differences. 
 The amount of research this guy did was incredible. It is a lot of anecdote, but that is what truly brings the book to life. It was a sociological study, a psychological study, and yet also a true testament to the power of parental love. 
 One thing I especially enjoyed is that the author didn't totally squelch his own opinions and insight out of the book. If he had some philosophical thoughts or perspective, he wasn't afraid to share those. I think that brought a humanity to the book that you wouldn't usually see in a non-fiction treatise that also has a bit of an academic bent to it. 
 At any rate, I would highly recommend this book as it fosters humility, empathy, and understanding as well as a deep appreciation for one's children. And gratitude on my part for having such an easy life by comparison. And admiration for those who carry big burdens, often with such love and grace.

I put a hold on this one primarily because of the cover, and secondarily because I liked the preview chapter on Overdrive. I don't regret having read it; it's got problems, but even so, I stayed up way too late finishing this one. 
 I liked the setting (publishing house) and the mock arguing between the two main characters, as well as the way they eventually admitted their mutual attraction. However, there were a few things I found not great: 
 -the speed with which they admitted this attraction (could have done with more of a slow burn) 
 -Lucy's weird obsession with how short and tiny she was and how tall and big Josh was 
 -the way Josh usually just seemed to be awkward, prickly and standoffish (Mr. Darcy, good), but then would occasionally be an actual asshole for real (Christian Grey, yuck) 
 That said, I really did think their chemistry was good and I enjoyed a lot of the dialogue. I also liked Lucy's relationship with her parents and with her boss. I liked Sally Thorne's writing and will probably read her next book.

In this re-read, Slaughter-House Five is still the seminal eye-opening experience that I thought it was when I first read it in the seventies. While there was certainly comedic qualities, it is actually Vonnegut's most serious work with the possible exception of Mother Night. Vonnegut has taken his own war experiences and examined them with eye of a man who have questioned too long and has never found answers but realizes that the non-answers may be the answer. This novel is one of the greatest anti-war novels ever. Yet Vonnegut is wise enough to state within the same novel that he may as well written an anti-glacier novel. A must-read for everyone on the planet.

"The Audition" is a 17 page novella prequel to "Seraphina" about the brief scene in which Seraphina had to go through to become the assistant music composer and Princess Glisselda's music tutor. 
 The story started with Seraphina and Orma who was on the way to the castle for the final audition with the court's composer and the princess. Seraphina was nervous after Orma had predicted that she had 12% chance to succeed even after a grueling pre-audition and it does nothing but annoy her. When Orma didn't come back after a walk, Seraphina went to find him but instead she encountered a very rude girl with a pail of fish sauce and hell bent on mischief. 
 The prequel introduced the reader to Seraphina, a young apprentice with a gift of music who was under the tutelage of her music teacher Orma. Her chanced encountered with Princess Glisselda provided their first impression to one another and their eventual friendship that were apparent in "Seraphina". For a short scene, it gave a nice insight to the main character and enhanced the interaction with multiple of characters as should with the subsequent book. 
 I would recommend reading the prequel first before you start reading "Seraphina" to slightly enhance your readincg experience.

Why I picked it up: Last in a trilogy. 
 This picks up not long after Red Glove ends. Cassel is in the agent-in-training program for worker kids. Lila is proving herself in her father's mob business. Sam & Danica are still fighting. Cassel's mom is on the run after working a politician. I do not recommend reading this if you have not read the first two. This is a layered story and while it could be enjoyed a la carte, it's better as a part of a whole. 
 I liked it. A lot. I wasn't sure I was going to, because moral ambiguity is not my thing. Not at all. I am very, very black and white. And the Curseworker world, Cassel's world, is nothing but shades of gray. But it is fascinating and unexpected and brilliant and it doesn't bother me that it doesn't fit into the right and wrong that I want it to. And that, in and of itself, speaks to its brilliance. That it can make me not care about the right and wrong I want there to be. A truly original, fascinating series. A really neat world. And fantastic execution. 
 I want to mention one aspect that exists throughout the series but is most prominent in this book. Hands are erotic. Because cursing is done through bare hands, everyone wears gloves. Bare hands are uncommon. At one point, a character describes the "tear away" gloves at a strip club. Old school pin-up girls have bare hands. Hands are erotic. I love that. I love how it is done in the book and I love the idea and it's just such a neat part of that world.

The Circle is a new bay area company, but is really Google+Facebook. It dominates search and social media, has a huge sprawling campus in the south bay, and is full of intelligent, ambitious young employees. This story is I think a take on where the connected nature of the internet might be taking us. It's essentially a discussion about privacy vs openness, and I think a serious 1984-esque warning about being too open. 
 I thought a lot of the book was kind of shallow and unrealistic. The characters weren't very well developed. And I can't imagine an HR department that would get on your case for not using social media or attending a brunch you were invited too - it was just too extreme to believe. But I suppose that was on purpose, as the author was just making a point. I appreciated the point (see below), but didn't love the story. 
 Mark Zuckerberg has been fairly public on saying that he believes a more open society is a better one. The notion is exactly the one Mae learns with the kayak incident - if your whole life is open to your friends and family, it's very hard to do anything dishonest or that you might regret. The premise of the Circle - that privacy and secrecy are bad - is taking this idea to an extreme that I doubt Zuckerberg or anyone else who runs a social network has ever contemplated: complete openness. Or as its motto says: 
 All That Happens Must Be Known. 
 It is easy to imagine us eventually living in a world like the Circle contemplates. With public video cameras everywhere that document everything we do, and tons more data (photos, videos, texts) available to search engines to scan through. Already there are startups like Dropcam that enable public video feeds that are archived. There are atm and building and traffic cameras everywhere that the police already use. I heard of another startup that puts a video camera on you and it takes photos of everything all day and creates a montage of your day that is searchable/sortable for you. In many ways, we should already start acting like everything we do at least outside of our homes is being recorded on camera. 
 I think the central question the book poses is the one Bailey contemplates with Mae: is there such a thing as a good secret? Should we have privacy at all? Or would the world at large be better off if all secrets are known? I think we know where Mr Eggers stands on the subject, as the book seemed to be written in a dystopian, mocking kind of way. But it is in an interesting thought experiment, as many secrets would ultimately be better overall (not necessarily for the disclosing party, but for the overall situation), if they were known. For example you don't want to tell your friend that you know their significant other is cheating on them b/c you aren't supposed to know, but ultimately it would be better for them to know. Can you think of a secret you know that should be a secret? 
 But of course, there are lots of secrets that should stay secrets. Ignorance often truly is bliss, and people often just need to be weird and express themselves in ways that not everyone would appreciate if it were open. We are private beings, and yet our dignity and sense of self-worth largely stems from how others perceive us. I think this book is a thought-provoking story that shows us how our society is changing.

 EDIT Upon reviewing my list of read books, I'm changing this to three stars simply because it was not very memorable. Seriously, I know I read a lot of books but I barely recall reading this! o.O 
 About three-quarters of my way through the book I was set on a three-star rating for this book, but the plot twist at the end convinced me that this book deserved four stars. 
 The basic idea for the plot (spore wars destroy everyone between the ages of 20-60) was interesting, but not all that realistic. The whole society that develops afterwards is a little odd, however. Many children are left parentless, and instead of doing anything productive about it, the government decides to ban them from working and round them up into an institution, which makes absolutely no sense. 
 The kids-on-the-run scenario isn't totally original, but I suppose it's believable in this story, because they have no one to look after them. I liked the idea of Prime Destinations - renting out teenage bodies to the elderly is a fascinating concept, and brings up an interesting ethical question as well. 
 I didn't mind Callie as a character, but she wasn't particularly interesting or smart. I question some of the decisions she makes in the book, such as her romance with Blake, and her decision to shoot the senator in the hand. 
 The whole situation with Blake was what originally made me want to rate this three stars. I kind of thought something fishy was going on with him from the start because of the way he was so incredibly interested in Callie. I mean I get the fact that she's extremely good looking and a new face in the club or whatever, but in the beginning she didn't give him that much to go on and it seemed like he was a little to into her. 
 The only other thing that wasn't great about this book was the fact that some of the characters were a little flat. Michael, for example. He was supposedly her neighbor/friend, but he's randomly gone at times and there were some traces of romance with Callie. He also never really develops-- he joins Prime Destinations because Callie did and because it was a good way to earn money. 
 The two characters I did like were little Sara and the Old Man. Sara was pretty realistic because of her young age and sweetness. I also liked how she originally was excited to be chosen and how Callie had to physically beat her so she wouldn't get chosen. The Old Man is also an excellent villain. He always seems to be one step ahead, and is fantastically creepy in the fact that he purposefully switches his face into the most disturbing profiles. 
 Overall I really enjoyed this book! There were several minor things that I wasn't too fond of but mostly I was hooked because it had a fast-paced plot and and interesting topic that made me want to read more. I would recommend if you like mild dystopias. Not sure if I'm going to read the sequel or not, but this was definitely a worthwile book.

 I actually had mixed feelings about this book, which is surprising looking at the amazing reviews. I actually ended up really enjoying it but found it took me ages to get into. I'm really not sure why - maybe it was the style of writing, maybe the narrative didn't grip me as much as I thought it would, but it took me a good third of the book to get into it. I actually stopped and started it a few times too, something I rarely do with books! 
 However, once I'd got into the swing of the story and the language, reading more about the characters and learning more about the wonderful Jane, and noticing the various ways it's based on and around Jane Eyre, a novel I am very fond of, I found that this is actually a really skilful retelling of the classic story and one I ended up really enjoying! 
 Jane is a fun, fiesty character that has a real zest for life (sorry for awful cliched phrase) - she takes everything in her stride despite having had some tricky situations occur during her troubled and tough life! I loved the witty way she narrates her own life, as if it's an autobiography, whilst taking the mickey out of the tropes of the gothic/ romance novel. Very witty! Plus there's an element of murder thrown in there too which appeals to me...! 
 I'd recommend this particularly to those who have read (whether they enjoyed or didn't enjoy) Jane Eyre, as the subtle (and not so subtle) nods to the genre are really fun to read!

 Logan lives in Spokie, and is about to receive the Swipe. The Swipe is a way to pay for things, go anywhere and everywhere. Ever since David's sister died after getting the Swipe, he's been paranoid thinking people are out to get him. He might not be wrong. With the help of the new girl Erin, he delves deeper into the mystery of the death of his sister. And what he finds out may be as dangerous as he thought it would be. 
 Logan is rather paranoid and his parents may actually think he's lying about someone following him. His paranoid delusions grow and in confidence he tells Erin. As soon as Erin appeared on the page, I thought, "Logan, don't trust her. She is completely loyal to the AU." I liked Logan. He was smart, but not when it came to Erin. Maybe boys get distracted by pretty girls. Erin was one character I didn't trust. She seemed too strong willed and intelligent to just be helping out Logan just because he's her friend. She had ulterior motives and she gave me warning bells the deeper I got into the book. 
 I happily devoured this book only because it was so exciting and the pacing was fast. I loved it. The world building had just enough detail, but I did wish there was more of it.I don't understand much about the American union. It was briefly explained. But what I do know is that they're planning something sinister. A selection process of sorts, and Logan is caught right in the middle of it. I can't wait until all the answers get unraveled. The mystery will finally be solved. That ending was definitely a cliff hanger and it just made me even more happy that I had the next book to read in the series.

This is a very short story that combines mistaken identity with an attraction that violates the "guy code." Dane wants Tina, who he really isn't supposed to want because she's the sister of Dane's best friend. 
 I think the relationship would have been more convincing if Tina hadn't been the only one pining away for so many years. If Dane had noticed her in the past, the depth of their physical attraction in the present would have been more believable for me. 
 Also, I love a Happily Ever After, but I would have been okay without the epilogue. The book stands fine on its own and I didn't think that the sudden inclusion of marriage and a baby was necessary.  However, the overall book is definitely entertaining and somehow manages to mix pretty hot scenes with some sweet moments. 
 Since it is such a short story, the relationships themselves aren't explored very deeply, which would have been nice. But it's still a fun read nonetheless.

I really, really loved this one. It's not the best book I've read but it is one of the most entertaining. For anyone who was born in the 70s or 80s, grew up playing video games and is a present day geek - this book is a love letter to you and your culture. I don't know how wide its appeal would be beyond those demographics, but for those of us who fit them it's a home run. 
 There are plenty of things I could nitpick. The plot is pretty straightforward. A couple of the characters, especially the villains, are pretty one dimensional. But honestly, even though I was aware of those problems throughout the entire read, I didn't care a bit. The book is so relentlessly entertaining that it more than overcomes its minor problems. 
 If you fit the demographics I described, do yourself a favor and pick this one up now. You won't be disappointed.

The Star-Touched Queen was a beautifully written tale inspired by Indian (and possibly Greek?) mythology. Steeped in darkness and mystery, the book follows Maya, a princess whose horoscope foretells chaos and destruction. 
 The Star-Touched Queen had this gorgeous prose that definitely aided in painting the picture of a dark world where our main character needs to use her cunning and curiosity to survive. The build-up of the tale was quite well done overall, with the book reaching a fantastic conclusion where the loose ends are tied in a well rounded stand-alone. I must say, there were some sections of the book which dragged along, and there were quite a few points in the story where I was sighing in frustration with the choices that Maya makes. While the choices were frustrating, it was good to see that she wasn't completely perfect, and overall they made her a much more rounded character with her own complete developmental arc. 
 The romance and general story reminded me very much of Cruel Beauty by Rosamund Hodge, probably because they both have some links to Greek mythology and because they both had a similar style of gorgeous writing. But where the love interest in that book was sly and witty, the love interest in The Star-Touched Queen is darker, more serious and more mysterious. I feel like I wasn't quite as connected to Amar as I was to Maya. His character wasn't quite as developed as I would have liked, I suppose because he is absent for many scenes in the novel. 
 I would definitely recommend that you give this book a go if you like books with slow, dark mysteries and stunningly beautiful writing. I look forward to seeing anything else that Chokshi writes.

 Flynn is becoming one of my favorite authors. She writes women villains so well, it's scary. There were some problematic or unbelievable parts of the story. Amma's whole story is unbelievable. Coming from a small town, a girl still being coddled by her mom would be seen as weird, especially a 13 year old who still plays with a doll house. Plus, Camille would never have been super popular after screwing 4 HS boys when she was 13. Small town mentality: you can be a little slutty but you most certainly can't be a slut.

I wasn't sure what rating to give this book. On the one hand, it's a fairly predictable and cliche plot line, and the writing relied heavily on character dialogue and wasn't particularly special in style. Only a select few characters are really fleshed out, and even then I felt like a lot of backstory and explanations for the main characters' behaviors was missing. While the book is lacking in its literary substance, from the first page I found myself completely engrossed in the story and simply could not put it down. So, clearly there are a lot of elements about this book that make it work as a suspenseful page-turner. 
 The book did a great job of depicting the horrific experiences domestic violence victims live through. In particular through emphasizing how the self-blame, lack of support from family and friends, and aftermath for the lucky few who survive abusive relationships is often harder for the victim than the abuse itself. I also thought Haynes painted a clear picture as to how a reasonable person could find herself trapped in a nightmare relationship for which there was no clear escape. The book is very graphic and violent, but that is to be expected given the subject matter. In any event, it was an great read that entertained me enough to keep me up all night reading it 'til the end.

"Winter, Spring, Summer, Fall; Death is the fifth, and master of all." 
 I wanted to like this. Great concept: a geologically active world with people who can interact with earth and stone. Periodic global catastrophes give rise to "stonelore" and a churning of society. Well written. 
 "You certainly weren't expecting to have to deal with the end of the world on top of everything else." 
 However, the three main story threads are further confused by varying person and tense, not to mention chronology. (Sometimes second person ("you") and present tense.) Distracts. 
 "Survival is not the same as living." 
 Unnecessarily crude and pornographic. Almost quit two-thirds through. She invented a clever world-appropriate set of curses, but peppered the text with offensive Anglo-Saxon words. 
 "Who misses what they never, ever even imagined?" 
 Jemisin is a talented writer, but am not inclined to try her works again. This book won Hugo and Nebula awards, whatever that means these days. 
 "Neither myth nor mysteries can hold a candle to the most infinitesimal spark of hope."

Last time we left off with Celaena Sardothien, she was broken. Heir of Fire unravels the story of how she pieced herself back together, though not without help. At the start of Heir of Fire, we see our leading lady barely scraping by in Wendlyn, living off bread and wine. Getting into brawls just to dodge the numbness. Her wounds raw from Nehemia's death and the departure from Rifthold, we wonder what's in store for our beloved heroine when Prince Rowan, who serves Queen Maeve of that land, arrives on the scene to seek her out. It has been revealed that she is none other than Aelin Ashryver Galathynius. The lost queen of Terrasen. 
 So what now? 
 New characters are introduced to us, and the marvelous world-building continues. Sarah J. Maas weaves the tale with a deft hand as we journey along with the characters we have grown to love. Their paths have diverged - it becomes apparent - as Celaena is now in Wendlyn, while Dorian and Chaol are in Rifthold. 
 Among the new characters are Rowan Whitethorn, the no-nonsense immortal Fae prince. 
 The initial meeting left me somewhat intrigued, when he and Celaena first cross paths. Celaena is at one of her worse-for-wear points when this happens. She goes with him - what could she lost at this point? 
 Queen Maeve, Celaena's antagonist aunt and essentially Rowan's master, delegates Rowan with a tall task: to train Celaena to hone her magic. 
 Rowan is a weapon forged in flesh. His magical prowess aside (as the dude can bend wind and ice), Rowan is equipped with a steel will and a sharp intellect. Celaena's first equal in every way. 
 Their relationship kicks off being antagonistic. They take swipes at each other, and this seems unrelenting. 
 But perhaps Rowan's snarly and icy demeanor was what fueled my suspicions that something happened to him. He'd been alive for centuries. Surely he wasn't always this acerbic? 
 The turning point comes when he begins to let down his guard around Celaena - whom he refers to by her birth name, Aelin - and we learn that by a tragedy of circumstances, his with-child mate was brutally slaughtered when he was off at war. He'd sworn allegiance to Queen Maeve to latch himself to some other purpose, some form of structure - to allay the grief. 
 From then, Rowan Whitethorn slowly unravels. 
 It is beautiful the way in which Rowan described his grief, his loss. He had been lost. He confided in Aelin that perhaps some part of him will always be lost. 
 And then came that pivotal moment in their budding friendship: 
 "But maybe," he said, quietly enough that she looked at him again. He didn't smile, but his eyes were inquisitive. "Maybe we could find the way back together." 
 He would not apologize for today, or yesterday, or for any of it. And she would not ask him to, not now that she understood that in the weeks she had been looking at him it had been like gazing at a reflection. No wonder she had loathed him. 
 "I think," she said, barely more than a whisper, "I would like that very much." 
 He held out a hand. "Together, then." 
 "Together," she said, and took his outstretched hand. And somewhere far and deep inside her, an ember began to glow. 
 With Rowan's help, Aelin learns to control her magic. It was more about self-control than anything. This leg of her journey saw her coming to terms with herself - acknowledgment and acceptance of what happened in her past, and willingness to rise to the imminent tasks of the future. 
 Reclaiming her throne, her birth right. 
 This will be an endeavor for which she will need all the allies she can get. 
 Her first ally being Rowan, as Maeve - by Aelin's request/blackmail/threat - freed him of his blood oath. 
 It was a powerful moment when he swore a blood oath to Celaena/Aelin. Something else we were given to chew on was the revelation that Rowan and Aelin were carranam, which is a rare bond among Fae that allows each party to share magic. Only the strongest connection can foster it. Their magic-sharing played a monumental role in the eventual vanquishing of the Valg princes. 
 Rowan and Aelin's friendship was a pleasant surprise for me. Here was a dude who did not take her shit, who pushed her towards becoming her best self, who helped raise her high while she was at one of her lowest points. He saw her through her initial shifts (to and from her Fae form), her transition from feebly summoning her fire to mastery of its control, severe burnouts/near deaths, and an almost fatal encounter with some gruesome Valg princes. 
 He was also the first to hear about her past, the memories she imprisoned in the shadows of her mind. 
 The flashbacks were both heartbreaking and wonderful. 
 We learn about the precise circumstances of her parents' deaths, as well as the sacrifice of Lady Marion that allowed Aelin to narrowly escape her would-be murderer. 
 One plunge into the water, and the next thing she knew, Aelin woke up and was face to face with Arobynn Hamel, the man who would make her into a killer. An assassin. 
 It came full circle, and we recall the start of the story when we were first introduced to Celaena. 
 Adarlan's most notorious assassin. 
 Lost queen, and a slave in enemy lands once she was captured. 
 A confrontation brews between Aelin and Arobynn, now that she realized he is in possession of the third Wyrdkey. 
 Not everyone dear to her in those memories perished. 
 Which leads us to the next new character, taking us back to Rifthold. 
 Her beloved cousin, her loyal protector and human shield, Aedion Ashryver, would grow up to become a skilled general serving the King of Adarlan. 
 At first glance, Aedion strikes us as an embodiment of arrogance and debauchery. 
 His cunning allowed him to hold up this initial layer, as we soon learn that his loyalties never swayed from Aelin. 
 Aedion had been working for the enemy all this time, his every movement rooted in plot. 
 Chaol Westfall, the captain of the Royal Guard, catches on when he discovers that Aedion Ashryver is strangely absent from his lavish parties. 
 Aedion gains a tail, and a tentative ally in his dealings with the rebels. 
 Above all, he learns from Chaol that Aelin is, in fact, still alive. 
 Aedion Ashryver had been called Wolf, general, prince, traitor, and murderer. And he was all of those things, and more. Liar, deceiver, and trickster were his particular favorites--the titles only those closest to him knew... Cousin--that had been his most beloved title. Cousin, kin, protector. Those were the secret names he harbored deep within, the names he whispered to himself when the northern wind was shrieking through the Staghorns. Sometimes that wind sounded like the screams of his people being led to the butchering blocks. And sometimes it sounded like Aelin--Aelin, whom he had loved, who should have been his queen, and to whom he would have one day sworn the blood oath. 
 Noble, incessantly loyal Aedion. He held on for ten years, not once losing sight of his transcending cause. 
 I'm certain many agree when I say that I fervently look forward to the reunion between Aelin and Aedion. It has been a long time coming. 
 I can't talk about Aedion without talking about Chaol. I understand that a myriad of readers were frustrated with Chaol in Heir of Fire, and this was mirrored in Aedion's dialog encasing Chaol's lack of allegiance to any particular side. 
 He'd earlier struck a bargain with his father to return to Anielle, where he would be its eventual rightful ruler, in exchange for his old man helping to orchestrate Aelin's send-off to Wendlyn. Chaol sold his freedom to protect the woman he loved. 
 In this third installment to this riveting series, Chaol is warring with himself. Having grown up in the land where Adarlan's king was revered and loved, he couldn't think otherwise overnight. 
 From my experience, when one is too close to a situation, it's easy to lose sight of the big picture, and harder still to view clearly the things that blur up close, our breath fogging up the details. 
 Chaol needed perspective. Heir of Fire was an internal journey for this man of honor. He was thinking for himself, in his own way and in his own pace, before he finally acknowledged the king's dark depths. Dorian had suffered being the man's son, and Celaena's world nearly ended from the geezer's twisted actions - but Chaol wasn't on the receiving end of the king's depravity. 
 In this way, it can be said that Chaol was, in some ways, more sheltered than Dorian, his Crown Prince. Instead of being angry at Chaol for his self-conflict, I rooted for him to see the truth that he deserved before he made a decision. 
 The shit hit the fan with the confrontation with the king, and Chaol finally chose. 
 Regardless of what went down in the past between them, Chaol's loyalty lays with Dorian. 
 We saw how many events transpired before Chaol became dead-set on his allegiance. From this, I think I can compare his hard-won loyalty to Rowan's. The fact that Chaol did not choose overnight lends a shade of finality to his commitment. 
 I really hope that in choosing Dorian, Chaol will eventually choose himself as well. 
 His departure to Anielle makes me think that Chaol is well on his way to forging his own path. 
 I still respect Chaol Westfall for all his straightforwardness and morally upright ways, and look forward to learning more of his journey in upcoming installments. 
 What happened to Aedion at the end of Heir of Fire was endlessly frustrating, and will no doubt further spur our heroine into action. 
 Not only will she return to take down the two men who ruined her life - Arobynn and Adarlan's ruler - she'll be the one to rescue Aedion, to wrestle him from darkness like he has waited far too long for. 
 I must say that Aedion Ashryver has gained my respect with his bravery and sacrifice. 
 Sarah J. Maas confirmed that Celaena/Aelin will survive the series, but damn it all if Aedion doesn't get his happy ending as well. 
 On the topic of forging a path away from darkness, I have to mention Manon Blackbeak - one of the heirs in a gathering of witch clans the king of Adarlan summoned to ride his dragons in the coming battle. 
 My initial impression of her was not pleasant. Tearing mens' throats out with her teeth? Girl had an uncanny appetite. 
 Until we meet Abraxos. He was the bait wyvern to the frontline beasts the witches were to pick for their rides. Despite his underdog status, Manon chose him because she recognized how resourceful and resilient his struggles made him out to be. 
 It is her bond with him that coaxes her to nourish some semblance of tender emotion - which is quite unlike what she was led to believe of herself and her fellow witches throughout the course of her upbringing. 
 That Manon Blackbeak has a heart - in the figurative sense - is confirmed when she decides to save Petrah, the Blueblood heir, from falling to her death in the War Games(on a side note, Iskrah is a blistering b&%$# for commanding her own wyvern to kill Keelie, Petrah's wyvern, in mid-flight). 
 I am intrigued to learn more about Manon in the upcoming Queen of Shadows, as well as how her character arc will scale off in the broader story. 
 I didn't discuss much about Dorian's arc in this story, as I was not particularly taken by his interactions with Sorscha, the healer. I didn't have a problem with their connection, but it paled in comparison to what was happening with Aelin & Rowan as well as Aedion & Chaol. 
 Everyone saw what happened to Dorian at the end, though. Our boy is a vessel for now. He's still in that body of his, somewhere... somewhere in that shell, we hope Dorian will hang on long enough... until hope and help arrive. 
 Overall, Heir of Fire encased plenty of world-building. We are introduced to new heroes and potential antagonists. That being said, it's not a tapestry of black and white or evil versus good in this world. The characters are multi-dimensional, and beautifully flawed. I can't help but root for nearly all the main players to get to their happy place. This enthralling third installment has left us with much to chew on as we wait with bated breath for Queen of Shadows. I eagerly await Aelin Galathynius Ashryver's return on September 1st. Cheers to Sarah J. Maas for gracing us with such a badass, resilient, fiery, complex, profound heroine!

(3.5 stars) In 1986, a 20-year-old man got out of his car and disappeared into a Maine forest. For 27 years, he lived in a blind spot of the forest 3 minutes away from civilization, by stealing food and provisions from unoccupied cabins in the area. He never even built a fire for fear of discovery, and was finally caught when burgling supplies. 
 I hadn't really heard of Christopher Knight before this, but the story is almost too crazy to be true. I wondered what would compel a person to turn away from society and become a hermit. The author wanted to know this as well, and met with Knight while in prison to try to find out more. 
 The story is partially about Knight and partially about hermits in general. The truth is that Knight is so hard to understand, even after interviews. Knight said it best himself: he's a square peg and society is a round hole. He just doesn't make sense to most of modern society (even his incarceration and rehabilitation doesn't make sense). The story was interesting, but because Knight has no answers, therapists (who haven't treated him but followed the story from afar) have no answers, the author/journalist has no answers... the story didn't leave me feeling any resolution.

 I really liked the growth of Lada and Radu separate from Mehmed. I think Radu is going to be alright, I think he has finally seen Mehmed for who he is now, and Lada is still in love with a man who can only love conquering places. Each character, including Mehmed have grown to ruthless characters: they are either in your face killing you, or using people and their weakness as an advantage.

Woohoo!! Amazing :) ! Looooooved it. 
 The bad stuff first (which isn't much): 
 Mainly that most of the 'action' in the books happened to Katy, so in that sense having the books written through Daemon's PoV took away a lot of the suspense. I also thought at times the pacing was off, but that's to be suspected when you condense three books down into one. 
 The rest probably contains spoilers if you have not read the series before. 
 Good Stuff: 
 One of the biggest things I loved about getting Daemon's PoV was that he brought so much more background into the story. We got so much more insight into his relationship with his siblings (mainly Dee), the Thompsons, the DOD, Matthew, and the other Luxen. Katy's PoV didn't get much of that. She had her mom... some school friends... but that was it. And none of the side characters in her life were really relevant to the story's plot. Daemon's perspective was rich in that regard, with us seeing his interactions with Dee, and getting more of his history with the DOD officials. 
 I especially appreciated the first book through Daemon's perspective. Daemon was a raging asshole in the first book, and while we were told through Katy's PoV that it was to protect his family, I didn't really think it justified how downright horrible he was to her. Yet in Oblivion, we got to see exactly the kind of pressure Daemon was put under from the Thompsons and Matthew because of Bethany & Dawson, and to hear his thoughts when he was being a jerk. I understood him a lot better, and Armentrout did a wonderful job of showing the progression of Daemon's feelings for Kat and the inner conflict he felt along the way from dislike to love. 
 Onyx still remains my least favorite book of the series, but let me tell you that I was able to endure it a lot better in Daemon's head than Katy's. Katy really pissed me off with her foolishness and stubbornness regarding Blake , her leading two guys on at the same time, and all of the things she kept a secret from Daemon and the others. Yeah, she sort of explained herself in the end which helped, but... Yeah. Onyx has always been a hard one for me to get through, but at least with Daemon's PoV I didn't have to spend most of it wanting to rip Katy's head off with my teeth. Onyx was still the weakest book, even in Daemon's PoV, because the intrigue of the mysteries being solved happened mostly with Katy. So we missed a lot of the plot progression being in Daemon's head. 
 Opal (and Origin) is still one of the strongest books in the series. I loved this book especially because of all of the interactions we got with Daemon and Dawson . And it was nice to finally see Kat and Daemon together without the stupid drama that was such a big part of the second book. Besides his relationships outside of Katy, Daemon's perspective didn't really bring anything new to the story. But it was still a fabulous book. 
 And as a side note - Luc. Luc is bae. I'd jump all over a book series written about him if it means I get more of his sassy devil-may-care attitude. 
 Anyway, Oblivion was a really great read. Daemon's sass, his humor, and his voice that Armentrout portrays beautifully in her story all make it a must-read. She did such a good job of giving Daemon his own voice, one so distinct from Katy. And she did an even more brilliant job keeping the chemistry between the two of them alive and sizzling. Honestly, I'd love nothing more than to read another series with Daemon and Katy and their kid? Because seeing them as parents, oh my god . Yes please. Let's start a petition.

IT HAPPENED ONE WEDDING is another delicious read by Julie James. I know I can always count on Julie James for an entertaining story, witty dialogue and interesting characters full of snarky comments. I wasn't disappointed. Sidney Sinclair is in her thirties and has just moved back to Chicago from New York after breaking up with her fiance. She is disillusioned and embarrassed after catching her fiance with a much younger woman and is having a hard time moving on. Vaughn Roberts and Sidney first meet when he tries to pick her up in a coffee shop and she turns him down cold. Vaughn is irked by Sidney's rejection. He has never been rejected by a woman and even though her assessment of him is dead on, he still finds it annoying. Vaughn likes having fun with women and isn't interested in settling down, but it bugs him when Sidney calls him on it, without even knowing him. They are both surprised when they are thrown together again when Vaughn's brother and Sidney's sister decide to get married. Vaughn reminds Sidney of her ex and every time they meet she makes sarcastic remarks to him. 
 Vaughn has all the elements for the perfect book boyfriend. He is ruggedly sexy, smart, an FBI agent, witty, down to earth and has a great body. Oh, and I can't forget, his masculine voice has a rough grit to it. Sidney is beautiful, smart and has a successful career, but her list of how to know when a man is ready for a permanent relationship, had me laughing. Julie James has written a fast paced, humorous story, yet it has touching emotional moments too. There are engaging secondary characters. Some of them make appearances from the previous books in this series. There is a lot of trash talking between the guys and it seems Vaughn can't make a move without someone commenting about it. I love all the verbal volleys Vaughn and Sidney throw at each other. This is the fifth book in the FBI/US Attorney series, but each one is a stand alone.

 The Moon and More is the latest book from Sarah Dessen, taking place in Colby, a fictional town that's been used or mentioned in a lot of her books. One thing I noticed right away is that the book mentions Colby is an island community, connected by a bridge to the mainland. I don't recall it ever being mentioned in the other books that use it, so while it's kind of nitpicky, I kind of got thrown-off by that since I'd assumed in the past that it was a coastal community. 
 The book itself succeeds as Dessen's books always do, however. The characters are well-developed and have their own personalities and lives, rather than simply living within the context of the book's plate. There are certain things about them that could've been introduced earlier, such as Emaline's tendency to go to the gym when she wakes up early. And I'd also like to congratulate Dessen on working with a plot point that usually annoys me: the love interest became extremely annoying, but rather than Emaline going along with it, or it being unintentional on the author's part and therefore ignored, it was meant to be that way and Emaline broke up with him rather than going along with it and losing her own identity. 
 The biggest criticism of the book would probably be that the writing gets repetitive when there's a lot of dialog. Dessen formats it the exact same way several times in a row, in a way that's supposed to be different and quirky but just gets annoying because she keeps using it. 
 Still a solid read, though, so one I'd say you should pick up. Happy reading!

 So - who loves The Lunar Chronicles! 
 "I do! I do!" 
 A few pages into book one, Cinder and I was hooked. It's just THAT GOOD. 
 With that said, I wasn't rushing to get my hands on a copy of Fairest. Possibly because I absolutely hate Levana and I was worried that in knowing her backstory I might actually start to feel sorry for her and possibly because I saw it as a fluff book that was only standing in the way of Winter coming! 
 I was wrong. 
 On both counts. 
 Because - OMG No! My hate for Levana was stronger then ever after finishing Fairest. 
 And because - not only was it a perfect story to read before delving into the 800+ page massiveness that is Winter, it gives some really good background to Winter as a character and some pretty cool insight into the Lunar world. 
 Do you need to read Fairest before reading Winter? No. 
 Do you need to read Fairest at all to still enjoy the series as a whole? No. 
 Should you read Fairest because Meyer is word magician and you love the world she has created so much you just want ALL OF IT? Yes. 
 Also, on it's own, it's a pretty great story. The backstory of Levena and her family seems to be one that existed all along and not something thrown together or created solely for the purpose of another book to add to the chronicles. It felt, to me, like the details of this story were always there, lurking beneath the surface of books one, two and three. 
 In essence, it's a pretty perfect backstory -- one where all the pieces fit. 
 I highly recommend Fairest to fans of The Lunar Chronicles and I highly recommend reading it as book 3.5 - after Cress and before Winter.

 Why I Read this Book: I'm going to be honest, when I first heard about Delirium from those who had attended BEA 2010, I had no interest in reading this book. Yes, I had read Before I Fall and yes, I thought it was a great, moving read. But for some reason or another I wasn't immediately captivated by Delirium. Then I started seeing the reviews and that's what got me. Next thing you know, I was itching to get my hands on this book. 
 What I Liked: At first, the premise for Delirium didn't really catch my attention. But as I started reading more dystopian novels, I've come to learn that I enjoy reading books from this genre. Before I Fall was well-written, not just as a debut novel but for a novel that focused on retelling the same day over and over - and over again - seven times. That's a hard feat to accomplish without losing a reader from boredom! 
 I liked that the pacing with Lena and Alex's relationship was believable. If there's one thing about YA novels that annoys me, it's those rapid fire I Love You's exchanged by the main characters after only a week of dating. Lena and Alex are both likeable characters, and each in their own way. At first, Lena is a sheep; she goes along with the program of 'love is bad'. But thanks to Alex, she reassesses her opinion and starts to think for herself and begins to have her own opinion on the matter. Alex is a very appealing character; he's the forbidden bad-boy. But he's the guy that makes you question all the rules. 
 The ending - OMG! - the ending! It sucker punched me. The whole time I was reading the ending, I was thinking No, no. no!!! It felt like I couldn't breathe. My head was spinning. Delirium put me in a funk for a few days. It's hard to let go of these characters. 
 What I Didn't Like: Delirium was a slow starter for me. It's told in first person narrative, from Lena's POV, so there's a lot of thinking and analyzing going on. Because of this, I wasn't pulled in right away. Delirium didn't grab me until page 131, about 1/3 of the way into the book. But after that, I was hooked. 
 Overall Impression: Delirium will leave a long lasting effect on your heartstrings. It doesn't just pull on them, it YANKS them. This is a book that will have you thinking and it will affect your emotions. It will take you a while, perhaps a couple of days, to recover. Be prepared for the anxiety that is sure to come after you read Delirium and as you wait for Pandemonium, book 2 in this trilogy. It will eat at you for days. Delirium is a definite must-read for YA readers. Fans of Before I Fall will definitely enjoy reading Delirium. I also think fans of Matched will enjoy this book as well. 
 Note to self: Re-read the last chapter in Delirium before starting Pandemonium.

This book cemented it: Eloisa James is hands-down my favorite HR author. Maybe it comes from being a professor of literature, but that woman can research like nobody's business. What's really impressive, though, is her ability to weave in those well-found facts into an interesting story. Although truthfully, I wouldn't even care if romance played a part or not: she paints Victorian England in such a fascinating, fresh light that I'd happily read about estate management. There is a realness to her writing that outshines any other author's ability I've seen. It's not that others lie, necessarily, but it's always clear that the setting is nothing much more than a setting. They'll throw in enough details to paint the picture, but it all seems so superficial compared to Eloisa James. Her dukes and duchesses act like they should -- a class above.

 I gave this book 4 stars. If you've ever had a really close best friend that you shared everything with and had an incredibly strong bond with then this book will resonate with you. The entire novel is witty and clever, you'll never be bored. 
 Most of the time I hate books written in this format, where you only get the story through two characters texting or emailing each other because I usually feel like I'm missing a lot of the story. That problem wasn't present here as I felt because these two characters were so close they would tell each other a lot so I could get a feel for them as characters and the people around them. 
 It was well written and something I couldn't seem to put down. It was also super realistic, there wasn't really a moment in this book where I thought to myself "yeah right, like that could actually happen". 
 While the story is about the lives of these characters and how they are trying to get through their early adulthood okay, it's first and foremost about the friendship between these two characters and it's beautiful. 
 What I found most relatable was that these people who went in and out of the protagonists' lives were all people I know. We've probably all met the people that are being written in this book. 
 Overall, amazing contemporary about friendship and life. Would highly recommend this to those who love a good YA contemporary.

So... after reading Taking a Shot I think I might "take a break" from this series. While I really enjoyed the first two books in the series, Taking a Shot felt like the exact same story again but with less likeable characters. I mean this is a contemporary romance series so it should be expected that the stories would be somewhat formulaic but this was just too identical plot wise and it got a little distracting. 
 I think the thing that pulled me out of connecting to the story was that Jenna was an entirely unlikable character. I freaking LOVED Jenna in the previous two books! She was sassy and quirky and I was so excited for her to get her own story. The thing is, in Taking a Shot Jenna became the whiniest person in the world. Honestly, she was bugging the hell out of me. If I were Ty, I'm not sure I would have wanted to bother with all her whining. Ty was about the same as all the other guys in the series. He was a good guy who treats women well and is spectacular in bed. He wasn't anything in particular to write home about. If I were to be blunt I would say he's pretty bland for a lead character. He was a great guy but besides that there wasn't anything else about him to really make him stand out. 
 Like with all of the other books in this series, the covers are really something to behold. They are always graced with a delicious bit of man candy which basically guarantees smutty delights will be found between the covers. As usual, the smutty delights here were top notch. Jaci Burton can really write some grade-A smut! The only thing is... the smut is getting to be formulaic. I think all the books in the series follow a similar smut trajectory. Here's an example: In all of the books I've read of the Play by Play series there's one anal sex scene and it happens chronologically in the same spot in all the books. So while the smut is still stellar and super-hot, it's also a bit predictable. 
 Overall, Taking a Shot was an ok, if predictable, romance. I didn't particularly connect with either of the main characters. Also, their romance is for the most part boring. Nothing exciting happens. NOTHING. I can see how the reader is supposed find Ty loveable and root for Jenna to achieve her dreams. However, Ty was boring and Jenna ended up being so whiny that I just didn't want to listen to her anymore. The saving grace here was a smut because that is really something special. So if the smut here wasn't as good as it was this may have been a 1 star book for me. As it stands now, I'm giving this 3 stars because it was just "ok."

Enjoyable for a fan of the Riyria Revelations but I think it would be a bit flat for someone new to the world. 
 The Good 
 ---------------------------- 
 Cast: the cast of characters is good and the Royce/Hadrian interaction is great. Sullivan is good at giving life to minor characters that appear in only a chapter or two. A tale is much better when everyone seems like a person not a cutout. 
 The Bad 
 ---------------------------- 
 Dramatic Tension: while not horrible there really is no serious drama. It is hard to have a lot of tension with a prequel when we know what will happen, but there is a lot of problem/solution/problem/solution/etc which can make a book interesting but not compelling. At the end Royce and Hadrian do fall into a series of problem/problem/problem but the tension is sabotaged by the reader finding out a few chapters earlier *exactly* how it will end. 
 Continuity: I could be wrong, but there seemed to be a few continuity issues with Revelations -- nothing huge but annoying. I remember Hadrian not knowing how Royce got out of Manzant, but he was told in this book. Gwen's prescience is much more blatant than it was in Revelations. And a few more. 
 The Meh 
 ---------------------------- 
 Story: Since the entire thing is a setup, it feels artificial that almost nothing in this book happens organically. I know some are attracted to stories where we discover the hidden puppet master that is carefully pulling strings to make everything happen -- I find them fake. When Royce and Hadrian finally get out on their own the story is at its best. The Gwen POV is good and has some great moments, but she just isn't imperiled enough. 
 Will read #2

The conclusion to Aguirre's Razorland Trilogy. Deuce, Fade, Tegan, and Stalker have been sent from Salvation (which is under seige by the Freaks) to bring back help from a nearby town... but they fear they will be too late to the save the town... which starts a long journey that ends with a truly epic battle for who will end up, not only surviving, by dominating what is left of the world. 
 This book does not stand on its own. Read the first two in the series first. (#1 - "Enclave" and #2 "Outpost".) 
 I really liked this book. I enjoyed the way the characters battle through PTSD from terrifying experiences, don't know or understand how to express their feelings, and grow throughout the book. The other thing I liked was that we did eventually get an explanation of the beginning and the start of the Muties/Freaks. Aguirre promised an explanation and we got one in this book. 
 The ending felt a tiny bit "deus ex machina"  when the younger muties found compassion and turned against the older muties and forged a treaty with the towns , but the explanation does make sense, so that can be set aside. I really liked the Epilogue. It put the whole story into perspective to me -- the fact that people who were one Heroes can find their place in life and eventually become just normal citizens. 
 My one criticism of this book (and of the series as a whole) is that it did not feel "young adult" to me. I know that the characters are teenagers... but that by itself does not make a book or a trilogy "Teen." I think that Aguirre should just label this "Adult" (as her other books are) and get off the teen bandwagon. But beyond that, I would recommend this to anyone looking for a good Sci-Fi Dystopia/Romance story.

Easy falls into the category of mis-marketed YA novels. The synopsis of this story suggests your typical love triangle romance - three or four guys all crushing on the same girl at the same time. In reality, Easy is a coming of age story about rape and it's effects, not only on the victim, but on bystanders as well. Although the love story really does overshadow this major theme throughout much of the book, it is still prevalent and most importantly, it is an idea and a concept that everyone, regardless of gender, should hope to understand. 
 When Jacqueline is assigned to be the designated driver for a Halloween party just weeks after her boyfriend unexpectedly dumps her, she doesn't expect to get almost raped by someone she knows. In fact, the only reason she's still sane is because of Lucas, the mysterious boy in the back of her economics class who saved her. Now, Jacqueline finds herself increasingly curious about her mysterious savior as well as her flirty economics tutor whom she only knows via email. To add to that, her ex seems to have realized his mistake and want her back. Yet, the worst thing is that her rapist, who didn't get to finish his job the night of the party, is still seeking her out with a vengeance and coming out with the truth is far from easy... 
 It is easy to dismiss this novel as being just another rape story as, in many ways, it is. Yet, there are distinct twists and valuable lessons that make it stand out from similar novels I've read. First and foremost, Jacqueline signs up for a self-defense class, something I'm seriously considering taking after reading this book. Furthermore, the level of support she receives from her best friend Erin is admirable. Although she never tells her mother about her near-rape incident until nearly the end of the novel, this reaction felt strangely realistic considering their relationship and Jacqueline's reactions and responses were all very real. Perhaps my favorite scene is one where all the frat-girls are discussing what to do about the issue of the rape and whether or not to report it. For me, that scene, more than anything else in the story, really got the message across that being raped is not the fault of the victim. Even though I wished Jacqueline's guilt was a little more tangible to the reader, it was still present and handled very well. 
 That being said, there were many aspects of this novel I didn't like. First and foremost, you should know that this is a typical love story featuring That Guy. Yes, That Guy who is dark and brooding and mysterious and who has been crushing on you from afar for what seems like forever without you even knowing. Yes, this story also features That Girl, the goody-two-shoes who has recently broken up with her boyfriend who didn't actually understand her worth but she's gorgeous so she can land any guy she really wants. Although there was a slight twist, for the most part the romance was nothing original. In fact, I found it to be a tad bit unrealistic and Jacqueline and Lucas' encounters were so hot/cold. When they were together it was steamy, and then they wouldn't talk for a bit, and then it got steamy again. Knowing their personalities, this interaction made very little sense to me until they began to get closer and closer, at which point it seemed like a normal relationship. Still, their initial interactions felt strained and a little odd. Furthermore, I felt as if Jacqueline was focusing on her love drama a little more than her recent rape, which was a huge letdown for me. I was really hoping for the author to play that point up and even though it was prevalent, it could have been emphasized more. 
 Despite these flaws, Easy proved to be a deep and provocative novel. Like most male protagonists, Lucas has a tortured past, but his is truly shocking. I loved how it related so well to the theme of the book and how the impact of that event reverberated throughout Lucas' life. What I didn't like however, was how eight years of being unable to cope with this situation lead to him healing in eight minutes. Although those eight minutes at the end were most definitely impactful, I wished to see a more gradual character growth for him. I was hoping for a small mention at least in the epilogue, but was left rather disappointed. Still, I have to give props to Webber for her unique integration of this idea. 
 Ultimately, Easy was an enjoyable read. Did it completely blow my mind and leave me crying and speechless? No, but it did fly by quickly, keep me turning the pages, and most definitely proved that even the same standard love story can be enjoyed again with a few meaningful changes. However, more than anything else in this story that could recommend it - from its characters to its plot to its love story - what truly makes me want every girl to pick up this story is its deep, heartfelt, and truly life-changing message. Tammara Webber may not have me rushing to read everything else she writes, but she has certainly earned my respect with this story and that, I can assure you, is not easy.

 This was my first book by Jeannine Colette and I really enjoyed it! Nothing too over the top here, just a sweet and sexy small-town romance featuring one hot cop and a feisty heroine. 
 Leah is determined to own the bar where she works and I loved that aspect of the book. The author also seems to have a wicked sense of humor which shows in the funny banter and the hilarious Matthew McConaughey references. Leah lost her first love to an overdose, and he also happened to be Adam's best friend - Adam, the rigid, by-the-book policeman who seems determined to punish Leah for her past mistakes. 
 Adam is charitable and gorgeous and kind and protective. He has made it his mission in life to rid the town of narcotics. When Leah is sentenced to community service under Adam's supervision, the sparks begin to fly. 
 Even though the setting is in the Midwest, this story has almost a sassy, Southern feel to it, reminiscent of Abbi Glines and Harper Sloan's early books. I love a blue-collar hero and Luke fits the bill perfectly! 
 Adam was cold and harsh and downright mean for much of the story, until Leah begins to break through to him. The chemistry between these two was HOT HOT HOT! I applaud Ms. Colette for her strong and sassy heroine and absolutely loved Leah. She wasn't just a party girl and earns the respect of everyone around her. 'Wrecked' is a funny, sexy, small-town romance that is a great way to spend a few hours.
