Book Added to TBR: IT'S REALLY HAPPENING!! And release day on Harry's birthday! Cheeky. I like it. 
 Initial Impressions 8/4/16: Hmmm I'm not sure what I want to rate this. It was kind of all over the place for me. The overall plot was interesting and I really, really loved certain parts. Obviously it was a unique experience reading it as a script and I think it lost a LOT. Less atmosphere, less dialogue, less development. I didn't feel like the characters were well-represented? Maybe because they're so much older... But a lot of them felt far off from their younger counter-parts (although I've changed exponentially since I was 17 so... Fair enough) but I hated that Ron came off the way he did. He was such a lump and a putz with little personality and essentially was Hermione's lesser half. Hermione was a stronger personality, as she usually is, but I feel like she lost a lot of her logic and wisdom... How do you LOSE wisdom over the years? Harry was always a bit all over the place for me so that was about the same and Ginny was a total movie Ginny, not book Ginny. Ugh. There was a weird sexual tension between the Albus and Scorpius (was that just me? Them always commenting on the hugging thing?) and I honestly thought it was going to be revealed that one had a crush on the other, which would have been fine expect for the fact that it didn't and I was confused by them always bringing up hugging and the deep friendship feelings which sounded almost romantic. Maybe I was reading too much into that because I was looking for more depth! There were also a few characters from the series who make appearances (though I won't reveal who they were) and some were AWESOME and some were confusing, to say the least. 
 Honestly, some of it was so much fun. Parts made me cry. Some made me laugh. But I also had moments where I scratched my head, questioned a lot, and even laughed out loud (not in a good way). Some of it was suuuuper cheesy and I can see why people said it read as fanfic. I think the fact that it was a rehearsal copy of a script really had a part in that too. You lose so much when you're not READING reactions, nuances, and tone of voice. Some of that is included but the atmosphere is greatly lost because of the format. So much is shown through the scenery and the acting (I imagine) that is not needed to include in a script, and I'm sure there are so many notes that aren't included to keep the book from being endless amounts of scenery and character notes. 
 The overall plot was... a really interesting concept but seemingly poorly executed. This was like cramming multiple books into one book (or I suppose, one play) and concepts were sort of flying all over the place. It was really fun to see things from the original series turn up but other times, the references back to the original series was very cheesy or just plain inaccurate. (Small inaccuracies, in my opinion but it's Harry freakin' Potter. You don't think the fandom will pick up on this, you guys??) 
 I mean, obviously this was specifically adapted for a play and that's how they wanted to tell this story... But I really, really wish it had been developed into an actual book instead of just giving us the rehearsal script. There was so much more of this story to tell! Things would have been a lot less cheesy if they had been developed or explained. (Although some things I'll never get over. They were just weird.) Everything felt really, really rushed and I would have rather had a simpler plot with more development instead of bursting from scene to scene. There was no time to really absorb anything and that also left very little room for character development. I don't care if we already know the majority of these characters -- they still need to have a personality. 
 So great to see the future for Harry Potter but I just really feel a little let down by a short story. Overall, it felt messy and rushed and after sleeping on it, I think I'm left more disappointed than excited about the development. I would have loved to see this really developed in a novel or in a series. We needed so much more time with Albus to understand him a little better. I would have loved to see this great friendship between the two boys and their complicated friendship with Rose (oh, and don't get me started about her role in the end of the book. An even cheesier way to wrap things up. Yay). I always love more time at Hogwarts. I would have loved to see those little clues along the way to the big reveal. I was okay with what the plot WAS but it really just needed way more development. I kind of feel like if it can't be done well, best to leave it alone. 
 I guess beggars can't be choosers! 
 Now can we have an Ilvermorny series pretty please? 
 Full and organized review as originally posted HERE on The Book Addict's Guide 8/16/16: Obviously there are a lot of mixed emotions before starting the infamous eighth Harry Potter book. Naturally I was excited -- because it's Harry freakin' Potter -- but I also just didn't quite feel as excited as I thought I should be. Before picking up the bound version of the play (since I guess we really shouldn't be calling it a book as it was never intended to be an actual book), I knew there were a few things that were hindering my excitement that I ultimately expected to affect my overall enjoyment of the experience (and in fact, they all did play a part in that). I knew that J.K. Rowling was involved in the plot and creation of CURSED CHILD, but ultimately, it was not her writing on the page. I knew that I was going to be reading a rehearsal script for the play and that the formatting might throw off my experience. And I knew that I'd be reading about adult Harry, Ron, Hermione, and company and I didn't know if I'd like where their characters were in their adult lives since we had some pretty cheesy things happen in the epilogue of DEATHLY HALLOWS, and that actually was J.K. Rowling's writing. 
 The short version of this review is that CURSED CHILD was kind of all over the place for me. The overall plot was interesting and I really, really loved certain parts but other parts of it just seemed so... I guess amateur is the best word I can think of at the moment, although that seems quite harsh. We've grown to love J.K. Rowling's stories and how detailed they are and there were just certain things about CURSED CHILD that didn't seem like they were plotted out very well. Other parts seemed completely random and totally uncharacteristic of the series. The overall concept of this story of the next generation was a really interesting concept but seemingly poorly executed. This was like cramming multiple books into one book (or I suppose, one play) and concepts were sort of flying all over the place. It was really fun to see things from the original series turn up but other times, the references back to the original series was very cheesy or just plain inaccurate. Small inaccuracies in some parts (it was "Happee Birthdae" not "Happy Birthday"), and some big timeline disagreements in others but it's Harry freakin' Potter. You don't think the fandom will pick up on these? (They totally did.) It was just things like that that really made me feel like this was sloppily put together and that these playwrights who put the CURSED CHILD play together were missing some really core feelings and elements of the series. 
 I knew that I was going to be reading a script when I started and it was definitely a unique experience but I think the format lost a LOT in translation. There was less atmosphere, less dialogue, and less development which obviously you'll get through the actors of the play and you won't see in a rehearsal script. I just felt like I lost so much not READING those reactions, nuances, tone of voice, sensory descriptions -- I mean, really a little of everything that brings the world of Harry Potter to life. Some of that is included in the script notes but the atmosphere is greatly lost because of the format. I mean, obviously this was specifically adapted for a play and that's how they wanted to tell this story... But I really, really wish it had been developed into an actual book instead of just giving us the rehearsal script. There was so much more of this story to tell! Things would have been a lot less cheesy if they had been developed or explained. (Although some things I'll never get over. They were just weird.) Everything felt really, really rushed and I would have rather had a simpler plot with more development instead of bursting from scene to scene. There was no time to really absorb anything and that also left very little room for character development. I don't care if we already know the majority of these characters -- they still need to have a personality. 
 I also didn't feel like the characters were well-represented at all. Part of it may be because they're so much older... But a lot of them felt far off from their younger counter-parts (although I've changed exponentially since I was 17 so... fair enough in some respects) but I hated that Ron came off the way he did. He was such a lump and a putz with little personality and he was essentially was Hermione's lesser half. Hermione was a stronger personality, as she usually is, but I feel like even she lost a lot of her logic and wisdom... How do you LOSE wisdom over the years? Harry was always a bit all over the place for me so that was about the same and Ginny was a total movie Ginny, not book Ginny. (Ugh.) The main adult characters (the aforementioned) seemed so stiff and one-dimensional which is hard to bear after spending a full series with them, reading the series multiple times, and watching the movies over and over. We know these characters. They are our childhood. They are our friends. We grew up with them. To see them underdeveloped and misrepresented in a sequel like this just felt so uncaring. There were also a few characters from the series who make appearances (though I won't reveal who they were) and some were AWESOME and some were confusing, to say the least. 
 There was a weird sexual tension between the Albus and Scorpius (which I thought was just me at first but there are tons of THINGS all over Buzzfeed and Tumblr about this so I'm not alone) and I honestly thought it was going to be revealed that one had a crush on the other, or that they both shared romantic feelings. That would have been fine expect for the fact that it didn't happen and I was confused by them always bringing up hugging and the deep friendship feelings which when described really sounded like something more than just a deep platonic friendship bond. 
 It was so great to see the future for Harry Potter but I just really feel a little let down by a short story. Some of it was so much fun. Parts made me cry. Some made me laugh. But I also had moments where I scratched my head, questioned a lot, and even laughed out loud (not in a good way). Some of it was suuuuper cheesy and I can see why people said it read as fanfic. Overall, it felt messy and rushed and the more I think about it and discuss it, the more I realize that I'm more disappointed than excited about the development. I would have loved to see this really developed in a novel or in a series. We needed so much more time with Albus to understand him a little better. I would have loved to see this great friendship between the two boys and their complicated friendship with Rose (oh, and don't get me started about her role in the end of the book. An even cheesier way to wrap things up. Yay). I always love more time at Hogwarts. I would have loved to see those little clues along the way to the big reveal. I was okay with what the plot WAS (except for some parts) but it really just needed way more development. I kind of feel like if it can't be done well, best to leave it alone, and I don't think CURSED CHILD did justice to this series at all. 
 We did beg for an eighth book though... so I guess beggars can't be choosers? 
 But now can we beg for an Ilvermorny series, pretty please? (Will I ever learn my lesson?)

There's reviews all over the board for this one and I understand why. 
 First of all, I feel like you have to be a "veteran" of historical fiction to even get into this in the first place. It's very slow and character-driven, even with a few "action" scenes sprinkled in. You have to really just appreciate setting and getting to know characters, and I do. Unfortunately, because of this, I feel like this book is very nichey. 
 I loved the first 75% of this book. I loved Violet and her relationships, both established and growing, with Laney, Seeley, SUNNY (oh God did I love Sunny..or more, I loved how much she grew and developed), Elsa, Dorian, Ruby Jewel & Jubal the VanZeldts...ALL of these, to me, were extremely interesting and felt important to the plot. At the time, anyway. 
 Without getting spoiler-y, I hated how the conflict with Dorian was resolved. I felt it was rushed and too easy. Like I understand its importance, in a sense, how he is (I'm guessing) supposed to be a kind of mirror to the VanZeldts throughout the majority of the book, and to help develop Sunny, and her relationship with Violet. But it fell flat for me, his last few appearance. To me there was no build-up to it, other than how he acted with Violet...I expected something much more creeping-up-on-the-reader, which was how Dorian acted with Violet and Sunny and Seeley...not something so demonstrative and in-your-face and oh then it's over. I felt it could have been mixed in better with the Thomas/voodoo plot instead of being pared away. Seriously, the whole Dorian arc knocks a whole star off this book for me. 
 Another half-star goes because of Thomas. Thomas. I thought Thomas was a nice love interest. I appreciated the lack of triangle (because oh God, Dorian does not count), and how much of a gentleman he was, and how he challenged Violet. But it was very TELL not show, their relationship, which left me so lukewarm on it. Like I'm not doubting how close they grew, because the scenes we do see, there is a spark, and it is sweet. So yes, I do believe that Violet could be in love with him but I didn't really feel it, from Violet's POV, the way I felt her relationships with Sunny and Seeley and Laney. 
 And speaking of relationships, I was dismayed to see how little of Rush was featured as the book came to an end. He's so prevalent in Violet's mind and heart and then it just kind of dissipates. She, at one point, vows not to grieve for him any longer but grief doesn't work that way. 
 I DON'T KNOW THE BALLAD OF TAM LIN so I can not attest to how close this was to the original. 
 All-in-all, I'd definitely recommend this to Historical Fiction fans, or fans of character-driven novels...if you are able to overlook the couple glaring flaws.

Plot: I love, love, love the mix of real life to paranormal. At the one side, you have the regular police and detective work which involves shitty, angry, stubborn, jealous, etc people beating you up and/or trying to shoot you. Every once in a while, I enjoy that, and the voice Jones uses for her story is perfect for me in that regard. On the other side, you have Charley talking to the dead to help solve their murders/cases, and all the issues that come with her having abilities which normal people, especially strictly logical cops, just cannot fanthom, and most don't even try. The mix is absolutely perfect! 
 In this first story, Charley has to solve the murders of three lawyers who worked together in the same firm. While she puts the pieces together, she's hunted by a shadowy prescence that gets her knees week, and she finds out it's a guy she knows from years back -- Reyes. He's comatose, which explains her kinda being able to see him, and about to be cut off life support. Desperately trying to find and save the one guy who ever made your heart beat -- and who could love you for you and what you are. Take that for drama! 
 Characters: Charley is truly one of a kind. She's snarky, badass, takes things as they come, a good friend and listener, but doesn't take shit from people who stand in her way. I have no idea how being the Grim Reaper from such a young age made her into this. It was probably her father's good influence, then her uncle's. She really knows how to chose her battles, with a strong sense of justice and a natural need to help. And through all that, she keeps her humor. I think it's because she has a small circle she can trust, and that's enough if you have a life like hers. 
 And Reyes, OMG! He was definitvely sin on two legs, and worse. It was pretty creepy at first, but so worth it. Although the package deal of secrets and complications he's having in tow isn't to be taken lightly -- not by a long shot. I'm really, really curious what's to happen with the two of them next. 
 Then, there's the ghosts... I think there'll be other like them in the sequels, yet I want to say their lives, deaths, and characters were a good background, solid and real for this paranormalcy to unfold. I truly hope there will be others like them in each story. 
 Area Scan: Flow: 5/5 -- Vocab: 5/5 -- Plot: 5/5 -- Heroes: 5/5 -- Sidekicks: 5/5 
 Romance: 4/5 -- Drama: 4/5 -- Action: 5/5 -- Suspense: 4/5 -- Humor: 4/5 -- Fantasy: 5/5 
 Overall: 5.5/5

This is a book my book group had read in the days before I became a member. Whenever we would discuss other books, the conversation would often loop back to IN THE LAKE OF THE WOODS, which I had never read. Finally, I decided I just had to read it. I'm glad I did. I can certainly see why this would be a great book for discussion because of the "did he or didn't he" ending. However, in certain ways I feel the characterization of Wade was sort of ham-handed: the alcoholic, super-critical father, the magic hobby, the politician's need to be loved all seem pretty obvious. I thought Kathy, the wife, was a much more subtle and interesting character. She seemed to know exactly who and what her husband was, but she chose to stay with him anyway. I would have liked to know more about her childhood and what made her tick. I suspect any soldier is capable of committing an atrocity under the terrifying circumstances of war, but O'Brien didn't really convince me that THIS soldier had returned to his murderous ways. The book prompted me to look up Lt. Calley on Wikipedia. It turns out he only served a few months of house arrest for his crimes and then spent the rest of his life working in a jewelry store--an example of the banality of evil.
This was funny! It was a little too easy to put down, but now that I'm done I'm craving the next one!

This volume really failed to live up to the high standard set by the previous two volumes, whose mind-game arcs created great tension and paid off in droves. This time around, the focus is on the new character, Misa: the second Kira. The second Kira concept could have been so much more interesting, but rather than utilizing an interesting character, the rather one-note Misa was included to throw in a love interest. The volume is labelled "Love," which is ironic considering that there is actually no love story really present here. Rather, Misa is a singularly infatuated and embarrassing female caricature who does nothing but screw things up throughout the volume. She acts like she has taken some type of absurd "love potion" from a Twilight Zone episode, as her actions are incomprehensible and she is far too willing to give up everything for absolutely nothing in return. On the other side, Misa could have given Light an opportunity to show off some complexity and challenge his drive to kill, but she simply turns into a pawn to be used in Light's plan. Yes, this certainly shows off how far Light has fallen in his humanity, but it doesn't necessarily make for interesting reading. 
 Meanwhile, the epic battle between Light and L is placed on hold and spins in circles for the duration of the volume. There are some great little moments here and there, but the lack of L in this volume certainly causes the narrative to suffer. Also, the lack of any type of explanation or build-up to L detecting Misa is incredibly anticlimactic. 
 There is certainly a level of tragedy in Misa's arc in this volume that is interesting, especially after being caught, but the arc doesn't pay off at all when it counts the most and is left hanging when it really should have been tied up. 
 The most emotionally beautiful aspects of this volume are actually the Shinigami who fall in love with Misa and the consequences of that love, but this is not explored nearly enough. 
 Still good, but not up with the best of Death Note.

As he navigates the weeds of his rather pathetic life, a woman dubbed the "Packer Attacker" throws [rocks, stones, pebbles, dirt, who can say?] at Sheldon Packer, an up-and-coming presidential candidate. Samuel and this woman are connected in a spoilerific way, and then it's off to the races. 
 The Line That Killed Me: The entirety of Laura Pottsdam's "Argumentum Verbosium" is life (46-48). 
 Best Character: Simon Rogers 
 Why [As] You Like It: This reads pretty quickly. Page 76 came around much faster than expected, especially with how long it is. We are definitely still in the exposition, and I don't know if I have any real feelings toward it yet, but I must like it for some reason? idk What that reason is. Current mood: *shrug* it's aight. 
 Why I'm Gone, Girl: As of now, Sam has some pretty stereotypical vices and character traits. Most of the people he interacts with do, too. While I'm sure Sam may evolve in different and nuanced ways in the upcoming 600 pages, committing to Hill's novel without that assurance is a lot to ask.  Will I turn the page, or toss it into Mount Doom? I hate to give up on this as there is so much more to go, but the assurance that it will get better is the only reason I would keep reading it. It's pretty bland so far, and not like vanilla ice cream. Sorry, Sam, but maybe you are a bit too washed-up for me.

Best-selling book of 1966. My brother lent me a copy some twenty years after its original publication. Not my usual fare, and wasn't that keen on reading it. 
 Is it still relevant? Absolutely, which means it's a timeless novel. It's also well-paced. As it happens, this was a ground-breaking, genre-making roman a clef which blazed the way for much more sordid authors. It deserves four out of five stars for being a landmark book. As I keep saying - judge things in their time. If nothing else, it allowed other female authors to make a great deal more money out of what was then a male-dominated industry in terms of successful authors and their pay-cheques. A positive thing for feminism? I think so.

My second read of this book. There are two major differences this time: first, I saw the TV show between the reads and second I listened to the audio. Well, the book is still that good. Entertaining, clever, disturbing, amusing, thrilling... name it, the novel has it. 
 The narrator did a great job interpreting a detached, kind of disconnected young man, coming alive only when confronted with (or doing) what sane people would consider as inconceivable. 
 The book is often creepier than the show, where Dexter's killings are mitigated for obvious reasons. Here, even if Jeff Lindsay doesn't go into too much graphic details, we take the full blow of the tortures inflicted to the victims. 
 The irony is, those victims are so monstrous, there is no possible empathy with them. No we are, as in the TV show, completely on Dexter's side. Marveling at his actions and reflections, his sense of humor, and intrigued by the glimpses of humanity he shows from time to time and that stay totally unconscious to him. He sees himself as a perfect sociopath, a "monster". But is he ?

He goes insane, but eventually meets up with his half-brother Mildmay, a former assassin on the run from the law, who takes him on a quest to the one place that can restore him.

I have been sitting with my thoughts about this book for over a week, trying to pry apart expectation and nostalgia from my reading experience. In the end, even when I take into account what this book actually is and is not, I still consider it a massive failure and I have a lot of feels about why it was so terrible. So welcome to my laundry list of crankiness and critique! 
 1. To begin, I know that this is just a script and will never capture the same magic and emotion that the full play would provide. On the other hand, without all the interesting visuals, it is easier to analyse the story based on its narrative strengths and weaknesses. Even the best visual masterpiece may fail at telling a good tale, and Cursed Child is not a well-crafted story. 
 2. The plot. Oh god, the plot of this mess. Cursed Child is based largely on a hackneyed time travel plot that you've read a billion times before. Scorpio and Albus change the past, which changed their present, and SHENANIGANS! Time travel always fit uncomfortably into Harry Potter, so much so that Rowling tried to write the offending items out of the universe so that she could preempt too many fans from pointing out the logical problems that they introduced. So of course they are back and seemingly even less thought out than before. To do a time travel story right, you have to nail the logic down while doing something more interesting than the butterfly effect. The Cursed Child does neither of these things, resulting in a lackluster, uninteresting set of problems that feel contrived and fail to spark much imagination. 
 3. Oyyyyyyyyy. Voldemort's daughter. I have been trying to avoid using comparisons to fanfic because I have read a lot of good fic. Fic is not shorthand for terrible writing. What this play reminds me of are the stories that young writers produce, filled with nonsensical plots, underdeveloped characters and a lot of general silliness. For young writers, this is perfectly acceptable! It is part of learning! The Cursed Child had an initial print run of something like 4.5 million copies. I expect better. Voldemort's daughter and time travel shenanigans are the types of things you find in early work by authors still experimenting and learning their craft. It's not that these concepts can't be done well, but that it takes a lot of finesse to manage it. Describing Augury as someone with silver hair with blue streaks did not make me confident about what I was going to experience in the coming pages. Giving her few, if any, defining traits didn't help matters. She's a boring character without personality, created more for shock value than actual narrative value. She's what I would expect from a writer still learning, not part of collaboration between multiple experienced writers. (Also, more powerful than Harry? He's a full grown, fully trained adult, a powerful wizard, and the head of magical law enforcement. Augury is barely out of her teens. Please, don't tell me she's magically wonderful just because of her father. Magic, while some of it seems inherited, depends a lot of a person's training and practice. Needing a GROUP of adults to take her down was just silly). 
 4. When The Cursed Child was first announced, I thought that it might go over poorly with fans given the fact that it was going to deal with an older Harry. The most interesting stories about his life would probably be fairly non-magical, I thought, and address the emotional repercussions from his childhood. I was half right. The play tries to make the best of both the magical world and the mundane. There are ridiculous magic fights (what is even with the Trolley Witch), but the script's best moments occur when focused on Harry and his attempts to cope as a father in the post-war period. Unfortunately, the play doesn't give these quieter moments the time that they deserve. There's so much Albus and Scorpio messing with time that the character relationships are neglected. We flash through years of the kids' lives without really getting into what makes either of them tick, and Harry's fears and struggles would have been fascinating to ruminate on more. The time travel issues were completely unnecessary to make this a powerful story. All we needed were the characters even if they didn't pick their wands up all that often. A Potter universe story like that would have been incredible, but alas, the script went with safe and marketable. 
 5. Part of the play felt like it was trying to justify the end of the Harry Potter series. Specifically, I was both irritated and concerned with the continual propping up of Ron and Hermione's marriage. I admit, I never shipped the two and thought that they were not particularly well-suited for each other as teenagers. More importantly, I thought it incredibly odd and unrealistic that everyone got married to their high school sweethearts, but hey, small population and post-war exuberance. I can get understand how it could have happened. This is all to say that I was not really the audience for sweet R/H moments. I would happily have ignored them save for the fact that for some reason the narrative really wanted us to like and support this marriage. That it was so important that R/H be together that we see how miserable they would be apart (Hermione is alone and not even Minister of Magic without Ron!). Sure, people's lives will be different when you change something as important as a partner, but the whole "one true love" message is damaging for children and there wasn't even a good reason for that plot to be in the play. H/R seem like they have a perfectly good marriage. Why the throwaway scenes? Heck, in a play that is supposed to be about Harry, why not more about his marriage with Ginny? Cementing more heteronormative junk into the Potter universe is what I had hoped this franchise had moved beyond... 
 6. Speaking of marriages, this play did absolutely nothing to help Ginny's poor characterisation. The Weasley family in general got pretty shafted as the focus was largely on Harry and Hermione (though I can't complain since they are my favourites). Characterisation in general was... odd. McGonagall wasn't nearly as feisty as she should have been, and Ron was goofy in a way that he never was in the original series (I did appreciate Ron's more subdued humour and quiet intelligence as a teen). 
 TL;DR - The Cursed Child suffers from a terrible plot, horrible characterisation, and teases readers with some excellent ideas that are so poorly addressed that it's an incredibly frustrating reading experience. I could go on about the little things that annoyed me (polyjuiced Albus kissing Hermione was particularly egregious), but I think my comments are sufficient to explain why The Cursed Child is a disappointment for long term fans of the Harry Potter universe, but also from a story telling perspective. 
 Oh, and might I add that the $40 cover price in Canada is truly ridiculous given how short the book is while other adult hard covers are usually only $32.99 or $34.99? And young adult hard covers range from $20-25?

Had it not been for Tiffany Reisz and her The Original Sinners series, I'm not sure it's a genre into which I'd have ventured. When Michael and Sam's one night stand comes to an end, neither of them expect to see the other again. But fate (as she often does) has other plans, and the sizzling chemistry between them is irresistible. Michael's already been part of an office romance that went sour, and he's not thrilled to find that Sam, the man who won't stop plaguing his thoughts, is his new boss. Sam is on a mission to keep his personal and professional lives from colliding. He spends his days in an office and the rest of his life in the closet. Michael and Sam were both likable characters. Michael's heart was in the company he'd helped build from the ground up, and it was obvious the people he worked with were important to him. He knew who he was, and he wasn't ashamed to admit it. I loved the descriptions of Michael's personal style, especially as it was in direct contrast to Sam's. Sam, on the other hand, was still struggling with merging his professional and personal lives. Who he was was at odds with who he felt he needed to be to maintain his intended career path. But if he wanted Michael to take a chance on him, he was going to have to conquer his inner struggle and let everyone see the man he truly was. 
 The pacing of this story was perfect. It held my attention from the first moment, and it didn't let up until the last page. The chemistry between the main characters was electric, and the love scenes were detailed and sexy. I felt like the bedroom (etc.) scenes were essential to the story, as they were a huge part of Sam discovering parts of himself he didn't know were there. The way Sam's feelings evolved (regarding Michael and himself) were credible, and I really enjoyed how authentic it came across. There was only one thing I didn't like about this story, and this was Sam's constant worry about putting his career in jeopardy if he were to come out of the closet and be openly gay. I don't doubt the validity of his thoughts, but it was so prevalent that in some parts, it was enough to interrupt the flow of the story. As a reader, I only need to be shown this a few times before I know it's something that is a huge concern for Sam. 
 Takeover was a wonderful read, and I'd recommend it if you're looking for a quick, hot M/M read! 
 This review was originally posted on Books & Beauty Are My Bag.

The Tales of Dunk and Egg is a series of short novels by George R.R. Martin (uber-short, when you consider the other stuff that he writes) set about 100 years in the past in the world of A Song of Ice and Fire. Dunk is Ser Duncan the Tall, a hedge knight (which is a knight who has no lord, sort of like a Ronin in feudal Japan), and Egg is ... well, if I tell you who Egg is, then it would spoil a bit of the first story. If you just have to know, you can run a quick Google search, but I'll leave that up to you. 
 The stories are good, and just as entertaining as the main series, even if they're not as robust. The characters are deftly-drawn, though not as complex, though we do get to know Dunk and Egg pretty well over the course of these three stories. In these stories, they're basically the Starks from A Game of Thrones: honorable, humble, and gracious. Egg is a little hot-headed, but is easily kept in line by Dunk. 
 The bad guys in the stories will be somewhat familiar, too, since they throw their weight around irresponsibly, by right of privilege alone. The good news is that in these stories, Martin forewent his usual trend of killing off all the characters you like, and let Dunk and Egg and the rest of the good guys survive a little bit longer. That might be what these stories are for, to be honest; palette-cleansers to remind us that there can still be a reason to hope in Westeros. 
 In The Hedge Knight, we're introduced to the characters, so a good chunk of the story is their background, and then the story becomes one of Dunk proving himself to be worthy of the title "Ser." In The Sworn Sword, we're introduced to Dunk swearing fealty to an older knight, and having to defend him against those who would steal his water during a drought. It has a cute and funny romantic subplot that felt so out of place in the overall series that I couldn't help but laugh and love it. The Mystery Knight is about as close as any of these stories get to being a standard Westeros story, as it involves political machinations and conspiracies, though not on the scale of what we've seen outside these stories. 
 What I like the most about these stories is how they fit in with the entire series. Dunk is mentioned in passing as having been a member of the Kingsguard in A Storm of Swords, and it's wild to see how he started off literally at the bottom of society and moved his way up to being one of the seven highest-regarded knights in Westeros. They also touch on the Blackfyre Rebellion, going into more detail, even though we don't see the rebellion as it takes place. We also see house names pop up here and there, and even get a few cameos of older characters who appear in the series proper. 
 I can't find anything wrong with these stories, but I didn't find a whole lot wrong with A Feast for Crows, either, despite other readers not liking it all that much. It's safe to say that I'm an A Song of Ice and Fire fanboy, as I look at the overall series when I consider how much I like one particular book. I'm even fine with having to wait for the books, since I want Martin to get them right. Even if all I can get in the meantime are these short snippets into the history of Westeros, that's fine with me.

 So this is the second book in the Fallen World trilogy by Megan Crewe, following The Way We Fall. I wouldn't necessarily categorize it as a dystopian since it's in present time, and there's really nothing supernatural that happens; it's just a big flu that kills a lot of people. 
 **Spoiler for The Way We Fall** 
 So at the end of The Way We Fall, Kaelyn's dad dies and Meredith is sick. I love how Megan ended the book. I literally flipped the page thinking there was going to be another chapters and BAM.. it was done! But basically Kaelyn can't really take it anymore and she almost jumps off a cliff to kill herself. But she doesn't, and continues on! And then she sees a book coming from the pier and WHO'S ON IT?? LEO!!!!!!!!!! 
 So in this book, Leo comes back with horrible news. There was a reason why they weren't receiving supplies from the mainland anymore! The virus was everywhere and had wiped out almost the entire population in Canada and the US. Furthermore, we learn from the start that the blood transfusion worked and that Meredith is as healthy as can be! Which I was really happy about! I mean throughout all three books I kept shouting IS EVERY BODY GONNA DIE? Over and over. So anyway Kaelyn wants to do something to save everyone so she searches her dad's lab and finds something in the fridge that looks like a vaccine along with notes on how to make it. Turns out her dad was working on a vaccine after he had failed to make one the first time, and had tried it on himself. He had lived 18 days after having taken it and hadn't gotten sick or shown any other weird symptoms. Could it work? Kaelyn had to find out. She planned a trip to Toronto with her friends in order to bring the vaccine to doctors who could replicate it and figure out whether it worked or not. However, things don't really go according to plan. A boat arrives close to the shore to warn them that everybody has to escape, that somebody was going to bomb the island. Kaelyn and her friends quickly leave when the bombing starts and instead of just being her and Gav, they end up being her, Gav, Leo, Tess and Meredith. Furthermore, they team up with the man who came to warn them, Tobias, so ends up being ex military. 
 Needless to say they go through many many MANY obstacles during their trip. I really loved that it was during winter so it was so cold. They couldn't really pass through the streets because of the snow and there was no electricity or gas in the houses so it was so cold. They also needed gas for cars which was extremely hard to find. And most importantly, they needed to keep the vaccines cold and safe. Furthermore, they have to worry about the people. They have to worry about not getting sick, but even more importantly, they have to worry about the healthy people who want to protect their resources and themselves. It reminded me of Walking Dead a little bit again. The sick people aren't the problem; it's easy enough to avoid them or wear masks. It's the healthy ones that are the threat. They want to protect what they have, and gain more. In this particular case, there is a gang of people obeying orders from a certain Michael. They are extremely dangerous and want to get their hands on the vaccine. 
 Now you may notice that I commented a lot and got very frustrated at the end of the book. Here's why:  Kaelyn has four samples of the vaccine, she decides to offer one to Leo, one to Tess and one to Gav, since she and Meredith are already immune since they had the virus and conquered it already. Leo and Tess take it, but Gav refuses... for a dumb bullshit reason might I add. Anyway you can probably guess what ends up happening eh? HE GETS SICK. I was so upset and was like speed reading towards the end because I happened to really like Gav. I know she's probably supposed to end up with Leo because of the whole history and everything but I really hoped she would stay with Gav. He loved her so much and he was so smart and just OMG it's so upsetting. Anyway you don't even find out if he dies or not in this book.. you have to read the other one. Can you imagine people who read these books as they were coming out?  
 Anyway, this book was very good. I was hooked from the very beginning and felt happiness and joy and pain and sadness and all of the emotions I should feel when reading a good book. READ IT.. it's worth it.

After a slow and clunky start, there were moments in this novel where I thought it was going to turn into something genuinely interesting. It didn't, though it works perfectly fine on a "nasty, brutish, and short" psychological thrillerish sort of way. Length apart--I knocked this back in a couple of hours--the publishers' comparisons of it with Gone Girl don't seem too far off. It's a decent rainy-afternoon read, but nothing more. 
 I think it was the cultural aspect of the book that intrigued me most, although it didn't cash out. The Dutch setting had a certain novelty for me, and I was hoping that the novel would give some kind of insight into the darker aspects of a country legendary for its civilization and tolerance, yet also capable of producing some of the most violent soccer fans in Europe. The Dinner makes gestures towards this kind of cultural-political investigation (one of the protagonists is a politician; another, a history teacher); yet it never really delivers on that front. 
 The Dinner is riven with implausibilities, but the restaurant setting looms large among them, as others have commented. The notion of a tale of violence and mayhem unfolding within the highly formalized structure of a high-end restaurant meal is a very neat one, with a built-in Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie-type element of social commentary, but for that to work, the restaurant frame has to be accurately rendered. It really doesn't work here. None of the dishes the diners order sound faintly liked anything you might find in a restaurant of the type described, and the (not exactly novel) satire of nouveau cuisine preciousness falls fatally flat as a result.

But when the book fast-forwards 10 years and Sabrina has moved to New York, WOW!! The Laurelin Paige that I know and love returned with a bang. 
 Sabrina is hired to work at the company run by Donovan and Weston. She is smart, driven and extremely competent. But yet she is still in many ways the insecure college student who felt out of her league with wealthy men like Donovan and Weston. 
 This book is EXTREMELY explicit and explores the taboo subject of rape fantasies. So if that is not your thing, then you will not like this story. But if you are a fan of rollercoaster emotions, then you will love this book. 
 Sabrina has always been obsessed with Donovan. But he is distant, cold, sarcastic. She and Weston have a fling, but she realizes that she still has deep feelings for Donovan, and cannot resist his allure. 
 "I don't want you to touch me like Weston," I said, once and for all. "I don't want Weston! I want you!" 
 Donovan let loose the smallest hint of a smile. "I know. I was waiting for you to know too." 
 Sabrina goes back and forth with her feelings for Donovan. He was downright cold to her BUT he is so hot, she cannot stay away. I felt that this book really picked up around the 40% mark and I would urge everyone to give this thrilling and extremely sexy story a try. 
 Why the 4 stars? I loved the absolutely electrifying chemistry between Sabrina and Donovan. The sexy times are off the charts. I did not love Sabrina's lack of self-esteem and her feelings of worthlessness. I hope in the next book she goes after what she wants. I found this book to be very engrossing, surprising and very, very adult. So that for me is a win. 
 I love these kind of books where the hero is damaged and unloveable yet becomes obsessed with the heroine. I hope we get Donovan's POV in the next book and I cannot wait for the conclusion to Sabrina and Donovan's story!!

 at this point i don't think china mieville could write a book i wouldn't give five stars to. i even had to go back and add a star to my review of the city & the city because i couldn't stop thinking about it for weeks after i finished it. and this, now, this little piece of genius has completely cemented him (over neil gaiman, holly black and stephen king) as my absolute favorite author. i would write him fan mail if it wouldn't be epically creepy to do so. 
 anyway-- an actual review of the book. kraken begins with an impossible theft, that of the preserved giant squid from inside london's natural history museum, and its discovery by a very average, slightly nerdy scientist who works there. billy harrow is a wonderful protagonist-- one of the genius aspects of mieville's writing; his characters are always completely real-- and his descent from his very average life into a hidden city of cults and magic is immediately gripping because of the way the writing pulls you along every step of the way. you're experiencing everything with billy-- the wonder, the fear, trying to reason out what's happening, rejecting the rules and deciding to do his own thing-- until you are in as deeply over your head as he is. and then along comes dane. if billy is the embodiment of everything familiar, dane is the exact opposite: a holy assassin playing security guard, a man on fire with faith and devotion to a god most would call him insane to worship, a self-made exile from everything he holds dear for the sake of protecting the man he believes can save it. everything about him is strange at first, but as billy goes further and further into dane's world, he becomes not only familiar but safe. and then, as a team, as partners, they dive all the way down the rabbit hole and try to save the world. 
 this book, like all of mieville's, is astonishing in its complexity. the amount of work that had to have gone into plotting this thing out-- imagining all the cults, the creatures, the characters that are all intricate and complete entities even if their totality is only hinted at-- it boggles the mind. chaos nazis! talking tattoos! tribbles and phasers that actually work! and characters like wati, once a spirit buried with an egyptian pharaoh to serve him in the afterlife, now the socialist strike leader for all the familiars of london. and goss and subby, a pair of croup-and-vandemar-esque assassins who meander around the book bumping off the good guys with excruciating enjoyment. and kath collingswood, who really defies description but is one of the best characters in any urban fantasy ever. but part of what i like best about the book is that london itself feels like a character. certainly it's living and breathing to the characters that populate it, and under mieville's pen it comes alive even for me, who's never seen it except in books and pictures. 
 this book combines all my favorite parts of Neverwhere with all my favorite parts of American Gods, with all of the chases and fighting and badassery my action-movie-loving heart could desire. i loved it beyond words-- despite the fact that i've just used several hundred to describe how much-- and if you pick it up, don't be surprised if it keeps you held tight in its tentacles until you're done.

It has been more than seven years since I first read Eragon. I was mighty impressed with the book, mainly because it appealed to my teenage sense of glory and sacrifice and all things heroic. Eldest came next, followed by the much-awaited (and much hyped) Brisingr. I read both and felt increasingly restless at how drawn out the plot had become. Lengthy sub-plots and over-described battle scenes became a consistent trait of Paolini's writing. But still I persisted; still I kept that little hope alive in me that in the end he will gain redemption. The last book will be better than the previous two, I thought. Though I was more than a little bugged when The Inheritance Trilogy became The Inheritance Cycle. I felt kind of cheated when Brisingr fell into my hands that evening in December 2008. It wasn't the end I'd been waiting for. But the optimist in me (a pretty stupid, naive, foolish aspect of my otherwise sensible persona *ahem ahem*) put up a silly little argument in favour of one of my childhood favourites, and I relented. 
 And now many, many years after it all started, the tale of the young Dragon Rider has finally come to an end. I will not lie to you, and therefore I must admit - it was disappointing. Maybe my standards of what a good book should be have risen since I first started reading the Inheritance Cycle, or maybe Christopher Paolini lost the charm that his writing once held. Either way, the rather obviously (and unimaginatively) named final instalment in the series, Inheritance failed to appease my literary yearning. I should really have seen that coming given how increasingly unsatisfactory the books were getting. Also, I had more or less forgotten the details of what had transpired thus far in the plot; and I was loath to read the previous books again. So, thankfully, Inheritance started with a brief summary of the story from the first three novels. Then, the plot picked up from where it had been left. Though "picked up" is hardly a good word for it. I hardly felt like turning the pages with an eagerness I had come to expect from the series. Instead, the writing seemed stunted, almost forced; like Mr. Paolini was trying (and trying hard) to sound regal, medieval, wise or whatever the characters and the situations demanded. I couldn't help but notice the failed attempt on his part to create a prose comparable to J.R.R. Tolkien's from Lord of the Rings. It was annoying how he always used just the wrong adjective of adverb to describe a sound, action or feeling. (FYI Chris dahling, a horse doesn't "scream"). How can you concentrate on the story when the writer keeps using all the wrong sights and sounds to paint a scene? Needless to say it hampered his chances at gaining my sympathy. The characters drone on and on about the upcoming battle, and how the Varden had faced umpteen difficulties, how their condition was so dismal and chances of winning zilch. I got it the first time, I got it the second time, but did he really have to overdo it so much? I didn't think so. He should really reign in his writing urges. Also, what was the editor doing? The plot could have been wrapped up within 500 to 600 pages. It had no reason to be 847 pages long. 
 The point of the whole novel was pretty obvious from the start. I had no illusions as to the fate of Galbatorix (hint hint!). But did it really have to be so quick and almost insubstantially short as compared to the rest of the detailed and overly described skirmishes? I mean, if you can describe how exactly Eragon dealt a blow to the soldier's hauberk resulting in a dent in the steel, surely you can write a bit more about the one man who has endangered the whole of Alagaesia? Would it have been too hard if, instead of telling the reader through the conversation of assorted small and big characters how dangerous, fearsome, loathsome and cunning the King of the Empire was, he could have shown us that in a few snippet scenes here and there. The only time we see Galbatorix is in the last quarter of the book, and then too he isn't that convincing. I should have felt the intimidation, the fear he inspired in the hearts of all beings of all races. But I was TOLD that he did, never SHOWN the instances of such tactics. Save for when he tortures a certain member of the Varden, or in Murtagh's reaction to his actions, there is hardly another instance of his wickedness before that. By the middle of the book, I was sure frustrated at how often everyone fretted about how many Eldunari dear old Galby possessed! And how big Shruikan was, my-oh-my!. SHOW ME!!! But no. Not until the very end did I really get a description of the ominously huge black dragon. There once came a moment when I wanted to shout out to Paolini to stop describing every swing of the sword and every blow of the hand and its consequences on the receiver. After that, I tried skipping a fight sequence or two. I did to, but then went back and read it anyway just to check if I missed anything important. Nope, I hadn't. I think it really is a flaw on the writer's part if you can skip a part of the story and still miss nothing important in a plot. And I'm not talking about a little paragraph here and there. Like almost a page or two at a time! I never do that, but this book tested my patience so much that I almost did! Also, I felt the interaction between the characters on an emotional level was lacking wherever it was required. For instance, when Roran says something emotional to Katrina, you would expect her to respond with something like, "And you too, my love." That would be quite a suitable response in an intense poignant situation as was being described. But instead she replies with, "And you too, my husband," and that downright ruins the whole mood! I mean, really now? How impersonal can a response get? 
 But the book had its good points too. Like the ingenious schemes Roran comes up with to overcome seeming stalemates; or the Vault of Souls. That was a good one; it was gratifying to read something like that when everything else was so depressing. I just wish there were more of such "chocolate chips" in that big huge undercooked cookie of a book. But alas! There weren't, and that left me quite high and dry. The end was, quite honestly, totally unsatisfying. Again, forgive me for the LOTR comparison, but it was nothing like Aragorn and Arwen's happily-ever-after! Not fair! 
 But anyhow, I again state how disappointing this book has been and how very wrong that seems when I've been waiting for this for the past seven years. Hope this doesn't happen with my other favourites. I won't reduce my Goodreads rating of the other three books, because I liked them at the time. But this one's sure not getting away that easily. 
 Verdict: Disappointment redefined :(

We've probably all read heartwarming stories of adoption. This is not one of those stories. In fact, this story may make you think twice about your romantic notions of adoption. Jaden is a 12-year-old boy adopted from Romania at age 8 by an American couple. Seeing life from his point of view may break your heart. He feels unable to love. He thinks constantly of the birth mother who abandoned him. He compulsively hurts himself, sets fires, steals, and lies. He is all too aware that he makes life very difficult for his parents. 
 Going into a story like this, I completely expected Jaden to have a big change of heart by the end of the story. We're supposed to believe that adoption is for the best, right? That it always has a happy ending? Well, spoiler alert, there's not a lot of consolation at the end of this story. Not that there's none, but it definitely left me with a sense of dread, even as I choked up over Jaden's final revelation. 
 It was hard for me to read this story objectively because I hope to adopt myself one day. It felt like a cautionary tale. I applaud Cynthia Kadohata for telling a hard story, and telling it so beautifully, as she always does. I'd recommend this for ages 11 and up, particularly if the reader is interested in stories of kids facing adversity and not necessarily triumphing, but surviving. It's bleak, but it's powerful and not without hope.

 I'm not really sure where I want to begin with Frigid. There is so much I want to say about it, but my thoughts are all jumbled and running around because I loved the book so much. JLA has outdone herself yet again. Just when you think she has given you her best book yet, she surprises you with yet another gem. Frigid is a fresh and welcome addition to the New Adult genre. It doesn't follow the pattern that most NA books seem to follow as of late and that makes it even better. 
 I'm not even going to dance around the topic... Kyler Quinn is fantastic! Every time I pick up a JLA book I add another character to the book boyfriend list, and this one was no exception. Kyler is so so so easy to fall in love with. I fell hard for Kyler very quickly. He is so confident and charming and sweet and we cannot forget that he is drool worthy. I may quite possibly have a new favorite. 
 What is even better about this book is that both Sydney and Kyler are relatable. They are probably Jenn's most relatable characters yet. Neither character has anything truly extraordinary about them, they are just two college kids getting ready to graduate and the situation they are thrown into while extreme is definitely feasible. Sydney and Kyler have been best friends since they were little and over time those feelings grew, but do you want to risk that kind of friendship? It is a hard line to cross and as a reader you can completely understand why both characters have been so hesitant for so long. You can understand why both Kyler and Sydney don't want to risk losing one another. 
 I'm pretty sure every girl has had a Kyler in their life at one point in time. That one guy you know everything about and he knows everything about you. That one guy that everyone outside of your relationship says "you two would be so cute together." That guy that you are perpetually stuck in the friend zone with. It is a very interesting scenario to read about, because I am sure every girl reading Frigid will think back to their Kyler and think "what if" or possibly "I was there once." 
 What really makes Frigid great is that it is not solely a romance. There is a twist to the story and a bit of intrigue and action that just proves to make the story better. I also loved that it switched up the perspectives. I loved seeing the parallel between Sydney and Kyler. While I had moments where I wanted to yell and scream at them both "you are thinking the same thing", the dual perspective proved to truly allow you to understand the characters. It was also cute seeing how insecure they both really were with each other despite knowing one another their whole life. It really put the emphasis one how and why they both hid their feelings as long as they did. 
 All in all, Frigid is an amazing read and one I know I will be able to visit over and over again. Kyler and Sydney are amazing characters and characters that you will easily make room for in your heart. I know I have built them their own little room where they now both live and they live there quite happily I might add. So whether you are a JLA die hard or not, please do yourself a favor and introduce yourself to Sydney and Kyler.

 Ahhhh I am so happy to be back in the Mesopotamian desert with Jayden and company! I loved Forbidden so, so much, and this sequel was a must-read for me- probably one of my most anticipated books of the year. And it was definitely worth the wait. While I didn't love it quite as much as Forbidden, it was still a very solid sequel, and I am very excited for the final installment! 
 The Good: 
 Jayden is amazing as always. In Forbidden, Jayden was a great main character. In Banished, she is freaking amazing. She's tough, but she's classy. She's willing to stand up for herself and those she loves, but is always mindful of the impact of her actions. An she had to go through so, so much already in her short life, and the desert definitely doesn't plan on letting up on her anytime soon. 
 Strong family ties are beautiful. Jayden will do about anything to keep her family close/find family that isn't currently together. She values them so, so much and it is refreshing to read. It isn't about obligation, Jayden simply loves them for who they are. While we're talking about family, Jayden's grandmother is just... I love her, okay? It's no wonder that Jayden is the strong and kind woman she is, because her grandma is that woman too. Their relationship is exquisite, and it reminded me of my relationship with my own beloved grandmother, which gave me even more of a connection. The fact that these women are so strong in such a patriarchal society speaks volumes. But the author handles it appropriately- it's very clear that sadly Jayden and her grandmother are not the norm here, no because other women aren't strong, but because it's extraordinarily hard for them to have a chance to show their strength. 
 Speaking of, the setting is on point. My goodness, the desert seems like hell on earth. I suppose it was, for the most part, at least outside the cities. And really, inside some of the cities too. One of my favorite things about Forbidden was that I could really sense the setting, could picture it vividly, and that is the same in Banished. The desert is harsh and unforgiving, much like a lot of the people Jayden encounters. But there are pockets of good- again, both in the desert and the people- which is probably quite accurate as well. 
 I ship the romance. In the interest of staying spoiler free, let's just say that I shipped it when I read Forbidden, and I still do now- maybe even more so. 
 The Not As Good: 
 None of it was bad so I am saying "not as good", okay? Great. So my only qualm with this particular book was that I did feel like I saw some of the bigger plot points coming, and I found it to be more predictable than its predecessor. 
 Bottom Line: 
 Lots of love for this series. If you haven't started it, you probably should, and if you've read Forbidden and loved it like I did, you'll want to get your hands on Banished. And then wait impatiently for book three in this unique and cruel world with the unexpectedly loveliest of protagonists.

 Thrilling, sexy, second-chance contemporary sports romance with a twist. Somehow it all works in this perfect summer read! 
 And they would fight to their end for me. This team was my family, my soul. And I think that was what made everything that happened so damn complicated. 
 Tyler has grown up traveling with a baseball team her whole life. Baseball IS her life. She has been home-schooled, innocent, yet stunning and complete unaware of her effect on men. Then baseball's bad boy Chase Stern enters her life. A larger-than-life character, Alessandra Torre could have made him a cliche, but he is deeply sensitive, devoted to the game, and ready to give up his fast-living ways for Ty. 
 Chase Stern. The best bat to hit our game since Barry Bonds. A shortstop who made Ripken look like a rookie. A body built for baseball, a face that made GQ editors swoon, and enough swagger to fill Dodger stands with females. 
 Of course, Ty is forbidden to go near him, she is only 17 at the time and he plays for the team her father works for. But they fall deeply in love with each other, through stolen nights on the baseball field and living life on the road. She knows that he is completely off-limits, but these two share a deep bond that goes beyond the game of baseball. 
 But it wasn't his looks that had sucked me in. It was his play. His effortless grip of a game that we all struggled with. His swing, his throw, the dip of his body when he scooped up a ball, the stretch of his six-foot body when he leapt in the air ... it was my porn. 
 But then...the emotional one-two punch from the author hits and these two are suddenly, irrevocably separated . My heart broke for them!! Flash-forward several years and these two, now adults with their own lives, meet again. I absolutely LOVE second-chance romances, and MOONSHOT has everything I love about this trope. 
 First loves were supposed to be flimsy and temperamental. They were supposed to burn bright and fade fast. They weren't supposed to stick. They weren't supposed to eat away at a man's heart, his capacity for life. 
 Interwoven with this forbidden love story is a thriller aspect which slowly builds toward a terrifying conclusion. Ms. Torre is one of the few authors I know who can perfectly pull off such a clever post twist!! I was totally blindsided by this turn of events and it blended in perfectly with the story. It must be said that the author knows a LOT about the game of baseball and I loved reading about this part of the story, she has fabulous insight in to the game and I almost felt like I was in the stands ready for the players to take the field. MOONSHOT has everything I love about contemporary romance: deeply-felt characters; the sweetness of first love; very adult, steamy love scenes; and the bittersweet pain of second-chance romance. Please keep in mind that there is cheating in this book: this aspect of a story NEVER bothers me or affects my enjoyment of a novel but it is here in MOONSHOT plain and simple. Does it resolve itself? Absolutely. 
 Alessandra Torre is an automatic one-click for me andI loved this story!! Happy reading!

Very thorough, very well written write-ups of many years' worth of interviews with emigrants/refugees/escapees from North Korea. It was very easy to follow the different stories. I was glad that the author focused on people who'd come from one part of North Korea so that she could clearly show their range of experiences and the different ways they escaped. She also made a point of finishing up their stories with where they ended up, explaining how their lives in NK made their adjustment to the outside world easier or more difficult. 
 Happily for the reader, there's not a lot of blood and gore. It's alluded to and occasionally mentioned but not in as much depth as a fictional NK story I read recently. The oppression and craziness of the NK regime still comes through very clearly. 
 As one might guess, this Westerner finds it horrific that various people in charge of NK over the years have starved their people and tried to cover it up rather than let outsiders in to help - or let their people out to get help. Cutting off their noses to spite their faces, and creating more problems than they had to begin with (the longtime stunting of their citizens; the destruction of their infrastructure and environment). All for their control and their greed and egos. 
 The upsides of the regime, what few there are, also come through: pride in one's country and family; guaranteed education, employment, food, and clothing (when those are available - the book clearly shows how problems cause them to become unavailable very easily); the beauty of the countryside before the famines; how the NK system seemed to work well - for a few years in the very beginning. 
 I was very surprised that NK residents with family in Japan could so easily get goods from Japan into the country. Would not have thought the NK government would have allowed that. 
 Hoping NK opens up completely at some date in the near future and the remaining residents are reunited with their outside relatives. It's a shame that the arbitrary division of their country happened and caused so much trouble, for such a long time. 
 I would really love to have the author write an epilogue or addendum about the changes in NK since her book was written, since Kim Jong-Un had not yet come to power when she wrote this one. Are things better or worse for ordinary people in NK under his leadership? Is it easier or harder for those who've gotten out to contact their family and friends within? How is the food situation these days? 
 A very good book.

The Blackhouse opens with the discovery of a mutilated body in the remote settlement of Ness, on Lewis in the Outer Hebrides. Elements of the killing appear similar to a recent case in Edinburgh investigated by Detective Inspector Fin Macleod, who is drafted in to advise on the case. Fin has ties to the affected community, growing up on the island then leaving it behind at seventeen. 
 I'd read the second installment of the trilogy, The Lewis Man (my review), before this one, so knew what to expect from May's writing. His vivid description of the starkly beautiful landscape, the distinctive influences of language and religion on the close-knit community, and the extraordinary tradition of the guga (juvenile gannet) hunt, raise this far above standard police procedural novels. The chapter recounting Fin's teenage experience as part of the hunting crew on An Sgeir (a fictional rendering of Sula Sgeir) is particularly enthralling, detailing the customs of a way of life now alien to most of us*, and culminating in tragedy. 
 The echoes of the past haunt the present, with chapters alternating between the ongoing investigation and Fin's childhood, building towards a charged confrontation and a thrilling climax, keeping the reader gripped to the end. 
 *I'd recommend that anyone interested in finding out more about the guga hunt look out The Guga Hunters by Donald S. Murray. May references Sula: Seabird Hunters of Lewis by John Beatty, although copies of this may be harder to come by.

OMG - At Peace is my new all time fave of Kristen Ashley's contemporary work. Anthony Joseph Callahan (aka Joe or Cal) is our broken hero and Violet his new next door neighbor. For the first 1/3 of the story, Cal is NOT a hero, he's anti-hero all the way. Violet and her teenaged daughters are trying to recover from a devastating loss and the story takes off from there. I was riveted by this story - it's one of those where you're doing anything to squeeze in time to read the next few pages. In my opinion, it ranks up there with Knight, KA's first in the Unfinished Heroes series. 
 This story is full of angst and most normal people would wonder why Vi sticks with Joe. I have no way of explaining it except to say that it's worth it in the end for her. Isn't that the way for us in real life? Our heroes aren't perfect and we have to decide when it's worth it to stick by them and when it isn't. As usual, KA's storytelling is well done and reasonably well edited for a self pub. Her attention to detail paints a bright and vivid picture but doesn't get in the way of the action. There is lots of bacon to go with the sizzle - the sex scenes are graphic and not for those who like soap opera sex (where all the good stuff happens off camera). There is also some violence and the normal amount of cussing in a KA book. As the second in the series, I don't recommend you start with At Peace, but I suggest you get to it as soon as possible. Awesome stuff!

I feel like this took me forever, but I have to see I can't think of anything I don't like about this book. It's long-ish, but nothing is drawn out for the sake of being long, everything has a purpose. Libba Bray set this novel in the 1920s, and she really did her research because it's almost difficult to believe that a modern 21st century woman wrote something so well I felt like I was emerged in '20s New York. 
 I loved Evie. She isn't your average YA heroine. She's fun, enthusiastic, selfish, self-involved, but protective with a good heart once you dig a little deeper. All of the characters were very well-written though. 
 It was very easy to be drawn in and captivated by the mystery of the book, and some parts were just downright creepy in the best way. I'm so excited this is a series and can't wait for the next book. 
 There is definitely a love triangle developing, but clearly the author is taking her time with it and not letting it distract from the main plot and conflict. At first I thought I was pro-Sam Lloyd, but the more I read, the more Jericho grew on me and now I just don't know. Which is odd, because in most books despite "attempts" at love triangles, you tend to know who they'll end up with and there is usually a character the author clearly favors. In this one, judging solely on this first book...I really have no clue how it will turn out. I'm excited to find out though.

So, Lindsey warned me about this book. She told me it was going to make me cry. But I, in my stupid arrogance, didn't listen. Oh, no, I scoffed, crying is for mere mortals. I don't cry at books! Boy, do I feel silly. Two weeks later, there I was, clutching the book and sobbing like someone just told Trump is going to be named Supreme Continual Ruler of the United States. Oh, how the mighty have fallen. 
 And dammit, I hate things that make me cry. But I adored this book. The writing is beautiful, and Audra's impossible not to root for. After all, she had a heart transplant. She didn't expect to live long enough to get to college. But now she's healthy and alive... and she's got a crush on the brother of the girl who died to make it possible. OUCH. 
 Jake is utterly swoon-worthy. He's hot, he's a photographer who plays piano, and he's really conflicted about falling for the girl who is carrying around his sister's heart. It's so easy to root for both of them, yet so easy to see why starting a relationship could feel weird and awkward. Especially at 18 and 20. 
 The entire book is a delight. The romance unfolds in a realistic manner, the pacing is spot-on, and the ending is absolutely perfect. 5 Stars. Highly recommended!

You know that movie that's considered "classic" because it was so revolutionary for its time, but starts to look really bad as it ages? That's this book. I do applaud Jules Verne's attempt at hard sci-fi, and he does have a great imagination, considering scientists at the time didn't have a firm grasp on the composition of Earth. 
 But Verne really doesn't have a good handle on plot and characters. The expedition team sees a lot of cool stuff, but any sense of plot arc was missing, and I didn't feel like the characters really changed as a result of their adventure. Also, I'm okay with characters who aren't likable, but these characters are straight up obnoxious. Axel is basically me having an anxiety attack, and he spends the whole book freaking out. Uncle Otto is the most irresponsible organizer of expeditions ever. Why would you make a journey like this with just a guide and your very nervous nephew? Why wouldn't you bring enough food and water for months and months? Why would you try to sail uncharted waters in a RAFT? On top of that, he just refused to accept when things were going wrong, which might have served him well, but was nonetheless annoying. 
 Overall, 2.5 stars. I'm not put off from reading other Jules Verne books, but this didn't give me the best impression.

 First: This story is 
 nothing 
 like Gone Girl. I was right when I expected a different flavor between the two, and that was what I got. The Girl Before is so eerily realistic, because it can happen (or is already happening) in real life. And that's what makes it as scary (but not as amazingly deranged) as Gone Girl. 
 I went through a whirlwind of emotions as I read this book: scared and angry, wistful and teary. What Clara went through was painful. Even as the reader, I felt it. I marveled at how Olsen accomplished that. The book shifts between then and now--a technique that was so skillfully demonstrated by Olsen when she seamlessly chronicled Clara's story. The stark contrast between her Then and Now showed a life of love, sins, regret and forgiveness. Glen and Clara's relationship also provided a different insight as to what victims of human trafficking go through, with realities questioned, and normalcies shadowed with fear and doubt. I wanted Glen redeemed because Clara loved him so much, but I know if that happens, it won't be realistic. And it would be a slap to the faces of his victims when justice isn't served. Clara's "sentence" actually wasn't enough for me. I wanted her healed, but I also think she got off easy with the punishment. But at the same time, I know that her painful recovery and intense guilt is punishment enough for her. I don't know, I'm a bit undecided on what I want for Clara at this point. 
 Up until the middle of the story, I was expecting a mind-blowing twist. Until I realized I won't get it, because as I've already known beforehand, this book is a psychological thriller, and not a mystery. I wasn't disappointed when it dawned on me though, because I was in too deep with Clara's story that I just had to know what happens next; I just had to know how her story plays out. 
 However, I cannot help but feel that Clara has been so special--too special. I couldn't understand why everyone wanted her. Why everyone was so keen on getting her. Is it only integral to the story as a plot point? What is it about her? This is actually one of the very few reasons why I didn't give this book a higher score. Don't get me wrong, I love strong girls and heroines, but I wanted a heroine who isn't the girl that often stands out because she's pretty. I wanted a heroine that isn't always the popular girl. I guess, I want a heroine that's not always easy to love and root for. 
 IMPORTANT: Clara's story is important because it sheds a light on human trafficking. Along with other important issues, human trafficking remains to be a worldwide problem affecting many individuals and their families. Let us show our support in combating human trafficking by research, spreading awareness, and reaching out to the victims. A quick Google search will show a list of non-profit organizations that fight against this issue.
