 This was a good book and a quick read for me, but there were some parts that didn't sit well with me. First of all, the main character Aileana reminded me a lot of Adelina from The Young Elites, in which her history and reasonings were very similar and the personalities were pretty similar. Sadly, I didn't like Adelina and didn't care much for Aileana either. I also didn't really like Aileana's bloodthirstiness. With all the other kick-butt assassin characters I've read in other books, they don't necessarily like killing people. Here, Aileana loves and craves killing the fae, which could've been an interesting aspect, but it just ended up a bit annoying. 
 The romance was very lacking in this book, and it would have been better if Gavin or Kiaran were more fleshed out characters, or even if there was no romance at all. The buildup to the romance with Kiaran seemed lackluster and didn't have me excited at all. 
 The plot itself was very intriguing! I just wish they went more into the "falconer" aspect (I mean it literally is the title). The name was thrown around a lot, but not much happened with it. Like it did, but it didn't. Where were the falcons???

This review is going to contain a lot of huge spoilers. I've clearly marked them, but seriously, don't even be tempted to click on them if you really don't want to know. 
 As far as Dystopia's go, the Divergent trilogy has kind of just bobbed along for me. It's interesting enough to keep me reading all three instalments, but I don't feel myself becoming overtly excited about them. To be honest, Allegiant left me feeling disappointed. 
 Plot 
 So at the end of Insurgent Tris showed the city the Edith Prior video which revealed that the world outside the fence was waiting for the Divergent to appear and save them all. The factionless crushed Jeanine and her faction system, but there is so much unrest in the city. Two sides have formed: those who side with the Factionless and want to eradicate the faction system, and those who remain loyal to some of the ideas of it. Tris and Co happen to fall into the middle, and decide instead to travel beyond the fence and investigate the people behind the Edith Prior video. 
 That's where they discover the Bureau of Genetic Welfare, a scientific compound which monitors city experiments to create genetically pure individuals who are less likely to cause pain and suffering. Tris' city is Chicago - not a spoiler. Pretty sure the first film tells us as such - and it is a social and biological experiment. 
 The people of the Bureau believe the more negative components of humanity - things like unkindness, cowardice, selfishness, ignorance and dishonesty - are a result of an individual's genetics and that it is these traits which lead to human suffering through war and rebellion. The Chicago experiment separated the people into the five factions which celebrated the opposite in the hope of encouraging the genetic growth of these traits which would be passed down through generations. The Divergent are the desired result. These individuals are considered genetically pure as they have the capability to be more than one trait, and all those who are not Divergent are deemed genetically damaged. 
 I have a huge issue with this explanation. It feels like such a weak reason after two books that have spent a lot of time explaining the purpose behind the faction system in depth. The idea of separating people into isolated groups doesn't match the aim to encourage genetic growth. If anything, it restricts genetic growth since large groups of people won't have access to the other preferred traits. Those who transfer factions only see two traits as it is. And these factions don't mix! They come together on the day of the Choosing Ceremony and that is it. Mixing is discourage with the motto 'faction before blood' 
 And that's the issues I have if I even believed in the damaged genetics theory in the first place. Personality is largely a product of environment and upbringing. Genetics is such a small piece of the pie. Countless psychologists have researched this by comparing the personalities of identical twins who have been separated from a very young age. The personalities are different, as you would expect them to be, and for some the difference is extreme. Personality difference can be extreme within a small family unit. Genetics are not the one source for a person's personality. So the whole reason behind the struggle in this novel is based on a bunch of stupid.  
 Despite the fact that our group are leaving the city - the only place they've ever known - for the mysterious outside, I felt nothing really happened. The pace was relatively slow in Divergent and Insurgent but things were happening and there was action. So far, I've seen more action in the film trailer for Allegiant than I have the whole book, and there'll be two films! Allegiant was filled with a lot of waiting and discussion, and whenever a character did something, it was wrong. And this leads me onto the other main issue I had and his name is Tobias. 
 Tobias - since we've grown up and dropped 'Four' - is different in this instalment. I don't know whether that's because we're treated to a dual perspective in the novel, meaning we have chapters from both Tris' and Tobias' point of view, but he isn't Four as we knew him. It makes sense that his name would change because to me, he's a totally different character. For example, he's so whiny and needy I became frustrated with him. 
 Leaving the city, Tobias brings with him his parental issues. I can excuse him; his father was abusive and his mother faked her death in order to leave her husband, but she abandoned her son in the process. It's a lot to deal with and it would be more insulting if Tobias didn't have some form of damage as a result. But Tobias has never been stupid, and these issues make him stupid. 
 It is clear to us early on that the Bureau are responsible for the attack on the Abnegation that killed so many, including Tris' parents. The Erudite were supplied with the attack serum; they did not make it. Within the Bureau are a small rebel group consisting of so-called GD's (Genetically Damaged) who oppose the prejudiced GPs (Genetically Pure). They plan to break into the weapon's lab and steal the serums kept there. 
 Tobias JOINS them! Doesn't know them, has no real interest in their cause, doesn't even know the full extent of their plans and Tris even warns him off it, but he joins them. Naturally, it blows up in his face - quite literally - and then he mopes around feeling sorry for himself. The rebellion he participated in resulted in the (eventual) death of Uriah, and it started the long chain of arguments between him and Tris. It puts a real strain on their relationship. Tobias is a hypocrite here; he resents Tris for lying to him (about going to the Erudite headquarters in Insurgent), but cannot be honest with her himself. 
 The one redeeming factor about all of this is that Tris and Tobias actually talk to each other after the failed rebellion. They communicate and if YA in general is lacking anything, it would be communication between a romantic couple. Too often, these characters do what they like, cause friction and then live happily ever after. This felt realistic, and while it slowed the pace a little, they became stronger and more believable as a couple after talking about the problems they were having. For me though, Tobias never really redeems himself.  
 I could talk about the events after but I've already spoken at length about my main problems. So far this review isn't reflecting the 3 star rating and this last plot section won't help either. Serious spoilers ahead! 
 This is the point which clearly divides the Divergent fan base and readers. Tris dies. I won't sugar coat it. In the grand finale of this trilogy, Beatrice Prior dies. And it's so stupid. 
 Before you start, no, I'm not one of those fans - 'NO! You can't kill Tris! Goddamnit Roth, you're so mean. All my favourite authors kill my favourite characters... you so mean *cries* - No. None of that. 
 I mean it was stupid for the story. It's one of the most pointless deaths I've come across. Personally, I can't agree with the martyr vein some readers are following. 
 The group made an elaborate plan to release the memory serum within the Bureau compound in order to reset those running the experiments. They would be 'rebuilt' without the GD/GP propaganda and the search for Divergents would be ceased. However, only David knew the code to get into the weapons lab and upon breaching the door by force, a death serum would be released into the air. Conveniently, only David had the means to inoculate against it and no one had yet been able to resist the serum. 
 As Caleb has no friends and made a few bad decisions, everyone nominates him to blow up the doors, come into contact with the death serum and release the memory serum throughout the compound. His great chance to redeem himself by sacrificing his life to a greater cause right? Well, Caleb was obviously nervous, but he had agreed to do it, albeit reluctantly. Tris and Tobias trained him towards his death. But his reason for agreeing was not out of love, but for a way out from his grief and self-hatred. His sacrifice didn't mean anything to him. 
 Tris finds her heart and holding her brother at gunpoint, takes the explosives from him. She can't bear to send her brother to his death - a bit of a redeeming quality, makes me like her a bit more but not enough to miss her. She's not overly worried about the death serum either. She's Divergent! One of the, if not the, purest Divergent to come out of Chicago. If anyone can resist a serum, it's good old Tris. 
 And she does. There's a moment where we're a little doubtful, but somehow Tris manages to resist and beat the death serum. There's a classic 'villain chat' from David within the chamber in order to distract David while Tris makes her way to the terminal to set off the memory serum. 
 And David shoots her. 
 Beatrice Prior. Divergent, Rebel, all-round pain in the arse to leader types can resist fear simulations, excessive testing at the hands of Jeanine and her brother, truth serum and can even shake off the effects of the death serum.... But she gets shot and dies. And that is why it's so pointless. There's no last ditch effort, sacrifice myself because it's the only way - she just gets shot and that's it. I feel cheated. 
 I don't even care that she was successful. The point is, she died when she didn't need to, and that's cheap.  
 Characters 
 I'm going to keep these next two sections quite short and succinct. I've waffled enough about the plot as it is. 
 I didn't connect with the characters as much as I wanted to this time around. I've already ranted about Tobias so I won't repeat myself. Tris comes into her own a bit here and I believe that's because she is sharing the narrative with Tobias. I'm certain my feelings towards her would be different if I had all 520 pages with her. 
 I wish the side characters were given more attention. Felt like they were only there to accommodate Tris and Tobias. They never felt fully formed and I didn't much care about any of them Uriah dies and, to be honest, I even forgot who he was. His death and Tobias' subsequent guilt chat to his Mum and brother, Zeke, didn't have any form of emotional impact on me.  It honestly felt that if we weren't centred on Tobias and Tris, we were wasting time. And it's such a shame because so many of the side characters had potential. 
 Structure 
 I briefly mentioned the novel was structured into two perspectives. I honestly can't say if it worked or not. I was surprised the first time Tobias' name cropped up at the beginning of a chapter. I think by the time I got to his fourth chapter, I realised it was slightly weaker than Tris' entries. There were far more similes and the lines grew cheesy. Plus Tobias whined so much more. In different places, I got confused about whose entry I was reading, and had to check back at the beginning of the chapter. This shouldn't happen because Tris and Tobias should be different characters with different voices that are not easily confused. 
 The pace was stunted throughout the novel, but there was still an edge that kept me reading. Which kind of sums up my whole experience with Allegiant. I wanted to keep reading for closure, to lay the series to rest and say goodbye to the characters properly. Unfortunately, it receives 3 stars while the first two received 4 because it was weaker and I found so much more to fault. I recommend reading it to end the series, but it's not something to get excited about.

"Something magical has happened to me: like a dream when one feels frightened and creepy, and suddenly wakes up to the knowledge that no such terrors exist. I have wakened up." 
 Anna Karenina is a story about an aristocratic woman trapped in an unhappy marriage who decides to have an affair with the charismatic Count Vronsky. Additionally, it follows the life of Constantine Levin, a country landowner, who is trying to find his identity in life. The novel explores themes such as social conventions, morality and the pursuit of happiness. 
 It's my first Tolstoy novel and I found his prose to be the most remarkable aspect of the book. His use of language is impeccable. Most of the characters are full of contradictions and self doubt which makes them very realistic. 
 But I must confess I'm a little underwhelmed by this Classic. 
 My biggest problem is Anna. Tolstoy's depiction of the love affair is some masterful storytelling like the quote that opens this review but I really loathe Karenina's character trajectory from then on. 
 She starts out as a very energetic woman and as the story progresses she becomes a shadow of her former self which I think was the intention of the author but in the end it becomes too exasperating. Her lack of self awareness and disregard for her children made it really hard to empathize with her. She ends up having no redeeming qualities. I don't usually have a problem with characters that make bad or immoral decisions but I feel like Anna is not compelling enough to make me care about what happens to her. She was my least favorite character in the novel. 
 The story also gets a bit tedious at times when it comes to Levin and his political views on the feudal system of that time. It comes across as the author inserting his beliefs onto the story and I found it a little distracting.  
 Ultimately Anna Karenina is a story about two people who are in pursuit of a fulfilling life. Anna must abandon an apathetic existence in order to find a more gratifying path for herself but her choices may not take her where she wants. Levin tries to find his way through a stable family life with a different outcome. 
 Overall I enjoyed this story mostly for the superb prose and I liked some of the characters, but I started reading with a lot of expectations that were not fulfilled. 
 I'll be trying luck with War and Peace next. Hopefully it'll be a more interesting read than this one.

Susie's voice was haunting : detached when describing the life of her murderer, full of love and ache when reminiscing about her past and following her family's present life. 
 Almost everyone in heaven has someone on Earth they watch, a loved one, a friend, or even a stranger who was once kind, who offered warm food or a bright smile when one of us had needed it. And when I wasn't watching I could hear the others talking to those they loved on Earth: just as fruitlessly as me, I'm afraid. A one-sided cajoling and coaching of the young, a one way loving and desiring of their mates, a single-sided card that could never be signed.

I discovered Control way, way before the cover was released (the first one? The first cover that showed up on Goodreads was actually this white background with red blood cells, I remember!), when it had a completely different synopsis on Goodreads, and when there were only a few adds. I pretty much immediately needed it and once I got my hands on a copy, I dropped everything and started reading. 
 Control is a rather fascinating book. It feels like it doesn't happen too much in the future, but enough so that there's a lot of new technology and secret scientific projects at work (although who knows, those may be going on today!) 
 The biggest thing about this book is how much of the plot relies on the science of the characters'...abilities? Genes? A lot of it is explained to the reader and I'm thoroughly impressed with the level of research and gene/DNA knowledge in the story--having a brainy main character can be hard, especially in sci-fi, but Lydia Kang does a masterful job pulling it off enough so that, while I didn't get lost in the explanation, it sounded legit and completely real. If, you know, it was genetically possible. 
 The characters were amazing, though maybe a bit cliche. 
 Zelia was a wonderful main character who was smart when it came to lab work, but was a bit less so when it came to real life application, but more on that later! I loved how grounded she was, how much passion she had for experimenting, and how absolutely loyal she was. Zelia didn't get overly emotional at the worst times like some characters, and she tended to look everything straight on, winning me over with her logic and passion. 
 There was Dyl, the prettier, younger sister, and I sort of hated her. Dyl was naive, impulsive, and seemed completely reckless to me, although we didn't get to see her often throughout the story. (Also, I hated how she started drooling over a boy immediately after finding out her dad was dead. What?) 
 Cy was the resident bad boy with a sweet side and I absolutely loved him. He was just as passionate about his work as Zelia and they made an amazing team. He was as loyal as Zelia and a bit arrogant besides. I suppose he is the typical bad boy of a story, but I couldn't help but fall in love with him, especially when he was with Ana. 
 The romance was absolutely swoon worthy and I was practically at the point where I wanted to smash Zelia and Cy's faces together and force them to kiss, before they kissed. Their relationship was a slow buildup that I loved reading (talk about sexual tension!) and watching their animosity turned into romance was absolutely thrilling! And the things Cy did for Zelia were just so adorable and sweet. 
 The twists, the shocking revelations, the secrets! There were so many in Control, it's a bit hard to keep track of, but each of them just shocked me to the core. I loved the pacing of the book, especially near the end when everything pretty much exploded! (And holy crap that ending.) 
 The only thing I was bothered by was that, in the beginning, Zelia trusted Micah even though it was evident that he was the enemy and she trusted him more than she trusted her new family, who had only tried to help and protect her. It made our heroine seem impulsive and naive and it bugged me throughout the entire story that she trusted him. Eventually, we learn the truth, but she still trusted him to keep his promise? Even though he'd broken his promises a thousand times before? 
 Control was a thrilling start to a new series with a heart racing plot and a killer ending. Lydia Kang's debut is a sci-fi that'll capture your attention and make you fall in love with most of the characters while breaking your heart a little bit throughout the story. Betrayals, mutations, secret organizations, familial love, and a hot love interest? What more can you ask for?

 Seventeen-year-old Caymen Meyers grew up thinking that all rich people are the same and after years of observation she's able to tell who's rich and who's not right away. Caymen finds the rich amusing, nothing more, that is until a boy named Xander Spence walks into the store to buy a doll for his grandmother, she can easily tell that he's super rich. Since then, he seems to want to spend time with Caymen and get to know her, but Caymen is sure that he'll lose interest in her quickly. Having been taught by her mother many things about the rich and to stay away from them, she's learned that the rich have a short attention span, so it's better not to get involved. Not only does she get a taste of being rich, she also discovers some secrets of her mom's past. 
 The beginning of the book was a little slow, so it was a bit hard to get into, but I ended up finishing it pretty quickly. It's basically about a teenage girl who helps her mom at her porcelain doll store. They find the rich amusing, until one day she learns that not all rich people are the same and ends up falling in love, despite what she's been taught. 
 One thing that sticks out for Caymen is that she's funny and a very sarcastic person. I love this about her, I love funny characters. At times it seemed like she doesn't care about anything, which she knows as well, since mentioned it in the beginning, but later we find out what she likes and enjoys. I think humour is a way for her to block people when they get close figuring out what's wrong, like fighting is for Gabrielle in Spark by Brigid Kemmerer. Caymen is also very responsible since tries to help her mom as much as she can with the doll store, despite the fact that she hates it. Although, once in a while (it might have just seemed like it to me), the sarcasm did seem a bit too much. 
 I also liked some of the other characters as well, like Caymen's best friend Skye, and some of her new friends like Mason. 
 Even some of the adults were 3D, like Caymen's mom and Xander's grandma. 
 While some serious stuff happens, overall it's a light, fun summer read. 
 As I've said before, while The Distance Between Us is a little slow in the beginning, it is entertaining, has great and fun characters, and it's a fun summer read. 
 I can't wait to read Kasie's other books, like Pivot Point. Even though they're different genres, I'm sure that I'll enjoy it, although I'm not sure when I'll read it.

 This book made me crazy and took forever to read. I haven't been entire sold on the second trilogy of this extended series. Books 1, 2, and 3 were a magical unit of action and character development and general swellness. Book 4, while introducing a new villain and storyline, was kind of boring until basically the last five pages when it became unbelievable and made me want to throw the book across the room. So I was really excited to get the next book and find out What Happens. 
 City of Lost Souls is Book 5, and I'll say the first 391 pages were kind of a draaaaaag. Jace is Not Jace. Sebastian (Jonathan) is Sebastian. Or is he? Team Good is in a tizzy (always). Team Evil Sons of Valentine is Planning Something Big. Again. Jace and Clary's True Love is in Jeopardy. Yada Yada Yada. 
 Anyway, the breakdown of my reading experience goes like this: 
 Part 1: The Set Up = snooze fest. 
 Part 2: The Getting Into It = raised eyebrows. Is this going to get interesting? No. Not yet. Not until page 392 wherein AWESOMENESS FINALLY OCCURS! 
 Part 3: The Payoff = All the aggravation and snooziness was worth the wait. I mean I wish the entire the story was as awesome as the last third. Because it was FANTASTIC! Jace being Jace and Not Jace. Clary being CRAY-CRAY, making terrible decisions again (At one point, I literally screamed "WHAT ARE YOU DOING?!  page 418. WTF?? ). Simon and Isabelle being... well, Simon and Isabelle  can they just get together already? . (Speaking of Simon... they cast this kid for the movie. Love it!) 
 What made the book so dull through Parts 1 and 2 is we didn't follow the action. No one in Team Good had any idea what was going on. It's hard to feel invested in a story where we don't know the stakes. We don't feel the pressure. There's nothing to get our hearts beating and our palms sweaty. Book 1 did this pretty well. Clary's mom is kidnapped and Clary is almost killed in like Chapter 3. But in this book, despite Clary's forays into adventure with the Sons of Evil Incarnate and despite Team Good's raising of demons and angels and faffing about, nothing was really happening! It was all very ugh... 
 And all too frequently when something did start to happen, we would shift to a different character's perspective for something oh so trivial *insert eyeroll here*. We interrupt this interesting potential plot development for an unnecessary mini-make-out scene between two basically unnecessary characters. (Yeah, I'm talking about you, Jordan and Maia! You had basically zero point in this story. Go away.) 
 ...But once we knew the stakes, what Team Basically Evil But Not Exactly It's Hard to Explain were doing... then it got CRAY. I wish we'd been following either Jace or Sebastian's perspective from the beginning, then this book might have hit 5 stars. As it is, I can only give it a 4. I love this series quite a bit. Can't wait to see how she's going to finish the series. With all this set up, it better be epic. Srsly. 
 Rating Breakdown: 
 Writing technique: 1/2 (It's not overly complicated, but she can be deep and poetic and interesting stylistically. Also I love how she refers back to things from the earlier books - quoting herself, but tying all the stories together. She could skip a few of the make-out tho...) 
 Character development: (Most of these characters are constantly learning about themselves. And I love it.) 
 Plot/Story development: (The last Part was 5 stars, but the first two were only like a two or three... so averaged out...) 
 Message/Theme: (This series so far has dealt a lot with family - if you become your parents. If your blood determines your essential goodness. This book was a lot about risk and betrayal and identity. If someone takes your free will away, but you're "happy," is it real? And the question of doing the wrong thing for the right reasons... It's all very interesting...) 
 Overall: I liked this book. I love this series. I adore most of these characters. I'm looking forward to the final installment.

Ahem. I haven't wrote a review for a while so I'll dust off my fingertips with this one. 
 Long story short. This is an apocalyptic read where the world was destroyed by humans and their fear. Silos were built to house humans and to be maintained by them. There is a hierarchy that exists, both politically and professionally. The brass is at the top and the lowly farmers and such, at the bottom. 
 There is a secret about the silo. Anyone voicing their concerns with the outside world will be "cleansed" (sent out to die) to eradicate any further questions about what it's like now and if anyone can survive. 
 One soul manages to make it farther than the others and her will to live will be tested. Now that she knows some of the truth behind the silo, will she be able to save the others who are being punished for helping her? 
 I don't know if it's because I did not read this during the great hype, or if it is because I listened to this on audio, but I really felt like this was a freshman read. Lots of boring dialogue that painstakingly tried to get me to feel for these people I had no attachments to. The pacing was too steady. No, "oh, my goodness!" or "Watch out!" in this read. We just waded on. 
 Juliette, whom the people chose for their mayor, was weak and often relied on others to see her through a situation. Well, pretty much all the situations. 
 There are many questions that were not answered in this omnibus that I thought should have been at least hinted at. 
 While many found this read enjoyable, I found it to be tedious and, for the most part, uneventful. 
 I may or may not read the next segment to see if things improve.

Mara Dyer can kill people with her raging thoughts. While I appreciate that there had to be somekind of explanation as to why, I thought that the science and all of the pages and pages of exposition and dialogue around it was simply too complicated. There didn't need to be a reason, a history, a cause, and an effect of Mara's power that was so detailed. I liked it better without the (complex, too overwrought) rationale. 
 And, yet, Mara walks out of the hospital scot-free because Jamie has a cousin who's a good lawyer? Come. On. We had 150 pages of mythology and 1 paragraph of explanation for how Mara got away with murdering three people in this book alone?  
 This book could have done with some serious editing. It was overly repetitive; I think Noah and Mara repeated the same lines and cycled like gerbils around the same thoughts for the last 150 pages or so of the book. Great - we got the sentiment, we didn't need to be hammered over the head with it a la New Moon. And I definitely did not need to be inside Noah's head (those chapters contributed nothing to the story emotionally nor did they carry any crucial plot points) and especially not for their sex scene. Come on. That was just gratuitous and weird. 
 In the end? The beginning of the series was more compelling than the end; the author gave into her need to neatly resolve the characters and explain the phenomena inside the book; and as a reader was I satisfied? Unfortunately, not really. There was so much potential here that, while I liked the characters and the originality of the story, I wish the author would have dared to drive it to a more adult place and so overall I'd rate the entire series with 3 stars.

Taste was an alright read. It wasn't especially fantastic, but it wasn't bad either. It did have flaws, but I loved the world building and the whole idea of the Zhamvy. 
 Taste is about a girl who stumbles onto a hidden city full of Zhamvy. The Zhamvy are actually zombies, but instead of eating brains, they eat flesh. 
 The MC, Phoenix was alright. She got onto my nerves sometimes. she was probably a bit plain, and I didn't really like her that much. She has issues with her dad, but the issues felt a bit out of place. She was a bit rebellious, and she would randomly drop things such as "I had kissed plenty of boys before" it was a bit random, and it didn't seem to fit in very well with her personality. 
 The secondary characters were alright. Many characters meshed together. The only characters that really stood out of my was Preya, Luka, Demitri, and Yana. I couldn't really remember the rest of the characters, and when someone popped upin the book, I was like: Wait, who's that? 
 Preya also gets a special mention here. Being, the main character's best friend, I expected her to be nice and likable. 
 Preya is a freaking spaz. She's crazy and annoying. She was always spazzing out on Phoenix, and I just wanted her to die. She was only in about 10% of the book, but she stuck in my mind as the most annoying character. 
 The plot was pretty cool. I liked the twists and turns, and everything was pretty original. However, the plot started off pretty slow, but it picked up around halfway. 
 Also, some things in the book I just didn't get. In one part of the story, someone says that Phoenix's father pushes her away because he doesn't want to lose her. Well, that just completely stuffed up my mind, and that doesn't make sense to me at all. Why would you push someone away if you were afraid of losing them? If anything, pushing someone away would make you lose them faster. 
 Also, at the end, I didn't get how making the Zhamvy human would save their race. If everyone is turned into a human, how is that saving a race? And they would also have a shorter lifespan as humans.  
 A good read, would definitely reccommend for someone looking for something a little different in the YA paranormal genre. 
 3/5 stars.

Jaz and Vayl typical missions involving taking down a target as quickly as possible, and then getting the heck outta dodge. Their current mission is a little different as they are teaming up with another team to take down one heck of a whopper necromancer called the Wizard. He's been causing mayhem for year and no ones been able to stop him. Despite this, things would be pretty simple for Jaz and Vayl if they also didn't have to figure out the Mole in the other unit that has been feeding the Wizard info. When you take into account their other problems with the reavers that are bent on revenge and the fact that Vayl's attention is straying towards someone else, that means Jaz is in for one heck of a bumpy ride. 
 I enjoyed the change of setting for this book. It was set overseas, fitting more into my ideas of where covert operations would be. As in the previous book, they are still working in the team format. Only this time their team also includes Jaz's twin brother David's team as well. I was happy to see them working together, even though it was incredibly strained at times due to the situations from the past. However, things are looking positive for their relationship in the future. Perhaps if David decides to forgive Jaz, then she might be able to take the first step in forgiving herself. 
 There was some major backtracking in the relationship between Jaz and Vayl, and I couldn't help but be disappointed. However, I do think some good might come out of this distance between them as now that she feels she is losing him, she realizes just how much he actually means. Hopefully this will give her the kick in the butt she needs to finally open herself to him. I'm not really sure what is holding her back at this point other than the fear of losing him. Yet, even if she doesn't have a fully romantic relationship with him, she would still be utterly destroyed if anything happened to Vayl. So, logically she should just make the most of whatever time they are given, and at least take the chance at happiness. 
 I was really surprised at some of the twist and turns in this book as they really caught me off guard. It can be hard to write without being predictable, so when a book catches me off guard, it definitely impresses me. With each new book that I read in this series I am finding myself more and more eager to read the next, as I just cannot wait to see what happens. The characters are so full of depth that you cannot help but to feel the emotions right along with them, making this a truly fantastic series.

Clementine is anything but over Ethan when she embarks--along with her family--on a summer-long journey on their boat, The Possibility. But along the way she meets James, who is also sailing the same route that Clementine is on and maybe, just maybe, he'll have what it takes to help her mend her broken heart and learn to smile again. 
 I loved James the moment that he ran into Clementine. He's funny, kind, and oh, by the way, he likes to draw. And did I mention that he's a red head? Maybe it's just me, but I don't think I've come across that many love interests that happen to have red hair--which meant this was definitely a refreshing change. More importantly, there's depth to his character--although you might not notice that about him at first. And surprisingly enough, I also really liked Olive, Clementine's younger sister, who is indeed wise beyond her years and she definitely loves her older sister. I should probably warn you that Clementine can be a bit touchy when Amanda is mentioned--and when Ethan is mentioned too. To be fair, I can completely understand Amanda's point of view on the whole thing as I've been in a similar predicament before. For the record, Amanda is Clementine's best friend and as the story jumps from the past (how the incident came about) to Clementine's summer on the boat so don't worry if this doesn't make a ton of sense to you right now. 
 Overall, Unbreak My Heart was a fun, light read that would be perfect for a spring break (or summer) read. It's my favorite sort of contemporary to read and you'll definitely see Clementine evolve; better yet, it leaves off at the end of the summer which is definitely perfect for Unbreak My Heart--although I certainly wouldn't have minded reading about what happened after the summer had ended. So yes, if Unbreak My Heart sounds like something that you'd be interested in reading, I'd definitely recommend it to you.

Espionage again. I guess I do go on a wild reading spree sometimes. Let's see. Oh, just look into my reading logs and research the genres. Recently, it was with the angels. Before that was... Finishing my to-read list/killing the numbers. Before that was... Fairy tale retelling. Before that was.... Greek Mythology, Persephone and Hades. And look at that! Espionage again. Heck, even the main character's name starts with James. Why hasn't there been a James Bond joke by now? Oh, perhaps James Bond is in MI6, not MI5. Still, I kind of expected Bond, James Bond to appear at any second. Perhaps Jones will make the cut? 
 Oh, sorry guys. No spoilers. I'm kind of forgetting that. 
 James is charming and smart. He is the lazy guy, but he is smart. Not smart like Jason Bourne or Michael Western (he is an ex-spy, same thing). But smart enough to not get caught. Plus, his background and gift with numbers (calculator guy) helps him with some works. I'm surprised he doesn't work hard to be the best he can be.  And relationships. I can't forget that.

But for the most part I was content to view this story through David's upright, compassionate, and ardently egalitarian, but sometimes blind, eyes. 
 There is a strong emphasis on historical injustice in this series, on the lack of women's rights, on poverty and the wealth-makes-right attitude of the times. It's well done and realistic, even if it makes me want to go back and knock heads together (which I could not have done, being female and therefore the property of some man - father, husband, guardian - from womb to tomb.) Thank all the gods for modern progress in that arena. 
 In this book David is almost recovered from the events in Beguiled and is contemplating the end of the painful but still idyllic time he has had with Murdo. The real world awaits them, with its complications and forces, none of which are likely to be kind to two men together. And despite everything, David is still unsure of Murdo's feelings and intentions. 
 I thought about halfway through the book that we were going to plunge into melodrama, but in the end the author managed to avoid that, and to resolve the crisis in a plausible and satisfying way. I think the second book was my favorite of the series, but I recommend all three to any lovers of historical romance.

The Spirit Thief by Rachel Aaron is terribly derivative. 
 And therein lies its charm. 
 Maybe it's because I've been in a massive reading slump, slogging through my pile of library books, finding mild entertainment, but no real joy. But The Spirit Thief, with its unabashed "D&D gaming session put to paper" approach is an awful lot of fun. 
 The novel's protagonist, by the author's own admission, is a D&D character concept. Eli Monpress, the thief protagonist, is cut from the mold of many a TSR novel, as are his companions, Josef, the warrior, and Miranda, the wizard (spiritualist). The only non-archetype is Nico, the demonseed within an ordinary human girl. At least, she doesn't feel like a fantasy RPG character; more like a goth girl from a vampire novel. 
 For Eli Monpress, being a thief extraordinaire isn't enough. Nope, he won't be satisfied until there is a million dollar gold bounty on his head. To that end, he cooks up a scheme where he will kidnap the King of Mellinor. The king's ransom will be the modest sum of 5,000 gold and a promise that Mellinor will pledge an additional 35-thousand to Eli's bounty. 
 The plan goes awry--well, of course it does--when the king's exiled (and embittered) older brother shows up. The brother, Renaud, was exiled because he is a magic user and wizards, even royal wizards, aren't allowed in Mellinor. The kidnapping of his younger brother is the perfect opportunity for Renaud to reclaim what is his. 
 Meanwhile, Miranda, a spiritualist, arrives in Mellinor, acting on order of the Spirit Court to apprehend Eli. Eli isn't just a thief. He's also a wizard, able wield spirit magic. In the world of The Spirit Thief, everything, trees, rock, doors, has a spirit, which can communicate with and do the bidding of wizards. In fact, when we first meet Eli, he is chatting away with the door to his prison cell. The Spirit Court objects to Eli's high-profile hi-jinks; hence, the arrest warrant. 
 Nice, civilized wizards find ways to gently coerce spirits to help in their endeavors. Enslavers, like Renaud, force spirits into servitude, which drives the spirits insane. Because loony spirits are dangerous, this kind of spirit magic is a no-no, and Miranda is forced to ally with Eli in order to stop Renaud from unleashing big, bad, batshit-crazy spirits on the world. 
 Eli's charming, devil-may-care attitude is a cute foil to Miranda's uptight, duty-bound approach to life. Josef and Nico are mostly along for companion value, but there's enough character there to make both at least intriguing. With both, a lot of backstory remains a mystery, left, I assume, for later novels. 
 The novel's biggest weakness is the almost complete absence of interior dialogue. There's rarely any sense of what the characters are feeling or thinking. Because the writing is tight and fast paced, I didn't notice this at first. But given my tendency to start "shipping" characters, I started to wonder what Eli thought of Miranda and vice versa. It isn't until the very end, that the reader is let into Eli and Miranda's mind. If the author had done that throughout the novel, The Spirit Thief would have been a keeper. 
 I'm looking forward to reading the next installment in the series.

 After reading and loving Lyga's other books, I had high expectations for his latest novel. Sadly, I fall into the Black Sheep category because this was just an alright read for me (2.5 stars). 
 Short recap: Sebastian has grown up being told that he shot and killed his baby sister when he was only four years old. It was an accident but Sebastian cannot forgive himself for what happened, while everyone else around him cannot forget. As a result, Sebastian plans to kill himself and end the suffering. 
 The big, overall problem I had with this was the narrative (Sebastian's POV) was not believable. He talks as if he is a college graduate yet he chooses not to apply himself at school. He is a good student but not special or gifted. Why should he go above and beyond since he is planning on ending his life? Speaking of school, why would his classmates still give him such a hard time over something that happened when he was four? No court in the country would hold a child that age accountable for their actions. Why did everyone pile the guilt on as if the event happened a month ago? There is also his friendship with Evan, who is supposed to be his best friend. How were they best friends if they had very little in common? Sebastian was quick to kick Evan to the curb to hang out with Aneesa, the new girl in town, so I would not and could not consider Evan a "best friend". Let's not forget about how apparently Sebastian really did remember everything that happened during that fateful evening with his sister yet he chose to act ignorant and clueless his entire life. Uh.. why? Why would he not talk to his therapist or parents about this? What purpose did it serve to lie to everyone for 10 years? (Don't forget, Sebastian is only 14 in this story.) 
 Here is where things got really weird for me with this story and I basically checked out: Sebastian and Aneesa decide to start making pizza videos on YouTube. That's right! In the midst of Sebastian making a life altering decision to kill himself, he decides to postpone ending his life to make pizza videos with his new friend, Aneesa, who happens to be Islamic. That plays a part in the story because several comments on the YouTube videos become hateful towards her and insulting. Sadly a good chunk of this story is dedicated to these two making videos over their summer vacation. Uh.. ok. Whatever. I can tell you that it really messed up the pacing of the story. It made no sense to me. He and his mother barely scrape by as it is so where does he come up with the money for the fancy ingredients for the pies? Also, how did he learn to combine such sophisticated ingredients if he has had no formal training? This mixed in with such a serious topic did not work. 
 I personally feel this should have had a stronger impact than it did. Yes, there were some very serious topics to cover (gun violence, suicide, and Islamophobia). It really bothered me how that was all Sebastian could think about, all he could imagine, all he wanted to do - end his life. He carried the guilt with him everyday because nobody would let him forget. Even his parents blame him and that was messed up. His mother needed help but never got any. They had a lifetime subscription to their issues. But this mixed with the stupid pizza tutorials just made me not care. 
 I never connected with these characters or the story. My lack of emotion with the story kept me from caring what happened to anyone. The ending alone did not work with the story. It felt slapped together and rushed. It was missing something that should have been powerful and outstanding. What we were given was anything but that. I know I'm the minority with this story and I am okay with that. I hope others find a way to enjoy it because I certainly did not.

This was a gentle Fantasy with all the traditional, read archetypal, side-characters, but it's real strength is in being a great character-driven novel. 
 I consider Orlan and Flidais to be side characters in this story, with Blackthorn and Grim being the true gift from the author. With Blackthorn and Grim, this shouldn't be much of a stretch to see, despite Orlan's PoV time, because that guy was just too idealistic and good-natured and romantic a prince to make it as anything other than the subject of the novel and not the real meat. :) 
 Flidais was much worse: being the put-upon trope princess who serves as a backdrop and not a real mover. Which is a shame, because her real role (Sans Spoilers) did have quite a few more opportunities for fun and mayhem, but alas, this would not have served, likely even supplanting, the true tale of Blackthorn and Grim. 
 I've spent all this time on the side characters, but what's all the hullabaloo? 
 Think a revenge-filled wise-woman with a hulk of a devoted man watching over her, forced into service under the Fae to do good in a small little land, and you've got just the tip of the ice-burg. The novel was complete unto itself, with a good take on an old, old celtic trope, missing almost all of the tripe twists that are expected on such an old tale, resting all of its strengths on characterization, depth of world-building, and serious attention to detail. 
 I fully enjoyed the novel. It was such a nice change of pace from all the war-driven fantasies I've plowed through, recently, returning to the roots of Fantasy, as in Fairy Tales. 
 There's a lot of plot-drive about men and women, the nature of justice with rape, with perceptions and misunderstanding, as well as truly good-hearted people being wrapped up in the whole mess. (And bad ones, too.) 
 What can I say? I think this is no way a flashy novel or ranking up there as anything I'd peg as the standard, but as a very good novel with great characters, I think it's damn sweet. :)

Dark Matter is a fantastic, sci-fi read about regret, love and quantum mechanics. 
 My book club picked this wild ride of a book and everybody took something different out of it. 
 We all enjoyed it, which is weird for us. Usually, we have opinions across the spectrum. This one, though, was universally loved. That's saying something. 
 "In the shadow of this moment, my life is achingly beautiful. "I have an amazing family. A fulfilling job. We're comfortable. Nobody's sick." pg 28. And then, something truly surprising happens. No spoilers! 
 I think that, as time passes, we grow comfortable in our lives, our marriages and relationships. Part of this book is about appreciating what you may take for granted. "He says, "It's like we get so set in our ways, so entrenched in those grooves, we stop seeing our loved ones for who they are. But tonight, right now, I see you again, like the first time we met, when the sound of your voice and your smell was this new country." pg 67. 
 The leader of my book club picked quotations that had to do about self-knowing and quantum mechanics. It was no surprise that mine were all about love. I'm one of the hopeless romantics of the group. 
 And one of the most open-minded: "We all live day to day completely oblivious to the fact that we're a part of a much larger and stranger reality that we can possibly imagine." pg 96. I truly believe that. 
 A local physics professor joined our circle and gave a short lecture on basic quantum mechanics and wave theory. But, you don't have to be an expert on the subject to enjoy this story. It's approachable science, like The Martian. 
 Recommended for book clubs, especially, but also anyone who wants an unbelievable story will probably love this too. 
 I heard that this is going to be made into a film- read the book anyway. It's always better.

This is one of a few books I've finished lately that I find a bit hard to rate and even hard to describe. First this book has significant flaws that weren't present (or at least weren't as present) in the first volume of this "series" Heroes Die. So...I'm going to say some slightly negative things about the book AND I'm going to be giving some significant warnings about it. Still please note that I have settled on a 4 star rating. Some books do transcend an "I like it" or "I don't like it" review. I considered dropping the rating to at least 3 and explaining why I would still recommend it "TO SOME PEOPLE" while dropping the rating but as I went on I decided I needed to keep the rating higher. 
 So, what's the negative? Well in the "simple column" the book at times gets a bit repetitive. You will I suspect feel that you've occasionally gone in circles. Also the storytelling isn't "quite" up to what it was in the first book so as a "pure novel" as a "story" it's good but not quite where it's predecessor was. 
 Beyond that we now leave actual negatives about the novel and move into the area of "BE AWARE OF THIS": 
 This is a dark, dank, oppressive, blood, vomit, deification (though the words used here are notably and purposefully more crude as in s_ _ t), mucus smeared story that many will find stomach turningly disgusting. I'm not using hyperbole here. If you have a weak stomach and scenes of violence, abuse, torture and rape are things you can't stand this is not the book for you. It's a well plotted well thought out book but the writer PURPOSEFULLY goes for the groin. 
 The book is also long on philosophy and philosophical debate. This is not in itself a negative and can be ignored (if you set your mind) but you should be aware. I am in disagreement with some of the authors conclusions and assumptions but that doesn't keep me from finding it interesting. And I do agree with much of his reasoning...but not all. 
 If someone who disagrees with your view of the world will annoy you to the point of distraction go into the book advisedly. The writer is not supporting a Christian world view (or for that matter a worldview that will support most religions), I am a Christian...a practicing one, but I still think the book worth reading. 
 I can't use the terms "like" or "enjoy" here, at least not comfortably. But I can say that I think most will be drawn into this novel and not only find it absorbing but thought provoking. While not agreeing with many conclusions and ideas promulgated here I do recommend that you try this if you think it won't badly offend. It's excellently written and I plan to get the next.

The only story I read from this collection is 'Black Dog,' as I wanted to continue on with Shadow, the protagonist of American Gods. It was a really good story, on par with The Monarch of the Glen, the other short story/novella about Shadow's continuing exploits.
Wow. That was intense!! & I cried. I actually cried! Highly recommend and need the next book NOW.

I have heard so many good things about this book and I was really hoping for that connection but it just didn't happen. Don't get me wrong, I loved the book! What made it seem less than a five star book is probably because I didn't get the "feels". I loved most part of the book but some scenes just didn't make me squeal or Fangirl. The book just made me satisfied. I liked the ending and I liked how the author incorporates the Marines in the book. I think it was very well done. But again, it was given a 4 star because it didn't give me the "chills" but it was very realistic and relatable and I did enjoy the relationship between Skylar and Josh :)

To recap An Ember in the Ashes: the Martial Empire has overtaken the Scholars, forcing them to live in slums or as slaves. The Scholars are forbidden from learning to read and are forced into menial jobs. Of course, the Scholars don't want to live this way forever--there is a resistance fighting to take down key members of the Martials. The Martial Empire is at a pivotal turning point, requiring that a new Emperor step up as a dynasty dies out. This leaves them feuding between themselves and momentarily weak to the machinations of the Scholar Resistance. 
 From the onset of A Torch Against the Night readers are dropped directly in the middle of action. Elias and Laia (our MCs) are fleeing for their lives in the middle of a Scholar uprising. Members of the Resistance attempt to fight back against the Scholars as a new Emperor is chosen. This raises tensions in the Empire as does the fact that the new Emperor is a Plebian and not a member of the Gens. Outside forces will try to exploit this moment of weakness. 
 Again we enter through the POVs of Elias and Laia. 
 Laia is a Scholar. She lived in the slums with her brother, Darin, and her grandparents. Her mother and father were leading members of the resistance until they were captured, tortured and killed along with Laia's older sister. Darin is her best friend and protector, but he makes a risky move and the Masks (soldiers of the Empire) catch on and come for him. Laia seeks a way to free her brother. 
 Elias was a Mask. He attended Blackcliff Academy and was chosen as an Aspirant. However, Elias finds the behavior of the Masks' abhorrent and flees from the Empire to help Laia. Laia's brother may be the key to stopping the tyranny of the Martials. 
 We also gain the perspective of Helene Aquilla. Helene was Elias' best friend and fellow student at Blackcliff Academy. She too was chosen as an aspirant but unlike Elias she gains the title of Blood Shrike to the Emperor (the second in command). Her family is one of the great Gens. 
 This story was a wild ride! A lot happens, that's for sure. I really enjoyed Helene's perspective. I rooted for her to figure a way out of the mess that is her life and cried alongside her at points. She was a great addition to this series. 
 The tension between Laia and Elias is ramped up a little bit in this novel though there are events that keep it from fully progressing. I definitely ship them! (Though I still feel bad for Helene.) 
 I was a little bit peeved when Keenan shows up and starts swaying Laia's affections. I really just didn't care for his character (& there's a good reason why!) and I was mad certain events take place between them. 
 The supernatural elements in this story are really interesting and add a lot to this story in my opinion. The Soul Catcher was an interesting one--I hope we'll learn her backstory at some point. 
 And this story is just as dark as the first if not more so! Would recommend!!!

Ooh this one was good. I'm really into this series. 
 Calla, our protagonist, has more than a couple personality flaws, but she is not your standard-issue young adult heroine unable to lift a finger to help herself, constantly selfish, and eternally virtuous. She is written so much like a real, strong, and headstrong teen with tons of responsibility (and guilt) that I find her utterly relatable. 
 I pretty much was just okay with the ending - it was alright where it ended, but clearly it's a big old setup for book three, which, thankfully, I already have checked out from the library.

I'm often skeptical about reading two-person perspective novels because they're often repetitive or it doesn't work out well. However, Marie Lu defied those odds for me. I read the entire Legend trilogy in about 10 days. It was such a refreshing dystopian story and it stands out among many other novels. I recommend this book to everyone. The book always get me guessing, which I liked. June is easily my favorite character in this series. She's so smart and determined, and although I liked Day too, I enjoyed June's chapters more. I'm so excited for the graphic novel to come out!!

I loved this book! It was amazing! It was an interesting retelling of Beauty and the Beast and I loved the characters! Especially Feyre. She was an interesting main character and I liked how she was determined to do something. From the beginning we see her as the one taking the initiative to take care of her family. And throughout the book, she wanted to help out those who have taken her away from her family with the curse. Also, I like how she didn't let the faeries taunting get to her. Her witty comments made me like her character even more. :D 
 And of course, who wouldn't love Tamlin? I liked him from the scene in which they first eat dinner at the manor. His attempts at flattery in the beginning was hilarious. :D And it was nice to see that he truly does care about Feyre more than ridding himself of the curse. He could have easily have told her about the curse but he put her before himself and his kingdom. 
 Now, while I like Rhysand, I really hope in the next book he isn't a love interest. I can see Feyre and Rhysand as good friends but I don't want a love triangle because I ship Feyre and Tamlin! But I do have respect for Rhysand for standing up to the anatagonist and for helping Feyre out (despite the deal she's now binded by). I'm also curious to see what will happen now that Feyre is an immortal fey. And, of course, what Rhysand saw that scared him so much.  
 Overall, this book was fantastic and I can't wait a whole year for the next one!!!

Not my kind of book. Catch-22 took me a while to finish because I found it so hard to get through. I understood the sub-text of the narrative after reading some analyses, but that didn't change my opinion. With that said, on my first attempt of "Pride and Prejudice", another popular classic, I thought the book was one of the worst I've ever laid my eyes on. On my second attempt it became one of my all-time favorites. Maybe if I ever decide to give Catch-22 another try, I'll find it a joy, but this review is certainly not focused on anything remotely joyful. 
 Joseph Heller was portraying the chaos and bureaucracy of war, the struggle between normalcy and insanity and the chasm between ambitious, power-hungry men and the regular guys who just wanted to see the light of tomorrow. The best criticism I can offer without going over-the-top is that reading over 400 pages of the same or similar jokes in Heller's writing style wasn't just hard, it was annoying. 
 Catch-22 started off well. In fact, I literally laughed out loud a few times when coming across some gems such as: "The Texan turned out to be good-natured, generous and likable. In three days no one could stand him." Reminds me of a few people I've met! 
 Unfortunately, a book is not a collection of occasionally witty one-liners. The rest of Catch-22 was dreadful and dreary. I give it a two star "It was okay" rating because the writing at least somewhat fit the bill of the setting, and hope to come back to this novel in a few years to re-evaluate my opinion. 
 PS: I'm confident that this isn't an issue of maturity, as I've seen people argue on other reviews. At 23 (as of Apr 15), I'm at an appropriate age to have the ability to read and independently evaluate these kinds of literary works.

Review Taken From The Pewter Wolf 
 In this, the fourth book in the 13 book saga, the Baudelaire orphans are sent to their new guardian at the Lucky Smells Lumbermill, expecting a safe future from Count Olaf. Expect they didn't expect to work at the lumbermill. They didn't expect to have a guardian that cares more about profit than any health and safety. They didn't expect their guardian to want to be called Sir nor did they expect that their new guardian would smoke so many cigars that they will never see his face because of the thick cigar cloud. They expect to be live with the workers in tiny bunk beds, have chewing gum for lunch or to be paid in coupons. But they do expect that, sooner or later, Count Olaf to turn up in another disguise, with a plot to steal their family fortune... 
 Now, I wanted something fast and I read this within two days. TWO DAYS! So this could be seen as a good thing, but while reading this, I remembered that basics of the story had been repeated in the previous books and a few more times in the next few books. 
 I'm having a tiny problem with writing this review. Because the book was ok. Not great, not rubbish, but ok. I remember why I didn't read the series back to back and I dip in and out of the series. However, I think this book is good if you're a fan of the series. If you're starting the series, start with The Bad Beginning and work onwards.

 I loved Eleanor & Park so much! Primarily because it is not your typical high school romance novel; in fact, it is defiant in setting itself apart from other YA novels of the same genre. 
 Eleanor is the new girl, owner of some crazy red hair and strange clothes. Park is the quiet Asian boy who avoids attention like the plague. When the two meet, they bond instantly over their obsession with comic books and good music before soon falling head over heels into first love territory. I love how the two come to find each other as a reverie of sorts; a place of solace where they can escape their sometimes troubled lives and be completely themselves without fear of judgement. 
 This is a beautifully written book. I marvelled at Rainbow Rowell's handling of the topics of domestic and child abuse, bullying and body image. That makes this book sound like a very serious read but while Rowell does tackle these important issues head on, she also manages to provide a brilliant balance, where this book is hopeful and funny, too. It masterfully captures the excitement and thrill of a high school romance but also the doubt and hurt that can come with opening up your heart. I also love how Eleanor & Park is structured to capture both Eleanor and Park's point of view. The characters are so vivid, unique and engaging, perfectly cast in this utterly gorgeous story of that special first love and both the awkwardness and elation that come with it. I found myself falling in love with these characters as I read their tale and was actually a little sad when it ended! My favourite of Rowell's books by far. A must-read for fans of YA and romance.

While Kozol's Fire in the Ashes: Twenty-Five Years Among the Poorest Children in America focuses on the emotional stories of the children who have educational issues as a result of poverty, Tough goes the theoretical route in regard to education. The two books go hand in hand and should be read in succession. 
 Although this book spends much time on the discussion of "character" education, there is so much more going on in this book. In the end though, it comes down how to best help the poor have more success in not only getting, but actually completing their education. Interestingly, Tough hits on something that Kozol emphasized in his book as well - it only takes one person who intervenes in a child's life to help that child become successful irrespective of economic status. 
 Tough doesn't just focus on poor children in his book. I liked that he also tackled issues that rich, private school kids face, which can impede their success after graduating from school. 
 All in all, a dense but very good read, chock full of information about education, parenting and chess - yes, chess! 
 I highly recommend it.

Asimov writes in the foreword that he agreed to make his Foundation sequels 140,000 words, twice as long as any previous book. That helps to explain why there are so many needless conversations and random tangents in these books. Trevize and his amazing powers of infallible intuition are back for a continuation of Foundation's Edge. The plot consists of searching for Earth for the vague purpose that somehow Earth holds the unknown reason why Trevize decided in favor of Gaia at the end of Foundation's Edge - or it holds the reason why he should change his mind. If he does change his mind then Gaia will listen to him and abandon Galaxia. So now we know that the ending to Foundation's Edge was pointless. This is a good indication of what to expect out of Foundation and Earth. There is no real motivation, mystery, or conflict driving this story. 
 Most of the time the descriptions of the various stops are interesting enough but there isn't any intrigue to hold attention for long. There are some good scientific discussions but they add nothing to the plot. Conversely the science fiction aspects weaken with the continued reliance on the powers of Bliss/Gaia. The poor sci-fi gets even worse with the introduction of transducers on Solaria. Asimov even abandons clever solutions to the problems facing the trio and relies on Bliss to solve them. Bliss even uses the function of the transducer herself. We find out that it was the transducer technology, at least the energy principle behind it, that captured Trevize's ship when he and Pelorat first approached Gaia in Foundation's Edge. 
 With nothing to drive the story it's up to the various and many tangents to hold interest. Asimov sprinkles in his ideas on almost everything. I liked some of the tangents but was always irritated by their frequency and how out of place they were in the context of the story. A lot of the tangenting scientific discussions read like one of Asimov's nonfiction education books. Some are pretty good but they lack the logical progression of his nonfiction making the arrangement awkward and still not providing adequate support to the story. The sci-fi asides do make the search for Earth more interesting. It almost reads like an astronomy puzzle. 
 The ending is weak.  It shows that previous actions relied on mental manipulations through hyperspace that aren't justified. Why didn't Daneel just have other robots go to Aurora and get a child that would have been killed or just kidnapped one? Why didn't Daneel just give Trevize instructions to go to Solaria and get a kid then give him instructions to get to Earth?  The explanations at the ending made the entire book even more pointless. Trevize's ability to make the right decision was of no consequence. Worst of all, having read the Robot and the Foundation books in chronological order, the ending was telegraphed.  The significance of Daneel is only apprectiated if you've read the other books but if you've read the other books you know what's going to happen.  It's the same situation as in Prelude to Foundation where having read the other books makes the ending both better and worse.

This was a beautiful novel. I'm glad my friend lent me her copy because even after she had recommended it to me a while back I still hadn't managed to get myself a copy (I had intended to right after I finished it, too, if not for her generosity in gifting it to me afterwards). 
 The narration and writing style was perfect from the very beginning. I was hooked from page one and I loved every second I read. There was no scene that was boring and though I may have skimmed through fight scenes I still did my best to pay attention to the writing. The author's descriptions were great, too; it was precise enough that I knew the image the author wanted to present yet vague enough that I could use my own imagination to fill things in (like descriptions of Thetis). 
 The friendship and romance between Achilles and Patroclus was so well done. The characters were made individuals first, shown how their identities were before their relationship began, and then they blossomed and changed from simple children to the men they became in tales. The sexuality was done simply but effectively and the sex scenes were just the right amount of intriguing without being vulgar (in fact, my favourite scene might be the "tell me again" scene). I cared for their relationship and was bothered by Achilles' experience with a woman and annoyed with Patroclus' own first-hand narration of sex with a woman (although I think it was more uncharacteristic of him in general; I don't believe that scene did much besides show how compassionate he was but it didn't feel necessary to me). 
 I cried at the end, from Patroclus' death to the very end of the novel . The way the novel fell into place so perfectly, and how all the characters met with fates so befitting to them, was just beautiful. Foreshadowing and the narration in general (like how Hector had never done anything to Achilles) was so well done that even though I knew what was going to happen the story compelled me to hope for a different ending. More so, I was almost hurt by what I thought was going to be a tragic end for Patroclus but the way Thetis gave in and saved his soul was so perfect that I cried even more at the finality of all the threads. 
 I wish I knew more about Greek mythology to appreciate the novel better but it wasn't necessary in order to fall in love with the writing and the plot. I wasn't sure whether a five star rating was too high for this book, but from the way I was captivated and how I cried at the end I felt like it deserves a place with my other five star books because it is definitely reread worthy and more so just a good book in general.

I couldn't get a visual of Sydney in my mind. 
 Ridge: 
 This is one of those stories you love to hate. I've read one other book by this author and I didn't like it because of the repetitiveness. This book had similar issues (aka, repeating perfectly 6 times in one paragraph ect...) but I pushed it away and forged ahead. I gave it a shot. 
 Things I couldn't stand 
 1) Maggie. Oh lawd I know this girl isn't to blame. I get it. But even with the illness and deafness I couldn't find it in my heart to sympathize with her when the truth about Syd and Ridge finally came out. Honestly, she was annoying as hell. "I will never leave Maggie for you"... "He will never leave Maggie for you..." I know how bad this is going to sound, but I have to say it: I feel like her disease was the one thing she had over Syd. 
 At first I thought Ridge had a connection with Maggie because she was deaf too. (To a certain degree.) But then after reading a few more chapters, I just knew there was more to it. And when it was revealed that she had Cystic Fibrosis, I was mentally telling Sydney to pack it in. Maggie had 5 years on her, a disease, deafness-basically, a long laundry list of sympathy and history that no one could compete with. 
 And yea, I know that's not how I'm supposed to think, but I can't help it. It's one of those moral dilemmas, understand? You want the lead guy and lead girl to be together, but there's this sweet, innocent, person standing in the way...And as innocent as that person may be, you see them as nothing but a problem, which is how I saw Maggie. 
 POINT BLANK: It's almost like Maggie's situation was created to justify the cheating. 
 2) The repetitive writing. I knew her style going into this, but still I cringed every time I read certain paragraphs that were meant to be emotional breakthroughs. Example: I liked such and such. I liked that he was this or that way...I liked that he could run and jump....ect... 
 Those sentences damn near killed me. 
 3)The speeches that would last up to 3 pages. Or as I like to call it: info dumping/E! True Hollywood Story material. I know you have to ask questions to get to know someone, but the way it was done in this book...Damn. After a while I just started skimming through pages. 
 4) The songs. In this case I think it would've been better to let the reader imagine what the lyrics were. 
 All and all the story wasn't bad. I liked Ridge and Syd in the beginning. But as the story progressed I found myself reading just to see how this author was going to make it all work. FYI: How she was going to bring Ridge out of this looking like the good guy. 
 Honestly, I never believed Ridge when he wrote that letter to Syd telling her she had his heart. I couldn't. If he had dumped Maggie I would've had a different opinion. But since he didn't, the audience is left wondering if Syd was second best/spare. Ridge breaking up with Maggie would've proved something to me. Loyalty, perhaps? I'm not sure. I do know if I had been in Syd's shoes and found out that my lovers girlfriend didn't accept his apology, I would've been iffy if he showed up at my door and claimed he wanted me. 
 No matter what Ridge says, it will always be in the back of Syd's mind. Would he still be with Maggie had she not broken up with him? Yes. Is he always going to love Maggie? Yes. No matter what these questions will always be in the back of Syd's mind. Whenever it got to the ending and he professed his love I didn't believe a word of it. Could've been because the ending was rushed, but I doubt it. 
 In the end I wound up disliking Ridge, hating Syd, despising Maggie for simply breathing. (I'm just being honest here, okay?) 
 There were times when I wanted more for certain characters and the author didn't deliver. (Primarily the ending.) I just never felt like Ridge cared about Syd as much as he claimed. I didn't believe it. This is where the Maggie thing comes into play. When I read the chapters were he's talking about Maggie, there was such passion...And then when he talked about Syd it seemed like she was more of a problem. 
 It was a clusterfuck ladies. 
 Conclusion: 3 stars for the plot and Warren. It would've been 4 had the ending been better. Was this redemption for "Hopeless". No. But I wouldn't knock reading something else by this author. 
 UPDATE: 
 I've had time to digest this book and I'm taking away a star. Just knowing that Syd was Ridge's second choice doesn't sit well with me. And I'm kinda starting to question what the purpose of this book was in the first place. What was the point?

This is my second of Lisa Genova's three books and I have loved them both. (I can't wait to read Love Anthony next.) Genova is a Harvard-educated neuroscientist, and her facsinating story lines reflect this. While I was more than a bit unnerved reading Still Alice (see my blog post, http://www.goodreads.com/author_blog_...), Left Neglected was a bit easier to tackle since it didn't make me feel as paranoid about having Alzheimers. (It did make me feel more worried about having a car accident, though!) With her pristine prose, Genova enlightens us about our fascinating gray matter while still delivering highly moving stories. And she is not above poking fun at the medical profession in the process. Genova is obviously a person of faith who believes in forces beyond medicine, and yet she never comes across as preachy or religious. A five-star read by one of my new favorite authors.

 All in all, I was very confused.

I enjoyed this book and flew through it! I loved the imaginative detail and references to the Wizard of Oz. This book has a really interesting premise, and Danielle Paige managed to paint a very dark picture of a place known for its optimism and carefree magic. I feel it could have been made darker in tone, rather than just the events, but I understand it's quite hard to do that when you have a normal teenage girl doing first person narrative. I also thought it was cool how Amy had pink hair. 
 However, I still do have a couple of criticisms: 
 There was a bit of cliche going on at the beginning - a bullied girl with a hard life who has to deal with some bitchy popular girl at school. 
 I think this book would have worked better if it was just one book than a trilogy. What are the bets that the publisher decided to squeeze money out of a brilliant stand alone by stretching it into a slightly washed out trilogy? 
 I felt that whilst a lot happened, nothing was really achieved.  None of the events described on the back of the book (Tinman's heart, Lion's courage, Scarecrow's brain, Dorothy Must Die) happened apart from the Tinman's heart was taken in the very last page. The synopsis of the first book is basically a spoiler for everything that will happen in the second. This is my main criticism of the book and I actually feel really aggravated about it. 
 The romance between Amy and Nox was not done well at all, I love them both individually, but I felt like their relationship was more like a rushed wish fulfilment for the author. (oops)  
 Overall, I really enjoyed the book, but it definitely had flaws. Great characters and imagination, but the plot could have been richer and I would have preferred a stand alone rather than a trilogy.

Andrew Smith's Winger flattened me. I was breezing along, laughing and cringing at the shenanigans Ryan Dean West gets into, and then the ending cold cocked me in the feels. Yes, I saw some kind of tragedy on the horizon, but I expected something different than what I received. I was a blubbering mess by the final page. Such a mess that my lovely wife said, "Dude, it's just a book." 
 Yet there are some books that rise above simple ink and paper, or collected kilobytes. There are some books that breathe. Some novels that are so well written they defy fiction and become real. That's Winger. 
 The cast of characters all have unique personalities, but my standout favorites were Joey, Chas, and Seanie. Ryan Dean was adequate as our narrator, but those three aforementioned teenagers truly stole the show. In my opinion, Chas, as our prerequisite soft-hearted bully, was probably the strongest and deepest character. We hear very little from him other than his constant berating of the rest of the cast, but when things go wrong for Chas it's heartbreaking. I must say, Smith pulled a fast one on me, because I didn't expect to care about Chas. Very nicely done. Joey was my second favorite, and Seanie exists on this list because I've never read about a character like him. Period. He was quirky and hilarious. MySites for EVERYONE! 
 In summation: I'm sorry this review is so short, but I have absolutely nothing bad to say about this book. If you only read one Young Adult novel in your life, make it this one. Funny, endearing, and shockingly tragic, Winger sets the bar for me as far as YA is concerned.
