The Taylors have been witches as far back as anyone can remember and they are the creme da la creme of Savannah magic society. Unfortunately, Mercy Taylor is a magical dud without a lick of magic at all. Her twin sister Maisie on the other hand got an extra huge helping of magical mojo and is the princess of the family - beautiful, talented and almost everyone's favorite. It's been that way since Mercy was a baby and she's use to her sister getting all the attention, she loves her sister and doesn't begrudge her the limelight. But she does lust after her sister's fiance. Ashamed of her feelings, Mercy turns to an infamous hoodoo root doctor - Mother Jilo, begging for a spell that will make Mercy love her best friend Peter and end her feelings for Jackson, her sister's intended. That one little spells sets of a chain of events that throws Mercy's entire world into turmoil, beginning most notably with the murder of her Great Aunt Ginny. 
 There's a ton of world building backed into this book with loving descriptions and lots of attention to a handful of characters. While the plot is fairly interesting and kept my attention I did feel like it dragged a little in the middle. More-over, while some characters were well fleshed out and fully detailed, others felt like thin caricatures without much detail - Jackson and Peter for example. Both are important character and yet they have little character development and don't really stand out. Overall it was an interesting book and yet just too drawn out. I probably won't continue with the series. 
 I have a couple of major pet peeves: First Maise's abrupt character reversal felt completely out of left field and unnatural. There were no hints early in the book that she was anything other than a loving sister so for her to abruptly turn out to be a villain felt contrived. Furthermore - the twist with Jackson turning out to be Ren was also completely out of left field with no earlier support in the book and contrived. The major plot twist, that Mercy was actually a powerful witch who's power was stolen, was predictable (or at least I had guessed that would happen halfway into the book). My only surprise was in who killed Ginny and that was cheapened by Ren turning out to be Jackson. Also the entire explanation that Mercy was in love with Jackson because he'd been absorbing her magic and part of her recognized that in him - that made me wince. So basically she's in love with him because she's in love with herself. Meh. The pregnancy bit at the end felt contrived as well and didn't seem to serve any real purpose. Mercy's sudden realization, literally in the very last moments of hte book, that she did love Peter also felt contrived and way, way too late.  
 Overall, excellent world building, inconsistent characters and a plot the limps along for most of the story. Despite my gripes I am sure that many urban fantasy readers will enjoy this series.

 Dark Skye is the 14th book in the Immortals After Dark series by Kresley Cole, which happens to be one of my absolute favorite go-to series when I want something sexy, emotional and full of angsty, action-packed goodness. This author isn't afraid of alpha males, kick ass heroines or the long, drawn out story arc. If you are reading this review chances are you have picked up at least a few books in this series or are familiar with this author. If that's not the case and you're thinking you might want some new paranormal romance in your life, let me just say up front that this is not where you want to begin. When I say long, drawn out story arc I am not kidding. 
 One of the things I like best about this series IS the long reaching story arc and how all the different plotlines intertwine with each other. I've been waiting on Thronos and Lanthe to get together since way back when I first saw them snarling at each other in Carrow and Malkom's story, Demon from the Dark. Especially since they looked to have so much backstory. I simply adore that Kresley Cole's not afraid to reach all the way back hundred of years to begin a love story. 
 "To me, you smell like no one else in the world ever has, or ever will." His gray irises glowed silver with emotion. A breeze ruffled his sandy brown hair. "It means you and I are going to be best friends. When we grow up, we'll be... more." 
 Lanthe and Thronos have a lengthy, difficult history between them. What started out as a unique and beautiful friendship as young children soon turned into hatred and fear on one blood soaked night. Lanthe, the Queen of Persuasion, and her sister have lived in terror for the last five hundred years as Vrekeners have again and again attacked them unmercifully. Thronos Talos, the Vrekener prince, has always known the beautiful Sorceri is his mate and at one time loved and confided in her. Now he just wants to punish the treacherous, unfaithful woman for a lifetime of physical and emotional pain. 
 Their story picks up exactly where the last several installments have... as they are escaping the Order's prison where so many Loreans are being held for experimentation. Thronos has been tracking his mate for so long that he is willing to do anything to catch and keep her. Even go into a Vrekener's worst nightmare and venture deep into the Order's tunnels, following her as she and her witch friend escape. Once he catches up with them and literally drags her unwillingly to safety their adventure begins. 
 Thronos is not kind to our heroine when they finally meet up again, he's rude and angry and just about as emotionally vicious as a five hundred year old immortal virgin who has chased his mate across the world as she lives her life without him can be. You heard me right, he's a five hundred year old virgin. (Angela falls over dead) Lanthe is the epitome of a bad ass, unapologetic heroine. She's wickedly sarcastic, powerful in her own right and is not about to apologize for her sexual history. No matter how many times Thronos verbally jabs at her and tries to make her feel small, she is not about to say she's sorry for living her life and having some experience. No way. Never. 
 Gahhhhh, I love this type of heroine. Love. 
 "I like myself!" she cried. "Did you never consider becoming what I need?" 
 This couple's journey takes them through portal after portal, through demon realms, deep underneath the sea and into danger time and again. The action never lets up for a minute as they learn the truth about each other's pasts and slowly discover how to let that past go and live in the present. Thronos is tortured by wanting his mate in spite of thinking that she has betrayed him repeatedly over the years. He's not just inexperienced sexually, he literally has no idea what romantic love means. Yet he has protective instincts that lead him to keep his mate safe under desperate circumstances and every time they make it thorough another life and death situation he finds something else to admire and respect about her. Lanthe forces him to accept her exactly as she is, through the slut shaming, aggressive anger and general douchery he keeps pumping out her way, she just stands her ground and refuses to be anybody but herself. Let me warn you, Thronos is like quite a few other KC heroes, he's a total asshat for a good portion of this book, but goes through an amazing transformation until he eventually becomes an understanding and loving husband. I thought he was completely, believably redeemed by the happily ever after. Also, he and Lanthe have some pretty scorching hot love scenes as she's teaching him how to be the lover she needs. 
 "That's right, Thronos. I want to make you remember that and everything else. Because our love story is epic." 
 As the Ascension draws ever closer, alliances are shifting with every new story and Nix the Ever-Knowing continues to play a deep game. There were several new developments that will hopefully finally, finally give readers what they've waited fourteen books for. I have no idea who book 15 will be about. Will it be Fury? Morgana, Queen of the Sorceri? Maybe Kristoff? I have absolutely no idea. The plotting in this series is so intricate that I can't imagine how Ms. Cole keeps it all straight. 
 I am completely addicted to this series, every new release is just as captivating as the previous one, once I picked Dark Skye up I found myself unable to put it down until I read the last word. I definitely recommend. Final Grade- A

 Maybe it's because I have such fond memories of Ella Enchanted (next on my to-re-read list), but I had a lot of difficulty getting into this book. I can't say I was comparing them, except to say Ella was simply a more enjoyable read, but still: the predictability of plot points and character relationships hit me over the head like a ten-ton brick. Obviously with the economy of characters and the slim size of the novel, any half-discerning reader could see Rhys and Addie were going to fall in love, that Drualt would make an appearance, and (duh) that Addie would save the day; but I would have at least liked to see more of the why and the how for how these things came about, rather than their happening simply because formula dictates it. Of course the male and female leads are going to fall in love, and the shy coward is going to find courage to save everyone. 
 There were some surprises (Meryl's fate, for example; I was on tenterhooks to see what would happen to her) and great sequences (i.e. Addie's imprisonment with Vollys, easily the best and most interesting part of the book), but I could have done without the Addie/Rhys courtship. Or Rhys, for that matter. Maybe I was reading him wrong, but there was a constant impression of over-the-top flattery and obsequiousness. With the shy, complimentary Addie even saying his bows and flourishes were extravagant, I could hardly see him as anything but wildly extravagant. Nice, yes, and caring, certainly; but I couldn't wrap my mind around quiet and stalwart Adelina falling so head over heels for someone so extreme--at least not with any sincerity. I was honestly hoping she might grow out of the crush by the end of the book, and even at their wedding, I couldn't really believe that they were in love. I would have much rather read 100 pages of Addie battling monsters and finding her courage than of Rhys' bowing and cloud-shifting and flourishing. 
 The ending went on entirely too long, as did the beginning. I would happily reread the segment with Addie and Vollys again, but I could skip the first 50 pages and stop after Meryl's revelation she was turned into a fairy and still not miss a thing.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Let's see what did I think... 
 Let me start with the bad points to the story first. 
 Things started off fine with the female heroine and the male hero in their character introductions but once they met the storyline just became silly. 
 Lucy gets shot at and she completely dismisses it. How do you dismiss getting shot at? Even if she was right and no one was shooting at her the fact that she sends uniform police after her so called "attacker" but she can't be bothered to stick around to see if they caught the guy or better yet file charges or a report or even give a description of her attacker? 
 Then the guy she thinks attacked her shows up at her house and she doesn't call the police she just lets him in to talk about what happened? 
 Once he inserts himself into her life he tries and fails to convince her that it might be possible that someone wants to hurt her. After finding out this guy might be legit she still denies the fact that anyone would make an attempt on her life. You would think a cop would show her better evidence or just leave, right? Nope. 
 That was my first clue that this was going to be one of THOSE books. 
 Randomly, for unknown reasons and prior to beginning of the book Lucy, our heroine, get her hair bleached blond. During the beginning of the book we find out she hates it. Lucy makes a lame attempt to correct her hair with an old expired box of hair dye that not only wrecks her hair but turns it green. Wow. I thought this woman was supposed to be smart? 
 In between all that the cop, Zack, continues to try to convince her that someone is trying to kill her. Not until her car blows up does she begin to believe him. This woman's car was bombed, and they clear the scene at lighting speed, and she asks if her car was totaled? Really? 
 Did it seem odd to anyone else that a robbery detective would invite himself to move into a house with a woman, who at this point isn't even a witness to any crime, to protect her 24/7? Why is a robbery detective investigating a crime that's not only out of his jurisdiction but it was above his pay grade since it was a federal crime? Also, why is Zack answering her house phone while he's there? 
 She's receiving hang-up calls on almost a daily basis and the best way they think to handle that is not to trace the calls but to let the one person the criminal won't talk to answer the phone. Brilliant. 
 Then another bomb is suspected to be planted in her bed but she doesn't call 911. She calls Zack. Cool great, WHATEVER. When he gets there does he call in the bomb unit? Nope. Let's just hide behind the door, tie string on the end of the blanket, and pull. GREAT idea! The PHYSICS teacher has nothing to add to this but agrees wholeheartedly. It blows up and takes the bedroom and part of the upper floor with it. And guess what? They stay in the house. YAY! And while staying in the house let's ignore the seriousness of the situation continue to refinish and varnish the kitchen floor while we're at it. 
 They continue forward like they're having a fun DIY week remodeling a cabin in the woods. 
 I get that this book was written prior to 2001 so no Homeland Security until 2002. But come on! After two bombs going off at the same house in a neighborhood no one bothers to call clue in the FBI or ATF? We're just going to sit back and let two robbery detectives continue forward with the case? 
 What also makes this story agonizing for me was the fact that this character, initially dressed up to look like a smart girl, seem more of an airhead and unable to take care of her own safety and well being. Her ineptitude was often reinforced by her sister, Zack and her ex-husband repeatedly. Either by saying things like, "She needs a handler." or "She needs someone to tell her what to do." or my personal favorite to forcibly grab her and direct her to do whatever. It was made worse by her bumbling around like she was having a sleepover and not having a cop, a stranger to her, stay in her house to protect her from an unknown threat while he invaded her privacy looking for clues. 
 What did I like about the book? 
 Well, I think that the author didn't really take the story serious and that's a good thing. She was just trying to tell a cute boy meets girl romance. I picked this up looking for something light. My thinking it would be along the lines of a Meg Ryan movie type deal, the Chick-Lit genre. I hate the term Chick-Lit. Instead, it was more along the lines of 13 going on 30. Not my kind of thing but I see the appeal. 
 I think there is a better way to execute a female lead in this genre. I think there is a better way to keep a story light with carefree and vibrant characters sound without them coming off as immature. 
 Something other than making an accomplished physics teacher sound like a tween in a Disney channel sitcom and a seasoned police detective sound like a petulant frat boy upset because he thinks his life will be over if he gets married.

2016 Reading Challenge - Read a New York Times Bestseller 
 The only things I knew about this book before I started reading it were as follows: 
 1) It was on the longer side, over 400 pages or so 
 2) It sold a CRAPTON of copies. Like, so many copies 
 3) Everyone and their mom loved it 
 4) It was about 2 sisters during World War II 
 That was enough for me! I finally dove in. The water was colder and calmer than I expected, and just too salty for me. I waded in the shallow end for a bit, then got out, dried off, participated in other water-based activities like water skiing, tubing, and tanning on an inner tube before deciding to return to this body of water, only to find the temperature warmer and the waves larger than last time. 
 My overall opinion of this book (excluding my own problems with the characters which isn't fair to pin on the author) is that it needed a better editor to fix pacing and reduce wordiness/redundancy. There were many slow chapters for the first half of the book it seemed, and the diction was repetitive. I noticed a lot of paragraphs that were either fully fledged or dangerously close to purple prose, which leaves me exasperated and bored. Also, for a 400+ page book that is about 2 sisters during World War II, there is little to no suspense. Seriously. There are plenty of opportunities for it to be used that would certainly make the story more interesting, but it's just no there. 
 The characters is a whole different issue. I loved Vianne's character development. She changed from a weak woman who refused to deal with anything and lived in this deluded world where her husband (who is a German POV) is alive and well and will be home soon and will take care of everything for her. She is like this for the first half of the book, which is another reason I found the book to be less enjoyable. However, she is greatly changed by war, and I think Kristin Hannah handles her transformation well (i.e. she doesn't become some super soldier overnight - she's still a flawed woman, but she becomes stronger and braver). 
 Isabelle, who is younger and more impetuous, becomes a member of the French Resistance. I loved her story line more, except for the instant "love at first sight" part, which caused eye rolls more than any other reaction. Luckily that part of her story isn't that prevalent for most of the book, but the theme reemerges later and makes it more frustrating. My other complaint with Isabelle's parts is the lack of suspense - as a resistance member, I highly doubt she'd come under no scrutiny by anyone besides her sister. That kinda took the wind out of my sails a bit (lots of nautical references for a book that never features any bodies of water). 
 This being said, I think Kristin Hannah did her research and really caused me to sympathize with survivors of the war. Surviving in a occupied France was fascinating and horrifying to read about, and learning a bit about how the resistance communicated was also interesting. 
 If you want a book that has better writing (in my opinion), a more interesting perspective, and more suspense, I would look to All the Light We Cannot See. That book did not take me a month to finish; more like a day. The writing is beautiful and I found the characters to be more interesting overall.

 They don't deserve any rants or any signs of garbage coming at them, because of some sort of "ugly ending" that I don't see at all, whatsoever. Can I just sit here, pretending that Goodreads isn't clogged with all of those negative reviews? Let's move on, and let me just say that this was one of the best books that I've ever read, and it certainly sparks up onto me as one of the best finales to a trilogy, or to any series that has ever climbed into my eager hands. 
 For the time being, I can tell you that it was love at first sight. From the first chapter to the last, it was a never-ending roller coaster ride that really messed up my feelings and emotions. I fell in love with the plot right away and I kept telling everyone around me that my heart is racing. I never have been this excited and anxious to let my feelings about a book out for a long time, and now here's my raving moment where I'm just about ready to explode. Every single masterful thing written in this book was meaning something, and I just never wanted to let anything leave out of the gorgeous pages that introverted into my heart. 
 Back in 2012 when the first book in the series was released, Burn for Burn, I picked it up as soon as it hit the shelves because at the time, I had been loving Jenny Han's other series and I wanted more, obviously. Little did I know that this would become a paranormal series by the end, as there were barely any hints given to us through the first two books but I can tell you that suspense and plot twists were two elements that both Han and Vivian are masters of. It's been more than a year and a half since I last put down the sequel to this one and I've always been thinking about what had happened to Rennie. Doesn't that tell you something? How often does a book's events stay in your mind? For me, if it's memorable, it can last a lifetime I'm sure, and the whole series is going to stick with me forever. 
 "A fiery anger begins to simmer inside me. I used to hate feeling angry. I used to fear it. Except now... it feels good. It feels like something." 
 This took off right where the sequel left us with. We're currently at Rennie's funeral, and Kat and Lillia can't seem to believe what's happening, and they feel like they have something to do with her death. Mary's also there, and she's witnessing it all, first thinking that it's her funeral. Later on, Lillia is mistaking her feelings with Reeve, and she doesn't know what to feel since it's absolutely forbidden in her case after Rennie's death. It's their senior year, and graduation is coming up, and everyone's trying to figure out what they'd like to do with their futures, but the only thing on Mary's mind is revenge and Lillia and Kat are stopped from following the mainstream, at least for now. 
 What this book has done to me is something unlike the usual situation with a 5 star read. I was sitting on my bed for 20 minutes, trying to figure out what my feelings were doing with me, and what the rating I should give this. It's no excuse to say that I shouldn't give this 5 stars. If my conscience told me that, I literally would've thought that it was messed up. Although yes, there had been some things that frustrated me, like Mary's character, everything in the end was perfect and it made up for all of the mishaps and tweaks needed. We started off this series with a 5 star rating, and we end it off with a 5 star rating. That definitely shows you how two fabulous authors can achieve something remarkable with just a thought that was shared over eating cupcakes, as the best ideas usually do. 
 "Years from now this will be what I remember when I remember my spring break senior year. Not the missed trip to Jamaica, or not being invited on Alex's yacht with all my friends. It will be this moment right here. The smell of chlorine on his skin. The way the sun dips slow into the water before it disappears. The first time I ever told a boy I loved him." 
 The pacing and everything about this plot was angelic and illusional. It's rare to find a book that puts you in a situation where you feel like you're burning into ashes because of your happiness, but in this case, I got all of that right in a matter of a few hours. The book made me want to devour and read this slowly, as I know it's my last chance to read a story of three girls who I can totally relate to and who I see as the best protagonists with different personalities and actions that they plan to do those those who they love and hate. Han and Vivian sucked me into the world of Lillia, Mary and Kat instantly, and I wasn't let out until the epilogue, where the questions were answered. 
 I honestly feel like I'm dying inside. The ending was so sad, but amazing and remarkable at the same time. I expected everything to end off differently, but we have achieved a classic ending where it all seemed right. There was some action as we all knew would come with Lillia, Kat and Reeve against Mary, who truly unlocked her sense of authority and power over everyone as she thought that her case of revenge gave her the allowance to be stubborn and use who she was against everyone else, including the two best friends who always were there for her. I just have to get my feelings of the ending out of me, or else I'll be stuck in this world for the rest of my life! 
 "He's alive. He's free. We all are. Because whatever Mary was in the end, she saved us." 
 Lillia had to be my favourite girl out of the three. Over the past three books, I have to tell you that she's changed and learned the most from them all. She's become confident, where she's now able to let her feelings and words be said without a bossy chick going over her. She demands to be in power, and she's looking for love. She's dealt with it now, of course, and Reeve's changed her, and she knows that the time to move on is the right time for her. I love her attitude, and her perspective was my favourite to read, where her leadership oozed my heart. 
 Kat has grown up from an immature reckless chick to someone who's been through so much but is there for her friends. Hey, she proves that she doesn't need a man in her life to be happy, and you can definitely see her obedience and connection to Lillia throughout the novel. You call Kat, she'll be parked on your driveway with a cup of coffee ready for you. She was loyal and most of all, she didn't care about the revenge anymore. It was like fate put her and Lillia in that revenge situation to find each other as they never had given each other a chance in the past. 
 And Mary? Well, through the middle of the book I would've told you that I hated her, but she was lost in her own world as well. She was a total mystery, and though she thought that she knew it all and what was really going on in her life, she didn't, but it was okay, as the other girls proved. Her authority went a little savaged and out of control, but I guess that's what happens when you're lonely and you don't give other experiences a chance. Of course, guilt and sorrow is what came out of Reeve and the girls in the end, and she needed it to make her stronger. Her ending was absolutely open, and I guess it all goes depending on your opinion of her to see what actually happened. 
 Some would agree to call this a chick-lit, or a contemporary-romance, but I believe that the contemporary and the romance absolutely stem away from each other. Yes, the novel had tons of romance (and kisses) in it, but the romance proved the strength of the characters and it was all about fate and the situation. Lillia and Reeve were really something else, I adored them together. And yeah, Lillia found herself in a love triangle with both Reeve and Alex, but I saw Alex more of a supporting friend who will always love Lil in a 'sister' way. Though in the end, everything was quite open, I feel that the connection had never subsided and left them. Reeve will always look at Lil and see a glint of the opal necklace that he bought her, and Lil will always see the fire in Reeve's eyes. But that's another thing to talk about--it was all real. 
 Happily ever afters? Not so much, if you really think about it. And that leads me to my last thought, where I'm telling you that this was unlike anything else I've ever read because although it is a fantasy, it's real as well. I can picture this happening in reality, and all of the events even changed my viewpoint of the way I see friendship and love. This was the normal way of seeing things, which gets us to realize that these characters are just teenagers, who had been in the wrong situation at the wrong time, but they surely had gotten something from it. 
 "What we had was perfect, and it was finite in the way that all good things are. Nothing gold can stay. I take off the necklace Reeve gave me and then I cry until the sun comes up. For what could have been and what will never be." 
 And that sends thick tears into my eyes, because the impossible is barely possible. And the authors got that. 
 This wasn't a miserable read, if you're kind of getting that from what I'm trying to say. This book was perfectly fabulous and gorgeous, and every time my eyes blink, I see ashes, ashes of what could've came out of this book, but then I realize, there's nothing else or else it wouldn't have been real. I won't even try to explain to you what this one meant to me, because it was truly something else. Reeve, Lillia, Kat, Mary, Alex, and even Rennie will always stay as real people, real characters in my heart who are walking on this Earth today. And maybe, just maybe, we're all one of them. Love's powerful, guys, but it can always change your fate.

In my review of Planet of the Dragons, I complained that there weren't enough dragons. Not so here. The Great Zoo of China is bursting at the seams with dragons of every color and size. Prince (horse-size), king (bus-size), and emperor (airplane-size) dragons. Yellow, red-bellied blacks, swamp dragons, etc. Possibly even too many dragons. Chalk it up to being careful what you wish for! 
 Regarding the debate about whether this book is too similar to Jurassic Park, I would say that the first half was too reminiscent, but that wasn't a deal killer for me any more so than The Land That Time Forgot capitalizing on the Lost World a hundred years ago. Building on the popularity of another book isn't a new development in the publishing industry. But like TLTTF and Lost World, the predecessor was superior to the successor. 
 The explanation for the origins of dragons and why different cultures have their own dragon legends is superb. It's a truly great premise. Coupling that with the military and cultural ambitions of modern China is even better. My qualms are not with the fundamental story, but more so with the execution. 
 The writing in the book is uneven. There are excessive explanations of exactly who is located where with exactly which groups. It's as if an attempt is being made to prove to the reader that the author hasn't forgotten where all the characters are. Too many times when Chinese people are speaking, the text reiterates that they spoke "in Mandarin." That got old. Generally, I assume the English speakers in the book are speaking English, and the Chinese ones are speaking Chinese. The only time it's somewhat helpful is when the main American character, CJ, speaks in Mandarin, but even then, it's not always needed. I didn't really care what language anybody speaks as long as the book is in English. 
 The book was also marred by an awkward transition from happy albeit VIP tour of the dragon zoo to a nightmare. One passage we've had a great experience learning about the exotic dragons. We step inside for a nice lunch, and by the time we come out, the dragons have pulled off their electronic monitors and eat the humans. It was too abrupt. 
 Another problem in the beginning and middle was a lack of suspense. I guess I was supposed to sense that something would go terribly wrong, but I never got too worked up or engaged wondering what would happen next. Maybe it was because the characters weren't quite compelling enough, or because the foreshadowing was too subtle or nonexistent. 
 But the book definitely picked up toward the end. The various details gelled together and Frey presented several very clever ideas. A great concept and a solid ending earn this book a favorable rating.

 Audrey, Wait! is a story about a girl that had simply broken up with her boyfriend, Evan, and thus, inspired him to write a song. It blows up into the next biggest American pop hit, and of course, Audrey ends up being hounded by the paparazzi. 
 I strongly disliked the characters of this book. Audrey was bearable (if a little stupid) but I really didn't like her best friend Victoria. The entire time I was reading I just felt the need to punch Victoria. Audrey is having trouble adjusting to the life of a celebrity and all Victoria can think about is the free stuff and perks of being well-known. Every time I saw her name, she was either asking about free make-up or if someone had invited her to some social event. The first time Audrey is called by a reporter, Victoria pressures her into answering the questions even though Audrey was definitely not of a mind-state to be smartly answering. Victoria becomes Audrey's "agent" without her even asking. She uses Audrey's name to get free things without even asking her! I felt like Victoria wasn't a true friend; Instead she was portrayed as a leeching, fake friend. 
 The romance in this book was painful. At first I thought that it would be cute for Audrey to end up dating her co-worker. That was, until the romance became the #1 example of terrible romantic development. 
 James, the love interest, is absent for much of the beginning of the book (probably because he's a really boring character). What attempts there were to develop the romance were quickly forgotten as his appearances were followed by four chapters of absence. There are probably three meaningful interactions between James and Audrey before they end up beginning to date (and no, that is not a spoiler because we all know it was going to happen). I found that the book used a lot of time skips to avoid having to describe events. The lack of build-up was partly salvaged with some teensy, teensy bit of chemistry between the two characters. 
 Audrey's character was annoying but her narration was pretty fun to read. The reckless, teenage voice was represented very well. I thought that it was believable how she handled the fame and breakup. 
 I really really liked the way this book ended. It's about as realistic as a unicorn flying into my house but nothing about this book screams verisimilitude. I liked how it was dramatic and showcased Audrey's change in attitude towards her whole situation. Although I didn't really like the trigger for her change, I enjoyed her I-don't-give-a-crap attitude and I loved the way that she kind of realized that her situation would be okay. It would all be okay.

 Pushing the Limits is a heart-wrenching story about family, love, and mental illness, told in alternating points of view between Echo and Noah. I could not put this book down! I stayed up until 3AM to finish and soaked my pillow. Yeah, I cried. A lot. 
 Echo is missing an entire day from her memory. She can't remember what happened the day/night she got the scars on her arms. The scars she hides with long sleeved t-shirts and gloves in the middle of summer. She went from being a social butterfly - dance team, art competitions, dating the "right guy", to a social recluse. 
 Then, through her therapist/social worker she meets Noah - a stoner whose reputation with the girls "walks down the hall before he does" - just as she's trying to get her life to some resemblance of normal. Her ex-boyfriend is interested again, and he might just put her back on the acceptable social list... but Noah doesn't cringe at the sight of her scars. 
 Noah's family was torn apart by tragedy, and he was separated from his brothers in the foster care system. He's been abused by the system, and in his anger and frustration he became the "bad boy". But Noah's determined to get his brothers back, and Echo might be able help him. 
 I really liked the dual narration, and appreciated getting to know both Echo and Noah from their perspectives. Katie McGarry did a great job with writing in a male POV; I was impressed how she was able to get inside a teenage guy's head. I also loved how Noah's family was his best friends Isaiah and Beth, and how they took care of each other. 
 Pushing the Limits is a fantastic debut by Katie Garry! I can't wait to read more from her, and I'm looking forward to her next book, Dare You To, which tells Beth's story.

 Review: Parasite is going to be a hit. This book is genetically engineered to be a success. To say I liked it isn't quite enough. I was disturbed and angry. I was completely engrossed. I was disgusted, fascinated and most of all I believe this book is completely possible. Perhaps not exactly the way it happens here, but in some way, I'm sure humanities hubris will be our downfall. 
 I have a fear of invertebrates. A deep seeded, sometimes phobic fear that keeps me up at night. I blame the movie Beast Master and the babysitter who let me watch it at age 5. In the movie A green-glowing worm or leech is inserted into a man's ear. It burrows into his brain and turns him into a mindless killer. I also blame my father for his ill-conceived pet name for me: Worm. A book about tapeworms? Let alone tapeworms in PEOPLE. THAT TAKE THEM OVER??? No way. 
 But marketing works, and the cover and display for this book at BEA certainly drew me in. So authors, when you ask yourself, do these events and giveaways result in reviews and sales? The answer is yes. I read this on the train home from BEA and will buy the rest of the series without even worrying about my book budget. 
 Of course, all books have their flaws. Unfortunately, this book's flaw in inherent in it's concept. While I loved the slow build, and the intermixing of science journal writing and narrative, it led to a final reveal that flopped. Seriously, if you didn't figure out the big "surprise" in this book by about the 5th chapter you're stupider than a Howler Monkey. Luckily, Grant's writing is of a high enough calibre and the story engaging enough on other levels that this let down was minor. Also, I'm not sure how she could have avoided it. Both the necessity of the main character not knowing for the plot, but also the character profile which makes her innocent enough to believe she really didn't know. 
 Parasite is an easily digestible (ha) nugget of grossness. I recommend it for any reader. It's a commercially accessible book but with enough teeth (ha!) to get into your brain like a colony of Neurocysticercosis parasites.

 Ten years ago, a community, consisting of Weir and Anaweir, flourished on the mines carved deep into the Brazilian hillside. Life could not have been better for the fleeing people. Until, a mysterious attack on the bases water supply left many dead and many more fighting for their lives. Most of the adults died, leaving behind their legacy with their weir children, who developed powerful abilities and clouded their stones. Only seven at the time, Jonah Kinlock knows first hand how powerful and dangerous he had become. With the help of Gabriel Mandrake, Jonah, his younger brother, McKenzie, and multiple future friends were able to beat the odds against survival, enrolling in Anchorage, Mandrake's school for those affected at Thorn Hill. Together, Jonah, Alison, Natalie, Mose, and Ruby make up Nightshade, battling the shades of Thorn Hill. Meanwhile, Emma Claire Greenwood spends most of her days in her grandfather's guitar studio, increasing her luthier skills. Her life soon gets turned upside down when she discovers her grandfather in a pool of blood in his guitar shop. Near death, Sonny Lee hands her a note, thrusting Emma into a world she believes is in fairy tales. Soon after meeting her long lost father, Emma learns more about her family and herself, only to have it all taken away in one night. Rowan DeVries, a wizard, takes Emma in, determined to find out what exactly happened the night his sister was killed. The only problem is, Emma cannot remember. As the story continues to go on, Jonah and Emma come together on common rocky grounds. 
 This book is so different from the first three. We are thrust into even darker character backstories and tragedies. I very much enjoyed the appearances of the original characters within this book. Some movies ruin books, some are better than the books, this fifth Grisham novel in publishing order is a little bit of both. I kept seeing former KKK (kluckers, as they are also known apparently) and death row inmate, Sam Cayhill, as the actor who played him so well in the movie, Gene Hackman. For those who fondly remember the Christopher Reeve Superman movies, Hackman will always be Lex Luthor! I wish Sam Cayhill had some of Lex Luthor's diabolical humor (OK, well maybe he has a tiny bit). 
 THE CHAMBER movie receive an abysmal 12% at Rotten Tomatoes, but fortunately the book is better. Without sifting through the various negative movie reviews, I'm pretty certain why this rated so poorly. It's not really a story, more a character study and drama, it's definitely not a thriller, and as for legal drama and suspense, everything hinges on whether or not Sam Cayhill's grandson and young attorney, Adam Hall can get a stay of execution (AKA The Big Question). This review won't spoil the story by answering The Big Question but if you've seen the movie you know the answer and, thus, reading the book becomes the equivalent of floating down a river in a semi-inflated raft. 
 Considering this as a slow-moving character study, let's examine the characters. Adam turns out to be the only likable one. Adam's father was Sam's brother and changed his name to get away from the family's dark secrets. The reader can get into his corner a little bit (some readers could be more compassionate than I based on Grisham's strong writing style), but it's hard to get fully on Adam's side trying to save his grandfather from being gassed because the man is such a rotten, racist bastard. His acts, even if the excuse in part, is that it was family tradition are just way too despicable to stomach. I felt zero sympathy for Sam Cayhill and as a result, it was difficult to be in favor of Adam's quest. Factor in Sam Cayhill's rich, alcoholic, drama-fueled daughter and a two-dimensional bad guy accomplice of Sam's that may or may not be important and the reader has two curious subplots that, in retrospect, seem like wasted opportunities. 
 Negativity aside, this book is significantly more literary than Grisham's other books, save for A TIME TO KILL, my personal favorite of his novels I've read. As mentioned in past reviews, I can enjoy a great character study, so this aspect kept me turning pages more than the answer to The Big Question. In some ways it returns to similar themes in ATTK (racism), but with less sympathetic characters. 
 There is a tremendous amount of capital punishment legal mumbo-jumbo involving death row appeals and assorted efforts to legally save a dying man, up to and including clemency from the Governor (should that become necessary), little of which actually happens in a courtroom, unfortunately. Again, for a legal book, I expect at least some courtroom drama and I was left hungry with this read. By going through the appeal process, as seen and experienced through Adam's eyes, the reader is supposed to be on Adam's side, wanting his grandfather client to go free. I really appreciated how hard Grisham tried to make me care about The Big Question through various characters eyes and perspectives. Grisham spares literally know angle unexplored in the four weeks leading up to finding out the answer to The Big Question. 
 To summarize, I think what hurts this novel most is the length. It's too exhaustive, too laborious, and tries way too hard using too much space. The reader gets it somewhere around half the words used. Answer The Big Question already! Either Cayhill is stayed or he's gassed, but stop stalling, quit trying to make us care. As a short novel or novella, THE CHAMBER would have been tighter and stronger. At least for this reader. 
 My review may sound harsher than I feel about the story. Despite the length, the mostly unlikable characters, I still enjoyed reading, primarily because Grisham's writing is free-flowing and easy on the eyes (it's popcorn fiction), thus earning a 3-star rating. Of the six novels I've read, this has been the weakest so far. 9,468 of 9,718 (story finishes at 97% with last 3% containing an excerpt of The Litigators).

 "We all know the definition of shattered: to break into pieces; to weaken, destroy; to damage, as by breaking or crushing. But my story isn't about being shattered. It's about surviving the pieces."-Haven 
 Nashoda Rose has done it again! She is undeniably one of the most dynamic and passionate writers of all time. Every time I pick up a book by Ms. Rose, I know that I am in for an amazing ride. Her storytelling is unique because of the detailed characters, the internal struggles they face, and the passionate heroes (and their heroine counterparts). Shattered by You was an excellent continuation of the Tear Assunder Series. I can only hope that she continues to explore every single character (even beyond the fourth book) so that I can continue to indulge in this delectable series. 
 Haven is Reams's twin sister. She has been battling the demons from her past and is constantly running. If she runs, she feels she can escape. 
 Unfortunately, there is no escape for her. The damage to her soul has burned deep. She is broken. Her broken soul has caused her to detach herself from everyone. Although she is trying to go back to school and rebuild her life, she cannot escape the panic attacks and depression weighing her down. 
 Crisis is the "fun-loving band member" of the group who has all the right moves. He loves the ladies and loves rock-n-roll. 
 "Imagine a rock star: hot, tatted skin-- which bordered on an addiction to pain-- muscled, and charismatic. He worked out obsessively; f*cked obsessively. Played music obsessively." 
 When he met Haven, his priorities shifted. He saw beauty in her and wanted to bring her out of her shell. He begins to pursue Haven gently. It all starts with a few text messages. As soon as the friendship begins, everything changes. After all, can't love heal all wounds? 
 "You will break. One day that cool exterior you're hiding behind will shatter. It has to. It has nowhere to go. And when it does happen, I intend to be there to help you pick up the pieces."-Crisis 
 Crisis' transformation is extreme. He offers Haven support and pushes her gently as she navigates through the darkness. Haven has been brutalized so violently. The pain you feel for her is immense. Yet as she begins to overcome, you feel joy through that pain. I genuinely loved every moment these two shared together. Often times, I find myself desperate for the romance to start. And yet, in this case the friendship was so beautiful as it bloomed into something more. 
 "I wanted to bust down her walls and force her to let me in. Her demons weren't black shadows. They were fuckin' monsters and the road ahead was one that was going to test every part of me and her. But for some reason, it didn't scare me. Because as long as she was in my arms, we'd be okay."-Crisis 
 Of course, in addition to Crisis and Haven's relationship, we have the opportunity to share in the mending of Ream and Haven's relationship as well. Twins share such a delicate bond and these siblings have been through hell together. It was quite momentous when things for Haven begin to clear and Crisis, Ream, and the entire crew is there waiting for her. 
 "This was what it was about. The feeling as if your heart beat right out of your chest and into theirs. Like you couldn't take another breath without them. As if everything inside united and there were no questions. No uncertainties." 
 What makes this read so beautiful? This is a love story full of heart and passion. When Crisis and Haven come together, everything becomes right in the world. Shattered by You has plenty of action, drama, and colorful text to keep you engaged the entire read. I simply cannot say enough about my love for this book. Every time I read a book by Ms. Rose, I am reminded of why I read. I read to escape. I read to feel joy. I read to experience love and passion. Thank you Ms. Rose for bringing all of these feelings out of me again! I will be anxiously waiting for Kite's story! Although, it will be hard to top Crisis and Haven. They will forever be etched in my heart, mind, and soul! 
 "She'd keep her promise to herself and find normal. Our normal. Mine and hers."-Crisis

So have you ever been scared that when you read a book for the second time, it will lose its luster? It has been almost one year since I first met these wonderful characters and the writing was just as beautiful as I remember. 
 Natsya has gone through a horrible trauma and she goes to live with her aunt. Her parents are not the typical absentee parents one usually sees in YA literature. They are kind of absent, but it is Natsya's choice. She wants to go to a new school where no one knows her and live with someone she feels doesn't expect anything from her. Every time her mom or brother tries to make an overture towards her, it's heartbreaking. Her family wants to reconnect so badly, but the problem is that they want the old Natsya. And that Natsya is dead. 
 Natsya does everything she can to push everyone away. Her trick? She doesn't speak at all. Natsya also dresses extremely provocatively. She wears really tight and revealing clothes. She figures any guy who pays attention to her will only want one thing and she is okay with that. She just isn't okay with them loving her or expecting any kind of attachment. So it's interesting that she manages to build friendships and a sort of family, even with the no speaking thing. She becomes friends with Drew, a harmless flirt, and Clay, an artist with a fascination for drawing her. Drew seemed like a jerk at first because of all the sexual innuendo he threw her way. But he was all talk. There was a scene where Natsya's mom asked what she was to them and he said, "Family." Awww. Try not to get emotional with that. Drew became so protective of her and it was really sweet. 
 As for Josh, I just completely fell in love with him and rooted so hard for their relationship. Josh has lost his entire family and he is now emancipated. He is very close to Drew's family, but other than that, he tries not to get too attached. He doesn't want to lose anyone else and that is his biggest fear. It's not really that difficult to understand why Natsya feels safe with him. He accepts her silence and her company without expecting anything in return. Their relationship is ADORABLE. He starts calling her "Sunshine" at the beginning of the book, mainly because she dresses in all black and never speaks or smiles. I kind of loved that. And after they hang out in silence for weeks, she actually starts speaking to him. He is the only one she feels safe talking to. I also thought they were so cute on their first date. Because they both have issues, it was actually a first date for both of them and they had no idea how to be "normal." 
 Of course there is drama because of Natsya's past. She refuses to tell Josh anything about her past. She feels completely ruined and undeserving of what Josh is offering. I got so frustrated when she pushed him away and I just wanted them to be together again. I adored the very slow buildup of their relationship and was anxiously awaiting the reveal of what happened to Natsya. I thought the ending was absolutely perfect and I really can't think of a single thing I would change about this book. 
 When I finished this book a year ago, I immediately wanted to read it again because I loved it so much. I felt the exact same way this time. I just did not want to let go of these characters.

After the end of 
 Fire Falling 
 , I flailed a bit waiting for the next book...to load because my Kindle decided to be obnoxiously slow. So it wasn't a dreadful long time, thank goodness; I don't want to imagine what the wait must have been like for those who read it when the book released. 
 Of all the Air Awakens books so far, I think Earth's End had to be the most action packed. I had an idea of how it started after reading 
 Tales from the Front 
 (a novella between books 2 and 3). But I wasn't prepared for this book AT ALL. Everything I loved about the first two was amplified in the third of the series. The action, the tension, the risks, the ROMANCE (y'all don't know how much I ship Vhalla and Aldrik...it's bad, real bad). 
 It's really hard to talk about a book in the middle of a series without spoiling too much from the previous books. But one thing that remains consistent is Vhalla. As the heroine, she could have gone one of two ways: not changing at all or changing so much that you lose what was amazing about her to begin with. Kova found the middle and Vhalla not only grows as a person but also keeps that relatable factor. She struggles. She is challenged. She must make tough decisions without knowing the outcome. Nothing is guaranteed. 
 Since this book is where the team has reached the warfront after spending the last book on the march, things are tough. Kova didn't skimp on the world-building as she creates a place where the Northern culture clashes with the Southern army camp. Death isn't uncommon and it's never an easy decision to make. That Vhalla goes through this and you really see her thought process made everything so much more real. 
 She's not the only one. The characters aren't spared just because it's their story. You really see a new side to them. While Earth's End features all my favorites from previous books, it also brings in a new set of supporting characters who are by no means easily cast off. Especially Jax. 
 I am SO excited he has his own prequel series because he quickly became one of my favorite characters. Him and the Golden Guard are amazing as a team, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. Plus Baldair is part of them and while Aldrik is great, is younger brother isn't half bad either. ;) 
 Okay, so far I've managed to keep from talking about my new favorite ship but let's chat quick about Vhalla and Aldrik. The end of Fire Falling is a MASSIVE cliffhanger and if you ship these two I HIGHLY recommend having this book ready to go because you're going to need it. What I love about these two is that they give me that romance I crave in the books I read while also keeping it grounded within the story. I never felt like the plot suffered so that these two could spend pages upon pages lusting after each other. Their relationship fits within the world, within the story, and is as integral as any other part. 
 It made my heart break a bit at the end but at the same time, I was comfortable with Vhalla's decision. It struck me as staying true to her character and the changes she's made over the course of the series. Plus, I have a feeling it's not over just yet. After all, there are two more books! 
 Now that I've sufficiently gushed about this book (definitely the best of the series so far), you can all go out and buy it so you can suffer with me.

This is the third John Green book I have read, the first being 'The Fault in Our Stars' (surprise, surprise) and the second being 'Paper Towns.' And unfortunately, his stories have started to disappoint me as I jump from one book to the next. TFiOS is one of my favorite books of all time; mainly because the plot wasn't overburdened with unnecessary characters, the characters felt real and were relatable to on a level way past the obvious, and the story was... killer, for lack of a better word. Paper Towns was okay; it wasn't great, but it wasn't bad either. The last 100 pages or so made up for the silliness of the rest of the book, but I liked it in the end. 
 THIS book, I'm not sure about. See, I liked the story. I didn't want to put it down. That having being said, I HATED the characters. What a shame! The story was good, the writing was wonderful, the John Green touches that I have grown to love (and those precise touches that keep me reading his books) were a delight. Certain aspects like the protagonist's love for biographies and last words made the book interesting. John Green has a certain air about him; he can write fluidly, efficiently while making life-changing remarks, thought-provoking statements as easily as one breathes. And that's what earned this book a 3 star. (Probably a 3.2 but GoodReads doesn't give me that option, does it?) 
 Now going back to the negative points: Alaska was a Mary-Sue. Now, the thing is, everybody has different perceptions of a Mary-Sue, but it all boils down to one thing: a Mary-Sue is perfect to everything and everybody around her, no matter how fucked up she actually is. So Alaska drinks and smokes, she's self-destructive and angry, mysterious and frustrating, but she's beautiful, sexy, gorgeous, smart because she reads poetry and quotes authors and reads intellectual books. She says things that make boys swoon, she does things that make boys run after her, she plays with people, and overall, she's a selfish bitch but everybody forgives her because she is Alaska and she is perfect in every possible way. John Green doesn't contradict that. He likes to point out the certain 'flaws' she has, but according to ALL the characters in the damn book, they weren't flaws at all, were they? Nobody was ever angry at Alaska for more than two seconds. Nobody was hurt by her aloof ways for more than two seconds. And OBVIOUSLY, she was everybody's love-interest from the moment they laid eyes on her. The only thing I liked about her character was her strong, and overly aggressive view of 'patriarchal paradigms' but that only popped up like thrice in the book, and in the end, everything ended up based on that. So, a big thumbs DOWN to Alaska, which sort of sucks because there wasn't ONE paragraph where she wasn't mentioned or yearned for. 
 Miles Halter was such a disgusting character. He annoyed the hell out of me. He was as selfish as Alaska, if not EVEN MORE. I mean, dude, you know a girl for four months and she dies, and you freak out and go batshit insane and start acting like she meant the most to you, when OBVIOUSLY you're surrounded by people who have known her for YEARS, even from a distance, that must count for something. And you have the NERVE to sit there and scoff at their grief while all you can think about is, "She said to be continued, so I wanted to love her and have sex with her, but I can't because she's dead, and now I can't feel that sexy girl in my arms anymore." And he fails to understand that there are people around him who cared more, who had more reason to grieve, and he shuts them out because he was a lousy bastard. 
 The only character I could stand a little bit was Chip aka The Colonel. I don't have many complains about him; he was a well-rounded, moralistic, humorous character, whereas everybody else from Lara (who basically was a damsel in oblivion) to Takumi (was that his name, because I can't remember, because he was so insignificant to the entire plot ugh) was absolutely shallow. 
 So I don't know. I'm wondering if I should even bother to read An Abundance of Katherines, because I'm seeing a pattern here. I gave TFiOS a 5. Paper Towns a 4. Alaska a 3. I really do not want to read a book that is worthy of a 2. :( John Green, ugh, I love you so much, and it pains me to read a book which I dislike.

So. Rites of Passage. Considering that the last memorable experience I had with teens in military school was the Disney channel movie Cadet Kelly with Hilary Duff, I wasn't entirely sure what to expect from this one. I just knew I wanted it to be good and that I wanted Sam McKenna to kick some misogynist butt. Luckily for me, RoP was just what I'd hoped for and more. 
 The military is a family tradition for the McKennas. So are dares. So when Sam gets a dare from her older brother, Amos -- the last one he gave her before he committed suicide -- she's determined to complete it, no matter the cost. This is how she ends up going into military school. But it takes so much more than just that dare to keep her there through all the hazing and intense hate that she faces as one of the first girls at the Denmark Military Academy (DMA). Sam proves time and time again over the course of the book how ridiculously strong and determined she is. Not just physically strong -- though she can definitely kick lots of her fellow cadets' butts -- but possessing an incredible amount of inner strength. Sam faces abuse that would drive everyone I know right out the front doors but she always manages to pull herself together and stand strong. Sometimes it takes a good cry or a few painful moments to get her there but that only serves to make her feel more real to me as a reader. I wish I had a friend like Sam to keep me going when things get rough because she is pretty incredible. 
 Speaking of incredible, let's talk about Drill, shall we? Drill (or Dean, but he is most commonly referred to by his rank of Drill Sergeant) is a hot, caring, and definitely not misogynistic military man who caught Sam's (and my) attention. Technically he's 17 but I actually kept forgetting that because he acts and comes across (especially with his strong military presence) as older... closer to 22 or 23 in my mind (whereas Sam, for context for you, felt closer to mid-to-late teens like she was supposed to... she's 16, I believe). He outranks her which makes any sort of canoodling of theirs strictly against DMA rules, but they are both very conflicted over this rule because they definitely (and understandably) have the hots for one another. The forbidden romance played out really well even though sometimes I thought they were being a little too lax on keeping things secret, especially considering how many people were out to get Sam. Occasionally, the fact that they weren't getting caught felt a little too good to be true, but overall I loved the tension of the "we can't but oh we so want to" (PG-rated) heat between them. 
 It's not just the central characters (and their romance) that made this such a fantastic story. The actual plot and action played a large role as well. I loved getting a glimpse inside the military academy, and watching the new recruits go through team building exercises and training was really interesting for me. The rituals of military school are foreign to me but clearly not foreign to Hensley, who showed them off very well. They even made me want to get up and exercise and feel fit and get stronger... well, after just one more chapter, that is. Tied into that is the whole idea of the secret society working to rid the DMA of its first female recruits. Seeing this develop and unravel both for Sam and for readers from a few nasty cadets into the work of an entire secret society was engrossing and I loved the way Hensley tied it all in with the background, rituals and routine of military school. 
 Overall, Rites of Passage kind of feels to me like the surprise book of the year so far. I didn't hear a lot about it before I dove in but it turned out to be a standout contemporary novel with action, tension, and great characters. I didn't really get into the side characters here (because I figured my review was already long enough and I have done enough rambling) but there are some excellent players who only serve to strengthen Sam's story, whether they're on her side or not. Her fellow recruits and everyone she meets at the DMA, good and bad, as well as her own family bring an array of conflict and comfort to Sam which only made the story richer. A great debut... I'm excited to see what Hensley writes next!

4.25 stars. 
 Kara Gillian is a detective at the Beaulac Police Department in Louisiana, and was recently transferred from Property Crimes to the Violent Crimes Division, something she's been wanting for quite some time. This means she'll be able to work on a case that has been cold for three years, that of the Symbol Man murders. Before they stopped cold, thirteen people had been ritualistically killed and when she happened to come across one of the victims while on patrol, Kara realized there were arcane traces on the body, alerting her to the fact that somehow another summoner was involved in the murders. 
 Rowland not only has a knack for writing about all aspects of crime scene investigation, (not too hard to understand why she's so great at it, given her background) but also for witty dialogue laced with humor and swearing, scenes of summoning and characters that are extremely likable. She also did a good job of not having a plot that was easy enough to figure out by page seventy-five (though with Monday morning quarterbacking you do go "aaahh" once you're done reading) and for creating a very believable storyline that had me spending every free minute reading it to find out who or what was responsible. 
 I love Kara. Due to the fact that she's a summoner, she's not only isolated physically (she's miles away from her nearest neighbor) but also socially, unable to share who she really is with any possible girlfriends and sort of inept at having a boyfriend. There are the usual douchebags on the force who look down on her for being a woman (of course they assume she had to screw her way to lead on such a prominent case) and for being newly promoted and being assigned such a prime case right away, overlooking the fact that she's the most familiar with the Symbol Man because she spent the last few weeks studying all of the cold case files. 
 The secondary characters are fantastic. You never know who might be hiding something or just what they're hiding. In fact, I'm pretty sure most of them are hiding something, whether they know it or not. Tessa is a terrific anchor for Kara. Being her aunt she's the only one who knows the truth about her, and FBI agent Ryan Kristoff, who works on a sort of occult task force, seems like a person who, though she disliked him initially, may be someone she can work with and trust. Others that she works with, such as Doc, Jill and even Crawford and a couple other detectives, add a lot to the story and will hopefully have bigger storylines in future books. And Lord Rhyzkahl is definitely a sexy and mysterious character, though I guess that comes with the Demonic Lord territory. That didn't stop me from wanting to crack him upside his head more than once, but I can't wait to find out more about him, as I'm sure all his little secrets and motivations won't be revealed for quite some time. 
 Between this series and her White Trash Zombie series, Rowland is quickly becoming one of my favorite authors. I can't wait to read the rest of the books in the series that are out so far, though my sister has warned me that I'll be screaming in frustration after I finish the last one as the next installment isn't due until next year.

"Sirensong" was a fitting end to this series and a good relief after the second book in the series, "Shadowspell". Black has some very unique and interesting ideas that I wish were executed more eloquently. Even though the voice in this novel was significantly better than it's previous there were still lines such as, "She looked at my hand like it was a dog turd and she didn't want to touch it." (Page 280) That line literally made me burst into laugher. 
 Finally, Black takes us into Faerie! Dana has been summoned to appear before the queen of the Seelie court and she takes a small entourage with her, which is pretty much everyone she knows in Avalon save her alcoholic mother. I was ecstatic to learn about Faerie and I don't feel like Black disappointed at all in her delivery of this fictional realm. The Green lady was one of my favorite and creative creatures of Faerie. 
 I feel as if the sexual themes in this series have not been very consistent. In the first novel we have reference to sex. Then, jump to the second novel where you have the bargaining of giving up virginity, near rape, and erect nipples. Finally, in the third novel there are all these build ups that lead no where because in the end *spoiler* we find out that Dana isn't ready to have sex. Groan! *End Spoiler Alert* 
 The Erlking is probably one of my favorite characters. How hot and sexy is that guy? I'm not sure I have thought of a character in a book before as hot and sexy but the Erlking definitely fits that description. I thought Ethan had great character development over the course of the three books even though this only spans like two months. It is sort of unbelievable that one character can change so much is such a short period of time. 
 I really wish Black would give her readers more credit and not stop to explain every minute detail. Yes, we get it the Fae are beautiful and yes we get it your mother is an alcoholic. And is it too much to ask to have a pretty protagonist? Does any one really believe that a girl who wears khaki pants and a button up to a ball would attract the attention from Keane, Ethan, AND the Erlking? No one even dresses like that any more! 
 I wish she would elevate her writing style and slightly alter her voice but oh well....the book really is what it is. Jenna Black had a story to tell and I sure found it interesting enough. Despite the turd remarks and comments to "get the hell out of Dodge" the book was a pretty solid success I would say. 
 I was even moved to tears once as Dana dealt with the struggles of her mother. I liked how nothing really resolved with Dana's mother, it was sad but realistic. Other than that, I wish Black had given us a better ending not one that seemed so neatly tied up. Is it too much to ask for a little romance? 
 Overall, once again I think the books are appropriate for older teens and is a fun and interesting read. There is only so much I expected out of this novel, after all I did read the first two and so I knew exactly what I was getting myself into. The book is super fast so even if it is a waste of time it doesn't waste much at least. I do wish she had chosen to continue this series. I think she could have gone on for quite a while.

*I recieved a copy of HOW TO BREAK A BOY via the publisher through a Goodreads giveaway. 
 If I had to describe HOW TO BREAK A BOY in one word, it would just be angst. 
 So. 
 Much. 
 ANGST. 
 Despite all of the ~feelingz~ being thrown around angrily in this novel, I still enjoyed it. A lot. The characters were fun, the story was fast-paced (even though I read it suuuper slowly), and the plot was fairly solid. 
 Now, that being said, there were things about HOW TO BREAK A BOY that I didn't really like. But we'll get into that in the actual review... 
 ...which starts now. Beware of spoilers. (There probably won't be many, though.) 
 P L O T: 
 Okay, I'd like to start off this little plot chat by saying the main trope in this novel is my favorite. Ever. Fake dating turning into real dating is what I LIVE FOR. (exhibit A: To All the Boys I've Loved Before.) So, I was absolutely thrilled when I won a copy of this book because yes, please. And trust me when I say that aspect was fulfilled perfectly, even though it wasn't as prominent as I'd like it to be. The plot aside from that was fairly strong; what goes down in HOW TO BREAK A BOY is basically what the description is. That being said, there were points where I was just like what are we even doing here??. 
 C H A R A C T E R S: 
 Whit. Although he could be pretty pretentious sometimes, Whit is probably my favorite character in this novel. He's witty (get it? whit-ty?), he's funny, he's quite pretty, etc etc. Whit is basically my dream boyfriend. My only complaint about him is how he acted at the end. I feel like a general apology was in order from him, but we didn't get one. Blame it on the length of the book, I guess. 
 Olivia. Well, hello, main girl. I get you're supposed to be kind of a horrible person and all, but why can't your actions start reflecting your thoughts? You're so inconsistent and your actions annoyed me a whole lot, but you pulled through in the end. I appreciate that. Thanks for not being an absolutely horrendous main character. 
 Adrienne. Oh, boy, I wanna fight her! I, the reader, am obviously supposed to hate her, and that goal was accomplished. She's so stuck up, so pretentious, so horrible. No excuses for her horrible-ness. 
 The characters & the plot are the main things about HOW TO BREAK A BOY I liked, but here's some other things I liked about it: 
 -the cover. it's gorgeous, duh. 
 -Olivia and her mom making up(ish) in the end 
 -honestly, most of the characters getting what they deserved :) 
 -how in-depth I could see into this novel since I defaced it, which was super fun!! 
 -the general sassiness 
 -the foreshadowing 
 You see, I liked a lot about this novel! I really did. But, here's some things I didn't like too much: 
 -ended way too early for our main couple to resolve everything?? 
 -the sexual assault towards the freshman cheerleaders?? like why 
 -the fact that we don't get to see what happens next. still salty 
 Anyways, that's my review of HOW TO BREAK A BOY! I recommend it to anyone who wants lots of angst, sass, and that great trope.

UNWIND. DONE. 
 I LOVE IT. YET I HAD SOME PROBLEMS WITH IT. 
 This started out with me just discussing the book with my awesome friend Binnudeya and as I looked upon my too long message. It seems fit to be a review. kind of? maybe. we'll call that. So here are my thoughts on the long awaited read of UNWIND! 
 SPOILERS coming your way! 
 Ah the ending was awesome. Lev being a clapper? surprised. But he was redeemed at the end. Awesome character development here. 
 Connor. Oh boy. In the beginning he was kind of naive and acting like a baby. I was expecting high character development from him. it came near the end. But the fact that he lost his eye? and then his arm was bad and gave him another one. ROLAND'S ARM! 
 ROLAND. I hated that little shit. But going in to the Unwind process. I felt really sad and was actually sympathetic for him. My hand was on my mouth through out that chapter. Horrible. That chapter was written perfectly. 
 THEY DON'T LIVE!(people who get Unwound) I MEAN HE DISAPPEARED NEAR THE END. SO HOW IS THAT POSSIBLE? 
 The world building was not the best. I mean this was after the American civil war. which ended in 1865 (our world). So did they have this high technology since then? or is this a civil war that was made near their future? where I-pods and plasma TV's are considered antique? that wasn't mentioned. 
 Risa. I really liked her. She was bad ass. But I don't know, we didn't see much of her for a while. Like sometimes we'd see her a lot and then nothing. She didn't get much character development. but getting paralyzed at the end. girl. tears. I want to know what happens in the next book for her. Hopefully something nice. 
 THE LOVE PLOT. I knew this was coming. but not like this. It happened so sudden and out of no where that I didn't even realize they were kissing the first time? They both never mentioned that they liked or had an attraction for one another. And then the secret meeting to make out? Rushed, sudden, was not well built. 
 I HATED Lev from the start and I never thought that he would be the one character that I would be rooting for in the next book. 
 The writing style, as I said before, was not my favorite. but I feel as we went along it progressed and was better. 
 The whole aspect of the Unwinding is still weird. And I think the question was not yet answered. I mean, why the hell would I get my child to be sent out and cut to pieces and then given to other people? at first I thought the parents were getting money for Unwinding their kids. But that was not mentioned so I don't thinks so. But still. Is it because the kids are trouble makers? that you just want to get rid of them? sending them off to chopped of is not the way. I mean you as a parent probably had to deal with the same thing when you were young, scared and worried your own parents would send you off to be Unwound. So why put your own child through that? Question unanswered.  
 This book though had a lot of plot twists and mind fuck moments. Which I really enjoyed. Overall the book was amazing. I was on the edge of my seat almost all the time and I would have to force my self to leave the book to study and save some pages to read the next day. 
 I think it's a 3.5 stars. but because I just really enjoyed it, on goodreads it'll be 4 stars. I think the second book is good? oh boy. 
 Long rant for the win.

 This is JD Ruskin's first book and she certainly opened with a bang. Characters with issues, a compelling story line and excellent writing will most certainly push When One Door Opens to the top of many reading lists. 
 Logan is fresh out of prison, finally sober and holding a job. It's only part time, but hey, everyone has to start somewhere. He's still at that phase when every superior's question makes his breath catch and every awkward situation makes him crave a beer, but he's taking it day by day and doing better than he had in years. Then his boss asks him to deliver groceries and check on his nephew Caleb as another part time job, and all that hard acquired control starts slipping away with a simple sight of too tight sweats. 
 Caleb is a whole different story, innocent, somewhat naive, gorgeous and agoraphobic. He hasn't left his apartment for three years and doesn't react well to change. But there is something about the ex-con giant who makes him laugh and tries his best to make Caleb happy. 
 When One Door Opens was a slow paced story, gradually developing the relationship between the two main characters, letting them fight their battles with staying sober and obeying the rules for Logan and making a simple trip to the store for Caleb without having a panic attack. 
 Their interactions were so fun I could have read about them for hours, but it was their flaws as well as the tension between the two studs that kept my attention and eventually kept me thinking about this book long after it was read. 
 The main conflict was subdued as well, there but not the harsh focus as one might expect and it suited the story well, letting the reader stay intent on what was important, without broken trust but with all the explicit details the characters' situations involved. 
 This is the one I will recommend, for everyone who likes imperfect characters and needs a comfortable book to relax to. It was a first, but I sincerely hope it's not the last we'll see of JD Ruskin.
