This isn't the best work about insanity from a literary point of view, other than the fact that this is Sylvia Plath and might mirror her own life. I found it disconcerting, not knowing which parts to accept as reality and which parts to see as her perception of reality. The disconnect between her life in New York and the rest of the book is clear, and points to the beginnings of the moving toward irreconcilable madness. 
 Isn't it strange how even in a disturbing book such as this, there can be feminist themes? Here is an interesting quote: 
 "I saw my life branching out before me like the green fig tree in the story. From the tip of every branch, like a fat purple fig, a wonderful future beckoned and winked. One fig was a husband and a happy home and children, and another fig was a famous poet and another fig was a brilliant professor, and another fig was Ee Gee, the amazing editor, and another fig was Europe and Africa and South America, and another fig was Constantin and Socrates and Attila and a pack of other lovers with queer names and offbeat professions, and another fig was an Olympic lady crew champion, and beyond and above these figs were many more figs I couldn't quite make out. 
 I saw myself sitting in the crotch of this fig tree, starving to death, just because I couldn't make up my mind which of the figs I would choose. I wanted each and every one of them, but choosing one meant losing all the rest, and, as I sat there, unable to decide, the figs began to wrinkle and go black, and, one by one, they plopped to the ground at my feet."

If you've ever been in a bad relationship with a church, you can probably relate to the nagging guilt, the tattling, the self-doubt, and the dogged belief that all the warning signs are mere tests of your faith. I thought this was going to make the book a dreary read, but Remini keeps it remarkably upbeat, which gives it an air of authenticity. I think if I were writing this, it would be a non-stop laundry list of crazy, but she starts out by describing all the wonderful things she thought Scientology was creating. She talks about what an egotistical loudmouth she could be and how for all those years her priority was to clear the planet and get lots of attention. The interesting thing is how up-and-down she seems to be in the church Sometimes she's the hero, and then she's getting punished, and then she's the hero again. By the end of the book, it's clear that the downs are outweighing the ups, but it's also clear that she has invested too much personally and emotionally (not to mention financially) for it to be a clear decision to just walk away. 
 Along with being an open-handed account of a painful experience, this was also an entertaining story about her personal journey into a fulfilling career in an unforgiving industry. The book is humorously written, paced well, and contains a satisfying quantity of gossip about Tom Cruise, although I would have liked to hear more about Xenu. Maybe she thought it would just seem to far off the deep end for her readers, but the more of that people generally know the easier it will (hopefully) be for the next people who decide to sever ties with Scientology.

 As I've reported in my previous reviews of this series there were times where it seemed as if my gray matter was going to be permanently fried by this epic sci-fi story. I finally got through to the end with most of my marbles still in the bag they came in. 
 It's almost impossible to give a summary of this without spoiling the previous book so I'll just say that Aenea and Raul Endymion continue their interstellar journey to fulfill her ultimate destiny as the powerful forces of a corrupted Catholic Church and the artificial intelligences of the TechnoCore try to stop them by increasingly desperate means. Oh, and the mysterious and deadly time-traveling Shrike continues to pop up. 
 This isn't just your standard sci-fi space opera about a chosen one saving the galaxy from the Death Star. What Simmons has done here is create a tale that spans time and space in which even Jesus was a player and the ultimate stakes are the fate of evolution of life in the entire universe. As with the other books, he's done an incredible job of building multiple stories and fusing them all together into a rich and diverse whole. Any one of his concepts could have been the basis for an entire book or series like a planet where the cities have been built high onto the tops of mountain peaks due an acidic ocean at lower altitudes. That's just one stop along the way for Aenea and Raul. 
 So how did I live through it? Dan Simmons finally revealed himself to be human and somewhat fallible here in the last book. Don't get me wrong. It's still an excellent series and one of the most ambitious sci-fi stories I've read. But there were a few things that irked me in this one that took it down from five stars to four and that probably kept my brain pan from overheating. 
 First is that Simmons goes back and alters some of what we're previously told in the earlier books. I'm not sure if he originally planned to end it after two books but carried it to four and had to do some changing to fit an ending he came up with later, or if he just discarded some ideas late in the game, but I didn't like that what we thought happened in the first two books turned out to be untrue. Simmons didn't commit any crimes against his fans on a George Lucas scale, but it bothered me, particularly the revisions to the Shrike's origin and ultimate fate. 
 I also don't think that Simmons knew when to turn off the creative mode and shift into resolution mode. He kept adding elaborate new settings and characters and events right up until the end game, and it started reminding me of how Lost just kept piling new characters and mysteries into its final season and didn't do nearly enough wrapping up. Simmons still managed to provide a mostly satisfy ending, but when he added yet another mind blowing new setting in the last quarter of the book, I found myself getting a little impatient. 
 Still, these are minor quibbles about a sci-fi story that swung for the fences and managed to deliver on almost all of it's potential.

 Well, there's no surprise that I absolutely LOVED the third book in the Fae Chronicle Series!

 Escaping Destiny takes off right where Tauting Destiny left us! Syn is about to be taken to the Horde Kingdom and the mystery behind the Hoard King is finally solved! I was so glad my theory was right!!! 
 But the biggest shock was not about who was and what happened to the Horde King. Oh no, prepare yourselves for some shocking news!!! I was speechless!! But I love all of the surprises! Well, almost all of them LOL 
 Ryder and Syn's chemistry is as sizzling as usual, or even more! Their banter is just as fun and the fights lead to epic make up time! 
 Even though I love Ryder to death, he was an ass to Syn through a lot of parts of the book! There were times that I loved his Beast better than him! Without the whole Fae Shenanigans to deal with, the Beast certainly can have a more clear vision of what he really wants! But I do understand his side and he more than make up for it!!! 
 I loved to see all the characters again in Faery, their interaction, the guard, and...Ristan!! I love the Demon so much!!If Ryder wasn't in the picture he'd be perfect for Synthia, but well no one's better for Syn than Ryder! 
 This book is packed with Fae politics and action...Ryder learns how to woo Syn (yes, even Royal Badass Fae needs to woo sometimes ;) ) and Syn needs to learn to accommodate her human life into her new Fae life. The fact that she's been raised human is what makes her Syn and also what makes her the perfect match for Ryder. He needs her human side. 
 It's certainly difficult for Synthia to understand how Fae's politics goes, and even more difficult since Ryder is so busy being immersed in it. But then the reason why he does it is to protect her. Both Ryder and Syn can be unreasonable sometimes, but I also give both of them reason most of the time. Ryder made me cry sometimes, I admit but then we get glimpses of how he thinks and why he does what he does and you just cry again from being much more in love with him! 
 I blame Amelia Hutchins for turning me into a hopeless lovestruck girl for her characters! This book has the right dosage of funny and snark and action and love and...well...HOTNESS! 
 Holy Hotness! I want to be a F***ing Fairy Happy Meal if I'd be treated like Syn is! Amelia certainly can make us fan ourselves while reading her books!! 
 I can't tell you what my favorite part of the book was, because there isn't just one! The whole book is a surprise after surprise and it's packed with what I love most: a hotter than sin male hero, a badass heroine (I want to be Syn when I grow up!!!), a funny and sarcastic Demon, some hot guards, a sweet Fae named Adam (I like him so much more now!!!) and action!! 
 I can't wait for the next book in the series, it will bring so much more into the story! I hope Syn continues with her badass backbone, Ryder needs it. And I hope Ryder pulls his head out of his a*** and just say he loves her forever!! We are all waiting for it! I also can't wait to know how things will turn out! This book doesn't end in a cliffy, but it will make you want more like RIGHT NOW!!

 When I first heard about this book, I wasn't super excited by it. Sci-Fi isn't really my thing, and space epics have been really hit or miss for me (looking at you, Across the Universe). But after reading an excerpt about a month ago, I was hooked - and for good reason! It's so hard to explain what this book is without giving anything away. Part romance, part action, part zombie thriller ? How do you classify this book? 
 I was surprised - but delighted? - by how dark this book is. It's laugh-out-loud funny at times, but there's also a lot of gore and death and general unpleasantness, at least to peripheral characters. It took me by surprised because the first few chapters I read as a preview didn't really hint at how gritty this book is, but all the grittiness feels justified. There's nothing here that's gore-y just for the sake of being gore-y or shocking. It's realistic, or at least as realistic as a space adventure can be. 
 Ironically for me, the romance was the least interesting part of this novel, at least the one between Kady and Erza. It's a bit juvenile, but I kind of like it because Erza speaks WAY more like a teenage boy than most YA heroes. If you're in this solely for the romance, you might be disappointed. But the action/adventure more than makes up for it, and that's coming from someone who doesn't normally care for action/adventure. 
 The biggest delight, though, was AIDAN.  He was by far my favorite character. For an evil robot, I just wanted to cuddle him and tell him everything was going to be fine. His sections were my favorite sections, and the complexity of being an AI was captured perfectly.  
 So yeah. Just read it. You'll find something you like.

Wow, this was amazing. And rough - really emotionally hard, because she is so good at evoking empathy in morally gray situations. Scratch that - Butler is so good at taking situations we tend to think of as morally black and white and evoking empathy to force the reader into the uncomfortable position of realizing their grayness. 
 I thought "Bloodchild" was a magnificent story, I was touched and shocked and completely drawn in to "Speech Sounds." But by the time I was partway through "Amnesty," I had to take a break to collect myself. It's a very brutal story - and I say that with admiration. Incredibly inventive and skillful, just dealing with harrowing subject matter. 
 I'm glad I forged on and finished though! It's easy to see how Butler became a preeminent name in science fiction - she has an astonishing ability to imagine novel situations and poignantly explore the real human issues they give rise to.

There she meets Lang, a MC Prez, at a bar, where he rescues her from other MC. He's doing the best he can to raise his 3 little sisters after the death of their parents. But he is struggling with Maya. The school set up a counselor for Maya, it happens to be Lily. Lang can't get Lily out of his head, he wants her, just as bad as she wants him. 
 Lang tries to be a badass, but he seems fake, like he doesn't really want to be there. Lily, she annoyed me after awhile. Lang schooled her on MC old ladies, yet she still got pissy about it. If you want the man, you take the entire package. Not bits and pieces and what works for you. 
 I liked this book, but there wasn't enough climax, both sexually and plot. My heart never jumped up to my throat in terror. And my heart never raced with the sex scenes, they were glossed over. Where other less important things were given depth, like the step mom's engagement ring. I know we like to keep things up to the reader to use their imagination, but I felt like enough wasn't given. Did it take away from the story? No. But it didn't help either. The two things that happened, one to Maya and one to Lily, seemed like no big deal. I expected a war.  The formula for this book is similar to that of other regency romances out there. You mix a beautiful, innocent girl with a handsome, roguish man and you've got a recipe for an enjoyable read. 
 However, Karen Hawkins's book managed to insert a few significant differences in the generally-used model. 
 For starters, the main character, Bronwyn (love, love the names in this book), is what the aristocracy considers a spinster. At twenty-four, she remains unmarried and does not wish to change that fact. Bookish, bespectacled and without any regard whatsoever towards fashion, Brownyn is an unconventional woman for her time, to say the least. 
 Then there's Alexey, Prince of Oxenburg, a man with very unusual tastes when it comes to women, who is visiting Brownyn's town. Needless to say, he's a total hunk. 
 His gypsy heritage - through his mother and represented for the most part by Tata Natasha, his grandmother - is another intriguing fact about the storyline. Also, the author invented a whole new country (I googled it to be sure), adorning it with some very accurate insights into romani culture. 
 These unusual aspects of the story brought some originality in what is becoming a very tiresome genre, what with the enormous similarities between books. It is a comfort-zone genre, soothing once in a while, but exausting when in rapid sucession.

4.5 stars 
 This was amazing! So, so good! I enjoyed the first installment but this was a whole lot better. 
 Without a doubt what makes this series great are the characters. Elisa is one of my favorite female protagonists ever! She is so intelligent, independent, selfless and determined, yet she isn't perfect, she struggles to find her confidence and authority and at times makes mistakes as a queen. She takes care of herself and does not depend upon authors to constantly save her. I was completely devoted to her and all I could think was how much I would love for her to be my best friend. At the end of The Girl of Fire and Thorns I was wondering how Rae Carson would handle Elisa's further character development since she already had a lot of the latter in the first book. It was handled wonderfully. Elisa really grows in this novel, finding out who she is, what makes her great and becoming the queen her people need. Rae Carson I applaud you! 
 However, not only is Elisa a wonderful protagonist, but the novel is also full of meaningful character interactions between Elisa, Hector, Mara and Ximena. The relationships portrayed were realistic and heart-warming. 
 Elisa and Hector....the perfect couple. I loved the romance in this book. No insta-love there. 
 Seeing how the relationship between Ximena and Elisa changes was simply phenomenal because it was both a true to life development of their relationship and simultaneously showed how much Elisa had come into her own. Ximena was definitely one of those characters I had very mixed feeling about. 
 And of course we cannot forget the relationship between Mara and Elisa. Guys, this YA novel has a real and deep girl-girl friendship in it and I enjoyed it almost as much as the romance. It just made me so happy! How often do we see a friendship like this between two girls without jealousy, slut-shaming etc. ? Not often enough! Mara, in her own way, is just as strong and independent as Elisa is. 
 Another thing I want to commend Rae Carson for is how she portrayed religion. Personally, I love fantasy books about religion (e.g. Mistborn by Brandon Sanderson) but it has to done the right way. The Crown of Embers did it the right way. Never did I feel like the author was trying to force a certain belief system on me. Religion was just an integral part of the world and it always felt respectful. 
 The writing in this book is also wonderful. The descriptions are gorgeous yet very easy to read and don't bog down the story. It was easy for me to get into and stay engaged. 
 The reason I took off half a star was the plot. By no means was the plot bad in any way, it was just something I had seen before and didn't really surprise me. However, this is clearly a character-driven story and so I could easily forgive a certain lack of excitement in the plot. 
 All in all, a fantastic read. I highly recommend this series to anyone who likes fantasy and is sick of reading about the same old female protagonist.
Picks right up where Eragon left off, and has me looking forward to the next in the series, Brisingr.

 What I liked in Hero : 
 1. Enemies-to-lovers

 4. low angst 
 Alexa Holland, the enemy's daughter who end up working as Caine Carraway's PA. This is a woman who know what she wants and chase after it. Despite Caine hatred and harsh treatment towards her, this woman never back down. Alexa is adamant to change Caine perception towards her and to admit that he wants her in his life permanently 
 Caine Carraway, self-made millionaire, brooding, confident and a hardass boss. After finding out about Alexa's identity, which link to the tragedy of his family, he decided to hire her and work her to an early grave. 
 Them working together brought forth an awesome love/hate relationship between the boss and the PA and some sensual office romance when they engage in an intimate affair. What is hotter than having sex on your boss' desk with the said boss? 
 Of course, things are not flower and roses despite them screwing each other. Alexa is a woman on a mission to demolish Caine's armor. She wants more than just sex between them. I laugh out loud at their boring morning after. I felt like I hear some cricket noise during that particular scene. It seems like when Caine proposed an affair, he only do sex and nothing more. 
 I honestly don't mind that Alexa is the one doing the chasing here because is refreshing to read and the feminist in me wants to cheer her on. She seems to be the most understanding heroine around who kept giving chances to Caine no matter how many times he rejected her desire for more. I lost count how many times Caine screwed up a situation and Alexa just forgive him for being a douche. 
 Caine is such a lovable asshole because I understand where he is coming from. He is not being an asshole just because. He never manipulate or lie, he was pretty upfront with what he is willing to give. He is a man reluctant to expose his vulnerability. Of course Caine had his own endearing quality when he is being jealous of Alexa having a social life and sometimes he can even show his sweeter side. But the number of times that he pull away from Alexa makes me want to knock some sense into him. He frustrate me to no end. Eventhough I whole-heartedly rooting for him, I felt that he needs to spend the rest of his life making up to Alexa. 
 Overall, Hero is a delightful and easy read despite the whole love/hate theme. Recommended for those who love romantic comedy with a bossy hero, smartass heroine and whole loads of sexy times.

It was an American classic, a short story written in 1930's. I love how the prose became poetic, and how the author switched Mitty from an ordinary husband doing a weekly chore to become a surgeon. And a hero - inscrutable to the last. 
 There is something about onomatopoeia that made the short story appealing. It adds up to the reader imagining how Mitty quickly triggers a daydream. At one moment he is an assassin. And then he became a surgeon. 
 The thing with this short story is it leaves you a sort of a plot hang-over. He just waited. Stood there. And just like death via firing squad, he stayed motionless. Yet proud. 
 I guess this is what the author wanted to impart to the reader. Once the pen stopped he became still. And he was proud of his creation. 
 Thanks for the free audiobook and the newyorker archive. :)

 After being consistently disappointed with one of my favourite author's recent offerings, Indigo Spell is the book that restored my faith in Richelle Mead. I found the first two books of the Bloodlines series to be held back by the main character, an alchemist called Sydney who I have described as being too cold, scientific and prudish to be interesting. However, this is the book that changed it all for me as Sydney undergoes some pretty major character developments after she got over her major hang ups in the previous book. 
 There's a lot happening in Indigo Spell, from Sydney being a target of a deadly witch, to struggling against Adrian's affections, and finding out a conspiracy that the alchemists may be involved in that will put the very Moroi she's assigned to protect in danger. After growing attached to Jill, Adrian, Angeline and Eddy, her vampire friends, Sydney is slowly overcoming the barriers to her rigid alchemist prejudice that she has been brought up with. 
 Although Sydney is confused about who she really is, this is the book where her strengths shine as she learns how to wield her 'womanly charms', wields some pretty powerful magic, while using her deduction and scientific skills to uncover some secrets behind the Alchemists. 
 Adrian is back to his old self as he resigns himself to 'loving Sydney from afar', and little does he know that it wouldn't be for long. We get to see how right Adrian and Sydney are for each other as she's pulled him out of his binge-drinking, mopey mess and uses his renewed confidence to chase after her. Even Sydney can't resist his charm and the two finally get together in some sizzling scenes (M rated mind you). 
 The turning point of the book for me was when we learnt that there may be a lot more to the golden lily tattoo that meets your eye. In previous books, I blamed Sydney's prudish, clinical personality on her strict upbringing and her identity as an Alchemist. The tattoo may have more of an impact than we thought, by constricting her thoughts and putting teachings into her mind about why she shouldn't trust a vampire. 
 Should I daresay that Sydney's clinical detachment is actually fun in this book?

I wanted to like this book more than I did. In the end, what I did appreciate ("like" is not the appropriate word, given the content of the book) is that I got a sense of what it feels like to know that you live in a world in which you can be shot by police (or others--angry citizens and so on) for no reason and that society will tolerate--even condone--the shooting. I got a sense of what it's like to know that you are never safe because of the broad cultural attitude toward the color of your skin. I got a sense of what it feels like to live a life in which you never feel that you have any true autonomy, and I got a sense of how the history of America as a nation has led us to this state of affairs, despite the absurd platitude that we "live in a post-racial world." A large chunk of white culture may be pretending that we live in a post-racial world, but Coates definitely shows that such a claim is nonsense, and the strength of the book is his ability to make the reader feel it, not just know it in her head. That experience is one that needs to be disseminated widely if we're ever to get to a post-racial world. People who think racism is not a problem need not to be comfortable; they need to walk around in others' shoes for awhile. I can't imagine that any white parent has to experience a black stranger shoving his six-year old child out of the way because the child isn't walking fast enough and then having the crowd around the scene turn on him when he defends his child. Coates had to live through just such a nightmarish experience.  That poignant story is the kind of story that people need to hear and understand because until we take a close look at the unconscionable behavior around us, I don't know any other way that society will really change. 
 The problem with the book, for me, at least, was its difficulty--not just the emotional difficulty, but the reading difficulty. I struggled through the first 1/3 of the book because it seemed almost as if Coates is writing in code. He writes to his son, and maybe he was literally writing just for his son and in so doing was using a vernacular common to them and their family but which is opaque to me. Maybe he was writing for all people whose black bodies are at risk because he knew that they would understand him from their own experience, and so was using a vernacular which is common to African Americans but not familiar to white people--or at least not to me! Maybe it's a matter of generation, as I am not quite old enough to be Coates' mother, but nearly, and certainly I'm enough older not to know some of the vernacular of people of his age. But whatever it is, I struggled with sentences such as these (to give just one example): "Schools did not reveal truths, they concealed them. Perhaps they must be burned away so that the heart of this thing might be known." The pronouns are confusing, and I couldn't work out what "this thing" was. I ran into many sentences such as this one which I couldn't parse. 
 Maybe it's a matter of a writing style which eschews specificity and concrete explanations, but I wrestled with too many abstractions and too many undefined--or not clearly defined--concepts. Coates has, for example, and idea of a "Dream" (capital D) which is not the same as "dream" (small d) and all through the book I was never sure what that meant. At one moment, I would think it was the dream he had for himself, but then I'd get to another passage and it would seem that the capital D Dream is a bad thing--a false dream that he perceives is offered as a lie. Maybe it was both and he now rejects the pursuit of the Dream. I never was able to resolve that dichotomy satisfactorily. 
 He writes throughout the book about "people who think they are white," and I thought for a long time that he meant people we call white but who don't understand that the human genome project long ago demonstrated that the reality is that there is no such thing as race on a genetic level, but then later in the book I ended up confused because I thought he was using that kind of description to describe people we call black who want to live like white people (related to the Dream?). Late in the book he finally says that people who think they are white are people who believe that they are exempt from human failings, but I'm not sure how that works in the context of all the earlier uses of the language. 
 Coates talkes about "The Mecca" which is Howard University, or, more precisely, somehow associated in his mind with Howard University, but which is not Howard University itself, as he says that Howard University and The Mecca are separate entities, though the latter is clearly at the former. I couldn't work out that relationship. 
 The latter 2/3 of the book were much easier for me. Maybe I finally got used to the style, but it seems to me that the writing got more concrete and I had to struggle much less to understand the language. The latter 2/3 tells about the death at the hands of police of a young man that Coates knew at Howard. He was minding his own business one night when a policeman took to trailing him for a long period of time and then ended up shooting him, claiming that the young man, Prince Jones, whom Coates describes a a model citizen of the kind we are all led to admire--God-fearing, hard-working college student, and good to everyone--tried to run him over with his jeep. No evidence of any kind exists to support such a non-sensical story as that a young man with no criminal history would suddenly decide to murder a policeman. The police officer was let off and sent back to work. We are all familiar with the story now of too many other young men who have been killed in similar circumstances in which the injustice has been enough to outrage huge numbers of people of all manner of skin color. It was from this part of the book that I was able to understand and appreciate the experience Coates was relating. 
 Maybe if I reread the book now I would have an easier time of the first 1/3. 
 In the end, I couldn't even work out exactly what the message was to his son. He said he didn't want his son to grow up terrified all the time, and he seems to be glad that his son's life has been happier than his own has been, but much of the book seemed designed to terrify. I'm not saying there is not good reason for terror: for me as an outside reader and a white person, that was the great value of the book: the inside view of conditions I already know, as a mostly cognitive fact, to be wrong from the perspective of the people who have to live with the possibility of that wrong every day. Nevertheless: I couldn't work out a clear message. Maybe there isn't one. Coates evidently wrote this book in the wake of his son's having to hear that Michael Brown's death in Ferguson, MO would not be avenged by the "justice" system, and so maybe the problem is trying to find an impossible middle road between terror of very real potential travesties and the hope that things will be better--if not for ourselves, for our children. 
 Regardless: I would say that this is a book worth reading; I only wish it were just that much easier to read so that more people could read it.

I was so excited for this book to come out in the Fallen series. The world and story Lauren Kate created is wonderful and the third installment did not disappoint. 
 Luce goes on a journey through the Announcers to better understand her relationship with Daniel. They've been in love through the ages, and she's desperate to make things work in the present. But she needs help. So what better way to figure it out than to witness it herself. 
 While Luce is traveling further and further back, those she left behind are anxious to bring her home. Including Daniel. And with trouble brewing that none of them could fathom, it might already be too late. Will Luce and Daniel, with the help of the other Fallen and Nephilim on their side, be able to prevent the worst danger yet? 
 I've been in love with the series from the very beginning. Even though some may be annoyed by the slow pace, I've enjoyed the suspense. Lauren has done a phenomenal job of building things up to this point, and I can only hope we'll get all our answers soon. 
 This most recent book definitely answered a lot of questions (not all, but quite a few) and has set the stage for the finale. Learning more about Daniel was the highlight for me, though. Being able to witness his love and devotion to Luce throughout the centuries through not only her eyes, but Daniel's as well made me like him a lot more. Because up until this point we saw Daniel tell her of their past, but he kept so many things from her. He was more of a frustrating character than anything else. 
 Luce and Daniel's struggle has been great and I loved seeing the different times and ways they came together in history. The research along that Lauren must of have done for this must have taken so much time. Thank you for doing that and giving us the wonderful sneak peeks into Luce and Daniel's romance Lauren! 
 And now I will sit and wait as patiently as I can for Rapture, the final book in the Fallen series *twiddles thumbs and whistles* Okay, not so patiently.

I'm having such a hard time writing this review. I'm so happy with this story, yet so disappointed that it is over. I love the way everthing played out, but I kept asking "but what about so and so?" and "wait, what happened then?" and I just kept telling myself to be happy with what I was being given. And I was...I am, but this story has made me a very greedy reader. 
 I became a sponge with when I started reading this, soaking up every detail I could. It captivated me from the beginning, and I could not even pinpoint what it was exactly that did it. There are so many layers to the characters, and I enjoyed every time one more of them was peeled away. 
 Silvio has become one of my all time favorite characters. Even though we have learned so much about him and his characteristics, at the end, I still feel as though he is hiding so much. I love that he has issues and is so complex. I would love to read more about his life with Franco and Sebastiano (not so much about his father though *shudders*), and/or his time with Battista. 
 While not nearly as complex and complicated as Silvio, it was a joy to get to know Stefano as well. He continually tries to make things right for everyone, and I was very happy he was able to fix things one more time. 
 The one scene with Donata, Stefano and Silvio was amazing. The same tone that carries on throughout this series holds steady in this scene as well. I found it very refreshing. 
 So, I was happy to read about everyone again and see how things would pan out and conclude, but I was saddened at the same time knowing it was all coming to an end. I can now put my efforts into finding something to help me cope with the withdrawals I already feel coming on.

I'm in-between about this. 
 Let me first say, I was so looking forward to reading this. I ordered this earlier this month and it took about eight years to actually be delivered. When I finally received it, I ran it to my room and started reading. Finished it in one day. It took me for one hell of a wild trip, that's for sure, and I didn't exactly know what to rate it because it wasn't good, it wasn't bad, and the characters weren't good - I mean, not good people, exactly - but given the situation, I couldn't imagine how I'd react either. 
 Sigh. This is a brilliant debut, nonetheless. But these people were horrible. All of them. Including Emma. 
 I know that sounds harsh, but I'll get to it. 
 The novel starts with Sara being interrogated at a law office - not for the first time -- because she's about to go on trial. She's one of the girls who viciously bullied and berated Emma, the so-called slut who committed suicide to escape the taunts. Emma was said to be so effortlessly beautiful that Sara greened with envy every time she saw her. 
 The story rotates between the aftermath of Emma's suicide and Sara and Brielle's upcoming trial, and the horrific extensiveness of what those girls put Emma through. I think at certain points we were meant to sympathize for Sara - even Brielle - but I definitely couldn't. Not in the slightest. Not even during the ending. An apology given too late.  And, really??? Love, Sara???  
 There were times where I wanted to chuck this book. Sara's mindset was so intolerable half the time, I couldn't deal. She refused to take the blame for Emma's death, pinpointed it back onto Emma 99.9% of the time, and had the audacity to say she was the only one who genuinely felt bad in the end. In writing this review, I ran back to my book to copy out this convo between Sara and her lawyer about the V-Day rose fiasco: 
 "You felt good at first?" 
 "Well, yeah," I say. "It was funny. It was just so many roses, you know? It looked ridiculous." 
 "You wanted Emma to look ridiculous?" 
 "She'd been making me look stupid." 
 "How so?" 
 "With Dylan." God, Teresa could be so stubborn. 
 This is my point. Although, Sara did admit, she did things simply to follow Brielle. Had sex with Dylan to be a non-virgin like Brielle, etc. She continued to torture Emma under her own power, then had the gall to wonder why Dylan wouldn't answer her phone calls/texts. Yes, her home-life sucked, same with Brielle, but a never-there dad or a tragic rape story would never give anyone any right to outright bully someone to the point of suicide. 
 Back to Emma. She did, after all, go after Dylan, knowing Sara was with him. But I do have sympathy for her. They treated her horrible - sent her Valentine's flowers as a cruel joke, parked a SLUT sign on her front lawn, made parody Facebook and Twitter accounts. Need I go on? I wish we had, at least, one chapter in Emma's POV to see if she actually had true feelings for him or her opinion on this general nastiness. 
 Of all of them, Dylan might be my favorite. He honestly didn't do anything wrong, except  you know, the cheating.  And in his final interaction with Sara, I was, at first, a little annoyed, but I went back and read it, then I understood. Of all of them, even his high school portions, he always remained mature. Praise to him. 
 This is slut-shaming in its finest. This is truly a raw, difficult read, and I'm not sure I'd recommend this. But if you would like to read something similar, something a tad lighter, check out, The Truth About Alice.

 This book was so cuuuuute! I guess I expected that from a Kasie West book anyway, but this one I enjoyed more than her other book, The Distance Between Us. I read this in one sitting, and I will say that I had a tear in my eye and I was smiling with such joy. 
 In this story we meet Charlotte "Charlie" Reynolds. She is a tom-boy sports fanatic who would rather be clean-faced and rolling around in mud with the boys, wearing loose and comfortable clothing. She lives with her 3 brothers and her father, so growing up in a male-dominated house have given her many male figures to look up to. Losing her mum at a young age, she spends her time trying to work out what really happened, as well as trying to earn money for a speeding ticket she couldn't get out of by using her father's name. After a few hours at her job, things start to change, and not just about her but due to a certain neighbour, Braden. 
 My favourite thing about this book was Charlie's brothers and her father. The whole family dynamic in this book actually caused a tear in my eye, and I adored how close and hilariously brilliant they were. It was full of chaos, fun, pranks and love, and even when she introduces them to boys, they put on a fake 'we're going to kill you' to him and laugh when he leaves the room. How lovely would it be knowing they will always have you back and be looking out for you? It was very endearing and sweet. At one point, Braden who was the neighbour and one of her brothers' best friend, says something along the lines of 'I wanted to be in your family'. 
 Me too, Braden. Me too. Please adopt meeee. 
 Her father was adorkable too. He was so clueless on girls and we were reminded of times when he had to do the period talks and mentioning that her female friend told him to get her a bra. Near the end of the book, they had a talk which got me emotional, and I think girls like her need to realise how lucky they are to have a father like that. Some of us aren't as lucky, but it was lovely to read. His punishments and actions were fair, and I think he was a great father, I liked reading about him. And my hat goes off to him for raising all of those boys - mischievous and boisterous one's, at that - and Charlie. My goodness. 
 What was also nice was to be reminded of West's other series, The Distance Between Us. We're reunited with some characters, Caymen even has a line, and Skye is in this book quite a lot. It was nice to be brought back to some similar faces, and I always liked it when authors did that. 
 The romance, well, of course there's the 'love triangle' but it's never as prominent as something like a fantasy series. It seems to be 'one is a distraction and the other I want to have children with' because we're already aware that she doesn't love the distraction. Charlie has nightmares, so when she can't sleep, she'll meet Braden at the fence in their garden and talk about things. And by things, I mean anything that's bothering them but they never mention their feelings towards one another. Obviously, with books like these, it's pretty clear who she ends up with because it pretty much says in the summary. They did just suddenly go ~omg i'm in love~ and I was like 'wait what', but that's to be expected with fluffy books like these. It all happened quite fast and I was thinking that it was a little bit silly, especially considering she found true love at 16. (Come on....) These kind of books, eh? 
 I do want to add something about Charlie - she can be kinda sexist towards her own gender. She was harping on so much about how girls are all about make-up, shopping and boys. I have to say, this isn't very accurate. I know she was brought up with her father and 3 (4 if you could Braden) boys, but she shouldn't keep saying that girls are these worthless airheads who just spend their time caking make-up on and caring literally only about their appearance and who never ever play sport. Charlie, you're not the only girl ever to like sport and hate make-up. She was constantly putting down her new friend Amber just because of who she is and that she's the 'typical girl', which did bother me, but if she's been brought up a specific way, who am I to judge. I'm glad she got over that though, but still. 
 Charlie even got to the point when she was like 'Y'know what, I'm a girl, I will dumb myself down for a guy because boys don't fancy tom-boys or sporty girls' and she actually does. She has the interest of a boy called Evan, and he's never see her without make-up and she spends her time with him asking him about the sports she already knows about. 
 gurrrrrl. You were bad-mouthing "the typical girl", and now you're doing that? But it's okay, because Braden and her father both have a brain, and they both said: 
 "We can't let boys define how we feel about ourselves. You have to know who you are before you should let any boy worth anything in" 
 "You don't have to change for a guy. If you can't be yourself around him, you shouldn't be dating him" 
 Yes. Someone has to tell her that she's being an idiot, and that's something that bothers me about dating shows we have here in the UK. Girls pretending their stupid so a boy likes them, because honestly, they don't find the ditzy blonde airhead act as cute as you think. I know these girls aren't like that, and that's what Charlie does. She even says that Evan is getting things wrong, but she says nothing. Thank goodness for Braden. 
 It wasn't a long book but it was enough. It was short but sweet, and I got out of this book what I went in hoping for. It was pleasant, made me laugh and smile, I cringed once or twice and ended up turning my Kindle off in happiness. I can't see how anyone can dislike Kasie West's books, they're there to lighten the mood and to also teach us a little lesson, and in this one it was to just be yourself. Don't let people change you, and you should know that family will always be there for you. 
 *turns into a goey mess* 
 Really enjoyed it. I'll be on the hunt for another West book very soon, I'm sure of it.

If ever an author was, is, and did write a novel about a marriage-of-convenience could, this is the book to study. The trope of hero-in-pursuit and marriage-of-convenience, and even tortured-hero, are all familiar elements of romance novels on the market. They're popular, they're entertaining, yes, but I doubt few accomplish telling those tropes within a story as well as Kleypas did in Tempt Me At Twilight. 
 The characters of the book were the very definition of excellent. Harry and Poppy were two people that were completely engaging, both within the context of the story, and for the reader, myself, personally. From the initial opening sequence, to the very end of the story, I felt myself drawn into the lives, and personalities, of the leading hero and heroine. Harry is a remarkably fascinating tortured hero. I say this, frankly, because this is a common, overused trope, in many respects, and it can work splendidly, or not at all. With Harry Ruttledge, his brokenness as a man was very much a part of his characterization, and yet done in such a way that was subtle and understated. 
 So, too, was the creation of Poppy. In her, there is a degree of both strength, and contentment, of spice, and milk. In some ways, too, I feel that while her character was often more of a "background" personality, this kept the book from becoming exceptionally melodramatic. This melodrama could have easily been the case if Poppy's personality were anything other than what it was, most especially in the face of the book's plot and story structure. 
 Fundamentally, Tempt Me At Twilight is the telling of trust. The romance is powerful, yet quiet. It is a tangible reality within the book's story, but worked in such a way that while the reader realizes the plot is internal, it's outward affects on the characters still make the book very fluid and structured. This, combined with the excellent pacing of the book, I feel, allowed for a truly remarkably enjoyable story. At no point during the course of the book did I feel any dead-air, either with the story itself, or the characters reactions to their situations. 
 My last and final point; the ending. Okay, wow. I thought I was cued up for Catherine and Leo's story, but holy-crap, I'm even more energetic than I was before. Even though their is relatively little story-action of Catherine's backstory, I'm still enthralled with what's been revealed so far. I have the distinct feeling that Cat is far more damaged as a heroine than even I first estimated.

 Presley Flynn is Dmitri's sub. She is head over heels in love with Dmitri. However, when someone tries to blackmail the club, Dmitri turns cold and distant. Now Presley needs to figure out either how to reach him, or if they are not as perfect as they seem. 
 The connection between Presley and Dmitri is intense. However, the lack of communication between Presley and Dmitri is troubling. In the end, it was never really resolved either. I remember seeing this book circulating the internet when it was first published. The title is what brought my attention to this book and the title is what kept bringing my attention to this book. The blurb was interesting enough, as well, but it never gave me enough information, there was never that hook that made me want to read it so bad I just had to have the book right now. But I kept seeing it around and eventually, my curiosity about this girl who was so cold that she surpassed everybody else in this "Coldtown". 
 I was not expecting vampires. I attribute this little surprise to my lack of attention at anything but the title, although there was really nothing in the blurbs that screamed at me that this was about vampires. Also, I've been trying to avoid reading reviews for books because I've been accidentally spoiled one too many times. So, when I realized three pages in what this was going to be about, I almost stopped reading. The subject of vampires is over-saturated, over-romanticized, and over-cliched. Frankly, I'm bored of vampires. They're all pretty much the same and the story hardly changes. If the story does change, people latch onto the one little thing that's different that might make the vampire genre a little more interesting and ruin it, making it just another thing to hate about the vampire craze. 
 However, I have been starting a lot of books and not finishing them lately, so I've given myself a goal to read at least 25% of a book before I quit. I'm glad I did. I found myself wanting to know more about this Cold world that Tana lived in. I wanted to experience was the Coldtowns were like. I was curious about whether or not Aiden was going to turn. Most of all, I wanted to know what was going to happen to Tana and how she was going to deal with it. 
 I think it was Tana that really made this book one that I don't regret reading and one that I'll remember for a long time. She was tough, smart, resourceful, and loyal. She did stupid things, but she tried to fix them. She was everything I love reading about. She really was the Coldest girl in Coldtown and I loved it! 
 I still don't like vampires, though. I still don't like the vampires in this story. But it worked and I'll probably reread this book when I've forgotten most of it. It's one of the better vampire books that I've read, that's for sure.

 1) Medusa ("Dusa") is a vibrant, well-adjusted (considering her circumstances) young woman who doesn't angst endlessly about the tortures of her life. Though she acts the victim at first, she eventually realizes that crap has to end and takes charge of her future. 
 2) Hermes has his secrets, but only once does he not ask for Medusa's permission before upending her life (and he does it because she's not acting in her best self-interests). He also apologizes profusely and from that point on makes it a point to ask her. 
 3) Love is not always the answer, but it can be the answer if you work for it. Love doesn't instantly make ANYONE'S life better in this book, but for those who use that love as a way to make their life and those around them lives better, its the most precious thing of all. 
 4) All the mythology you can shake a stick at, but not quite what you may have learned from Bulfinch's or Edith Hamilton. 
 5) Jocko is awesome. I won't say who he is to the story, but gosh he was one of my favorite iterations yet. 
 So there you have it. What more do you need?

Really good series ... but I can't help but feel weary of Zoey. 
 The only thing worst than being an outcast in your own family is being Marked. And this is exactly what happens to Zoey. When her best friend Kayla witnesses the Change, instead of helping her like a true best friend would do, she runs. Leaving Zoey heart broken she heads home hoping for her mom and step-loser dad to understand, but boy was she wrong. Knowing that she has to get to The House of Night, the local vampyre school soon because if she doesn't, she'll die, she heads to her grandmothers farm, knowing she'll understand. But when she arrives at her grandmothers house she is left a note that her grandmother is in the lavender field. Zoey has been over the trail to the top of the hill many times, but on this particular trek she found it extremely exhausting. Soon she wasn't able to see straight and didn't see the branch that she tripped over. As she fell to the ground, her head hit a rock and made her head bleed. After she passed out she experienced and OBE, out of body experience. She felt her soul drift towards what sounded like her grandmothers voice, going through a set of rocks searching for her. But what she finds isn't her grandmother but Nyx, the vampyre goddess herself. shocked by her encountering the great goddess she asks why she is here. Nyx, then says that Zoey is older than she appears and that she has great powers, not understanding Zoey questions the great goddess. The great goddess than goes over to Zoey and kisses her on her forehead. Feeling the burn of her vampyre mark she wakes up to see her grandmother singing to her. When the High Priestess (principle) comments on how bizarre her mark is Zoey is confused. Just before at school it looked normal, and outline of a crescent moon on her forehead, like every other fledgling, but when she looks in the mirror she sees a fuelled in crescent moon that is only awarded to adult vampyres. The High Priestess questions why Nyx would mark Zoey with such a great gift and asks Zoey how she attained this mark, Zoey gets a feeling that she shouldn't tell the great High Priestess, so instead she dodges the part about her dream. Why would the great goddess award Zoey with such powerful gifts? Is there danger around the corner?

Wow. Just... Wow.

 Maybe it's because Sandy just tore through the East Coast and it's so fresh in my mind that things can literally change overnight, but this book was pretty intense. Yeah, it's written as a diary of a teenage girl, but once you try and see where she's coming from (I mean, I was once a teenage girl, so I can get it) with all the talk of being bored with things or just wanting to get a damn date to prom! 
 Really though, this one sucked me in and I honestly felt the dread that she did. The dwindling food supply, the fear of gangs roaming about, the wonder if things will get better... Makes me wonder just how many people are prepared for a disaster like this, because I know I'm not! 
 When I read reviews and people complain that it seems like it's just focused too much on her life and her own little world, well, I don't know what they expected. There were no adventurous journeys, no love triangles, no overbearing enemy, and it was perfect just the way it was.

It's a setting that just full of possibilities: the Greek Gods of Olympus are still around and most of the principles are living in a rundown house in modern London. With characters like Apollo and Athena and Hermes, there's no end to complications and plot twists, right? Phillips does come up with jobs suitable of her cast - Aphrodite as a phone sex operator just makes perfect sense. And if Apollo and Aphrodite live in the same house, they probably would end up having sex with each other, considering their particular strengths, and despite being half siblings. Altogether, wouldn't we expect the whole clan to be just as dysfunctional in this age as the one they originated in? But that's the problem with this book - the characters do act all too often just as you'd expect. They have almost no arc. I guess that's the problem with characters so deitic - they have no where to go but down, and if that's not your ending, you really don't have much of a story. There are two mortals that get mixed up with this crazy family, and they do have a journey, but you'd think with people like Zeus and Hades getting involved, the whole thing would be more.....epic?

A nice frothy read for a sleepless night, but disappointing in spots. I know Christie is known for recycling her plots (and even publishing the same book or story under different titles), but come on. So far every Battle/Bundle book has a political house party and a dashing adventuress, and people blundering around in a library in the dark, going in and out of other people's bedrooms in the middle of the night. Not to mention the secret society wearing masks to their meetings. Yeah, right. They know each other's names and therefore presumably their mutual identities, so what is the point of that? And what, dear Aggie, is "a typical foreign gesture", may I ask? Which foreign did you have in mind, dear--African? Asian? American? Inuit? At one point Battle actually says with a straight face, "Now, if anyone is in the room, you can hardly help hearing their breathing if you are listening for it." Really, dear? True, for much of my life my hearing was uncomfortably sharp, but even for me it would depend on the size and acoustics of the room. For most people, in a large library (ie room lined with books, and paper absorbs sound beautifully) that would be quite a trick. 
 Patricia Wentworth's first novel, Grey Mask, was published the year before this one. Do I detect imitation on the part of Mrs Christie? Oh not the plot, but a lot of the elements...but then, as I say, Battle 2 is dangerously close to a remake of Battle 1 in many ways. Whatever. When I have a cycle of insomnia, I will read anything that isn't too much effort, which explains the preponderance of cosy mysteries and children's lit in my reviews just now. In spite of the typical Christie "rabbit out of hat" tell-not-show ending, the red herrings were rather good, if there were rather too many of them. Beats the crap out of Julian Barnes.

4.25 Stars? I'm not sure how to rate this. I absolutely adored Rebel Belle, but it wasn't like a 5-star book to me. 
 Rebel Belle is about Harper, a girl who's one of the most popular girls in her city. She's in every AP-class, she's like the School President and she's in every club there is. On the day of her homecoming dance, something peculiar happens and Harper finds herself being a Paladin, one of an ancient line of guardians with agility, super strength and lethal fighting instincts. Her mission is to protect David Stark, school reporter, subject of a mysterious prophecy and possibly Harper's least favorite person in the entire world. 
 This book was so much fun to read. It was so clever and hilarious. I loved Harper because even though she may be one of those typical popular High-School girls, you could still relate to her and see how much she changed during this book. She's smart, witty, kickass and not afraid to speak up. Her being a Paladin was just so contrast to who she was before and Rachel Hawkins manages to intervene Harper and the whole Paladin thing so well. 
 David Stark was such a great male-character to read about. I could relate to him so much, and even though I sometimes didn't like the things he did to Harper, he turned out to be such a cute and sweet guy that was so funny and sarcastic as well. 
 The plot and the writing in this book was so good and hilarious. Even though this book may look girly (and some parts are girly) it was still action-packed and really dark. 
 This book made me laugh out loud several times, even though it is a really dark book with some heavy themes. That's what I loved about this book the most. Ever since I read Hex Hall I've absolutely LOVED Rachel Hawkins writing. She's such a clever writer with such an original plot, even though I felt it lacked some of the charm that I found in Hex Hall. The end felt a bit too cheesy for me as well, but overall this book did not disappoint me. It was hilarious and definitely what I needed to read since I was falling in a sort-off reading slump. I was overall really pleasantly surprised by Rebel Belle. I highly recommend Rebel Belle to someone who wants a light, funny and action-packed book.

To summary this in one paragraph would be impossible. There were a few bits that niggled me (listed in the cons sections below), but due to the fact I believe I am to blame on part for those, for not having read any earlier titles in the series, rather than the author, I decided it would be wrong to hold that against my rating--because once I'd figured out the who's who, the author pretty much had me hooked. See below for more details: 
 What bugged me: 
 The opening bothered me. The first person writing, giving a rundown (or a recap) of the main characters of the book. 1) It jarred my flow when it suddenly then switched to third person from three differing POV's. 2) I'd much rather have learned about them as I went through, but that's probably just me. But, when I reached the end and discovered a closing summary written in exactly the same style as the opening, I then wondered if this might be a quirk/tradition of the series, which I might have got had I read the preceding titles. 
 Also, because there were three differing POV's, and I wasn't familiar with the characters from not having read the earlier books, it then took me to around 12% to keep up with which character/personality I was dealing with each time the switch was made. 
 What I loved: 
 Well, I pretty much loved everything else. This is possibly one of the most beautiful yet saddest stories I have read in a very long time. From beginning to end. Yes, the three ladies were 'lost' before the pinnacle moment of the tale that pretty much pushed them all over the edge. But it took something as devastatingly shocking as that occurrence for them to realise exactly what they had but had just forgotten was there. I suspected from the off that Tibby hadn't committed the suicide the other three had (in their grief and frustration and desperation) believed of her. I suspected, in fact, pretty early on that a terminal illness would be to blame. 
 However, I never once predicted the possibility of a child for her, or pretty much anything that followed. 
 The only outcome I guessed correctly was the inevitable one (to me) for Lena and the man she'd never quite fallen out of love with. I prayed and prayed the entire way through that they would find their way to each other. Thank you so much for delivery of that because I doubt I'd have forgiven the author had it ended differently for them. 
 Carmen's path: I hoped she wouldn't go through with the wedding, yet some little part of me worried the whole way through that she might. Then her train journey pretty much undid me, her interactions with the father she met and how they somehow connected. Although it didn't happen in this book, I'd like to think they might one day speak again. 
 Bridget: Damn, that was one lost and fragile woman. And God bless that beautiful man of hers for forever being there for her. I almost felt proud of her during the moment when she finally figured out what her heart needed again. 
 And then back to Tibby: Tibby who knew them all so well that she understood what they needed way more than they knew themselves. 
 I've seriously never cried quite so much. For around the final 40% of the novel, there must have been something wrong with my Kindle, because the words were constantly blurry. ;o) This is quite possible the most moving story of self discovery I've ever read. Just beautiful.

I am acting out part of a scene for my World Drama class (the very first exchange between Thomasina and Septimus in Act 1, Scene 1, right up until Jellaby enters), so I had to read the play quickly along with my other assigned plays. 
 I simply can't write an intelligent review for such an intelligent, funny, and heartbreaking play without re-reading it. I just know that I closed my book and had that niggling feeling of, "God damn it, why did I wait so long to read these words?" 
 Stunning. Amazing story, excellent characters, and a perfect concept for a stage play. I, a reader and writer who has no aspirations to EVER take the stage, cannot appreciate a play the same way an actor can appreciate it, but it still makes my chest ache when I think of it. 
 If this ever comes to the theaters in my city, I'll be in the front row. 
 (By the way, I'm playing Septimus).

I went into this book not knowing anything, and all of those people who recommended I read this were right; you need to go in not knowing. I didn't put the book down. I needed to find out what was going on. By the end, I actually gasped. Great ending, and I'm so happy I got around to reading this novel.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The beginning was 3 stars. The ending salvaged it for 4 stars. 
 Brief summary 
 It picks up immediately where the last book left off. Kylie is wondering what it means to be a chameleon. Derek is in love with her but is willing to just be her supportive friend, and Derek is her absentee boyfriend. He's hiding his relationship with Kylie so he can get on the werewolf council. Kylie is working with a ghost Of a murdered girl. She's come to warn Kylie that the murdere is at shadow falls and to protect Holiday. Her grandfather wants Kylie to come live with her own kind both to be safe and to learn all the skills she has. It ends with Kylie saving the day, Lucas betraying Kylie's trust and feelings and Kylie taking the next step to understanding her heritage. 
 What I thought: 
 The beginning and middle dragged for me. I found Kylie more whiny in this book. I also got frustrated with her supposed lack of understanding about what the ghost wanted and who the killer could be. Willful ignorance if you ask me. Don't read these books for the "mystery," as it is all pretty transparent. 
 I liked Kylie using her gifts as a chameleon. The love triangle was well done because Derek was not pushy. He was just a constant, supportive presence. There were a couple of sexy scenes with Lucas which definitely got my pulse racing a bit. It was gratifying to see Holiday and Bernett finally embrace their love. Lastly, the book ends in such a way that it does pique your interest for the next book. There's bound to be a whole bunch of new characters, new scenery, and, I think, a whole new different kind of ghost.
Actual Rating: 4.5

Going into this I was expecting a light, supernatural mystery, but it turned out to be more UF. The heroine was a bit annoying at times, but is also in her early twenties, which could explain some of it. There are a bunch of cliches in this book, but I'm still interested enough to read the next one and see what happens. 
 What I liked: 
 * Sinjin. He's an interesting one. 
 * Jolie when she wasn't being stupid, so for about half the book. 
 * The finding your animal part was cool. 
 * The interview with Rand and Sinjin at the end of the book, that was fun. 
 What could have been better: 
 * Jolie had a few TSTL moments and I was kind of rooting for her to lose a fight to teach her a lesson. Since this would have involved her death, I guess it probably wasn't meant to be.  Then she had non life-threatening stupid behavior just to drag out the tension. 
 * Seriously, when older, more experienced supernaturals drag you into their world, why do they insist on not telling you everything? It always ends badly. 
 * And then, why does every powerful supernatural male the heroine meets instantly want her? That is getting really old, really fast.

A warm, witty take on sexuality, the difficulties of high school and growing up. 4/5 stars. 
 I read the last 30-40 pages with a smile plastered across my face. This is very good. 
 The titular Simon is our first person narrator and I warmed to him pretty much instantly. He makes a few dubious decisions, but he's basically a good kid trying to do his best. We root for him and want him to be happy. 
 The book's particular world of friends, family and high school reminded me of the film Easy A. If you haven't seen this movie, I recommend it. Emma Stone is marvellous, as always, and Stanley Tucci and Patricia Clarkson turn in hilarious performances as her parents. Anyway, if you have seen the film, this should give you some idea of tone and atmosphere of Simon vs. the Homo Sapiens Agenda. 
 A sympathetic narrator, great characters and a central mystery make Simon vs. the Homo Sapiens Agenda a great read. I guessed Blue's identity half way through but it didn't matter. Mostly because I got to chuckle with glee when I was right - ha! 
 I recommend this for everyone and particularly those who enjoy contemporary YA

I really enjoyed this book. I didn't have a problem with the voice of the narrator as some reviewers did. She was a fluffy, rainbow colored southern lamb blundering through an Unseelie infested Dublin. It reminded me of what I loved so much about the Anita Blake (the first couple books in the series) and Sookie books, of a utterly vulnerable human completely out of her depths and surviving the darkness that surrounds her by sheer luck. Loved it and can't wait for the next installment to be available.

Well, I can say that I enjoy reading this, especially since I've missed my OTP, Elizabeth Bennet & Mr. Darcy. 
 I like that the author gave this story a modern vibe, with issues such as LGBT, transgender, pregnancy not in the traditional way. I like that the characters really resemble in the former Pride and Prejudice. 
 I like the setting of the story, I like the different distinctive characters. However, not very much fond of Darcy & Liz here. It feels like the romance is too force and I don't feel anything from it. I like that the author gave more insight on the Bennet family, especially the three younger sisters, who are fun to read. 
 What I don't enjoy is the writing style here, because I felt like there's too much rambling and I am so close to skim some parts.
WOW! Surprised at how much I loved this. Usually I prefer sweet and easy reads and this is the total opposite. I can't wait for the next book.
Adding this just based on the guy on the cover -- the same guy from one of my fave reads this year, Easy.

So awesome. It has the mixture of fun and peril that I love in my magic-school stories, and it all feels very fresh and vivid. Funny, too - no trope is left uninterrogated, and the excerpts from the beginners' magic textbook written by the world's greatest juju snob cracked me up. Sunny's a great character and one I'd love to see more of. And it looks, according to the Goodreads page, like there's going to be a sequel. Sweet! \o/

As with many people who have read this series, I originally knew it under "The Last Vampire" title. I admit I was a little annoyed at finding out the entire series had been renamed. Not sure why this was done, necessarily. I had to keep correcting myself after I put it on my Christmas list. 
 Anyways, I really enjoyed the book. The character of Sita was still familiar even after all these years. I applaud Pike at being able to reconnect with her character so well. I'm not sure if I like the explanation of the end of "Creatures of Forever" but I'm willing to let it slide by. I really don't know if I liked the way this book ended, but it's Sita, and I will be reading the next one too. Really hoping we get some good answers.

Another thriller in the Rizzoli and Isles series, I could not put this down in the evenings! Gerritsen keeps me coming back for more. I much prefer her to James Patterson and most other thriller/suspense authors I've read lately, as her writing is better, her plots more intriguing, and I love the characters. Can't wait to see what happens next.
Very different from the movie.

TBH this was less fun than I'd expect from the blurb and the cool premise. The huge chunk in the middle is the guys hiding in the safe house, arguing/having sex/brooding/arguing more/having more sex, and yet the characters' personalities (while likeable and interesting) were never explored to the extent that would satisfy me in a book that has relatively little action, considering the genre. It's a solid book, but it doesn't flow as well as it should.

Note to self: do not read three Jackson Brodie mysteries in a row; it's depressing. Though the writing is as good as ever, and the incidental characters are great, if one reads #2, #3, and #4 on a binge, Atkinson's trick of leaving out huge chunks of how new characters came to be in Brodie's life becomes more obvious. And at the end of each book, some characters who one expects to be continuing, and whom one wants to know more about, apparently disappear, because in the next book it's as if they've never been. 
 Nice twisty plot on this one, anyway. But will we ever meet Tracy Waterhouse again? Probably not. Will we ever meet Brian Jackson again? Probably not. 
 Love the dog.

I loved this book. 
 I LOVED THIS BOOK 
 Seriously, I loved this book. 
 Get it yet? 
 The Infernal Devices has bypassed the mortal instruments and risen to my favourites pile - which may or may not have to with the fact that it consists of the most heart-breaking love triangle I will probably ever read about. The love Will, Tessa and Jem share for each other is both amazing and excruciating, which essentially means that this is the one love triangle where I couldn't pick a side. It also means that I was a teary mess. Seriously, the dam broke open the second Jem told Charlotte that his one regret was that he would have liked to see her child. Cue me becoming an emotional wreck. By the time I'd reached the epilogue, I thought I was all teared out, but somehow I managed to dreg up a few more tears for the most bittersweet, heart-wrenching closure to a series I've ever read, and then spent the rest of the night staring at the blank wall opposite me trying to feel something that wasn't outright depression. 
 Kudos, Cassandra Clare. Kudos. 
 Other than me becoming emotionally unstable, however.... 
 Gabriel and Cecily's relationship was the best. Will's reaction to it was also downright hilarious (though when is William Herondale not downright hilarious?) Had to love all the TMI references - finding out Izzy's necklace came from Magnus, Henry invented portals, Jace's scar's origin (Magnus finding Will and Tessa together was SOO funny), and how Church ended up in The New York Institute. Also, finding out Ithurial was the angel locked in Tessa's necklace was hilarious, because really? How is Ithurial the one angel to always be captured by shadowhunters? What are you doing, man? My favourite parts of this book were probably all the Will/Jem parts, though, because their parabatai bond and friendship never ceases to amaze me. I loved the flashback to when they first met, and the scene when they said goodbye to each other - both when he was Jem and when he was Brother Zachariah. 
 All in all, this book was amazing. Definitely recommend to anyone who's as obsessed with the shadowhunter world as I am.

I couldn't put A Beautiful Lie down, and ended up finishing it in one day. If you are looking for the typical college love triangle, this is not it. There is nothing typical about it. It has a little bit of criminal investigation, too many secrets, a whole lot of betrayal, and a heartbreaking story line. 
 Anabelle Parker was starting her last year of college when Garrett McCarthy, and Milo Roberts walked into the coffee shop. She felt the chemistry with Garrett immediately, as did he. Her past wouldn't allow her to give her heart to someone like him, and when Milo asked her out first she knew he was the safe bet. Since that time they have all three been best friends, sharing their lives together. When one of them dies too young, the other two are left to figure out how to move on. 
 ***Spoilers*** 
 Parker's dad was destroyed when her mother died. She vowed at that time, never to let anyone have so much of her that she couldn't function if they were gone. When she met Garrett & Milo, she knew Garrett had the power to break her heart, and so she chose the safer option when Milo asked her out. All these years, the two of them have loved one another, even though she is planning her life with Milo. When Milo is killed in a Navy Seal operation in the Dominican, Garrett asked to be assigned there to find out the truth of his death. Parker sneaks her way in when the photographer can't make the trip, and Garrett finds out she has been working for the CIA the entire time he has known her. She joined up with them right before meeting the guys, when they approached telling her that her dad owed a lot of money to the mob. They agreed to pay her last year of college that she couldn't afford, as well as pay off her dads debt if she joined them. She has been pretending to be a free lance photographer while secretly investigating Fernandez,the president of the Dominican. What we later find out is that her dad was also CIA, and was investigating him as well. When Fernandez found out he had a daughter, they got her recruited hoping the CIA would give her the tools to keep herself safe. When Garrett and Parker get to the Dominican, the evidence of Milo's involvement in some shady dealings show a side of their friend they never knew about. Garrett and Parker end up getting together, and confessing their feelings, right before Milo shows up- alive. He tells them he has been working undercover, and had no choice but to fake his death. In the end, it turns out he is Fernandez's son, and he's training to take over the family business. He kidnaps Parker, and Garrett is captured while trying to rescue her. The get themselves out, but not before Parker is seriously injured, and must spend months in recovery and rehab. Garrett is forced to testify in the trial, and unable to see her for the majority of that time. Even though Parker knows he has no choice, going through the aftermath of their ordeal alone is almost more than she can take. Once he is released, he immediately finds Parker and they live HEA. The epilogue reveals that the two of them do get married, and have a little girl.
Short and sweet and cute.

I heard and saw so many people talk about the Percy Jackson series and other series by Rick Riordan and how much they love his books with different mythological backgrounds. 
 I think a younger version of me would have liked this book more than I did and especially would have liked the humor more. Don't get me wrong, I appreciated Riordan's action-packed story andespecially the growing friendship between Percy, Annabeth and Grover. Other topics I thought this book portrayed well were family and belonging. But at the end, this book is categorized as middle-grade and aimed at kids far younger than I am. So I often felt it way too predictable and some solutions for problems a bit overly convenient. That being said, I am still going to continue with the series to read more about greek mythology, which I really love reading about.

I liked this book, but not quite as much as I enjoyed The Thief and The Queen of Attolia. I think mostly because this one was almost purely politics and introduced so many new characters with not very different names, so I got confused really quickly. 
  
 I think overall, this book was about the relationship between Eugenides and Irene. Gen married the Queen of Attolia for love, but he is also forced to become the King of Attolia for the sake of the kingdom and uniting it in order to be successful in the impending war. I absolutely loved the scenes where Gen and Irene prove their love for each other. The only reason why Gen agrees to be King is to protect her. (aww, isn't that adorable) 
  
 There were so many lovely scenes in this book, and I do love the character of Costis, but it seems that each scene that I enjoyed was followed by other scenes that muddled the plot and got me confused as to what just happened. I suppose that's MWT's writing style; she loves to hide important details and only after reading a bit later do we see her genius (and Gen's genius--seriously!) 
 4 stars, and I'm really looking forward to reading A Conspiracy of Kings. Attolia is an interesting place, and its palace is full of both loyalty and distrust, but  Gen is smart enough and clever enough to prove himself . However, I would LOVE to know what is happening in Eddis or Sounis. Attolia is just as foreign a place to me as to  Gen .

** spoiler alert ** 
 Make it a 4 1/2. Really reminded me of Touch not the Cat, which is why I saw the final twist coming. There were still a few surprises: the identity of aunt Freda, and of John Howard.
