 Wow guys, were do I start with this one? How about - IT WAS REALLY GOOD. That's a good start right?? This is a series I have had my eye on for a while because almost everyone I know and follow loves this series. I wanted to see what all the fuss was about! I was worried this book wouldn't live up to the hype for me, but it totally did! I loved it all! 
 Reincarnation? 
 When I first read the summary of this book - I wasn't sure what I thought about it. The reincarnation premise was definitely a fresh idea to me, one I haven't seen done before. The idea that everyone in the world is constantly reincarnated (that is until Ana comes around!) is an interesting one, but I didn't really grasp the full impact of what that meant until I got further into the story. I love it when this happens in books for me! It's like, I didn't really understand the world, not all the implications of of that world (in this case, reincarnation), until I really got into the story and saw how the characters thought and felt. In a way, this book reminded me of the Matched series, because the same thing happened to me with that series. If this explanation is a little vague, click the spoiler tag. :) There were a few things I didn't realize right away that were a consequence of everyone being reincarnated. One, everyone knows everybody else. They have had thousands and thousands of years to run across each other at some point. Secondly, knowing you will definitely be reincarnated also means that you don't mind dying as much as people who don't get reincarnated (seems pretty "duh!" but it hadn't occurred to me!  
 Music 
 I loved the role music played in this book. Music has always played a big part in my life - I grew up playing instruments and I'm almost always listening to music. The way Jodi Meadows writes about music and the feelings it brings out in the characters (and myself!) were great and I really enjoyed it. You can tell that Jodi Meadows is a music lover and really understands how music makes me feel, haha. 
 Love Story 
 The love story is very interesting too. At first - I didn't really buy it. I mean, this guy is thousands of years older than this girl. I mean, I am all about being open minded about these things - after all, when I first started dating my now-fiance I was only 18 and he was 24. It was pretty scandalous at the time (not so much anymore haha! - funny how the age gap matters less the older we get). Ana is a teenager and it was hard for me to understand how someone that much older than her could grow to love her - but by the end of the book I was sold. I totally ship Ana and Sam!! :) 
 In Summary 
 This book definitely lived up to the hype for me. I can't wait to read the rest of the series. I didn't mention the story line much in this review, but it was such a good story! In fact, there was a part that took me by surprise that I LOVED.  There are dragons! I love dragons!  If you enjoy fantasy books, give this series a shot - even if you're not sure what you think about reincarnation. I wasn't sure how the reincarnation bit would sit with me, but in the end it totally worked for me!

I received a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review. Thank you to the author for her generosity. 
 As a lover of mythology, I was excited to read a new take on the Persephone myth. The battle which helps open the story is bloody and violent. We learn what happens when Death refuses to let anyone die. The descriptions are both chilling, and powerfully evocative. 
 We meet a murdered princess, convinced she is Death's Cobweb Bride, and her murderer, as they join girls from all walks of life. One such person, Percy, is unloved and mistreated by her family. They don't understand the gift she has. We follow Percy and the other brides as they venture to Death's keep. Along the way, there is intrigue, camaraderie, and heartbreak. Even though she comes from a poor family, we see the strength and kindness Percy has inside of her despite how she has been treated so far in her life. 
 In this novel, death is not the real enemy, but a selfish Duke who is determined to stay "alive" (or un-dead) no matter what pain and suffering it may bring to the world. He shows us the depths to which man will sink when confronted with his own mortality. By the end of the book, I found myself rooting for Percy, and for Death. 
 I am looking forward to reading more on Percy and her adventures to find the Cobweb Bride.

Lia and Alice Milthorpe have just lost their father and soon after his death, a strange circular scar appears on Lia's wrist. It marks her as a part of the prophecy, although she doesn't precisely know her role. Is she the Guardian? Or is she the Gate? Truth be told, she doesn't figure that out for a while and it's James--the boy that she's known for quite some time and fell in love with--who finds the book that contains a single page of the prophecy. Throughout Prophecy of the Sisters Lia learns about well, the prophecy and her role in it; she also witnesses a scary change within her sister who plays for the opposing side of the prophecy and learns about the Keys which can either help release Samael or destroy him--although ultimately the decision rests with the Angel of Chaos. 
 Unlike Alice, Lia begins with no knowledge of the prophecy or her powers. Through a series of events, she stumbles across the prophecy with James' help and from there she meets several minor characters who help her learn bits and pieces of the prophecy. Meanwhile, Alice tries to sway Lia to join her cause and Lia--rather obviously--resists. 
 There's more that I could add to my summary, but I won't, because they're spoilers. But I will say that I loved Michelle Zink's writing style and that it flows really well in my opinion (beautiful and lyrical). Alice is frightening. No, really, she's pretty scary and I can't believe her level of crazy--although one could blame the Souls. Lia on the other hand it pretty oblivious when the story begins and slowly, she learns to see things for what they really are (figuratively). And then there's James--who Lia has known for quite a while and happens to be in love with. If it wasn't for him, Lia would've never even heard of the prophecy and although she tells him nothing of the prophecy, he does pop up often enough--as he was cataloging her father's library. 
 Prophecy of the Sisters is set in 1890 and a bit north of New York City--which automatically meant that my interest was piqued. It features two twin sisters set on opposite sides of an age old prophecy and did I mention that the cover is gorgeous? Admittedly this has been compared to Libba Bray's Gemma Doyle series and well, the only thing that I feel that they have in common is magic and the fact that they're both set in the Victorian era. This is a book that I'd recommend and although perhaps not everyone will love it, I personally feel that this is definitely a book to try.

The plot 
 The book starts with Alyssa ignoring bugs that are talking to her. You heard me: bugs. They talk to her and she thinks she's going crazy like her mother who's in an insane asylum. She realizes her mother is acting insane in order to protect her and stumbles into wonderland to save her. Jeb - Alyssa's next door neighbor and crush - ends up going on the adventure as well. They meet characters in the original Wonderland story but with a dark twist. She teams up with Morpheus who was her childhood friend to save her mother. 
 Let's start with Alyssa 
 What I love about Alyssa is how strong her character is portrayed. Her childhood is a bit of a blur but she holds on to her sanity and follows her heart. She's scared in Wonderland (who wouldn't be? I mean, it's seriously a dark place) but Jeb keeps her in reality. At first, she's confused about everything and unsure of herself. After a while she grows into what she was born to do - save Wonderland - and you see the transformation from beginning to end. It's always fun to watch characters change through out the book! When she meets Morpheus the love interest flips from Jeb and she's confused about who her heart belongs to. 
 Jeb - Alyssa's neighbor and love interest 
 Jeb is very strong and reliable. You can see how much he cares for Alyssa; it's adorable! He's the rock Alyssa leans on when she's in trouble emotionally and physically. Some people who are on team Morpheus say that Jeb is too overprotective and controlling. I don't believe this... Alyssa is strong enough to be on her own, Jeb is there to help her. He can get bossy sometimes but it's not insanely pushy and it's for Alyssa's own good. Jeb has a kind heart and he's perfect! 
 Morpheus - Member of Wonderland and Alyssa's other love interest 
 Morpheus is an interesting character to read. He always has ulterior motive and you never know what going on in his head. You can't trust him; he's a willy one. I'm sitting here trying to think what to say about him but it's hard since he's so complex. Just like Jeb, he cares for Alyssa greatly. It's harder to see it because he's so aloof. I believe Alyssa is only attracted to Morpheus because he's a part of the madness and mayhem and she's getting addicted to that (and doesn't like that part about herself). It's hard... he does care for her but he's also selfish and vain. I can't get a good grip on him. 
 The writing 
 The world building is amazing! Wonderland is, again, very dark and twisted. Characters are kind of freaky looking and I know if I stumbled in Wonderland I'd run away because the whole world is full of nightmares. The characters were written with passion; my feelings towards them were deep. All the emotions going through Alyssa's head and her actions where well thought out. Splintered is definitely one of my favorite books this year! PICK IT UP!

At first, I felt great sympathy for Clara. But as the novel wore on, Clara wore on my nerves. I can only blame sleep deprivation and the suddenness of being a single mother to a certain extent, because gradually, Clara came across as an unhinged, entitled, paranoid *itch. Nick's downward spiral, in contrast, was more sympathetic and logical. That's not to say the decisions he made were logical, just that his desperation seemed more justified (and even visceral). 
 As Clara goes through the infamous stages of grief, she seemed perpetually stuck at denial, instead blaming anyone and everyone else for Nick's death. Although one part of me says good on her for seeking to find her husband's "true killer", another part read it all in horrid fascination (like a train wreck you can't look away from) because it culminates in her massive beat down of someone completely innocent in Nick's demise. And this, by the way, was a big question mark left dangling by the end of the book because we never find out if Izzy pressed charges against Clara for assault and battery. 
 Still, even with these demerits, "Every Last Lie" was a decent read. I suppose one could say that most of the characters in the book were just doing the best they could, the best way they knew how. And that includes poor Emily who refuses to leave her abusive husband because she didn't think she could stand on her own, even had she not had a child to think about. Someone you definitely could not say that about Connor. Wow - talk about someone with inflated ideas about himself and what life "owes" him! In fact, I'd say Izzy was more deserving of a fair shake in life that this a**hat. It's sad that someone his age still had a frat boy mentality. 
 The plot of this novel was intriguing, and keeps one guessing until the very end. The pace was good. The characters complex, and the story telling captured my attention throughout. I thought after a time, the dual, alternating narration from Clara and Nick's POV would become tiresome, but surprisingly, it didn't. If you have some time to spare, "Every Last Lie" is worth a read.

4.5 Eleanor Oliphant comes across as another socially maladjusted (lovable) misanthrope like Ove or Don Tillman. (he's technically not the same category, I know) She dislikes and harshly judges her co-workers in the accounts dept. of a graphic design firm in Glasgow Scotland, and holds herself aloof from pretty much the rest of humanity. Her strict adherence to dated manners and conventions, her formidable vocabulary and her precise diction made me think she was twice the age of her 30 years. The reader is instantly in on the joke as she narrates her self-imposed dull life defined by routine. But things take a darker turn than the above books with references to "Mummy" and her weekend routine of consuming 2 liters of vodka. Eleanor is hurting, though she refuses to acknowledge it and others are incapable of seeing it due to the impenetrable defenses she has built. She describes herself: "There are days I feel so lightly connected to the earth that the threads that tether me to the planet are gossamer thin, spun sugar. A strong gust of wind could dislodge me completely, and I'd life off and blow away, like one of those seeds in a dandelion clock." (5) Others describe her as "a bit mental" and "a nutter." What starts the breakdown of these defenses are a random series of events that put her in close contact with others: her computer at work malfunctions and she meets Raymond Gibbons, an affable, comfortable-in-his-own-skin IT guy. They witness the medical emergency of Sammy Thom, a retiree who collapses in the street and needs EMT services. She goes to a concert and fixates on a singer whom she determines is "the one" and embarks on a plan of self-improvement in order to ensnare him. All these events are peppered with her critical commentary and her wonder (and ineptitude) at human interaction as well as weekly phone calls with "Mummy" who grows increasingly more hateful and hurtful. Eleanor, ready or not, is propelled into human relationships and also into facing her horrific past and hurt. This book would be hilarious if it weren't so heartbreaking. That emotional swing is what keeps it from 5 stars for me. And the ending is a little mind-twisting, though thankfully not cliche. Raymond is a hero and worth the read, and the Scottish terms and tone that authenticate the book are lovely. Impressive debut novel.

This book was picked out for me by my significant other from a pile of romance novels. "Which one should I read next?" I said. "This one's about an earl," he said. "You've been reading a lot about dukes lately. Maybe an earl would be a nice change?" Thus far the only difference noted is that the earl has a younger half-brother who is a duke, so presumably another (the next?) book in the series can be about a duke. 
 Anyway, this book is what it is and you know what you are going to get once you read the back cover. If you don't, you figure it out pretty quickly when you open the book and find yourself reading a sex scene. Between the hero and his mistress. He hies back to his house, musing on his Sad, Sad Story as he goes, and discovers his estranged wife (the heroine) waiting for him. We quickly learn that they are estranged because he discovered her in bed with his younger brother (not the duke, a different one) on their wedding night, which she agreed to only because the brother told her that this was the only way the earl wouldn't insist on consummating their marriage too soon, but he would totally chill out after he was mad for a bit so it would be fine. This struck her as a good idea. 
 At this point, you probably have a pretty good idea of how the novel is going to go. Where has she been for the last couple of years? Well, running his estates wisely, of course. Why is she back in London? To save her beloved younger sister from marriage to an elderly roue, of course. The hero angsts over his inability to love - of course. We get a scene of the hero's mom in bed with an artist fifteen years her junior and musing on the fact that she's been in love with another man throughout her last two marriages, which made me want to read HER novel instead. 
 That said, why one star? Because I just couldn't finish this thing. I kept getting distracted by other books and annoyed by minor details, and the authorial meddling was just too obvious - the hero kept ping-ponging between being wildly attracted to his wife and asking her for a divorce so he could marry his mistress, although he wasn't actually in love with the mistress. The villain of the book is, in fact, the mistress, who turns out to be totally insane and obsessively in love with the hero; I just can't deal with that plotline. For me to believe in a Happily Ever After, there would have to be an insane amount of groveling from the hero, which there wasn't (hey, guys, the mistress was really good at hiding her insanity, so how could he know?). Additionally, I really hate it when most/all of the prominent female characters in a romance besides the heroine are Evil with a capital E. Have the courage to believe that the heroine's awesomeness is sufficient in and of itself without needing comparators to demonstrate that she's "better" than them.  I skimmed through the last few chapters, was thoroughly irritated by them, and did not force myself to read the rest of the book more thoroughly.

I know that might sound weird, but all I knew was the vaguest details (the synopsis on book and on some reviews), it's a trilogy and it's a dystopia (something I haven't read in a while because... well, I got sick of dystopian books and needed time away). That's it. So, I went into this kinda blind. 
 And you know what? I was genuinely surprised how much I enjoyed reading this. 
 I got caught up in the world and the pacing was great once June and Day actually meet. Before that, I felt it was a bit slow, but once they met, it was like reading a thriller with the fastness and the chapter point-of-views going back and forth. I liked reading from both their point-of-views (that's rare, I think. To like both characters equally) so I never felt like I had to rush back to a character as the other was boring it. There was always something happening and that kept me turning pages.

And the relationship - I'm not 100% certain that I buy it. It feels a bit like insta-love. But this is a trilogy, so Marie could explore this in the next two books (and with the film rights bought by the team that bought us the Twilight Saga, I think the movie's in safe hands). 
 I am surprised how much I enjoyed the mad ride. I do hope I get to read the second book in the series, Prodigy, soon. The very first thing I thought when my copy of The Twelve fell through my mailbox was whether I needed to re-read The Passage before throwing myself back into Justin Cronin's world. In the end, I did re-read it, but in hindsight it wasn't strictly necessary as I remembered far more than I thought I would, and the first part of The Twelve recaps what happened in The Passage in biblical verse. It sounds like an odd way to recap a book, but it works pretty well from my perspective. 
 One feeling I had from The Passage is that the world building would be revealed bit by bit in the next book, and I'm happy to say I was right. The fall of Denver is particularly closely examined, and the fates of survivors are spread through the first part of the book. More on the background of characters that only flashed up in The Passage are also revealed, and although some of the character interactions have a strong feeling of familiarity, not having these connections would have lessened the tension and emotion of the story. There's also more information on the infection, and the different strains and how they were discovered and introduced to the public. Most of the characters from The Passage are back in The Twelve, and almost all of them have changed and matured in the intervening period. 
 There are also new characters introduced, which for anyone that has read The Passage is enough to sound overwhelming, but they are all quite unique and it's actually good to have a few fresh faces after the intensity of the first book. 
 After The Passage I really didn't think Justin Cronin could rachet up the horror and tension any further, but he definitely succeeds in doing so with The Twelve. A new community is introduced, and the cruelty and deprivation of the regime that controls is in huge contrast to the community introduced in The Passage. I don't want to give too much away, but in some ways it mirrors real events in human history that shocked and appalled the world. 
 Although not told in flashbacks as such, the time period shifts back to the outbreak and moves forward from there, eventually jumping past the period that the majority of The Passage was set it, to five years after the ending of The Passage. 
 Unfortunately, once again, there is a lull in the middle of this book, despite it being significantly shorter than The Passage. However, because it is a shorter lull, it doesn't feel like stalling quite as much as The Passage. 
 Overall, I did enjoy The Twelve more than The Passage, and mostly that is due to the world-building. However, I'm giving them both the same rating as The Passage had a more epic feel to the journey.

Before I started reading this my husband told me a) I would love it and b) the threat of Greg Stillson's political ascension would be particularly disturbing to read in Trump's America. He was right on both counts. 
 I loved this book so very much. It is clever and twisty but not convoluted. The reactions to Johnny's clairvoyance feel very realistic. I am a big believer in supernatural stories that have authentic characters with reactions to supernatural phenomena that feel plausible and grounded. Johnny gets famous, he gets publicly roasted as a crank, his coma and subsequent reawakening make his mother's religious mania even more acute. His friends are compassionate but also scared of him. This book is so poignant. The reader becomes so emotionally attached to the characters so quickly. My heart really broke over the thwarted love of Johnny and Sarah. My emotions were completely engaged from page one until the end. 
 And then we get to Stillson. Even though King provides a few excellent vignettes highlighting Stillson's character early in the text, Stillson is not a major player until the third act. The specter of him percolates in the background as Johnny confronts other villainy (such as the Castle Rock strangler) and struggles to reorient himself in the world. He is a shadow lurking at the edges of this story. Stillson is an excellent villain when he finally emerges as a formidable politician and head of his own "America Now" splinter party. Try to read his comments in 2017 without a chill running down your spine. King does such a good job capturing the politicial milieu of the 1970's, yet this also feels so disturbingly relevant. A book that totally nails a specific moment in time that nonetheless feels timeless is quite special indeed.

 I've wanted to read this one for a long time but kept putting it off because I didn't want the hard cover version, but I eventually gave in (Christmas present to myself) and bought it, and I'm not sorry I did. 
 A couple of years ago I read a wonderful graphic novel (MYth: My Seasons by Zelda C. Wang - read it!) based on the myth of Persephone & Hades and I LOVED it. So I was excited to find another version of the myth in which P&H actually love each other instead of him ravishing her and locking her away in his dreadful, dreary underworld. 
 I liked Radiant Darkness in general and enjoyed it whilst I was reading it (stayed up til the early hours of the morning to do so) but afterwards it seems just a little flat. The character of Persephone is believable, though a little naive, but everyone else remained fairly vague and elusive. I couldn't really tell how her mother felt about her; who was her father; why did Zeus allow Hades to cross the border to fetch Persephone; and surely Hermes and Thanatos were the same character just re-packaged with different names!? 
 The book is well-written, the pace is ok (although it does flounder around for a long while in the middle) and the plot is essentially sound. It's a good light read, but if you're looking for something really 'meaty' with complex characters, politics, settings, etc, then it probably won't satisfy you for long. 
 Is there a Happy Ending? Yes. It's much the same as the original ending but happier.  
 Content Rating: PG 
 Ok for Teens, approx 14+. Persephone marries Hades (no surprises there, so no spoiler tag) and they sleep together but it happens entirely off-screen and is barely mentioned, other than that she wakes up alone (a lot!) and she likes to have his arm around her at night (mentioned retrospectively, not witnessed in real-time). It's also mentioned that Zeus regularly disguises himself (to fool his wife Hera) and seduces mortal women, but it doesn't occur 'on-screen'. 
 There are one or two very rare occurrences of coarse language (the D word I think) but no violence that I can recall, other than one brief mention of piglets being thrown into fires as part of some fertility rite. 
 Romance Rating: OK 
 Hades was attractive in a barely-described-at-all-but-still-handsome-and-powerful-nonetheless way. The story is told entirely from Persephone's point of view, and while that means we get to know her pretty well (to which I have no objection), it also means we barely get to know him at all. Our understanding of him is limited to what Persephone sees and assumes, and she's not always the brightest spark out there! 
 So, he basically stays the same elusive, handsome, powerful and remote stranger as he was when we first met him. Which means it's a little difficult for a proper romance to develop because we've essentially only got one character to work with. He's like a handsome paper cut-out wafting around somewhere in the underworld (which, I might add is a remarkably pleasant place - heaven anyone?) popping in only for key plot points to assert his possessiveness and tell her much he loves her and no they will not talk about earth or anything else important. And she basically goes along with it - every time! - saying "you know best dear Hades" and that's the end of that! 
 So, no, I didn't really feel there was a good romance, or even a healthy one to be honest, but I still liked the book for trying something new and putting a happier face on this myth.

 One of the first things that you have to know about Starry Nights is that it's not a conventional YA. 
 It's been frequently described as Night at the Museum meet DaVinci Code, but I - like Heather at FlyLeaf Reviews - actually think that it's closer to a fairytale. 
 It has the same foundation of an ordinary person gaining the ability to do extraordinary things, with just a hint of magic, mythology and the battle between good and (semi) evil, thrown in for good measure. 
 This emphasis on the fairytale aspect turns an already intriguing idea, into a YA book that reaches new and extremely entertaining heights. 
 *** 
 Things that worked: 
 * Characterizations 
 I loved the fact that from the get-go, Whitney makes it perfectly clear that Julien is delightfully ordinary. His grades are mediocre, his drawings are good but not brilliant, and he's been feeling at a loss since being dumped by his girlfriend. 
 This is not only a refreshing change from either the slacker hero or the super-powered superhero that seems to populate YA these days, but it also makes it easier for readers to cheer Julien on. We want nothing more than for him to gain his groove back - much like a fairytale hero, who is about to prove their greatness - which sets off the following chain of events at the museum perfectly. 
 As for the secondary characters, they're the perfect supporting cast - especially if viewed through that fairy tale framework. There are siblings who are there to offer guidance and insight, a pretty girl who helps set off Julien's abilities, and a best friend who acts as both side-kick and confident. 
 Whitney gives them life, personality and wit, even for the brief scenes that they're in. 
 * The setting 
 I've seen some readers critique the lack of French ambiance in the book, but I think Whitney's sparsely sketched Paris is actually perfect for the story she's trying to tell. 
 By not overloading readers with descriptions of the museum or of Paris, she really reinforces the idea that this is a story about art, and how people can use art to interact and interpret the world around them, verses just how we see the world, point blank. 
 And more importantly, this also reinforces the idea that this is Julien's journey, from being unsure about himself and his art, to proving that he is in fact, a hero. 
 * The writing 
 I saw another reviewer/author mention how impressed she is with Daisy Whitney's ability to reinvent herself with every book, and I would have to concur. 
 While I wasn't a huge fan of When You Were Here, the writing was breathtaking for a contemporary book. She ups the ante again with Starry Nights - Whitney fuses both her beautiful contemporary writing, with a lyrical reinvention of the Muses and art history. 
 I would say that even without the Paris ambiance, Whitney's writing alone is enough to immerse you. 
 *** 
 Things that didn't work/Things to consider: 
 I did have two minor quibbles with Starry Nights. Even if I were to view the story in the framework of a fairytale, I still struggled with the idea that: 
 1)	Julien's friends would so readily believe his powers. 
 I think that even for people who were the best of friends, would find it difficult to swallow someone suddenly saying "Hey, not only does my presence bring art to life, but I have the ability to protect from decaying..." 
 I would have loved it if Whitney had fleshed out the relationship, or at least the disbelief a little more. 
 2)	Julien's lack of French-ness. 
 (yes, yes - I realize that's not a word.) 
 While I thought that Julien was charming as heck, nothing about him really said "French boy in Paris." His narrative voice sounded really American, and would occasionally take me out of the moment. 
 Now, the plus side to this? It really emphasizes the idea that fairytales like this are universal. The downside? Readers may be disappointed that he's not more... French. 
 *** 
 Final verdict: 
 Starry Nights is an extremely charming and whimsical fairytale, which reminds readers to reexamine the world around them with different eyes. 
 While there are definitely some issues that some readers will likely have with the book - e.g. the romance aspect - I would say that this is still a lively tale that will enchant and delight readers. 
 I recommend this book for fans of contemporary YA fiction, but also for fans who like books where fantasy meets contemporary - e.g. readers who may have grown up reading books like The Chronicles of Narnia, and are looking for something that gives off the same ambiance, but with more of a contemporary feeling.

 I wish we could give .5 stars on GR, because I'd clearly put this one at 4.5/5 stars. Well, I'd put a 5/5 if not for one thing, that I'll expand on later on. 
 Having read David Estes's first novel, "Angel Evolution", barely a few days ago, I was amazed to discover to which extent this author's writing has developed in this new, beginning trilogy. This is clearly a work for which said author took into account various critiques, and used them to improve his writing and storytelling. The result is, frankly, very good. 
 "The Moon Dwellers" follows two characters on two opposite ends on the social scale: Adele, a young woman who's been sentenced to jail for life, but decides to escape with her friends Tawni and Cole and find her scattered family again; and Tristan, elder son of the allmighty President, born with a silver spoon in his mouth, but intent on estranging himself from this life that doesn't feel like his own. The story is told in the first person, from the alternating points of view pf Adele and Tristan; while such an exercise in writing can be quite hazardous, here it works well, allowing us to learn more and more about those characters and what their lives are like. 
 I especially enjoyed said characters' personalities. Adele and her friends have had to become strong during their stay in jail, and they don't let anyone dictate them how to behave--they don't hesitate to fight, and they do it well and with spunk, too, both physically and through sarcasm. As for Tristan and Roc, the one isn't such the pampered prince as a lot of people believe him to be, and the other, albeit not the best when it comes to handling a weapon, is terrific in the way he managed to keep his sense of humour throughout dark times. Their friendship, too, is made of solid mettle, and feels genuine and very much present. 
 The one thing I wasn't too keen on was the 'insta-connection' between Adele and Tristan; it has nothing to do with "The Moond Dwellers" per se, it's simply I as a reader who's never felt convinced by such strong attractions upon first sight. Also, I thought that at times, events unfolded a little too neatly (the various bomb attacks, especially), reinforcing that aspect of 'destiny bringing everyone and everything together'. I suppose you either like it or not. 
 This said, I am nonetheless eager to read the next volume! 
 (As a side note, I find the cover's composition absolutely fascinating. The more I look at it, the more it grows on me.)

However, given that I haven't read the rest of the series, he might not have been overreacting nearly as much as it seemed without the full context of the story. 
 If you haven't read the rest of the books and don't mind a few spoilers to get you started, Elixir may be a good novella to start with. It doesn't take long to read, and it still introduces you to a few interesting components of the world. And if you have read the previous books... then I'm going to guess that this one will give you a few nice insights about what's going on before the next book.

This is book 1 of the Septimus Heap series, which I have read all of. It leans closer to the Narnia series than Harry Potter or Percy Jackson, because while there are continuing threads and cause-and-effect between the books, there is no overarching threat that unites it all by driving the plot of the series. Somewhat more connectivity than the Narnia books, since they are continuous in time. 
 This is the one that starts with the take-over. Silas Heap, returning to where his wife Sarah is having their seventh son, finds a newborn baby girl in the snow. And he is intercepted on the way by Marcia, who tells him that they must say she was born to them, and who is inexplicably wearing the amulet of the Extra-Ordinary Wizard. On the arrival home, the Midwife is rushing off with the bandaged body of their son, and Sarah weeps at the sight of the baby, whom they name Jenna. 
 Only later do they learn that the Queen and the former Extraordinary Wizard had been murdered, the newborn baby Princess had vanished, and that the kingdom had been taken over by the Supreme Custodian. 
 Ten years later, Alther, being a ghost, learns that they have learned where the princess is. Marcia arrives at the Heaps' to announce it and take Jenna with her while they scatter to escape. On their return to the Wizard's Tower, they find a ten-year-old boy trapped in the Young Army -- Boy 412, as they call him -- and set to guard the Tower, half-dead from cold, and bring him to save him. When Silas and his son Nicko arrive, they are followed and must go down the garbage shoot. 
 And so the adventures continue. Including a message rat; their Aunt Zelda, the Keeper; too much cabbage; a ring and a boat, both about dragons; an apprentice called Septimus Heap; the return of a necromancer; and a tavern burning down. It all works together to build to a grand resolution. 
 The world is an interesting mish-mash of modern day and pseudo-medieval -- the Supreme Custodian is far more totalitarian than an Evil Overlord's lieutenant. The magic has some interesting twists. And the tendency toward Capital Letters and the use of bold for magickal words works quite well.

 Cold Fire picks up exactly where Cold Magic left off. Kate Elliott even backtracks through the last chapter of Cold Magic as a recap adding a few more details to break up any monotony. Cat and Bee are trying to escape the Mage House and turn to the trolls at Godwick & Clutch Cat had previously met. 
 What they couldn't anticipate is the arrival of General Camjiata, the radical who wants to usurp the current ruling Prince of Europa and wants to use Bee and Cat to do so. Upon deciding to leave the General's company the girls become embroiled in a quest that leads to us discovering Cat's sire as well as saving Bee from becoming a casualty of the Wild Hunt. 
 I'll admit, the political goings on in this series thus far have been a whirlwind. While they have an influence on the world in which the series takes place, and while Cat may navigate the inner workings of impending revolution from time to time, I've never found it is by her choice unless someone she cares about is entangled within as well. 
 I found that Cold Fire focused more on the decision of Cat's emotions. After a trip through the spirit realm, she comes out the other end on the islands of the Antilles in the Caribbean with a far warmer climate. Since time moves differently in the spirit realm, she ended up being gone for seven months. And because anything can happen in Kate Elliott's novels, Vai, Cat's estranged husband, happens to be on the island when she comes ashore. 
 From the beginning, Cat's marriage to Andevai has been a driving force. Not knowing what to make of his character exactly, always seeming vain, arrogant, and despising of Cat, my mind was immediately changed in his last scene in Cold Magic when he told Cat: 
 "When I saw you coming down the stairs that evening, it was as if I were seeing the other half of my soul descending to greet me." 
 How can you not want to explore more of their dynamic after that startling out-of-nowhere statement? Elliott must have thought the same because Cold Fire certainly explores Vai much, much more. His motives for being in the Caribbean are unknown; although he claims to everyone he came looking for his missing wife, Cat knows there's more to his story. Regardless of this, with almost everyone else around her being of unknown association, Cat finally has to make a decision of what she feels for Vai and if those feelings lead to trust as well. 
 I was really happy that Elliott didn't prolong the inevitable when it came to their relationship. We finally got to see a different side of Vai. Still being vain and arrogant, we begin to see that he is more than his Mage House affiliation. This was something we saw very briefly in Cold Magic when they visited his village, but it becomes something more when he's conversing with people who are not kin. 
 As in Cold Magic, the down times are few and far between for Cat. And what middle book wouldn't be complete with a little cliffhanger ending to lead us into the third? I'm just glad all books in the series are out.

Future Chicago is nothing like it is today. Many ancient skyscrapers are crumbling and vacant, Lake Michigan is a brown, stinky Marsh, and every citizen is divided into one of five factions - Candor (the honest), Abnegation (the selfless), Dauntless (the brave), Amity (the peaceful), and Erudite (the intelligent). Once a year, anyone who is sixteen has the chance to choose which faction they will belong too. Most stay within the faction in which they are raised, and those who choose to switch often disgrace their family and, if they fail the rigorous initiation period, risk becoming a member of the dreaded factionless - a group of poverty stricken people who live on the outskirts of society, starving, wearing rags, and preforming jobs that no one else will. 
 Beatrice has always known, deep in her heart, that she is not Abnegation, but to admit it and go to another faction would be such an insult to her family that she isn't sure she has the will to do it. Then during testing day, her results are not at all what she, or anyone, expects, and on choosing day, she makes the choice to join Dauntless, which is nearly as shocking to her as it is to her family. Within minutes, as she is jumping from trains onto the roofs of buildings, she wonders if she made the right choice, but has no other option but to stick it out. Her determination and will are the best things she has going for her to make it through Dauntless initiation in the hopes that she will not become factionless. 
 Dark, ominous, and foreboding. Biggest issue is that it follows a pretty common dystopian formula - someone comes of age, someone chooses or gets chosen for a job, someone trains in said job, someone is a key player in a larger plot taking place. Still, the formula works and is a page turner that is sure to please the masses who are clamoring for another Hunger Games like series.

This book has pretty much every element of young-adult angst that can be packed into one book: drugs, teen pregnancy, questioning sexuality, molestation, suicide, distant parents, first kiss, dating, non-parent adult mentor, and I've probably forgotten at least a half dozen. 
 I'm amazed at how much I forgot from the book. The last time I read it was at least ten years ago. Some parts were surprisingly vivid, others completely new. I think I plucked what was relevant to me, as a teenager, from the above themes and discarded all the rest. 
 One new thing that struck me in this book was how it read so similarly to The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time, so much so that I started to question where Charlie might fall on the autism spectrum. The main difference between this book and that was Curious Incident takes place within the narrator's mind, which doesn't change. Perks is a series of letters, and Charlie's English skills do improve, as does his writing, as the school-year progresses. Still, he's a little different in his odd bouts of honesty. 
 The adult reader in me gives this book three stars, the teen in me gives it five, so I've averaged that out to four.

 The sex scenes aren't great even though they're obviously necessary for the story. Not that I mind a well placed (and well written) sex scene in a good thriller, but these are crude. The male ego in them is pretty obvious. 
 This was my first Ken Follett book and I'll definitely read more.

This is the second of a three-part series from Dark Horse Comics. It's a great companion to the beloved Nickelodeon show. The action is filling in some of the gaps that show how the world progressed to the point it was in for the follow-up series, The Legend of Korra. This book is exactly like watching an episode, only shorter. (I imagine all three parts together will be like a full episode). The artistry is beautiful, the bending looks badass even in still images, and the characters are exactly the way we remember them. I'm really loving getting to see Zuko's continued struggles to figure out what the right thing is, now that he's the Firelord. And the fact that this is from show creators Bryan Konietzko and Michael Dante DiMartino means it's all canon. (Is Zuko going to end up with Mai or Suki?!! What about Sokka?!!) Can't wait to see the conclusion!

I absolutely adored this book, inside and out. The characters, their development, the plot line, the evasiveness that Maggie Stiefvater had this entire book, it was absolutely amazing. I feel like the plot that we had been building up since The Raven Boys was completely resolved and just overall, amazing.While there were a few confusing parts about this book, they all really happened in the end, when everything just changed for everyone. 
 The characters and their development throughout this book, and really the entire series, was absolutely fantastic. Blue and Gansey's relationship within this book really sold me throughout the entire thing. It wasn't too forced and I felt like they evolved together and in a good way. Blue and Ronan's relationship took a turn for a better in this book as well, and I feel like this really helped me warm up to him, as he finally let the group in, emotionally. With this, he was also letting the reader in finally, and you learn a lot about him and his past in the Raven King. 
 Adam defiantly fell lower on my list during the first half of this book, mostly because I felt like he was kind of upset and a Debby-downer the entire time. That was until a major spoiler (that I won't get to until the end of this review). At that point, and when Gansey and Blue finally admit their relationship to everyone, he finally started to move back up. 
 Finally, there's Noah. I really don't have any words for this boy, because anything I'd want to say about this precious angel, would be spoiling the ending. I just love him, and I'm so happy how his character ended up. 
 I loved this book more than any other in this series, and overall, it was hard to give this book anything else than a 5/5 stars! 
 Now onto the spoilery goodness! 
  
 Once again, I'm really just going in order of how these events occurred, and then going to talk about my thoughts on each topic! 
 First off, finding out that Ronan accidently brought Orphan Girl out into the real world? That seriously fucked me up. Especially when Henry Cheng saw her in the back of the SUV. That made my heart stop. 
 Later finding out that Ronan dreamt up Cabeswater? That came out of left field for me, but after thinking more about it, It started to make sense, especially everything they learned while there the first time. 
 And then the moment that we all had been waiting for since book one, the Ronan/Adam kiss(es). I squealed so much when these happened. Although I didn't catch this relationship starting until the third book, but when I did, I shipped it so hard. 
 Then, when Gansey sacrificed himself to kill the demon that was going to unmake everything? I mean, I did kind of see that death coming, but not like that. While I hoped that they'd find Glendower and he would make everything better and all of that fun stuff, but part of me knew that it wasn't going to end well from book one. At least the way he died was the one I had predicted from the minute Blue had see his soul. She was going to fall in love with him, and her kiss was going to kill him. And it did. 
 The whole issue with Noah though? What I think happened was that he was also letting go when he saw Gansey spirit pass through the 'Middle realm' or whatever its called. And Noah let go to our world so that Gansey could come back, and because of that, Blue was able to 'wake him' like they were planning on waking Glendower. 
  
 To wrap things up, I adored this book. It was amazing in every way and I pray that Maggie Stiefvater will someday return to this world and maybe even these characters. I'm going to miss them dearly!
Far better than the disappointing last outing. Compelling plot, really interesting setting (getting outside London was a good idea), lots of development in the ongoing story as well. Cracking read.

I raced through this sequel to Delirium, and I don't think fans of the first will be disappointed... although, I did see all the plot twists coming from a mile away. Still, I'm caught up in the story now and I'll be reading the rest of it for sure.

If you stick 6 high school kids in the same room for a month, they will all pair off and lots of drama will happen. That's basically all the book is. It tries so hard to be a decent zombie apocalypse novle, but mostly it's about the kids trying not to kill each other.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Soooo, I'm really torn about this one. While I did almost fly through this 700-page-monster, I didn't think it was the best out of the series. I definitely enjoyed ACOMAF more than this, but I think it's a step up from ACOTAR. 
 I had some serious issues with the pacing of the story and while I do understand why so much of the build-up to the final battle is necessary, it slowed down the story so much that it almost came to a halt at times. There were scenes that I really, really enjoyed but didn't think were completely crucial to the core plot line, and felt superfluous within the story. 
 Secondly, I also didn't appreciate nor enjoy the weak attempt at diversity that SJM seemed to strive for in ACOWAR. I do see that she was trying but to me it felt like too little too late. Helion's (if that's his name) sexuality and the fact that he's black just felt like SJM was trying too hard to get some diversity in there. I honestly didn't think that he was crucial enough to the plot to be an adequate pillar for the diverse representation that I would have loved to have seen in ACOTAR and ACOMAF. 
 I was also very disappointed with how Mor's storyline was treated. I didn't think that her coming out was handled sensibly enough and I, as a bisexual person, felt misrepresented. SJM might have meant well, but to me, it backfired. 
 Finally (and I have many more thoughts on this book but I want to keep it short), I wasn't satisfied with the ending. It might just be my cold dark heart that wanted more death and despair, but I felt like we got cheated with the ending. Amren's decision felt weirdly OOC to me. Plus, it felt too good to be true. Yes, I did appreciate that the core group survived and I definitely would have ranted if any of them had died. However, war demands sacrifices and while I see that both Rhys and Feyre made some, it wasn't at their personal expense but rather at their people's. None of the core group suffered any long-lasting consequences from the war and that just doesn't seem realistic to me. 
 And don't even get me started on the Deus-Ex-Machina... 
 ACOWAR did have some redeeming qualities: The characters (except for Amren's ending) and their developments were incredibly well written. Rhys is my special, extra-dark muffin that still has me crying for more feminism in Prythian. Azriel and Cassian also took up more space in my heart. 
 I also enjoyed the extension of the world building and the introduction of the other High Lords as well as some peak at the mainland High Fae territory.

"The Caged Graves," by Dianne K. Salerni, is a mediocre historical romance/mystery novel set in a small, rural town in 1867. Verity Boone, sent to The Big City to live with family after her mother's death, returns to the home of her infancy and her father to scope out the dude her dad arranged for her to marry (if she decides she likes him). Verity's family is wealthy, her uncle's family is wealthy, her fiance is wealthy, there's really nothing standing in the way of her romantic attachment except for the flirty and handsome young doctor in town who is slightly anachronistically fond of soap. As she settles into her new life, Verity discovers there's ~~MYSTERIES~~ about her mom and her uncle's first wife. Fortunately, her mom left behind a giant stack of diaries. 
 There's some good in the book, including the serious treatment of PTSD in soldiers returned from the way, and the way Verity is all ~Progressive~ and ~Liberal~ and ~Judgy~ toward her rural townmates, but then goes on to make a bunch of racist and classist assumptions. POC provide a powerful assist in the book, although of course the POV is rich white people. Salerni also touches briefly- too briefly!- on rural Vampire myths in the USA. 
 The writing isn't bad per se, but the mystery element is super SUPER obvious... like, I figured it out within the first few pages... and there is no real threat to the romance element. I also did not really LIKE Verity and found her smug insistence that she NEVER faints irritating, in the same vein of "I'm not like those OTHER girls" comments. I also kept waiting for Verity's fiance and flirty doctor to start making out or something, I don't know. 
 All in all, it was a fast and ok read, and I'd be interested in reading a more mature book by Salerni, something with a bit tighter editing. It's also possible that I should have waited longer after finishing "Coldest Girl in Coldtown" before diving into another YA fiction book with a plucky female protagonist. YMMV.

After reading the Lunar Chronicles last year, I've been wanting to explore some more fairy tale retellings, so I was excited to jump into this retelling of Aladdin. 
 Overall, this was a pretty solid read for me. I enjoyed the writing style, I enjoyed the character development, and I found the plot to be engaging well-paced. 
 The development of Aladdin and Zhara as individual characters was solid and I really enjoyed getting to know Zhara in particular, as she's so different from the genie most of us associate with the Aladdin story thanks to Disney. She was a rather complex, layered character who struggled with motivations and emotions and a whole slew of other things and I felt Khoury did a wonderful job developing and portraying the struggle Zhara goes through as the story progresses. 
 One of my absolute favorite things about this book was Princess Caspida and her Watchmaidens. I have always loved seeing strong female friendships portrayed in books and lately have been leaning toward stories that prominently feature those kinds of relationships instead everything being love and romance. And let me just tell you, these women were baller. Fierce, loyal, and strong, they love each other and their city and their kingdom and in so many ways they completely made this story for me. 
 My biggest struggle with the book was the relationship between Aladdin and Zhara. Partly because it felt rather insta-lovey to me and partly because I have some major issues with all these stories where a hundreds-year-old immortal something or other falls in love with a teenager. Even though we know from the beginning that Aladdin and Zhara are gonna fall in love (because it says so on the dust jacket), I would've like there to be more of a slow development of feelings. Yes, Zhara fights against her instincts and struggles to come to terms with her feelings for Aladdin, but from the beginning there's the whole "connection" thing and yea. I'm sort of okay with the hundreds-year-old jinni falling for a teenager because of the fact that the hundreds-year-old jinni was basically frozen in time as a teenager herself and has spent the last 500 years just chilling along in her lamp, but I still just struggle with that whole concept and I wish writers would stop doing it. 
 Though I can't necessarily think of a better way for it to end, the ending bothered me. It all felt very tied up, neat and pretty, in a lovely bow and I get that that's what fairy tales are, but I don't know...it felt too sweet and sappy and happy. Mostly because of the last line. If that had been taken out, I might've been more okay with the ending. 
 Overall, like I said, a pretty solid read with some wonderful characters. Just a few things that irked me a bit, but very much a "it's me, not the book" kind of things.

I'll admit that when I first heard of Kevin Hearne, I thought that Barenaked Ladies' keyboardist was writing books now and got very excited. Different Kevin Hearne, but still an interesting book. I got my copy through First Reads, which is always fun too. 
 The thing I enjoyed most about Hounded is the magic system. I did have my own Druid phase in college, so that aspect appealed to me right away, but even aside from the historical roots, the magic system is extremely tight. It doesn't work all the time, and has a strict set of rules, making it entirely believable that you need a solid 2,000 years to master it. Hearne has an extensive knowledge of all sorts of mythology, and he doesn't take cheats around the characters he borrows, either. At times it feel like a few too many mythological creatures (witches, werewolves, vampires, Irish gods, Norse gods, fae folk, partridges in pear trees), but he does approach each character from a solid base of rules. That's neat. Irish wolfhounds are also neat, and I've always wanted one. 
 A lot of people compare this book to the Dresden Files, and that's easy enough to do. One thing that struck me though is that Harry Dresden is constantly in trouble and always starts out behind the gate. Atticus, on the other hand, always seems to be a step ahead and over-prepared. He kills two gods in this book and kisses three goddesses, even having sex with one just because she's board,  From this standpoint, Atticus is a bit MarySue. He's so good at everything, all the ladies love him and all the dudes are jealous of him. I got a bit frustrated with that aspect, especially the fawning women angle. 
 I'm still interested to see where the story goes, and will likely continue the series when my own "to read" list gets shorter (which it will one day... I swear). If you like urban fantasy, but are a little tired of the noir detective trope, this is a great alternative. It's a fine popcorn read for the weekend.

 I guess I prefer Tris' Chicago when there is a greater focus on one of the factions and not all of them. I found the emphasis on who belongs in what faction and "oh today you're being such a Stiff" jibing really distracting. And it also didn't make much sense to me that EVERYONE should fit in one of these five very narrow factions. For some reason, this issue didn't bother me during Divergent but since everyone kept talking about how so-and-so TOTALLY belonged in this faction, it really got me to thinking. Seems like the contingent of factionless would be much bigger than all the factions combined, especially since you get kicked out of Dauntless if you're not in the top ten of initiates. 
 I guess we know now that the factions serve a specific purpose, but I thought that reveal was weak. So at some time in the past, everyone became too violent? And then they put everyone into a burnt out version of Chicago so they could learn how to be less violent? And the test subject responded...by beginning a violent war that killed dozens, if not hundreds of people? So the project/experiment failed? Am I missing something? 
 I actually enjoyed reading about Tris' response to killing Will and her mother and father dying. Her pain and difficulty coping were palpable and also made her a compelling character. I didn't really care too much about her and Four/Tobias, though it was interesting to learn about Tobias' mom and dad. 
 In short, I think I'd be factionless.

 It is rare to find a book and actually call it "epic." It is also rare to fall in love with a book from the first page and read it in a sitting, or at least, it has been difficult for me to do that lately when every book I have been reading is a three star. Lynn Weingarten's Suicide Notes From Beautiful Girls saved me from jumping into a reading slump and feeling useless with myself. She takes a real-life, crazy situation and makes it believable, switching between genres and making this a grief-bound-loss-story, to one that is a pure and favourite of mine, a psychological thriller. 
 Weingarten uses everything that she could in her writing style to capture the attention of readers. I fell in love from the first page, couldn't stop reading, and made sure that the atmosphere around me was not distracting, and certainly not loud and noisy. This precious, precious novel saved me from drowning and collapsing in all of the books I own, perhaps even saving me from giving up on books that are contemporary after all. As time goes by, I have found myself to be picky with novels, but this is love at first sight. The tricking plot that Weingarten creates is captivating, and a true adventure within an adventure that the main character, June, goes through. I adore this novel, and I seriously promise readers that it will be on my year's favourite list. 
 "Later, Delia would explain to June that finding a best friend is like finding a true love: When you meet yours, you just know." (61) 
 Lynn's characters just fall under so many topics and parts of life that it truly is difficult to pronounce what this book actually focuses on. It shares elements of murder, abuse, hallucination, jealousy, death, eeriness and mystery. But then again, June, the main character, falls under so many other things like having a horrible life which really leaves readers not being able to understand what the truth really is. In this case, it is totally acceptable to just not know. You will not know. You will not know anything until the last page where your world will collapse. Or at least, mine did. I seriously had to make sure that the book was seriously over and that there wasn't some invisible ink on the final back pages because I was shocked, and kind of in a good way. If you cannot handle the suspense, then I pray for you. 
 Weingarten moves from perspective to perspective, from different periods of time when there are hints and clues that really give you the solemn answer to this mystery that June herself is bound to solve. Readers see the start of the toxic, addicting friendship that Delia and June make from the sixth grade, and how quickly things tear apart because of jealousy and really... because nobody had no freaking idea why. Friendships are like that, and instead of an author handing readers a cheeky, one-sided tale about two girls who become friends again or who go through loss, this is the ultimate truth. And we are seriously lucky to see both sides of the story, if you know what I mean. 
 You see... this book makes me contemplate some theories as I did with Michelle Hodkin's Mara Dyer trilogy. Because the ending was so abrupt and beautiful, every reader could make their own guess and see what would happen with that. I cannot stop thinking about what Weingarten left us with. Humans are savages, we all are in some way, and instead of hitting the violent side of things (well, we kind of did in a few ways), we get to take a look at sociopathy, lies, and desperation. The writing is very, very lyrical and melancholic, and I just kept guessing and guessing. I still do not know what to think and what to do with myself. I feel like I am in this clear bubble of nothing, trying to discover what the truth is to this novel. There is a point and main idea--destructiveness, in fact, but I love how readers are able to discuss and have their own say on this. It's not a clear, special ending, if you know what I mean. 
 "Evan, Ashling, Sebastian. They all smile. Who are these people? Who is Sebastian? Who is Delia? What the fuck have we done?" (310) 
 I cannot digress anything more about this story--it is my love and I am so glad to have enjoyed it as much as I did. There is a slight romance, but as we get to know June more and more, we see that friendship is more important to her than guys. 
 Suicide Notes From Beautiful Girls really is beautiful and pure. I could definitely see it as one of the best books, ever, period, and it such a savaged, interesting psychological thriller. Your heart will pound, you will be shocked and unsure of what will actually happen in the end. The characters are all so complex, but each have their own spark that makes them different. And in the end, this is a book solemnly about reality and the things that can occur if you're not careful. Agh.

 The world building was great and I liked seeing different parts of Venda from Lia's point-of-view even though I'm still a bit confused how the Sanctum works. Seeing the reaction of Vendans to Lia was interesting and I liked how she got people on her side. I was very impressed by how "many" allies she had in the end! 
 I really enjoyed the plot twists in this book even though I was able to see many of them before hand. Will the Morrighan royal family know the truth of what really happened with Lia? What about the war? What about the prochery? I can't wait to find out!

As much as I enjoy this series and these characters, the foreshadowing felt too heavy-handed this time out. The crimes themselves were shocking, but there weren't many real surprises - even among the more personal elements of the plot. 
 I also get a little bored when most of an investigation revolves around repeated visits to a small group of suspects until the killer makes a mistake.

"Don't look so glum. This is going to be an adventure." 
 I'm impressed. 
 ==>Characters: Morgan is a teenage girl who is too curious for her own good and refuses to take things as they are told. She questions the gaps in her understanding of Interment, but is clever enough to not disrupt the system. In short, she is a dreamer, but one with common sense. She strives to do the right thing and be good to those around her. As the narrator, she is likable and her thoughts as she navigate a new and dangerous Interment paints a vivid picture in the reader's mind. 
 The side characters, unlike too many YAs, are given clear personalities through Morgan's eyes. What's especially fascinating to read about are the relationships between them. We have her best friend Pen, her betrothed Basil, her depressed and drug addled mother, her blind brother. We see Morgan's growing desperation and complex bonds tying the people around her together. Even better are people like Amy and Judas, who, through snatches of knowledge, impart their own tales of life on Interment and their quest for an exit. 
 ==>Romance: I find it extremely lucky that all betrothed love each other. Alice and Lex, Morgan and Basil, Pen and Thomas. It presents an interesting question: can you make yourself fall in love with someone, when you know you have no choice? Does it come naturally? Is it a biological determined by a factor from birth? 
 ==>Setting and Plot: Plot was nicely paced, but the second half I found too sudden. The plot twist was rushed and not placed well. 
 What I like most about the setting is the question it rises: Who manufactured the earth exactly? Throughout the story Morgan discovers that events she thought were godly were actually achieved through science. There is a great disillusionment happening, but my biggest question is how they got into the air in the first place? It's a floating piece of land dragged up from the ground. Hopefully, this will be answered in the upcoming books.  It's an interesting, paranoid, unhinged novel but lacks the hypnotic quality of the first because it's more of a character study than anything else: "let's take a well-trained but insecure man (the POV character John/Control), and put him into this bizarre situation and see what happens." And this POV character is a little less endearing than the Biologist of Book 1, even though they both intentionally keep the reader at a remove. 
 I liked how this book related back to Book 1, but wish it had done more of that, and also spent more time on the prior expeditions into Area X and such, rather than spending so much time on John/Control's relationship to his mother (also an agent), and his past assignments, and that kind of thing. The ending was fun, but by the time it came around I was not as invested as I'd been in the beginning. All in all, enjoyable, but not quite as fresh and exhilarating as I'd hoped. 
 Random note: the paperback copy that I read had the text canted at a slight, regular angle so it was not parallel with the binding or the edges of each page. I'm not sure if it was intentionally printed like that or if it was a fluke, but this actually added nicely to the novel's sense of disorientation. Neat!

I picked this book up because I recognized the name of one of James Patterson's many collaborators - who, most recently, has been working on the CBS adaptation of Zoo. Is this Gout's first solo work? It's the first I know of, anyway. 
 The intro feels like classic Max Ride, being presented in the form of a letter demanding your attention, and then we jump into the story itself. It alternates between three very diverse POVs of talented but underprivileged teenagers all over the world. We get the Mexican-American hacker Rex, who's looking for his missing brother, then Tunde, a Nigerian boy whose engineering knowledge is being exploited by a corrupt general, and Painted Wolf, the alias of punky Chinese hacktivist Cai. (From her, I got a distinct "teenage version of Skye from Agents of SHIELD" vibe.) The book itself is also peppered with unusual graphic illustrations to help you tell which POV you're on - Rex's POV has these weird little molecular things, Tunde's POV is loaded with graffiti on the edges and hand-drawn illustrations of his designs, and Cai's POV has these square target things on each page, certain words highlighted in a way that makes them look like printing glitches, and occasionally, very blurry video screenshots like Person of Interest. 
 Visually, the book is pretty cool, a hybrid of the graffiti designs from the covers of Olivia Samms' Sketchy series (which, if I remember, was also recommended by James Patterson) and the rule-breaking use of illustrations as part of the text like in Illuminae. Unfortunately, visually stunning though the book was, it did make it hard to read sometimes, particularly in Tunde's chapters, where the graffiti often distracts from the actual story. And as for the actual story, the main plot is pretty predictable, and the three narrators' backstories aren't all equally interesting. Cai, in particular, is hard to get invested in, mostly because her primary persona is a notorious mask - although given how boring her home life seems to be otherwise, that's no surprise. Tunde and Rex, however, you can't help but root for. Especially Rex, who really needs to find his brother, yesterday. 
 This book is quite clearly just the first in a series, and while I wasn't super-duper-thrilled with it, I'll be keeping an eye out for the sequel. And in the meantime, this reminds me, I need to get my hands on John Sandford's third Singular Menace book sooner rather than later.

I've never read anything by C.S. Lewis before, and given that he's a favorite of most of my friends, I thought I'd give him a try this holiday season. I'd seen the movies based off the Chronicles of Narnia, so I had a basic idea of the series, but I never grew up with the stories. 
 I'm also not very familiar with the Bible or any of its stories, so I'm judging this book as a fictional story alone, not as an allegory. 
 Off the bat though, his writing doesn't impress: 
 "(their names were ____, _____, and ____, but they do not come into the story much.)" 
 . . . Thanks? I don't know if this is supposed to be added for narrative charm or something, but it just seems awkward and intrusive. 
 Also: 
 "Whatever is this?" said Peter's voice, sounding tired and pale in the darkness. (I hope you know what I mean about a voice sounding pale.) 
 This doesn't read as stylistic charm. This is more like laziness, as if he came across it in an edit and just didn't feel like changing it. 
 The story itself is charming, though, and moves quite quickly--more like a fairy tale than a book. Especially when it comes to telling telling instead of showing; character emotions are talked about to the audience in a way that they aren't experienced in real time but summarized. 
 Characters also seem to know things they previously had no knowledge of (or they had actually stated they had no knowledge of)--like the Witch not knowing how Edmund came to Narnia and then showing him how to get home a single conversation later. 
 Speaking of characters, the four main characters here (Peter, Edmund, Susan, & Lucy) felt more like board game pieces to be talked at or pushed around than protagonists of their own story. Seldom did they ever do anything of their own will. Everything is placed in their hands, or they're manipulated or charmed into doing something. The beavers particularly moved the plot forward by instructing the kids what to do, where and when, for about a fourth of the story. I know this was written in a different time, but as a reader in the present time reading for enjoyment, all this seems like an info dump at best to keep the book short and moving forward. 
 Maybe if I'd read this when I was a child, this would be dearer to my heart, but for now, it's just a quick and ok read.

 Through the wonder that is Twitter, I made a connection with someone at Quirk Books. I wasn't searching for their review copies actually, but one of their people was offering up another book I really wanted to read to a reviewer (Note to self: read that book) and I responded. I didn't even follow him, but saw the message through a retweet. Anyway, when he emailed me about that book, he asked if I would like to review for Quirk Books. I looked at their catalog and gave a tentative yes, mostly on the proviso that I would review if they published something I was interested in. Well, the first book offered was The Last Policeman, and, yes, I was interested. 
 The Last Policeman has an awesome premise. It is what I would call pre-apocalyptic, which is something I've read a couple of recently (another such book being Unraveling). In these books, everyone knows the world's going to end, or at least they expect it. The world could go post-apocalyptic, but it might get saved. As a huge dystopian/post-apocalyptic fan, I am naturally intrigued by these. 
 In The Last Policeman, a tremendously gimongous asteroid is going to collide with the earth. The scientists have proved it, and there's no way out of it. A lot of people will die immediately and the rest will hang on for a while in post-apocalyptic conditions, but odds of survival for anyone are low. The asteroid is coming in mere months. 
 What's so fascinating is that this shows you the response of society. Of course, society kind of falls apart. Suicides become commonplace, people abandon workplaces to go in pursuit of their bucket lists, drug use skyrockets. All of this in an attempt to squeeze the most life possible out of what time remains, or to avoid the inevitable conclusion by concluding everything immediately. From a philosophical standpoint, this question of how the world would react in the face of such inevitable destruction is incredibly riveting. Winters does an amazing job showing a number of different possibilities. 
 Like with a number of the books I've read recently, though, I didn't hugely connect to the characters. With the number of books this has happened in, I'm starting to wonder if the problem is me. Either way, this was my personal reaction. I do like Henry. I like his dedication to his job, and I do think it's true to life that some people would be so much more comfortable with the end of the world if they just ignored it, focusing on their day to day lives. 
 Henry focuses on this possible murder case, desperate to solve it, despite the fact that, ultimately, it won't matter. At most, the murderer, if there is one, will die earlier or spend his last few months in prison. They're still all going to die. Perhaps this futility is what kept me from caring about the characters? I don't know, but Henry was the only one I bonded with at all, and, even then, I was not particularly bothered about whether he got what he wanted. 
 This is my first experience with Quirk Books, aside from the Pride & Prejudice & Zombies books, and I'm glad that I gave them another go. I highly recommend this lightly humorous and bleak novel as a readalike of The Postmortal. The concept and clever writing definitely make this a worthwhile read.

 I liked this book. I liked it a lot. If I hadn't read Rowell before I probably wouldn't have picked it up, but knowing that she's fair to her nerd characters and doesn't mock them for being nerds (I'm using nerd as a descriptive term) made me willing to give it a chance. Books written about fandom by outsiders tend to get it wrong, and this book avoids that by being written by someone who's been in the inside (I mean, that opening portal for Cath's fic writing site? Clearly based on AO3 with a different age rule). There's plenty of professional writers who are snotty about fanfiction, especially those who are almost write fanfiction themselves (yes, Jasper Fforde, that means you), so it's always encouraging to see writers who aren't. 
 It's more of a coming of age story than anything else, and even though my own first year experience was more like Wren's than Cath's (minus getting hospitalised, I wasn't that much of a freshman) I could relate to Cath's struggle to find a place for herself in a big bad world without her twin. The development of her relationship with both her family and with her new friends and boyfriend felt natural, and I really liked that Cath wasn't expected to give up what she was interested in writing because she gained a boyfriend. Too often there's an expectation that a woman's got to give up whatever she's interested in as soon as she gets a partner, and it's heartening to see a YA book not go down that route. Levi being genuinely supportive of her interests too was a really nice development, even if he's possibly a little too good to be true. 
 There's a couple of things I would have changed - for one, don't have anyone mention Harry Potter if the series your character's writing for is a parody of Harry Potter and I would have liked to have seen more of both Wren and Reagan. I'm not sure if you could write an entire book about Reagan, but Rowell, if you're reading this, consider it! Or maybe I should write my own fanfic about it. Despite that, I really enjoyed this book and if it sounds like something you'd like to read, I'd recommend it.

 That's not to mention the instant dislike/lust that they both found themselves in from the start, and the chemistry between them was delicious. 
 One thing that really stood out about this story for me was my discovery of just how much I dislike "time jumps". You know, the ones where it's "a week passed by..." type of thing? It led to far too much "telling" and not enough actually experiencing things through the eyes of the characters. While I understood the necessity of it, it still left a bad taste in my mouth. 
 That said, however, I enjoyed the unconventional (divorced) heroine, the forbidden romance, and the honorable-to-a-fault hero. The Aileen's sister made me want to murder her on more than one occasion, and I can't wait to read her story in the next installment of the series and see if another man does a better job of taming her. 
 There was another aspect of the story that I absolutely adored, though I fear that including it would be a spoiler, so I must only hint at it -- the presence and storyline of Tara's former love, Raury. I was very leery of reading it when the story began, but I was very pleased with the outcome.
