Rating: 1/5 
 ***Minor spoilers*** 
 Allyson is currently on a trip around Europe with her best friend Melanie. The trip was a graduation present from her parents before she went to college in Boston. The thing is, she isn't really enjoying it as much as she feels she should. She's underwhelmed by the cities they visit and she isn't into going to the pubs like her best friend is. At a Shakespeare performance in one of the places she's visiting, she meets a man named Willem. As fate would have him, she meets him again at the train station when she's meant to stay in London for a few days before heading home. Instead, she takes Willem up on his offer of him taking her to Paris for just one day. 
 I didn't really like this book. I found Allyson a very annoying character to deal with. First of all, she's on a trip around Europe that her parents paid for as a gift and she's complaining because she doesn't think the cities look the same as they did in movies she saw? Are you kidding me? There are so many people that would love to be in your shoes and you're complaining that you get to travel across Europe. She's entirely too trusting and naive. Taking off with a guy you just met to a city you've never been to and where you don't even speak the native language? Trusting him to pay for everything for you?  Having sex with him?  Shel even gave him her watch to wear, which was another graduation present that probably costed hundreds of dollars. And then after literally a day in Paris with him she's madly in love with him. This girl is like 18, how can someone be so naive? 
 Most of the issues I had with this book were the characters. There was barely a likeable one at all. Allyson's mother is forcing her own hopes and dreams on Allyson. Allyson's grades start dipping in college because she's both upset over Willem and the classes are hard. Her mother doesn't stop to consider that something is wrong with her daughter. She just "punishes" her for doing worse than usual, then when Allyson is noticeably upset, she dismisses the notion that Allyson may be depressed and simply says that she's just upset she's being punished. Her best friend doesn't contact her at all, doesn't send a birthday present (or even a card!) and pressures her to be both the Allyson she's used to and the Allyson she wants her to be. 
 Overall, I didn't like this book very much. The characters are annoying and I feel like they never stopped for a moment and thought about how they were acting. I hated the insta-love (falling in love in a day?) and how naively trusting Allyson was. And then after, I was sick of her pining. The last third of the book wasn't as bad as the first parts, but by that time I was already tired of the book and wanted it to be over. I definitely don't recommend if you're into great characters and a well developed romance.

I've been wanting to read books by Sarah Dessen for a while now. The Truth About Forever is my first read. I find it very enjoyable and light reading. If you want to just take your mind off things for a while, I recommend this book and it is a perfect read for the summer. It remind me of Cecelia Ahern. 
 The storyline is simple, Macy spending her summer job at the library; finding that her life is too stiff, too tight, that out of sudden she got a job helping Delia with the catering. That's when the chaotic, messy moment begins. That's when things started to change. She made new friends, she deals with different things everytime, a totally new from the constant phase at the info desk. She met Kristy, Wes, who taught her to be more spontaneous, who taught her that some things just happened, you don't need to plan. I love the Truth game she played with Wes, where they just talked about things. 
 It's simple, but if you look closely, like how Macy and her mom deal with the grieving, differently with her sister; how Macy and Wes shared the same painful loss; this story actually tell on more big stuff. A relationship between Macy and her mom, Macy with Jason. Everything that happened during that summer changed her to be a better person, to be happy; helped her dealing with the loss. 
 It's a good story, about life, about forever. The characters are loveable, relatable, the type of characters that you want to meet and can't help but love; especially Kristy and Wes. 
 It was becoming clear to me that I shouldn't bother to get too attached to anything. Turn your back and you lose it. Just like that. 
 That was the hard thing about grief, and the grieving. They spoke another language, and the words we knew always fell short of what we wanted them to say.

It's like narcotics in YA-chicklit form. I shouldn't love it as much as I do, and I shouldn't be thinking about it for days after I finish, but it calls to me. 
 *Addict hands shaking* "I need book 8!"

Stephen Crane's 'The Red Badge of Courage' is a seminal text as regards to war narratives, being considered by many literary critics to be the first modern war novel ever written. However, what is also really surprising, in my opinion, is that this "classic study in the psychology of fear" was written by an author, just twenty-two years old, who had never been enlisted in war himself. 
 How could a novel, so famous for its realism, be written by someone so inexperienced? That was a question which most critics asked since 'The Red Badge of Courage' was first released in 1895. Crane's "feverish imagination" was criticized by one reviewer as the cause of this novel. What they failed to mention was how Crane still managed to write a book which is "true to life, whether it is to be taken as a literal transcript of a soldier's experiences in his first battle, or... a great parable of the inner battle which every man must fight". In a rather Shakespearean fashion, Crane focuses on Fleming's inner experience rather than on the external world around him. In fact, Henry Fleming, the protagonist, is constantly referred to as 'the youth'. Neither the battle, the war, nor the armies are even mentioned. 
 'The Red Badge of Courage' is all about Henry Fleming, with all his typical misconceptions on war. In real life, if you happen to get shot, there are no 're-spawns', as in an online computer game. There is nothing glorious about death, even if it is for one's own country, as we can see from this description from Chapter Six: 
 "He was being looked at by a dead man who was seated with his back against a columnlike tree. The corpse was dressed in a uniform that once had been blue, but was now faded to a melancholy shade of green. The eyes, staring at the youth, had changed to the dull hue to be seen on the side of a dead fish. The mouth was open. Its red had changed to an appalling yellow. Over the gray skin of the face ran little ants. One was trundling some sort of a bundle along the upper lip." 
 There are many more horrific descriptions of corpses throughout the book. "The old Lie: Dulce et Decorum est/ Pro Patria Mori". 
 I am disappointed to notice all the negative contemporary reviews here on Goodreads. It is true that 'The Red Badge of Courage' is somewhat archaic, but what do you expect from a novel written in 1895? I especially like the novel's particular phraseology and diction, . Overall, it is a gem that deserves to be studied and read for many more centuries to come. As a novel emphasizing the "psychological portrayal of fear", 'The Red Badge of Courage' is unique. Its ironic tone is also peculiar, since the red badge of courage was actually inflicted on Fleming from a soldier from his own side. Comparatively, Fleming thought that running away from imminent death, fear being one of the universal laws of nature, was "the sore badge of his dishonor"; "his fall", as though he was another Lucifer. Stallman commented that "the education of the hero ends as it began, in self-deception", as though Fleming envisioning the "existence of a soft and eternal peace" as being a mere illusion. I do not believe that comment to be entirely correct, however, for the youth did blossom into a mature and self-assured individual. He achieved what is known as 'prudentia' in literary criticism terms. 
 I loved every part of 'The Red Badge of Courage', and I do so desire to read it over and over again when I get the chance. I also recommend the brilliant John Huston 1951 movie adaptation of the same name, available for free on many internet movie archives nowadays, with a commendable performance by Audie Murphy, the most decorated American soldier from World War Two.

Wow. The complexity of Morton's writing is astounding. She jumps between narrators and time periods with such alacrity. The really amazing thing is how she builds the layers of the story a molecule at a time such that by the time the story ends you can't imagine how you got there. There has to be some kind of alchemy going on here......
This was a cute, fun read. 3.5 stars.

Uglies is set in the far dystopic future where the cities of the current world have been abandoned. In the new world, children live with their parent's until they're twelve, then they leave home and live in dorms. The dorms are in ugly town. Once they turn 16, they get an operation that turns them pretty. At the start of the story, Tally Youngblood is weeks away from turning 16. She is sick of seeing her "ugly" face with it's lack of perfect symmetry, her nose that's too long or her squinty, watery, eyes. Her best-friend-for-life, Peris (a boy) turned 16 four months before she did, so that left her alone. Feeling friendless, she finds Shay (a girl) and they become friends. Shay tells her about people that don't want the operation. Tally can hardly believe anyone would actually want to stay ugly for life. Blah blah blah 
 So basically, the story had bad pacing, underwhelming world building, unbelievable characters, boring and unbelievable conversations, and plenty of hitting over the head preaching, which frankly, marred the book's goodness for me, not to mention the head ache it gave. I fought through the first half of the book (since I keep hearing about this series), but thankfully, it picked up in the second half. Overall though, the book was a waste of my time. I like knowing how a story ends and this one is part of series, so I couldn't resist reading the plot summaries of the other books on wikipedia. I'm glad I won't have to waste more time reading the other books to know how unresolved it ends.

A lovely dytopian YA romance, Feuds was a wonderful read. It wasn't perfect. I felt like it had a lot of potential, but didn't go all the way. However, I still quite liked it and enjoyed reading it. From the sweet romance to the game-changing secrets and manipulations, this book was great. 
 Davis was a good heroine. I went back and forth on her. It was odd. One minute she would be thinking independently, the next she would fall back in line to what she was told to think. But, in the end, she chose to go her own way, so I ended up being okay with that. Overall, she was a likable heroine, though I'm hoping she has a chance to grow stronger in book 2. 
 Cole was very sweet. He was very loyal to his family and determined to protect his loved ones. Two issues with his character: 1) I wish I had gotten to know his character more. He felt oddly shallow for a main character. 2) I found it odd that, despite being so dedicated to his family, he was suddenly contemplating leaving them behind so that he could run away with Davis. That didn't fit his character and knocked him down a few notches because it made him seem fickle. But, overall, I liked him too. 
 The romance was very sweet. There were definitely some very adorable moments. However, I wish that I had actually seen them get to know each other. I don't mind characters falling in love quickly, as long as I believe that they know each other well enough to claim love. That didn't happen with this romance so it felt a bit shallow. But, I still thought they were cute together. 
 The plot was well paced and I was kept interested the entire way through. The world that that author created was interesting, though I wanted more description, particularly about how exactly the Priors were made. There were a few twists as some game-changing secrets were revealed. I enjoyed the story and I'm curious to see what's coming next. 
 Feuds was a wonderful YA read. Though it wasn't perfect, I still liked it and found it to be an enjoyable read. YA lovers, this is a book you might want to check out.

4.5 Gut-wrenching, hair-pulling, kick-someone's ass Stars 
 By the first "Patience" chapter, I was ready to throw up. What Patience has to endure in her own home is horrific and the author will give you that horror in descriptive detail. 
 You cannot help but put yourself in her shoes. 
 You cannot help but want to pull her from the book and give her a new life. 
 You cannot help but want to kill her demons for her. 
 Sometimes, I secretly prayed for an eternal sleep, one where there is no pain and he didn't exist. 
 Zeke is not without his demons as well. Used as a punching bag by his alcoholic father, he uses alcohol, drugs, women, and music to drown out his own anger and worthlessness. He could not have been more different from Patience than the devil is to an angel. But he saves her, time and time again and together they help each other heal. 
 [image error] 
 The story is both heartbreaking and uplifting. The subject matter has been discussed in other books and is not unique per say. But, I did find the author sensitive and at the same time wanting to give you the realism and consequences of these teenagers' problems. 
 Writing: Excellent 
 Character: Love and want to adopt them 
 Recommend: Yes and only when you have a box of tissues handy

Evening Winterrose, one of the oldest faerie in San Francisco, is murdered; but not before laying a curse on October Daye to ensure that the killer will be found. It's been fourteen years since October had anything to do with the world of faerie, a world that largely looks with disdain upon changelings such as herself; a lot can change in fourteen years. 
 Rosemary and Rue spun a good mystery. The urban fantasy genre isn't one that I normally go for, but this book did end up making me enjoy it. The amount of detail that McGuire put into the fairy tales that she brought to life within her pages was one that anyone with a more than passing interest in folklore would appreciate. I also must say, it was a relief to have something other than vampires and werewolves and other such 'stock' monsters on the pages. 
 I think Sasha and Krissy would enjoy this; she does urban fantasy well, and the mystery, though easy enough to solve for a reader, was still respectfully brought off.

There is a lot of buzz about the murder complex, a story about a futuristic wold where there is no illness, no death so population booms. The only thing keeping populations under control is the murders, crime and murder is rife and everyone knows that it could happen to any one of them, at any time. Meadow is 15 and has been trained by her father to survive, who goes into testing for a role within the governing organisation, but to get the job she has to do the unthinkable. Once she's in her new role things get worse, she meets Zephyr, a ward of the state who appears to be unimportant, but who has more influence on her life than either one of them realise until its almost too late. 
 A fast pace, gory and dark book, the MC is what some would term a 'gripping read' and I did enjoy the book, but I'm not sure why! The story was good, not great, the writing the same - there was nothing spectacular about the book. It was very gritty and I can see the direction Cummings was headed for but it just didn't make it for me, it felt to TEEN for me, which a good YA avoids. 
 I'm glad I read it, and there was nothing wrong with the book, but i found that when I picked my reader up to resume the story I had to think hard about what had happened, what the plot was so far and what I expected next. It was almost like I'd forgotten the story so far, which is strange. I love books that invade my non-reading world, that I think back to when I'm in real life, and the MC didn't do that for me. 
 I'd recommend it as a read for those who are between books, but not as a must read, there is promise there and I'd consider reading a second book, but my expectations would be lower.

This books starts off awfully slowly. I was a good 1/4-1/3 of the way in before I started to enjoy it. The characters are beautifully developed. Steinbeck has depicted life during the Great Depression not only in Oklahoma but all the way to California as the Joads travel. He lauds family farms and denounces the disparity between those families and the few wealthy. It seemed like Steinbeck was unsure about how society would progress. He shows both possibilities: kindness and support or selfishness. I would have rated it higher, but I felt that these themes were beaten to death by the end. They were drilled in with example after example. Perhaps that is what he intended, though. Who am I to say?

Don't let Goodreads confuse you. It says it took me 5 days to read this book; but in reality, it took me 4 days to read 80 pages and one day to read the rest. 
 I had a little bit of a hard time getting into this installment, clearly. I don't know if that was at the fault of me or the book. I'm not sure if I just wasn't in the mood for this story when I first grabbed it a few days ago, or if something felt off kilter about the opening 50ish pages. The novels in this series always start off with A LOT of action, so it definitely isn't slow to get into plot wise. Despite me having a rocky start, once I got into this final book, I WAS HOOKED. Like I said, I pretty much read it in one day. 
 I thought this was a very solid conclusion to this trilogy. The action was on point. The stakes were raised. The romance, oh man the romance. I swooned so hard for this couple. The love and loss and grief and friendships and relationships, all of it was at stake and all of it was heightened. Even though the treasure-hunting/quest aspect, which for so long had been my favorite part of this series, came to a head and ended in this installment, I really felt the characters and their connections with each other and the implications of their choices carried the novel to the end. It showed that, although the quest was fun and alluring, it wasn't the only thing carrying the novel forward. The absence of it deepened the bonds between our four main characters in a way I wasn't expecting I would love so much. 
 There is a very heavy presence of science in this installment that I found wasn't explained very well, but I got the gist of what the consequences of it were enough to realize that the outcomes were dire. I would have liked to see this plot line delivered in a more articulate way though. It became a little convoluted and nonsensical at times, just because of how the author attempted to explain the science behind it. However, it definitely wasn't distracting enough to take away from my enjoyment of the novel as a whole. As I mentioned, I was able to get the point of what the author was trying to imply. 
 In the end, I was extremely satisfied with the conclusion. I am happy with where our characters ended up and what paths they decided to follow. It made sense for all the individual characters and gave me enough closure to know what to expect from them after the final sentence. With that being said, I love these characters so much that I do really wish there was more to their story. I was satisfied but still want more. I just love Avery, Stellan, Jack, and Elodie too much to already have to say goodbye to them. 
 10/10 would recommend this trilogy. I cannot wait to see what else Maggie Hall comes out with in the future :)

 Talk about blowing expectations out of the water! I have heard very mixed reviews about this story and have been very hesitant to pick it up. However, since I will be seeing this on stage during the coming week, I figured it was about time. 
 Maybe it was because of the low expectations I harboured, but this completely blew me away! 
 A few things I do want to mention, you could say in defense of this story/script, or just simply call it my stand on some points that have been raised in the wider bookish community. 
 1. This is indeed not a script written by J.K. Rowling but it is so obviously one she was heavily involved in. I don't want to question the skills of John Tiffany but this is clearly a Harry Potter story written in a different format which is why I assume it was created in collaboration. 
 2. On that note, I disagree with some people who say this should have been a novel. In fact, I'd go as far as saying that this would have been a disaster. This story is an afterthought, it was clearly created to meet a demand. Don't get me wrong, it is all kinds of wonderful, but Harry Potter was done, completed, finished, 'The End' was written. So J.K. Rowling caved and got help doing it but she decided to bring something new to the table in exchange for the fact that this story is somewhat an add-on, a #7.5 rather than an #8. So I really don't see why this should have been novelised. 
 Overall, I loved every minute I spent with these characters and it was great to return to their world. I cannot wait to see the play(s), I think it will be a truly unique experience! What is left is this - this is a play, it is not a novel, it is a new and magical story that mostly stays true to the original series (some character misdevelopments included), but it does not majorly enrich the story that Rowling finished a few years ago, it's a bonus. If you go into this bearing these things in mind, I think you're in for a treat! Of course, script reading is not for everyone so there is that, unfortunately. 
 --- 
 After seeing the play in theater, I have decided to drop a star. Don't get me wrong, I still absolutely loved it, but I also see its faults more clearly now: some things (writing-related) did not work on stage at all in my opinion.

There were many times I would have happily walked away from this absurdly overlong story. What kept me slogging through was the decision to finish it just so my opinion wasn't left in doubt. 
 No, I didn't end with any doubt: I'm astonished that King has the reputation he's got. There was so much in here that was laughably poor craftsmanship. He frequently has his characters do nonsensical things [see spoiler 1], or otherwise adjusts reality to make his storytelling easier [see spoilers 2 and 3]. 
 Some of his characters were compelling and enjoyable to visit. Many others were mildly elaborated stereotypes. Isn't it somewhat distasteful that the one and only character whose race was mentioned (over and over again) was amped up into a comic book stereotype of religiosity? 
 In fiction sub-genres such as this, we grant the author quite a bit of latitude. This post-apocalyptic story already has one big fictional element at its heart: that a disease will wipe out the overwhelming majority of humanity. But King isn't writing science fiction here, he writes paranormal horror stories. I get that: I've skipped reading King for several decades because I'm not interested in horror, or paranormal, much less both. I thought at least that he crafted his stories well, however, and this book -- well, I still don't know why people like it so much. It sucked. 
 Spoiler 1: Nonsensical actions by characters: There were two that grated. 
 First, what was with the huge traffic jams? When people feel like the world is threatening, they retreat to a safe place, which for the vast majority of us means we shut ourselves up in our homes. If you happened to have a loved one who you think has a better place to hole up in, or who you want to be with at the end of the world, then a sudden urge to drive somewhere would be plausible, but since The Stand's pandemic took place over the course of at least a week, massive acute traffic jams make no sense. That's even more true far, far from a metropolitan center, such as the passes over the rocky mountains, or in the middle of corn and wheat fields in Iowa. 
 Second, people working until they dropped dead on the spot. This is somewhat reasonable for doctors, nurses and scientists who may think their sacrifice may reverse the pandemic. But what about those soldiers who died at traffic stops -- or even with weapons aimed at and used on civilians? Does King really think soldiers will stand there, shooting at panicked people, even as their fellows are coughing their lungs out and collapsing?  
 Spoiler 2: Reality bent to make things easy, one: The big one is the course of the disease. This partially relates to the "people working 'til they drop dead" issue, because he portrays a lot of people who apparently died so quickly that you still saw them engaged in the activity of daily life. Remember the guy with his head in his stew? Are we really to believe that he was dying of this horrible influenza, but still wanted to eat, walked to the cafeteria and got himself some chow, and then sat down and -- plop! -- decided to drop dead? Or the scientist working with the centrifuge? No, he apparently didn't feel like crawling to a corner and wrapping himself in a bunch of blankets as he shivered with chills and whimpered. 
 Apparently all the people the characters could talk to and interact with (and watch die) were suffering from a disease the took several days or more, and completely incapacitated most of them, whereas all the characters that died before we met them died of a different and much, much faster disease. Or, I guess, we could accuse King of wanting it both ways, because that let him portray multiple forms of melodrama without having to work at it.  
 Spoiler 3: Reality bent to make things easy, two: The second one are the superpowers King granted to his Villain and Saint. Sometimes the big bad guy can send his "eye" to see almost anything he wants, and sometimes he can't. Sometimes he can even teleport! Oh, but not always. Why the difference? Well, we got some mumbo jumbo about the Saint's opposition -- oh, except there was that time he threatened her with weasels, and visited her in dreams, wasn't there? Again, things were allowed when it made King's story easier, and disallowed when that was what made his story easier.

 I'm going to be up front: I'm not a big fan of The Maze Runner series. 
 CONSTERNATION, UPROAR! 
 It's true, it's true. I've read each one, all (now) five books, and I gotta admit, it's not the best series I've ever read. And Thomas is not among my favorite protagonists. But to be fair, the idea is certainly compelling, and I was just as flabbergasted as anyone with the reveal at the end of the third book about WICKED. Maze Runner is a good pulpy action story, and it's actually a little amazing the movies have failed so hard, because the style of writing and narrative really does suit the big screen. 
 So all that being true, why did I read The Fever Code? Well, curiosity. I wanted to know about the Maze and how it was constructed and more about Thomas's life at WICKED before it all went down. I was, ah, a little fuzzy on the details, it being quite a while since I read the other books. So I read the extensive wiki to understand what had happened and what would referenced in this prequel book, but much like reading No Fear Shakespeare SparkNotes for school (which, as an English major, I of course have never done this), it was merely to pass the test. I had no emotional investment in what would happen to the characters (nearly all of them die, anyway), and I didn't like any of them enough to care about them pre-Maze. Again, it was mostly idle curiosity that carried me through (and for 
 some books 
 , that still isn't enough). 
 I feel that if you're going to enjoy The Fever Code, you really must be invested in the series as a whole, as this does give detailed information about WICKED life and some backstory for the characters. But it really could've just been a novella, or even a short story; there's not that much substance to warrant an entire novel. And as it is, the book itself is not that long. And I had wanted information about building the Maze itself, but the hand-wavy science of how the Maze works obviously wasn't going to withstand intense scrutiny, so it's merely touched on. And it was interesting reading the excerpt from The Maze Runner at the end and noticing how different it is, how much . . . well, how much better written it is, despite it being older. Honestly, I think I just don't like Dashner's style. But that's me! Everyone has different preferences and that's fine~ 
 Basically, if you love The Maze Runner series, from the titular first book to The Kill Order, you're gonna love this one too.

But I finished book #2 while out in the country without much a signal.  Finally, for the first time, I can honestly say I love Rose. Her character is wonderful! I love how fierce and determined she is and how much she loves and cares about people. I admired her and her reasons for venturing out on her own. Even in her worst and weakest moment, I felt like I understood her. And Dimitri... Oh, god. Though the book was written from Rose's point of view, like all of them, through her bond with Lissa, I was able to experience her adventures despite the distance between Rose and Lissa. There were two different storylines in this book, but both of them equally captivating. 
 Rose's adventures in Russia and meeting Sydney and Dimitri's family were great. I loved being introduced to another layer of conflict in the Vampire Academy world with Sydney's character. I keep saying that and I never really expand on that, but I don't really know how. I feel like I need more to happen, but I love him regardless and for now, that's all I can say.

Slowly these stories wind and connect, with just the right amount of absurdities and visits to a vivid memory-powered dreamworld. When Kafka lands a position and a place to stay at an old, private library, he is befriended by the androgynous, philosophical Oshima, and finds himself drawn to the reclusive and elegant head librarian, Miss Saeki, who harbors a tragic love story and secrets painted and sung into delicate chords of the past. 
 Kafka on the Shore spills over with beautiful sentences, and I found all these lyrical lines especially fitting to the story's atmosphere, which laps the shore of unreality just as it sings the dissonance of all-too-real painful memories and personal, private destinies. I was completely captured by these characters, each adrift on their own odyssey, in need of another's tide to pull them in.

Having finished #3, I now look at Mistborn the way I look at series like Lord of the Rings, The Dark Tower, or The Secret Texts. While each book tells a cohesive story, it's really one long arc of a plot told over multiple volumes. I think of The Fellowship of the Ring, The Two Towers and The Return of the King as 3 volumes, not 3 books, even though I know they are. I think Mistborn works the same way. You could pick up each individual book and read it, but you don't really understand the story until you've reached the end. 
 And what an end it was. 
 I'm still processing it, and I finished it almost a week ago. I can't think of another modern series that ended with not one, but two major characters reaching actual, literal godhood. I 100% didn't see the ending, any of it, coming. I'm depressed about who died, and almost annoyed about who lived--Spook  and Breeze  were two of my least favorite characters of the original crew, and to lose TenSoon  instead of them made me sad. But I do think it closed off his character arc and completed his journey, just as Vin and Elend completed their journeys. 
 Sazed...his journey is nowhere near complete, no matter what the ending seemed. I'm not sure how comfortable I am with his final position, although I'll have to go back and read from the beginning to see if it makes more sense than I feel like it does right now. 
 But this is a brilliant, extravagant, beautiful end to an outstandingly original series. I became more impressed with each page I read, and the way he tied all of his threads together at the end--even from the very first chapter of the very first book--was astonishing. Do yourself a favor and find these books. You won't regret it.

 All the reviews mentioned the Harry Potter angle (kid gets invitation to magical college), but there was less said of Narnia, which surprised me because that seemed more important to the story. Let's see -- jaded kid goes to college, meets friends (also jaded), gets a girlfriend, graduates, messes around with magic to no good end. And the characters ARE annoying with how jaded and dissatisfied they are for absolutely no reason. 
 But, even with that, I could not resist the snappy dialogue that's much too witty and cutting to ever be realistic (plus everyone had the same voice), but it reminded me of being up too late with drama club friends and being overly sardonic and catty and drinking too much gin. Cripes, I right now realized what I liked about this book -- it made me nostalgic for being 20 and slightly stuck on myself. Yeah, so that's probably a bit indulgent. Josh I found to be especially hilarious, and even when at the end things were supposed to be all very sad, I was snorting like a crazy person over the vaguely Germanic centaurs. 
 Naggingly, it doesn't quite hold together plot-wise, either. I have a list of questions I would like to ask Mr. Grossman about many of the choices he made. I still liked it well enough that if I had a magic time machine watch, I would go into the future and get the sequel. 
 Grade: B. 
 Recommended: Not to anyone who likes fantasy to include magic and wonder. This includes complaining and snarkiness. It combines two of my favorite genres, College Stories and Clever People Behaving Badly.

The Veil is an urban paranormal novel. But there is really nothing novel about it. This genre has been, in my opinion, beaten to death to the point where nothing is fresh or new. The Veil tries to be an NA book and it somehow doesn't fall victim to the many tropes and pitfalls that plague this virgin-riddled genre but unfortunately, The Veil winds up reverting back into a YA novel. It doesn't matter that the main character, Claire, is 24--she acts like she's 16 by blatantly disobeying every rule given to her. Someone tells her not to move and the second they walk away she is off, trying to save the day with her meager skills. It's not like they're treating her poorly--she is completely out of her element and unequipped to face the dangers coming her way. 
 But let's talk about those meager skills of hers--skills that she barely knows how to use or even invoke but she thinks she can do anything she wants and repeatedly throws herself into violent situations despite everyone else's best wishes. She thinks that she alone has the ability to save New Orleans from another paranormal war when she herself just came into her crappy barely useable telekinetic powers six months ago. She only has two damn training session on how to get rid of excess magic and all of a sudden she forgets that she doesn't know how to truly work her own magic. But this becomes totally irrelevant as she apparently has almost limitless strength and ability when it comes to moving large heavy objects. At one point she seriously considers trying to telekinetically move a helicopter. Give me a break. 
 Claire is also a shitty shitty friend. She doesn't trust her closest friends and knows very little about their personal lives. She's keeping big secrets from them and vice versa. There is a distinct lack of trust in all her friendships which reflects poorly on her. For some reason her and her gay friend Gunnar are trying really hard to push some guy on their mutual friend who she isn't even interested in. The main character goes so far a admits in the beginning that they have no spark but for some reason the two characters wind up getting forced together. 
 Let's not forget the absolutely bizarre aside in the final battle where she needs three separate times to get told to pay attention to the battle going on around her. What the hell. How oblivious can you be that you totally ignore your surroundings in a war zone. Even better is  her suddenly seeing a similar looking woman and deciding that's her mother.  In the middle of a damn battle field. 
 I totally give up. This book is a ridiculous mix of practicality and outlandish characters.

I've seen The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society many times and never even picked it up to read the blurb. The cover looks like boring and the title is just silly-sounding. I knew that it had sold a gazillion copies, but I had no idea what it was about. When it was recommended to me by a GoodReads friend, I decided to check it out at the library. 
 I have to say that I'm so glad I read this book. The story is told with a series of letters between a London author, her friends and a group of people on the island of Guernsey in 1946. The book made me smile, it made me laugh, it made me cry and I often smiled and cried at the same time. The epistolary style made it a very quick read and made each of the characters seem real. I learned so much about the German occupation of England's Channel Islands and of England during and after WWII. (I didn't even know that the Germans had occupied English soil.) 
 I highly recommend The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society for everyone. It will make you laugh, make you cry, make you laugh and cry at the same time, and will teach you things you probably didn't know.

This is the sequel to The Just City, a strange yet compelling mix of philosophy, Greek mythology, history and science fiction. Pretty much the most unorthodox genre combination ever, but Jo Walton handles it fantastically. 
 The cliffhanger at the end of 
 The Just City 
 centered around the fact that not all of its Children were happy with Plato's ideology and were convinced they could improve on it. Enter the fragmentation of the Just City into various Just Cit(ies), and the ensuing wars over arts, culture, and forays into colonialism. 
 While the first book was heavier on the actual philosophy and society-building, 
 The Philosopher Kings 
 plot placed a stronger emphasis on science fiction and Greek mythology. Debate and democracy still exist here, but characters have to confront the fact that their civilization exists outside of linear time, and that they are essentially experiments at the mercy of the Olympic gods. Their attempts to grapple with this, and the fallout that can only come from warring nations (and religions, as Christianity also emerges to make things that much more complicated) are what drive the story now. 
 I rated the initial book in the series a full 5 stars but I can't do that here, primarily because of the narration. We flip between several perspectives, and at a good pace, but even though theoretically each character is vastly different their tones all sounded similar. If my mind wandered I would have to backtrack a few pages to remember whose voice I was reading and reorient myself. From what I remember I didn't have as much of a problem with that in 
 The Just City 
 . Still, this was a strong sequel, and, even better news - there's going to be one more after this! I don't know where things will go from here, but if these first two books are any indication I'm going to really enjoy finding out.

 This is a review of the audiobook, narrated by Kate Reading, who did a wonderful job on this charming intro to the Pink Carnation series. I cannot recall hearing her before; but, luckily she reads the rest of the audio series as well, so I certainly look forward to listening to her. 
 I guess you could call this one an "historical chick-lit" with two stories running throughout. I didn't really mind being pulled back to Eloise's story in the present day, as I quite liked it. She's a recently cheated-on doctoral student writing a dissertation on spies of the French Revolution. Did I say I didn't mind the interruption to present day? That is, until, I was about half-way done! By then I hated being yanked back to the 21st Century! 
 This is because most of the story is about the iridescent romance between Amy and Richard, set in London and France, 1803. By that point I was deep into the intrigue of the many mistaken identities of a spy with the Nom de Plume of "The Purple Gentian," the mystery of who was going to be "The Pink Carnation," and the witty calamity that ensues when two young people are headed irrevocably toward romance. 
 It was fun doing this as a "buddy read" - to see which of us got what right. No rapes or torturous angst takes place here; this one is a pure sparkling glass of pink champagne.

Things I liked about this book: 
 - Good pacing. New plot developments happen regularly enough to keep things from dragging, but it doesn't fall into the trap of constant chapter cliff hangers that some action books do. 
 - Believable central characters. While the less central characters in this series tend to be relatively flat and forgettable, the central characters have some degree of depth, and some amount of growth and development over time. 
 Things I did not like about this book: 
 - Continuity break. In the first book, it is made explicitly clear that Luna's curse only affects accidents which may happen to her -- any intentional harm is unaffected. In this book, intentional attempts at harming her are rendered ineffective due to her curse. This doesn't make sense within the universe's rules. 
 - Politics still vague and relatively nonsensical. For the most part, it seems like the only functional difference between Light and Dark mages is whether they torture their apprentices and/or enslave non-mages. The Light mages we've met, for the most part, seem just as willing to completely disregard magical law for personal gain as the Dark mages are, and just as willing to kill their rivals.

It's so disappointing to read a series that has once started out so strong, progress into something so... flat. 
 I have loved this series from the start. Laughed, worried, cringed, and fangirled about Charley and Reyes' story and their preternatural connection. 
 But eight books in, a child in their arms, and the story has become somewhat confusing. We're given one description about Charley's origins and in the next, we find out it's something else. It's like we're all blindsided in every book, leaving with more questions instead of answers. Normally, I would have been okay with some surprises but really, after all these books, we still don't have a clear idea on what's really happening. It's annoying. 
 I still love this series though. So I'll still probably stick it out until the end (whenever Ms. Jones decides that will be).

 Echo is a human, but her only true home is with the Avicen, a race of bird people who nest beneath New York city. However, when she steals a strange music box she sets in motion a series of events that The Ala hopes will lead to the legendary Firebird. The only hope the Avicen have of ending the century old war between themselves and the Drakharin. 
 My hopes going into this novel were entirely too high. The book boasted of LGBT representation, which would have been great if it hadn't been between two side characters. One of whom is in love with his straight friend for a majority of the novel, but will obviously fall for the only other gay man he's ever met because he doesn't have any other options. It's not just this romance that's poorly written though, every romance in the novel is. Aside from one that is only remembered. 
 Echo isn't really anything noteworthy. She's a classic chosen one, who's tough and has trouble trusting people. At least that's what the author tells us. Unfortunately characters with trust issues seem to throw those out the window. The book takes place over about a week but that's enough for untrusting Echo to put her trust in several strangers because they're pretty. No substantial romance can develop over such a small time frame but the author pushes for two of them which feel rushed and inorganic. The characters know almost nothing about each other other than how warm they are, or how good looking they are. The love triangle is even more irritating, it's just as badly written as every other romance related thing. The romances offer near nothing to the story and were completely unnecessary. 
 Aside from the romance the book itself was pretty rough. It throws you into thew world far too fast, frantically trying to explain things as it goes leaving the reader confused. they throw the story into the world without adequately building it up first. Echo is a quintessential chosen one, leaving much to be desired, I'm less than interested in her because she's so predictable. It was a very standard fantasy novel littered with bad romances and only a few interesting plot points that made it enjoyable at all.

Wintergirls is a story that goes inside the mind and life of an 18 year old anorexic, Lia. In many ways, it deserves more than three stars. And you all know how I like magical realism (NOT!). It turns out not to be exactly that, but too late - - this whole portion of the story line never resonates with me and seems superfluous. It ends up making Lia seem less accessible to the reader and more mentally ill than I think most people with anorexia appear to be. I went to an all womens college so believe me, I saw more than my share of eating disorders . . .and Lia didn't quite fit the mold. That's okay - - I mean it is a fictional book, and the character doesn't have to be the precise typical model of an anorexic - - but certain elements just made the whole story less believable to me.

 Two-second recap: Like the city it takes place in, Elizabeth Ross's Belle Epoque is a gem of a novel. 
 Maude Pichon's coming-of-age in the most unlikely of circumstances, is detailed by Ross with delicate precision and finesse. This is a book that is both entertaining and incredibly informative, and will likely charm readers everywhere. 
 *** 
 Full review: 
 If you follow the publishing industry at all, you'll likely be aware of two things: 
 1)	The dominance of the YA dystopian novel is finally subsiding, and 
 2)	Stand-alone YA contemporaries and YA historical works are being touted as the next big thing. 
 When I read the synopsis for Belle Epoque in 2012, I knew that number two had to be true. I both read a lot of YA books in the past couple of years, but nothing I've read was as unique as what Belle Epoque's synopsis purported to be. 
 So after a lot of shameless begging - thank you for not laughing at us! - Random House kindly sent me a beautiful bound manuscript for me to read. 
 *** 
 Plot overview: 
 After fleeing her live in provincial Brittany, Maude Pichon has arrived in Paris, determined to make a new life for herself. 
 Maude has dreams of working in a shop, selling clothes or delicatessens to Parsians, but quickly learns that without a reference or the necessary accouterments, she won't be able to find a job. 
 So she takes on the only job that she can find: joining an agency that provides repoussoirs for the societal elite. 
 As a repoussoir, Maude is a foil; a plain, unattractive ornament that is used to garnish already beautiful debutantes. By appearing in public with them, Maude will only emphasize their beauty and their grace. 
 Maude is deemed to be the perfect foil for Isabelle, the headstrong daughter of the wealthy Countess Dubern. However, as Maude begins to form a true friendship with Isabelle, she begins to find herself at odds with what her job requires, and what her heart believes. 
 *** 
 Things that worked: 
 * Characterizations 
 For a book that's very character-driven, it's important to state outright that Ross's primary and secondary characters are like miniature works of art. They're rich, vibrant and bold, all serving as the brush strokes to create the final story. 
 As the main character, Maude is a wonderful study in contrasts. She's often shy and unsure about herself - especially when it comes to her appearance and her interactions with higher society - but she can also be gutsy, headstrong and opinionated when the moment calls for it. 
 Ross does a fantastic job of capturing Maude's voice, and showing the reader just how she begins to evolve after taking on her job as a foil. She's tougher and more willing to believe in herself, but she's also more arrogant; she desperately wants to believe that she's not destined to be the so-called ugly friend for the rest of her life. 
 As for the secondary characters, they're all well sketched-out in their own right. 
 Though we don't necessarily get to spend a lot of time with the other repoussoirs from the agency, the details that Ross does include shows us that they too are women who have fallen into this profession by circumstance, but still want to believe that they have more to offer society than their so-called lack of looks. 
 Ross does such a wonderful detail of adding those necessary details that make us invested in their triumphs and heartbreaks, and cheer when they finally get their happy ending. 
 * The romance 
 While there is something of a love triangle in Belle Epoque,, I highly appreciated the fact that Ross made sure that the both men played second fiddle to Maude's personal journey. She daydreams about them and admires them, but she never lets its get in the way of her job and her responsibilities. 
 In many ways, the inclusion of both Paul and the Duke are actually used to emphasize Maude's growth and developing worldliness as she serves as a repoussoir. 
 Without giving spoilers away, Ross crafts a wonderfully understated scene in the latter half of the book where Maude, after receiving some surprising news about one of the young men she's admired, realizes that everything she's assumed about him was merely a projection of her own desires. 
 She connects this back to her own role as a repoussoir and how she's made assumptions about individuals like her colleagues at the agency, and has allowed others to make assumptions about her as well. It's very much a eureka moment for her, and Ross plays it beautifully. 
 * Isabelle's relationship with Maude 
 The friendship between Isabelle and Maude was definitely my favorite part of the book. 
 Even though they were from opposite ends of the social spectrum, they just worked together in a way that seemed effortless. They each had faults, hang-ups and issues, which the other helped to compensate. 
 I especially loved the fact that Isabelle never seemed to look down upon Maude's lack of education. Instead, she just assumes that Maude is as capable of accomplishing what she has in academia, which helps Maude gain the confidence to overcome her previous hurdles about her background. 
 At the same time, I enjoyed watching Maude buoy and support Isabelle's ambitions. She's the one person who's not going to be impressed by Isabelle's status or morning, and can give her an opinion that is genuine and true. 
 * Paris, as a character 
 Like some of the greatest French writers in history, Ross does a spectacular job of incorporating the city of Paris into her story as its own character. 
 From Maude's first harsh, unforgiving introduction to the city, to the jeweled, accessories-laden homes of the societal elite on the Right Bank, the city lives and breathes right along with Maude, as she slowly becomes who she's meant to be. 
 Ross has clearly done her research about what Paris was like during the period, and relays it in Belle Epoque spectacularly. As someone who actually used to live in Paris, I felt like I could perfectly see everything that she was describing. 
 * The plot, and the bigger issues. 
 Whereas the majority of YA books will have the standard theme of the hero or heroine discovering something positive about themselves - whether it's a superpower, intellectual capability, etc. - Belle Epoque focuses on the supposedly worst aspects of our heroine, and puts her in a position where people are able to profit off of those traits. 
 It's absolutely morally repugnant, and we feel every hurt, every ashamed thought, and every disgusted moment that Maude experiences when working for the agency. 
 But at the same time, we also feel greater joy and greater success, whenever Maude does something that shows that she's not defined by her looks or her status in life. Without spoiling the plot, Ross's daring start does reap greater rewards. 
 * The ending 
 As someone who's studied quite a bit of French literature over the years, I thought that Ross's ending was wonderfully executed and very genre appropriate. 
 The idea that Maude loses everything and must rebuild again, and she does so with grace and an eye toward her future, shows just how much she's grown within the scope of the novel. It also proves definitively, that she - and others like her -should never be judged merely by their face. 
 *** 
 Things that didn't work: 
 Nothing. Absolutely nothing. If I could go back in time and recommend this book to Balzac, I totally would. That's how perfect this book is. 
 *** 
 Final verdict: 
 With Belle Epoque, Elizabeth Ross has proven that she is a rising star in the world of YA fiction. She has the type of skill and finesse of a novelist with dozens of novels under their belt, and I look forward to seeing what she'll write next. 
 I recommendBelle Epoque for fans of YA and adult historical novels, but I also recommend this book for readers who read some spectacular writing and want an unusual, imperfect heroine to root for. 
 Get this book - you won't regret it! 
 ***

Deanna Raybourn excels at creating strong, sassy heroines with a flair for adventure, who aren't afraid to break from the confines of society's expectations and seize life (and love) whenever they get the chance. 
 Poppy Hammond certainly fits the bill. After her dramatic exit as a runaway bride, Poppy is restless and yearning, knowing only that she needs more in her life. The nice man who helped her flee the wedding is someone she'd like to at least thank for his efforts, leading to an impulsive escapade in which Poppy winds up in Damascus under an assumed identity... right in the midst of political upheaval, treasure hunters, danger and intrigue. Definitely all the ingredients needed to please a girl seeking adventure! 
 Sebastian is a heroic leading man, insultingly misunderstood by Poppy to start with, only revealing his true character and capabilities to her over time, as they plunge from one dangerous situation to another, fleeing across deserts, hiding out in old ruins, and evading bad guys with a flair that would put Indiana Jones to shame. 
 As in City of Jasmine, the Middle East of the 1920s offers just the right combination of beauty, danger, and old-timey espionage thrills to make Night of a Thousand Stars a romantic, exciting adventure story. The politics and history of the region in that tumultuous time are well-explained, but never in a way that's boring or instructional. Instead, the intrigue serves as an exhilarating backdrop to Poppy and Sebastian's growing flirtation and affections, and the two play off each other marvelously, displaying the mingled exasperation and amusement you might encounter in an old movie a la The African Queen. 
 While Night of a Thousand Stars works as a stand-alone novel, characters from the author's earlier works (City of Jasmine, the Lady Julia books) are referenced. There's no reason that you couldn't enjoy Night on its own, but if you're so inclined, I'd recommend reading City of Jasmine (and its companion novella, Whisper of Jasmine) first. 
 Overall, I found Night of a Thousand Stars to be a fun, engaging, romantic read. If you're a fan of romantic espionage tales, don't miss it!

Well, let me start by saying that I am a MORON - and this is SO ME (I usually do this with movies but apparently it has now extended to books) - b/c I missed a major plot point that occurs at the very beginning of the book. (The main character kills someone, and I thought who she kills was a mystery, but you are supposed to know who it is.) I figured it out later but it definitely impacted the way I read the book. Fortunately for me and the book, I think I might actually have liked it even less had I read it properly, but who can say? So my caveat is that basically my whole review is tainted by my stupidity. 
 Overall, I reject the tagline of the book and found the primary plot device very problematic. The plot device is that each time the character dies, she comes back and lives life over again, and tagline is, "What if you had the chance to live your life again and again, until you finally got it right?" However, that's not actually what happens, because unlike in, say, Groundhog Day, in which the main character learns from his mistakes and improves the next time around, the main character in this novel is not consciously aware of what she's going through. She struggles with deju vu and somehow knows unconsciously to avoid certain events in her next life, but there is no conscious learning, which to me kind of defeats the whole point. The other main problem I saw is that major plot points that didn't even have to do with the main character also changed - how would that have been possible? It was not well explained. The most prime/annoying example of that for me was  when her parents decide to keep Izzy's baby. The main character was still a baby and other than the fact that she lived instead of died, how could she have influenced that choice?  The way she formatted the device changed, as well - it went primarily in chronological order, and then when the character died she went back to where it would have changed and started over. However, at one point she jumped far ahead and I was completely turned off and didn't understand what I had missed, and other times it didn't work exactly the same, either. The book was also long and I read it over a week or so and could not even remember which life she was on, what had changed, etc. 
 I found the first 20% or so fairly interesting except that her deaths/rebirths did not seem to change anything. Then it jumped really far ahead in her life which made me feel disconnected and that I had missed something (I really hadn't, that time!). Then I just started getting annoyed with everything I listed above. I also thought the inclusion of the historical figure and her impact on history was cheesy - especially since it didn't show the impact of what happened after she changed it. (I guess we were just supposed to assume that things got better.) This made me compare it to 11/22/63, in which he changes history but you get to see the impact that it made, which I thought was much better. I then enjoyed the end again, because it sort of ran through every aspect of her life and how she managed to side-step all of her previous issues (still though, without her really being conscious of what she was doing or why). Then the very end fell flat for me again.  Apparently she didn't stick with the history-changing life as her ending, and chose Teddy's life instead, but I was unclear on how the history change would NOT have saved Teddy's life or how whatever she did in the subsequent life DID save it. Also, were we supposed to know who was responsible for the missing girls? I never figured that out.  I feel like even besides my big miss at the beginning that there may have been a lot I missed or didn't understand (maybe in part b/c I didn't really like it and may have been reading too fast?). I had some questions about the ending which I discussed in the spoiler above. Maybe I was too dumb for this book, but I don't think I'm generally a stupid person so if it was that confusing, maybe that's at least somewhat the author's fault and not just my own? 
 As you can see, there is plenty to discuss, whether you like it or not. I can't remember the last time I wrote such a long review for a book I didn't really like. I might not personally recommend the book as the most enjoyable read because of everything I disliked about it, but it's certainly a good book to discuss with others and I therefore might still recommend it as a book club selection (not for my own book club, since I already read it, but for others).

 Don't fucking call this a rip-off or a knockoff-read of The Hunger Games or else I'll seriously punch you. Okay, I'm not making a threat here, haha, I'm just kidding. But really, the haters need to back off. Just because the summary makes it sound like there's a game and in order for there to be one winner, everyone has to die, THAT DOESN'T MEAN ANYTHING, OKAY? This book was honestly fucking amazing--and here is a long list of reasons why this isn't like THG in any way: 
 1. This doesn't have ONE protagonist--there's many protagonists, basically one per every Player. 
 Basically, we don't have a Katniss Everdeen here. There are so many characters here who we get a least a few chapters of thoughts of to really get to know them. It was actually really easy to remember who they were because Frey and Johnson-Shelton created such memorable characters. 
 2. This wasn't your average dystopian world where everyone's poor and there's Factions or Districts or whatever. 
 In a way, this is like a present-based atmosphere with the Endgame there to balance the population. In fact for Sarah, she was at her graduating ceremony when the meteor hit, so like, yes this was very believable. Piano lessons and soccer and high school were a thing in this book. 
 3. It wasn't all about killing everyone and being the last one left. 
 Here, you have to find the Earth Key and the Sky Key and the keys in order to achieve your winning. And if you die, it's not only your soul that dies--it's every single person in your bloodline. Imagine if you were part of the biggest bloodline in the world and something happens... 
 And yes, those are just some of the ways how it differs. But it's a completely different novel and I just want to throw my head against the nearest wall when I see people hating on it. Endgame was such a racing and captivating novel that I devoured in one sitting, remembering that it's such a long book. 
 You see, you'd think that the key idea of this would be really difficult to understand as there's many POVs and locations and everything--but this was my kind of novel. There're puzzles and mysteries and after finishing it, I feel so dumb, especially since there's some repetition pattern and puzzle that the authors want the public to solve for a grand prize of $500,000. Like really, how amazing is that? 
 So every once in a while when the population is too high for the world to hold or when there's too much war, the Endgame begins. You don't know when, and you never expect it to happen, but there's always people training and getting ready. You're eligible when you're ages 13 to in your twenties, and after that, you can go on with your life living normally. All 12 Players never saw it coming, but they were chosen randomly. There are 12 different bloodlines in the world, and each Player comes from one of them. Die or lose the Endgame, your entire bloodline dies as well. It's as simple as that. And all you need to do is search the world, looking for the keys and solve the puzzle. 
 "He has a new friend. The beautiful Player of the 233rd. A new friend. Maybe more." 
 It's been a little over a week since I finished this (as I'm writing this review) and I still can't get my thoughts together. As I'm seeing my friends in school, I feel like all I'm talking about is this book and how they should read it. I even heard that a MOVIE may be coming out for this one? It's already got so much fame in such little time, and I'm clapping my hands rapidly as I feel so proud for that matter hehe. 
 Okay--so this is such a kick-ass story.You have 12 teenagers who basically get to travel the world to win a game, wherever they'd like to. They all come from different races, countries, cultures, and they meet in China where everything begins. I guess you can say that they all have their own special talents--there's even a bomb maker. Now you can really realize and accept the fact that your talent can help you. ;) 
 It was so amazing because as you're in the middle half of the book, you sincerely realize that someone will get the Earth Key and you're wondering who it'll be... And the theories begin sprouting up in your mind. I KIND OF SAW IT COMING BUT THEN IT WAS LIKE THEY STOLE IT. They basically ran and grabbed it from someone who sincerely needed it and then they killed that person. AND I LOVED THAT PERSON! 
 After I finished reading, I originally thought of this to be a 4.5 star rating for me as there were some dull moments in the middle, but then I thought about how the ending made up for it and how much I really adored and became obsessed with the book. This is probably going to be one of the best books of the year coming from me. 
 My favourite character was Chiyoko. She was so kick-ass and worked so well on her own, not needing Sarah or some other guy with her. (BUT HER LOVE WITH AN-LIU, THOUGH!) Really, Frey and Johnson-Shelton both created amazing character-development and even KILLED OFF SUCH AMAZING CHARACTERS LIKE IT WAS NO BIG DEAL. But that's a little better, because we never saw it coming, unlike THG. 
 "As she says that, a part of Sarah hopes it isn't true. She hopes this is just a wild teenage whim and that she's no actually falling for Jago. Falling in love with a rival would be about the worst thing that could happen. But then they kiss. And kiss. And kiss. And Sarah forgets." 
 AHH OMG SARAH AND JAGO WERE SO CUTE. And remember that checking scene and Sarah blushing and wanting to see more? I began fanning myself. Too bad she had an obsessive addicted psychopath guy at her shoulders stalking her because she left him for good and he loves her too much. Some people have to let go, no? 
 So this book was perfect and gorgeous and fast-paced and I was left shocked at the end of every chapter. Frey and Johnson-Shelton are such amazing writers, and I'd pay a million dollars to get a peek at the sequel, because I just can't wait. 2015 is going to be an amazing year for great books, I can already tell. I'LL BE AT THE MOVIE PREMIERE ON THE RED CARPET, PEOPLE.

So Atlanta continued to grow, the trains continued to disgorge new residents and the tenements grew more crowded and the moonshine continued to be driven down from the mountains and the streets spilled over with even yet more passion and schemes and brawls, because there on the Georgia piedmont something had been set loose that might never again be contained. 
 Darktown is a great, immersive, complex work of historical fiction wrapped around a slightly unstable but still enjoyable mystery. It has a large cast, with nearly everyone eventually getting a small segment of the novel from their point of view, but the two central figures are Officer Lucius Boggs, one of the first eight black police officers in Atlanta, and Officer Dennis Rakestraw, a shading-towards-liberal white cop perturbed by his partner's violence. They're partnered up with Tommy Smith, more openly passionate than Boggs, and Dunlow, a veteran and viciously racist patrolman proud of his familiarity with and control of "Darktown." The four of them intersect one night when Boggs and Smith call in for white patrol officers to arrest a man who has run into a streetlight--black cops had virtually no authority over white criminals. ("'Stop or I'll call the real cops'?" Smith shook his head. "Funny how that don't work.") Rake is willing, but Dunlow isn't, and nothing is done. Meanwhile, the young black woman with the bruised lip in the passenger seat of the car has disappeared. 
 She resurfaces, having been shot in the chest, and neither Boggs nor Rake can let it go. Boggs wants to protect his community, and his time on the job has disillusioned him as to the likelihood of that: solving Lily Ellsworth's murder would be a concrete and valuable accomplishment, especially when it's done in the face of an utterly indifferent white authority. Rake, on the other hand, mostly wants to differentiate himself from his partner's callousness--without attracting too much attention or conceding "too much" equality. Their separate investigations twist throughout the book and their eventual information-sharing is productive but tentative, with Rake openly surprised by how much Boggs and Smith were able to find out on their own. (He thanks Boggs for helping him with "his" investigation.) 
 The complexity of the characterization and the richness of the historical setting are the two great strengths of Darktown. While the supporting characters never quite make the leap into three dimensions (And as much as I genuinely appreciate multifaceted antagonists, Dunlow's lengthy monologue to Rake about his past love of a black child who died feels both cheap and way too neat ), Boggs and Rakestraw are really well-handled. Boggs is a minister's son struggling with the knowledge that even perfection will probably not be enough to ensure that he's treated with respect by his ostensible colleagues and in the meantime facing occasional derision from people in his community who either think that he's sold out or think that he's not willing to go far enough. Even his own partner is perturbed by Boggs's careful lack of expression. But all the calculation that has gone into his every move serves him well as he tries to find the truth behind Lily Ellsworth's murder, and the further he goes, the more he's willing to risk. Rake, too, knows about being careful, but he's being careful because he wants to walk the line between commitments: better than his partner's open racism, violence, and corruption, but still ambivalent about a black family moving into his neighborhood and distasteful of patrolling black areas. He expects credit for standing up to his partner at all. He looks into the Ellsworth murder out of the desire to prove he's a good person and because he suspect his partner's involvement. 
 The attention to the detail of Boggs's community and Rake's lukewarm liberalism is part of how well Mullen renders 1950s Atlanta as a whole, ever attentive to the details of the maddening rules the black police officers have to follow--they can't wear their uniforms to or from work, directly submit their own reports, or reliably pull arrest records--and the grinding effect they have on Boggs and Smith. But the city--and eventually some of the countryside--come alive even apart from that, with Rake using Southern hospitality as an in to places where he's not really wanted and a YMCA owner giving his basement over to the police to prevent further break-ins. It's an illusion, I'm sure, and of course I'm not an expert, but at times it feels like there's nothing Mullen has forgotten to account for. 
 The plotting and mystery don't quite live up to everything else--the plot resolutions come a little too quickly and haphazardly, with some fairly pointless stalling: there's no need to imply a character has been shot only to have them alive a few scenes later and then find out a few scenes after that the truth behind the coy implication, and overall Mullen uses that "then she told us everything" approach where the characters learn truths that the reader isn't permitted to overhear too much. There's one pretty amazing coincidence. Certain conspiratorial actions don't quite cohere as part of a reasonable plan. 
 But most of these flaws only surface at the end, and the time we spend with Boggs and Rakestraw following their separate investigations is time well-spent, even if it doesn't resolve with too much impact. The point is for the case to resolve and the emotions to stay messy. And indeed the novel ends with Boggs more aware of his frustration but going about the life-long process of containing it and taking what achievements he can, with Rake taking full credit (and no little blame) for solving the case and letting Dunlow's sons get away with burning down the house of the black family in their neighborhood. But Boggs has a date, which is nice, and a better relationship with his immediate supervisor.  I immediately Googled "Darktown Thomas Mullen sequel" and was disappointed not to see one already in the works. Fingers crossed, though.

This is a book about bad people. That's the first thing the reader needs to know. Almost everyone in the book has some skeletons in their closet or in the well near their childhood home  and it is delightful seeing them all be awful to each other. 
 This book wasn't groundbreaking, but it was fun. Once I got into it, it was difficult to put down. A lot of the plot twists can be called fairly early on, but there were some in there that actually surprised me. 
 The general gist of the book is that Ted meets a beautiful red-headed woman on a plane trip home, and he confesses to her that he knows his wife is cheating on him and that he wishes to kill her. The woman, Lily, surprises him by going along with the idea, and telling him she will help. They make plans to meet and things spiral out of control from there. 
 My main problem with this book isn't its extreme coincidences (that's just often part of these types of books, and they lampshade it from time to time so I am not too bothered by it) but the fact that some of the writing is...well, dude writing . I don't mean the writing is bad! Most of the time, it is good and has a nice flow to it. But then there are passages like this: 
 "...you could tell she was pretty, and had probably once been beautiful. Natural blond hair, blue eyes, and large breasts that she was showing off in a V-neck shirt and cardigan sweater. The portion of her chest that was visible was deeply tanned and freckled." 
 When I read descriptions like that, whether they are written by a guy or not, I just have to roll my eyes. Not that I'm not guilty of writing in a similar fashion, mind. 
 That minor nitpick aside, I thoroughly enjoyed this book and would recommend it, like most other people reviewing it, to fans of Gone Girl or Girl on the Train (though the book should really have "girl" in the title if it wants to make it big in the book club world. The Girl Worth Killing maybe? I digress.)

Bound by Honor starts out with us learning that Aria is being forced to marry Luca "The Vice" Vitiello through an arranged marriage between two feuding Italian mafia gangs. Aria's father has betrothed her at only age fifteen to Luca, whom she is to marry at eighteen. Aria sees Luca as a monster, a killer, whom she has nothing in common with and she is terrified to marry him. Their wedding is not about love, it is only about Aria being a good daughter and living up to her duty as a female in the mafia circle. 
 This started off interesting but it lost two stars immediately due to the cheating. I just can't believe Luca cheated on his wife only a few days after their wedding! Such a turn-off...I am not sure what the author was thinking. She used cheating as a way to actually bring Luca and Aria back together after they had been avoiding each other and made it a tool to have them actually talk about their relationship, but Aria was such a completely naive doormat. She forgave Luca instantly for no reason. She was a bit too naive, meek, and timid for my liking. 
 Another star was lost because I did not like the slut-shaming in this novel. It wasn't too extreme but Luca called Grace a whore for no reason, and he called the girls he used to sleep with sluts. Umm okay, what does that make you then Luca? A huge manwhore and slut, womaniser, and player? Not exactly qualities I like in the main love interest... 
 I also found their whole mafia world fascinating. It was incredibly sad, women basically being sold off as slaves, their virginity up for auction and worshipped by the men in a creepy way. I can't say I found any of this romantic, but it was a very interesting and unique plot. 
 I have a feeling the next novels might prove to be better, especially Gianna and Matteo. Aria's sister definitely isn't timid and I have a feeling I will like their story a lot more. The next novel Bound by Duty is about Dante and Valentina. We barely got to see Dante in this novel, I have no idea what his personality is like but Valentina seemed interesting, so we will see where the series goes!

 - Violet's grandmother's diaries - Through these diaries Violet learns more about herself, her abilities and the organization she works for. 
 - More mystery/insight into the organization - Although it was clear in the previous book that the organization that Dr. Lee, Sara, and Violet works for isn't completely benign, we're given more substantive clues. I can't wait to learn more about the original group of men and women with special abilities and the organization's ulterior motives. 
 - Violet's growth - Violet has this terrible habit of closing herself off from her family, friends, team members and Jay. In this book she's forced to deal with this and make a decision. I am looking forward to seeing how she works with her team members. 
 - Jay, Jay and more Jay. Jay is loving, protective, and loyal but he's not a doormat. He knows when enough is enough and puts his foot down.
