 I have to admit, I was a little apprehensive when I started Dare You To. Beth was definitely a prickly character in Pushing the Limits and I wasn't sure how I'd take to her in this one. I was wrong! In classic Katie McGarry fashion, she writes fantastic characters and stories and relationships that pull you in and doesn't let you go! 
 In Dare You To, Beth Risk is forced to go live with her uncle after an unfortunate incident after which she's forced to choose to protect her mom or herself. She chooses to protect her mom because that's what she's done her entire life -- she takes care of her, drags her back home after she passes out at the bar and tries her hardest to shield her from her mom's piece-of-crap, abusive boyfriend. Heavy burdens for a 17 year girl. It really made my heart ache. 
 So she ends up in another town, in a new school and she struggles like a fish out of water. Who knew that the one person to make her feel wanted would be the one person that seems like her complete opposite -- perfect, put together, all star baseball player Ryan Stone. You know, I don't even like baseball but I would watch Ryan Stone pitch ANY day. 
 I really liked how Dare You To showed that sometimes, no matter how hard you try, you can't take care of people that don't want to be taken care of. Sometimes, you have to let people go in order to be able to live yourself. You have to be able to recognize that you can't always save people all by yourself. Beth has spent so much time protecting her mom, covering for her from the law, that she doesn't see in the long run that it can be damaging. She loves her and just wants to take care of her... Beth's tale is one of knowing when to stop running and when to start living and trust. Ryan's is one of self discovery and finding himself apart from what his parents want of him. His life may be perfection to the outside observer but it is quite the opposite. Having no one to tell, he takes to writing. I loved how Ryan was three dimensional -- not just a jock but also smart and an amazing writer to boot. 
 Beth and Ryan's love story is beautiful. I love how Katie's writing just sucks you in. I was so invested in these characters and their lives, I just wanted them to be able to figure it out and start to heal! 
 The swoon factor... Ryan Stone is hot. And, yes, Katie can sure write those kisses! So, ever since forever, I have been obsessed with rain kisses. Pouring rain, soaked to the skin, type kisses. 
 Well, Katie wrote one of the best kisses of all time. It is going up there on my list of favorite kisses ever! And it really was one of my favorite scenes in the book. Three words: bottle of rain. My heart kind of melted and yours will too! 
 Katie McGarry has a way of writing that makes each of her characters so real and I feel like I know them and I care about them! She brings such life and emotion to their stories. I absolutely adore her writing, you must read this. I dare you to! =)

Right--another Kagawa review. It's starting to become habit; I should've known, seeing how gleefully ecstatic I was when I saw the Iron Queen cover. I should've known... 
 Some Background 
 The Lost Prince--as has been mentioned numerous times by the reviewers and the blurb--is a spin-off from the Iron Fey series. Spin-offs, usually, lead to tears and disappointment; and the Lost Prince--though hardly disappointing--does have some flaws because of this. 
 For one, our new protagonist-in-chief--monsieur Ethan Chase, whiny teenager extraordinaire and surprising brother of Meghan--is, to put it quite bluntly, a pain in the arse. And this, my dear, is coming from another teenager. 
 Anyway: our new character is Ethan Chase, and his girlfriend Kenzie. Thankfully, Julie has not left our old darlings from the Iron Fey a stranded--Meghan, Ash, Grimalkin and Puck all make notable appearances (particularly the latter two) and we even get the charming Leanansidhe starring. It's all one big party, right? 
 Well, not quite... 
 Characters 
 Since the perhaps greatest difference between the Iron Fey and this usurper is that of the characters, it seems fitting to start with them first. 
 Firstly: Ethan. As mentioned, he's whiny. But--unlike most teenagers--he's not whiny because he's not getting everything he's entitled to, or some other false stereotype. No: Ethan is angry--angry to be without his sister (whom he still holds dearly, despite thinking her to be some cold faerie queen a la Mab), angry that the Fae won't leave him alone (he's constantly whingeing about that) and really... angry that he's ineluctably tied to the strange, fabulous world that is Faerie. 
 Since this is a decent enough reason to be whiny, I could just about tolerate him. He's also got some good traits to him: he's tough, he's good with a sword, and he's really a nice enough guy behind that exterior. 
 Even so, I can't help but feel disappointed. It's not just the constant anger--often directed at himself, too--or all the fear and mistrust of the Fae. It's not even the lack of awe; of wonder, to be able to experience this extraordinary hidden world. (Though that does annoy me, make no mistake.) No: what annoys me is that he isn't as good a character as Meghan--not as loving, not as powerfully determined, not as magical--or, for that matter, Ash. 
 Honestly, I enjoy the other characters more than him. Grimalkin is a far more amusing personality; Puck, genuinely hillarious; Leanansidhe, so wonderfully charming; the Forgotten Queen, so complex a character... 
 That's the irony, with this book. All of the characters are great, except for the main characters. That kinda defeats the point, don't it? 
 Kenzie, now, Kenzie! In many ways she was a much more likable character than her brooding boyfriend (indeed she jokes about this, to great effect: 'Tough guy, if brooding were a sport, you'd have gold medals with scowling faces lining the walls of your room'). I enjoy her charm, vivacity; but also her strength, her ability to see what is great in the world. 
 My only point of complaint (yes, I am such a nitpicking bastard; shoot me, why don't you?) is that she's too dependent on Mr Brooding to keep her safe. In part I can understand this (most people don't need to kill faeries) but it does play into the hands of that tired old trope: the princess in need of saving, and the knight ready to do it. I would have thought Kagawa would know better. 
 Finally: Kierran. Our three quarter human, one quarter Iron, Winter and Summer faerie; and all trouble prodigy. He's... slightly disappointing. Sure, his powers are awesome; his personality, unusual, charming, and surprisingly gentle. But he doesn't set your pulse a-racing the way Ash did (does?). He's not the deadly, entrancing faerie you think he is. 
 And his love of Annwyl, the Summer girl? Not the best matchup. In fact, I found it rather tedious. 
 All in all, I'm glad to be re-acquainted with the Iron characters. But of these new characters, I remain to be convinced. 
 Plot 
 This new foe--these Forgotten Ones--are excellent. For one, they're a great way to tie up that old knot (by turning them into an entirely new series--have to admire Kagawa's creativity). For two, they're genuinely fucking scary. This is good. 
 The plot, as usual, leaves no error in pacing; no overly drawn out moments, or scenes drawn too hastily. In this regard it excels. 
 Nevertheless, I found the finale... slightly anti-climatic. For that matter, I found the manner by which it was reached anti-climatic. This is not because of the antagonist--for she, thankfully, was both deeply frightening and yet somehow utterly fascinating--but because the motivation and mode of action of the protagonists just reeked of naivety and foolishness. Kierran, in particular, seemed a fool to be so easily lured; a fact exacerbated by the already lukewarm love affair. 
 I also found Ethan's deliberations for Todd mildly irritating. This is not because I didn't understand why (for Ethan is still a determined do-gooder) but because I found Todd himself to be terribly unlikeable. 
 That's the weakness of the plot--it can be anticlimatic, yes, but mainly it is character-driven, and lacks suitably motivated characters. 
 On a side-note, I found Kierran's willingness to collaborate with the Forgotten Queen disturbing, and bizarre. I am left to wonder whether he is indeed under the thrall of some magic. Also, I do wish Ethan would drop the ever-tedious mistrust of faeries and open-up to his nephew. But, let us move on... 
 Writing 
 I am pleased to note that Kagawa's writing tic--the excessive use of double similes, as mentioned in my previous review--no longer makes an appearance: the book flows smoothly and without hiccups. 
 In terms of aesthetic prose, we are treated to very little; but aesthetic prose is no prequisitry to a good book, and indeed may be considered counterproductive for the Lost Prince. Still: I would have enjoyed more vivid imagery of Faerie. I complain of this with every Iron book, though--and since I'm always back for more, I can only guess the realm of Faerie is deeply captivating regardless. 
 In other ways, Kagawa's writing is fluent but unremarkable. Though there are a few wonderful snippets--Puck, unsurprisingly, being the source--it is clear Kagawa isn't a master of punchy one-liners. Then again: greatness is not perfection, and this book comes rather close in the latter. 
 Conclusion 
 Allow me to be brief: the Lost Prince is in many ways an exciting book. It contains much of the same old magic that imbued former works; and it's got an entirely new direction. It does leave wanting in terms of Ethan's and Kierran's character, but this is their first book; a great deal is yet to be seen. 
 My rating is ultimately a benefit of the doubt. And now, if you'll excuse me, I have a sequel to read...

Wow, just wow! 
 First thing readers need to know is that this is not a romance novel. It is a brilliant story of obsession, manipulation, and utter madness. 
 It is the story of Joe and his twisted perspective on what love is. Its the type of obsessive love that would send any sane person running, but in Joe's mind, he is the ultimate romantic lover. 
 Joe Goldberg works in a bookshop where he judges the customers literary choices, and believes that he is far more superior in his knowledge and taste. 
 Enter Guinevere Beck. An aspiring writer who moved to New York on a scholarship. 
 She makes the unfortunate decision to walk into Joe's bookshop, and in Joe's twisted mind, there is an instant connection. 
 I've had the choice of either reading it, or listening to an audio book, I chose the later. I believe that in this book's case, listening to it has made it creepier [for me at least]. Santino Fontana has done a wonderful job narrating this book, he really brought Joe to life. 
 This books also makes you question your online privacy, and not in a subtle way. All Joe needed to find out everything about Beck's life, is access to her social media accounts. He used all this information to insert himself in her life in a way she couldn't escape him, even if she wanted.. He knew EVERYTHING about her and made himself appear to be what she really wants. In front of our eyes, Joe turns from a stalker, to a friend, and then becomes a boyfriend. 
 Caroline Kepnes has done a brilliant job with this book, I couldn't believe that this was her debut novel! I can't wait for part 2, Hidden Bodies. She managed to give Joe the ability to pull us into his world, make his insanity appear normal (even if it was just for a few moments), and we even develop a bit of misguided sympathy. 
 This book is one of my ultimate favorites in 2015, I highly recommend it. A small warring though, it contains some strong adult language and swearing, but I hope that wouldn't stop you from enjoying this awesome book.

Her hero is reasonably typical of her work, but I did like that despite his gruff ways and rude behaviour, he was very capable of understanding the heroine's feelings and giving her space to work them out. 
 I recognise a lot of this stuff from Heyer's other novels, though, which is a little sad. I hope I'm not coming to the end of my love affair with Heyer's work, with thirteen(ish?) novels left to go! But since I've read them in no particular order, that's not very likely -- and there is still something compelling about even the least of Heyer's work, from the silliest of her characters to the most rakish.

Everything that annoys me in YA series is not in this book! to a minimum... 
 Nina Kane struggles to survive and care for her sister and mother. She will go through any means to support the two of them. When she finds out her sister Melanie committed a horrible sin, her life suddenly goes for the worst. Let me rephrase that. Her sister's sin was just the beginning of a horrible situation, not the cause. Within one day Nina finds herself amongst a group of runaway teenagers who are real exorcists. 
 The world building and setting was executed brilliantly. I rarely go into depth about the setting because most of them are either the same or not that great. But this one was amazing. If you've read The Handmaid's Tale by Atwood, it's similar to that. 
 After demons attacked the souls of millions of people, the Church stepped in and saved the day. Because of this, they now run the country and society. The future has reverted back to Puritan era. Of course everyone knows the Church isn't the most reliable or credible organization. (Back off ya damn Christians!) I didn't care much how much they repressed people. I was impressed about the soul giving part. Each baby needs a soul donated to them in order to live. For example, a grandparent would sacrifice their soul (life) for their grandchild. It makes having a soul more meaningful. The exchange presents a conflict that would resurface later in the series but it raises a philosophical question. Would you sacrifice your life for an innocent newborn? Another part I was surprised by was the sterilization of young girls. At 15, girls go through an exam where if they aren't a suitable carrier, then they will be sterilized. That is some hard stuff. Who does the church think they are by saying I can't have kids because of a few imperfections? 
 Now the subject of demons. I haven't really read books regarding demons, but how they explained them was amazing. 
 Let's go back to the actually story. What YA cliche was debunked? Well, when the protagonist is thrown into a situation where she is exposed to something new and unnerving, of course she'll have a series of questions. Sometimes they'll be annoying and demand the questions now or the person helping them will refuse to answer anything. Thank GOD this didn't happen. Finn, who is the first to help Nina, sits her down and explains everything in a calm setting. Nothing is going on so we can focus on the situation. 
 The romance...the romance...the...romance. It was unique. The romance was obvious and happened quickly. However I liked the set up and the issues it will offer. Finn's condition is going to create a problem with the relationship. 
 Overall, the book left enough out to have you want to continue on. I can't wait for the next book and I will consider reading the author's other works because she knows what she's writing.

Yup. I admit it. I picked up Shadow Lands thinking it will be an awesome YA thriller. For weeks now, I've been craving for a book that incorporates Taken (starring Liam Neeson) elements, because damn, psychological thrillers are just so much fun, you know? I wanted something that was capable of gripping my heart at its throat, a book that could leave me in so much suspense and action, and I absolutely hoped that Shadow Lands would be the answer to that longing. If you're in the same shoes I had back then, let me tell you this now - don't let the synopsis fool you. This book was a disappointment, and I'll tell you why. 
 Psychological Thriller? Um. 
 I'll give credit where credit is due - Shadowlands had a pretty awesome and mean start that will get you certainly pumped up with excitement. Here we have a serial killer who takes on many identities to get closer to his victims, an uncanny ability of his that allowed him to get away from the authorities such as the FBI for at least a decade. Finally, at the opening chapter, he decided to finally reveal his true colors and take his kill, Rory becoming his 15th victim. Having luck at her side, she was able to escape and call for help, and consequently got her and her family into a witness protection program courtesy of the FBI to a new town somewhere out there. 
 It could've been good. I tell you, it could've been good, but it fell short really fast and really hard. Reiterating what Wendy Darling said in her review, the plot "...quickly devolves into a cable movie of the week thriller with flat characters and an uninspired storyline..." I think I became disappointed mainly because I wanted a real thriller in a contemporary setting, but instead we get thrown into an all new, weird town in the middle of nowhere with obviously supernatural elements. The reader gets the feeling that everything is going a little too well, and that there must be something fishy about this place, that something just isn't right. There is something off about the place, and of course the mystery is revealed at the very end (literally). But the thing is, in these scenarios, you're supposed to keep the reader guessing - you're supposed to keep them hanging, damnit. This is where the "mystery" ends, I guess, because everything is just so damn obvious from the get-go. I won't say what they were, but the author left several clues behind, which were clever I admit, but didn't have any discreetness of any kind to make the huge ending a surprise. Sure, I got a WTF moment at the end, but it was more of an exclamation of annoyance than of awe. 
 I also thought there were too many scenes and situations that were put there just for the heck of it and served no purpose at all, making it feel like the plot was just dragging in an attempt to prolong the "suspense"... And you know what sucks more? The plot could've been wrapped up in one book. But no. We get this ridiculous, dragging premise, with obvious clues all over the place, a bizarre ending... and... and there's supposed to be more, but why there's supposed to be more does not make sense at all. I think there would have been more impact if the story ended right there and then after the big revelation. Certainly, there are still lingering questions, but right now in the state I'm in, I don't think I want to be bothered to know the answers to those. 
 "I'm not beautiful but all the hot guys like me" 
 OK, so Rory considers herself inferior looks-wise compared to her gorgeous sister, Darcy. She's a "nerdy science geek", wears a t-shirt flaunting Einstein's theory of relativity, and has pretty much low self-esteem. But not only did she get to attract her sister's handsome boyfriend, Christopher, but every boy she met in her new town kept on glancing at her, too. While I'm okay with all the supernatural shiz going on, I find myself uneasy with this. I couldn't buy it, and sometimes I get frustrated whenever she reminded herself that she wasn't not as pretty as Darcy or she that she's a nerdy geek, so how could they like her?!. Ugh. Whatever. 
 ...and etc. 
 There were many illogical stuff going on in this book. First of all, if you're going to be under a Witness Protection Program, shouldn't the FBI be more meticulous and careful in transporting you to somewhere else? They were portrayed very poorly here, and made them look like a bunch of incompetent nincompoops. Most characters were very 2-dimensional as well, and lacked character depth. The sister is a gorgeous senior who loves partying, and fuck you if you keep her from her parties. She is the gorgeous one, the guys go ga-ga for, and it's simply 
 unacceptable 
 that her sister is getting all the attention from the hot guys. Like, seriously, right?! 
 Uh-huh. 
 Overall, this was a pretty frustrating and bizarre book. I get what the author is trying to do here, and in some ways, it worked... but the opposite thing happened to me, and right now, I'm more annoyed than anything else and don't want to be bothered with the succeeding books anymore. If what I said don't bother you, you may want to read this, but please, read with caution.

"It's almost insurmountable. I don't know how to tell them something like this and still come out of it feeling like Simon." 
 Buddy Read with the delightful Bella 
 I was dubious about this novel. The title and the blurb gave me the impression it would be either stuffed full of angst and a depressing slog or a trite and misjudged attempt at being "topical". 
 I have no idea why I was so harshly prejudging Simon vs. but I'm so glad Bella picked it because this is a hilarious, uplifting story which manages to be incredibly honest, without veering into cynicism OR hallmark territory. 
 "Oh my God," says Leah. "It's happening. We're finally witnessing something more painful than Nick's bar mitzvah." 
 "Awkwardness achievement unlocked." 
 "Should we be filming this?" 
 "Just savor it." 
 And it was funny. There were so many times I giggled or groaned because it was relatable, cringe worthy and totally hilarious. 
 The characters were well drawn and diverse. I wanted to give them all a hug. The other thing I loved was how believable they all are. There were instances where the situations described were so relatable that I couldn't help nodding my head at "yes, that's true, I remember that feeling/ situation/ conversation. It felt authentic. It was a massive cut above YA novels with their quippy, painfully confident super model stars a.k.a Cassandra Clare style. 
 I only have one quibble and it was a structural one. All the plot points were resolved by page 160 in a 200 page book. That extra 40 pages was a very sweet love fest but all narrative urge had evaporated and the denouncement felt too long for what was a very slim narrative. 
 The other niggle was I guessed who Blue was the second time we met him irl (as opposed to the emails). I probably sound like a bit of a wanker cause I feel like I say this stuff a lot- but it just seemed so clearly telegraphed. I didn't mind it, it made for some nerve wracking and exciting reading moments- although the email where he described Cal instead of who Blue really is I was just dying from horror... omg noooo O_o 
 Overall this was a positive, feel good coming of age story. 
 Recommend for: people who enjoy contemporary fiction, people looking for positive, uplifting stories about LGBT protagonists, teenagers 12+ 
 Other books you might like if you enjoyed Simon vs.: Unbecoming, Looking for Alibrandi.

Shattered King is a sexy, suspenseful second chance romance. Hunter King spent 3 long years in prison for a crime he didn't commit. And the worst part is that he was put there by the one person he never thought would betray him - the love of his life, Lulu (Lucinda), who took off after she sent him to prison. But now that he's out, he's determined to get some answers from her, even if he has to kidnap her to get those answers. 
 In the beginning of Shattered King, Hunter was full of vengeful anger toward Lulu, and he treated her like she was a common whore. He literally kidnapped her, held her hostage and screwed her as if she was a prostitute with no dignity. I can't say I liked him too much at that point. Yes, he was angry at her perceived betrayal, but really? Kidnapping, holding her hostage and using her obvious attraction for him against her, all with no care for her physical and emotional state?!?! Nope, just nope! 
 But, as time went on and Hunter realized that Lulu had no choice back when she put him away, he was all in and his true alpha tendencies took over and that's when he redeemed himself. I never fell in love with him the way Lulu obviously did, but I could finally see the attraction. He was a sexy, protective, dirty talking, dirty doing man whom she loved, so of course she couldn't resist falling back in love with him. Well, she never fell out of love with him, so I'd guess she just finally gave into those feelings. Can't exactly blame her for that, but sometimes I wanted her to be stronger and resist him so it'd maybe slap some sense into him in the beginning. 
 I do have one minor little quibble and it's that as sexy as they are together, sometimes I felt as if the sex scenes were a little too plentiful. I wanted a little more dialogue and emotional times, and a little less sex. Sometimes, ok, MOST of the time, they used sex as communication, and it got a little old after awhile. Other than that, though, I like Shattered King. Both Lulu and Hunter are interesting, vibrant characters and their chemistry is smokin hot. The pacing is good and the action is enough to help propel the story along when it started to lag a little. 
 I really like the world Sherilee Gray has created with Hunter, his brother Van and their associates and am looking forward to more. The excerpt of Neco (Hunter's friend and associate) and Ruby's story (Broken Rebel) sounds like it's going to be even better than Hunter and Lulu's story, can't wait to read it!

This would make a terrific graphic novel or action movie. I enjoyed it while it lasted and was so ready for it to be over because nothing really changes. I think for a dystopian setting that works extremely well. 
 My only complaint is the pacing. It almost moved TOO fast for me. There some places where I just wanted a little more dialogue or an "extended scene" or something. Basically, just me being greedy and wanting more of the book. I hope in the next one there's more exploration of the cities outside this one, the other Queens's and populations. It was a very unique world combining royalty and a dystopian society and the next one has a lot of promise.

He sees her smiling with another guy and then gets the hell out of there? Didn't he wonder why she left in the first place?  I guess that Will needed some time to grow up into the man he was destined to be. What can I say? Men should and must fight for their women! Women are the hard ones to crack, after all. It's their job to do the cracking.. 
 ~~anyway 
 In conclusion, I liked the book! Rating it properly is quite hard for me, since I feel a little ambiguous about it. Don't get me wrong! Carey Heywood is a talented author and a good writer. Some points of the story could be better, regarding their reflection to reality. 
 In the end of the day, it is a good book about 2 people growing up into their own personalities and never falling out of love with each other, even though they weren't together. You can't challenge fate, after all...

The Dystopic/ Dystopian Cannon, what is on it? Here's my list, you can tell me what I'm missing. The review will follow. 
 1. We should probably start with Thomas More's Utopia. I've heard that "U"topia is a pun meaning both "good" place and "no" place, but what do I know? I didn't read the book, and it's Greek to me. 
 2. 1984 and Brave New World are tied because people are always arguing over which one is better - although it's pretty clear that 1984 wins out. 
 4. Fahrenheit 451 is next on the list, although I recently reread it, and while I was impressed by some of the technological advancements Bradbury mentioned - the shells for instance - I wasn't particularly impressed with the book. I was surprised that the book wasn't about the government burning books as much as people not reading them. 
 5. Anthem (I'm getting tired of writing tons of boring crap after each one, so I'll stop. You're welcome.) 
 6. The Handmaid's Tale 
 7. The Hunger Games 
 8. I'm lumping all other current YA dystopian fiction into number 8, so that's The Uglies, Divergent, The Maze Runner... am I forgetting any? Probably. 
 9. The Giver gets it's own spot. 
 10. The Road 
 Did I miss any? If so, let me know and I'll take it under advisement. Rest assured, this is THE definitive list. I, a random goodreads reviewer, am THE authority here. 
 *The Review* 
 In my estimation, this is the book in a nutshell: words matter. 
 The book is about a number of other things as well: freedom (from and to), love, religion, exploitation, feminism, obedience, propaganda, fundamentalism... but it all comes back to the premise that words matter. 
 Atwood makes this clear in a literary sense, as well as more or less overtly stating it. 
 For instance, she is constantly talking about etymologies, phraseology, expressions, and puns. This is constant, constant - like never ending. Constant, like in math a number that significant. It's funny, isn't it that she is constantly using this literary tactic - which can mean both significant in one sense, or it can mean ever-occuring in another. 
 "Steel yourself, my mother used to say, before examinations I didn't want to take or swims in cold water. I never thought that much about what the phrase meant, but it had something to do with metal, with armor, and that's what I would do, I would steel myself." p. 160 
 "Why is it that night falls, instead of rising, like the dawn? Yet if you look east..." p. 191 
 "I compose myself. My self is a thing I must now compose, as one composes a speech. What I must present is a made thing, not something born." p. 66 
 Basically, you can flip to any page of the book and find some such evidence of her thesis that words matter. 
 But she uses other tactics as well. When she plays games with the Commander, what does she play? Scrabble. Why Scrabble? Why not Monopoly, or Parcheesi, or Snakes and Freaking Ladders? Words matter. 
 And Atwood ties all of this into the other points/ social commentary of the book. Take love or religion for instance: 
 "The more difficult it was to love the particular man beside us, the more we believed in Love, abstract and total. We were waiting, always, for the incarnation. That word, made flesh." p. 226. Once again, it's about words. Words matter, in this case she's talking about love. Love. And religion. 
 John 1:1 "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." 
 1 John 4:8 "God is love." 
 "Incarnation" in this context is a very biblical and Christian reference. Atwood's commentary on religious fundamentalism, and Love stems from the argument that words matter. 
 What was her commentary on love and religion? In Evangelical/Fundamentalist Christian circles I don't think you can go a year without hearing a sermon or reference on the different types of love in the Greek language: agape, phileo, and eros. We could have a long discussion on what love is. Is it a choice? Is it sex? Is it commitment? I love sleep. I love poetry. I love my daughters. I love my wife. I love my students. I love reading. I don't love any of these things the same way. 
 I fully believe that one of the biggest components in love is commitment. And in The Handmaid's Tale, there was commitment. But that was about the only aspect of love left. Intimacy, and companionship were non-existent. Because words matter. Women weren't allowed to read the Bible to see the context of the passages. The changing of words and their meaning changed the culture, and irreparably damaged it. 
 People weren't allowed to speak out - to use words, and when the proverbial ball started rolling no one stood up for what was right. They were swept up in a media frenzy, and by the time they realized what was going on, the changes were already in place. 
 The Handmaid's Tale was decent as far as dystopic fiction goes. It's not high on the official cannon, but it's there. I had some problems with it: as in it didn't seem as realistic to me as 1984. (if you know what I mean...) Granted, I wasn't living in Iran in 1979 "the veil stands for freedom." 
 It also had some problems dating itself. I don't think 200 years in future people will be referring to the 1990s as "the 90s." And writing about the 80s in a faux-future that's already come and gone... well... it must have been difficult. 
 Last thing, I had the benefit of reading this with the Physical Plant Summer Book Club at Goshen College. If you made it this far into the review and you haven't gone to college yet, you may want to check them out. They've got a pretty sweet International Studies program and if their Phys. Plant has a summer book club, what's that say about their academics?

 Love is not easy. It's not always sunshine and rainbows. It comes down to very different people relating to one another. Like a conjoined twin, I think fear is a close companion to love. When we are young, we fear that you will never find the right person to love. When we find them, we fear that the other person will not love you back. When we have love, we always fear that this person who has become so vital to your world could be lost. The Rules of Magic is about love. Love between siblings, parents, children, lovers and friends. It is about letting your love flow freely, not bottling it up with fear, guilt, doubt or anger. 
 I loved this book. I was offered the ARC by the publisher through Netgalley. I vaguely remembered hearing about the first book in the series, Practical Magic, when the movie was released. I think Sandra Bullock was in it? I never got to see it, but ok! Knowing that The Rules of Magic was a prequel to that book I decided to read Practical Magic first. It is not necessary to do that, though I am glad I did. Both books can easily stand on their own. I think if I were to do it again, I would have read this book first and then Practical Magic. 
 Both books are a slow burn. It took a good 25% before the story really gets into swing. Don't misunderstand me, it is a good, well written 25%. The methodical layering of personal relationships between the characters and the world they live in takes skill and above all else time. 
 As the descendants of witches, the Owens family are magical people. I found them fascinating. They know everything about curses and charms. Which herbs will cure fever and which will shake loose an unwanted lover. Black cats are not bad. Witches can't drown and always carry lavender in your pocket. Even with all their knowledge, some parts of life cannot be tricked, manipulated or avoided. 
 Life was short, it was over in an instant, but some things lasted. Hate and love, kindness and cruelty, all lingered and, in their case, all had been passed on. 
 The Owens family suffers from a curse. Despite the curse, they each must come to learn to: 
 Love more, her aunt had said. Not less. 
 It is a short but sweet thought from a lovely book. It is what we should all strive to do, with or without the help of magic. This book is one I'm going to think about for some time. I will likely revisit it as well. If you have a chance, I highly recommend getting to know this author and her beautiful books. You won't be sorry

 What an unexpected pleasure. Heroes versus heroes has been done before, but not this well in a long time. With the gloves off, Tom Taylor, seems to have been given free reign to do pretty much whatever he wants and uses it to great effect. Really like his familiar, yet different, takes on all the DC Universe's Big Guns. Of course, Batman and Superman take center stage. But the lesser players get lots of attention to. Great scenes involving Green Arrow and Harley Quinn that add a little levity to the story. Another follows the Flash as he grapples with his conscience and his role in Superman's new world order. Finally, the confrontation at Arkham Asylum was pretty badass as well. Taylor does a good job voicing classic characters so as to make this "world" seem as if it is a realistic possibility within the current DC continuity. 
 Also gotta give a shout out to Jheremy Raapack. His style reminds me a little of Darick Robertson's stuff (and that's a good thing). While all of the contributing artists are pretty good, his stuff really shines. His dark line work, slight changes to traditional costumes, and distinctive style all add to the uniqueness of the book. Sad to see he isn't returning for the second volume, but the story alone is enough to make the next book required reading for me.

The best thing about this novel (maybe the only good thing?) was Casper. I just fell in love with this character. Not only did he come across as an authentic teen boy, but he wasn't uber model handsome (as almost all the other boys in this novel were - unrealistic as THAT was!), he wasn't moody/edgy, or a constantly smirking playa as so many other YA boys are portrayed. In short, he was just a normal, average guy. Casper was so comfortable in his own skin. Hannah even acknowledged it. She recognized that Casper didn't act like someone he's not, he wasn't fake. Rather, he knew who he was and was OK with that. I so wish Casper had been the main character of this novel, as I'm sure that would have been immensely more enjoyable to read about than the actual main characters of "A Totally Awkward Love Story". 
 Sam was a fairly typical teen boy: ordinary (but not in a bad way), moderately cute, fairly intelligent, up for fun with his mates, and sometimes, insecure and confused about the opposite sex. Even what transpired between him and Miranda (aka Panda) in a "certain" scene in the novel, egregious as it was, was believable. 
 Hannah on the other hand, to paraphrase Chandler Bing (since I think the whole lobster thing might have been a Friends reference), could she BE more of a doormat?! I didn't think I'd ever read about a teen girl who was as spineless as Hannah. Do they truly exist? Even when Hannah does find a spine (for like 2 seconds), and finally, gives both Stella and Sam the reaming they so richly deserve, she forgives them a nanosecond later. Now, some folks might applaud her for sticking by her friend (Stella) or having a generous personality because she gave Sam a second chance, but for me, I read it as her reverting back to her spineless self. Thus for me, Hannah was not a very sympathetic, let alone authentic voice of a teen girl when she constantly subverts her true feelings just so she can have a "friend" back or have a boyfriend. If someone can't speak up for themself, why should I do it for them? She's a fairly pathetic character, really - the "Gretchen" of this Mean Girls set. [I think all those who've read this novel know that Stella is the Regina character, yes?] 
  Toward novel's end, I'm glad Casper tells Hannah that no, lobsters don't in fact mate for life. I think that, together with the passages where Hannah and Sam finally have sex seem to portend that the two are not destined to be together forever. [But I must give props to the authors for writing a really plausible scene of one's "first time".] None of the couples or near-couples in this novel were even close to being each other's "lobster" - and for me, that includes Sam and Hannah.  
 As it has been some time since I experienced the summer between finishing high school (or the British equivalent) and the start of university, I thought it was ridiculous that not a single character had anything else in mind besides partying, sex, alcoholic stupors, and fabulous adventures (Kavos and Woodland Festival). The only part of "real life" that ever affected any of them was worry about whether their final grades were good enough to get into the uni of their choice. Otherwise, this novel was pretty much a mash up of just about every glossy, gilded, vapid teen drama depicted on film or television. 
 There truly was nothing original about this novel. Having said that, if the authors write a book with Casper as the main character, I'm in. Too bad he only had cameos in this feature.

Synopsis: 
 Sarah's family rarely stays in one place for long in an attempt to outrun the cold her mother hates. But one winter night, Sarah's mother walks out on the family. Her father is unable to keep up the pretenses of a normal life as he slowly turns into something more beast than human in front of Sarah's eyes. With her best intentions at heart, her father takes her to live with a grandmother she didn't even know existed. In the dilapidated castle, in the middle of the forest, Sarah begins to uncover the truth of her families history and the curse that she's inherited. The curse that will trigger the first time she falls in love. 
 Thoughts: 
 This was a surprising little book. The description of it being a Beauty and the Beast retelling with the female being the beast had me instantly intrigued. Throw in the twist on the curse being that falling in love for the first time is the trigger and I could not contain my grabby hands. 
 Hellisen's writing is full of wonderfully figurative language. There are so many lines that jumped out at me with their thoughtfulness and creativity. Even the character descriptions had a wonderful level of uniqueness: "She looked like the kind of woman who would put arsenic in the soup and tenderly nurse someone to death, spoonful by spoonful." Instantly wanted to stear clear of that old lady. I just can't get over how beautiful the language is. 
 That being said, I'm not sure how well this will do with the middle grade audience it's being marketed to. It has a lot of deep topics wrapped up in its fantasy. It's a book that I feel like teachers make kids reads and kids go "What? I don't get it." That said, it was a unique take on a frequently retold fairy tale and I thoroughly enjoyed it! 
 Thanks to the publisher and NetGalley for the ARC. 
 Publication Date: February 3,2015

I loved this book, since I'm a complete sucker for time traveling and historical stuff. I liked that there was a clear description given for the time traveling storyline, although its origin was never really mentioned. The historical references were incorporated quite nicely into the novel. There were all these mysterious aspects involved, the explanations for which were gradually revealed. While some questions were left unanswered, these actually make me all the more excited for the sequel! 
 Regarding the characters, I would have to say that my favorite was probably Ben. He may have seemed like a jerk at first, but he turned out to have such a sweet personality. I was really enjoying the moments between Ben and Jenny, but then somewhere in the middle of the plot, Nikolai was introduced, and that kind of ruined it for me. I mean, love at first sight? Instalove? Seriously? (I hate instalove.) And after that, it seemed like Jenny completely pushed Ben out of her life. I'm sad to say that I didn't feel much connection or depth when it came to Nikolai. I have to admit, the Nikolai-Jenny romance was quite endearing, but I'd choose Ben over Nikolai any day. 
 All in all, I consider this a really good book, and it's something that is sure to interest the time traveling fanatics out there.

Maybe my expectations were too high. I loved The Girl with All the Gifts and was so excited when I learned the author had also written a prequel. What a letdown! 
 Boy on the Bridge is basically a complete reboot of Girl with the Gifts, think - 1984 Footloose vs. 2011 Footloose. Same characters, same mystery, same story. But instead of expanding on the universe and adding to the narrative, this book adds absolutely nothing to the series as a whole. Readers already know what the "twist" is; we're all aware that there are hungry children out there  and we get no new information to build upon everything from the first book. Boy on the Bridge lacked the slow-burn, creepy style that made Girl with the Gifts unique.
Of course, this is a classic and there are some great quotes that have come from this work. It was a fun read but at times it became a bit too silly.

What a pleasant, comforting, great low-angst read. Miss Walker can really do no wrong. 
 Jack loves his life and job in Tasmania...but he's lonely. He luckily runs into Lawson at the airport and offers the flustered, cute, geeky guy a ride. They hit it off and thus begins the best adventure of their lives.

Early on, while looking up the chronological order of Agatha Christie's books, I thought I accidentally spoiled myself about the murderer. I only saw it for a second, but I was quite sure I messed up the experience of a good mystery. Well, I resigned myself into reading it as a howdunit, fully expecting this one character to be revealed as the killer. 
 Only it turns out that I was wrong. I read the "spoiler" wrong and made assumptions, basically chasing a red herring. I cannot even rely on my own observation skills; definitely more of a Hastings than a Poirot. 
 For that surprise alone I enjoyed it a lot more, because it was something far different from what I was expecting. Also Hastings is nowhere to be found, which is a definite plus, although interestingly, Poirot misses him very much. They'd only been written together for two novels and a dozen short stories by this time though so I wasn't buying that at all.

 This book is a tough one for me to rate, so I'll wait until the end to get to that part. First, it's important to note that this book is told through a series of interviews with an unnamed (probably) government agent, who interviews all the characters for his files (I assume it is a "he" based on a comment one of the characters made). If that just isn't your style of book, skip this. There are very, very few chapters that aren't told in interview form. The good news is that this format makes it a very quick read. 
 The next thing is that this is science fiction. Not sci-fi mixed with some other more approachable element, but real sci-fi, with significant bits talking about science. That's not exactly my thing, but I thought it was easy to skim those parts. But again, if pure science fiction isn't your thing, you probably won't like this. 
 Now, all of that said, this was a really fascinating story, and I think very creative. I like the idea that there are aliens (or, there is an implication of them, anyway) without it getting too crazy. I also like that there seem to be real-world ramifications to this science and research. These people aren't operating in a vacuum and there are international responses to what's going on. I really liked that, and I thought it made it seem more real. 
 As far as the characters go, they were decent, but we didn't get to learn a whole lot about them because of the format. This book was really about telling a story as it happened, through the lens of the people involved. We skip some bits that are likely less interesting and see instead the highlights of this otherworldly experiment. And that's okay, because those parts are really interesting. 
 It makes you wonder whether the government is doing some of these things (not the alien part, necessarily, but some of the other things mentioned). I don't know whether I hope they are or hope they aren't, but either way, this was a fast-paced story about a pretty cool subject. There's also a character that's definitely hatable, which I think is pretty important. Also, the ending was pretty awesome. Not going to say why, but it's worth getting to, I think. 
 So, why so much trouble deciding on a rating? Well, it was quick and had an interesting story, but I didn't love the format and there were some parts that got bogged down in science. I've been going back and forth between three and four stars, but because of the ending, which I really liked, I'll go with four. That said, I'd only recommend this if you're okay with this format!

This is a book I was eagerly anticipating. I devoured Throne of Glass and Crown of Midnight earlier in the year and I immediately marked my calendar for the September release date of Heir of Fire. September came and went and it turns out a lot of other people were also excited about this book (read: LONG library waiting list). I almost purchased the book at my local bookstore, but I don't yet own the first two and it felt wrong to start buying at book three (and I wasn't quite ready to purchase all three in one shot). Alas, I finally got my hands on the book in November by borrowing it from a coworker's daughter. Yes I am 25 years old, borrowing books from a 12 year old, WHATEVER. Now it is December and here is my review of Heir of Fire (long preamble over). 
 Heir of Fire opens a few weeks (months?) after the final events of Crown of Midnight. Assassin Celaena Sardothien has arrived in Wendlyn, supposedly on a mission to kill the rulers for the King of Adarlan. Her secret mission is to obtain the information she needs to locate the final Wyrdkey, stop the King of Adarlan from amassing more power, and keep her promise to her departed friend Nehemia to free the people of Ellwye. However, as the story begins we find that Celaena is rather depressed, doubting her ability to achieve any of her goals and her worthiness as a "hero".This changes as she meets her mysterious and dangerous Aunt Maeve and the Fae, along with a whole new set of side characters, and begins to discover who she really is. Meanwhile Dorian and Chaol are living their lives without Celaena back in Adarlan. Each of them is also on a path of self discovery and ultimately deciding what role, if any, they will play in overthrowing the King of Adarlan. 
 I think there is a lot to like in this installment of the series. We are introduced to several new characters, Celaena's cousin Aedion, Fae warrior Rowan, a bunch of demi-Fae, a new lover for Dorian, LOTS of people. For the most part I think all of these characters are interesting, and well fleshed out. Especially Aedion and Rowan. It was interesting reading the about Celaena's childhood, her relationship with Aedion, and his devotion to her then and now. Now Rowan, at first I was thinking ,"Oh, boo! We left behind one love triangle (Celaena, Chaol, Dorian) simply to step right into another. WHY????", but Maas took the relationship in a different, and far more interesting in my opinion, direction. Now there is some hinting that we may be in store for yet another love triangle (Aedion) but for some reason that possibility doesn't bother me as much. Maybe because the history between Aedion and Celaena is set up in this book, as well as the idea that Aedion has always been, and will remain, loyal to her (I am also TOTALLY willing to overlook the cousin thing, maybe that says something about me, but I don't care!). 
 Speaking of new characters, in Crown of Midnight we were briefly introduced to the witch clans of Erilea, and Heir of Fire delves much deeper into this aspect of the story. One of the witches, Magnon, is basically a main character with several chapter from her POV. At first I thought I would not like this, I believe my actual thought was something along the lines of, "Ugh I DO NOT CARE! LET'S GET BACK TO THE ASSASSIN AND THE FAE!". At a certain point however I was all in and I actually almost started to enjoy Magnon's chapters more than Celaena's (and definitely more than Dorian's).This storyline also explains the rumors surrounding the Wvyerns and the screaming heard in the Ferian Gap, referenced in the earlier books. This could have been a boring new plotline needlessly added to fill space (and some may argue that it is) but I think it is fresh, interesting, and entertaining. 
 I also enjoyed the development of the main characters, specifically Celaena and Chaol. Celaena is really on a journey of self discovery in this book and I think it is done pretty well. It's gradual over the course of the book. She is aided along the way by the new friends she has made, but in the end the progress she makes comes from her own determination to become who she wants to be, and I like that. Chaol's is also somewhat of a journey of self discovery, but really I am just glad that he finally SPOILER ALERT starts to see the King of Adarlan for who and what he really is and takes a stance on what role he is going to play in the inevitable conflict to come. I mean FINALLY! Chaol has been described as the "good guy" throughout the series and yet he still mindlessly stood by the king because of some sense of duty. That changes in this book and it's definitely a good thing. Even Dorian looks within himself and makes some decisions about his future. He also finally starts standing up for himself and not relying on Chaol or Celaena, but I didn't enjoy Dorian's storyline as much as the others, more on that later. 
 I've read some reviews that argued the tone of this book varies too much from the previous books or that Maas was trying to do too much/trying to emulate other fantasy stories/authors and not entirely succeeding (multiple POVs, lots of new characters, new settings, history info dump, sound familiar??), and while I definitely see where they are coming from, I don't entirely agree. Yes, this book seems more ambitious than the other two but I think it is a good thing, it shows the author is growing and trying new things. And yes, it does appear to be borrowing some style from other fantasy books, but I don't really see any problem with that either. Most importantly, I didn't find it boring. I liked learning more about the world Maas has created. The Fae, Celaena's own personal history, the witches, I found it all to be pretty interesting and if the planned six books actually happen it makes sense to introduce more characters and mythology into the series. 
 Though I did enjoy all of the above aspects, Heir of Fire isn't all roses. One thing that didn't work for me was Dorian's storyline. Almost immediately we are introduced to a new love interest for him, and to me she mostly seems like an empty, throw away character. I understand showing Dorian moving on from Celaena or making him fall in love with someone else so that we as readers don't feel sorry for him, but it made his character feel like nothing more than a love interest. I think it would have been more powerful to see him move on and discover more about his magic on his own. That also would have fit more with the self discovery storylines of the other two main characters. Dorian does ultimately embrace his power and take a stance, but it is only after he experiences more love and heartbreak. It would have been nice to see him do those things solely for himself. 
 I also think Heir of Fire does drag a little more than the previous two installments. This may be due to it's length or the attempt to keep the momentum sustained in all of the storylines. Though I still immensely enjoyed it, I didn't breeze through it the way I did with Throne of Glass and Crown of Midnight. It also definitely reads like a middle book within a series. There are more tiny revelations than big reveals. More stage setting than huge plot turning events. It slightly makes up for these aspects by being heavy on the character development. The ending does contain some cliffhangers that are clearly set up for (perhaps predictable) outcomes in the next book. This "middle book syndrome" doesn't bother me so much, I think it unfortunately happens in many book series, but I could see it being irksome for many readers. 
 Overall I think Heir of Fire does its job. It is entertaining, introduces interesting new characters, pushes the plot closer to the final endgame, and (probably most importantly in terms of any book within a series) made me excited for the next chapter in the Throne of Glass series. If you enjoyed Throne of Glass and Crown of Midnight, I say read Heir of Fire. If you haven't started this series before, WHAT ARE YOU WAITING FOR? Magic, adventure, romance, a kickass heroine who is also an assassin! Get going!

This book was just as good the second time as the first. It's one of those rare books that you wish was longer because it's just. So. Good. Honestly, I can't say enough good things about it. 
 In a nutshell: The characters are varied and they grow as the book progresses; there's humor sprinkled throughout the book; plenty of action; a really cool system of 'magic' that's not really magic, but science; a (very fine-looking) alien race from Atlantis; and a bit of romance. Even though there's an 'end-of-the-world' scenario, it doesn't bother me like most other dystopian novels usually do. For one, it's not exactly dystopian. And for another, I think that well-developed characters (and a great, edge-of-your-seat plot like this story has) can overcome most setting problems. 
 I'd give it more than five stars if I could. Recommended for ages 12 and up.

 Revenge of the Girl with the Great Personality delivers exactly what the title says; we get revenge and a girl with a great personality. Make that an awesome personality, because I loved Lexi so much! She was so snarky and sweet and innocent, and she was just so funny! I wish I had half the sense of humor that this girl does! 
 Not only was she funny, she was so three dimensional and such a fan character to read about! She has some strange worries for sure, with her little sister being such a drama queen....at seven. I really have to applaud Mackenzie as a character-- I could see how she could be so nasty, but she's just a little girl. I mean, I get super grumpy when people prod at me too! 
 It's no excuse, but she's just a kid-- and we see phenomenal character from her and Lexi. I think that they truly learned from their mistakes, and I don't think they'll be repeating them. I love when characters have growth like that! 
 I also liked the family dynamic-- it wasn't functional by any means, but it gave us such insight into Lexi. Her mother is so terrible. I think that I would have strangled the woman long before she had so much control over my life. o.O 
 She made a really good villain. 
 Moving on, before I start ranting. I loved all of the secondary characters. Logan, Taylor, Benny and Cam all just made my day. They were each fairly good friends to Lexi, and I was constantly rooting for all of them. I was so proud when Benny talked to Chris, and when Lexi went out on a date...and I was especially proud of Cam for being such a good friend! 
 All in all, Revenge of the Girl with the Great Personality was a fantastically unique read with awesome characters.

I've recently discovered the joy of listening to audio books rather than reading on my phone or in the physical form. I put on my sneakers and put in my earbuds. Then I start walking. Or perhaps I catch a bus to work or wherever it is that I'm going. 
 It works great. I lose a lot of time daily on commuting and this way it doesn't feel like it's gone to waste. The amount of reading I do now has gone up and I do less of anxious over thinking I unavoidably do when my mind isn't focused on other things. 
 Contact was the perfect audiobook. I had the edition read by Laurel Lefkow and I wouldn't have it any other way. There's another one read by Jodie Foster, who is famous and all, but the way Lefkow read this amazing piece of fiction was just perfect. The way she adjusted her accent and the depth of her voice to suit the characters really enhanced my experience and made me feel the book more deeply than I would have if I was just reading it. 
 That being said, I was pleasantly surprised by the way Carl Sagan writes. It's vivid, easily understood even when he talks about complex topics and endlessly vibrant. Since the original Cosmos was way before my time, I had little knowledge of his work, let alone that he wrote amazing fiction. 
 Ellie Arroway is a radio astronomer and a director of "Project Argus", an array of radio telescopes who are a part of SETI or the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. One day they pick up a strange signal from a star called Vega which is 26 light years away and the brightest star in the constellation Lyra. As it turns out, the signal contains a reflected transmission of 1936 Summer Olympic games in Berlin and Hitler's speech at the opening. Under the original message, there is another one containing blueprints of a strange machine and a handbook how to build it. 
 This novel is a fantastic blend of discussions about philosophy, science, religion and the future of the human kind. It entertains the idea (and the very probable fact!) that we aren't alone in the universe, but are just one of many endless civilisations out there. It's as scary as it is exciting to think about it. 
 There are about 7 billion of human beings on Earth at the Earth at the moment and we all like to think that we are different and that something like our religion, race, political affiliations or even just our career makes us better than the others. But far from it. We all forget that we all are just human beings. And if it takes a machine sent from beings from the outer space to makes us unite and stop killing each other as much, I really hope there is a radio signal on its way to Earth from the star Vega. 
 The characters occasionally seem secondary to the whole plot but they are the carriers of the conversations that discuss the values of humanity. Hadden, the eccentric billionaire, was my favourite character, apart from Ellie. He represents the human ingenuity and the courage to not conform to anything that sets our progress. 
 What we often forget and this book reflects is that we are as technologically advanced as we have ever been as species. WE may not have commercial space flight yet nor we've terraformed Mars (looking at you, Elon), but we have small technological wonders that we use on daily basis. Powerful computers of the size of a palm, panels that convert the Sun into energy that conserves our food, bring us light at night and warms us in the cold months and so many machines that make us lazier. 
 But we're getting there. It's only exponentially upwards from here. Our world is a beautiful one.

Robert M. Pirsig's Zen & the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance embodies that 70's spirit of road trips and the search for enlightenment. 
 The story follows the narrator and his son on a motorcycle trip across the North-Western USA. It's a very personal and moving account, which is not only testament to their father and son bond, but also feels incredibly raw and real. 
 Along the way, the father and son duo have many philosophical discussions which they call Chautauquas, ranging from ethical emotivism to the philosophy of science. Unfortunately, the son, Chris, does not often get a word in edgeways. His father, or Phaedrus as he refers to his past self, has a lot to say. And while his teachings are solid, they are a mere introduction to philosophy and touch on the great philosophers who should be explored more after reading the book. 
 Despite the name, there is not as much Zen Buddhism, or motorcycle maintenance come to think of it, as one would expect. That being said, the explanation of the scientific method and how we as a society and as individuals go about discovering the truth, and the analogy of working on a motorcycle is beautifully written. 
 Road trips have this habit of serving as time for contemplation and finding oneself. The open road can do that to you. And discussing philosophical aspects and teachings with a fellow traveller is a valid past-time. Towards the end of the book, Zen & the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance really tips over into preaching, though. It's no longer a discussion or an anecdote seen for its philosophical value. And that's when the reading turns from being fun into being tedious. The search for enlightenment has turned into a lesson. 
 As a road trip story between father and son, during which the father wants to share some life advice, this would be great! But the author apparently could not resist temptation to turn absolutely everything into a philosophy lesson, which takes away from the story at the heart of this novel.

Though this book was entertaining and insightful . . . not much actually happened. The ending hardly felt like an ending to me, and I was left a little bit confused. What was the point of reading a 325 page book if there was no ending in sight? 
 Now, maybe the "ending" was written that way because sometimes that's how life happens, there is no clear cut ending or fairytale-esque happily ever after. BUT . . . This is a book. There should be at least some kind of clear ending, don't you think? Since there's no sequel, I would like to know what happens. 
 Ultimately, I would recommend the read, but be prepared for the story not to end.

Looking for Alaska was the only John Green book I hadn't read yet (except for his Let it Snow novella) and I have to come to the conclusion that it is definitely not one of my favorite authors. I always end up a bit disappointed by his books and the only novel from him that really moved me was Will Grayson, Will Grayson. I had often been told that Alaska was by far his greatest novel. Objectively, that might be true. But that doesn't mean it's the one I enjoyed the most. I have to admit it was more intense, you could feel he had put a lot of work in it, but I didn't like the characters and it took me too long to get into the story. 
 Everything starts with a protagonist who, like in every John Green book, doesn't really have friends and has some kind of obsession with something - which, in Miles' case, are famous people's last words and reading biographies - yeah, you kind of expect that kind of thing when you've read a few of his books. The book starts with a mysterious countdown that took me by surprise when it stopped. I have to say I didn't expect the story to become so intense and moving, I was more expecting a light read. I can't say anything more without spoilers but I wasn't exactly ready for this kind of story. Of course, I thought some parts were very beautiful and I was moved several times, but I think it is just because I could relate to some things that happened in real life just a few weeks ago. 
 The book is very short, but it took me almost a week to get to page 100 in this story that it really slow paced at the start. I didn't get attached to the characters at all and I was rather bored. What bothered me the most was the idealistic vision of boarding school that teenagers tend to have. To be honest, I really wanted to go to boarding school when I was younger and when you see the cliches from American or British books and movies, this doesn't come as a surprise. I mean, Miles has never had friends and is rather antisocial but as soon as he gets to this boarding school, his roommate takes him everywhere with him and he has an amazing social life and the best friends ever. Seriously, I've seen more realistic John Green books. 
 The strength of this novel lies once again in his outstanding writing skills. He knows how to use words to make beautiful poetry. This is the kind of novel you should absolutely read in its original version. Not that I say this is the kind of book you should absolutely read. I got annoyed at the characters, the story doesn't move forward, everything is cliche, etc. I am really disappointed by this book which I had been told was this author's masterpiece. I have to say I am quite puzzled at all the positive reviews, maybe I just didn't get the book. Friendship, pain, love and hope are themes that the book deals well with, but all these themes are too recurrent in this author novels. A good first novel, but you soon realize the author didn't manage to renew himself. Maybe if I hadn't read all his other novels before I wouldn't have seen so many similarities in his characters and plots, but I am starting to feel like I am always reading the same thing even though the book isn't bad itself.

 Sometimes you get to read a book with a certain idea about it, but as reading, your impression changes radically. 
 I liked the cover of this book (I love stories about fighters!!), but this one is much more than that. It is the story of a family overcoming. A family of three children, and a fourth, which ultimately meet one of them in an unusual circumstance and become friends for life. 
 Till Page was a fighter for life. His parents were irresponsible: his father was a villain who just wanted to get along in life, and his mother was much more concerned with taking care of herself (and her nails) than taking care of the house and three children. Exactly why, at 13, Till had to take care of two younger brothers, Flint and Quarry. 
 It was not enough to carry this responsibility on his shoulders, in this same age he discovers that has a hearing disorder that will make him lose his hearing - this could occur gradually or instantly. On that occasion he meets Eliza Reynolds. Her parents was not bad, but lived fighting over the little money and that made the daughter invisible to them. 
 Eliza spent much of the day in an abandoned apartment, where she could make her drawings and develop her talent, something that her mother hated because it reminded her father was a frustrated artist and not looking for a decent job to support the family. 
 In this empty apartment she knows Till. There, the two create a private world; a world where there is no hunger, anger, poverty; charges, fights, deafness. 
 This friendship comes a special affection that develops into something greater, but neither has the courage to admit to each other. The years pass, they are dating other people, but the daily meeting in the fantasy world of Eliza and Till remained. 
 Having to work two jobs to care for siblings and pay the rent, Till can appease some frustrations in the new gym in the neighborhood, the On the Ropes, where he works in exchange for his training. With so many responsibilities, he can not graduate in high school , but he was there in Eliza's graduation. That night they finally take courage and open their hearts, have their night of love ... and are separated by six months. 
 Eliza went to live in another city because of college, rented a small apartment - in which the neighbors could hear everything she did - and tried to take her life ahead without Till. 
 When Till was involved in an illegal situation by his father, Till managed to escape and realized that his only safe haven was Eliza, and he seeks for her. 
 From this new reunion, the two begin, comings and goings, to establish rules that wanted to live. Till felt he was unworthy of love such a beautiful, intelligent and talented girl, but Eliza could see a Till he himself did not know. His inner strength was huge and day by day he managed to keep his family together and made come true the dream of his life. 
 Of course his disease came to collect its payment, this was another obstacle he had to overcome, still fearing that his brothers also had this disease. 
 The book moved me in many ways. The fight this boy to survive was such that sometimes you wonder how humans can be so strong, so resilient. 
 A beautiful story. Highly recommended.

 The Boy in the Striped Pajamas is a short novel that is both a coming of age story and a brief glimpse into a dark period in history. 
 Boyne cleverly draw the reader deep into the tale by trusting that our knowledge of the Holocaust exceeds Bruno's, a young German boy who is frankly baffled by this strange new place called "Out-With" where he and his family have moved. 
 With every experience that Bruno has, the reader cringes- for we understand the horrors that he has yet to grasp. Readers can only continue to turn the pages and hope that when epiphany does come to Bruno, the consequences of his knowledge will not demand too high a price. 
 This tale does have weaknesses. The brevity of the book might be the reason why the titular character felt a bit two-dimensional. In addition, I would have been happier had there been more character development for Bruno, who remained self-absorbed throughout most of the story. Even Bruno's naive misunderstandings and innocent confusions about his situation eventually got slightly wearing and belabored. 
 Despite that, the whole of the story was captivating, with an ending that a young adult reader won't soon forget.

So, it felt like a missed opportunity to do as Pratchett usually does, and take on contemporary issues in the guise of hilarious buffoonery. And some of the sidepaths the book wandered down got a little--dare I say it?--tedious. Still, he's a great writer, and the main character, his family and cohorts are very likable people, so I certainly don't feel like I wasted my time. Just...he's spoiled me, and I was hoping for greatness. It alarms me that Pratchett is frail and suffering Alzheimer's, because I, selfishly, would like a few more great books from him.

So... the writing in this was brilliant. Very clever. But... it was also boring. While I can appreciate the style and structure of this type of book, that doesn't mean I liked it. And I did NOT like it. 
 The Good: 
 The structure is wonderful. Very clever. The author arranges it like a syllabus, and each chapter is named after a well known literary work. Then the themes in each chapter connect to the original theme of title. Super cool, right? 
 The protagonist is consistent and well developed. She has a witty voice and I liked it. 
 The Bad: 
 This book is SLOW. It takes 350 pages for anything to actually happen. And shockingly, it spends all this time building to this event, but then the few pages before the event, it skips through months! It didn't make sense. Why spend 350 pages building up these tedious events to suddenly say, "Well, now we'll skip ahead three months and talk about this thing." It frustrated me. 
 This book is what I would consider very high literature. It makes about a million references and actual CITATIONS to other books. While this was cool in the beginning, it began to grate on me. Why would I want to read a 500 pages research paper? I don't! 
 Things rushed at the end. It would seem that it is impossible for a 500 pages book to have a rushed ending, but this somehow managed it. And all of the discovery of this was very much in summary, not in scene. As a person who strives for a fast moving plot and interaction with other people, this grated on my nerves. 
 Overall, the structure was interesting, but the book and content was boring. My advice: Skim it until about page 350 to get a sense of the structure, then go find a summary somewhere and read that afterwards.

Whoa! This book has to be one of the strangest reads I've come across. I can see how its eccentric nature will not be for everyone, but for me the beautiful, often disturbing, writing style captivated me and never let go. It's not the type of story that just anyone could pull off, the author definitely did some thinking outside the box for this one, and Quinn has my two thumbs up. 
 Calling this book Another Little Piece is quite fitting, as it felt like with every turn of a page, another piece of this mind-boggling puzzle was put in place - or at least moved a tiny bit closer. And this review is especially hard, because in almost every piece lies a spoiler. The first of these spoilers comes at the 15% mark, thus I'm not able to go into the plot itself, but let me just promise you that you will not have read anything quite like this before! I was shocked by what I was taking in at regular intervals in this book - and from someone who reads as much as I do, shock is a good thing! My advice: be very careful what reviews you read beforehand. 
 Annaliese has no recollection of the past year of her life, the year she disappeared. The character growth in this novel is substantial; we see Annaliese go through a complete remodeling from who we first meet. The girl at the start is timid and confused, yet she surprises you with the strength of character she possesses even then. As she finds out what happened to her, she transforms into the tough person she needs to be to weather this information, even refusing part of who she is. Because she gets to know her old self through flashbacks, and she's learning who she is now, all the while fighting her inner demon, it makes it difficult to connect with this type of disjointed character. I wouldn't have changed anything about her, however; this strangeness makes her character. Due to the nature of the plot, the secondary characters can take some situating, but they all become important players in this mystery. I especially liked Dex who has an oddity of his own to add even more complexity to this bizarre plot. 
 The writing is what makes or breaks a book like this, and this one makes it, completely and thoroughly. Quinn's writing is at once terrifying and wonderfully addicting. I was haunted by some of the images that she produced, yet I was unable to stop imagining them, in greater detail each time. Suffice it to say, those who are easily queasy may have to skip a few passages in this one. Aside from her skill for the disturbing, Quinn is also a master at intricately layering her tale. It begins as what feels like a jumble of words and events, until, little by little, we begin the deciphering process. With her show rather than tell manner, we're left to our devices to bring this story together with what we're given, which I highly appreciate even though I was confused as all heck at the end. A re-reading of the last chapter and a discussion with a friend amended that, some, but I'm still not sure how I feel about it. 
 Profoundly original and disturbingly odd, I think everyone should experience Another Little Piece. Not because I believe everyone will love it, but because I think everyone should experience the anomaly that it is.

I think the only appropriate initial response to finishing The Stand is "....wow." 
 Calling something "epic" gets thrown around a lot these days, 9 times out of 10 in places it has no places being. But I think it is safe to call this truly epic, and not just because of its size (this unabridged version runs about 1200 pages). The grand scale of the clash of good and evil is something that most fiction now can't support, and most authors don't try; those that do try, usually fail. 
 The first 300 pages or so are kind of a hard slog, not because they're badly written, but because they are so vivid that the descriptions of mass-scale death and rotting bodies is a little hard to get through. I don't scare easily, but I had to stop reading this right before bed, because I had to give myself lectures just to turn off the light. After that the characters come more into focus and the grand visions start to move as the scattered ones and twos start to come together. 
 I read a lot of Stephen King because it's kind of a guilty pleasure and I enjoy it, but I wouldn't normally call them literary masterpieces, and I think even King would agree with that. This, though, shows what he can do at his best, and his best is spectacular.
Weaker than most of Neil Gaiman's books with tenuous plot. It's stretched a bit too far, but is still an enjoyable read.
