The perfect balance of thrills, chills and feels with an epic twist both brilliant and compelling. 
 Clare Mackintosh's poignant narrative grabs you from the very beginning with the story of a mother whose entire world shatters when her five-year-old son decided to race her home. Hers is a perspective laden with emotion, a broken woman who walks out of her home, out of her life, to the comforts of the unknown, to forget the sounds and sights that haunt her every minute. Not only does Mackintosh lace every word with feeling, but suspense mounts as the story unravels in multiple perspectives, building up to a twist so unexpected that the entirety of what you've read flips and morphs into something new, exciting and scary. As a frequent suspense reader, I've become quiet adept at predicting twists, but this one is so masterfully plotted and executed that I gasped the moment it happened. I Let You Go truly has it all--secrets, suspense, love, loss, chills and thrills. I couldn't get enough, and even its end delivers jaw-dropping moments which makes the story linger long after the flip of the final page. 
 "What sort of bastard kills a five-year old boy, then drives off?..." 
 "That's exactly what we're going to find out." 
 After 5-year-old Jacob's tragic death, a mother loses everything while two Bristol detectives pledge to find the individual responsible for his death. 
 "Such a small impact on the world, yet the very center of my own." 
 Jenna Gray moves to a small rickety cottage on the Welsh coast, to escape the reality of her life, of that horrible accident. The story follows Jenna as she attempts to survive each day, slowly opening up to those around her. The bitter-cold weather of the coast coupled with Jenna's melancholic perspective, set a somber tone that makes her brokenness palpable. 
 "I want to fix an image of him in my head, but all I can see when I close my eyes is his body, still and lifeless in my arms. I let him go, and I will never forgive myself for that." 
 Halfway through, Mackintosh drops the aforementioned twist that changes everything, and the rest of the story untangles with huge impact. 
 I can't imagine anyone not loving this multifaceted, emotionally haunting novel. The character development is so rich, the plot so well thought out, the emotions so raw and real. There is just so much to consider... from the grave outcomes of momentary choices to the intricate, emotional relationships that often set the course of our lives. This book instantly became one my all-time favorite psychological thrillers--a must-read for readers of all genres.

This is one of those books that really needs the half star rating - I gave it 5 stars, but it probably should be a 4.5. I decided to round up... 
 This is a fun book. Anything that pokes fun at Revelations and Armageddon is right up my alley - I've noticed a lot of comparisons to Douglass Adams, and this was reminiscent of the Hitchhiker's Guide, with quirky British humor and bizarre scenes. 
 This was very much a character-driven book - and the characters were all balanced in a strange way. The four 'bikers' of the Apocalypse (3 men and 1 woman) - the four of 'Them' - 3 boys and 1 girl. A young couple and an old couple. The Angel and the Demon. 
 Parody and satire were also strong points of the novel. Famine and the fast food restaurant, with Elvis working as a fry cook, are good examples. 
 I also enjoyed the historical and classical references, although I'm sure I missed many of these (examples: comparing Adam to Napoleon, with an exile to Elba, references to historic events in the Agnes Nutter prophecies) 
 The book looses half a star in not tying everything together well - or perhaps, making things work too neatly. I never felt the sense of doom required - something was going to happen to make everything 'all right.' This was apparent from the tone throughout the book. You knew too well what 'side' everyone was on - (although one of the philosophical questions raised is what purpose the traditional sides of good/evil serve). 
 Given the subject matter, and the characters, I felt a little bit cheated by the weakness of the plot. But overall, it was a great book - very funny, and a quick read (I finished it in less than a day.)

But after seeing the beautiful see-through dust jacket and stunning cover art I HAD TO GET THIS and boy, I'm happy that I did. 
 This is a crossover retelling of Sleeping Beauty and Snow White. Two fairy tales that I know of but am not too overly fond of. Slowly but surely I'm starting to despise all things "damsel in distress" and so I was a little apprehensive going into this. BUT LET ME TELL YOU ... MY FEARS WERE ILL-FOUNDED. Instead of two damsels we have severall badass female characters who kick ass, are clever and sassy and independant and who fuck shit up! It was very refreshing and I'd rather read Gaiman's tale to my kids than the original two (my imaginary kids, that is...)! 
 So the premise of this book reminded me a little bit of Gaiman's Sandman (a body of work that seems to overshadow all of his works but well THE SANDMAN IS JUST THAT BRILLIANT, READ IT!) because there is a sleeping sickness in the lands. And it's spreading fast. Sleeping Beauty is locked into her tower and no hero managed to get past the roses and give her a good peck on the mouth. When Snow White hears of this, she fears for her people (and *coughs* also sees an excellent opportunity to delay her shitty wedding to some shitty king) and sets out to free Sleeping Beauty. 
 This is a tale about bravery and doing the right thing. About being strong and finding what makes you happy. To take your own freedom and just to be a badass lady! 
 Chris Riddell's illustrations are STUNNING and accompany this tale beautifully.

 I am a huge fan of books about music especially if there are guitars in it. But what makes Another Little Piece of My Heart extra special for me is that it is a retelling of Jane Austen's Persuasion. I haven't actually read Persuasion yet but so far, I have enjoyed all its retellings that I have read and Tracey Martin's take on Persuasion is not an exemption. 
 Claire and Jared's relationship before was perfect - save for the fact that Claire's parents are against Jared's family's economic status. They were kindred spirits and both truly loved each other. They had lots of fun and made music together and planned about their future together. I rooted for them the moment they met and so even though I knew where the plot would lead their relationship, I still shed tears when they broke up. What Claire did to Jared was probably wrong but at the same time, it was also understandable. 
 Fast forward to the present. I thought that Jared would turn into an asshole like what the summary makes him sound like but he didn't. He has his own reasons for why he wrote the song about Claire even though it is full of lies. I was actually surprised that he was kind of ashamed of the song and other than being indifferent (but still privately hating on Claire), he still seemed like the same perfect boyfriend he once was. Claire on the other hand is more eager to make it big in the music industry. She practices much harder now with her bandmates. She doesn't show it but Jared's song has totally affected her. But still, I love that instead of letting it be a weakness, Claire somehow shaped it into strength and she uses it to propel her forward. 
 Claire also is a very likable character. Gods, I LOVE her. She's independent, strong-willed, and sarcastic and her narration is such a delight to read. Her family is a very difficult one with a father that's self-centered and conceited and a suck-up annoying little sister, April. But among the two, I enjoyed April more especially when they started getting along together and bonding over hating a common enemy. Honestly, you need to meet April. She's incredibly annoying and I love her! 
 Claire and Jared are both genuine characters. They are not ones without flaws and they make mistakes that take them way too long to fix, but at the end of the day, they still managed to set everything back in their rightful places. The character development in this book is superb. I wanted the story to go on and on and on. But sadly, everything has to end and there was nothing I can do when I reached the final page. Tracey has created this beautiful piece and I cannot wait to read more of her works. Please, Tracey, write some more awesome books!

Ask Again Later is the kind of book that you'll immediately associate with the word cute. It's the first adjective I thought of when someone asked me for my opinion of the book. You can even tell just by looking at the cover.

She's kickass if you ask me. It had all the elements that make a cute story but I wasn't so amused at first. Heart just had too much bad luck. 
 You see, she had two prom dates. No, she didn't juggle two dates at once. For some reason she was able to go to two proms when she flipped a coin to decide which date she'll go with. Same events happened but a little differently based on who she's with. In addition to that, she somehow gets the feeling of deja vu whenever certain events overlap. Towards the end, the story met at one point. I don't quite understand how it happened but it did. It's confusing but as long as you don't over analyze, you're good. 
 Going back, two prom dates meant twice as much chaos. Something's bound to go wrong on prom night, right? Heart definitely had her share of bad luck... over and over again. I get that it's part of the coin toss magic but it was too repetitive for me. Some parts were really funny (albeit cringe worthy) that I laughed out loud but some were just meh. 
 What changed my mind was when the love interest started dropping hints here and there. It was too cute for me to resist. I started enjoying the book more. It's like the guy was the only constant thing between two very different events. It was endearing how they got together. Heart was so clueless that it was frustrating but when she finally allowed herself to break her no dating policy, it was soooooooo cute! (there's that word again) 
 If you're looking for a fun YA contemporary, then you should definitely read Liz Czukas' Ask Again Later. Some parts were a bit cliche but overall it's undeniably enjoyable.

Let me start this review with a small rant about steampunk. 
 Steampunk, or mechanical fantasy as I call it, is a genre of fiction featuring a historical setting with advanced, often whimsical, technology. It is often set in the Victorian period, although there are exceptions. Dirigibles, automatons, spider-like vehicles, and weapons masquerading as ladies' accessories are popular pieces of steampunk machinery. 
 I DO NOT LIKE IT! 
 I dislike how steampunk machinery makes no scientific sense whatsoever. I also dislike how steampunk books are often choked with genre cliches and tropes. 
 That being said, I can tolerate it in small doses. My favorite series of all time, Lindsay Buroker's The Emperor's Edge, has steampunk elements to it. However, for the most part, the technology in Buroker's series make sense, and the characters are often slaving over hot boilers or wrangling awkward machinery gone awry. I like that Buroker's machines are bulky and malfunctioning and hinder the heroes as often as they help them. 
 On the other hand, Elizabeth May's The Falconer has the kind of steampunk technology that I'm not overly fond of -- mechanical hands that shoot out to pour tea and fold bustles. There are implausible helicopters ornithopters and and little ornate devices that hold tremendous power. Um, what kind of power and how does the device harness it? Nevermind that! Tremendous power!! 
 I connect the star and the remaining knife. Power flows from the objects as they melt together to form the larger star. The metal is smooth in my palm again. 
 See what I mean? It's nonsense, I tell you! 
 As for the rest of the book, it's good. It's a fun read, with kick-ass heroine and lots of action and antics. The Falconer follows a young Victorian lady of Edinburgh, Aileana Kameron, whose mother was brutally murdered by a faery. In the days after her mother's death, Aileana learned that her country has a bit of a faery infestation and humans are being slaughtered because of it. Shortly after, she met her... unique... tutor, Kiaran McKay, who instructs her in all things murderous and violent. With his help she goes on a supernatural killing spree. Her life of wreaking revenge is upended, however, when she learns that the faeries below ground, imprisoned in their kingdom, are very close to breaking out. 
 My favorite part of the book, funnily enough, was a character called Derrick. He plays the comical sidekick, which is usually a part that I care little for. But Derrick was truly hilarious. He's a pixie, a male Tinkerbell, and lives in Aileana's closet, mending her gowns for honey, which intoxicates him. His scenes caused me to laugh quite often. More than that, he also served to make the fae folk more accessible. Athough Derrick doesn't kill humans like his larger kinfolk, he is still an uncanny creature. I liked how May made the villains slightly more sympathetic by giving them a spectrum of behavior that we got to witness. 
 However, there were issues with the book besides the steampunk. I found myself arguing with Aileana's logic and the behavior of other characters quite a bit. The writing also seemed to be... manipulative, unkind, coy? I felt strung along, as a reader, having things withheld that didn't have to be. Did the romance really have to unfold that way? It was strung out for so long that when something did happen it felt too little too late. And the cliffhanger. By god. What a disservice to readers. 
 All in all, I give The Falconer three stars. It had good elements and frustrations in equal measure. However, I will surely be picking up the sequel, which comes out this November.

 First off, it was a teensy bit insta lovey feeling. I liked both Nicholas and Etta and I enjoy the dynamic of their relationship, but I'm not sure what their love for one another is based off of. Like, the journey throughout this book literally happened within, what, like ten days max? Sorry, not enough time to convince me that their soulmates. Also, if my mother was being held hostage and was waiting on me to come rescue her and I only had nine days, I'd have my ass in gear. You wouldn't catch me wasting time making out with some guy I met three days ago. 
 That being said, a lot of the moments between Nicholas and Etta were cute, I just think I would've enjoyed them more if there was more of a build up in their relationship. For instance, when they're in the Underground bomb shelter and the couple is dancing to the music and then later, Nicholas asks Etta if in her time, the two of them would be able to dance like that. I thought that was adorable. 
 Speaking of the events that were convenient, the whole scavenger thing was. I like riddles or plot twists in books that I can solve. I mean, I love being surprised by a plot twist, but once I know the plot twist, I want all the little clues to fall into place. My reaction should be "oh, duh, stupid me." In this book, there wasn't really any way for me to solve the riddles. A lot of them are based off Etta's knowledge of her mother's paintings, which the reader knows nothing about. And all of it just seemed to happen so quickly. 
 The fact that Etta's mother escaped the men holding her hostage seemed a little abrupt too. Like, she meets up with Nicholas in the desert and he's all shocked and she's all like "pfft did you really expect anything less from me?" Well, um, YEAH. Nicholas doesn't actually know you, or what you're capable of. And if you were going to escape anyways, why send your daughter (who has no prior knowledge or experience in time traveling, btw) to go get the astrolabe? All that succeeded in doing was leading the Thorns right to it! 
 I will say, I didn't suspect Julian was alive until the end. When Etta disappears the same way Julian did, I started to wonder because OBVIOUSLY Etta didn't die. And lo and behold, Julian's alive. 
 The book was a good, quick read and I did enjoy it. I'm just not buying that the whole next book will be based off Nicholas finding the astrolabe to restore Etta to her time because he's dedicating his life to finding her because he can't live without her because he met her a week ago and they're in love and so living without her isn't living at all.
Soooo not my cup of tea.

It's bittersweet, but at the same time satisfying coz it's not your cliche battle-romance type of novel.

"The man in black fled across the desert, and the Gunslinger followed." 
 This is the first line to The Dark Tower series; eight dark fantasy/horror/western books which King describes as the magnum opus of all his writing. It's an incredible first line, and quote possibly the greatest first line I have ever read. 
 It's a shame that I hated almost every moment which followed. 
 From the beginning, you are thrown into King's universe with no explanations. You don't know who the Man in Black is, who The Gunslinger is, where they are, why The Gunslinger is chasing him, or why the Man in Black is fleeing. Or if he is even fleeing. Or what the heck is going on. All we know is that the Gunslinger follows. 
 The problem is that as we continue, nothing is really explained to us. We get some background on the Gunslinger, but not enough. We experience the world with the Gunslinger as he progresses through the desert, but that's it. This means that I had no idea what was going on, or why is was happening, for 98% of the book. I didn't care about the events that were happening, or what happened to the characters. There was no way to identify if there was good or evil, or if any of the characters fell into those paradigms. No characters had any relationships to speak of, nor relationships to the world around them. 
 I found myself constantly thinking, "Why am I even reading this book?" 
 I'm sure the story improves and dots are connected as one reads on. I knew this wouldn't be the greatest of King's work since it's the first story he ever wrote. For a 19-year-old, this is still great. But I detested it. 
 If anyone I know has read this series and wants to let me know what I'm missing, I'll gladly listen. I want this book to be great. Alas. Until such a time arises that this is bested, I shall leave this my least favorite book of 2016. By a lot.

Rating: 5+ stars 
 "Sure, jock," he smiled. I'm all yours." 
 I don't know about you, but I think that was the darn cutest thing Jason could have said, but I'm still pissed! Tushmore, how can you freaking leave it at that? With so many questions left unanswered? 
 I wanted a more in-depth look into Jason's past. Did Mike's leaving have an influence into his harder substance usage? What did he feel during those lost three years? Did he actually enjoy Mike's company when he was getting paid? What was going into his mind when he woke up at Fulbourne? When he learnt it was Mike's doing? When Mike went to visit him? When Mike told him he loved him? 
 Argh, I want my answers! I really wish it had been told from Jason's point-of-view, or better yet, from both of Jason's and Mike's point-of-views. And why was it so short? 
 The more I think about it, the more surprised I am at how much I actually liked it loved it. There are issues I had at the beginning, for example, at the prices Jason charged Mike. How Mike was somewhat naive and how much of a pushover he was. At times, I was outraged and wanted him to get over Jason. I thought he deserved better, but then I realized how broken Jason was. How he desperately needed someone to believe in him and push him. He did deserve Mike's love. Yes, it also has a few editing errors, and sorry, but Tushmore's writing isn't spectacular, but you know what? Despite all my complaints, it somehow made sense; it just worked. I know this isn't for everyone. There is substance and emotional abuse, addiction, paid sex, and perhaps unhealthy love; it's provoking, but yet so rewarding. Mike's faith and love is absolutely grounding and stunning, definitely something extraordinary to read about.

Kate rarely comes out and makes a positive personality judgment like that, and it seemed out of place--added in in revisions, maybe. And then, when Armitage says something about loyalty when he has Kate hostage, it's obvious immediately that Maddie is in on the whole thing, but Kate doesn't pick up on it.  Those are small issues, though, as I wasn't certain I was right about the main killer, but I do think she gave away the game a little. Other than that, a tightly-plotted mystery full of suspense and good storytelling. I'm glad the Daniel Lapp storyline is moving forward, too. I hope the next book resolves it entirely.

Few things frustrate me more than loving the first book in a series, only to be completely let down by the second. Such was the case with this book. I adored the first, and almost bought the second rather than waiting for it at the library. However, I'm glad I didn't buy it, because this isn't a book I'll ever be returning to. 
 For starters, there isn't really a plot in this book. Basically, Calla spends the whole time learning about these people she always thought were her enemies. Chapter upon chapter of explanation ensure, with Calla and Shay saying interesting things like, "I don't understand," and, "How is that possible?" These comments are sometimes the only break in what is really a 300 page explanation of Searcher history. Yawn. 
 Calla herself is wildly annoying, vacillating between Shay and Ren at the drop of a hat. More than a bit angst-y, and there wasn't enough of a plot for me to overlook the annoyance. She also allowed Shay to push her around more than I was comfortable with...where is the kick-ass female alpha she's supposed to be? 
 A lot of new characters are thrown at us, especially in the beginning. The author includes a number of pointless interactions between them, to what purpose I can't imagine. (To show readers that the Searchers are normal, nice people?) Some of the Searchers were a bit over-the-top, and I wished we could have seen more of Calla's pack rather than this new group. 
 I will be reading the next (last?) book in the series, mainly because I'm hoping that now all the backstory bs is done, we can get back to an actual storyline. I'm also rooting for Ren (Shay really pissed me off in this book), and I hope Calla ends up with him in the next book.

 God, how irritating this book was. With all the drama and shit.

 "Yeah, I still make her nervous. I wish I knew how to fix that, but I'm not a Hailey expert yet. I'm still just getting to know her and what makes her tick" Chapter 11 ("Hanging Upside Down From A Chandelier").

I wasn't quite as enamored of this book as I was with "The Name of the Star." I'm not sure quite what it was about this second book in the Shades of London series that didn't quite do it for me as well as the first, and I'm still giving it 4 stars, but I felt like *something* was missing. 
 The elements I loved about the first book were there. An interesting paranormal mystery! A snarky and fun main character! Snarky and fun secondary characters! London! Boo! Jazza! Alastair! 
 I think I know what it was. I realize that Rory was traumatized by nearly being killed by a ghost. I get that and can accept that. But... I saw from the second Charlotte recommended Rory see her psychiatrist that this psychiatrist was bad news. Why did it take Rory so dang long to figure it out? And she didn't even really figure it out, it was shoved in her face! Ack!  
 After giving myself a week or two to mull the book over, I've decided that the book itself is so much fun to read, this doesn't matter all that much (though it is annoying). Maureen Johnson has a ridiculously fun writing style and the book itself is a fast romp that is a bit darker than the first book. 
 Without giving anything away, I will say that the ending of this book doesn't wrap up nearly as neatly as the first book, so if you're looking for the sense of closure and satisfaction you had when you finished "The Name of the Star," I'm afraid you won't find it until the next book. Now that I'm thinking through it, that is the other major component that left me not quite as happy with this book as the previous - but it isn't something that should keep you from checking it out if you're looking for a book with just about everything - a bit of mystery, a bit of humor, a bit of supernatural weirdness and creepiness, and a just a hint of romance.

FACTS: 
 - It's not really a romance. There are a few bits and pieces, but it's ultimately sooo not the focus of the story, which is kind of appropriate. 
 - It seemed like it would be a fantasy book, but it's not really. I mean, it is, because it's about some imaginary land/kingdom. But I guess it didn't feel like a fantasy since it's so rooted in science and there's no magic. 
 WHAT I LIKED: 
 - I really liked the overall story. This girl who never in a million years expected to be queen is suddenly queen. 
 - I liked the main character a lot. She was super down to earth and probably ended up being the best possible person who could become queen. 
 - It has a good mystery. The whole book is really a murder mystery. The MC is trying to figure out who killed everyone. I enjoyed her investigation! 
 THINGS I DIDN'T LIKE: 
 - The ending felt anti-climactic to me. We went through so much to get to the end, then it just fell a bit flat. I think because the murderer ended up being a nice (but misguided) person so it was hard to really truly hate her, and the MC clearly felt the same way so she let her off easy. I think this just made the whole thing feel unsatisfying. I wanted to be able to truly hate someone and see them punished, but I didn't get that.  
 - The book was missing a little X factor that would have made me truly love it. It wasn't a soul shattering, all-consuming type book. More like a fun, enjoyable read that may fade from my memory pretty quickly. I enjoyed it, but I don't see it lasting with me forever, if you know what I mean.

I have read and enjoyed Ms Fitzpatrick's Hush, Hush series very much, so when I saw this book on Netgalley I had to request it, as I wanted to see if the Author could write a good YA that was non paranormal, I do like suspense books as much as Paranormal books and I can say that I enjoyed this book too. 
 The main character is Britt and she has planned a hiking/camping trip in the Grand Teton Mountains in Wyoming with her best friend Korbie. Just before heading off Britt bumps into Korbie's older brother Calvin who had split up with Britt 8 months ago, Britt still harbours feelings for Calvin and when they have a bit of a spat in the Gas Station, Britt steals some items out of Calvins Glove compartment in his car... And I had no issue with her little escapade, he was a complete jerk, and my opinion didn't really change through the book. This little act of spitefulness ends up being a life saver for Britt in the near future! 
 Korbie's parents own a lodge in the Teton's and thats where the girls plan to use for their base, on the drive up, they run into a blizzard, after some thought the girls decide its better to try to set out on foot for the Lodge or another cabin... And thats when the adventure really gets going! 
 I really took to Britt's character, she's spent most of her life relying on her father/brother/Calvin to protect her, and after Calvin's betrayal she decided that enough was enough and she planned this trip to show once and for all that she could fend for herself. As you read the story you watch her grow, she finds courage and determination throughout the trials that are set in front of her. 
 Korbie on the other hand hasn't changed - her family treat her like a princess (a point that Calvin hates as his parents have constantly belittled him and never supported him, down to actual physical abuse) Britt even looks out for Korbie, and sticks her neck out to ensure her safety is paramount. This was another aspect I liked about Britt, she thought of others before herself. 
 As the plot unravelled I had my suspicions to what and who was responsible for certain things, but Becca Fitzpatrick still managed to sneak in a plot twists to keep me guessing. 
 If you enjoy a suspense story with well developed characters, then I would recommend this book without hesitation. I will certainly be looking out for it in the bookstores come Release Day.

 To be honest, the writing style was a major issue for me. It was in Molly's voice, so it was written in the slang-ish 'snarky' way that a 16-year-old would talk. Or supposed to be, anyway. To me it seemed much more juvenile than 16 and I felt like the attempts at humor and sarcasm just tried to hard. The points that were probably supposed to be funny didn't even draw a twitch of the lips from me. Instead I was like: 
 Loser. 
 I couldn't stand Molly. She was snobby, judgmental, and petulant. Sometimes I forgot she was supposed to be 16 (at least that's what I think she was anyway) because she acted more like she was 12. (Seriously, at times I felt like I was reading a 12-year-old's diary.) Plus some of the things she said made me want to punch her, such as: 
 There were only a handful [of necros] that attended my school, and most of them were to dark and angsty for my taste. Plus, I didn't look good with kohl on my eyes and my nose was too cute to be pierced. 
 Maybe I'm overreacting, but the stereotypes in this sentence just pissed me off. So just because you have your nose pierced and wear dark eyeliner you're 'dark and angsty?' Bitch, please. And this: 
 Ally was fourteen, tall and gangly, still flat-chested and had braces, too. She had the best hair - long, silky chestnut waves with auburn highlights, but did she care? No. She also liked to wear baggy clothes in blah colors. Even though I would never admit it to her (not ever), one day she'd be gorgeous. Y'know, after she lost the metalwork, got some boobs and developed some fashion sense. 
 What, just because she has a few flaws and isn't snobby like you, she's not beautiful? Because she wears what she wants and likes to be comfortable, she's ugly? Ugh. This just rubbed me the wrong way. And Molly had something like that to say about pretty much anyone she saw. Like she was better than everyone else. At one point she even said something judgmental and shallow and then was like "oops...my shallowness was showing again" like she was trying to make it a joke. Hahahaha-NO, how 'bout I knock some of your perfect teeth right out of your pretty, shallow little head. ARGH. I hated her. And when her dad drops a major bomb she goes all Hulk, smash! on everyone: 
 "No," I yelled. "I'm not! I hate you! I hate all of you! [...] I'm not going to boarding school. I'm not gonna be a reaper. Or Anubis's bitch. You hear me? I choose my life. Not you!" 
 Back to the writing style: It grated on my nerves and made my eye twitch. Let's get something straight, I use the word 'woot.' I happen to love that word. Plus I felt like there was too much mixing of the terms 'necromancer' and 'reaper.' The lines were a bit blurred, even though those two paranormals are totally different. I did skip through and read the end, and was underwhelmed and unsurprised by that, too. 
 Really? Sigh.

Who doesn't know the famous Miss Marple and her investigation talents? When it comes to well-known detectives in classic literature, along with Sherlock Holmes and Hercule Poirot she will belong to those who are mentioned first. I can almost imagine the gossipy, annoying and very inquisitive lady snooping around the village, and it's easy to understand why a smart character like her earned such a recognition beneath crime and mystery novels. "Murder at the Vicarage" is called the first book in the Miss Marple series, yet she only appears in a handful of scenes, irregularly interspersed in the course of this novel. 
 In the first place, Agatha Christie writes about a colonel's death and the small town's vicar who tries to discover the murderer's identity. Most of the characters will at some point of the novel be suspected of being the wanted murderer, but the reader should expect the final reveal to be somehow unpredictable. I thought I had figured out who the killer was halfway through the novel, but the outcome was ... I could not have been more wrong. And it would indeed be surprising if anyone else was as smart as Miss Marple in the quest of figuring out the identity of the culprit. However, this also caused another one of this book's weak spots: Although it is only 270 pages long, it dragged on for the second half, as nearly no new information were added and the investigators were more or less left groping in the dark. 
 Agatha Christie writes about very different characters trying to live in a small town where nothing ever happens - until this highly disliked man is murdered at the vicarage. As the novel is written from the first-person-perspective of the vicar, Leonard Clement, the reader has to rely on his observations, which made it even harder to guess the outcome of the murder mystery. After all, the author managed to write complicated and confusing murder mysteries with nearly no loose ends, however, something else fell by the wayside: the characters. With nearly no character development or interesting relationships present, it is hardly possible to get invested into the plot itself, and with Miss Marple being only a side character, the most interesting part of the novel was ignored for most of the time. 
 My first Miss Marple novel, my second Agatha Christie novel, and still no fan of her works. I guess I'll be staying faithful to Sherlock Holmes!

On the Saturday morning, I took my girlfriend to work, drove home, picked up the book and didn't stop reading until I'd finished all 400 pages of it--I swear the font is small too! The speed at which I read the book is itself a testament to Cline's easy to read style. 
 The earth is a dystopian husk of what it used to be, and even the short spells that we spend there paint a vivid picture of the brutality Wade, our main character, faces. In stark contrast, the OASIS--the virtual world where the majority of the populations finds its escape--is simply enchanting. Its universe spanning scope and depth are brilliant. One of the best things about this story is that it's something I could envision happening. It doesn't sit completely outside the realms of possibility. 
 Then, of course, there are the endless 80's references that, even as a child of the 90's, I could appreciate. These references firmly place the story in our world, and give it that realistic edge that draws you in. As a gamer or a child or a fan of the 80's, the nostalgia factor is a major player in your enjoyment of the story--in fact they are a major plot point! That being said, you definitely don't need to have seen, played and listened to every popular movie, game and album of the 80's to enjoy the story, as the important details are given to us along the way. 
 All the characters were real and relatable--even the in-game avatars showed a great deal of emotion (thanks to immersive interfacing that some OASIS users possess) and I found myself driving through the story not just because of the intriguing plot, but because I HAD to know what happened to our average tinkerer Wade. 
 All in all, I wholeheartedly recommend this story to anyone who's a fan of dystopian fiction, gaming, or the 80's. Or anyone who's a fan of a god-damn fantastic, character driven story. I think that covers pretty much all of you.

Kokoro is the kind of novel that I would call good, but brings to mind the phrasing "good literature" rather than "exciting story-telling." The story itself is rather unspectacular and doesn't exactly seduce the reader with cliff-hangers; instead, it focuses on a more philosophical topic for which the story is more the medium than an end. The story is not bad (though structured with a bit of unbalance), but pure entertainment is not the focal point of this novel. 
 To me (and who knows how grossly off from the generally accepted meaning my interpretation is), the story was ultimately about the consequences of choices and actions -- not on a physical level, but on a philosophical and moral level. It is about the heartfelt pangs of consequence rather than action-driven reaction to action. 
 It is about a young man's discovery of such an understanding of consequence via his connection to his older friend, Sensei, who himself is deeply searching for meaningful resolution to the consequences of his own actions -- and in doing so is falling into a life of almost utter inaction. At the novel's start, the younger man is almost startlingly insensitive (not appreciating how a trip to the graveyard might be a emotionally endowed event for his companion). By the end, the young man is forced into retrospective of the person for whom he what might, at best, have been said to have had a naive curiosity for -- and hopefully an implied retrospective of his own person. Abstracted to the most general sense, the book is about, not the extraordinary, but the growing discovery of a need for recognizing the meaning in the hopes and failures of everyday existence. 
 Despite the utter lack of specificity in my above description of the novel, that is very much the feel of the novel: it does not pinpoint nor articulate any specific message nor universal epitaph to bind all together, but rather leaves the impression of the uncertain, but existent meaning created by and embedded in the actions of everyday characters. 
 The outstanding quality of the novel is the setting of Japan of approximately one hundred years ago does nothing to take away from the philosophical implications of the work. It has a timelessness -- even if it's not much of a page-turner.

While Beauty Slept is a bleak rendition of the Sleeping Beauty tale. I liked it well enough, yet I couldn't help but compare it to Spindle's End, a book with a similar plot but much more magic, both in the story and in the telling. 
 I'm a fan of retold fairy tales, and this one imagines how actual events might have been embellished into the Sleeping Beauty legend, over time. That means there's almost no magic, although there are a few "magic?" moments that make you wonder how much power the "witches" in the story really had. You could put their powers down to persuasion, charisma, and herbal knowledge, or you could see them as something more. I liked the idea that this was something that could have actually happened in medieval times, with the "enchanted sleep" a euphemism for a real disease, but the story still carries a hint of fantasy, as the place names are pretty much made up. 
 (I might have liked the book better if it had swung harder in one direction than another--either straight-up historical fiction or straight-up medieval fantasy. As it was, it didn't have enough world-building to satisfy my fantasy tastes, and not enough reality for a true work of historical fiction.) 
 Like Spindle's End, the story is told mostly from the perspective of an older-sister figure of the princess, and (vague ending spoilers) the twist at the end is virtually identical , albeit with more death and less magic. So I couldn't help but compare the two. I realize there are only so many ways to retell a fairy tale, but the similarities were enough to made me feel like I'd read this version before. 
 I did like the narrator, Elise, and her romance with Marcus. However, Elise spent far too much of the book going "If only I had known then what would happen later! Would I have made the same choice? I'll never know!" which can be effective when used sparingly, but it gets old fast. 
 A diverting enough way to spend an afternoon, but for me it doesn't come close to Spindle's End, which will always be one of my favorites.

Turtles All The Way Down is definitely a John Green book, with all the pros and cons that statement comes with. That being said, I did like it. Quite a bit. Turtles All The Way Down is the latest novel written by John Green. The novel follows the story of Aza Holmes, a sixteen-year-old girl with a pretty severe anxiety disorder. Sixteen-year-old Aza never intended to pursue the mystery of fugitive billionaire Russell Pickett, but there's a hundred-thousand-dollar reward at stake and her Best and Most Fearless Friend, Daisy, is eager to investigate. So together, they navigate the short distance and broad divides that separate them from Russell Pickett's son, Davis. Aza is trying. She is trying to be a good daughter, a good friend, a good student, and maybe even a good detective, while also living within the ever-tightening spiral of her own thoughts. (Mild spoilers follow) 
 So, I don't know if it was just me or if the marketing campaign really screwed up, but I was definitely under the impression that this book was more of a mystery novel. It is not a mystery novel. It is not a mystery novel. IT IS NOT A MYSTERY NOVEL. Everybody all clear on that? Good. I wish the advertising for the novel had been a bit more forthcoming about the fact that this book is really about a girl with a pretty severe anxiety disorder. I was not mentally prepared for a book like that, and the longer I read, the more anxious I became. That's not to say the book is bad or anything, it's genuinely really, really good. I just think that everybody needs to know what they're getting into when they start this book. If you find yourself in need of a trigger warning before consuming potentially triggering content, this is your trigger warning. 
 The vast majority of Turtles All The Way Down deals with Aza and her anxiety. It's handled in a really, really realistic and respectful way. Almost too realistic. If I had to bet money, I'd bet that much of this novel is autobiographical in one way or another. While I went into this expecting a mystery novel, I really liked that I ended up getting a novel that dealt so much with anxiety. As someone with anxiety, so much of this hit home so well for me. The way Green describes invasive thoughts and anxiety spirals as this thing that you can't escape that just gets tighter and tighter as it keeps winding its way down your brain really was amazing. I've never seen that concept explained in such an accurate way before and it was such a joy to read in this novel. 
 His characters, as always, feel a bit... fake in that no teenager talks the way he has them talk and they always think in these pretentious philosophical ways and it always feels just a little bit off. They're well written and developed characters, but they still suffer from that factor that John Green has always been known for suffering from. One thing that's worth noting, though, is that this book very much doesn't glorify or romanticize mental illness (or any illness). That's an accusation that's been lobbed at John Green for pretty much his entire career, and I'm happy to say that it's not a problem that's in this book. Anxiety is painted in a sympathetic but ugly light. A lot of detail goes into explaining just how awful mental illness can be. Green is careful not to stigmatize or demonize mental illnesses, but he also makes sure to properly show just how awful and unappealing it is. It's definite growth in his depiction of mental illness and it's a welcome growth. 
 It's hard to talk about the "plot" of the novel as it really revolves around Aza coming to grips with her anxiety and how it impacts the people around her and how her life and Davis Pickett's life interacts and weaves with each other's. I thought it was paced really well. It never dragged nor did it move unrealistically quickly. Things happened at the speed they needed to happen and plenty of time was spent on things that needed time spent on them. It's a quick read; it's not a particularly long book nor is it a particularly challenging read. But it's a well-paced read. You feel satisfied with how things went by the end of the novel. 
 Honestly, this is probably my favorite of John Green's books. I loved The Fault in Our Stars, but he ran awfully close to romanticizing illness there and I enjoyed Paper Towns (and never understood the criticism it got for the fact that Margot was a "manic-pixie dream girl"; that was sorta the point of the book. Q had to learn to stop viewing her like that and understand that she was an actual person and not an idealized construct), while I never managed to finish Looking For Alaska and haven't looked at An Abundance of Katherines or Will Grayson, Will Grayson. Turtles All The Way Down is a surprising book. It's not a mystery novel; it's a genuinely moving look at how anxiety can impact the life of the sufferer and those who care for them. It's a sweet story about friendship and young love. It's heartbreaking and funny and entertaining and it's worth reading, especially if you or anyone you know has ever suffered from an anxiety disorder.

Such gorgeous writing. 
 Too often authors have incredible ideas of stories to write. So we're excited about them and want only to find a time-machine to transport us into the future with the intention to read said stories. 
 And then we do, after months of waiting (still waiting on that time-machine, by the way) and we're disappointed because, although the author had a great idea, the execution was so-so or completely mediocre. 
 Am I right? Which is why I am so extremely happy and proud to be able to say that ''Wintersong'' is as good as it sounds (and looks--exquisite cover!), because the narration is absolutely captivating. 
 It's a dark but romantic and magical fantasy poem--I mean novel. But it's so poetic that, at some point, you're going to stop thinking of this as being just another book and look at it with reverence and wonder, ''Was this marvel written in another world? Somewhere with real magic?'' 
 Whenever I will feel uninspired or uninspiring, I will read a chapter of this book. 
 The story is very interesting, especially because there aren't many like this one (that I know of). How often are goblins featured in fantasy novels, anyway? Rarely. And, I don't know about you, but I find love-hate relationships kind of really sexy, especially when there's a touch of mystery and darkness to the romance. 
 Though, do not expect adventure, action, a large series of events or even elemental magic. There is more showing than telling, but the telling is done so well that I simply did not care for the repetition or slow-pacing. 
 What I did not like as much was how important multiple characters were in the beginning of the story, but then not anymore as the story progressed. I missed Kathe and I missed Josef. And, really, if you're to include a gay character in your story, why not actually focus a little bit on their romance story as well, huh? 
 It is true, sadly, that this book will not work for everyone. If, however, you love lyrical writing and character-driven stories with an emphasis on romance and a dark atmosphere, this may just be your fantasy win of 2017.

I am going to review all of these books together. If that is a problem for you, stop reading. 
 I read these books quick. As in I started on Sunday afternoon and was done by Monday evening (and yes, I worked a full day on Monday). They were captivating and easy to read. If these are YA reading then they are certainly a more challenging type than existed when I was younger or than I have encountered as an adult reading YA. 
 There is practically nothing new about the themes or devices in these books. There have to be a million novels and movies about people being forced to fight to the death. Its not surprising that those having to fight are teenagers; sacrificing the innocent has happened since civilizations started tossing maidens into the sea. The government having a drawing to select the people they are going to have citizens kill isn't new either (in fact, all I could see during that scene was Shirley Jackson's short story). 
 So it wasn't the plot that made me love these books, although there was nothing wrong with the plot. What made me love these books (and probably made others love it as well) was the characters. Katniss is a wonderfully complicated and conflicted hero. She has so much disdain and venom for her mother that I was surprised. But she has a valid reason: her mother lost her shit after Katniss' father died and Katniss and her little sister almost starved to death. Katniss is a very parenitfied teenager. She has been taking care of her sister and mother for years when we are first introduced to her. Although her mother has returned to some sembalence of functionality, Katniss is still the one who makes the household run. 
 She is also the one who tries so hard to take care of and protect her sister. What's really interesting is how much she underestimates her sister. She has a vision of Prim as a fragile child that she has to keep safe and has a very hard time seeing Prim's strengths. In fact, she sees Prim like a lot of adults see children: without a reserve of resilience and nothing to contribute to society at large. Its an interesting commentary on how even those who have been underestimated or who don't have status in society can't see when they commit the same sins against someone further down society's ladder. 
 Katniss spends the books unsure about a lot of things. She can't sort out how she feels about two boys (men? teenagers?)and ends up stringing them both along for almost the entirety of the trilogy. The love triangle isn't interesting, at least not any more interesting than any other love triangle. What is interesting is watching those relationships deteriorate over time. You can't string two people along for a year or more without creating hard feelings and animosity. I can't say that's a theme I've seen in a YA novel do well before. 
 Collins is at her best in these books when depicting the dark underbelly of human emotions. There's a lot of love, justice and heroism in these novels, but what really shines is the doubt, vengence and torment. 
 Everyone's motives are muddled, and even Katniss isn't sure where she stands on what is going on around her. The only person who is singularly good and pure is Peeta, and frankly he bored the shit out of me until the third book. Not that I wasn't rooting for them to end up together (hey, I'm only human), but I wanted him to really lose his shit on Katniss or refuse to have a veneer of love but not the real thing. Maybe I'm just projecting how I'd act/feel onto him. 
 Watching Katniss and Gale grow apart was beautifully done and completely nostalgic. Who hasn't experienced a relationship that was close during a hard time fall apart when circumstances change? Or had a childhood friendship disintegrate? Its not something that teens think about because many of them haven't had that experience. As people experience differnt life events, their relationship changes, and many times bonds can't flex to accommodate who you become. Not something that you'd really have to teach adults, but what a fabulous choice of themes for YA. 
 And speaking of fabulous themes, Collins portrays addiction with gentleness and ugliness. Haymitch is the obvious depiction, he's an alcoholic who begins the books by making an ass of himself. Not unusual for a drunk. But he also is insightful, funny and more dependable than you'd expect. He's been through some horrific events and its perfectly understandable why he doesn't want to face reality any more. He fucks some things up, he vomits all over himself and passes out frequently (sounds about right for an alcoholic). However, he is great at strategy, he's insightful and he really comes through for Katniss and Peeta. Its nice to see an alcoholic being portrayed in complex ways. They aren't all bad, but we don't usually admit that in our society. Even more interesting are the drug addicts. Some of the victors have developed opiate addications. They are mostly portrayed as happy, artistic and harmless. Also pitiable and very unhealthy. But those characters are some of the most at peace in the whole trilogy. 
 In all, these books are wonderful. There aren't a lot of gender stereotypes or too much political propoganda to put the reader off. The plot devices aren't new, but they don't feel worn out. The characters are rich and the relationships are realistic and ambivalent. Now if only this series would gain the cultural popularity of Twilight I might feel better about what teenagers are reading...

An Ember in the Ashes by Sabaa Tahir is a solid 4.5. I usually round up, but I just couldn't bring my self to do it in this case because of one itty bitty but super annoying issue I found with this otherwise spectacular read. I will get to that later, but first let me rave. 
 Laia is a Scholar living in a Martial world. Once a free people, Scholars were conquered by the Martials 500 years ago and have been living under the brutal regime ever since. Her brother Darin is captured and imprisoned, facing possible execution. Laia volunteers to spy for the Resistance, a rebel group trying to take down the Martials, and her best hope to rescue Darin. She allows herself to be sold as a slave. Now in a position to gather intel she believes will save her brother, Laia embarks on a dangerous mission in a violent world. 
 Elias is a Martial soldier at the Empire's military academy. Though he has friends, family, and prestige, he longs to escape the ruthless system he secretly deplores. He plans to desert upon graduation, a crime punishable by death if he is caught, but an ancient prophecy persuades him to stay. A new Emperor is to be named, and he finds himself among the contenders. As the following weeks unfold, Elias struggles to survive and must decide what price he is willing to pay to become a free man. 
 The world building in this book is fabulous. Tahir weaves a magical tale combining just the right amount of history and ethnology and current events. The different languages, traditions, and societal structures of the Scholars, Martials, Tribesmen, and Mariners bring some diversity to the story. Though it is supposed to resemble ancient Rome, and succeeds in many ways, I feel there is also a Middle Eastern influence as well due to the surrounding desert and the presence of jinns and guls. Wriths also exist in this world and I would have enjoyed a more significant presence of all these mythical beings. However, this book is definitely low fantasy, not high, so the relationships take center stage. 
 The imagery in AEITA is absolutely mesmerizing. Tahir has a definite talent for making emotions nearly tangible and painted pictures in my mind without becoming too wordy or sounding too silly. However her real skill is bringing a scene to life using the sense of smell to portray the environment as well as the characters. Laia smells of fruit and sugar, Elias of spice and rain. Keenan smells like cedarwood and Helene like grass and snow. I found these descriptions seriously intoxicating and felt they effortlessly furthered my understanding of who the characters were, like secret glimpses of their souls. 
 Overall, I loved the characters. Laia took a little while to grow on me while I adored Elias all most immediately. Laia starts off as a frightened, fragile, slightly self-righteous 17 year old. All of which is understandable, but not desirable characteristics for a heroine in a fantasy novel. However Tahir works some magic with her character development, and along the way, Laia blossoms into something more. She becomes strong and courageous and capable. Elias starts off kind and fearless and loyal. He only gets better. He desires freedom more than anything, which strikes me as the central theme in AEITA (and just happens to be one of my favorite subjects). It is what many of the major characters yearn for to varying degrees, but he is the one who pursues it without support from anyone else. 
 Other themes include guilt, courage, family, and friendship. All are important; all are powerful, but freedom is always my favorite. 
 So this story included a "love square." I have grown quite weary of the love triangle over all, but I found the existence of a love square did not irk me one bit. However the one thing that did annoy me so greatly that I chopped off half a star from this otherwise exquisite story is how Elias responded to the presence of Laia or Helene in every. Single. Scene. Yes, he is a young male with raging hormones. I get it. Laia and Helene are both beautiful and brave and smell so good. But when you are balancing on a ledge with enemies attacking from above and death waiting below, and you are distracted by Helene's body being so close to yours, can you not freaking focus on the situation at hand, Elias? I understand attraction can leave you feeling intoxicated, but you're kinda in a dire situation here. Surely the instinct to survive is greater than the instinct to copulate at this particular moment. Overkill, Sabaa. Overkill. 
 Beware, in the world of AEITA, the threat of rape, torture, and murder always loom. This is a violent, gruesome setting. People die. A lot. If you can stomach a fair amount of cruelty and bloodshed, An Ember in the Ashes is a fantastic book with incredible heart and soul.

If Kleypas had stated at the outset that everyone in this book were time-travelers who'd gone 30-40 years into the past, I might have given this a 4. As it is, a couple of glaring historical inaccuracies made me knock this down to a 3. (I actually wonder if someone changed the time period of this series late in the game, as all of the historical issues would be absent if this took place in 1880.) 
 This book had great characters, possibly some of my faves of all of Kleypas' novels. It referenced other books I didn't even know were interconnected with this series, and I was delighted to see that characters I had enjoyed in other books were continuing on happily elsewhere. 
 But...holy historical inaccuracy, Batman! 
 First off, the entire premise is that many wealthy American heiresses (including our heroine) are going to Europe to marry titled British men. If this story had been set between 1874 (when Jennie Jerome married Lord Churchill) and 1900s, this would make sense. (Actually, if the story had taken place 20 years earlier, it might also be believable - but this takes place in the period when heiresses weren't doing that.) It's sort of like having people go to Woodstock in the 1930s. 
 The girls also refer to sneaking a greased piglet into Mrs. Astor's parlor. However, at this time "the Mrs. Astor" was the 14-year-old Caroline Webster Schermerhorn. She didn't marry William Astor Jr. for another 10 years, and she didn't become the grand dame of society until the 1860s. (They could be referring to Margaret Astor, but that's a bit of a stretch.) 
 Lillian tells St. Vincent "about wintertime in Central Park, when the pond at Fifty-ninth Street had frozen over and weekly ice carnivals were held." And this is the part where we learn Lillian is a time traveler, because the book takes place in 1843, and no one had even TALKED about building Central Park yet. William Cullen Bryant didn't start calling for a public park of some kind until 1844. At the time this novel takes place, the area that is now Central Park hosted villages lived in by free African Americans, Irish pig farmers and German gardeners. She also talks about the "row of stone mansions on Fifth Avenue," which didn't exist at the time (or for close to another 20 years). 
 I'm happy to give a romance novel a pass on anachronistic characterization (if you read even romance novels from 30 years ago it can be hard to get into just how submissive the women were expected to be), but stuff like this just drives me bonkers. BONKERS, I tell you. 
 The fact that he took advantage of her when she was drunk was probably more historically accurate, but it made me dislike him a LOT. If you are drunk you are NOT CONSENTING. Period. That gave me a case of the icks.

Meh. The concept is interesting, but the world and characters didn't really work for me. The language was too full of modernisms to fit the world. Fayre is rather mopey, except when she is burning with lust, and some of the language got repetitive.

Bravo, Mr. Wallach, bravo. 
 Review originally posted on @ Princessica of Books. 
 *Thank you to Simon & Schuster for the complimentary copy! This in no way affects my review; all opinions are my own.* 
 I previously read We All Looked Up back in August and gave it 4.5 states. It's obvious that I enjoy his work and I looked forward to more. If you read that review, I'm about to mention some of the same things because Wallach delivers again, but this time better. 
 Introducing: The Manic Pixie Girl Trope 
 You know, that one girl who is quirky in all the right places and brings existential crises wherever she goes. Silver hair? Spends time in hotel lobbies? Is 245 years old (supposedly)? That's right, we get one in Thanks for the Trouble and I adore Zelda. I enjoy this trope in general and it's one of the lesser ones. Wallach makes it so fun and quirky. 
 Where's the Diversity? There it is! 
 Shoutout to Wallach for constantly making his characters diverse! Told in a male POV, the main character is a Latino as is the rest of his family and one other character. Even the side characters are Asian, though they are put in a stereotypical environment. In addition, mental health is involved and it is done correctly (see "It's in the Words" section later). 
 A New Best Friend (or 2 or 3) 
 I loved all the characters! Alana provided comedic relief, while the chess players pop in at the right times. Each person has their own voice and it's so apparent that I find myself reading some characters' parts faster, in an accent, and with hand motions. 
 Tell Me A Story (or 2 or 3) 
 Wallach is one of THE best story tellers. Like I mention before, each character comes to life and everything is told perfectly. Oh my gosh, just writing this review makes me want to read it again! I read this like a movie and books that read like movies are the best. 
 A Weekend Road Trip 
 Wallach chooses the San Francisco as the setting, a place I am very familiar with. It has a dash of everything and there is so much to do. The setting really ties everything together and bolsters the whole road trip romance. Even to those unfamiliar with SF, he'll make it familiar to you. And make you want to go to every place mentioned. 
 It's in the Words. 
 There are three main themes in this novel: taking risks, moving on but not letting go, and as I previously mentioned, mental health. 
 As I said before, mental health is done correctly. I recently read a guest post by Paula Stokes in which she shows how she is breaking the stereotypical mental health story and making it accurate. One of those points is: a romance cannot cure their issue(s). And Wallach follows through with that. Zelda and Parker's romance does not cure either of them. As Zelda says, it's going to take months, not a weekend. I appreciate that their love isn't used in that way. 
 In other words, 
 I flipping LOVED Thanks for the Trouble and I recommend it to those who are quirky, or not, those who are indie, or not, and those who love contemporary. His writing style is beautiful and very smooth. At the end of We All Looked Up, I eagerly anticipated this one. At the end of Thanks for the Trouble, I am eagerly anticipating whatever he has in store because you know damn well I'm going to read it. 
 Final rating: 5 stars 
 How much do I recommend? Buy a hardcover NOW (and buy me one, too, please!)

 As first impressions go, Cassandra Campbell's voice is real professional even if I don't agree with all of her interpretations of the book. And that impression lasted all the way through the ending. But despite the wonderful narration, this book started out slow for me even with the easiness and convenience of an audiobook, that I abandoned it twice to pick-up another book to read/listen to. The opening volley just isn't very catchy. [Demonica Caduceus] Or maybe it is just my interest that couldn't be reeled in by doctors trying to save lives they really want to kill. No, that medical drama is overrated. However I like their modified caduceus though. Now that, is inventive! Which speaks of an interesting world building.... Interesting, but got a big whole in it. 
 The premise of this world is that there is a supernatural community hiding in plain sight among ordinary humans and that there is a guerrilla war going on between the demonkind and the humankind. The way this world is presented, is that the supernatural beings are very prolific, they are everywhere. And nobody slipped up after all these centuries? These millions of supernaturals and humans-in-the-know never slipped up all these time? No traitors on both sides whatsoever? No money-grabbing, self-serving among their ranks who sees an opportunity to better themselves by betraying supernatural secrets to the rest of the world? Somehow that is not believable. Unless there is a great big spell that prevents everybody from doing so, which there isn't. So that is one great big gaping hole in the world building that could swallow the grand canyon whole. That sank the suspension of disbelief to the bottom of the ocean! And that is not the only hole, just the biggest one. However, if you get past that and ignore the grand canyon hole, the world building is wonderful! It is full of vampires, demons, werewolves and every interesting fantasy elements living in our everyday world! Fantastic!! 
 Another downer for this book is that Tayla, our heroine, is too stupid to live (TSTL). Not only once, but repeatedly stupid with stunted sense of self-preservation! Yet described as a kick-ass demon hunter who survived a tough childhood and tougher work as a hunter for years on end. Which is really difficult to believe because if she acts as stupidly as she does in the story she ought to be dead a long time ago... That knocks the suspension of disbelief two more rungs lower. And there is just too many contradictory elements for the character development to rate any higher than 2, not to mention annoying! 
 Now I know that first books in a series are not usually the best so I will give this series another try and hopefully the next book would be better.

Furious 
 is a super intelligent, wonderfully challenging, and entertaining young adult novel. Jill Wolfson's take on the Furies, is incredibly clever and definitely makes for a compelling novel. Steeped in Greek mythology, it is intriguing and a bit scary, to see the Furies portrayed as three teenagers that are dealing with a lot of pain and heartache in their lives. I have to admit, Wolfson, is pretty clever in choosing to go this route with her re-telling. To date, it's probably one of my favorite of the re-telling's involving the Furies. 
 Wolfson, employs some interesting witty narrative, for the reader to enjoy. The twists and turns in the plot, are highly captivating, and are frightening on a whole other level of degree. The character development and growth of the three main characters, only add a new layer of depth to the novel. It's terrifying to see how these girls come into their power and then begin to abuse them, as they work through their own pain and tragedies. The complicated twists and entanglements in their arcs are fantastically creative and clever. 
 The world building is probably one of the most interesting facets about this novel. The blending together of an external world and an inner world, is such a complicated and fascinating element of this story. It came together in such a way that was seamless and was integrated into the plot line in such an interesting way that it piques the readers interest more. The exploration of both worlds were inherently important when it came to this story and the three main characters Wolfson invested in. Getting to see both worlds from each of their point of views, is incredibly emotionally charged and highly intense. 
 If you're looking for a way to escape and read an enjoyable story that features Greek mythology, then this is probably that book you are looking for. I would definitely recommend it to anyone who is looking for a highly intense, interesting, and creative take on the mythology, if not for the double world building alone, and the intriguing characters.

I really wanted to review this when I finished it but it's been a busy couple of months so I'm a little late... 
 I've always loved time travel stories (who doesn't?) and I've always been fascinated by the JFK assassination. I've read several non-fiction books about the event--some focused on the conspiracy theories, others on the details of what was known about Oswald, Ruby, Tippit, et al. I've seen many films and TV shows about the event (Quantum Leap did an amazing 3-episode arc where Sam kept leaping in and out of Lee's body; The X-Files blamed the whole thing on CSM; I even vaguely recall a [possibly] made for TV movie about a man who wanted to go back & save Kennedy because his brother was killed in Vietnam and he thought saving JFK would save his brother [or something]). Obviously, when I heard what Stephen King's latest novel was about, how could I resist?! 
 Simple answer: 849 pages 
 But, thanks to this and Under the Dome, I bought myself a Kindle and after a year, I finally bought the ebook copy of 11/22/63 and devoured the book in three weeks. It's so much more than a time travel story about saving JFK. King creates a series of characters (not nearly as many as there were in Under the Dome, but still pretty many) that you grow to love (and sometimes hate). 
 The setup is simple-Jake Epping, a divorced English teacher, is given the mission of preventing JFK's assassination using a time portal that connects present day to September 9, 1958. This means living in the past for over 5 years, but it's not as simple as you would think. You see, "the past is obdurate;" it doesn't want to be changed. The novel becomes a sort of video game where Jake has to try his hand at changing smaller events before building up to the "big boss" of Lee Harvey Oswald. There is even a game over/reset option of coming back to the present and going back to September 9, 1958 again to try again. 
 The events Jake has to change, the people he meets, the woman he falls in love with and the eventual fateful day are all so real, I sometimes had to remind myself this was just a novel and not really possible. King does amazing work with the details he put into the historical portions (thanks to years of research; King actually had this idea all the way back in 1971 before he published his first novel, Carrie), and when you think the story's over, it's actually just starting to get interesting. 
 I've found King sometimes has a great idea that fizzles out into a disappointing ending, but this is definitely one of his best. Even two months later, I remember a feeling of "Well, of course that's how it had to end. Just perfect" while not predicting the ending at all. If you have any interest in JFK, this book is for you. If you like pondering the hows and whys of time travel, this book is for you. If you like swing dancing, sports betting, historical dramas, love stories, teachers or references to It, this book is for you. 
 Go. Read. It. ("It" referring to 11/22/63. I've yet to read It)

Emelina Flores has come home to Ruina. After rescuing her sister Olivia from imprisonment in rival kingdom Lera, Em and Olivia together vow to rebuild Ruina to its former glory. But their fight has only begun. Olivia is determined to destroy everyone who acts against Ruina, but Em isn't as sure. Ever since Em posed as Prince Casimir's betrothed in Lera, she's started to see another side to this war. And now that Cas has taken the throne, Em believes a truce is within reach. But Olivia suspects that Em's romantic feelings for Cas are just coloring her judgement. Em is determined to bring peace to her home. But when winning the war could mean betraying her family, Em faces an impossible choice between loyalty and love. Em must stay one step ahead of her enemies--and her blood--before she's the next victim in this battle for sovereignty. 
 Avenged is dangerous and complicated, the next step in saving the Ruined, in rebuilding their home. But other kingdoms have other plans, and Em still has to deal with a rather furious sister hellbent on claiming her revenge. 
 Em is sure that, with Olivia rescued, they'll be able to return to Ruina. That the Ruined will finally have a home again, that they won't be hunted across the land and driven away by those that fear their abilities. But Em is also sure that Olivia is furious and bloodthirsty, full of rage from her being imprisoned for the past year, that she won't rest until every human who stands against her is dead. Until every royal in Lera is dead. And that includes Cas. On the other side, Cas is busy worrying about what to do next now that he's been named king. Now that his cousin is pressing him to declare war on the Ruined. Now that his advisers are losing faith in him. Now that he's not sure if he even wants to be king when all he really wants is to be back with Em. 
 There's a lot that happens in this book, much more than I was expecting. Revenge and death, plots and plans and subterfuge, political deals and calls to war. Em worrying about how far Olivia will go in her quest for vengeance, in her desire make Lera pay for what they did to her. At the rate events are unfolding, at how many people are dying around them, I imagine the third book will be the final explosion where every party will come together. And who's to say who will still be alive at the end?

 Told their stories in alternating chapters, both Wills have problems. 
 The first, lets call him say, Will1 (the one who narrates the first chapter) is best friends with Tiny Cooper, the "biggest and gayest" boy in school. At first Will believes you cant pick your friends, which is evident when he says if you could, he would never pick Tiny, as he feel he has been stuck with the worst person to be best friends with ever. Will1 only at the end of the book realises how much he has taken for granted in Tiny, and how much Tiny goes underappreciated when he is always loyal and always "trying to make the world better". 
 Will2 is extremely moody and begins with narrating the second chapter. He is struggling with depression, a single mother after his father walked out, and coming out about being gay. But, in a night of unpredictable events, he ends up meeting Will1 in none other than a porn shop? Classy huh? Which is funny, and i think it was seeing Will2 through the narration of Will1 that really got me to see that this is just some poor kid. He then meets Will1's best friend, Tiny. After meeting Tiny, he begins on the long journey of accepting himself in a world that he thinks hates him. I felt most sympathetic for him when he finally lets his thoughts free, in the quote: 
 *SPOILERS** 
 "Heres the sick twisted thing: part of me thinks i deserve this. If I wasnt such a lame excuse for a person, something right might happen to me. It's not fair, because i didn't ask for dad to leave, and I didn't ask to be depressed, and I didn't ask for us to have no money, and I didn't ask to want to fuck boys, and I didn't ask to be so stupid, and I didn't ask to have no real friends and I didn't ask to have half the shit that comes out of my mouth come out of my mouth. All i wanted was a break, one idiotic good thing, that was clearly too much to ask for, too much to want." 
 *** 
 Both Wills taught me that everybody has their problems. That everyboyd needs a friend, comeone they can talk to about the shit that goes on at home. Someone who can buy you fake IDs (that may or may not even have the right age on them to get you into the club anyway...)Someone who you will get up out of bed for at 5.00 in the morning and drag you out of the house without knowing why. But most importantly, they taught me the importance of appreciating people. That realising everybody has their shit. That I'm not the only person in the world that isn't always 100% happy in life.
