With the help of her best friend, she's raising her son in a town that doesn't want her. After moving to be closer to her son's father, she realized that he never intended to make her a legitimate part of his life. So she's moved on. Or at least tried to. But when her best friend gets a new neighbor everything she thought she knew is thrown out the window. As Coen and she become friends, her life gets complicated all over again because she's finally found someone who wants her for her but so does her best friend. She may have sworn off love especially that of firefighters, but there is just something undeniable about Coen. Now she just wishes she knew what to do. 
 The blurb of this book hooked me. While I was anticipating major angst, it wasn't really so much an angsty book as an emotional one. There were definitely hints of angst enough to keep me flipping the pages though. As the story unfolded, I came to really love Coen. He was perfect book boyfriend material. I also really liked Elle even when some of her reactions to things frustrated me at times. And as the conflict came to a culmination, I wanted a bit more meat to it. It kind of seemed a bit too easy without much fallout (at least for my angst loving heart). Overall, though, this was a wonderful story full of heart and some heat that left a smile on my face.

Mermaids have been popping up on my radar a lot lately, and I have to give a lot of credit to the authors I've read lately--the stories have each been unique enough to capture and hold my attention without begging comparison to other stories. Of Poseidon was no exception.It was a fun read with a great mermaid Syrena mythology woven in. 
 The mythology that Ms. Banks crafted for this story was probably my favorite part of this novel. The lore that surrounds the mermaids, from their special abilities to the rift between two "factions," created a world that made me curious--made me want to dive below the surface to experience it for myself. The back-story that it created for the characters made them more complex and added that extra layer of intrigue to their personalities. 
 In terms of the characters, I have to say that my absolute favorite was Toraf. He's genuinely fun to experience in every moment we're with him. I loved his undying devotion to Rayna and scheming with Emma to get her to pay him attention was so cute! If I could hang out with one character from this book, it would totally be him. As for the rest of the characters, I liked them quite a bit, but they all had a lot of moments where I was like "No. That's so not you. Stop that." You know? Those moments that seem really out of character and seem to come from nowhere? But overall, Emma won me over with her feisty personality, even if she came across as a bit juvenile at times. Galen's alpha-male personality is hard to resist, even if he's more than a little overbearing at times. 
 Of Poseidon is a fun, quick read--perfect for reading on vacation this summer if you haven't picked it up already. The quirky characters and well-crafted mermaid lore will pull in all fans of mermaid stories.But be prepared, the cliffhanger ending will leave you wondering if you're missing something and then begging for the next book--which you'll have to wait until 2013 to read!

The Gift is one of those books that keeps you hooked, from first page to last. I was genuinely gripped throughout and it got to the point where I literally had no idea what had happened to Callie, or if Callie was even real, or is perhaps Jenna was just slowly losing her mind. Which is actually a terrible thing to wonder, but it's hard to trust someone who can barely remember if she locked her front door or not, that's shocking. Not to mention the fact Jenna doubted herself so how in the world were we supposed to believe her? She was just as baffled as we were and that's what made this such a compelling, intriguing, hard to put down book. It's why I kept reading, reading, reading despite the fact my eyes are literally beginning to be put to sleep. It was intoxicating. 
 It's incredibly hard to explain the part of the book, and depending on where you fall on the scale of someone having someone else's organ in their body, and that organ effecting their life will make your decision on how you see this book. On the one hand, there's a part of me that things an organ is just an organ. It doesn't have feelings, it can't make you feel another person, but then there's the romantic side of me that kind of likes the idea that you can feel someone else inside you. That there is such a thing as cell memory theory, because it lets me believe that even though someone you love may have passed away, they can live on in someone else and that's amazing. And that's basically the premise for The Gift. Jenna has a new heart (although I'm not sure it's ever explained why her old one wasn't good enough - it's hinted at a major emotional moment, but never fully explained, imo) and she's absolutely sure that the girl whose heart she has, Callie, didn't just die on a random road, with no seatbelt, for no reason. She's sure there's something more at play, and she's determined to find out the truth, no matter what. 
 Like I said, it's tough to really believe Jenna, when she feels she's being stalked, or that she really is feeling Callie's memories because there's no proof. Jenna has no luck when it comes to actual, tangible, physical proof and so a lot of it is based on gut instincts, and pretty lucky plot devices. Would Nathan, Callie's ex, really be so forward with a girl he doesn't even know? He helps her up after she faints, and all of a sudden he's calling her the next day? That's debateable, but it moves the story along, and I was okay with it. The plot really motors on, as Jenna finds herself putting clues together, and figuring stuff out, and I cannot deny at all that her narrative was so compelling. From her mind maps, to her seeing a random man in a hoody, to things at work being tampered with (her orders, a pet dying) it all adds up, and it gets to the point where you're on the edge of your seat like, "WHO IS RESPONSIBLE FOR THIS?!?!?!?!?!" Why are they doing this? Jenna was not, by any means, a terrible person. She just wanted the truth - whether it was her truth to find or not, at least she was being pro-active about it. 
 I really, really enjoyed The Gift. Louise Jensen really has a knack for telling a gripping story and there's no doubt at all that she left me on the edge of my seat throughout. I really liked Jenna, she was a compelling heroine, and I appreciated the fact that she wanted to know what had happened to Callie, I'm not saying that no one else cared - they thought it was indeed just a tragic accident, but I liked that Jenna had the force in her to go hell for leather, no matter if it made her scared for her life, all in a bit to find the truth, for someone she didn't even really know. That's impressive. This is such a good thriller, one you definitely won't regret reading, although be warned: It will keep you up late into the night!

 My book club ladies probably think I'm weird, because I'm always recommending books that are like: This book is like Jane Eyre but with evil fairies or this book is Jane Austen with magic or this is a future scifi retelling of Persuasion. Well I'm doing it yet again. Here is a lovely beautiful scifi retelling of The Scarlet Pimpernel. The Scarlet Pimpernel is one of my all time favorite books and I really really loved how it was done here. 
 This book is in the same Universe and as For Darkness Shows the Stars and it's on a future Post-apocalyptic earth. Way way into the future. There's all this scifi stuff going on and that's fun. 16 year old Persis Blake is the Wild Poppy aka Scarlet Pimpernel. Justen Helo is her "fake" love interest. Revolutionary scifi shenanigans ensue. 
 As a Book: Well-written, invisible prose. Strong female characters. I liked Persis and Isla and even remy and Vania a lot. They all felt real. Very real characters there. Tero and Andrine were more side characters so that was ok, but they could have been fleshed out more. Justen was a little weak as the male lead. He was a strong character in theory; he had all the elements of one, but something about him was off as he came across the page. I like that he had flaws, but he was kind of prejudiced. Like he couldn't see through Persis' cover. I know it was part of the story but I didn't like it. And the love portion was a little weak. Why do they like each other? I did enjoy seein fake Persis through his eyes. She's so...sweet lol. 
 I really enjoyed the world-building. This is such a believable world and to make a completely separate society from the first book? Job well done. I like the way this book follows up the first book but not as a sequel. I also enjoyed the revolutionary rhetoric it was done very intelligently. And with Justen and Vania on two different sides of the revolutionary coin. And Persis makes some really good points too. I found it interesting that Persis and Isla were such strong female characters and albion is like the one place in the world females don't have equal rights. The next job for the Wild Poppy? 
 As a retelling of Scarlet Pimpernel: It did a really great job. I was telling my husband the plot of the original Scarlet Pimpernel and I hadn't even really realized that certain aspects were added. Like Remy being like Marguerite's brother and Vania being Chauvelin. I just thought it fit really well into this very detailed and interesting new world and that it added all the Pimpernel elements was really amazing. He was constantly slut shaming and then lusting over the same women he slut shamed. I can't stand when guys do that; I find it to be a statement of superiority and objectification of women, and I have no respect for men like that. I also found Stan to be extremely creepy and stalker-like in some cases. I completely cringed every time he did anything, and dreaded reading his sections. 
 The other main character, Charmaine, clearly had issues and seemed to be an expert at deluding herself and covering up everything she considered bad. Despite this, I did enjoy her character. She turned out to be a lot more clever than she let on and I understand how she could make the decisions she made that may not have been the most righteous. 
 While I was intrigued by the plot line, and definitely enjoyed Atwood's writing style, I found that the story flew so far away from the initial situation and premises of the book. There were a lot of questionable situations with high moral dilemmas that were being carried out by the supposed "good guys", and I found the ending to be left very open-ended. 
 All of that being said, I did like the book and the plot did keep me wondering what, of all things, was going to happen next. It wasn't a favourite by far, and I'm glad I didn't buy it, but it was still good.

 I had this book in my TBR pile for a while, but by the time January rolled around and I realised that the movie was coming out, I decided to read the book. When I started the novel I was in the middle of another series, the Mortal Instruments, and had just finished City of Glass, so it took me a while to get out of the fantasy world and into the science fiction one. 
 Despite my belief that dystopian books and movies have been WAY overdone in the past couple of years, I enjoyed this book. It wasn't by far the most original story I've come across, and probably not the most entertaining, but I had my share of laughs, and the plot was (usually) not boring. 
 However, the organisation of this book was confusing. I didn't understand at first who was telling the story (by Part II of the book, I still thought that Cassie was telling the story rather than Ben, and it took me a while to realise otherwise). Also, I didn't like how the story changed from first to third person when Sammy was telling his part. 
 I'm not against romance in books, and most of the time it's enjoyable, but if it's not contemporary, lovey-dovey moments can get in the way of character and plot development REALLY easily. Especially in this book. Cassie spends a good third of the novel falling for the weird Evan Walker in what I imagined as a log cabin in the middle of the woods while the readers are stuck with Cassie's ridiculous internal conflict on whether or not to trust the guy. I may not have had a problem with it, but their relationship was so AWKWARD, I could feel myself cringing every time Evan said something stalkerish to Cassie about wanting to take care of her and going after her brother himself (what a control freak). The only thing I could think during these long and tedious chapters was, "when can we go back to Ben's POV?" 
 I loved the chapters that explained Ben's side of the story. Absolutely LOVED them. Maybe it was because of the amazing character development brought about by the military training, maybe it was because of the whole mystery surrounding Camp Haven, or maybe it was just because of the hardcore characters like Ringer, but these chapters were the brilliance of the novel, the part that gave it its WOW factor. (By the way, when Sammy went up to Ringer and believed she was Cassie, I really believed it. Got me there.) 
 Onto characters... I didn't particularly LOVE any of them, and definitely had some frustrated feelings for particular ones (*ahem* Evan). However, they constantly admitted that they weren't perfect, and they all had their flaws, which I admired. I want to see more bonds between the characters, especially friendships rather than relationships. I want to see Cassie and Ben developing a good friendship in the next book (I can't really see anything happening romantically). I hated Evan at first, and hated Evan even more in the middle of the book, but by the end I started feeling sorry for him (maybe he really is a good alien, and he was just trying to find his place in the world). However, I'm still suspicious, since he didn't show up at the end of the book and decided rather on blowing up the whole military base. Also, I felt like Cassie was really shadowing her abilities while she was around Evan, but by the end of the book she was seriously outshining Ben (and she didn't have any military training). Also, I'm oddly curious to know what Ringer's real name is... I feel like there's more to her than meets the eye. 
 I really liked the symbolism in this book. It was really cute how Cassie held on to Bear for Sammy, and Cassie's sarcasm was HILARIOUS (I loved when she referred to the M16 as her "bestie"). Also, it was kind of adorable how she wanted chocolate and the next morning she found a Hershey Kiss on her nightstand... but that also got me paranoid about how I thought Evan could read her mind, which of course got me started on the suspicious thoughts (who knows, maybe he CAN read her mind). 
 What kind of bugged me was the thought that the only reason Sammy was prevalent to the plot was so that Cassie could rescue him. I get that the kid is only five years old, but at this point he just seems like a burden to the other characters, and he's a really likable character. I love how Cassie always said how smart he is for his age. I definitely want to see some character development in the future for Sammy.

It's a good 3.5, but the humor tips it over to 4 stars for me. One thing I was not expecting to do during this book was laugh out loud, but it happened quite frequently. 
 Obviously that's not the main draw of the story - it's a real page-turner, and while the technobabble was on the verge of getting overwhelming at times, it never actually bothered me that much cause it lent such a huge amount of realness to the story. 
 I actually can't wait to see the movie version of this, because the book itself was so cinematic, I could see everything playing in my head while reading.

"At the heart of every legend there is a grain of truth." 
 Actual Rating: 3.5 Stars 
 * I really liked how the different Mythologies were explained and handled differently and made out to be something else. Instead of worshiping real gods, humans worshiped the Old Generation in this book, the ones that were firstborn, without knowing that their gods are pretty much alive. Also all legends are part true in this book, meaning that were people were created and they are werewolves as well as vampires, but with a different origin than usually. Some creatures also belong to the Second Generation and are several thousand years old. Therefore, we got to see "gods" like Hecate or Bastet and saw the World Tree Yggdrasil, here as a part of Hekate's shadow world in which she lived. There's also the codex and the famous Flamel, full of the elixir of life and prophecies. The firstborns were actually present when it was written by Abraham and went under, when Humai (humans) were created and evolved. With the discovery of iron they were pushed back, keeping to their own realms, but some firstborns, now known as the Dark Old Generation, still stayed here, waiting to reclaim their world and enslave humanity. There also was an Atlantis which was ripped apart by two people. I loved all those elements, because they were re-imagined by the author and made to be something else. That is what I always enjoy and why I say that reusing certain elements is no problem, since every authors creates a new meaning with them. I also loved that there were different types of magic, like alchemy, necromancy, pure magic and much more. 
 * I particularly liked Scatty, she was a fierce warrior goddess and quite enjoyable because of her strength and humor. She's probably my fave character in this series and I'm very curious how everything will go for her in the upcoming books. Please let her live. I also ship her with Josh, I'm sorry I cannot help myself, I think they would be a great, interesting couple, because they are so different. 
 * I did like Josh as well, a little better than his twin Sophie. Josh was impulsive and acted before he thought, even though he has a good heart and a great sense of loyalty. I could really feel with him when he felt like an outsider and frustrated, as well as a little jealous. I found him to be relatable and especially his fear to be left out. Sophie was cool as well, but I connected with Josh a little more. She's the more rational, diplomatic part of the twins, who knows when to be more tactful. 
 * Nicholas was fascinating as well, because he was a little ambiguous and the reader couldn't fail to notice that there are many different perspectives on him and different people judge him differently. The question arises which the truth is, why I found quite suspenseful. The Villain, Dee, was amusing and reminded me of another beloved Villain of mine, because he doesn't like getting his hands dirty, but also is really smart and knows how to manipulate people. 
 * I liked the plot, even though I heard some people say it was to slow paced. I personally did think that there was enough suspense and action and that the book just had the right pace. As for the writing style I'm careful to say too much, because I think it's different if you read the translation. However, I can say that I got quickly through this book and finished it in nearly one day. 
 IN CONCLUSION: I would recommend The Alchemyst to fans of mythology and people wanting to read about the famous Nicholas Flamel. This book is labeled YA but I would recommend it for Middle Grade as well, because it's surely greatly enjoyable for younger readers with it's rich fantasy world.

 ChooOOOooom

Maybe a little bit too 'sweet' for my tastes, and I can't say that I'm really satisfied with the Dead King 'twist' that I guessed a quarter way through, but it was an ending that actually ended. Review Appears First on my Blog: The Life of a Bibliophile 
 I am forever in love with Hayao Miyazaki's Howl's Moving Castle. I didn't even realize it was a book until I watched the anime for the fourth time and actually read the credits for once. So I put it on my to-read list and forgot about it for a little while. Then when I was getting back into my 'I need to watch all my favorite animes again' phase, I remembered about Diana Wynne Jone's book. Luckily, It was available in eBook (A very smart decision on their part). I've come to terms with both book and movie, keeping them in my mind as separate entities to preserve my love for each. 
 Howl's Moving Castle is not one of those books that I had to think about what the author had in mind verus what the author actually writes. Diana Wynne Jones is blunt. She tells you what is happening, what it looks like, and what the characters are feeling. No guess work, no 'author says this, but means this' nonsense. It was so utterly refreshing that I couldn't put this book down. 
 Jones is able to balance character development and plot advancement brilliantly, yet I believe leaning a bit more heavy on the plot. Despite what the anime leads you to believe, this isn't a strictly romantic story. It is a story of doing what you never thought possible and about finding out that you are so much more than you thought you could be. It's about love, yes, but it's not solely about romantic love. It's about love for family, for self, for friends. 
 Some differences between the Anime and the Book: 
 Jones also did not write Howl to be everyone's dream man. She wrote him as a cowardly drama queen who can't get through a breakup without sliming all over the floors. In an interview she said she would never want to date Howl and doesn't understand the readers who do. 
 Sophie isn't an insecure young girl who believes she is plain or hideous. She is a woman who thinks she is set into her ways because she is the eldest. She believes she has a destiny that, though boring, is what she has to do. 
 Overall, if you're a fan of the anime, or a fan of fantasy, of strong women, of bluntness, of fun, I'd suggest this book to you, Curious Reader. 
 xx 
 A Bibliophile 
 More differences (but may be considered spoilers, so click with caution): 
  
 Sophie has sisters (Martha & Lettie) 
 Sophie is actually a powerful witch, she talks life into inanimate objects 
 Sophie doesn't switch between being an old person and a young person depending on her self esteem 
 Sophie isn't insecure about her appearances 
 Howl isn't romantic with Sophie at all. He is dramatic and annoying. [Big Drama Queen] 
 Howl is constantly dating through the novel. 
 Howl's apprentice, Michael, is actually 15 and falls in love with Sophie's sister Martha 
 The Witch of the Waste doesn't come to live with Howl and Sophie at the end or ever becomes more important than a rival to Howl 
 Howl is actually from Wales, that's where the black spot on the dial by the door leads him. He has a sister, niece, and nephew in Wales. 
 Obviously, a lot more backstory

Park has a knack for making the swooniest, realist love stories (don't judge my English). Allison is in college. Growing up in the system hasn't helped her trust many people, including her great adoptive father. She tries though, but just with Simon her dad. Her only friend and the only person to break down her barriers is Steffie, another girl who grew up in the system. 180 seconds is about to change her world. 
 When Allison suddenly participates in a social experiment for Esben, a famous YouTuber who does amazing work in social experiments, she finds herself in one of her worst nightmares. Instead of being in the shadows, she is now in the spotlight. For 180 seconds Allison and Esben must look at each other without saying a word. In the seconds Allison begins to feel a pull towards Esben, something she wants to deny. At the end of the 180 seconds there are feelings both cannot control, and a kiss ends it all. Now Allison is virally famous, after thousands of shares and views in one night. She can't deny what happened but she'll try, because she can't fall for Esben-she can't let him in. 
 This was such a heartfelt story of love, trust, and friendship. It's corny and delicious. 
 4 stars

October 7-8, 2015. 
 This is book 6 of the Maiden Lane series and is about the 3rd (and for Pete's sake, hopefully the last, Ghost of St. Giles, Maximus Batten, the Duke of Wakefield (brother of Lady Hero Batten, who married Griffin Reading, and Phoebe Batten, who is going blind). There are so many characters in this series that I constantly must remind myself of how they are related. Not that this is a bad thing. 
 Actually, this book has almost nothing to do with the actual Maiden Lane, although some scenes do occur in St. Giles, where Maximus, as the Ghost, has been searching for his parents' murderer for 19 years. 
 Artemis Greaves is the quintessential impoverished gentlewoman. Her brother is Viscount Kilbourne, and for 4 years, he has been locked up in Bedlam after he awoke with the dead bodies of 3 friends with no memory of what happened to them. Artemis has spent that time as companion to Lady Penelope, a sweet but extremely shallow and ditzy heiress who is determined to marry a duke - specifically the Duke of Wakefield (the only other available Duke is Scarborough, who is considerably older. 
 Wakefield begins to notice Artemis, in spite of her ability to fade into the background, and he gradually comes to realize there is more to her than just a drab lady's companion. They begin a really torrid love affair, even though he knows he cannot marry her. 
 I have mentioned in previous reviews that I disliked Wakefield and found him cold and pompous. This book reveals why he became so and reveals the man beneath the Duke. I really enjoyed their story. Once again, secondary characters are well drawn, some of whom are to have their own stories told (Trevillion and Phoebe, for example) and some who are to remain in the background (Miss Picklewood - isn't that a lovely name?). 
 4 1/2 stars for a stellar love story well told. 
 ********* 
 Reread January 21-22, 2017. 
 Ah, the Batman book! Just as maddening and delightful as I remembered. 
 I absolutely love Artemis and have since we were first introduced to her several books ago. Although her sad lot in life is as lady's companion to that widgeon, Lady Penelope, she is everything Penelope isn't: intelligent, witty, brave, loyal, loving. She even truly cares for her silly relation. 
 It's so satisfying to watch the stiff and proper Maximus begin to wilt around the edges and eventually, completely crumble and admit that he can't imagine life without Artemis as his duchess. 
 And incidentally, in the Epilogue, we meet wicked Val, the Duke of Montgomery, for the first time. *shivers with pleasure*

I found this book from my library's recommendations of books like The Hunger Games. This young adult book also takes place in a future dystopia. I only give it three out of five because while it's a fascinating story, the characters didn't do much for me. 
 Mary is a young girl in a village surrounded by the Unconsecrated, creatures who were once human before they were Infected. When her parents both succumb to the Infection, her brother leaves her with the Sisterhood, the mysterious religious council that runs the village. She learns more about the Sisterhood's secrets and slowly begins to learn that there is a world outside of her village. 
 Carrie Ryan has a great way of building up suspense, and she writes amazing action scenes. I read through the first half of the book in one setting. But I wasn't sold on the romance that was supposed to carry most of the book, and I still don't have a very good grasp on Mary's character. 
 The author creates an eery world and effectively pulls us into Mary's doubt and fear as well as her hopes and dreams. I get scared pretty easily, so the thoughts of the Unconsecrated and their constant hunger were on my mind when I wasn't reading it. I still wish I could have seen more of the characters, though. Cass seemed pretty superficial, I knew nothing about Travis aside from Mary's undying love for him, and Harry and Jed weren't very distinguishable, either. My library has the second book, so I'll probably pick it up to see what happens to the characters.

Ugh. It's never a good sign when the dedication page of a book pisses you off...the Casts said they dedicated this book to LGBT teens. Which is great, really. I'm glad they show their support. However, how can they do that and then depict Damien and Jack so poorly and as cut out stereotypes of what ignorant people assume gay people are and how gay people act? It just bothers me so much. And no, I'm not talking about how Damien was so upset over Jack's death. They were in love and Jack died a horrible death and they couldn't prove it was really Neferet. Damien's reaction was how many people, gay or straight, would act . No, I'm talking about how Aphrodite has to point out that Damien and Jack are gay at every mention of something girly. How Jack sobs like a baby at every little thing and characters repeatedly (mainly Aphrodite) say how girly and gay he is. Authors, we get it. Jack is gay. How about you give him real qualities instead of saying he's off decorating everywhere he goes.  Oh, wait, you can't because you killed him.  
 Now that that is off of my chest, lets move on, shall we? I was disappointed that we had to hear from Zoey again. I also noticed a few things in this book that I didn't notice before. I don't know if that was because I just ignored them, or because they just weren't as obvious as they were in this book. Such as all the characters saying "We heart _____" instead of saying "We love ____" and "Heehees" instead of saying "So-and-so giggled." That really got on my nerves. So did all of the pop culture and product placement references that were mentioned. I actually had the urge to go through and count them all, but at that point I was about halfway through and didn't feel it was really worth it. Now, looking back, I wish I did. It seems that every other sentence was some reference to a popular song (they had Defying Gravity from Wicked in one scene) or product (iPhones. iPhones everywhere) or movie or book...they're everywhere. I know that there was a lot of mention of Star Trek and Star Wars in the other books, but it just feels like this one went over board. 
 ON TO MY STICKY NOTES 
 27 pages in, and Zoey and Stark are already sucking face in an enchanted forest. Wonderful. 
 35 pages in and they're off having sex. After Zoey is all depressed and crying and shit. Another problem I have with this series; the characters seem to use sex as an answer to get rid of pain and suffering and forgetting all of their problems. On one hand, I get it. From a science stand point, sex brings out all of your happy hormones that makes your body forget pain. On the other hand, THE WORLD IS GOING TO SHIT AND YOU'RE HAVING SEX ON PAGE 35. Not a whole lot of build up, and really, authors? That's how you're going to begin this book and your newly found heroine who has repaired her shattered soul? I just...I don't understand their logic. 
 On page 38, Glee is referenced. Oh yeah, did I mention that the version of Defying Gravity wasn't the good one from the musical, but the rip off one from Glee? Yeah. It was. Also, another pop culture reference. Inserting them does NOT make your book automatically cool. It just means that in a few years, your book will be considered out dated and people will laugh at how silly these things keep being mentioned. 
 Page 51. Kramisha is talking about Jack decorating the school yard for a big celebration upon Zoey's return from Happy Island Sex Life with Stark the Guardian. 
 "If he tries to hang rainbows and unicorns everywhere and make us wear them feather boas-again-I'm just gonna say 'ah hell no'" 
 As stated before, how can you dedicate this book to LGBT and then depict them like this? Maybe I'm just being over sensitive, but this just seems way too stereotypical. I just wish that they'd portrayed this characters in a more realistic way. 
 Also on page 51... 
 Stevia Rae was still grinning when Lenobia called the Council Meeting to order. In the days that followed, she would remember her grin and wish she could hold on to the image of Jack making purple swords out of paper singing "Defying Gravity," eternally looking on the bright side of life, eternally sweet, eternally happy, and, most important, eternally safe. 
 OBVIOUS FORESHADOWING IS OBVIOUS Sorry, but I thought the best foreshadowing happened when after the big reveal you look back and go "Oooooh so that's what that meant!" Not this where it's way too obvious something is going to happen to Jack. Then it becomes much less of a shock when something actually happens and we as readers aren't left with as big of an impact as we could have been. Now, with characters as bland as most of these, it's really hard to feel anything, but that's not really the point. 
 Page 114 it is revealed that Kalona is basically Neferet's immortal sex slave. When did this series get so obsessed with sex and S&M? 
 Page 119 we get a little more insight on our lovely heroine, Zoey Redbird. The world is going to hell, people are dying, Neferet is, as always, an evfil bitch obsessed with pain and darkness, and where is our dear Zoey? Making sweet, sweet Queen/Guardian love to Stark on Peace Island where darkness can't touch them. This is who we have as our heroine? Really? 
 Page 158. 
 "...where even the rocks and trees and souls had names....People today...believe that the earth is just a dead thing that they live on..." 
 Did this sound familiar to anyone else? Because what immediately popped into my mind was "Colors of the Wind" from Disney's Pocahontas . Now, admittedly, that movie is nowhere near historically accurate, but I have a feeling our wonderful authors wouldn't care about that. Seriously, the words to that song "You think you own whatever land you land on/ The earth is just a dead thing you can claim/ But I know every rock and tree and creature/ Has a life, has a spirit, has a name." 
 Maybe I'm just nitpicking here. Or maybe this is legit and that's where they got their "inspiration" from. I mean, they do take a lot from the Native American culture, so who knows? 
 Page 183. Stevie Rae is out and about wondering what on earth she is going to do about her and Rephaim and wishing she had someone she could talk to when all of a sudden, BAM. Her mom is right there. This scene was so out of place. I mean, Rephaim kept telling Stevie Rae she had to go to her mother, but she kept putting it off which made this scene seem so out of place. It almost felt like the authors realized they needed someone Stevie Rae could confide in and decided HEY LETS PUT HER MOTHER INTO THE PICTURE JUST FOR THE LULS. Like no thought actually went into it, or what did was very little. 
 Page 198. Zoey notices Stark isn't quite himself. So she Googles his symptoms. Okay, one, everyone knows that's a horrible idea and the results always tell you you have cancer and/or you're going to die. Two, she came up with the idea that Stark had PTSD. Based on the symptoms of tired, distracted, grumpy, and forgetting things. Please, correct me if I'm wrong, but that doesn't sound like Post Traumatic Stress Disorder to me. That sounds like exactly what's wrong with Stark, which is that he hasn't been sleeping well. I wonder if the authors actually did any research for this at all. 
 And another thing: at the end Zoey and Stark are all lovey dovey in the tunnels and suddenly Stark has Zoey pinned and starts hurting her and doing things Zoey isn't okay with. She tells him to stop, but he doesn't hear her. She's obviously upset, and Stark is all apologetic and says he loves her and didn't mean to hurt her. Then like a switch, Zoey says she loves him and forgets that HE BASICALLY JUST TRIED TO RAPE HER. This has Abusive Relationship written all over it. 
 That's the end of my wonderful sticky notes. I still wonder why I've continued with this series for so long. And I'm constantly reminded at the end of each book. Throughout each book, I drag myself along thinking okay this is the last one, I'm done. Then those last 60 or so pages come along and I'm pulled into the book and have the need to know more. This time, though, I don't think I could care if I read the next book or even finish the series. The characters are dry, the dialogue is painful most of the time and is usually very cheesy, there are so many pop culture references that this series will be even more foolish in a few years, but once the action actually happens it's pretty good. It's action. There's suspense, there's curiosity, there's WTF IS NEFERET DOING RIDING A BULL IN THE MIDDLE OF THE NIGHT WHEN SHE IS BUTT NAKED moments that just make you stop and wonder what was going on in the authors' heads. Sometimes that's a good thing, sometimes it's not. 
 I kind of wish we knew more about Dallas in this book. I'm curious as to what, exactly, happened to him. All we know is that now he's having sex with the former leader of the Red Fledglings. That's all. Anyway, those last 60 or so pages is what keeps this book at a 3 star and not down to 2. I think I'll take another break from the series. There were many times I just wanted to chuck the book across the room or stab it with a knife. Books shouldn't do that to a person.

THE UNLEASHING has a running joke where the Crows love Kera's dog more than they tolerate their new battle sister. This joke became less and less funny as I began to prefer the dog myself. This is a relatively fun urban fantasy, and Laurenston's trademark over the top violence and romance are beautifully edited to fit a tight plot. Still, none of these characters rise far above caricature. Vig and Brodie and lovable on basically the same level, which isn't much of an endorsement. So far, this series can't compete with the established (and very similar) world of Kresley Cole's Immortals After Dark.

This novel, the third outing for Harvard Professor Robert Langdon, finally brings the fun speculative histories of Dan Brown to an American setting. With such a rich history, I thought Brown did a fine job in plotting a thriller through American landmarks. Unfortunately, I felt somewhat bogged down by Browns formulaic approach. I did find myself unable to stop reading this book, but I think Brown needs to think of a new formula before Langdon's next inevitable adventure.

I acknowledge this as a piece of literary history. Starting the Beat Generation, Kerouac wrote about his trips around the country with his friend Neal Cassady (here: Sal and Dean Moriarty). They travel, they are out of money, they drink, they fight, they have girls, they cheat on their wives, then they stop traveling. A few months later, they start traveling again, they get out of money, they drink, they cheat,... And so it goes on and on and on. These protagonists have no ambitions, no goals in life, no deeper intellectual thoughts. I pity them for real. Even more so as I consider this book as a real time witness. It has happened (more or less) like this and I get why Kerouac - who seems to be so much more intelligent than his surrounding travelers - got so bitter later on in his life. 
 I wouldn't have traded my life so far for the world for being with them. 
 I admit that I might have thought very differently about this book if I had read it about 10 years ago, when being a teenager. This might have been more appealing to me, all the doing nothing and traveling and freedom. Maybe it wasn't the right time for me reading it. 
 But still I rate 3 Stars for I appreciate the "new" and modern literature it was back then in the 50s and thank the late author for introducing me into a way of life which I would have never known without him.
Enchanting and bittersweet. It was a magical journey, though I think characters could have been better explored.

A 'cut and shut' is when two cars are welded together to create a vehicle which, while on the outside looks as good as any other used car, actually has the problems of both vehicles. To be fair, the reason most people dislike cut and shuts is that when they buy they're totally unaware it was originally two different motorcars. So perhaps drawing an analogy between this used car dealer's practice and 'Pride and Prejudice and Zombies' is an unfair one, as you could hardly expect to get something other than what's advertised in the title. 
 However this hypergamy of a book is like a cut and shut in that the bringing together just creates its own problems. The wit and sharpness of Austin's prose is blunted, while the excitement of the zombie attacks falls away when we return to Regency romance. By the end I was just mainly concerned with spotting the new bits to the text, and determining how a book works is not the best way to enjoy it. 
 If it had been a short story (or even a television sketch, the Harry Enfield bit where The Terminator is in the cast of 'The Remains of the Day' comes to mind), this may have worked better. But at book length I just felt the conceit was stretched far beyond breaking point.
I couldn't put the book down.

 Needing a break from a lot of the darker books I've been reading lately, Slow Hand was a welcome change. It was light and romantic and the characters were sweet and interesting. 
 Wade is my new cowboy book boyfriend. He's the gentleman rancher you can take home to your mama. He'll pull out your chair and open your car door. He's the sexy attorney that can handle your problems. And he's a stallion in bed (or truck or cabin floor or...). He comes to Nikki's rescue time and time again, and aside from being sexy as hell, he seems like a genuinely good guy. I love his aw, shucks demeanor and his Midwest charm, and he shows that chivalry is not dead. 
 Nikki took me a little more time to like. She complained about not wanting to get involved with cowboys time and time again, and I wanted her to give Wade more of a fair chance than she was wanting to give him. Actually, what I wanted to do was shove her aside and take Wade for myself, but if that wasn't happening, I just wanted her to stop lumping him in with all of the other losers she had apparently chosen in her life. But she was a sympathetic character, and she grew on me. 
 With a charming cowboy and a damsel in distress, this book was a nice escape from reality. The supporting characters were just as interesting (if not more so!) than Wade and Nikki, and I feel as if the author is setting them up for stories of their own. 
 The one thing that I will call out, however, was some of the sexual banter. I love a dirty talker, but I was literally cringing when I read some of this. I will never look at cattle the same way again after reading Nikki's argument to have sexually satisfied cows as some sort of sexual innuendo, alluding to Wade's performance. So wrong. 
 But, cow porn aside, Slow Hand was a pleasure to read. It was sweet, romantic, sexy and gives me a hankering for some boots and spurs! Looking forward to reading about Wade's brother, Dirk, Nikki's sister Shelby, and even Allie, Wade's former lover who I expected to hate, but had to admire for her ambition. Any books with these characters will be welcome on my "to be read" shelf! 
 Review copy provided for an honest review.

I absolutely loved this book. It was a million times deeper than I expected it to be and it tore my heart out reading it. I cannot praise this book enough. 
 I knew I wanted to read this because I'm always interested in dystopian novels. I skimmed a few reviews and saw a few negative ones that mentioned it was a rip off of The Giver by Lois Lowry with a love triangle. I don't know what I expected, but maybe in some ways I did expect it to be slightly too focused on a teenaged romance. But that's not what I got at all. 
 There are similarities in Cassia's world to the one in The Giver. It didn't bother me because The Giver is one of my favorite books and I am eager to gobble up anything similar. It's not too similar that I feel like it's a rip off. It's similar enough to sate my appetite and easily understand how it is set up. The love triangle was far from what I expected. It lacked immaturity to me, as Cassia was far from flighty or stupid or confused. The entire premise made perfect sense to me and flowed elegantly and I have zero complaints. 
 I loved Cassia as a main character. She was perfect. Unlike Tally, from the Uglies series by Scott Westerfeld, she was stronger and curious by nature and not completely blind to society even after discovering things that don't quite fit. It didn't take other people to sway her views on Society. And unlike Katniss, from The Hunger Games Trilogy, she wasn't automatically skeptical and distrusting of authority without provocation. She was in the middle of these two dystopian characters. She was believable in the sense that she was used to how things have been her entire life and didn't automatically assume anything was wrong, but her curiosity led her to make certain decisions that left her feeling more and more skeptical throughout the book. She was exactly how I would want a character in a dystopian society to be and completely believable without being annoyingly blind or suspiciously all knowing. 
 While there was a love triangle, it was great. Cassia is matched with her long time friend, Xander at her Matching ceremony on her seventeenth birthday. But when she looks at Xander's information on her microcard, she sees another person, Ky. She has known Ky throughout her childhood as well. The Officials tell her there was a mistake and Ky is unable to be matched and was never in the matching pool and her true match is definitely Xander. But her curiosity leads to her to wonder more and more about Ky. When she starts noticing him a little more, she begins to form a friendship with him on a deeper level. 
 I feel like I can't give anything more away without ruining the story, it was all incredibly interesting. It leads Cassia to question more and more about her life. She holds on to snippets of poetry given to her by her Grandfather before his death, which also leads her to question things. She discovers the power of words and pays attention to the things around her, all while trying to act as normal as possible. 
 Cassia's internal conflict resonated with me. Ky's story broke my heart. Xander's loyalty and ability to always do the right thing in times of crisis really spoke to me. Cassia's parent's love her one another and their family was strong and I cared deeply about virtually every character. 
 I couldn't stop turning the pages of this book and thought the story was believable, original, and completely captivating. I was sad when I was finished and even more sad that I didn't purchase the second book in the series. I cannot rave about this book enough. I thought it was mature and well written and wonderfully dystopian. I couldn't find any plot holes. While it will definitely appeal to fans of YA dystopians, it was so great that I'd recommend it to fans of more classic dystopians as well. Definitely well done.

Yes, I really didn't ever read this when I was a kid. I actually don't know if I read anything by Konigsburg. I have to say, this book was not what I expected. I thought it was going to be all exciting and fun about these kids sleeping in the museum and trying to solve the mystery. But it was not exciting. I found it pretty boring. I found both the main characters to be obnoxious and didn't think the book was as fun as I expected it to be. It did go by quickly though.

Also, the heavy handed message oh hope is just so obvious. Like, that stuff's supposed to come out as a result of the story, not just through monologuing. Eh, well see!

The Circle (in the book) is what, I feel, Google+ wishes to be. So this is excellent satire.

 And, wow, does this book make me remember with fondness when the internet was for anonymity.

An entertaining and uplifting book once again (it's weird how Greg seems to do nothing but complain and yet he always cheers me up), but somehow I felt this didn't quite live up to the roll Kinney was on with the previous couple of books in this series. Looking back, I can think of a lot of things I found funny, but they weren't laugh-out-loud, how-does-he-come-up-with-this-stuff, it's-so-relatable-yet-so-genius funny, you know? I guess whether the humour works for you will differ for each reader, and some of the jokes just seemed to miss for me in this one. Still, a solid addition to the series, and a fun read.

I was disappointed. 
 This book was recommended as a 'readers also enjoyed' from the Golem and the Djinn but the only similarities between the books appear to be that both draw on mythic figures. The writing, plot development and character descriptions were rather superficial compared to The Golem and the Djinn. 
 But enough of comparing this to other books: 
 This is meant to be Loki's side of the saga stories, which often paint him in less than flattering terms. As I am into Viking history and Norse mythology I was very excited by the idea of this book. Loki is a key character in the sagas, an integral complex character without whom the Norse mythology would lack a lot of its dynamic integrity. Because of his trickster element I felt it would be especially suitable to retell his story in a more modern voice. The first few chapters however were a bit dull; all we learnt is that the gods were not nice people and that Odin cheated him. To anyone who has actually read the sagas the fact that the gods were not nice is no surprise and that Odin was terrifyingly not nice is, well, DUH! 
 The language of the book is cheerful modern, something I often quite like in retelling stories and which does not bother me, as such, here. If however, anyone out there has doubts about enjoying a novel where Loki is told to 'chillax' by Balder, maybe skip this one. This leads me to the thing I am most disappointed about; the writing and story are sadly very superficial and while entirely from Loki's view point merely recapitulate the sagas with little added content. In addition to having no added depth to the stories there is no insight into the characters, who are much more one dimensional than they are in the sagas. There is none of the descriptive brilliance that so delighted me in the book this one was meant to be 'like' and no exploration of humanity, no inner voyage. To me the whole notion of retelling the old myths is to make them more accessible and give them greater dimensionality. Make them live and breathe for the modern day reader in the way that they would have lived and breathed for someone in the ninth century, sitting around a fire at night, enthralled by the story of the gods... 
 This is not achieved at all. 
 For example, on completion of the story of the building of Valhalla and the origin of Sleipnir, a story I have always been very fond of: 
 From Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda; 
 "Loki, however had had such dealings with Svathilfari that some time latter he bore a foal." 
 The Gospel of Loki; 
 Loki: "I took one for the team". 
 Heimdall: "smartass". 
 So, I think it comes down to whether you enjoy reading the myths as rich challenging prose with complex concepts, intricate motivations and damn near unpronounceable names or the exact, unadulterated same stories with slipstick modern characters and contemporary slang. It is not a bad book, it is not badly written or badly done, if you are not into Norse mythology, just mildly curious, you will probably quite enjoy it. 
 I personally infinitely preferred Neil Gaimans interpretation of the Norse gods in "American Gods" which had the increased complexity and character development that I was so disappointed not to find in this book.

I've been wanting to read The Road for quite a while, but I was never sure how I would feel about it, so I kept putting it off. 
 After having someone highly praise the book and exclaim that it was their favourite, I couldn't resist it any longer, and I decided that now was the time to read it. I'm so glad that I did. I can be a bit picky about non-traditional dialogue, so I was a bit hesitant at first once I saw how the book was written, but with Cormac McCarthy's mastery over the modernist genre...it complemented the narrative PERFECTLY!! And I was surprised to find that I actually really enjoyed the way that the dialogue was organized because it mirrored how society had fallen apart and it allowed for a seamless narrative that felt so real and immediate. 
 As soon as I started reading The Road...I COULD NOT PUT IT DOWN! I devoured it, and I know that it will be a book that I will return to in the future because it captivated me in a way that I really didn't expect.

I don't read a lot of MM PNR so I wasn't sure what to expect with this one. I was pleasantly surprised. I enjoyed the world building here and liked the werewolves a lot. 
 Chay and Keaton working through their attraction was a fun read for me. I liked them and I was rooting for them. I did really enjoy Keaton, I love a snarky character. He's got attitude but he also has heart so he came across very sweet to me and Chay was really wonderful. 
 I do like Langley's writing so I'm not surprised that I enjoyed this, I am surprised it took me so long to read it though.

3.5 Stars 
 I'm not going to lie to you: my deep desire for MILA 2.0 was entirely superficial. I mean, can you blame me? Look at that cover! It's the cover that The Adoration of Jenna Fox was trying to be. As soon as I saw this cover, MILA 2.0 went to the top of my WANT WITH THE FIRE OF A THOUSAND SUNS pile. Still, I'd been burned before by books from this pile and was naturally hesitant. Well, lucky me, because MILA 2.0 turned out to be a fast-paced thrill ride. 
 MILA 2.0 is about a girl who discovers she's a robot. That premise pretty much can't fail to make me excited. I really like the way Mila's abilities are handled in here. Sure, there are things where I wasn't entirely sure about whether they would be possible, but it wasn't hard to suspend disbelief. Driza's not trying to heavy science fiction on her readers, so she gives you just enough information, without ever feeling the need to over-burden you with technical terms or infodumps. Obviously, this might be a disappointment for hardcore science fiction readers, but it was perfect for a person like me, who has a rather tenuous grasp on science. 
 Driza does a great job with her action scenes. They're clear and concise, easily distinguishing between commands issued from other people, from Mila's programming, or from Mila's own mind. Some of the robotic features could have been confusing, depending on formatting and handling in the text, but they're really well-integrated, and not used so often as to be annoying. The real focus of the plot is on the action, which is great. I love when a book knows what kind of a book it is and runs with it. 
 Mila makes such a great character and is one of the best robot/manufactured main characters I've read. Most authors feel the need to make the character read as robotic, giving them stilted ways of speaking and limited vocabularies. Driza did not fall into this trap. Mila acts like a completely normal person, which is precisely the point. Since Mila is nigh indistinguishable emotionally from a person, it highlights the question of whether she has humanity. What makes a human human? I'm not going to pretend this is an original theme or even treatment thereof, but it's well done, and way less preachy than most. Also, Mila is hardcore. She does some things in here that really took me by surprise. Let's just say she's willing to get her hands dirty. 
 The main weakness in MILA 2.0 lies in the more realistic side of the story. The opening where Mila thinks she's just a regular student moves a bit slowly. Though I did find her dramas with her friend Kaylee very believable and unfortunate, I would have liked to see that element pulled out as something she learned from. On top of that, there's a new boy in school (of course), who is immediately drawn to Mila (surprise!). They bond way too quickly. While I do understand her obsession with whom throughout the book, since he's the only real, positive link to her human self, his side of things does not make sense to me. 
 Though I'm not completely sold on what, admittedly little, romance there is in this first book, I'm looking forward to the developments in the next...I hope. There's a possible love triangle brewing, and I really hope so, because I'm rooting for Lucas, whether that's happening or not. I would love to see a romantic hero with a limp because of his club foot. All kinds of people can be hot! Also, he probably wouldn't feel the need to protect her, since he knows himself and his limitations so well. 
 MILA 2.0 is out today, so, if you enjoy fast-paced books with a lot of action and science fiction-y goodness, go out and find a copy! Now I just have to wait a full year to find out what happens next. C'est la vie.

 This is a strange, claustrophobic tale told from the point of view of Linus, the first resident of the bunker. He quickly notes that there's a communal area next to a kitchen, six bedrooms and a bathroom. Then there's the lift. The bunker is quickly filled with six residents, from the youngest, Jenny, who's nine to Russell, who's described as nearly seventy by Linus. As a lover of films like Saw and Cube, this story really appealed to me. 
 The characters are an eclectic bunch, seemingly picked out at random by someone Linus describes as Him. A nine year old, a homeless boy with a rich background, a woman in her late twenties that sells property, a herion addict, an management consulant and a natural philosopher. I found it interesting that no two people were alike, and I think that's why they were chosen. 
 The person that kidnapped them was the most interesting character in this. He's quickly referred to as Him or He, with a capital, like God is in the Bible. His motives are unclear, there's cameras installed in every room that are unbreakable and have their own defense mechanisms, so my guess is that he's curious, wants to find out what will happen. 
 The Bunker Diary took 10 years of battling to get it printed and I can see why. This book touches on a lot of issues that some parents would not want their children to read - drugs, violence, suicide, murder. I was surprised to find that there was no warning on this book as to what lay inside, as there's even warnings for swearing on books now. I'm not sure I would recommend it for children younger than thirteen, but that depends on the child. For parents, I would recommend reading this book first to decide. I'm not for censoring but this book is brutal and not for everyone.

But my favorite kind of mysteries are the ones with the Agatha Christie-style reveal at the end, where you're slapping your forehead and saying to yourself, "How could I not have seen that coming? It was right in front of me all along!" 
 But the narration of Flavia de Luce is just... delightful, and it's wonderfully read by the voice actor. Everyone should listen to this autiobook! Everyone! :D 
 EDITED TO ADD: 
 After reading some reviews, I see that people are having trouble with suspension of disbelief, on grounds that Flavia's voice sounds too old or too learned. However, it's clear that the author deliberately kept separate the mind of the 11-year-old child from the older narrative voice. Flavia's actions and speech are often immature and ill-considered, obviously contrasting with the Flavia who tells the story. For me, it was easy enough to imagine that an older Flavia was reminiscing about the events that had happened, and was filling in many details she obviously learned later in life. But after reading reviews here, I see that the narrative device the author employed (and I understood) fell flat for many because it was too subtle.  Mindy McGinnis's Not a Drop to Drink was an excellent book. It was a little dry in the beginning, no pun intended, but I think it had to be to paint the stark, desperate world where fresh water was not readily available unless you were willing and able to pay for it. It was impossible not to be moved by the tragedy Lynn incurs, to be delighted by Lucy, adore Stebbs, respect Lauren and Vera, be angry with and heartbroken by Neva, and fall in love with Eli. This book is brimming with amazing characters. The story is a great balance between character-driven and situational plots. There was a lot more action than I expected. I thought the writing was fantastic; descriptive when it needed to be, well organized and well paced. McGinnis managed to keep some innocence in the story, and it brought parity to the harshness of the plot. My complaint, if I have any at all, is the way women were treated by the group to the south. As realistic as the situation was, it was difficult to read about women's bodies being traded for goods or the implied rape of others. And try as I might, I can't reconcile the reason for the direction the author took the romance part of the story. That said, I absolutely loved watching Lynn and Eli become so much more than what they'd begun as, both personally and together. Lynn's humanizing was perfectly executed, and it along with the romance were my favourite parts of the book. And let's not forget Lynn's interaction with Jasper. Poetic justice if you ask me. I would recommend this book to anyone who loves dystopian stories or loves a strong female lead.

 I quickly and wholeheartedly fell in love with Shatter Me and Tahereh Mafi's distinctive writing style, so I was absurdly pumped to read Unravel Me, especially after getting Warner's perspective in Destroy Me. At the same time, I was a little scared because I loved Shatter Me so much. Luckily, no worries here! There a lot of things I could talk about to fill space here, but only a couple I'd like to touch upon, since I'd much rather you go off and read the book than sit here reading my review. :) 
 Juliette has been placed in an utterly new environment, one where she's not physically separated from the world, one where she's supposed to contribute to a community and reap the benefits of being surrounded by people who are different, just like her. The problem is that she's so different--and potentially dangerous--that the people want little to do with her when she arrives. Instead of working to make people accept her, Juliette retreats into herself and into Adam's company--what little of it she can get, at least. This is where we find her at the beginning of the book: scared, lonely, and frustrated. She 's been trying to hone her abilities for a short time, to no avail. What I loved reading, though, was how Juliette--with the help of Castle and Kenji (KENJIIIIIIII)--grows, how she learns to befriend people, become part of a community, and care what happens to those people. She's whiny and self-absorbed at the beginning, but she becomes fierce and dedicated to helping those people she's quickly come to care about. It's a lovely transformation to watch. 
 I don't believe I can stress enough how big of a dilemma we are put in when it comes to Adam and Warner. Love triangles tend to make me gag a little bit. There's always the guy who it's obvious the girl is going to choose in the end and the guy who's just put there for some conflict, generally the bad boy. In Shatter Me, this was totally the case, but in Unravel Me and Destroy Me Warner has come into his own as... Something I really don't have a word for. 
 I couldn't help but think about him in relation to Shylock in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice (I know, I know, but I'm in a Shakespeare class right now and we JUST finished reading it!) My professor talked about how scholars deliberate over Shakespeare's intentions when it came to Shylock. He starts off as a clear villain, wanting to take down our nice, generous hero, but by the end of the play, he is easily the most complex and compelling character in the show, and one really can't help but root for him. Some scholars like to say Shylock got away from Shakespeare, that he became more than was intended, but I don't think that was the case. The ambiguity presented when Shylock speaks brings the play to a higher level; it makes it a powerful commentary, rather than just a play where the bad guy gets his dues. While I don't think Tahereh Mafi is making some huge commentary, I do think her intentions with Warner are clear. The "bad guy" is not just a bad guy. Taking Warner from a stereotypical villain to a very human, suffering character makes the reader think about labeling people from the beginning, and it makes me adore the book even more. 
 Now that I'm done with that rant.... I honestly don't have much to say past: Get to reading! Unravel Me takes the world and the characters established in Shatter Me to a whole new level. There's more action, more romance, more funny lines from Kenji, and just more to love all around. 
 You can find this review and many more fun things on my blog: Paper Cuts.

Okay, I have to be honest here. I personally find the Percy Jackson series, overrated. I don't think it's bad, I just don't love it like everyone else does. I have also read Kane Chronicles and enjoyed it. Heroes of Olympus I couldn't get into. So, long story short, I have an interesting relationship with Rick Riordan books. 
 However, when I heard that he was writing a Norse series, I knew that I had to check it out. So a couple of days after the book came out, I got it and just finished reading it recently. Here's what I have to say. 
 First, some cons: 
 I notice that on other reviews in here, some of the lower rated ones complain that this is basically Percy Jackson but Norse. 
 I will admit that while I was reading this, I did have the feeling that I was reading something familiar. I think this is the reason why I never read most of Riordan's books. It's the same stuff but with different mythology. I'm a person who highly encourages authors to try different things. In fact, I have two books I'm working on that are two completely different genres. 
 Some of the dialogue, lines, etc. felt awkward to me. 
 Every time I read a pop culture reference, I honestly cringed a little. Some other lines weren't much better. 
 This book felt like a comedy first, and an action packed Norse mythology adventure second 
 I'm not saying that I hate comedy (total opposite of truth) but I feel this book had it at some inappropriate times. Like, possible emotional or dark moment ruined by some witty line. 
 The fact that Magnus is Annabeth's cousin 
 Doing this honestly serves no point other than giving Magnus his last name. I feel this was just a cheap way to get PJ fans interested. 
 Those are all of the cons I can think about. 
 Now, to the pros: 
 This book is FUNNY 
 I said earlier that this book did have some comedy in the wrong places, but I never said that it was comedy that didn't work. I don't know how many times I laughed over the course of this book. I don't even want to say any of the lines, because you'll have to read it for yourself. 
 The references to previous series are minimal 
 Other than the few appearances of Annabeth, there really isn't any other references or nods to the past series. In fact, the only other ones I found were the reference to Jason Grace in a chapter title, and a reference to Percy's pen sword I found really funny.  This made the book much more enjoyable to me, as the very reason why I didn't enjoy HoO was because references to PJ were EVERYWHERE (I know it's kind of a sequel, but still.) 
 Out of all of the Riordan protagonists I have read about, Magnus is my favorite BY FAR 
 I don't know what, but there was something I felt when reading from Magnus's POV that I didn't get from reading Percy's, Carter's, Sadie's, Jason's, Piper's, or Leo's. He was a very entertaining narrator, and having only one narrator in a Riordan book again is nice. (As much as I enjoyed Kane Chronicles, that got annoying) 
 Character diversity 
 When I started this book, I was not expecting the main female lead to be Muslim, and for the other two sidekicks to be a dwarf with an interest in fashion and a deaf elf. Seeing these characters made me very happy, and I hope more diverse characters continue to come out of this series. 
 Those chapter titles 
 Do I need to say anything more? 
 FINAL THOUGHTS 
 For my first Rick Riordan book since 2011, I was not disappointed. I got some of the same feelings I got when reading PJ and KC, yet I got some new ones as well. While the book is not perfect, I think anyone familiar with Riordan should try to read it at least once. I think I will continue on with this series as well, as I'm curious as where it will go (in fact, I'm disappointed that this is getting the KC treatment of three books while ANOTHER Greek myth series is getting five) 
 So, until Hammer of Thor comes around, I will leave this series with four out of five stars. We'll see what happens from there.

A mind-blowing read. But definitely not for everyone. You've gotta WORK to read this book. I had to find an online annotated page of translations and explanations so I could figure out what Diaz was talking about. It's full of Spanish words, Spanglish words, references to gaming and Lord of the Rings, loaded with slang of all kinds, references to the history and culture of the Dominican Republic - especially the brutal dictator Trujillo, not to mention a ton of sexual language and expletives used in creative ways. No one should start reading this book without knowing ahead of time that this is NOT your grandfather's novel. 
 It's told by a narrator who gives you his opinion about everything and everyone while he's telling you the story of Oscar, (an overweight nerd who's afraid he'll die a virgin,) his sister, Lola, their mother Beli, their grandfather Abalard, and Beli's "foster" mother, La Inca. All the while, painting a vivid portrait of the nightmarish brutality under President Rafael Trujillo - who the narrator (Yunior) compares to a fuku - a curse that afflicted the country and its people for decades. Oscar's family is also cursed by a fuku. And boy, do they suffer. I'm glad I read it. 
 I can see why it won some prestigious awards - breaking with traditional fiction the way it does. I like reading immigrant fiction and this story will definitely stick with me. Still - I cannot recommend anyone start reading it unless they know what they're getting into. When the narrator describes a room as "smelling like ripe ass" and uses the word "nigger," (in a friendly, hail fellow well met sort of way) as often as he does, along with a host of other unpleasant images and vocabulary, it can make you cringe. But what a tour de force (if you can stomach it.) I, myself would never have read it if my son hadn't given it to me for Christmas, not realizing I might not fall within the book's target demo.

 Of course, the romance is a huge part of the story, but there is also a big focus on the love that you have for all of the people in your life, and the sacrifices you make for them. 
 Layken lost her father recently, and due to her mother's financial strain, they move across the country during Laken's senior year in high school. The neighbor boy immediately catches her eye, and a bond is almost instantly formed. But as soon as Will and Layken realize what they could mean to each other, they also realize how impossible their relationship is. It was doomed from the start. Will's circumstances are so different from what Layken expected, but her situation also changes quickly, pulling her even further away from him. 
 I kept thinking, "My gosh! How many knocks does this girl have to take?" Come to find out, even more than I originally thought. Fortunately, she has a fast growing friendship with Eddie, an energetic and quirky girl at school who has also had an awfully hard life. Eddie: 
 It wasn't death that punched you, Layken. It was life. Life happens. Shit happens. And it happens a lot. To a lot of people. 
 I can't say much about Will without giving out some spoilers. But here's a convo between Layken and Eddie that made me tear up, in the context that it was given: 
 "God, Layken. How do you do it?" she says. 
 She blows her nose and grabs another tissue out of the box. 
 "How do I do what?" I sniff as I continue to wipe the tears from my eyes. 
 "How do you not fall in love with him?" 
 The tears begin flowing just as quickly as they were ceasing. I grab yet another tissue. "I don't not fall in love with him. I don't not fall in love with him a lot! 
 And I was also in love with Will about forty page in. He's not a bad boy; in fact, he's the opposite. He's got so much responsibility and goodness weighing him down, you can't help but fall in love. He goes straight to my favorite heroes shelf. Because he's a modern day hero, the best kind there is.
Thoroughly enjoyed this book. Although I must say that the ending left me with panoply of unanswered questions ... aargh!!

The Bill of Life 
 The Second Civil War, also known as 'The Heartland War', was a long and bloody conflict fought over a single issue. 
 To end the war, a set of constitutional amendments known as 'The Bill of Life' was passed. 
 It satisfied both the Pro-life and the Pro-choice armies. 
 The Bill of Life states that human life may not be touched from the moment of conception until a child reaches the age of thirteen. 
 However, between the ages of thirteen and eighteen, a parent may choose to retroactively 'abort' a child... 
 ...on the condition that the child's life doesn't 'technically' end. 
 The process by which a child is both terminated and yet kept alive is called 'unwinding' 
 Unwinding is now a common and accepted practice in society.
Turns out this is my favorite part of the trilogy. I have quite a few issues with this series but the closure isn't one of them.

Guys. Guys. I met John Scalzi last week. He didn't come to my town as part of his book tour, but he did come to one that was just about ninety minutes away, so I made a special trip to (a) buy the book, (b) get it signed, and (c) meet John Scalzi! It was definitely a squee-worthy moment, especially when he called me a jerk in front of the whole crowd! 
 The End of All Things is the latest book in the Old Man's War series, and like its predecessor The Human Division, it's a compilation of shorter works that were originally published online. This time, though, the works are longer. I think this is a good thing. While I liked the idea behind The Human Division, I feel like Scalzi is better at long-form fiction than short-form fiction. I still think I prefer his stuff when it's novel-length, but with The End of All Things, he's a bit closer to that than he was with the last book. 
 The first story in the book, The Life of the Mind, is a brain-in-a-box story. This isn't a spoiler, though; it's mentioned in the second sentence of the story. The main character, Rafe Daquin, is a pilot who is a last-minute addition to the crew of a cargo ship, which is also taking the Assistant Secretary of State on a vacation. Since Rafe eventually winds up as a brain-in-a-box, you can probably expect that things don't go quite according to plan. 
 Rafe makes an appearance in the second story, This Hollow Union, but his part is important to the story; in fact, his part is the link between the two stories that makes this feel more like a novel that The Human Division. In this story, the Conclave is teetering on the brink of failure, with the two human factions playing a key role in how it plays out. This story, to me, represents the best of what Scalzi can do: political intrigue; behind the scenes machinations; and a complex sequence of events that's easy to follow. 
 With Can Long Endure, I was reminded that Scalzi is a liberal man. This doesn't bother me at all; I tend to agree with much of what he writes about politics and society on his blog, so it's more like reading something my Facebook friends would write. This particular story reminded me of a series of articles I've seen over the past several weeks, usually prefaced with "We have a police problem." It's also a reminder that in Scalzi's universe, even the police tend to think the way I do about things. 
 To Stand or Fall, the final novella, takes the themes set forward in the previous three novellas and concludes the overarching story of the book. Since this book does read more like a complete novel than The Human Division, I won't go into a lot of detail about it, but I will say that, in true Scalzi fashion, the ultimate solution involves more diplomacy than explosions, and everything that happened in the previous three novellas has an impact on how this story plays out. 
 There was some bonus material at the end of the book, comprised of an alternate take of the first story in the collection. It was interesting to read, especially if, like me, you're into how the creative process works, but it's also like deleted scenes or demo tracks; ultimately, you see why these things weren't the final product. I recognize that this version of the story was a rough cut, but it doesn't convey the story and events as well as was done in the final take. 
 Given that The Human Division ended pretty much where it started, and that The End of All Things concludes the events that began in the preceding book, I would consider these two books to be a duology of their own, best read together. Together, they take the universe of Old Man's War to a logical place (I hesitate to call it a conclusion, since the universe is ripe for more stories), and at least with this collection we see that there is a conclusion to those events.
