Taming the Beast is a story of forbidden, often cruel passion. Sarah Clark is an innocent 14 year old lover of literature, but all that changes when she meets Daniel Carr, her 38 year old English teacher. Soon they become entangled in a powerful affair in which Daniel quotes literature as a tool of seduction to use on Sarah. As quickly as the relationship began, it ends when Daniels moves away with his wife and children to teach elsewhere. Sarah's world comes crashing down at this point, and she begins seeking demeaning, often anonymous sex with hundreds of men to fill the void left in her by Daniel. 
 Seven years later, Sarah and Daniel encounter one another and their sadomasochistic relationship begins once more. They are destructive of one another and themselves, but they feed off of brutality of their passion. It's as if the only way they can sustain themselves is by selfishly using the other in a malicious, vicious, and hurtful way without a single thought as to the consequences. 
 Taming the Beast is an intense read with complex characters in a violent, obsessive, and often erotic relationship. Sarah and Daniel are the most dysfunctional, disturbing characters I've come across in a long time, but that is a huge allure for the reader. It's impossible to turn away from the horrifying, destructive nature of these people because perhaps we are all a little curious about the intensity and borderline scary eroticism displayed within the pages of this book. 
 Sarah is a hard character to figure out or even develop an opinion of. She's definitely three-dimensional. On one hand she's so overly sexual that it's easy to pity her. She's self-destructive and weak at times, which is very frustrating. However, she does possess qualities that allow the reader to sympathize with her or like her on some level. Her love of literature was a draw for me because I felt like it was something human and easy to relate to. Sarah's development (or should I say downfall) throughout the novel is painful, but very well written. 
 At times the story felt a little chaotic, but this suited the plot and characters. I wouldn't have felt appropriate if the ambience was calm and mellow because the interactions between the many characters was anything but calm. The writing style was very forceful and fluid. I found myself saying "just one more page," but ending up reading 25 more before I could put it down. Every sentence felt very full of important content and like it was a crucial part of the story. I took in every word with utter delight. Emily Maguire is a talented writer with the ability to captivate. 
 Taming the Beast is a novel I would highly recommend to those with a fondness for the forbidden and intense. This novel is capable of evoking disgust, pity, sadness in the reader, but it's a truly fascinating story.

And this is how both have to team up to find this mysterious killer who presumably had killed the other Vaudreys (Crane's brother and father) as well. 
 There wasn't something extraordinarily special about the plot or so I felt but it somehow had the satisfying feel to it. Everything wrapped up pretty quickly and nicely and the main focus wasn't just the romance or the the mystic magic parts. Everything was balanced out. 
 Talking about the romance, I don't know. I feel that it could have been a little better. Not saying it was bad or anything. It was infact splendid, and pretty hot and steamy too. I feel that it could have been more detailed . Or something like that. 
 So, finally, if you are into m-m romance books, then you need to give this one a try. I am pretty sure you won't be disappointed. :) 
 Oh, and yeah, No Cliffhanger so yay.

** spoiler alert ** 
 In a highly technological world, humans still shy away from mechs in Robin Wasserman's Skinned, the first part of a new trilogy. 
 The car crash was deadly. But Lia Kahn's parents downloaded her brain and gave it a new body, and though she mostly looks quite human, others view her as a 
 "skinner", a mech. Or, as her new acquaintances call her, a machine. 
 Lia is frustrating, and there are moments when she needs to be slapped. She's superficial, and considers herself above...well, everyone. Thus being shunned is a total shock to her, and she gets her comeuppance. But otherwise Lia thinks and reacts realistically. She does a lot of stupid things, but so do others. Heck, other people need to be slapped, too, and these characteristics stop this novel from being a 5-star read. But the content and plot are so fascinating that Skinned is well worth reading through all the way. 
 The world-building is richly enhanced, turning even clothing into a thing of technological wonder. Humanity, machinery, and how far each can go is put to the test and explored. For your bitchy teen fix, the supposedly secret relationship is blindingly obvious. Written in first-person from Lia's point of view, she should realise it, too, but denial makes a fool... 
 Admittedly read during an hormonal time, I very nearly cried, and that rarely happens when books are involved. If you've read this, email me with your guess of when I was teary. (Please don't do it in the comments here at the blog - let's protect readers from spoilers.) 
 Theology, philosophy, science, technology, medicine, relationships and self-discovery combine to create this engaging and thought-provoking futuristic story. But be warned that one's eyes may leak... 
 September's release of Book 2, Crashed, can't come soon enough.

Same feelings basically as the other books in the trilogy, but I started to get tired of Gemma's angst. It felt like so many of the chapters ended with her expressing again how alone she feels, and I get it at this point. I had less patience for the stuff in the realms again, and wanted more of the social negotiations of the Victorian world. I think I wanted everything to be more...supernatural, rather than fantasy. The fantasy elements took away from the gothic-ness of it. In fact, I didn't really feel the gothic at all, which is quite different from how I felt about the first book. Oh well. I still liked reading it. I don't think I was really in the best mood for this book right now (her constantly questioning her decisions, hesitating at making them, etc.), but overall it was fun. I think I just needed different timing and had incorrect expectations.

The Peculiar Life of a Lonely Postman is such a lovely title. I think this is how my interest for this novel was sparked in the first place. The premise got me even more excited. A curious but shy postman with a passion for human interaction, intercepting and reading people's personal letters: love it! 
 The whole thing is written without a single dialogue. I only realized this about halfway in and I found it kind of interesting because it at no point bothered me. It just fit the book perfectly. 
 The story is also incredibly poetic, both in its story and its writing. Even the short length of the story felt to me like a nod to the haiku. The story was wrapped up so, so beautifully. It dealt with quite harsh themes and yet I felt as though there was nothing harsh about it at all. It was all just so beautiful. 
 I loved Bilobo, the main character. I loved how much attention is given to his inner psyche. You realize that he's more than just a strange man going through people's private mail. He's a dreamer, he's a romantic, maybe socially inept,.. Such an interesting character. I actually found myself relating to him a lot. 
 My only critique is that some things were left quite unexplained. I'm talking about technical things like, how can the guy afford two apartments?? But I realize that those small details aren't what this book is about. Theriault describes Lonely Postman as 'a psychological novel that flirts with the fantastic'. I think that says enough. 
 So yeah, good read, very good read!
Persuasion is my favorite of the Jane Austen novels, so it was hard to stop comparing this to that. Overall, however, I enjoyed this take on the original, and it was different in good ways.

OMG! 
 This is my first ever ARC and I am so excited that I got to read this a full...six months before it was even published! 
 Yay me! 
 I am not sure how much I should reveal about it since it hasn't been published yet so I'll keep it short and sweet until...January. 
 At first I wasn't exactly feeling the writing style the author had taken on (and it is third person, boo) but I got used to some of the corny phrases eventually. Clearly the author was inspired by like, Across the Universe because the protagonists have generally the same characteristics. The main female character is a strong, opinionated red head and the main male character is like olive skinned and...alien (like Amy and Elder in Across the Universe). 
 Don't get me wrong, however. The author put a whole new spin to it. Cara, an Earthling, is chosen as one of three worldwide exchange students to house beings from an alien planet, whose inhabitants have DNA that resembles humans. However, they are more advanced and feel superior to Earthlings, causing a rift between the two species. 
 I don't feel like summarizing much right now. Later. I promise. 
 Really looking forward to what can come out of this and what others will say once it is published in 2014 (yes I'm boasting). Boo for me, but I have to wait TWO YEARS for the sequel.

Depending on which is in control some things (appliances, cars, magic, etc) will work better than others. There are also two factions fighting for control, the Pack (all manner of were-creatures) and the People (necromancers who control the vampires). As always with me, introductions too big for reviews that are quite possibly not helpful at all. Also, lots of gifs because I can. 
 3.5* 
 Well. 
 I mean- 
 I don't know how to say this. It's not that I didn't like it. It's not that I didn't love parts of it. It's just that, I don't know. Expectations, people. Expectations. 
 I discovered Penny Reid on a hot summer day, the air conditioner literally making me sick. I didn't care, I was fearless (and really hot and humid, since I live in Buenos Aires, so don't judge me). After reading Tara Sivec's Seduction and Snacks, quite possibly the funniest book I've ever read, I was looking for something similar. Light-hearted, hilarious romance that you want to re-read every time you're feeling down. (And I do not say blue, because that never really made sense to me. Blue is not a sad color. The sky is not always sad, the sea is not always sad, and I'm not feeling like a Smurf. Seriously, English-talking people are crazy.) 
 Where was I? Funny Contemporary Romances. But not the cheesy, stereotypical ones. I like my humor a little ridiculous, to be honest. And sometimes a tiny bit offensive, you know, not taking itself too seriously. Because in real life, people with outrageous, dry humor are just the best for me. So, in this search for a kind of humor that walks a very fine line, I found a recommendation that was said to be in the same style as Tara Sivec. And this is how I found her. 
 Penny Reid. 
 As I started a book with a ridiculous title, with an even more ridiculous series name, I did not realize my life was about to change. I did not realize what I had found. 
 Now, I don't believe we have one love in our lives. What if they die, or we never find them? I don't believe in destiny, written in the stars, meant to be. I do believe sometimes we click with people, that they complete us and make us more. But the whole concept of The One simply doesn't agree with the fact that people change in different and unpredictable ways, inevitably changing the way they interact with the rest of the world. 
 Even know, dramatically telling you about my level of love for this author, I can't say she is my favorite author of all times. (Since I do like to make lists, I can tell you she's the third after Nalini Goddess of All Things Mortal and Immortal Singh and Ilona Making Life Worth Living Andrews.) (Because J.K. Rowling is not an author, she's a religion.) 
 However, the things she made me feel. With Penny Reid's Knitting in the City (I know, ridiculous) series, I found love, and hate. I laughed, and I cried. I understood the power of coincidence, and the value of doing everything you can to make what you want happen. I was overjoyed when my favorite promps appeared, and surprised when I loved just as much the ones I can never like. Mountain-loving guys, famous actors, childhood friends turned lovers, old poetry lovers. All things I historically hated, she made me love. 
 This is my too long way of saying that expectations suck but there were no good expectation gifs so I had to write this long, unnecessary text. 
 I went into The Hooker and the Hermit (that's the book I'm reviewing, in case you forgot with my nonsense babbling) with too many expectations, and that's what broke me in the end. It didn't matter that it was co-written, in my mind this was Penny Reid, the woman who can do no wrong. Perhaps that was the problem, not the book itself. 
 My mind was conditioned, and this made everything just not perfect enough. I liked how quirky Annie was, but she wasn't as quirky as Janie. I liked the humor and depth Lucy's character introduced, but she wasn't as hilarious or complex as the Winston brothers. I could get behind the plot, but nothing can beat Fiona and Greg's crazy adventures. Ronan's courting was intense, but Drew's letters make me feel things I didn't know I could feel. As far as romance and characterization in general go, Sandra and Alex. Just Sandra and Alex. 
 Expectations are not why I rated the 3.5* down, though. I did have two big issues with this book. 
 First, romantic obstacles. It was just ridiculous, okay? While I kind of liked how Annie was shown as a hermit, her reservations were dragged too much. And Ronan's secrets keeping was just dumb. The BDSM, her identity, just everything. At first it was too soon for them to be together, and then it was too late. It just seemed like their lives would have been so much easier if they hadn't been so obstinate, even for a book. 
 Second, and most important, Ronan. 
 I didn't like him. I know it seems too simple a main problem for a review that is too long, but it's just the truth. I didn't hate him, either. He was too intense, and too underwhelming. Annie deserved less and more. He just didn't do it for me. Especially after all of Penny Reid's male leads. I just would honestly not date this guy, even in fantasy land. No feelings whatsoever were had. 
 (I'm watching Scrubs and I just wanted Perry on my review, okay?) 
 After all that, I must give credit where credit is due. It wasn't the worst CR ever. It was a good CR, I simply expected more. And in spite of it, I will not give up on my Empress. 
 Penny Reid is still one of my true loves. I still look forward to anything she writes, including the sequel of this series. My respect for her has not been diminished, for a little challenge is nothing for the trust I have put in her. Lucy and Sean, I am ready.

It was just another spin off novel that didn't even compare to the original. And it barely was a spin off. Specifically in the summary, which I didn't type this part, it said there would be appearances from people from Blue Blood. Only three chapters had those said characters. And it was only two characters. I wasn't impressed by this whatsoever. I want her to branch out and try something more than keep going back to her old characters that help her. 3.5 stars. An entertaining read, and an interesting extension of the current political landscape of the US into the future. The focus on bizarre outgrowths of the military and queer culture were a bit daunting at first, but they served largely as window-dressing on the world building. It reads less like a military/covert rescue novel, however, than as a camping trip in the wild, going from one place to another with only faceless opposition. If they had been fighting nature rather than the Red States it wouldn't have changed the story much. It would have been nice to have seen a better developed villain to oppose them, or see some of the personal basis of the Red State opposition, but the political underpinnings of this speculative world are largely understood, and therefore unexplained. Other than that, I enjoyed the book, and I'll certainly tune in again if there is a sequel.

 Author: Pierce Brown 
 Source: I Own It 
 Not as good as the first book but still pretty damn good. Good and sad, unfortunately. 
 I can't believe I'm saying this but Tactus became one of my favourite characters (along with Sevro of course but thats a given). I didn't like him per se, but he was a complicated character. We got to learn a bit more about him and I found myself liking him more and more, weird I know. 
 One person I didn't like too much was Virginia. Perhaps it was because Darrow was a bit more distanced from her in this book, but I didn't feel the spark of the girl who cleaned him up and basically inspired him while he was losing all of his hope. Instead she seemed insensitive sometimes, or only appeared in the book to 'humanise' Darrow. Which btw, was not needed. His treatment of the other colours is something to be aspired to.

Don't read this book during the work week. If you do, you'll end up staying up too late several nights in a row and then skipping "work" one morning to finish it off. (Or maybe that's just me?) 
 Daughter of the Forest is a beautiful (but harrowing) fairy tale retelling. The world, the characters, and the plot are all spot on. At one point, our heroine takes a vow of silence, and I was so engrossed in the story I almost felt like I shouldn't speak when I took a break for dinner. 
 The book is comparable to Robin McKinley, but darker. At one point, I felt like begging the author to take pity on our heroine and not make quite so many bad things happen to her. But there are good parts too, and it's definitely worth reading.

I read this book with Reign, Veronica and Gabriella! 
 I actually didn't know if this book deserved 4 stars, I feel like I didn't like it as much as I could've because it was so overhyped. 
 Even though so much happened, it felt like (at least to me) nothing did at all, everything moved too slowly and there were a lot of uninteresting parts. I don't usually like comparing books of the same genre like those "this book is like the hunger games" people but I feel like it's necessary here for the sake of the review: this book is very similar to The Wrath and the Dawn which is one of my favorite books ever, but while I fell in love with the characters in TWATD, the ones in this book didn't spark my interest at all, they lacked depth and the story didn't enthral me as much. 
 What I did love and think is important in this book is how realistic it was: *trigger warning* the horrors of war are so well represented in this book and although sometimes the mentions of rape were too much they were used in appropriate contexts. 
 I might change my mind and give this book 3.5 stars instead of 5, it wasn't a solid debut novel in my opinion but I'll definitely give A Torch Against the Night a chance!

3.5 stars. I liked this book, but I really wanted to love it. All the elements that push my buttons were there (gangster/criminal hero, cold yet strong heroine, historical...) but there was just a little something missing that didn't make it perfect for me. I understand the heroine is supposed to be cold and distant, but as a reader, we're supposed to understand why she acts the ways she does. We may not agree with her actions, but they should make enough sense to the reader that we empathize with her. For some reason, I felt like didn't get enough of this and I had a hard time connecting with her and sometimes was a teensy bit annoyed with her. Regardless, I still love this author and look forward to her next book.

Good stuff, though I admit to being a bit disappointed as I'm used to being blown away by Sanderson. A lot of the action was just plain hard to follow, and I lacked the patience to go back and pick through all the little details. Which frankly surprised me; usually action is one of Sanderson's strong points, but here there was just a bit too much of it.

A psychological thriller and survival story rather than the true horror King is known for, but still a great story. Everything starts out so mundane, and even once Trisha gets lost, things still don't seem that awful. But as days go by and she remains unfound, Trisha has to find her own way to survive. I loved how Trisha reacted to her predicament. She used what she'd learned from her mother and in school to try to find civilization, but at the same time, she acted just like a scared nine year old, reaching out for some source of comfort through her Walkman and the Red Sox games. At first you think the story is just going to be Trisha's fight to survive, but then that 'special thing' out in the woods begins to make itself known, and from then on, it becomes more of a cat and mouse game. I found Trisha funny and admirable. She kept it together for as long as she was physically and mentally able, she was resourceful and brave, but she wasn't afraid to cry. I loved the way that her hallucinations of Tom Gordon eventually helped her find a path back to people, even though his presence at all was a sure sign the end was near. But when Trisha channeled Tom to face down the bear/the God of the Lost, I had to cheer. And I loved the way she communicated with her dad in the end through Tom's signature move. I also really liked the asides about how the search was going or about the reality of the direction Trisha chose to go; seeing how close she came to being saved and how her tenacity actually made her rescue harder really kept me invested in Trisha and hoping for her to survive. A great and mind-trippy story even without King's normal brand of scary.

This book was quite interesting. It sorta had this "catch me if you can" (movie and book of the same name) feel to it, except that this one felt much more romanticised and had characters that felt too typical to the point of being made-up (see Axel Emmerman). The writing style was a little too simple for my liking as well. It sounded like a teenage fiction novel at points and doesn't lend to the credibility of the reality of the 'heist'. Overall, though, it was enjoyable and a quick read.
Book burning is a thing in this book and it's very very scary.

Look if you're okay with every character telling you how beautiful, amazing, graceful, and strong the MC is, and your cool with world building being dropped in only when it's convenient for the plot, and you want to do a lot of eye rolling, this is for you.

 I wanted to like this book more than the prequels, because I liked the series less and less with each book. Sadly the process continued with Haunted. 
 Paul turns out to be even crazier than I thought and we get more of the whole Jesse-drama-llama. Haunted was thinly disguised as a paranormal story when all it was is a love story between Susannah and Jesse. 
 Suze is more dense and stupid than I ever thought possible. I laughed out loud when she said she isn't stupid. Didn't all that happened before prove to her that she is very, very stupid? 
 I've become so frustrated with her, I don't even know what to say anymore. 
 She's become even lamer in this book than she already was. All she's concerned about is Jesse, Jesse, Jesse. Oh and fashion, wheee! All her rambling about clothes annoyed me. I simply didn't care about it. It seemed like bought advertisement for Jimmy Choo shoes. 
 The only one who was able to coax something else out of Suze and make her think of something else was Paul. But OF COURSE Paul had to turn out even crazier than he was portrayed as before. 
 And am I the only one who thought Jesse completely overreacted when he went at Paul with the goal of killing him? That turned me off Jesse so fast you wouldn't believe it. Beating someone up/trying to kill that person, just because they're being an a-hole? How about no. 
 I laughed out loud maybe four times during it and only two times was because of something that was supposed to be funny. The other two times was more of sad laugh or a laugh of how ridiculous it turned out to be. 
 I just can't with this series anymore. I'm glad when I'm finally done with it.

Beatrix, you are one interesting girl. I knew your story would be interesting, and of course it was, but not in the way that I had planned. For some reason, I was almost expecting you to imitate a repeat of Poppy's meeting with her hotelier. I certainly didn't expect you to fall for a tortured war hero. Nor did I expect for you to sit and wait in the shadows, secretly afraid to show your true self to the real world. Who knew you were really the scared one in the family? You, the girl who ran wild and free with the animals. 
 What a sweet story. It wasn't what I had imagined for Beatrix, but it was still satisfying nonetheless, and a pleasant ending to my time spent with the Hathaways. I will most certainly miss this fun and eccentric family.

I became acquainted with the "Under the Red Hood" storyline via the animated movie, and it is definitely a very dark part of the Batman history. I have recently embarked on exploring the Batman graphic novels, and decided to give this one a swing. This was very good. 
 This serves as a bit of a prequel to when the Red Hood enters the Gotham scene. It's not about Batman. It's about Jason Todd, who was found in the ruins of the warehouse that the Joker brought down on his head after beating and torturing him nearly to death. Initially, Jason is catatonic, but Talia Al'Ghul sees him as a pawn in destroying Batman and mentors him into the dangerous and murderous vigilante/assassin he becomes. He learns everything that Batman doesn't teach him about the darker Arts of War, with the goal of getting revenge on Joker (and peripherally Batman). In the process, he realizes that deep down, he still believes in fighting for good, but is willing to use extreme methods to deal with evil that Batman would never countenance. 
 This feels like a credible action/suspense story. Jason goes deep into the darkest pits of corruption and criminality, learns the skills he needs for his ultimate quest, and finds he can't turn a blind eye when innocents are harmed, or the tutors that Talia acquires for him turn out to be reprehensible in their habits. He also realizes that not all the means are justified for a desired end. Jason has a phenomenal brain and the incredible acrobatic and martial arts skills that demonstrate very clearly why he was Batman's Robin. Ultimately, I don't see that he has departed to far from the path that Batman sent him down. Maybe he is lost, but I think he will find his way. I need to read Batman: Under the Red Hood soon! 
 Definitely worthy of a 4.5/5.0 star rating.

I feel like all the YA books I read have a definite "she's going to end up with him" vibe by the first few chapters. But aside from her attaching to a boy right away, it was good. I liked the story, the writing, and of course the boy. Noah gave me butterflies cause he's just to damn self assured and quick. I didn't guess anything that happened and that's always a plus(other than the pairing but who didn't know that was coming by the first sighting of him?) and I read it in a night (a long night but still). I usually adore Picoult's books, but I never quite latched on to the premise of this one.

I strongly recommend reading a few of the series that directly preceed this one. I have read the first 3 or 4, then #10, then this one and I found myself slightly confused at who certain people are and what their stories were. Most importantly the new 'big bad' and 'no-fanger'. It was 3/4ths into the book before I learned both who and what it was. The mystery that is in the background for the entire novel make you want to keep reading and, while it is not solved in this novel, it is solved in the next one. I was a little frustrated at the fact that, throughout the books readers have been told that the enforcers of the council are warriors trained to hunt Immortals. This novel makes them seem like bumbling oafs. I know it was to make the main character look better when he is saving the girl but I thought it was incredibly OOC and distracted me away from the 'danger' of the story.

I want to keep this review brief, so let me just begin by saying that reading this book was like riding through a roller coaster. I had a lot of mixed emotions while doing so, yet thankfully, half of it were good. 
 There were times when Cath annoyed me, times when I felt like she's one of the most relatable young adult females I could realistically relate with. And there where also times in the middle part wherein I almost wanted to stop reading. It's just that, she acts too selfish sometimes. And though I could understand her reasons, It still pissed me off. 
 But she's not at all that bad. And the other characters were all okay too. The writing was good. The Simon and Baz fanfics/scenes were splendid--I admit, I just became a fan of a book in a book. The story was amazing, and except for my little downfall during the middle, maybe I could even say that I loved the book. 
 So yeah. I recommend this to everyone who wants a light, quirky read. Especially those who belong to a fandom, or writes fanfictions like I do. You won't regret it.
Well that was an interesting twist. I love books where you don't see the end coming!

Howl's Moving Castle has to be my favorite book of all time. I'm so often looking for books that are magical and whimsical without being epically fantastical, and HMC is exactly that. My profile picture is even Howl and Sophie because I love them so much. The movie version of it is inaccurate, but I couldn't imagine anybody but Miyazaki adapting it. It just feels like a Ghibli book to me - filled with wonder and fun and love. 
 Sophie is brazen and headstrong and humble and hardworking all at the same time. She's insecure, yet confident, and I love who she becomes by the end of the novel. Also, the mistakes she makes with Howl's suit and such are hilarious, and probably something I would do were I in her shoes. 
 However, if I'm like any character, I'm like Howl. From his drama to his selfishness to his overall antisocial-ness, he's pretty much me in male form. He's just a lot funnier than me. His sass and sarcasm and exaggerations really make the story light-hearted and funny. 
 Together, they're adorable. He gives excitement to a girl who never expected much. She's the voice of reason and gives him a relatively level head. Their relationship gets so much better in the sequels, especially with Morgan. (Don't even get me started on Morgan.) 
 I love all the other characters too, from Michael to Prince Justin to Calcifer to Lettie to Ben to Martha. The writing is warm and whimsical almost nostalgic. It's reminiscent of old fairy tales, what with all the tropes and the world they live in. 
 I think my favorite part by far is Wales. I've always loved Wales, and the Wales scene is absolutely amazing. Sophie and Michael's shock is hilarious and I really started to love Howl's character when we met his family and we learned that he actually did have something he cared about. 
 Overall, Howl's Moving Castle is a great book. I love the characters, the writing, the dialogue - everything. I only wish the movie was more accurate...

I loved the back-story to "Wool" probably more than the original - more so because the broad outlines seem so plausible they are terrifying... BUT I had ONE major problem with Howey that simply cannot be overcome by anything in the story (Spoiler, sort of, below....) Hence, what should have been a 4-star rating is downgraded to 2, for Howey's usage of ONE term a handful of times. 
 Basically, we did this-the US destroyed the world-but not only that, Howey claims it was a Democrat's Master Plan. He does not dwell on this, does not explain it, just casually mentions the "Shepherd's" affiliation a few times. Now, there have been PLENTY of authors who have managed to stay out of current politics, alienating readers of either side, by making broad generalizations such as talking about "the opposing party" and the like, without mentioning which side is which. Also, the Democrat angle was not only not explored AT ALL, but it simply had absolutely nothing to do with anything other than to pin the blame on A Side--and I found it utterly repelling (yes, as a far-left liberal democrat), especially without evidence of *why* it had to be a Democrat vs. a libertarian or a Green Party supporter or a Republican or an Independent. So, why mention Democrats at all? Ugh. 
 Definitely NOT a fan of the implied message: "Democrats have good intentions but they will destroy the world. They think they know better than everyone else, and they are comfortable making decisions for all people. They feel no remorse in pushing the "kill" switch for all of humanity, because they sincerely believe they are creating a better world..." 
 HAD Howey replaced: "Some of those in power" for "Democrats" I would 100% BUY this message and rate this novel at a 4/5. As it stands: GAH, No!

I am not a what I'd call a Murakami fan. In my twenties I liked Hard Boiled Wonderland; I enjoyed Sputnik Sweetheart, too, and Norwegian Wood. Later, I was pressed to read - and expected to love - Wind-Up Bird Chronicle. I still don't own my own opinions of Wind-Up, since I was berated for expressing indifference. Later read his running/writing memoir and was starting to understand the man-behind-the curtain. Eventually, I just wasn't interested anymore (at least for now). In my personal experience then, Murakami is best read in one's twenties. (Also Paul Auster, ha!) 
 Observations on After Dark: Listening to Murakami by audiobook made me realize that his work is conducive to audio. And Janet Song's reading was fine. But this book was really bad, I think. This is an odd thing to say about fiction but ... but ... it seemed like Murakami was making it up as he went along. And it was so plodding, as if profundity was supposed to emerge out of the quotidian details and the Americana dropped into each scene like color, to add a level of cheap nostalgia. "He did this. Then he did this. Then a cat crossed the road. Then they ate a sandwich." The surreal spiritual bits didn't work for me either - quasi-mystical mumbo jumbo without any meaning. I just had to grit my teeth and persevere to finish the (short) book, but I distracted myself by furtive fantasies of running home and writing a Murakami pastiche.

Full disclosure, I had no clue what a Margay was so I had to look up pictures. And now I want one! Christmas present maybe? 
 Harley Vincent is a half Margay shifter, half human who chooses to live in the human world. When she was younger her own pride was a bunch of partiers and was hated by the pack of wolf shifters that lived near them. But Harley was hated by that pack more than anyone and they made her childhood hell until her human aunt came and got her out of there. But Jesse, a wolf shifter, knew that she would be his one day. 
 He had lost his mate as a child and it changed him in a big way. He was no longer a carefree little boy, instead he became a hardened man that was quick to distrust people. Now that he's grown up and no longer part of the same pack, he's ready to claim Harley as his. And the he's done giving her time to run away, especially when he learns that her life is in danger. 
 Obviously I'm a huge fan of Suzanne Wright and this book is just another reason why. Jesse now has a place in my heart and I just loved him so much. He was so fierce and protector over Harley and I loved seeing that. Even with his own family and pack he wouldn't let them even think about hurting her. I love me some Alpha men, and Jesse is the true embodiment of one. 
 But Jesse isn't the only reason why this book was so good, Harley had a lot to do with it as well. I love how SW can create a kick ass heroine and makes them tough but lovable. Harley was just that, and I liked seeing her hold her own against her and the packs enemies. Even though her cat was smaller than any of the wolves she still fought with them and helped them protect their land. 
 I really enjoyed the fact that this wasn't the same "oh wow you actually are my true mate" type of story. Jesse lost his mate as a young boy, and Harley has never met hers but they loved each other enough that they wanted to mate with one another no matter what. I thought that it was handled really well so it made the story all the more perfect instead of taking away from it. 
 Overall, if you haven't read this series or author yet then you are missing out. Her characters are amazing and I can't wait for more. I have a feeling that Cain will be getting a story and if I'm right I may know his mate? I'm probably wrong, but I'm going to keep a look out for that to happen.

This book (and series) is an interesting glimpse into a strange world where Angels are nearly immortal and are the makers of vampires. Elena, a Guild Hunter (hunter of vampires that have broken their "contracts" with the Angels that made them), became an angel when she nearly died fulfilling a contract that threw her into a battle between archangels, the most powerful beings in her world. When Raphael saved her life, an unheard of thing happened and she became an Angel - the first made Angel in living memory. Unfortunately, that throws her right into the middle of Angel politics, which is a bloody world where power and violence reign. She is too young and fragile for most of the angels, and nearly everyone around her wants her dead. She must battle to earn respect and keep herself alive, plus keep from being her lover's downfall. She also finds herself battling nightmares from her past when her family was slaughtered, which adds another layer of weakness. Yet, her inner strength shines through and with Raphael by her side, she stands up to her many enemies. This series is more urban fantasy than PNR, but the love between these two is fascinating. Elena is a kick-butt heroine even when surrounded by physically stronger beings. She proves strength of mind is as important as that of body.  All in all, a satisfying read and I will be continuing to read this series.

As The Strangely Beautiful Tale of Miss Percy Parker opens, six London youngsters are chosen for a special destiny. Plucked from their ordinary lives, they are brought together by a mysterious goddess. Their mission: to protect humanity from the forces of evil. The goddess promises the six that, in time, they will be joined by a seventh. 
 Nineteen years later, timid orphan Percy Parker arrives at the Athens Academy, where two of the six "chosen ones" have made their careers. Percy is brilliant with languages, abysmal at mathematics, haunted by strange dreams, and gifted with the ability to see ghosts. She settles uneasily into life at Athens Academy, and soon finds herself infatuated with Alexi Rychman, her mathematics instructor. 
 Much of The Strangely Beautiful Tale revolves around the developing relationship between Percy and Alexi; this is definitely "romantic fantasy." They begin an unlikely friendship, with an undercurrent of forbidden attraction (though Percy is an adult, Alexi is her teacher). As he gets to know Percy, Alexi comes to believe that the shy young woman may be the fated seventh member of the group. 
 Meanwhile, another woman has appeared in London who appears to bear all the hallmarks of the goddess's prophecy. It's pretty clear, early in the story, which is the real seventh and which is the false one. Watching Alexi and his colleagues attempt to figure this out, then, is less like reading a mystery, more like reading a fairy tale, where the suspense comes from hoping against hope that the truth will out. 
 Then there's the Ripper, whose real-life murder spree is incorporated into the plot and given a supernatural explanation. Alexi and his friends must find the seventh member and stop the Ripper before things get even worse. 
 I had a lot of fun reading The Strangely Beautiful Tale of Miss Percy Parker. Leanna Renee Hieber creates a sense of enchantment from the very beginning, and the novel caught me up in its spell during a week when my real life went completely haywire. It has the feel of a fairy tale, which is not an easy mood to sustain in a full-length novel. The Strangely Beautiful Tale is elegantly written and chock full of interesting characters and mythic themes. I especially loved watching the development of Percy from a meek mouse to a woman who knows what she's willing to fight for. 
 I was briefly bothered by Percy's mathematical bumbling, since I've spent much of my life bristling at "girls can't do math" stereotypes, but when I thought about it a little more, Percy's lack of math skills makes perfect sense for her times. Because of those same stereotypes, a woman in the Victorian era would not have received much math education before enrolling at an unconventional school like Athens. 
 The plot of The Strangely Beautiful Tale of Miss Percy Parker is satisfactorily wrapped up at book's end, but there's plenty of room for future world-saving. Hieber has planned a series of four books. I'm definitely looking forward to them! 
 Recommended for fans of historical fantasies like Marie Brennan's Onyx Court series and romantic fantasies like Maria Snyder's Study series.

This book makes me sad that I can't read French. The most amazing thing about Hedgehog is the language, the prose is so fun and fanciful. This makes me sad because the original words were in French and that is not even what I got to read - maybe in French it was even better! Full credit to the translator Alison Anderson (Translator) for what I assume was an excellent job. 
 Otherwise, this book makes me happy! It seems strange to describe a novel about a suicidal little girl and a lonely widow as happy, but somehow reading this story was so uplifting. 
 Brief synopsis: Renee is a lady living alone working as a concierge for wealthy Parisiens. Paloma, age 12, is one of these wealthy Parisiens. Although they hardly know each other, they share the same secret - they are both far more intelligent than they seem. They deliberately hide their brilliance from those around them, but they are both unhappy. 
 I could understand that some people wouldn't enjoy this book. If you hate books without a plot, you probably won't love this. But the language and characterisation really got me. Although maybe I just liked this book because of all the cats!

Unsteady is actually my first Melissa Collins read, and only my second M/M read! I happened to really enjoy it! 
 Micah is a veteran who suffers from PTSD. On top of that he is living a lie. A HUGE lie. He has so many feelings that he has buried down deep and on top of the PTSD he's barely treading water. 
 Jude is someone who was Micah's best friend for awhile during their last years of high school. He has been taking care of his alcoholic father for a very long time, and spent the rest of it hiding who he really is. When Micah comes back into his life, both of those things change. 
 Micah and Jude coming back together is sad and beautiful at the same time. What they had in the past was so much more than friendship, but Micah isn't sure things will still be the same when he leaves the life he's torn apart about and goes back to his one time hometown to see Jude. 
 Both of these men are hiding things. When those things come to light so much angsty stuff happens. This story is extremely well written, and it was a page turner for sure. At some points I got aggravated with the characters, but I think that was the point. They were both flawed, and they were both likable. They felt real, and I really enjoy that in an angsty read like this one. 
 The intimate scenes were emotional, but didn't get me hot and bothered. This was more about the couples connection and I think Collins showed that well! 
 All in all this was an enjoyable read. If you enjoy angsty M/M romance, I would highly recommend this one!
Definitely can't wait to read the rest of the series!

"One dinner. One night. No repeats." 
 Aubrey aka Alyssa is a Junior in college with a double major in pre-law and ballet. Her dream is to be a dancer, that's her true passion, not the law. But her parents want her to be lawyers like them, and the only way they'll pay for her tuition is if she pursues the career that they think is best. Needing help with her classes she joins a lawyer-chat site and meets "Thoreau." 
 Andrew aka 'Thoreau' is a high profile lawyer that's used to getting his way. He wants no commitment to a woman, only one night to get his fill of pussy and then to never see her again. Then he meets Alyssa on and helps her on a few of her cases, becoming more and more interested in her. That is until he meets her in person and realizes she's a liar just like everyone else. She's not Alyssa, a fellow lawyer, she's Aubrey, law student and ten years younger than him. 
 I just have to say, Andrew was a complete and utter asshole...and I loved every second of him! He never apologized for his personality, and for me that's what made me fall for his character. Would I like him in real life? Not a shot in hell. But in the fictional world, I loved how much of a bastard he was. I especially liked that it never changed, this wasn't one of those cliffhanger books where the characters seem to change out of no where. Andrew started as an asshole and ended as one, there was none of that "her magical vagina made me a better person" bullshit that I don't really like. 
 "Andrew was the epitome of what it meant to be an asshole." 
 Aubrey was kind of hot and cold throughout the story and there were times that I liked her character, but there were also moments when I didn't. She had some fight in her, and the times she stood up to Andrew and showed her backbone, I really liked. I thought it was great that she wasn't someone that he could push around all the time. But then also she had her moments when she cam off as being a little weak, and I didn't like her then. 
 The books were off the charts sexy, and I couldn't get enough of Andrew's filthy mouth. From book one we got these crazy things that he would say, and they lit my panties on fire. I honestly can't even say that they were the hottest things I've ever heard, but the way they were written and coming from such an intense character, that's what made them so sexy. 
 My rating for the third book went down a little because there was so much angst and drama, which started to annoy me a little bit since I'm not a huge fan of a lot of angst. But that was my only issue with this series, and the rest was highly enjoyable. 
 Overall, this is a great series that I'm glad I finally found out about and read. Each book goes together very well and the story flows smoothly through each volume, which I liked. If you enjoy reading an angst filled story about a dirty talking lawyer, and his younger intern, this is the book for you!

It's a sad fact that so many favorite books from our childhood fail the test of time. That's why I'm delighted this book was every bit as good, if not better, than I remembered. Much has changed in the 15 years since I first read Assassin's Apprentice, but it seems my taste for well written fantasy books filled with intrigue and believable characters is not one of them. The pace is a little slow but that does not make the story or the characters any less engaging. 
 This book was told from the point of view of FitzChivalry Farseer, royal bastard and apprentice assassin. Fitz was a surprisingly easy character to like and not the typical type of assassin one might expect. I enjoyed the plots and intrigue that was abundant in the Farseer court. I was impressed by how Fitz slowly developed as a character as he grew older. I also enjoyed his relationships with the many interesting and well drawn secondary characters. Especially Chade and the Fool. 
 Rating 4.5 stars. Only the lack of any heart stopping moments of real excitement held me back from giving this the full 5 stars. 
 Audio Note: Paul Boehmer gave a good performance. I'd have preferred a different voice for the Fool, but that's a minor quibble.

This story is one of the best things I've read this year. And it was difficult to find - so definitely worth the effort. 
 The story is set in an old amusement park which is about to be reopened. It also acts as a prison for 5 demons from hell. The Guardia are demon hunters who are jailors for these demons. 
 This story was like discovering a new planet because the blurb doesn't prepare you for the Wild Ride. (The title is apt. Major frappe points) 
 The Guardia is going through some changes but the new recruits dont have the time to be excited, bothered, invested or scared. They have their own dreams and baggages weighing them down, isolating them. The demons are not their concern and they won't think twice before walking away. 
 Mab is an art restorer with a detatched existence. Ethan is a former Green Beret with a bullet in his heart. Both of them have roots here but this is not where they would choose to be. 
 But what happens when the prison gives you hope, perspective, possibility? 
 The picture I've painted sounds depressing but these are just the lead characters and this book handles heavy issues with a lot of humor and an excellent plot. Even the leads don't feel bad about their lives but work with odd coping mechanisms. 
 Add some escaped demons for adventure, action and an adrenaline rush - you still can't imagine how incredible this was. 
 I'm not telling you the plot points, twists or best scenes because you deserve to experience this on your own. 
 All I can say is this book made me introspect, dig deep, feel a little blue, very happy and oddly inspired. 
 Give this a try when you're looking for something different ;)

Ready Player One is straight up a tribute to all things 80s. If there were one book that a gamer should read it would have to be this one! Not only would gamers love it but any child of the 80s because there are so many movies, games and music references strung throughout the entire book that it was like one big ride of nostalgia for me. I remember fondly every science fiction and fantasy movie or game I played as a child and to have them mentioned in the book and frankly pretty much turned into a guide of all things awesome just blew my mind away. 
 If you couldn't guess already I thought Ready Player One was fantastic! Beyond fantastic really because not only is this a great book for teens (the main characters being teenagers) but this is an excellent book for adults - especially those adults like me that are still big kids at heart. That's right I'm looking at you folks who still like to RPG, Game, Cosplay and do anything at all SFF related. This book was written for us! It didn't just speak to me as a fan and lover of all things SFF this spoke to my soul. Am I getting sappy there? - Yes, I can't help it, I'm a big geek and I love what I love. Each one of those teens I could see reflected back at me anytime I talk to one of my genre loving friends. 
 I know this might have been hyped up all over the place, even while reading it, my friends who had already read it were all 'Oh I loved that," "Oh I couldn't put it down"...yadda yadda yadda. So it was really hyped up and I admit I was very hesitant to read it because I have been let down in the past by hyped up books and I was scared to be let down again. So I let it flounder on my shelf for 2 years! Don't let that be you LOL because man, this is already one I'll be reading again asap. I'll give you a moment to go click the buy button...done? Ok good. 
 So maybe you don't want to listen to the hype? Good don't! Don't listen to the hype, don't anticipate anything - just go along for the ride and enjoy. Approach and handle with caution because your head might explode in radtastic proportions...ok there I go hyping it up again. 
 All I have to say is this is more than just a coming of age story. While I think Ready Player One is reaching out to a specific generation, I also think it really could be for everyone. It is simply that entertaining. The comedy, the action, the pain, and pangs of love, there is so much to enjoy. I don't even want to go into the contents of the book one iota because the description tells you everything you need to know to reel you in - and I guarantee within the first chapter Ernest Cline will have you hook, line and sinker. You don't stand a chance.

So this was a weird one for me. 
 I went into this book with the mind set of getting through it so I could watch the TV show. (which btw im watching and its SO much better) So you could suggest that I was setting myself up for failure. Before reading this I heard so many bad reviews and I kinda agreed with them without even reading the book.

 I like the whole message this sends of "be careful of your actions as you dont know what effect that could have on someones life" and how we dont know what crap people are going through. I got that. I totally understand and appreciate that. But where is the mentioning of mental health? Its such an important topic and Hannah obviously wasnt mentally well and that wasnt noticed? Or even discussed after her death? 
 Like many other readers, I also didnt agree with how she handled it. Im going to sound totally insensitive, but Hannah seemed so whiny and arrogant to me. I know this wasnt how she was meant to be portrayed by the author but she just was. I hate how she handed out those tapes in an act of revenge? Two wrongs dont make a right. All throughout the book Clay was saying how unfair it was and I have to agree, the tapes were unfair. She essentially blackmailed 13 people into listening to her suicide note, which could be harming to them- the same way they were to her. I dont believe in taking people down with you. Hannah was being to hypocritical.

As there was so much switching between Hannah's recording and Clay's inner monologue, there wasn't much time for elaborate descriptions, the writing was just plain. However it did pick up and my favourite part of the novel was when Clay heard his tape, I really liked that chapter as we got to see more of his and Hannah's relationship.

Vinge has a vision of a plausible, interesting future, filled with wearable technology that allows users to transcend geographic boundaries and collaborate for good and evil. In fact, the detail Vinge invested in his world made it worth exploring regardless of the underlying story. And, one of the best things Vinge did as an author was remain neutral about the technology in the world. You could see the good and the bad, but he never told the reader what to think about it. 
 Beyond Vinge's world was an interesting plot that started with a bang, rolled along for a while with seeming little connection to the overarching plot, and then brought everything together beautifully in a fantastic climax. The ending left quite a few loose ends, but that only made me want a sequel more. And even if a sequel is never made, this book stands on its own as a great piece of literature.

I believe this is probably the third or fourth time I've read this book from cover to cover. I've read bits of it in addition since I bought the paperback sometime in 04/05. I recommended it to a friend of mine a few years ago and she couldn't get past the really long, almost run-on sentences. They'd never bothered me, but this time I did notice them. 
 I don't usually like stories that don't stick to the point and go off in other directions like major tangents throughout a narrative. But I liked Sunshine's tangents because they were about her world, her baking, and just her. She can come off bitchy and whiney and I'm pretty sure she and I wouldn't be friends, but I like reading her thoughts. 
 Sometimes a good book doesn't have to 'get to the point' all the time. Sometimes it can meander along, giving the reader insight and a laugh and some new ideas about what exists in the supernatural world. These characters do not act like typical vampires and humans, or partbloods. The world is McKinley's own and I love being there. It's so open-ended that I'm desperate to have a sequel, but as Ms. McKinley said in an email she replied to (I was all flustered), she wouldn't write it unless the story (characters and whatnot) came back. It was more eloquent than that (what she said), but I like that she wouldn't write a sequel just to write because it's probably not be true to the world and characters. 
 So if you can get over the lengthy sentences and lack of chapters (it's divided into four parts), it's fabulous. 
 This is also one of the only books that had me sold before I flipped to the second page. That could just be my affinity (a sunshine word) for bakery goods.

STATION ELEVEN, BY EMILY ST. JOHN MANDEL 
 Another one from the Goodreads "best science fiction of 2014" list. Coincidentally (or maybe not?), another miss. I'm now determined to stop taking recommendations from sites' lists. 
 Synopsis: An aging actor dies. In the next day, a pandemic spreads and kills most of the population of the world. Many years later, a group of artists, known as the Travelling Symphony, travels around the remains of civilization performing Shakespeare for the survivors. 
 Overall enjoyment: One of my biggest peeves when it comes to books about diseases, and something that happened in this book, is when the author tries to make the disease seem more scary by making it move too fast, so it has a very short incubation period. In this case, she specifically stated that the Georgia Flu had an incubation period of only three to four hours. A disease with an incubation period that short DOESN'T SPREAD. It could take over a city, it might take over a country (if they are absurdly over-populated, with the population insanely packed into a single place, and criminally negligent with emergency measures), but it will never take over the world. On top of that, the book was SO BORING. I kept forcing myself to go back to it, and it still took me a while to read because I kept falling asleep every time I tried. I don't recommend it. 
 Plot: There isn't one. In the first half of the book, nothing happens. Then, right in the middle of it a few things happen, which are promptly abandoned for more nothings to happen. Then, near the end, there is a huge anti-climax, when the things that happened in the middle of the book are resolved Deus-ex-machina style and the dramatic moment is ruined by being stretched out way longer than acceptable. After that, about 50 more pages of nothing happening, and the end. 
 Characters: I couldn't find it in myself to care about any of them. They're all haphazard, their personalities and motivations seem unclear. But that may be because they have no motivation, since they do nothing. 
 World/setting: The dystopia she describes takes some suspension of belief. For some reason, for instance, none of the characters described in the book have the brilliant notion to read a book and try to find out how they could improve their lives by fixing some of the luxuries that existed before the collapse; 20 years after the pandemic and everyone is still living off foraging. Plus, she keeps saying that the world is a lot more dangerous, and that it changes people, but all of her characters are suicidally reluctant to engage in violence. 
 Writing style: So over-dramatic. In the chapters after the pandemic, in every five sentences, one will be about how "things were before". In the chapters before the pandemic, the same thing will happen, but about how little time this lifestyle will last. "The last orange", "five days before the collapse", "his last breakfast", "the last flight". She repeats herself and drags things out so much it seems she's testing the reader's patience. I found myself skimming through the words, trying to get to the end. 
 Representation: There is one gay man. I can't remember if there are any POC in it, I don't think there were, but maybe that was one of the things I skimmed over. 
 Political correctness: Not too bad. Could be better, of course, but then, so many things in this book could have been better. 
 I should probably add that I'm not sure if this book was really as boring as it seemed to me, or if I'm so stressed out right now that I've become too intolerant. I really don't think that is the problem here, I tried really hard to get some enjoyment out of this book. There just wasn't any. 
 Up next: Doc, by Mary Doria Russell

 With each release in the Black Dagger Brotherhood series, one thing can be certain. Fans will get passionate and protective over their favorite characters - and will either love or hate the direction Ward is taking them. The Chosen is a perfect example as readers get vocal expressing their opinion. One thing I know - any book/series that can evoke that kind of emotion is going to be one h*ll of a ride and on my "read right now" list. There was never any question in my mind as to whether or not I would read it . . . seriously? I'm a fan who waited on pins and needles for this release just as I'm now awaiting the next one! I avoided all reviews and comments until I finished it and highly recommend (if it's even possible now) that you do the same. There are no spoilers in my review. 
 Like every other book in the series, The Chosen is rich in details and multiple plotlines. Unlike some readers, I love it! Talk about more bang for your buck. I have no problem following the storyline as it shifts between characters, scenes, and plots. While I freely admit that Layla is on the low end of my fav heroine scale, I was intrigued to see where The Warden would take her and Xcor and what kind of h*ll they'd walk through to get there. Talk about an explosion that rocked the BDB world - when the truth comes out about their relationship, the consequences and repercussions are earthshattering. The reaction of some characters cost them everything. 
 Relationship issues, shocking revelations, nonstop action - all are prevalent in The Chosen. So many characters face life-altering decisions and situations. It seems some are at a crossroad in their life - a bend in the road. Which way will they go? You'll get a lot of answers by the end of the book, but not all. I'm okay with that...it's part of what keeps me reading on. I have to say that given past history and ill feelings, I was a little surprised at the things Ward tied up and delivered with a neat little hea bow near the end. Some of it didn't ring true for me because it was such an about face for these characters who both hate and love with a passion. It's the reason I gave this book 4 stars instead of 5. Having said that, The Chosen evoked all the same emotions in me as previous books. Intense, on the edge of my seat suspense, passion, heartbreak, and nail-biting worry over who might not survive. Another Page Burning Must Read by J.R. Ward! More Please!

 I am sorry Night Circus, I love you with all my heart and will always cherish you but this is my favorite standalone book of all time 
 I mean, seriously. It talks about love, and friendship, and self discovery, and family, and strength, and bravery to face every inner demon we all have, and summer, and winter, and just everything I could wish for. It is the story of a boy named Ari Mendoza, a person who wouldn't admit his love to himself, and another boy named Dante Quintana, a person who had come to terms with who he was and would always stand for it, even if people hurt him. 
 It was the story of these two guys who fell in love, a love so beautiful and strong, so inspiring, like a poem. It was a love so true, so raw and full of honesty, so full of intimacy and discovery of both each other and themselves. 
 The plot was flowing like the way rain rolls down the windows. It was heartwarming and heartbreaking, addictive and compelling and utterly enchanting. I still find myself in utter shock that my favorite standalone of all time is a contemporary novel. The writing was poetic and wonderful and I found myself longing to jump back in this book seconds after I left it to do other things. It has so many inspirational quotes and explored so many issues that it opened my mind and heart to the world in ways I find myself unable to explain. Some of my favorite quotes were: 
 I got to thinking that poems were like people. Some people you got right off the bat. Some people you just didn't get--and never would get. 
 Another secret of the universe: Sometimes pain was like a storm that came out of nowhere. The clearest summer could end in a downpour. Could end in lightning and thunder. 
 To be careful with people and with words was a rare and beautiful thing. 
 And it seemed to me that Dante's face was a map of the world. A world without any darkness. 
 Wow, a world without darkness. How beautiful was that? 
 The characters were also so perfect. The book treated them all with such kindness and fairness, with such love and care. I just loved every single one of them and wanted them all to be happy. I wanted Ari to realize his love for Dante, Dante himself to be happy and proud of who he is, Dante's parents to have a healthy, wonderful baby that would live to be Dante's sibling, Ari's parents to heal, in their own way each one and I could honestly go on and on with how deeply I fell in love with all these characters and how much I wished I could give them all a world without darkness. 
 In general, I strongly believe this book brought so much light into my life and even when I finished, I still had the weird urge to reread it right then and there. I really, really needed something to remind me that we shall never be afraid of who we are and, no matter what, we shall never turn down the people we know are important for us and will always bring brightness to our life 
 I recommend this to every single person out there, whether you want to read a nice LGBTQIAP tale, or a story about finding yourself, or something poetic, or just something that will put you into thinking and will keep your heart warm and your mind content till the rest of your life 
 Until our next review, keep being strong, and bold and brave. 
 And explore, until you figure out all the secrets of the universe 
 ~Mary

What a surprisingly amazing book. What is it about the truly tortured hero that makes me melt? Lazarus Caire has had a horrible life. Better to say, I suppose, a horrible childhood that he allowed to turn into a horrible life. His emotions have shut down and he is now known throughout London for his debauched preferences in bed. He likes his women helpless. Temperance Dews is a widow in dire need of...something. She thinks she needs money to help keep her family's charity orphanage afloat. Little does she realize that her life is one big blank spot. She's lived this half life for so long that she, like Caire, doesn't even realize that she's shut everyone out. 
 This is a dark, story that turns magical. These two people don't seem to care that they have let their lives turn meaningless, until they see in each other what they don't want to admit about themselves. This is also a lot more erotic than the normal historical romance, so for those who feel uncomfortable with a little naughty talk and a slight bit of eroticism, this may not be for you. But for those of you that can take it, it's actually done very tastefully, I thought, and added a lot to the story. The passion that Caire and Temperance share with each other is what leads them to open up emotionally to each other. And by the end of the book, I felt as if they had connected in a way that many couples in books can't. They literally fulfill a need in each other, and the result is an extremely moving, poignant love story. 
 One of my favorite parts of the book, when Temperance finally talks to Caire a little about her dead husband. 
 "She inhaled. "He was a good man - a wonderful man - and I didn't deserve him." 
 Lord Caire closed his eyes and for a moment seemed to have fallen asleep. then he murmured, "I've never been married, but I think it would be quite awful to have to deserve one's spouse." 
 What a great line from a man who feels no emotion! Marriage is a constant give and take. There is no score, or there shouldn't be. But what a perfect way to think of it. I'll remember that forever, I think. And what a gem to find in such an unexpected place! Isn't if funny how certain words can mean so much to you at a certain point of life? 
 Beautifully broken people, and a beautiful story of how they came to accept themselves and each other.

Full of drama... liked you're reading a telenovela where the man is involved with another woman who was previously married to this another character that everyone hated and in the end, their lives get tangled and untangled and tangled again. Ugh. 
 Fallen Crest High is about Sam, who discovered that her bestfriend had been sleeping with her boyfriend behind her back. Then her mother dropped the bomb about her parents' divorce and had to move in to her stepbrother's house, The Kade Mansion. Heart-broken and betrayed, Sam soon found solace and protection from two unlikely allies, the Kade brothers - Logan & Mason. These two guys are party animals, all the ladies in Fall Crest want them, all the men want to be like them. But only Sam seem to get the best of both worlds. 
 If there's one thing I really liked about the Kade Brothers, it is that these are the guys that you love to hate and you hate to love. Storywise though, it got me brain-dead. Samantha just standing there while her two new-found "brothers-friends" slugged some beer down her mom's throat to make her pay was just ridiculous. Ugh. The parking lot scene? Hot and heavy and a bit awkward for me. Hmm. 
 So do I like this or not? You guess..

I truly think this book deserves a shelf all of its own, called "DAFUQ DID I JUST READ". 
 I mean, what's with that absurd story? The guy is absolutely atrocious, and the girl goes from "so frightened I could actually die" to "omg I wanna rip his pants off" in what seems like miliseconds (it take a few hours, actually. But you get my point.) 
 The guy knows he frightens her to death, BUT HE STILL DOES ALL KINDS OF AWFUL THINGS TO HER. With no explanations. He manhandles her, abducts her, then decides he'll keep her "because he doesn't feel pain when he's with her"... And, of course, he fails to tell her that. Or anything, for that matter. 
 And since she accepts that and finds it (and him) attractive and oh so manly and hot, she's obviously NOT the kind of heroine I want to cheer on. She's actually the kind I want to kill painfully for being TSTL. 
 Enough said.

3 stars for plot (what? All romance plots are derivative as hell!), -2 stars for making me actually think about my life, +1 star for being written by Elle Kennedy, +1 star for making Allie so feisty and badass, and +1 star because Dean. Just Dean.
Too long, terribly heartbreaking but loved it nonetheless.
No Sam in this novella (sigh), but Celaena continues to amaze me as a character.

When I read RUIN, I knew that Gabe would steal my heart, so TOXIC was not going to be left for months on time, hell no. It was going to be read the second I finished RUIN. I definitely gobbled this book down and it caused me numerous tears, heartache, different theories (one which I actually got right!) but I also got my laughs, my smiles, the banter and the amazing friendship from Kiersten, Weston, Gabe and Lisa too. God I love these characters. 
 Toxic is much more deeper (if it can be because Ruin ruined me) than Ruin. From the synopsis, we know that Gabe is hiding his identity, so in a way we know that probably isn't his name. So what is? What is he hiding? Throughout the book, until it is revealed, you are sat trying to work out who Gabe is, what his secret is, why he is hiding. I unlocked one name, one secret and when that was revealed, it still came as a surprise because I hardly ever guess right. 
 Gabe, as we know, is the happy guy. The guy who sleeps around because he doesn't drink anymore. The guy who can banter like hell, can be a sarcastic idiot but the guy who is protective of his friends, who will do anything to make sure they are okay, and would die for them - much like he told Wes in Ruin, but underneath he is broken, and depressed and feeling guilty for his past. 
 It's hard not fall for Gabe (maybe more than Wes) because you feel for him, you go through the motions with him and dear god, his life is just one torment after the other. You have Gabe with the secret, Gabe with different identities, Gabe with his friends and Gabe with Saylor. But who is he truly? 
 You watch conflictions, you watch love and hurt and pain and it all rolls into one massive fuckball when the identity comes to life. You get frustrated with him but in the back of you mind you know why he is doing it and you understand it so much throughout the book. But despite the lies and secrets, Gabe is completely loyal to his friends and your heart will break for him but then be put back together in the form of Saylor and the gang. 
 Enter Saylor. She comes flying, literally, into Gabe's life when his past is lying on his shoulders, when his past is moments away from unravelling. They don't get off to the best of starts, but they seem to be integrating into each others lives more and its hard to keep their feelings from each other. I definitely thought Saylor was going to be weak, that she wouldn't stand up to Gabe and his mean words in the beginning but I was wrong. She did and I love that about a heroine who doesnt shy away from biting back. 
 The more time Gabe and Saylor spend together, the more feelings are transpiring. They connect firstly through music and that is the one constant between them. The one constant that could express what they were both feeling, especially Gabe with his guilt and sorrow. Saylor was strong, she was there for Gabe when shit went down and she was completely selfless - which I admired from her. Not many people could do what she did, not many people would stay but she did and she helped him with everything, with the pain and the guilt, especially through the goodbyes. 
 She taught him to love again, to be okay with being your true self after so many years and to accept yourself for who you are. She really is inspirational. 
 Toxic is raw, its tear worthy, its heartbreaking but it also comes with pages full of love. Love for Gabe, love for Saylor, love for the gang and the little secret hiding. Rachel draws you completely in with her writing, you feel everything, you connect on a personal level and you just have to keep turning pages; turning pages to find out more about Gabe, about his secrets. Such a beautiful and emotional book and you all should get reading this series ASAP. 
 Delve into the lives of such amazing characters and get your heart broken and then fixed up once again. Rachel, I cannot wait to meet you at the Edinburgh signing. Be aware of The Book Lovers ;)

This is a difficult book to rate. I absolutely cannot give it five or even four stars, but it doesn't suck quite so terribly as to receive one or two stars. I suppose three is a solid middle ground. 
 Before reading this book, I was expecting something so much more than what I got when I finished it. When I purchased the book, the clerk told me that people had to be wait-listed to receive this book because it was flying off the shelves. I also heard that women were reading this book and feeling completely new and invigorated. I was positively ecstatic to read this book. 
 Upon completing it, I was left utterly disappointed. I'm not sure exactly what I was expecting from this read, but it's certainly not what I got. I suppose if you're a middle-aged housewife or an angsty teenager, this book may be worthy of five stars. The smutty sex scenes are just that--smutty. There is hardly any character development and there is barely a relationship development. Everything that you hope for over the course of the story just hangs there and never comes to any fruition. 
 While in some off-handed way, I can see why women are coming away from this book feeling invigorated. With the--can I even say "triumphant?"--Ana walking away from the "love of her life" after being beaten (even if it was for sexual purposes), I can understand how some women can relate to this personally.  It still did nothing for me and I was left feeling absolutely nothing but disappointed when I finished. 
 For such a lengthy book I feel like nothing happened at all. The only thing I enjoyed were the quirky e-mails the characters often exchanged. Aside from that, I'd say this book is not worth reading at all. Will I be following up this cliff-hanger ending by reading the next two books in the trilogy? Absolutely not.

A little girl goes off the trail to go the bathroom in privacy and ends up in a disorienting odyssey trying to find her way back to the path--and civilization. To keep her spirits, she listens to Boston Red Sox games, particularly her favorite closer, Tom Gordon on her Walkman. At least as long as her batteries stay alive. 
 Mr. King loves the Red Sox almost as much as he loves telling spooky stories, there's simply no missing that passion in this tale. What hurts this one, like some of King's other efforts is too much crap that isn't that interesting. Cut this book in half, maybe by two-thirds and it would probably have made a heckuva tight short story. As a novel, it feels like my stomach after too much milk. I had to keep reading to find out what happens to the girl, but that's King's gift rather than this being an awesome story. The ending didn't disappoint me, but it did feel a bit like King was out of gas and had to do something to finish the story. Then, like Rod Serling, he steps in at the ending and brilliantly bookends the tale. 
 From a chapter structure standpoint, and definitely gimmicky, it was neat how he made it like a baseball game (pregame, first inning, bottom of ninth-save situation, postgame). At the end of Mr. King's career, I doubt this book-which-should-have-been-a-great-short-story will fare very well. Not recommended except for diehard fans who want to read everything King has written.
