I first heard about this book because of the cover controversy--basically the publisher marketed this book with a white girl on the cover when the main character is a biracial girl. And while I was outraged on behalf of the author of a book I hadn't read, I had to wonder if being biracial was made clear in the book or had any importance. 
 I have to say, Justine Larbalestier's Liar had a really interesting voice for a narrator. There was only a background plot for a while (meaning, little to no action for about 70% of the book) and was heavy on the exposition and talking about the past. That, combined with the paranormal stuff, would normally make me rage. Add to that a white woman writing about a minority character, and I would throw my hands up and say, "I can't..." 
 However, Micah's character is surprisingly engaging, and, if you'll excuse the description, refreshingly honest in her assessments of people. While I did feel it was weird that she'd say in the beginning of the book that Zack was only a so-so boyfriend and then be devastated by his death, as the novel progresses, you get a feeling as to why. Zack seems an artificial way to rebel, and yet he has a sweet side, or at least a side that kind of likes her for her wildness, which is something her parents cannot appreciate. 
 For all the hullabaloo over race and the book, I'm glad the author made it somewhat realistic: there are interesting cross-sections of race and class. Sarah and Teyshawn represent two facets of black culture: Sarah is the rich person and Teyshawn, like Micah, is poor. Zack is a white Hispanic (because Hispanic refers to language and not race; even Latino, while more often used for race, can actually refer to any Latin American of any color). There is an Indian woman who teaches English, and a Japanese woman who teaches biology. Finally, NYC is written as diversely as it actually is! 
 An interesting aspect of the book is that not only does it take on racial stereotypes, but that it subverts the commonly seen paranormal trope of late where the male is the one with weird powers. Here, it's the women (mostly) who change, and only rarely do the men get affected. I'm tired of all the Edward Cullens and Sam Roths out there getting to be the only ones with cool powers. 
 One critique I have is one that I have with nearly every book that attempts to use biology/biological explanations for paranormal beings. As an actual scientist, these explanations always fall short and are usually unnecessary. If there is a science included in books, it's always biology...because it's the "easy" hard science, SMH. And here too the explanation is totally unnecessary. While I liked the part about hormones triggering Micah's change, I didn't like all the extra biology information, especially about horizontal gene transfer, because the way Larbalestier wrote about it gives a very inaccurate picture. She basically make it seem like HGT isn't seen in multicellular organisms (there is documented evidence that it occurs in plants, at the very least), and that the hypothesis is that it can occur by organisms being near each other or mating. HGT pretty much only occurs in large organisms if a virus or bacterium breaks off some DNA and moves it to the other organism or if the bacterium itself is the DNA that is transferred. The latter case is almost always what happens, meaning it would be almost impossible for a bacterium to seek a particular DNA segment, break it off perfectly, and then move it to another organism without being stopped by the immune system. Again, explanation was totally not necessary; the reader could have made up her own mind about why werewolves actually exist. 
 Another criticism I have is that because we hear so much background, when there's action, there's really not enough time to go through it all. The last third of the book seemed really rushed.

Later in the book, we end up at a national swimming competition, and again, it just didn't feel very authentic. I didn't feel like that author had much knowledge about competitive swimming, and it showed.

The main female characters is a genius mad scientist, but other than being in her shed making high tech gadgets a few times, she didn't seem very smart, or very scientific. The whole novel felt more like a first draft, than an ARC. The stilted, dialogue and lack of depth kept it from being the deconstruction of the genre I was hoping for. I just can't see many people being satisfied with this book.

It's 1922 and Sarah Piper is making ends meet by temping. Her jobs usually involve boring secretarial work, but not the latest job she's offered by her temp agency. Her employer would be Alistair Gellis, a wealthy young war veteran, and what Alistair wants from Sarah isn't secretarial work. Far from it; Alistair is a ghost hunter, and his latest case involves a haunting by a man-hating ghost. He hopes Sarah will be able to do the direct contacting of the ghost, which is the bit that won't work quite as well for him. 
 Sarah is reluctant initially, but she accepts and sets off with him to the small village where the ghost resides. There they are joined by Matthew Ryder, Alistair's usual assistant and also a war veteran. Sarah doesn't quite believe in ghosts, but is willing to go along with the man who's paying her salary. However, before too long, there are no doubts left in her mind. 
 The ghost is real. She's the ghost of Maddy Clare, a young maid who hanged herself in a barn and is now haunting it, terrifying anyone who comes close. Alistair's plan works, and Sarah is able to communicate with her, after a fashion. Maddy is very angry and very powerful. She wants revenge for whatever it was that drove her to suicide, and she demands Sarah help. 
 This one was a bit of a mixed bag for me. There were certain things that I thought worked wonderfully. First and foremost, the haunting itself is really well done. The ghost of Maddy Clare really is quite scary, and the author succeeds in creating an extremely creepy atmosphere. I also liked Sarah very much. She is a woman who really does value her independence, even if it means that she has to scrimp and save. She's sensible and knows her own mind, and this manifests in a low-key way. Finally, I liked the setting, even if it was a bit shallow, more atmosphere than exploration of the world in the 20s (to be honest, this story could have been set in quite a few other time periods with a tiny number of adjustments). 
 There are several negatives, though. Much as I enjoyed the ghost story, I found myself very uncomfortable with the priorities of our ghost-hunters. The focus seemed to be a lot more on the threat from Maddy, and how to make the scary ghost go away, and not so much on what happened to her and making sure the culprits be made to pay for it. Those Maddy wanted revenge against were dangerous people; who's to say they wouldn't do the same thing to someone else? That doesn't seem to worry them particularly. 
 I was just as uncomfortable with the romance. It felt tacked on and unnecessary, with Sarah's love interest being paper-thin as a character. I was also quite disturbed by the rapey way in which it starts, especially considering what we're discovering at the same time about what happened to Maddy. It would have been a better book with that element pruned out. 
 MY GRADE: A C+.

This was really good. There were lots of things I liked about it, but also some things that kept me from rating it higher. 
 I really liked the writing, it was nicely descriptive, occasionally rather witty, and seemed to fit the setting really well. I'm not very knowledgeable about this time period, but the book seemed realistic to me. I liked Kit and Griffin a great deal, as well as a lot of the side characters. I really didn't want to put the book down while reading. This is definitely the best M/M pirate book I've read so far. 
 There were some things that annoyed me though. Occasionally things were mentioned but then never fully explained to the reader, which left me really confused at times. For example,  when the Africa rescues Runyon, his story of how he ended up in need of rescue is summarized as "He answered Kit's questions fully and succinctly." But we never get to know what Kit's questions were or what Runyon's answers were, so I was really confused how Runyon had gone from being a "top man on the Miranda" to being on the ship sunk by pirates. I was also really confused which captain they were talking about - the Miranda's captain, the pirate captain, or the sunken ship's captain . Maybe if my knowledge of the nautical terms of the time was better I would have been less confused? I read those pages at least 5 times before eventually giving up and moving on. There were also times when Kit, as narrator, would withhold information from the reader for reasons that were not apparent to me, so I would be really confused during whatever was happening and only finally understand pages later when it was explained retroactively, like for example  the plans to take the Spanish ship that Kit was part of . That may have been done for a bit of narrative tension but instead it mostly just left me confused. There was a big reveal at the end that wasn't explained either, which left me a bit frustrated. I kind of feel like I need to reread the entire book just to see if all of these things make more sense now that I've gotten to the end. Also, we never got the backstory of how Griffin went from Major to pirate , which I really really wanted to know. 
 Despite my confusion I had a lot of fun reading this book, and I'd like to come back and reread it, although who knows when I'll have time for that. I'd definitely recommend it to anyone interested in pirates during this time period who doesn't mind minimal romance and lots of nautical terms.

They were both strong, if damaged, characters and they both needed someone to lean on. I loved how that brought them together. Of course, things weren't perfect. I was worried about how the secrets and lies would impact them, and while I'm not going to get down into the weeds of the plot, I'll just say that it was handled realistically. (That doesn't mean it didn't hurt.) 
 While The Debt is a standalone, I have to say I was selfishly glad to see some of my favorite couples from Karina's other novels show up at various points. It's always great to catch up with beloved characters long after their books have ended. I'm not sure if Karina plans to write books for any of the other characters we've met in this world, but I hope she does. I've fallen in love with each and every one of them and would always be happy to have more. 
 This was just a phenomenal book all the way around. Even if you've not read any of Karina's books, pick this one up. It's a beautiful book about healing, second chances and what happens when you find the person who makes you want to have it all.

Lisa Schroeder is one of the writers I find very interesting: she deals with quite difficult themes in an emotional way. She writes her book in free prose from the first person perspective, which basically makes all of her books a stream of consciousness. All the thoughts of her characters in a short time span, in Amber's case, her thoughts during one day. 
 It's the story of Amber and Cade, who spend one day alone on the beach before the big day.. they meet and end up spending the day together. It seems a case of insta-love, so be warned if that's a real turn-off for you. It generally is for me, though I think this is just a case of teenagers liking each other a lot, and seeking an escape for the day. Amber and Cade each have their own story, which in Amber's case is a shocking one. 
 Amber's story is why I have such problems with this book. I'll explain behind the cut, but if you don't want to be spoiled, you know what to do.. Amber has been switched as a baby.. which didn't necessarily have to be a problem, until the other baby-swapped girl (Charlotte) got cancer and the story got out. Charlotte died, now Amber's biological parents want to have custody over her. Why? I understand Charlotte's death was sad, the fact that they couldn't have more kids is heartbreaking, but is that reason enough to take your biological daughter away from everything and everyone she loves, those she calls family? Is it necessary? Is it good for her? I think it's incredibly selfish. Being blood-related isn't the only thing that counts, and hell, it certainly isn't the most important thing. If you have a good relationship with (those you call) your family, being away from them against your will is the worst thing ever. I don't care it's 'only' 6 months, I don't care the new people seemed to be treating her well and Amber seemed to be okay in the end of the book - it doesn't work that way!! It has the possibility to fuck you up mentally. That's what it did for me, when the university forced me to go abroad and I couldn't see my parents for ages. Having to be reminded of that in this book was extremely painful. It's different when you choose to go, though of course you can still get homesick.. but being forced to go away from those you love? If anything, Amber seemed to take all of it too lightly.  
 Though Schroeder's books always give you things to think about, this particular book bothered me more than I enjoyed it. It still had its good points, but the whole theme of Amber's story bothered me too much. I can't say this was my favourite book of Schroeder's so far.

This book ruined my life in the best way. 
 Christina Henry's novel imagines that James Cook wasn't originally a villain. Once, James was a boy named Jamie, and he was Peter Pan's first playmate. His most beloved one. 
 But after years and years and years of living with Peter, Jamie has aged in some ways -- not physically, but mentally. He sees the arbitrary, insane cruelty of Peter Pan -- someone who yearns only for fun, but whose idea of fun includes real bloodshed and death -- and Jamie eventually tires of it. 
 I haven't actually read any of Barrie's original work on Peter Pan, but am familiar with the story as portrayed by Disney and popular culture. Henry's take is so achingly good, because when you get down to it, there is something horrifically vicious in Peter's behavior and world. Jamie -- who wants nothing more than to just love Peter as he once did, and be loved in return -- is all of us, yearning for innocence but unable to stop witnessing the truth. 
 What else can I say without revealing too much? I just loved this book; I read it in about a day and half, literally waving off people to keep reading (although, given that there's a very sweet, tender young child in this story, I did also spend lots of time squishing my toddler). It's gruesome, but not gory; horrifying but not horror. It's just wonderful -- a chilly take on a beloved story (my catnip!) -- and I'm going back to inhale all of Henry's previous books. 
 Initial Thoughts 
 So delicious. I'm already predisposed toward Hook because I'm quite fond of Jason Isaacs, and Henry's take -- how Hook became Hook -- is just delightful. Peter is a complete monster, and I am amazed I didn't see it sooner. Longer review to come.

When it comes to an issue such as mental illness, it is important that the issue is tackled in a way that depicts its seriousness and gravity in today's society. In this book however, it was more of a humourous approach -- which may rub people the wrong way -- but it was still compelling in its own way. 
 Finding Audrey is about a teenage girl, Audrey, who suffers from General and Social Anxiety Disorder. She was diagnosed after an incident that happened at her old school involving a couple of mean girls, and has been living at home ever since. She wears dark sunglasses (she can't stand eye contact), has her own private den, and gets really nervous around outsiders. Then, in comes Linus, her brother's gaming buddy who really brings her out of her comfort zone. 
 The book was written as if Audrey herself was writing in her own private journal. And the thing about that is you never really get to know the details of what actually happened at her old school. As Audrey puts it, it's okay not to share everything. There were also transcripts of the documentary Audrey had to make as an effort to take the first step in connecting with the world again. I have to say, reading about Audrey's family is hilarious. Especially her neurotic mother who makes it her life's mission to stop her brother, Frank, from playing video games. Their family banters were funny and witty and I found myself laughing out loud at times. 
 However, in terms of the impact that the book has made on me as a reader, it was a small one. I do find myself relating to Audrey in certain situations like overthinking (God only knows how I overanalyse situations to the point where it keeps me up all night). But the fact that the presence of a boy (a love interest) was able to bring out the better part of someone who is mentally ill, I believe, has been done many times before. I was more interested in how her family supported her through her tough times.

I knew before I started this book that Something Big happens. I avoid spoilers like the plague and I didn't even read this series when this book came out. But despite that, there was so much chatter that you'd have to live under a rock to have missed the outcry. And even knowing all that, I was still utterly and completely decimated by this book. 
 It all starts out innocently enough. The mayor is putting the screws to Merit and Ethan to put an end to the blood raves in the city. And the same time, Darius, a bigwig from the governing vampire council, comes to town to check out the Chicago vamps. Merit believes Celina has a hand in it all.  In the meantime, Ethan is working to redeem himself for his behavior in the last book. He now accepts how he feels about Merit and is trying desperately to win her back. It's an intricate dance between them and their eventually acquiescence feels inevitable. 
 I'm not going to spoil the details of what happens, in the off chance you are one of the five people in the world who doesn't know how the book ends.  It sets up a juicy, thematically interesting plot, and it looks like all the plot elements are going to come together in a big dramatic climax, but September 11 happens instead. Is that a statement? I can see why a book that didn't have momentum would use 9/11 to shake things up, but why does this one? All those plot elements that don't come to fruition are like the gun in the scene that doesn't go off.

Our narrators are also repetitive and dense, which doesn't make me care about either of them even more. Bart in particular seems very fond of soliloquies (I can't think what else to call them) and just blathers on about the most boring aspects of whatever he's talking about. From the beginning I wanted to smack Ana upside the head and ask her what she could possibly have seen in her ex Max for four years, especially when they keep breaking up, and how she didn't see this coming to the point she's an emotional wreck. "You're a vulnerability," he ground out. "MY vulnerability. I have no vulnerabilities. I spent years shaving' every last one away from me so there was nothin' left. Now I got one, a big one, and I do not give one f*ck as long as she's in Colorado, sitting' on her porch, waiting' for me to get back." 
 KA and her anti-heroes rock! I love the combination. Not only does she give us our dirty-mouthed, alpha-male who is hawt as ... But she has an uncanny ability to make each one vulnerable. Here, Deacon hides a past that has him drowning in self-loathing and guilt. He is passionate and can be incredibly sweet and tender - vulnerable. It is a dichotomy, really. The perfect character, one that isn't singular. Which makes him relatable as well as lovable. The perfect anti-hero. One whose acts make you struggle with your morals to love, but whose character is so endearing you can't help but love. While Deacon may have lacked the traditional attributes of a hero, he certainly made up for those in the way he worshipped and took care of Cassidy. 
 KA doesn't stop with her rockin' anti-heroes, she pairs them with kick ass heroines, as she did with Cassidy. They are bossy, yet submissive, tender, yet strong, smart-alecky yet sweet. 
 Cassidy set out to follow her dreams. Running a set of cabins in the Colorado Mountains was living the life for her, even if it took every penny she had earned and some blood sweat and tears to fix them up the way she wanted, naming them Glacier Lily. Bringing her boyfriend with her, she thinks her fairy tale is about to come true. Only to find his idea of living is far different from hers. While fighting over money, relationship and work of the cabin, they receive a renter. John 'Deacon' Priest. 
 Over the years things change, she dumps her boyfriend, Deacon continues to visit his room #11, and she continues to beautify the cabins. Eventually, one Christmas when they are both without family and his trusty room #11 is booked when he needs respite from work, she offers a guest bedroom. Things change between them that night, a little Christmas kiss would be the slow start of Deacon's healing. 
 "That's why," he stated confusingly and I looked to him again. 
 "What?" 
 "That and your eyes." 
 I didn't say anything, just watched him drive. 
 He said something. "And your Christmas kiss" 
 Oh my God. 
 My Christmas kiss. He remembered my Christmas kiss. 
 "Deacon," I whispered. 
 "And a hundred other things," he stated. 
 He had a lot of healing to do, and thankfully Cassidy had a lot of patience. A very steamy, sexy read, but also a lovely story. 
 Tally: #33 KA books read, verdict: I loved it!

 Okay, before I even begin my review, I will admit I finished Dividing Eden way back in March. Yup, March. Normally after completing my first read through of anything I write a summary of my thoughts or formulate some kind of pre-review before I write my big review. However, after finishing Dividing Eden, and thinking about it, and thinking about it, and well ... thinking about it some more, none of this occurred. 
 Initially, I was on board with the whole novel. Heck, I even posted a status update on Goodreads that I loved it (and I don't use the big "L" word unless I mean it). Truth be told, I did love it and if asked about it in person, I might have raved about it. But, unfortunately the longer I sat on the review, the more I realized why it was taking me so long to put pen to paper and just whip something up. 
 I loved the concept of this fantasy: brother against sister, family drama, death, magic, a curse. Who doesn't love curses, especially the good versus evil ones? It had all the aspects needed to successfully create a wonderful and enjoyable read. And to its credit, I devoured Dividing Eden over the course of two evenings. Why then, dear book gods, can I not simply love it? 
 Well, it all boils down to one simple thing... 
 Dividing Eden failed to leave an impression on me. The writing was descent, the plot pretty good; the characters (while I liked them mostly) failed to pull an emotion from me. I kept reading because I wanted to know what happened next. Who would be nearer to the throne at the end. There were several things that weren't well explained (like the magic) and the quick division between siblings. According to the novel, the twins, Carys and Andreus, are supposed to be extremely close. However, their relationship deteriorated almost immediately. Why? Andreus seemed way too eager just to give up on his sister and easy to manipulate. By the end I just wanted him dead. Lol (sorry) 
 The good stuff... 
 The Trial of Succession was pretty dang cool. I also enjoyed some aspects of the world building such as the windmills, the secrecy and manipulations, and how the siblings were so different, Carys the adventurer, and Andreus the scholar. I enjoyed Carys's protective nature over her brother, even though I did feel she protected him a tad bit too much. To be honest, I think I just wanted more. And while the book is long and the pace is pretty slow and steady, so much more could have happened! 
 Overall, if you enjoy fantasy novels about siblings and don't mind stories that are just okay, then give it a try. I didn't love it but I am interested to see what happens in the next installment.

I always enjoy books in which the characters' lives intersect in small and unexpected ways, allowing these connections to be revealed to the reader and to the other characters as the plot unfolds. And I also always enjoy those books that surprise the reader with that last little twist. And this, the second Jackson Brodie novel by Kate Atkinson, features both of those characteristics. 
 So what was it about this book that didn't allow me to really settle in and enjoy? Call me a Pollyanna, but it bothered me that there didn't seem to be a single relationship in this book that was happy or satisfying. Jackson Brodie, the main character, still thinks of his ex-wife as his wife even though she has remarried, and his relationship with his current girlfriend is unbalanced, to say the least. Martin Canning still hears his emotionally abusive father shouting insults in his ear. Gloria Hatter has a philandering husband and a "best friend" that she doesn't particularly like. I could go on, but you get the idea. I realize that in the real world everyone has challenges in their closest relationships, but the dreariness of these characters' personal lives' permeated the atmosphere to a degree that I found unpleasant. Perhaps Atkinson decided to intentionally imbue the characters with the Scottish stereotypes of alcohol and pessimism. If that was her intent, she succeeded. Hence my tepid rating of 3 stars.

Mental disorders can be crippling to teenagers, especially when they carry a stigma and that stigma, coupled with ignorance, can make trying to live a "normal" life difficult. YA authors are doing a fantastic job of handling these stories and now debut author, McCall Hoyle can add her name to the list with one difference. Her protagonist doesn't suffer a mental illness but epilepsy. I liken the two, although one is physical the other mental, because of the stigma and the mental anguish that goes along with a physical disability. Both subjects are touched on in this quick but powerful story about a girl who dares to hope. 
 Emilie spends her days being homeschooled in her pajamas, playing with her therapy dog and best friend, Hitch, taking her meds, and slogging through life waiting for the next big one to hit. The next seizure that is, until her mother decides the unthinkable. It is time for her to attend school. She's on new meds and has been doing great. Her mom and shrink think that her "socioemotional well-being" isn't being developed enough and school is the solution. Emilie notices that her mom is wearing nail polish and keeps making excuses when a new phone number keeps popping up on her screen. She can't help but wonder if her mom is using this to work on her own socioemotional well-being. She's not ready for her mom to date, not when the hurt of her father's death three years ago is still so raw. Emilie has different ideas about school but agrees to stick it out ninety days in whatever hell that high school actually is. It isn't that she's afraid of people or the work (she's super smart), it's what they will think of her when they find out she has epilepsy and might die in front of them, or worse see her vomiting and pissing herself. 
 Watching teenage movies about high school prepared her for the stereotypes, but after her first few days Emilie is rethinking all of those movies and drawing some conclusions of her own. Like basketball star Chatham York, who should be the epitome of a dumb jock who doesn't care about anything but sports but she is so very wrong about him. Good thing, because she's pretty sure he's the hottest guy she's ever seen and now that he somehow convinced her to be his English tutor, it looks like she's going to be spending a lot more time with him. She manages to make a new friend in bubbly and confident Ayla, artist extraordinaire and editor of the school's lit magazine. She does a good job of pushing Emilie into new things without being too much, and Emilie knows she should tell them both about her epilepsy, but she doesn't want to them to think differently of her. She's going on three months without any seizures, which hasn't happened since she was seven, but with the stress of school, friends, a boyfriend and her mom's new social life she's having a hard time handling it all. The reader knows where this is going and although, predictable, I had no problems rooting for her Emilie and her new found life. Bonus points for an awesome English teacher, supportive mom, and perfect first boyfriend.

Perhaps this book should have been preceded by the author's definition of cheating because I take issue with that word in relation to the majority of situations in this book. Cheating was when my good friend's husband had sex with a female colleague while she was pregnant. Cheating was when my friend's boyfriend kissed another girl at a party when they were drunk. Those are my definitions of cheating. When I was in college, I went out with several guys. Was I cheating on them? We weren't "going steady". I was just having fun. Adults can do that. Polygamy was when my friend's father, a travelling salesman was found to also be legally (or not) married to another woman in another town and had a family with her too. 
 I believe at around twenty percent the Lucas Thorne called the heroine a "judgmental psycho". He practically took the words right out of my mouth because I had stopped not five minutes before that to complain to my husband about how I was sick of the heroine for calling the hero a "cheater" every two minutes in reference to his dating/sleeping with multiple women. He was not married and none of these women were his "girlfriend" so what is the problem? Personally, I probably would have called her a judgmental bitch. 
 This is exactly the reason I very rarely read books about twenty-two year old heroines who just don't have enough life experience yet. I guess I should blame the author for this one? Is she unaware? Polygamy is not the same thing as polyamory. Am I taking a romance novel too seriously? Probably. Again, I like a dose of reality with my romance novels. 
 And yes, my dear innocent Avery, there are women in the world who actually want no strings attached sex. It's not a fantasy a la Santa Claus and the Easter Bunny. Not every woman on the planet wants to get married, have 2.5 kids and the white picket fence. And guess what? There's nothing wrong with us. Okay, there's currently a husband in my living room, two furry beasts with four legs, and (crap!) there's a white vinyl fence on my lawn (does that count?). 
 If Avery were religious and she had an objection to Lucas's lifestyle based on her belief that a man should not have sex with a woman before marriage. Okay. But that does not seem to be her problem with him. Did he cheat on her sister? You will have to read the book to figure out how you feel about that one and personally I did not think it was worth it but I did it anyway. However, dating multiple women while telling them that he is not interested in a relationship and with the knowledge beforehand that he is dating other women (he even checked with a lawyer on that one) is not cheating. Harping about it every two minutes does not make it so. It just makes you look like a harping bitch. 
 I love a good hate/love story and the banter in this book showed promise until it descended into childish accusations of "cheating" on seven women, polygamy and other such nonsense. The story about Lucas and his guilt over what happened and why he only casually dates multiple women could have been a fascinating story in and of itself, one that I was interested in reading. Lucas Thorne was a fascinating character and I loved his complexity. However, the rest of the story was ruined by the antics and judgments of a childish heroine who apparently needs to get out in the world and experience a little more of what life has to offer before she starts judging other women and their choices to agree to such "relationships". As I recall she even refers to the women he dates as "skanks" and even "whores" at times but none of them were portrayed as such, most of them were described as "nice". And I am not even going to go into the whole OB/GYN scenario and the revelation that entailed about the heroine. 
 I wrote most of the above except the intro at about twenty percent of the way through the book and should have known that if I had to put the book down and rant about it at that point, I should never have picked it back it back up again but I did. Big mistake. I should have marked it DNF and left it at that, but since that is not what I did, I will tell you that it just descended further. Lucas's own best friend called him a "cheater" for dating multiple women while doing the same, then his sister called him a "cheater" for dating multiple women, then revelations of the past turned around and showed that the silly heroine was not only judgmental but a hypocrite too. And then there was this... 
 Lucas to his best friend "Low blow, you cock-sucking bastard." 
 Lucas thoughts "...doing Irish car bombs and puking in the streets." Really, of all the cocktails in America you pick that one? I thought I liked Lucas and now I don't. 
 I wanted to give this book 2 stars because there were some passages of banter between the main characters that genuinely made me laugh out loud and the heroine had some interesting quirks. 
 "When I was little, I was convinced my teddy bear was real-and all these years, later, I still found him in different spots throughout the house, though I was pretty sure my dad moved him around to freak me out, the bastard." 
 However, these moments were not worth the offensive remarks and the juvenile ranting and tantrums of the heroine and others who later followed her lead. I just cannot bring myself to say that I was okay with this so it has to be one star.

LIST OF REASONS WHY YOU SHOULD/SHOULD NOT READ FALLEN FLAME: 
 It is incredibly boring. 
 Like really. 
 Let's get started. 
 1. The characters were horribly bland. 2 dimensional at best. 
 - Miller somehow has successfully written the most boring Prince in all of YA fantasy history. 
 He does absolutely nothing. 
 There's nothing attractive about him, nothing swoon worthy, nothing distinct about him at all. 
 He's just a Prince, thats it. Vala talks about how gentle and kind he is but... bish where? We don't get much from him that makes a lasting impression. The only thing I remember about him is how he let Vala be whipped after she saved him. And that's not gentle or kind.. 
 - For a person whose skin can burn you with a single touch, Vala is pretty tame. The most interesting part of her obviously, is her skin condition. And because this is a YA novel she's obviously in love with the Prince. BORING! 
 -Xavyn, How the hell do you pronounce this? Why do authors think its cool to create names that can't be read? How did she even come up with this? To be fair he is the most interesting character in this book. But that isn't saying much, is it? 
 -All other characters just fall to the wayside. We have the evil queen, the rival or evil stepsister, and the devious princess. 
 2. It also wouldn't be a YA fantasy novel without the eradication of magic through some convoluted events that happened in the past. So yea, another played out story plot, thanks Miller. 
 3. Fallen Flame devoted too much time detailing the politics of the kingdom it featured. Miller spent an unfortunate amount of time boring us with the menial work Vala does as a guard, and the day to day politics of this supposed marriage alliance. Basically it boiled down to a lot of "they want our crops" this and "they want our soil" that and "They'll take over our kingdom" ... blah blah blah. 
 4. Fortunately, the writing was good. It read really well and flowed quite nicely. 
 5. But there were way too many info dumps. The characters who, mind you, were already boring me out of my mind, would then proceed to go on these page long speeches about the kingdoms history. 
 6. Perhaps the most infuriating aspect of the book is the complete lack of urgency, of tension and of a goal to be honest. Until I stopped reading the plot consisted of simply trying to find out who Xavyn was and what he wanted. 
 And that wasn't interesting enough. And then Vala befriended him , so that plot line was toast. 
 The only reason to continue reading was the hope that Xavyn knew what she was and where she came from. 
 But then he revealed his power: mimicry, which meant that he had no idea what she was because he was just copying the power she had! 
 Mind you, this is all done in the calmest writing possible. 
 There was no need for me to continue reading ... and so I didn't. I had no intense desire to find out what would happen next. I didn't care for the characters, and I couldn't connect with them. The world didn't draw me in, and I couldn't loose myself while reading this book. It's safe to say that Fallen Flame is not a page turner.

"Anybody who has had the temerity to write about Jane Austen is aware of two facts: First, that of all great writers she is the most difficult to catch in the act of greatness; second, that there are 25 elderly gentlemen living in the neighborhood of London who resent any slight upon her genius as if it were an insult offered to the chastity of their aunts." Virginia Woolf 
 Update: March / 2017 
 I had a strange feeling when I started reading the book this time & at first I did not really know why. Then suddenly I realized that I was reading the book in spring, which may sound stupid, but fact is that until now, I always re-read the book in autumn (or winter). It was unconsciously done, but my mind got in tune with the time and atmosphere of the novel (listening to Chopin waltzes while reading heightens the experience even more). Jane Austen's writing just has this power over me. :) 
 Her pleasure in the walk must arise from the exercise and the day, from the view of the last smiles of the year upon the tawny leaves and withered hedges, and from repeating to herself some few of the thousand poetical descriptions extant of autumn--that season of peculiar and inexhaustible influence on the mind of taste and tenderness--that season which has drawn from every poet worthy of being read some attempt at description, or some lines of feeling. 
 Autumn is the time for intro- and retrospection & these characteristics are exploited to the full in Anne Elliot. 
 So who is she? An introvert spinster of 27 who - in that day and age - is considered almos too old to have any chances in the marriage market and destined to be sidelined by society (spinsterhood meant lower social standing, even if you are a daughter of a baronet) and in Anne's case: by her family as well. 
 At the age of nineteen she met the "love of her life", but due to the persuasion of her friend, Lady Russel ("you are too young, he has no social position, no fortune to support a wife, PLUS he is a naval officer, whos life is always in danger" - this is during the Napoleonic wars with France) & the cold disregard of her family, she gave up the engagement. The rejected lover, Frederic Wentworth, thinking her weak-minded and entirely too persuadable, left her for good & Anne, with only a memory of their love, realises -too late- that she made the wrong decision. 
 She had been forced into prudence in her youth, she learned romance as she grew older: the natural sequel of an unnatural beginning. 
 This summary may sound quite melodramatic and very unlike any of Jane Austen's former novels, but her genius is at work, and the book is anything but. 
 Anne is the most isolated of all Austen's heroines. She is to all intents and purposes a "nobody" to her family & to society, with the exception of Lady Russel. Nobody sees her, nobody hears her, her whole existence does not count (curiously, we do not even meet her until the end of chapter 3) and yet it takes Austen's genius to put her in the centre at the same time. We see through her eyes and mind what is happening. She is not noticed, but she notices everything. 
 In addition, she is also forced into a passivity that not even Fanny Price can surpass. In the first part of the novel, JA barely allows her to speak. Her replies/thoughts are always reported (that famous invention of free indirect speech), but we cannot hear her. 
 After 8 years of separation Captain Wentworth (a now successful, rich & high-ranking officer) reappears on the scene - vowing, of course, to have nothing to do with Anne Elliot - and this seems to liberate Anne's repressed energy (which is natural in a way as he was the only one who understood her completely). From that point on, slowly, but gradually Anne's presence becomes stronger: she talks more, she acts more, and she is capable to show the qualities of resoluteness and independence which he thought she totally lacked. 
 This is an amazingly powerful novel and though the notion of "Romantic Love" seems to be much more pronounced, Jane Austen is Jane Austen still -thank Heaven! For the romance is the result of realism (money makes the world go round): when Capt. Wentworth first proposed, he had nothing to offer socially or financially. When he proposes again he has high social standing / fortune through his own merits; and for Jane Austen -always acutely aware of social expectations & pecuniary realities of life - this is necessary for a happy ending. 
 "Autumn is a second spring when every leaf is a flower." - Albert Camus

If you've read Rick Yancey's other series, The Fifth Wave, you know that he's a good writer. In fact, he's fast becoming one of my favorites. The Monstrumologist is totally different from The Fifth Wave and in it's own ways, is still equally amazing. A lot of authors tend to stick to a certain genre, their characters tend to follow same patterns and similar tropes appear throughout the stories. This is not the case with Yancey. And the fact that he can create two completely different worlds and various completely different characters and two stories with little to no parallels, amazes me. Perhaps the only similarities between the two is the fact that they keep you hooked. 
 My favorite part of The Monstrumologist was the characters. I love when a book keeps me guessing about characters. I like them to be consistent, but I like them to keep me guessing. While the man character of Will Henry is clearly defined throughout the story, the others are harder to decipher. Pellinore Winthrop begins the story as a driven, stubborn, almost unlikeable (but still unintentionally quirky) character. Based on his attitude towards Will Henry and the cold, calculating way he acts towards the victims of the Anthrophophagi, you're not sure whether you're meant to like him. John Kearns (aka Richard Cory, John J. J. Schmidt, and possibly Jack the Ripper) is introduced as a charming, charismatic, humorous and likeable character. The way Yancey is able to turn around your view of these two characters is stunning. 
 Which brings me to another aspect of this book that I liked. Philosophy. It's subtle, not up in your face, but it's there. The seemingly unlikeable face of Pellinore Winthrop disguises a man who is ultimately, caring and gentle and moral to an extent. On the other hand, Kearns, whose mannerisms are nothing less than polite and good natured, is merely masking his truly evil nature. Many times throughout the book I found myself writing down quotes that struck me. 
 I was a little worried when I started this book because the story, you find out, is actually being told from the perspective of a man reading the diaries left by Will Henry. To me, diary entries as a way of writing always seems to leave a little bit to be desired. It can be creative, but it leaves out the first hand perspective of events. However, other than the first and last chapters which are told from the perspective of the man reading the diaries, the book is told by Will Henry and not the in form of actual diary entries. So in this case, I'd say the ruse of the man reading this story from the future, worked in the book's favor. 
 The final action scene in this book is maybe the one thing that I found lacking. It just didn't seem to jive with the rest of the story, but ultimately wasn't enough to make me even come close to not liking this book. The ending of the actual book though, was good. I definitely recommend it if you like a little bit of horror, you don't mind quite a bit of gore and you like reading books that leave you wanting more.

Reagan's been through so many secret identities and innumerable amount of lies that she barely remembers who she truly is. When she finally begins to grow attached to her and her parents' newest home, bad news strikes. Now she has to fight between wanting to be a Black Angel like her parents or giving away that life of danger and secrets. 
 If you enjoyed The Naturals series by Jennifer Lynn Barnes, I highly suggest You Don't Know My Name. Both deal with responsible and incredibly talented teenagers surrounded by serious government matters. While Cassie solves serial killer mysteries, Reagan is on her way to being a top spy for the Black Angels. Both characters struggle with conflicts like not being taken seriously because of their age, family loyalty, and intelligent villains. 
 Reagan is undeniably talented and collected. She's been dealt a pretty sad hand in life, but takes it all without complaint. Family is something that's very important to her, to a point where she'll do nearly anything to save them. This is not the same as Tris's (from Divergent) wild and dumb selfless behavior. Reagan is responsible enough to actually listen to others while also fighting for what she believes is right. 
 Her neighbor Luke is a great character who wants to go into the military when he's older. Luke and Reagan match one another and don't hold each other back. Starting as friends, their relationship grows at a reasonable pace and their ability to comfort one another reveals cute sentimental moments between the two. 
 I was fairly annoyed with the fact that because of her and Luke's ages, they were kept in the dark about a lot of information. It's just so unfair that they're expected to act like adults when they're still being held in the dark like children. But, this is to be expected in a government/spy book like this. 
 The plot grows slowly. You're learning about Reagan and the aspects of her life for a majority. It was a really quick read so I didn't have a trouble with any super slow parts. The ending was great with a really good set-up for the next novel. Honestly, I really want will happen next in this series.

I have already gotten rid of the book, so I'm going to have to paraphrase how Jesse Andrews begins it: You can hate this book, or you can love it. It's up to you. That sounds like a challenge! I think he's saying if you like it, cool. If you don't, if you wanna be a hater, you're playing into my point that hating is so easy and that when we hate things, in part, we actually love them. 
 I don't like to feel tricked or trapped, and I did not like this book. I didn't hate it in a good way--I know what hate-love is! I LOVE to hate-read books. A hate-read has to drive me crazy like a sexy/insane girlfriend who I just can't quit. A hate-read has to make me so angry that I feel personally invested. I have to feel joy somewhere in the pages of a hate-read. Joy because I see some of myself in the awful characters, joy because I feel like I could write a better book, joy because it's just GOOD AWFUL SHIT, exactly what the worst part of me wants to read. This list could be much longer. But The Haters included none of this. 
 The characters were unlikeable and obnoxious, I didn't want to go on this road trip with them!!! But Jesse Andrews made me do it!!! I was being held hostage!!!! I wanted to jump out of the car!!! 
 I know Jesse Andrews is not a well-spoken thirteen-year-old, but can we be sure that he's not? I don't want to read something that I think I could have overheard on the subway. None of the writing was inspiring or brought me to another place or made me think of things in a new way. I could just FEEL Jesse Andrews laughing at himself after some of the "cool/hilarious" dialogue. 
 Jesse Andrews reminded me of Amy Poehler in Mean Girls. "I'm not like those other authors, who are stuffy and actually are good writers. I'm a COOL author, I write like a twelve-year-old talks! I write in lists!" 
 I will tell you another thing about a hate-read--you might get pissed, but you won't get bored. And toward the end, when they were like at the final concert or whatever, I mean, I couldn't even tell you what happened. My eyes were on the words but my brain was not there. I didn't care. 
 If you ask me, they should have stayed at that fucking camp longer. That place offered some real promise. 
 The resolution was unenjoyable and underwhelming. I felt like Jesse Andrews actually missed a great opportunity to write about what it means to hate-love something. He mentions it at the beginning and talks about it at the end, but that idea could have driven this whole book and made it much better. 
 There is a chance Jesse Andrews would read this review and say, "This girl say she hated my book, but I know that she secretly loved it." Which is exactly what cocky asshole high school guys when a girl doesn't like them. But I actually, 100% did not like this book. When I was done I took a shower and picked up 
 Devil in the White City 
 , which isn't even something I'd usually read, but I needed something that could be the opposite of The Haters. And I'm loving it. 
 By the way, hating is far too easy. It's awful if you hate everything. But it's okay to hate things if you use it as a constructive exercise in making yourself and your experiences better. If you use it as a chance to be funny but not mean. If you make sure it doesn't drive you so insane that you come away worse. In that way, hate can be wonderful. But deep down I do believe that optimism and positivity and passion and giddyness conquer all. 
 Caitlin Moran has a great quotation about cynicism. 
 "The whole thing about being cynical is that you put on armor to protect you because you are too ashamed to admit that you are innocent and naive and that you are inexperienced. So you put on this armor to protect you. The thing about armor is you don't grow in armor. You can't dance in armor. You can't run in armor. You can't change in armor. Today the game on social media is to be cynical, is to be snarky. It is to want to tear people down and not believe in things and war over who is going to be the most bitchy that week. Have the bravery. It takes far more balls to be a giddy optimist. Keep believing, keep yourself optimistic. Always have the balls to say, I love this." 
 So guys, FYI, I do love stuff. Just not The Haters.

 'I thought Munsell said that colour was here to give our life meaning?' 
 'Its function is to give life apparent meaning. It is an abstraction, a misdirection- nothing more than a sideshow at Jollity Fair. As long as your minds are full of Chromatic betterment, there can be no room for other, more destructive, thoughts. Do you understand?' 
 "Shades of Grey" is set in what used to be Wales, hundred of years after the mysterious Something That Happened. Nobody knows what the Something That Happened actually was, but it seems to have been linked to the disappearance of the Previous (i.e homo sapiens) and the establishment of the Colourtocracy, a society where your social status is based on which colours of the spectrum you are able to see, and the population lives according to a series of rules, with their conduct being rewarded or otherwise by the award of merits and demerits. Their society is gradually regressing technologically, as every few years there is a Leapback, when certain subjects are 'defacted' and all books on those subjects removed from the increasingly empty libraries, and the use of certain items becomes forbidden. Telephones, any cars more advanced than a Model 'T' Ford, and even riding horses are some of the things that have been forbidden in previous Leapbacks. The few remaining artefacts made by the Previous are now incomprehensible to the populace, but the Oz Memorial made me laugh when I realised who the figures on the statue were. 
 For most of the book, not a huge amount happens, but I liked the way that information about this strange rule-bound society is drip-fed as the story progresses - there are no info-dumps but you gradually get to understand how this strange society works (or so you think). The action picks up towards the end of the book, and I was surprised (shocked, even) at just how dark the story became. I'm really looking forward to the next book in the series and am hoping that we it will reveal more about the Something That Happened, who the the Riff Raff are, and where the Fallen Man fell from. 
 While reading the book, it gradually becomes clear just how bad the characters' eyesight is, even leaving aside their problems with colour perception. Eddie remarks more then once about the hollow, empty appearance of the Previous, due to their large pupils, and it seems that people have tiny pupils which don't change size to adapt to different lighting conditions like ours do. So their eyesight is poor even in daylight (hence the complicated arrangements of heliostats bringing sunlight into their buildings), while at night, they are completely blind (and terrified of the dark). They can't see by moonlight, although they know that some animals can, and they are unable to see the stars at all. 
 As well as the Apocryphal Man telling Eddie that the function of colour is to give life apparent meaning, Jane also says 'Someone remade the night as a barrier to restrict movement, and sightless people who have no fear of the darkness would give the game away.' So I don't think that the differences between the characters in this book and the Previous are due to evolution. It's not as if they live in caves or underground, so what evolutionary benefit could there be for the deterioration in their eyesight? If there were no colour-based rules on who you could marry, colour-vision would soon even out amongst the population. There is also no logical reason for social status to increase as you move along the spectrum from red to ultra-violet. I think that at some point someone must have made an arbitrary decision that that was the way it would be (maybe based on the historical role of purple as a colour for royalty). But whether it was brought about by genetic meddling or selective breeding, and why it would only affect the ability to see 'natural' colours I have no idea.

I really wanted to love Ancillary Sword, but sadly it just didn't click for me. It wasn't for lack of effort. In a way it was frustrating because Leckie's prose can be quite amazing at times. 
 The first book, Ancillary Justice, was universally beloved and won just about every scifi book award that there was to win. I understood what people saw in it, but there was so much in the book that frustrated me. Leckie showed her skills as a tremendous world builder (as everyone has noted), but sadly the characters were a bit lacking. 
 Leckie set out to fix that in the second book by having it mostly a long character study of Justice of Toren/Breq, the corpse AI that lost her ship that served as her central hub sentenced to a life in a human body. Her tale of vengeance led to a climatic face off in the first book and this one picked up directly after and at times it was hard to grasp where the plot was heading. 
 It wasn't due to depth or complication but instead because of the pacing and what the main focus of the book turned out to be. Leckie has proven to be a slow starter, in fact, I almost put down Ancillary Justice until I got to about the 40% mark when it picked up, with Ancillary Sword it probably didn't pick up until somewhere near the realm of 70%. 
 Her prose can be great, like I said, but at other times frustrating. Why is everyone gesturing? The word "gesture" appears in some form what feels like every page on both books and while I can understand that Breq is an AI who views things a bit differently, she seems to have a superior intellect and I'm sure can break down these gestures into more depth than just "she gestured agreement" and so forth. 
 Most of the book felt like something that most authors would have summed up briefly within a a few pages, a few chapters at most. Instead most of our time is spent with Breq seeing how the common people live. It was a valuable thing for the character to experience in her quest, undoubtedly, but the presentation and the events felt rather uninspired. There was also the fact that the reader was given no real insight as to what Breq was after throughout most of the journey. 
 There was similar insight missing from the first book early on, which made it such a slog to endure. I've seen a lot of people saying "well, I didn't understand it, but maybe I'm just smart enough." Readers have to be unafraid to take authors to task on things like this. Ancillary Justice wasn't confusing because it flew over the readers' heads, but because there wasn't enough detail or insight into the characters to get the reader invested. This book was similar to that. 
 So if AJ was missing character development and had a fascinating plot, AS was missing the plot and saw a lot of character development. Hopefully Ancillary Mercy pieces it all together because I truly want to love these books and Leckie's writing, but there are just a few little things that make these books more of a chore than they should be.

This story had me on the edge of my seat. Hawk is great at fast, plot-driven paranormal mysteries, and I think I like the plot to this one better than I did with the first book. It felt like a nice, contained story that still furthered our affection for Griffin and Whyborne as a couple as well as supporting characters like Christine and Whyborne's mother. Even though some of the creatures, creepy-crawlies, horrid lab experiments, and cramped mining shafts can be terrifying, this series still feels cozy, like the characters welcome you back with open arms to go on adventures with them. 
 Even though it is a common enough romantic device, I liked the conflict of "I don't deserve him" that both men feel. Griffin still feels like a broken man after he was committed to a mental institution after the death of his partner, and Whyborne still feels gawky and naive compared to his more worldly lover. The introduction of a shady man from Griffin's past doesn't help with the jealousy, but the stakes feel appropriately low in light of the, you know, demon alien creatures swooping down and body-snatching the citizens of a mining boomtown . I also really got a kick out of how Griffin demands Whyborne tell him something only the two of them would know to prove he hasn't been compromised and Whyborne basically yells in a panic "YOU LICKED MY ASSHOLE LAST NIGHT." And Griffin was like okay, yeah, this is him. 
 Hawk knows how to tell a great story while adding bits of romance at just the right times. Even when our heroes are saving a mining town from ruin or quarreling about past lovers, a perfectly-placed kiss, nuzzle, or "my dear" is enough to make it all right again. Only two books in and these have fallen into a beautiful domesticity throughout whatever they have to deal with. I'm hopelessly endeared by Whyborne's slightly fussy characterization, especially the way he won't even be outside the bedroom with Griffin in something as risque as shirtsleeves. Unbuttoning him is always a treat. 
 I read this one very quickly and I am currently devouring the next.

This book is so nuts! I kind of love it, but I'm pretty sure that's because I have absolutely no intention of actually trying to slavishly adhere to its advice. 
 I knew this book and I were in trouble when it asked if I could possibly be happy surrounded by old papers and unread books and accessories that I never wear. "The answer SHOULD BE 'No,'" it said. For me, the answer is a resounding YES! I LOVE finding old scraps of story ideas, and I do, in fact, go back to ancient story ideas... things that I wrote when I was 12, etc. I am at home in a library of unread books, handed down to me from other people who also never read them. There, I see possibility, hope, dreams. 
 Nonetheless, I love this idea of visualizing the kind of space, and the kind of life that you want to have. But this whole thing, where  you're supposed to go through each item, touch it, and FEEL whether or not it brings you joy , is not only kinda crazy, it's clearly only going to work on a specific type of person. The kind of person who has already developed a sense of "when to throw things out." Also, Kondo's going to be right there at my back telling me whether or not it brings me joy. 
 The further I go in this book, the more it sounds like Kondo is a freakish obsessive about throwing things out. A kind of reverse hoarder. This book advises things like "don't own any seasonally appropriate clothes, because we live in a temperature-controlled environment." I mean, this is the actual advice. Ignore the cost and climate damage that come from life in a hermetically sealed bubble-- what you really need is a near-empty, orderly closet! 
 How are you ever supposed to apply this when you live with someone else, who has a radically different vision of what brings them joy in a room? When you have small children who love nothing more than to collect and squirrel away? Sure, these things should be curtailed, but the "my way or the highway" overtone here doesn't have much place in family life. 
 It's got some great advice about throwing things out and parting with things when the time has come, and reading it has me actually wearing some of the accessories that normally just bring me joy by sitting in a wad at the bottom of a drawer. It also has me actually tackling some of the "shit boxes" that have been moved twice and contain papers that say "open immediately" and are dated from 2013.

 Corianne is fascinating to read and though it doesn't reveal who topped her by the end, a fairly good case could be made for suicide. The short story written in the style of her diary lays out her life before, after and during her marriage to the King. We meet Elara and get to see what she's like before it all and of course, book mad Julian and others. It's a fair reading of the character and I liked it. 
 Farley's story is a little different. From the Lakeland's it follows her mission to.... well that's just it.. I'm not sure. She makes a broadcast, finds Mare's brother and of course, meets Mare, but I'm not sure what her focus is. She's a great character and I liked reading more about her. 
 All in all, Cruel Crown is a good read and a must if you love the Red Queen series. It offers a nice tantalising view on the rest of the Red Queen universe and I did read it very quickly.

I found myself forgetting how young they really were until there was a scene from their school to remind me. 
 Another surprise was Bronagh herself. She's described as the quiet loner in school. Teachers give her some extra privileges because she such a good kid, other kids torment her just for fun. Then Dominic shows up. Around him, she's a totally different person. She lashes out, screams, swears, and is even violent toward him. I felt terrible for how his father treated him and I couldn't begin to imagine how that would shape a little kid as they grew up. Did he actually like Ruby?  Hopefully, this will come up in the next book.

It should be illegal for authors to finish a book on a certain note and then make you wait a whole year. Nothing terribly outlandishly shocking happened. However, there are just so many things left hanging that my mind couldn't really process it. I can't believe that Ruby erased Liam's mind!! As I kept reading, I thought for sure that she was going to stop or decide not to do it. I wonder how their relationship will be in the next book. Is there a way to reverse it? Will Liam remember? A Court of Thornes and Roses is becoming one of my favourite books series. It's the first book I've read by Sarah J. Maas and right from the beginning I fell absolutely in love with the world and the characters. The story- and world building are excellent and well balanced and I don't have any criticism. 
 Sarah J. Maas's writing style is one of my favourite. I can completely envision every setting in great detail and the unearthly beauty she describes. I usually have an extremely hard time to imagine the characters' appearance and the look of the surroundings but not in this series. Right from the beginning I could picture everything and the slow developing world building is perfectly constructed so you never feel lost or confused. A lot of YA authors (especially in fantasy of course) neglect the world building or don't balance it well but Maas did an excellent job. 
 The characters: 
 Feyre is an amazing character. Yes, she can be a bit too stubborn at times and when you tell her to "not do a thing" she will most definitely "do the thing" which can be a bit frustrating but besides that she's a pretty cool character. She never does anything that she does not want to and never lets anyone dictate her how to live her life (unless she would be killed otherwise). Compared to other YA novels I found her to be a lot stronger and emancipated female character who is smart, headstrong and a lethal opponent if you dare to hurt her loved ones. Her character development is already strong in the first novel but appears small in comparison to the sequel. 
 I grew to like the character of Tamlin in the first instalment even though you can already sense his strong protective behaviour, his stubbornness and his unwillingness to do absolutely anything to protect his friends and loved ones. He's no match for Feyre whose fortitude exceeds his own but it appeared to me that Tamlin honestly cared for her and since he never forced Feyre to do anything she doesn't want, I liked him despite his flaws. (What happened in the sequel is another thing...). 
 Rhysand is my fictional husband even though he appears to have some flaws in A Court of Thornes and Roses. The thing I absolutely didn't like is what he forced Feyre to do around the end. I understand why he did it and his motives are totally plausible but still... I really think that Sarah J. Maas should have come up with another idea... something less assaulting since this is something I can't tolerate no matter what. I wished she wouldn't have done that. 
 Another thing that bucked me is a bit of a spoiler: After they won Feyre and Tamlin had sex even though she just murdered two faes, died herself and saw Amarantha being murdered in a brutal and gory way. How can she feel like having sex after all of that. It was totally unnecessary and unrealistic.  
 But despite some flaws I love the ending and the set up for the sequel. :3

It really breaks my heart to give this only 2-stars, because I wanted to love this so badly. Rehvenge's backstory and subplot has been one of my favorite over the past few books, and I was looking forward to getting to hear his own story and voice. 
 I think Ward did a number of things wrong here: first and foremost was his relationship with Elehna. While I liked them both in their own right, I never really felt the chemistry between them that Ward so often described. It echoed too much of the instaluv relationship that went on between Wrath and Beth in the first book, and there was no amazing chemistry or deep-seated conversations and relationship build-up to make up for it. Yeah, there's a ton of personal shit that Rehvenge has to tell, but the entire thing just felt a bit... stunted. Elehna was rather flat as a heroine, and I never got the how of how they fell in love so fast. 
 I think this is due to Ward devoting WAY too much subplot towards her other characters. Yeah, it's always been in the other books, but it's especially so in this book. I really couldn't be bothered about the whole Wrath storyline (I mean really, his book is already over, and since his book was one of my least favorites, I was completely bored reading about him again). The John/Xhex storyline was great, and a look into the creepy Lash's head as the leader of the lessers was interesting as well. However, I felt like Ward spent an unnecessarily long amount of time with the subplot, to the point where it probably took up more than half of the book. If you're going to write a paranormal romance series with each book focusing on both a couple and the subplots, but you are catering yourself as paranormal romance first and foremost, it makes sense to have the love story be a driving force, no? 
 idk, I'm just not feeling it. I desperately wished that I'd felt differently about this, but I guess it wasn't meant to be. :( I'm so excited about the next book, though! John/Xhex, ahhhh...

The blurb for this novel claims "grotesque madness" and on that it certainly delivers. Howard has taken the classic story and given it a new side that further explores the dark elements of the original tale while also giving it its own life and conflicts. I must say that I didn't love every aspect of this re-imagining, but there were plenty of elements that I did enjoy. 
 I was greatly impressed by the twisted version of Wonderland Howard has created. The imagination this world clearly took is astounding, as Howard has come up with many interesting elements. Her take on having Alyssa "undo" the things that the original Alice left wrong was creative and a fun play on the original story. The imagery created was absolutely wonderful to read, as it was richly described and really quite exciting to follow. This was probably the aspect of the novel that most drew me in and kept me entertained because I thought the creative twists and the world Howard created were the strongest elements. 
 When it came to characters, I quite enjoyed Alyssa and Jeb. They both felt like genuine, emotional characters with strengths and faults, wants and fears. Not only was their friendship/something more pretty enjoyable to watch unfold, but Alyssa's family complications were also very explored in a very interesting way. Her strained relationship (almost non-relationship) with her mother was captivating and heartbreaking to watch, but well developed. However, in terms of the last main character, I was not impressed by Morpheus until near the end (though many others love him deeply, so this is largely personal preference). He really just came off as more creepy and invasive than appealing and seductive, which I think is what a lot of others see in him. I don't see the attraction at all, nor did I love his character for most of the book. I did come around on the "interested" side by the end, but still not the "attracted." 
 I also felt like many of the minor characters, while often extremely interesting, were not developed enough to leave a lasting impression beyond the strange way they fit into Wonderland. I understand that in a story like this, a large cast of characters certainly makes sense and fits well, but I often felt like I was just getting to know a few interesting side characters when suddenly their parts were finished and they were gone from the story. I'm definitely hoping that some of this wide cast makes further appearances in the next two installments because they added a certain something fun and creative to the story and I'm very interested in seeing more! 
 Overall, this was certainly an imaginative and wildly creative Wonderland re-imagining. While I didn't love all the aspects and completely don't understand the appeal of one of the points of the love triangle, I did enjoy the main character, the complex and well developed world in which she lands, and the crazy side characters that make it so unique. 
 3 stars.

 Our main character Monty is bisexual, there's a character that is gay and epileptic AND mixed race. There's a M/M romance. There was lot involved and the representation was great.

 The most impressive thing to me about this book is Gemma Hardy. Livesey has done what I, and so many other writers, struggle with. She has managed to create a very real human being. Gemma is bright, kind, and helpful. She's also ruthless, rude, and a leap-before-she-looks kind of person. As a reader I felt like I was listening to the story of a good friend - someone who I know and trust is a beautiful person but who, inevitably, I don't always agree with. Gemma lived a life where bad things happened to her that she couldn't control, she also lived a life where bad things happened to her because of her actions. I loved that, as a reader, I learned what those things were. As Gemma grew up and started to understand the impact of her decisions, so did I. It was a really great experience. 
 So why don't I love the book? I don't know exactly. Maybe because too many strangers were nice to Gemma. Maybe because things were just a little slow. I'm just now seeing that this is, apparently, a re-telling of Jane Eyre, a book I haven't yet gotten to. Perhaps I will better understand Gemma when I get to know a little more about Jane. 
 Oh - for anyone partial to Scotland or Iceland, you might get an extra kick out of this book. :-)
