What a story of strength and misunderstandings. I slowly came to know the story of 4 little children and their amazing mother. She had a hell of a time. It was hard to read, understand and then absorb her feelings and the decisions she made during her journey. The prose was palpable, her writing makes it impossible to be left untouched by Anya's remarkable story as she explains how she survived the siege of Leningrad and I was compelled to dry my eyes and press on. I'm glad I did, it was well worth it.

I would bet it would raise a lot of questions for kids who have never had experiences like the main character and it would raise a lot of emotion in children who have. My suggestion for this would be to partner read it with your child so you can discuss it with them.

My recap: 
 Trey attacked his father and broke from his pack--forming his own pack--when he was just 14 years old. He has a tendency to go feral when he fights. Now his father is dead and his uncle has taken over the old pack. His uncle wants Trey to come back and submit to him. Trey's response? Over my dead body. After a cooling off period, a battle to the death will take place. 
 Trey needs allies. He schemes to pretend to be a true mate with Taryn, a latent wolf and a member of the hated Warner family. Taryn agrees, to get out of a forced mating with an abusive jerk. 
 Both Trey and Taryn believe that their true mates died young, and therefore they plan to separate after the three months is up and Trey has defeated his uncle. But can they fight the unusual pull of attraction that they feel for each other? 
 My thoughts: 
 Trey is a damaged hero who had no childhood. He's dark and dominant, in the bedroom and out of it. 
 Taryn might be a latent, but she also a strong alpha female. She fights Trey at every turn. In the bedroom and out of it. Nevertheless, she's good for him. She also brings comic relief to the story with her sarcastic potty mouth. 
 This book is a scorcher. There is a lot of dirty talk and dominance in the bedroom. It fit Trey's personality, but I do have issues with the hero calling the heroine his %itch. 
 The plot includes the building of alliances, the build-up to the battle, and betrayal within the pack. But in the end, this is the story of Taryn and Trey, a poignant love story.

I remember years ago a friend recommended I read this novel that she was just in love with...I procrastinated since at that time I was heavily into reading suspense/thrillers but she pushed and pushed and finally bought the paperback and gifted it to me. I gave in and read it out of respect for my friend and absolutely loved it. It was my first venture into Urban Fantasy..as a matter of fact I didn't even know what Urban Fantasy was....but this book just knocked me on my ass and I fell in love with the characters, the writers and the story...This novel was the first in the Kate Daniel series. I have been a huge Ilona Andrews fan ever since. They are on my autobuy list and I have them in both ebook and audiobook so I can reread in a different media. Well, you can guess my excitement when I heard they wrote a new series in a similar vein. The Hidden Legacy series. 
 I went into the read telling myself that nothing could be as good as Kate Daniels so to keep my expectations down. I was 2 pages in and I was hooked. I LOVED Nevada and her quirky family. I adored that this extended family lives and works under one roof. IA writes fantastically strong female main characters and supports them with a strong supporting cast..in this case her family of younger brothers/sisters/cousins and a wacky Grandma and brittle Mother. I adored each and everyone and in the novel all their various characters traits, and personalities shone through. Nevada's nemesis and future love interest is Connor "Mad" Rogan is a man of mystery. He is uncontrolled, wild, a bit psycho but extremely powerful and lacks in any empathy for the human plyte at all. He is grumpy, rude, and you just have to love him. This is not a cuddly Curran but a nutso Mad...a wonderful love interest and I can't wait to read more and see how this relationship grows and changes. 
 One the the things IA does best is build a world that is close to our own but so different that you can get lost in the fantasy of it. This world allows for the intrigue of politics, the grisled ground of battle and the mystery of magic and allows IA to take her story in so many different directions that it will be easy to keep the stories fresh many books down the way! 
 Usually the first book in Urban Fantasy series is the worst...and if you go by this ...and this is the worst I so can't wait to read more they will only get better...and since I give this a strong 5 star rating...I'm excited to see how it can get better. For all you fans of Kate Daniels and Urban Fantasy, or magic based fantasy you will adore this...for those of you who love PNR there is enough hints to the love to come that you too will fall in love with Nevada and Mad. If you are looking for a great romp full of intrigue, action, battle, explosions and a great dose of humor you not 'should' but you 'HAVE' to read this first book in the exciting Hidden Legacy series. I so can't wait for book 2....it can't come quick enough!

This is one of Shakespeare's tragedies. It revolves around a man, Macbeth, who commits a series of murders to become and maintain his role as King. This play is a great look into a mind of someone who is so overcome with power and madness that he would risk everything to maintain the throne.

When you've exposed a weakness in battle, attack, don't retreat. 
 While I really like the hero, I wish I could say the same about the story. I felt that the romance was quite rushed up and there was just too much sex, too explicit for my taste. And they fell in love too fast. Personally, I felt that the characters could have been given much more depth and characterisation because the story had a great beginning. And Isabel found out Winter's secrets too fast..not much development there. 
 "Every gentleman you meet must voice his admiration, his wish to make love to you. And those are only the ones who may voice such thoughts. All about you are men who cannot speak their admiration, who must remain mute from lack of social standing or fear of offending you. Only their thoughts light the air about you, following you like a trail of perfume, heady but invisible." 
 Anyway, here is why I liked the hero-Winter. He does not believe in casual sex and is in fact a virgin.And once he falls in love, he does not mind that Isabel can't have children, he values her more than dreams which never existed. 
 I'm not like your society rogues, Isabel. I regard physical lovemaking as something sacrosanct to love. And if I loved a woman enough to take her to my bed, then I would love her enough to marry her. I don't intend ever to marry, ergo, I do not intend to ever get close enough to a woman--physically or emotionally--to make love to her." 
 Plus he takes tasks in his own hand-he does not depend on anyone else to do work. For instance, how he rescues kidnapped children and sets up a home for them even though he may risk losing his life in the process. He's protective, patient and can rein in his anger very well. And he's awfully blunt - something I like a lot ! 
 "Wear you social mask at your balls and parties and when you visit your friends out there, but when we are alone, just the two of us in here, promise me this: that you'll show me only your real face, no matter how ugly you might think it. That's our true intimacy, not sex, but the ability to be ourselves when we are together.

My initial impression of this book ended up being much more impressive than my actual feelings after reading it. I was intrigued by both the cover and the premise, both of which turned out to be, in my opinion, more interesting than the book. 
 I found this book to have an intriguing plot, which is what kept me reading until the end. I was hoping to get more from it by the end of the novel, but I found a few things to be missing from what could have been a very entertaining and unique story. For instance, the lack of world-building made it difficult to feel immersed in the story. We get only very vague explanations of what kind of world the characters live in, where the protagonist came from and how she came to be where she is now. I would have liked to have been given more details about how she learned to dreamstride and what exactly it entailed. After the initial prologue, you're taken directly into a scenario where she dreamstrides, which could have worked well if the author had taken the time afterwards to explain how the process works and how Livia came to become a dreamstrider. I also would have liked to know more about Livia's backstory and what the tunnel world is like, as well as the aristocratic world and how Livia fits into it. We only get Livia's feelings and memories about these things, but it would have felt more complete to know facts about them as well. 
 I also felt that for a majority of the book, things just seemed to be going around in circles. While each mission that Livia and her friends go on involved different people and one overarching goal, it felt like everything was just kind of repeating itself and that there wasn't anything new about what they underwent each time. The dreamstriding and the undercover operations began to feel formulaic after the first mission. I also found that Livia was very repetitive as well, harping on the same feelings and anxieties throughout pretty much the entirety of the novel with very little character growth. I found it difficult to like her as a character when she acted in a very self-deprecating manner for most of the story, and even her eventually belief in herself came at the very end, and only because it seemed convenient for the plot. 
 The ending felt a little rushed, with so much happening in the last 30 pages that it felt somewhat forced. I also found the ending to be a little cheesy and unrealistic, even for a fantasy novel. 
 Overall, I found that I kept reading because I was interested in the plot and was hoping for something to match my initial opinion of the book.

 Set during the American Civil War (my second favorite civil war, just short of the Marvel Superhero Civil War), it follows a hard-on-his-luck lad on his journey for....just...goddamned survival. This is all it takes for people to plunge into insanity: one night alone with themselves and what they fear the most. 
 Except this book is about what happens when you are forced to live with your greatest fear day in, day out, from the moment you're born to the day you die, generation to generation. Because it's hell on earth to face your fears alone; it's another level to know that your children will suffer under them, too. 
 All that said: Welcome to Black Spring! The little town with the big witchy secret. 
 Katherine was one of the 17th-century witches in the United States who was accused, tried, convicted, and then executed for witchcraft. But when she popped back up again and laid some black magic down, the townspeople realized they had only one way to keep her from cursing them further: capture her, suture her eyes and mouth shut, and bind her with iron chains. 
 Fast-forward to our day, the era of security cameras and apps that let you alert Big Brother whenever Katherine appears in your house and stares at your children while they sleep. The people of Black Spring know by now that you can't beat the witch, so they do the next best thing: they keep track of her comings and goings and hide her from "Outsiders" who come to visit the quaint old town. 
 Mostly, this works like a charm. But it's been three hundred years, and Katherine has plans... 
 On the whole, I really, really enjoyed this book. My only complaint is that pacing was a little even-tempo for my tastes, and I felt that it robbed the ending of some of its urgency. That said, I had more than one moment where I was scared, and I was recommending it to people before I even hit the halfway mark. 
 You shouldn't read this if animal death bothers you, but Heuvelt handles all the gritty issues in his novel with grace instead of rushing in for simple shock value. Meaning a lot of issues that I normally don't like reading about are in this book, but they're written so well that they never shoved me out of the story. Instead, they unnerved the bejeezus out of me in all the right ways. 
 I recommend this book to anyone who likes psychological thrillers, or if you're a fan of Stephen King's early work because this has the same surreal-but-close-to-home bite.

"If a violent battle destroyed everything you've ever known, would you be brave enough to save who was left?" 
 Kiernan and Wavery have spent their entire lives on the generational ship heading for a new planet where they will establish a human colony. As the oldest children, it is expected that they will wed and produce more children. However, when Kiernan proposes, Waverly isn't sure if she's happy or not. She should be happy, right? She should feel something more than friendship toward him, shouldn't she? Then things start happening that could affect not only their present, but the future for the entire colony. 
 Their sister ship, The New Horizon, should be a year ahead of them. When it shows up in the portholes, it is an object of concern and excitement. Excitement turns to terror when rebels from the New Horizon attack Wavery's ship and kidnap all the girls. In the melee, most of the adults are killed. 
 What follows is an interesting dual story between what's happening to Waverly and the kidnapped girls on the New Horizon, and events with Kiernan on his ship. Mildly reminiscent of "The Lord of the Flies", I found the story violent and disturbing with heavy emphasis on religion and fanaticism. 
 A dystopian story, the characters are complex, realistic and compelling. There is action (a lot) and romance (a little), and twists that will keep you guessing the outcome until the last page. According to the blurb, this is the first in a series. 
 Did I like the book? Not particularly. It is well written, excellently crafted, but it didn't appeal to me. There is no happily ever after, no satisfying conclusion, though it does end as it should. It's not a bad book, just not my kind of book. Those who love dystopian stories full of violence, fanatics, and with not so happy endings may like it more than I did.

I enjoyed this one much more than Nobody's Angel. 
 It's part 3 of the continuing Masters at Arms saga and this really is a saga. The story continues from one book to the next, there's a lot of story building in each one and they really wouldn't work as stand alones. 
 This time, we have the story of Master Adam and his sub Karla who is 25 years his junior. He rescued her from a potentially dangerous situation in a bus station when she was just 16. She's been in love with him ever since and they've become penpals in the intervening years. Adam, who was newly widowed at the time, thinks of her as just a kid and nothing more. He was aware of her infatuation but considered it to be a childish crush. He was wrong. 
 Karla walks back into Adam's life as a singer in his BDSM club several years later. Adam has a passionately physical reaction to seeing her and is horrified at himself. He has a traumatic childhood behind him and is beset in adulthood with all kinds of feelings of inadequacy and unworthiness. He believes he may have killed his father, he feels he was a bad husband to his first wife who suffered and died of cancer mostly in his absence due to his military commitments and he feels responsible for deaths of his fallen colleagues. Hence the book's title, Nobody's Hero. 
 Karla, on the other hand, considers him to be a hero and is still deeply in love with him. She knows he won't make a move and goes after him as a power submissive on turbo charge. Adam, knowing he can't escape her, decides to push her into an agreement she will consider intolerable to force her to safeword out and they start an extreme TPE master/slave agreement. 
 Karla takes to this like a duck to water, to Adam's surprise, and it isn't her that eventually has to safeword but both of them are aware that Karla's personality is fading to grey with this agreement. He's losing the feisty women he was, unknowingly, falling in love with. 
 And so the story continues on much in this vein with Karla constantly topping him - she's brought him to his knees before, can she do it again one more and final time? 
 I loved this story - Adam's deep lack of self worth was really tangible and he almost reduced me to tears on more than one occasion. Karla, also grief stricken due to the recent loss of her brother, is a character to admire - she's strong, resolute and cares deeply for Adam and will do anything for him. 
 There are a few supernatural elements to this series now with Cassie's spirit drawings in book 2 and Joni's (Adam's late wife) voice a constant presence throughout this one. 
 These stories are strongly about the emotional journey the central couple take. Of course there's a whole lot of sex, it's a BDSM novel after all, which is very hot, but it's more of a backdrop to the personal strife and problems and not the reason for being of the novel. 
 As always, we have world building besides the central couple. The next book, Damian and Savi, is set up nicely here especially with the epilogue and really has left me howling for the next one. Thankfully, it is due out next week. 
 So, all in all, a big improvement on book 2, I felt, and I'm deeply invested in these characters now and can't wait for Nobody's Perfect. Bring it on.

The best description I can think to give of Before I Fall is Groundhog Day meets Mean Girls. The main character, Samantha, and her friends are the high school girls that you love to hate: they're popular, mean, pretty, shallow, and have a strong sense of self-entitlement. From the outside, they're living the perfect life - until one day changes everything. 
 Lauren Oliver's writing is beautiful. Everything is described so well that you won't just visualize it; you'll experience it. All of the characters are so real - multifaceted and flawed with authentic teenage voices. Kent in particular was such a wonderfully crafted, unconditionally loving character that he has been added to my ever-growing list of book boyfriends. While I honestly didn't like Sam and her friends at the beginning of the book, I found myself quickly sympathizing with them as they became more self-aware and adjusted their personalities accordingly. 
 Before I Fall touches on many important themes: grief, loss, change, forgiveness. It teaches us that even the smallest actions can have drastic effects - both on our lives and the lives of others - and that we shouldn't take anything for granted. By the end of the book, you'll find yourself wondering what changes you would make if you were given a second chance.

I was lucky enough to receive an advanced electronic copy of this book from the First to Read program in exchange for an honest review. 
 This is the second book in a retelling of the Alice in Wonderland stories. I had not read the first book; in fact, I selected this book on a whim because my daughter has been an Alice fan-girl for the past year and I thought she might be interested in this series. Well, this book pulled me in from the start. 
 Alice and Hatcher have just escaped from some awful events in the city. They are trying to find a new place and a new life, and looking for Hatcher's long-lost daughter. They stumble into a long-running feud between the White Queen and the Black King that has threatened the existence of a village. When the witch enchants Hatcher, Alice is left to rescue him and the village children on her own. 
 It has been years since I've read the original Alice books and I can't say they caught my attention like this one. I remember the characters being original and the writing being clever but I don't remember being emotionally invested. In this book, I made a connection with Alice at the beginning. While it was somehow horrible to imagine Alice as the victim of human trafficking and later as an inmate of an asylum, I could empathize with the internal struggle she was undergoing to maintain a positive outlook as she headed into the unknown. 
 This book had a mystical, fairy-tale feel with dark undertones, yet somehow it manages to maintain a level of optimism and innocence that is appealing. If you like fairy tale retellings, I strongly recommend this book.

 I came across this book when I was skimming through some Listopia's on Goodreads. The list was named 'The Most Disturbing Books EVER Written' and I was curious. When I began this book, I kept wondering what possibly could be so disturbing about a bunch of small boys trapped in an island ( I was quite sure that this book did not contain any supernatural elements to suggest otherwise). Oh! how very wrong I was. As the book progressed, things started going out of hand rather quickly. This book deeply explores how unpredictable and animalistic humans tend to be when removed from the confines of a proper civilization. It is also a satire about power-play and in wrong hands, it takes no time to turn us all into savages. I was horrified at the outcome imagining all the violence and chaos. Even though I did not find the writing appealing; I am certainly trying to figure out whether the portrayal of human behavior and the circumstances in this novel have not been exaggerated at the very least. But then again we never know ourselves truly, do we?

The protagonist Honor Bright is a very principled Quaker. She is surrounded by other Quakers all of whom are opposed to slavery. Yet not all of them are willing to act on their principles. I feel that this is the central theme of The Last Runaway. Why are so many people afraid or unwilling to take a stand? Should they be judged for their inaction? When it comes to an important issue such as slavery, there were consequences for both action and inaction which are fully illustrated in this book. 
 I found this book compelling and provocative. It gave me a more complex view of 19th century Quakers.

Big step down from #0.5, and a let-down from 1.0. Sort of seeing why the series never went anywhere because there have been two two books where the story has been "bad monster, people die. more people die. even more people die. look, people dying. die, people die. monster monster die people die....quick victory" 
 It's wearying, drudgery, and a shame because this world had such potential. What it's lacking in these volumes is growth and development. I know there's always a sense of "avoid special snowflakes" in urban fantasy writing but that is exactly what this series needs, a bildungsroman that actually bildungs during its telling of the roman. 
 In both books 1 and 2, our hero has been strategically removed from the mentor, giving him greater agency but no way to learn and expand his powers. He discovers spells? They're taken away or burned. He creates something unusual? No one remarks on it but one minor villain. 
 Each bit is more frustrating than the last because while the first (0.5) book was exciting, books 1 and 2 have been repetitive, frustrating, and full of carnage without hope. There's no overarching story to root for or invest in. 
 I'm going to push on to book 3 and see where it takes me. I like the author's written "voice" and may try some other titles but this series didn't pay off the way I'd hoped.

 Recently I have felt slightly disappointed with the books I have picked up. I enjoyed them but I didn't seem to be sucked in. I needed Scarlet. I needed a book which shows me, after a busy month, how much fun kicking back with an amazing book can be. Scarlet is an amazing book. 
 '"Are you sure you don't want the tomatoes? They're the best part and they were grown in my own garden ..." 
 "Some of the intensity drained from the fighter's face. "I've never tried them." 
 Scarlet arched an eyebrow, "Never?" 
 After a hesitant moment, he released his drinking glass and picked up the two slices of tomato ... "Not what I expected." 
 I love books that grab you from the first chapter and does not let up. No "everything seems to be calmer now, let's wait for the next person to end up dead". Oh no, none of that here; constant action from the start. Answers lead to more questions, new challenges. I was kept on my toes the entire time. I would have read this book in one sitting if it were not for a postponed exam I had to revise for. Blasted weather. There was plot twist after plot twist, minor ones to major ones. There may even been a red herring, or maybe I was looking too much into it. It happens when you are constantly thinking, "What next, what next?" 
 One of the things I was most worried about when I read the summary for Scarlet, after finishing Cinder, was that all the focus would be on Scarlet's story and Cinder's would just be something happening in the background. I was genuinely worried. Thank heavens. It isn't like that. We get Cinder's point of view, quiet frequently actually. And it starts off just where Cinder ended. I loved finding how Cinder develops as a person and into her new lunar powers. 
 Having gotten to know and love Cinder's character in book one, it was definitely a risky move to introduce a brand new heroine into book two. I didn't know if I was going to be able to connect with Scarlet because she was not Cinder. Don't worry. There was no point in the book where the chapter switched points of view and I was disappointed; maybe only when there was agonising cliff-hanger. 
 Reading both Scarlet's and Cinder's story together gave Scarlet an added layer of depth that book one didn't have. I love how the slow development of understanding of how they are connected. This is Marissa Meyer, of course there has to be slow but delicious torture. 
 Out of all the new characters introduced in Scarlet, the one that most intrigued me was Wolf. Who is he? What is his past? Whose side is he on? Plus, he has the bad boy sex appeal hands down. The book only takes place over a short period of time, a very short period of time. It isn't very long for Scarlet and Wolf's relationship to grow. Billy Pilgrim has become unstuck in time. After being abducted by aliens from the planet Tralfamadore, Billy drifts in time through various parts of his life focusing heavily on his experiences in a POW camp after WWII. Historical fiction mixed with science fiction mixed with elements of a psychological novel, and oh yeah, partly true as it is based on Kurt Vonnegut's experiences as a prisoner of war during the firebombing of Dresden, Germany. Vonnegut writes, "There are almost no characters in this story, and almost no dramatic confrontations, because most of the people in it are so sick, and so much the listless playthings of enormous forces. One of the main effects of war, after all, is that people are discouraged from being characters." This is an apt description. It's easy to see why this has become a "classic" especially in the category of war (or, more accurately, anti-war) novels, but it won't be everyone's cup of tea (not that any book ever is really). I can't say that I necessarily enjoyed this book (so it goes), but I am glad that I finally read it. And it was interesting to look at Goodreads and see what my friends thought and actually discuss the book with several of them who vividly remembered reading and loving the book when they were in high school. Clearly it has the power to resonate with a lot of people. I definitely recommend it for those students with an interest in American literature as it holds an important spot in that cannon.

*SIGH* yet another book in which a promising premise ("fourteen viewpoints, one love story") is poorly executed. 
 Don't get me wrong, it's a cute, breezy little read and is perfect if you're looking to read something that doesn't require a lot of thought or if you're really into romantic comedies. 
 Gabe & Lea are painfully shy college students who have chemistry that they can't see but literally everyone in their lives notice. Even random people they don't interact with much, like a bus driver and the take-out delivery guy. EVEN A PARK BENCH AND A SQUIRREL NOTICE. It makes sense for their friends and creative writing professor to notice the (alleged) spark between them but I have a hard time buying that a waitress in a diner who interacts with them a couple times would root for them to get together. And do college aged guys really try to set their friends up rom-com style? 
 Most of their interactions are limited to them stealing glances at one another and blushing. IT'S 96 PAGES BEFORE THEY EVEN *SPEAK* TO ONE ANOTHER. The many, many POVs are annoying at times because they're often less than a page long and come off as choppy or really don't provide any information to advance the story - oftentimes, it's just someone rehashing that "YES, LEA AND GABE ARE BOTH ADORABLE AND SHOULD BE TOGETHER." A lot of the POVs sound the same, to the point where I was flipping to the previous page constantly to see whether it was Sam (Gabe's older brother) or Maxine (an 80-year-old waitress). 
 There are a lot of standard rom-com tropes that get in their way. Gabe has a "big dark secret". There are multiple misunderstandings involving one of the POVs, Lea's gay friend Danny. (Danny's gaydar tells him that Gabe is gay so he stalks Gabe in hopes of dating him. Another of Lea's friends asks around and finds out that Gabe is *NOT* gay, so while Danny is bummed, he decides to help Lea woo him. But when Gabe sees Danny & Lea together, he assumes they're a couple and that he should give up on Lea.) The "villain" of the story is a classmate of Gabe & Lea's named Hillary, whose sole flaw is that she's written as a one-note character. Basically she has a crush on Gabe and beats Lea to the punch when it comes to asking Gabe to be her partner in creative writing, which earns her the title of "skank queen of Cockblockville" from Lea's friends (who've never even met Hillary). 
 (Randomly, I really really really hope that there aren't a lot of college professors out there who blatantly try to sabotage their students like Inga does with Hillary, when she tries to get Hillary to give up creative writing - despite being a good writer - so that she can't interfere with Gabe & Lea getting together.) 
 I think this novel could've been improved with better editing - maybe cutting down on the number of POVs (or if the 14 POVs is a necessity, at least cutting down the number of POV 'chapters') to make the story tighter & move faster. The pacing also needs fixed. Like I mentioned before, it takes 96 pages for Lea & Gabe to even speak to one another. Their friends don't do the obvious and try to set them up until about 150 pages in. And nothing really happens to their "relationship" until the last 30 pages, so basically it's a lot of the same ol', same ol' and then a big rush at the end to fit everything in before the end of the book. I don't know much about Swoon Reads but I'm pretty it's sort of a vanity press which prints books based on votes by online readers. Maybe they should tighten their voting standards and hire some better editors. 
 I would give this book 2 stars for being so infuriating (SERIOULSY 3RD GRADERS WHO PASS NOTES WHICH SAY "DO YOU LIKE ME, MARK YES OR NO" COME OFF AS MORE MATURE. IN FACT, THINGS MIGHT HAVE HAPPENED SOONER FOR GABE & LEA IF THEY'D PASSED EACH OTHER THAT KIND OF NOTE) but the squirrel's POV is the highlight of the book and adds a full star.

The fourth in the Dublin Murder Squad series of mysteries, and once again it is very different than the other books. This one is practically a gothic novel, set in a creepy housing development that is largely abandoned and crumbling, located (of course) close to the location of a terrible event from our protagonist's childhood. 
 Our protagonist this time is Michael "Scorcher" Kennedy, who was the lead investigator (but not the protagonist) in the last novel, Faithful Place. Mick Kennedy is an interesting guy, hauling around a cubic ton of family baggage, largely in the form of his younger sister. This sister is a wrecking ball for Mick and everyone else in his family, who all coddle and excuse her manipulative and destructive behavior, never require her to actually seek medical treatment, etc. I spent most of the book debating whether Mick was a saint or major enabler, and ended up with he wasn't actually helping the sister with his drop everything and run attitude. Hopefully that will change with her latest antics, but I'm betting against it. 
 The most interesting relationship in the book is between Kennedy and his rookie murder detective partner, Curren. Kennedy's paternalistic attitude towards Curren and his secret desire for it to turn into the kind of partnership he's only viewed from afar - that was quite interesting. Moreso than the murder mystery anyway. 
 And for this murder mystery - I called it pretty early on. Doesn't detract too much from the book, as the mystery pretty much serves just as a background in these character driven novels. It was still entirely sad and horrific, but served the purpose. The thankless task of investigating what appears to be a domestic dispute rang true. 
 What didn't ring true and actually took me out of the story was the "American" dialect in the section where we were reading message boards (on pest control and wild animals). It wasn't a major or very important part of the story, but there was a chapter with a decent amount of message board comments that were supposed to be from Americans. But they were so poorly written (I say, as an American) that it was distracting. I have no idea if the many variations of Irish and English dialects used in these books are accurate, but that isn't distracting, as I don't know the difference. But using the Irish verb choices and just inserting in some stereotypical "American" slang was so weird to read. Not that I would do any better with an Irish dialect, but I'd bring someone else in - editing could have fixed this. 
 Other than that, it was transfixing and I read it in two days. Well done.

This is one of the best historical romances I have read in a whole- over 2 years, I believe. 
 I wasn't going to give this baby here 5 stars, but it made me teary in certain places, and just for that, it deserves full accolades. 
 I really enjoyed the story, which overflowed with tenderness. 
 The protagonists were a delight. 
 Coming off twitter and several conversations delineating how men are socialized to be these hard, unfeeling creatures, to not show emotion and to regard nurturing, empathy, and child are as effeminate, inferior qualities, women's qualities; and thinking about how much more strictly these norms must've held for men in years past ( yes I know this is a run-on sentence, but work with me here), I adored how Ms. Hoyt flipped the script with our hero. 
 Winter Makepeace embodies the stern, cold, impossibly self-controlled paragon of masculinity society so loves. But he is also, and it is plain for all to see - not hidden somewhere where only those closest to him can observe - he is as well nurturing, and has of his own volition dedicated his life to raise the kids in his orphanage. The care and worry and obvious love he has for his job and the kids under his care is evident in every page. 
 And of course, it also helps that Winter is our 'ghost of St. Giles' - a caped crusader who goes about vigilante style, righting the wrongs done to the poor, oppressed inhabitants of the dangerous slums of St. Giles. 
 It helps even more that due to his swashbuckling activities, Winter is a good male specimen - having lean muscles in all the right places. 
 It helps tremendously that Winter had a job and was a commoner, not nobility (As I read more about the aristocracy I am more appalled by them: how can anyone NOT be expected to work, because he/she happens to be gentry/nobility? Mind boggles). 
 I loved that Ms. Hoyt took time to explore a character who is so completely different from society's expectations and who was so secure in being such an anomaly. 
 As well I loved the heroine, who also bucked the trend. Here was a woman who was not nurturing in the least when we first met her. Of course there was a reason for that - barrenness. And for a time when bearing children must have been so important to a woman's identity, we get precious few stories about women who want to but cannot bear children. The emotion of Isabel's story was very moving for me. 
 And oh yes, I liked that Isabel was self-assured and knew what she wanted and would not apologise for living life on her own terms. 
 These two were people I really enjoyed meeting. I was entranced by their love story, which was so exquisitely tender, and by its resolution. I will say that while the ending a rather pat - it was still very believable for this couple, and managed to provide and excellent solution for the children issue while not taking away the sting of Isabel's barrenness. 
 There were a few flaws, but who cares about what the book got wrong/coulda done better after all this goodness? 
 Love, social justice, unusual characters which are unusual in an unusual way (not the standard for a romance novel at all); simple and tender story. 
 What more could you ask for? 
 But this book is a jewel. 
 Really, really liked it.
