The Law of Moses is a paranormal, new-adult romance novel written by the amazing Amy Harmon. I have read every book Ms. Harmon has written to date, and they all are wonderful, this one included! I knew nothing about this book going in to the reading experience so I was surprised to see her revisiting the paranormal genre. Her Purgatory series has a similar paranormal theme, which also presents an underlying mystery that keeps the reader guessing right up until the end. But that's not where the similarities end within her bibliography. Remember Josie and Samuel from Running Barefoot?? They make a few cameos in here too, along with the same geographical setting of Levan, Utah. Seeing Ms. Harmon pay tribute to her first few books made me smile, and it also gave me pause as I celebrated her much deserved success as a writer who consistently puts her heart and soul into what she creates. You're amazing Ms. Harmon! 
 The Law of Moses integrates family, spiritual, cultural, and emotional health themes throughout its story, while expanding the reader's horizon as to what (or who) just might be waiting for us on "the other side". This is one constant in Ms. Harmon's writing: her books are never "open and shut" types of reading experiences. Her writing is layered and the issues that have been gently incorporated within the characters and their journey stay with you, altering your perspective. But beware! The Law of Moses will have your emotions ricocheting from one extreme to the next and then back again! I felt joy, enthusiastic optimism, and the wildness that comes with growing up in rural living, but I also felt suspicion, hopelessness, and complete and utter devastation. I was shocked at where Ms. Harmon took these characters! But on both sides of the emotional scale, a feeling of love is consistent, even if it's just humming softly in the background. Because as the synopsis suggests, The Law of Moses is indeed a love story...it just happens to take the long-distance, backroad scenic route to get there. 
 My favorite quote: 
 "My mom always said negative attention is better than no attention at all. She was usually talking about foster kids who acted out. But apparently it also applied to seventeen-year-old girls who were in love with boys who didn't love them back." 
 If you have not read any of Amy Harmon's work before, do yourself a favor and take a look at what she has to offer. Each fan has their personal favorite(s), me included, but you can't go wrong with any of them. Check them out!!

Fortune's Pawn was a an exciting and entertaining read featuring a strong and capable heroine in the form of Paradoxian mercenary Devi Morris. Devi returns in Honor's Knight and Bach amps things up somewhere close to 11 for this sci-fi action outing. In the process Bach somehow manages to improve upon the already excellent Fortune's Pawn in almost every conceivable way. If you've yet to read Fortune's Pawn and you like action-packed science fiction with a strong female you should go do that now...there are definitely spoilers ahead. 
 Honor's Knight opens up almost right where Fortune's Pawn ended. Devi, can't remember much of anything from the last few month and every time she sees the ship's cook, Rupert, she feels a deep and physical revulsion. Of course, business must go on and Devi is forced to work the security on the Glorious Fool all by herself; at least for a little while. Meanwhile, she continues to see strange creatures that only Ren, the captain's daughter, can also see. Where Fortune's Pawn hinted at the major over-arching plot of the series Honor's Knight delves right into it...headfirst and with plasma shotgun blazing. 
 Bach, lays just about all the cards out on the table over the course of Honor's Knight putting Devi through the proverbial ringer in the process. Just about every question raised and every mystery hinted at in the previous novel is addressed in some way during Honor's Knight. The novel is packed to the gills with action; almost to a Michael Bay-sian extent. There are shattered planets, explosions, gladiatorial fights, underwater escapes, and giant invisible monsters. Honor's Knight definitely amps up the action and Bach proves herself as adept as her protagonist at handling the nigh fervent pace. 
 Bach fleshes out her world in Honor's Knight and I was particularly entranced by the Caldswell's daughter Ren. I love that Bach isn't afraid to inject a little bit of horror into her story and while she does lean on the creepy little girl trope (whenever I imagine Ren I see Alma) she also manages to interject a bit of the human horror and tragedy into the proceedings. Bach fleshes out the Aeon, the race of the Glorious Fool's XO Basil, as the ship visits one of their worlds and it was good to finally get a glimpse of a non-human world and learn more about one of the series' alien races. There is also more detail about the Xith-Cal and a further exploration of the events on the ghost ship encountered in the first book. 
 "More" seems about par for the course in Honor's Knight as Bach expands just about every aspect of the series. That also includes Devi's relationship with Rupert. This was, as in the last volume, my least favorite part of the story. That being said it's a fairly unobtrusive part of the story and its presence does little harm the pacing or the plot. If the only complaint I can really level at Honor's Knight was that the romance was unobtrusively present than I'm willing to call that a win. Bottom line if you like, fun, action heavy stories set in an interesting universe that you should be reading Rachel Bach's Paradox series. As much I enjoyed my time with Eli Monpress I have consistently found Devi to me a more engaging and purely entertaining read. Honor's Knight is a tight, thrilling, page-turner that highly recommend all fans of action-packed science fiction read.

Having spent some time in Asia teaching English, I had an unexpectedly large amount of overlapping experience to Kim in this book. Granted, my students were the rural poor of the (comparatively) open China, and not the elite of a despotic murderous gangster-cult of North Korea. But there was a lot that rang true when it comes to bonding with, and being both delighted and befuddled by, classrooms full of students from a different culture. 
 That part of the book was great, even if Kim seemed to squeeze 100+ pages of drama and pathos out of a fleetingly brief summer semester. Where this book really fell down for me was how limited the scope was seen looking at North Korea as a whole. Kim clearly has the experience and background to give us a lot more about this country and its path from the Korean War and into the 21st century. But she tacks pretty close to being mostly pure memoir here; a shame, because she could easily reach out beyond the gates of PUST and tell us a lot more about the country as a whole. That she doesn't, even after making a career from working with escapees and others working to clean up after North Korea, is just a shame and a missed opportunity. As a memoir concerned with a tiny slice of life in North Korea this is a solid B+. But as a book that tells me about North Korea, it comes up short. 
 Much like her students and her time at PUST, if only Kim could look beyond the confines of that campus and tell us more about this bizarre land of North Korea ...

I thought I'd like this more, I really did.

 Maybe it was the idea that women would allow themselves to be treated this way that really did it for me, Of course saying it could never happen is somewhat idealistic, as women are in fact treated that way and even worse to this day. But the idea that a whole civilization of educated women would allow such a society to take form? I just can't find it believable. (I know it may just be wishful thinking, but I hope not. I hope I am not wrong in assuming women would put a hell lot more of a fight.) 
 Then there was the fact that I heard of this as a feminist book, yet I don't see the feminist element. I hardly saw any strong women in this book. (Perhaps Ofglen only.) I suppose there is a certain kind of strength in quite resistance. In simply wanting to live as our MC did, but still for me it wasn't enough. She wasn't a bad character, she wasn't even weak, but to me she also wasn't strong enough. 
 The writing itself I liked. It was strange, but when you reach the end and realize what the author intended as the true nature of it, it made sense. I do however think the book could have flowed a little better. Sometimes it did seem to just stop. 
 Now the ending, I just don't know. I liked the ending of the story well enough. There was a certain sweetness to it, leaving it so open and still shrouded in mystery. However the ending of the book, the history notes. Those I was no sure about. It seemed like a very creative way to cover up an info dump. Creative, yes, but a dump nonetheless. 
 Now as for my confession, I think looking at the praise and the prizes it is very probable that the problem lies with me, but I just didn't get the message this book was trying to send. Was it a cautionary tale? meant to warn and scare? Was it about resistance? Was it suppose to show how easy a society can change? Or did it meant to say that people go along with anything and get used to any sort of life? 
 I just didn't get it. I'm not sure what it wanted to say. 
 On the other hand I believe it is going to stay with me, for a while at least. And that alone is worth something.

I love these books. Kristen Callihan has rocked my world for the second installment in a row, with a fantastic new story in an already extraordinary series. She made me laugh. She made me cry. And she made me love these characters. This book is sexy, surprising, and poignant, delivering 100% on the promise of its premise. I just finished reading it and I already want to go back and read parts of it again. 
 This is Adam and Eliza's story, one that Callihan has already laid the groundwork for in earlier books. Just to recap, Eliza kind of hates Adam's guts because he chained her spirit to him for years. The thing is, Adam recognized her as his soul mate and knew she was his only chance to end his 700 year curse. He was terrified of losing her, but handled everything terribly wrong. Now she has escaped him, but finds herself in another prison of sorts. Her grandmother, the Fairy Queen, is grooming her for something horrible. She lives in a gilded cage, but it's a cage all the same. As she learns more about what kind of monster Mab really is, she realizes she needs to get away. 
 Unbeknownst to Eliza, Mab has been keeping Adam prisoner for months, torturing him daily. Once Eliza learns the truth, she teams up with her old enemy so they can help each other escape. They set out together, trying to help Adam regain the strength Mab stole and searching for Fae artifacts. All this, while learning if they have a chance to mean something to one another. 
 Adam has been such an idiot in how he tried to force a relationship with Eliza, but here, I loved him so much. He has been unable to feel during all his centuries as the king of the GIM. Now that Eliza is in his life, he has so much to sort through... so much to lose. There is no doubt how much she means to him and watching her feelings grow for him is so very satisfying. I felt his fear and desperation, and later his joy, his wonder, and even his heartbreaking sacrifice. I cried, I'll admit it. 
 Eliza was pretty great, too. I appreciate how she stood up for herself, yet still kept an open mind. And when she opens her heart to Adam, when she finally tells him, ohmigod it is so good. There is no game game playing or artifice. Plus, the ending --wow-- I never saw it coming. I worry that some people might take issue with it, but I thought it was amazing. This. Book. Is. Amazing. 
 By the way, we also have some groundwork in place for Sin's book. It looks to be a doozy. I can't wait. 
 If you aren't reading this series, you should be. Simply among the very best of the genre.

I'm not sure what to say about this book, other than "Wow." From the first sentence, I was drawn into this dark, disturbing, and amazing (and amazingly well-written) story. I went into it thinking it was M/M romance, but it's not. There is a love story, yes, but it's not a romantic one in the traditional sense. It's a twisted, violent, and raw story of flawed people coming together in a highly charged environment (the Mafia) and learning to love and care for each other. The characters are human, deeply human, and deeply real and imperfect. 
 This is not a story for the faint of heart. There's violence (including sexual violence) and other behavior that most people would consider immoral or disgusting. And yet, even if I didn't like everything that happened, I was able to understand it and why the characters had done it. Mr. Voinov is truly skilled; he made me empathize with these characters even when their behavior was so far removed from anything I'd ever consider "right." 
 Was this book perfect? No. Is it for everybody? No. Will I remember it for the rest of my life? Yes. Will I read more by Mr. Voinov? Hell yes. He's an incredible talent, and my hat is off to him.

The Corrections is the story of the Lambert family - wife, Enid, husband Alfred, and their three adult children, Gary, Denise and Chip. The family is going through a crisis as Alfred's mental and physical health swiftly declines due to Parkinson's disease. In a last ditch effort to hold her dysfunctional family together, Enid makes a request that the family spend one last Christmas together. In the beginning of the book, none of the characters is likable and the family dynamics are bizarre and strained. But as the story unfolds, each of the lives of the various family members is described from childhood to the present and all of them become, not quite lovable, but at least understandable - and very human. 
 I was hesitant to read this book. Franzen's latest, Freedom, was not one of my favorites, in spite of all the praise and awards it has received. But more importantly, the similarities between the Lambert's and my family are very strong. There are 3 adult children in my family, and my father has been struggling with Parkinson's these past 4 years. I would absolutely DENY that our family is dysfunctional...but we do have our personality quirks and some of our interactions are a little strange. But aren't all families a bit quirky and strange? What I loved about this book was the ever present sarcasm and humor, surrounding, at it's heart, a sad story. I also enjoyed the stories told through Enid and Alfred's eyes. Old people never see themselves as old, and I found it encouraging and hopeful to realize that there is a young person inside all of us.

 "Hope can be a powerful force. Maybe there's no actual magic in it, but when you know what you hope for most and hold it like a light within you, you can make things happen, almost like magic." 
 *takes deep, shuddering breath* 
 I-I... 
 *sighs* 
 Where do I start? How to begin? How could I possibly find words to describe this utterly beautiful, perfect story? Anything I say won't do Daughter of Smoke and Bone any justice. 
 It's one of those books that you just... have to read, to understand where the praise is coming from. It's not your typical story (although some aspects can be easily referred to as cliche) and it's woven with magic. It's a story within a story, and one that will hook you from page one. 
 Summary 
 "Errand requiring immediate attention. Come." 
 In general, Karou has managed to keep her two lives in balance. On the one hand, she's a seventeen year old art student in Prague; on the other, errand-girl to a monstrous creature who is the closest thing she had to family. Raised half in our world, half in 'Elsewhere', she has never understood Brimstone's dark work now how she came into his keeping. She is a secret even to herself, plagued by the sensation that she isn't whole. 
 Now the doors to Elsewhere are closing, and Karou must choose between the safety of her human life and the dangers of a war-ravaged world that may hold the answers she has always sought. 
 When I first read the blurb, the first question I had was, "What is Elsewhere? Where is Elsewhere?" and it's a question that will plague you, dear reader, until the very end. The truth is, Elsewhere is Elsewhere. It has no place of it's own and, like in limbo, it is stuck between a rock and a hard place. 
 Karou's not your typical heroine, but at the same time she is. She questions everything and everyone and constantly carries this feeling of being split, of not being whole, around on her small shoulders. She's an art student whose life is split in two and who seeks answers from her loved ones. So when the truth begins to leak in the form of black, scorched hand prints on Portal doors, she needs to make a decision. 
 And fast. 
 The setting 
 We're in Prague! No, really, it feels like you are. The cobblestones, the buildings, the shining sun on your skin... it feels so real when described by Laini Taylor 
 It feels so real, like you're walking alongside Karou. Everything is described in detail, but not so much as to bore you, just enough to paint a vivid, gorgeous picture in your mind's eye. It's the perfect setting for the book, and so pretty. 
 WHO WANTS TO GO?! 
 Karou 
 Goddamn, it's been a while. Who doesn't love a real, true, kick-ass heroine? A punky girl with blue hair and tattoos, that Karou. I immediately fell in love with her persona - she's funny, sweet but a real teenager in the sense that she will have a bitchfit if she feels like it. She doesn't take no for an answer, expresses wishes on little and is just awesome. 
 I loved her. I loved her sass (that is now a word, ok?), her bitch-please attitude towards her ex-boyfriend and I adored that she could turn from normal teenage girl to kick-ass, angel-fighting badass in a matter of seconds. 
 At the same moment, she became aware of the pulse in her palms that had made her curl her hands into fists at her first sight of him. It thrummed there still, a pent-up energy, and she was jolted by the certainty that it emanated from her tattoos. An impulse overcame her to throw up her hands, and she did, not in cringing surrender, but with palms powerfully outthrust, inked with the eyes she'd worn all her life without ever knowing why. 
 She has got to be my favourite MC of all time. You just can't get enough of her. 
 This is coming from someone who rarely becomes attached to an MC, purely because they're always so boring. Karou, though, is not. 
 Akiva 
 He's a sexy mofo. Like, really sexy. It's easy to believe that such sexiness/beauty/whatever you want to call it, because Akiva isn't normal. 
 He's an angel. 
 He's kickass (if not a bit whiny at times, but that's okay). 
 He's beautiful. 
 Into kohl-rimmed eyes in a sun-bronzed face. Fire-colored eyes with a charge like sparks that seared a path through the air and kindled it... 
 Angel indeed. 
 He stood revealed. The blade of his long sword gleamed white from the incandescence of his wings - vast shimmering wings, their reach so great they swept the walls on either side of the alley, each feather like the wind-tugged lick of a candle flame. 
 Those eyes. 
 He's a perfect love interest and one you will love too. 
 Overall: a 
 must read 
 . If you're not into fantasy, magic or anything that isn't considered 'normal', then this isn't for you. But if you are... well, I have no idea what you're waiting for. Start reading already! 
 PS I will write a more coherent review at some point this week. Excuse my gushy fangirling feels.

I read a bunch of books in 2013, but I don't believe any of them captivated me quite like 11/22/63. 
 Full disclosure - I'm fascinated by the Kennedy assassination, and have been since childhood. Downtown Dallas, the Book Depository, the Grassy Knoll, the Zapruder film - the whole nine yards. So obviously, I was intent on getting to the heart of this story and what King had in mind for an alternate version of the events that unfolded in our timeline. 
 I wasn't disappointed at all by the re-imagining of those events, but I was very surprised by how emotionally affecting this story ended up being, and just how invested I ended up being in the protagonist's well-being. it's been a very long time since I've read a Stephen King novel to completion (at least the early 00s) and I'd forgotten how good he can be at making the reader care about a character. I guess the simple fact that by the end I was so busy rooting for the protagonist that I almost didn't care what happened to Kennedy is proof enough of the author's skill. 
 An aside - this book caused me to read 338 pages in one single day. For many people that might not be a big deal, but I am a V E R Y S L O W reader. Like, 300 words per minute deliberate. So for me to devour the entire final third of a nearly 900-page book in one day is telling of just how riveting that ending was. In my opinion Stephen King cemented himself as one of the great modern American storytellers with this novel. 
 I can't recommend this enough. It's imaginative, chilling, gripping, bittersweet and evocative all at the same time.

This is a story about Samantha and Jaxson, two people from two different worlds, yet they get each other and have more in common than they ever thought possible. Samantha's a senator's daughter, yet life couldn't be any more complicated for her. Jaxson has a troubled past that he can't seem to escape. Yet when their paths cross, love blooms. Although, it wasn't an easy journey there. Samantha's understandably slightly out of touch and Jaxson is so angry and brooding. But Samantha refuses to give up on him. 
 This story was so beautiful. I devoured every single word. The story was so believable, the characters were so believable and I fell in love with both of them. My heart also ached for them. They couldn't have been dealt a worse hand, yet all their troubles seemed so insignificant when in each other's company. The romance that developed between the two of them was slow-building and believable. And that ending...boy, that ending. I was not expecting that. It was so tragic yet beautiful and perfect. You'll have to read it to know exactly what I mean. Just make sure you have Kleenex handy. 
 Overall, this story is as close to perfect as it gets, and I strongly recommend this book to fans of Unlit Star and Bright Side. 
 **Review copy generously provided in exchange for this review.**

Light, fun, and totally sweet, Wish You Were Italian was a true delight. From the wonderfully described Italian scenery, to the adorable romance, this book was fantastic. Loved it! 
 The best part of this book, hands down, was the wonderful description of the Italian sites the characters visit. Not only the visual of the monuments, but the awestruck feeling you get when you see something so old and magnificent. The author did a great job encompassing what it feels like to see the ancient sites, which the history nerd in me really appreciated. 
 Pippa was a lovely heroine. She was a realistic, likable character. After being constantly pressured by her mother, she uses her exile to an art school in Italy to break free and follow her dream of photographing historical sites. I really liked her character and I thought she was great. 
 The two love interests were Bruno (the Italian) and Darren (the American archaeology student). They were both adorable in their own ways. Bruno was, well, as super hot Italian. What more do I need to say? But, seriously, he was utterly charming and could be a real sweetie when he wanted to be. 
 Darren was also amazing. This guy was so sweet and adorable and so heart-meltingly nice. He was the kind of sweetie that you can't help but fall for. Needless to say, I adored him as well. 
 The romance was very sweet. I won't say which guy won out, but I will say that the romance was well done an totally cute. 
 The plot was well paced and I was hooked the entire way through. The story was so fun and sweet as a spoonful of gelato (sorry, I couldn't help myself). I enjoyed every bit of it and the ending was absolutely lovely. 
 Wish You Were Italian was a wonderful, light, and fun YA romance. I really enjoyed reading this fantastic book. From beginning to end, this delight of a book and just lovely. YA lovers, if you want a light read that's guaranteed to make you smile, then this is your book. 
 *I received a complimentary copy from the publisher in exchange for an honest review
one sound I made during and after I read this one. UUUUUUUUUUUUUUUGGGGGGGGGHHHHHHHHHHHH
The best book in the series by far. This is the story I was waiting for.

MERMAIDS WITHOUT TAILS YES YOU HEARD ME NO LITTLE MERMAID IN THIS BOOK. 
 ooo JACKSON PEARCE I love your books. Yes I loved this one as much as the first two books. I was so happy when I saw my local library had this, didn't recognise it at first though due to the cover change. What is that about I loved the beautiful old style cover's. This book was as good as the first two books, which is unusual for me usually by now in a series the books are going downhill. Oh not in this one. 
 If you think this is about the little mermaid think again to me it was nothing like the little mermaid which I thought was a good move. I like the little mermaid but I think it would have made this book quite dull and boring. Which is the opposite to what I got from this. 
 Yet again this book has element's from a fairy tale just like the first two. Unlike the first two that had the bones of the Grimm brother's stories, this was based very loosely on the little mermaid which was wrote by Hans christen Anderson. 
 To me this was a mixture of different tales making up an original and enchanting mysterious book. It was also very dark in parts which I liked as it could have been more focused on romance. 
 Yes the mermaids don't have tails but have kept their legs shocking I know. The mythology in this book was intriguing always kept me wondering and hooked in this world. 
 I liked all the character's I always like that Pearce always focuses on her female character's. Also the fact that mostly all of the female character's in all the books in the series so far are strong willed and minded. Which makes a big change to what we normally get. 
 The writing again was extremely enjoyable and easy to read and get hooked into. 
 Overall a very intriguing fun fast paced fairy tale story would recommend to people who love fairy tales with a dark twist. 
 I think there is another book to this series so can't wait til I get round to it so far really amazing series :)

Can Hansel and Gretel get more creepy than the Grimm's version.... YES! SO F CREEPY!!! 
 Wow! Dark. Mysterious. Creepy. (Did I say creepy already, sorry!) 
 If you're into that kind of story you should read this, it doesn't matter if you haven't read Shadow and Bone, is some town folks... and all towns are the same. 
 So shut the window tight and make sure the latch is fastened. Dark things have a way of slipping in through narrow spaces.

Laurelyn is a one of a kind type of girl. Heart broken and jaded by the world she joins her best friend on a summer holiday to Australia. They plan on just having fun and being tourist for 3 months. Until Laurelyn meets Jack. Or Lachlan. Agh who knows anyway :P . They agree to a 3 month relationship. No strings attached and no real names. After the 3 months they will part ways. The best kind of relationship. Right? 
 I was told by a friend that I just had to read this book. She started reading it and just couldn't put it down. It was actually quite funny watching her rush through lunch hour to get as much of it in as possible. Now just imagine her enjoyment when the same thing happened to me. This really was a very hard to put down work of art. I loved it to bits. The characters were fantastic. Mrs McLachlan most probably my favourite character in many a book. Jack pretty much too. His straightforwardness was very refreshing and fun to read. 
 Jack and Laurelyn had some a sweet story. Their romance pretty much non existent, but still Jack manages to be one of the most romantic fella's I have read. I mean, what girl wouldn't love to get their feet rubbed after wearing some wicked heels? 
 Now, the ending... what is one to say? Uhhhh!!!! Torture. Safe to say, Cliffhanger of the year. But rest easy my lovely's, Book two Pain in Surrender is already out and already in my very eager hands so pretty soon you will be hearing about that too!
I simple adore, reminds me so much of me when I was that age...

Will write a longer review later, but damn, I forgot how much I loved this series. 
 I went back and reread book 1, and then read this in two sittings, and my big takeaway from this is that Helen is way too awesome for both of her love interests. They do not deserve a badass like her. She should just ride off into the distance with Darby and reign hell on her enemies as a lone warrior or something. 
 And it looks like she might just! 
 TLDR: not as great as book 1, but a strong defender against the dreaded "middle-book" syndrome.

Who's afraid of the big bad(ass) feminist? 
 Answer: Many, many boys. 
 It's a shame Marvel canceled this because it's fun, sly and smartass. And that scary F word -- feminist. Unabashedly so, in fact. Deal with it.

I loved this book. Zarek is definitely my favorite Dark-Hunter. Then Ash and now Jess. I loved Simi, too. She's impossible not to love. And despite his attitude, I liked Sasha, too. Nick is still my favorite Squire. Astrid was a gem. She didn't do anything to annoy me. I always worry about that with the heroine, but she did well in her job to judge Zarek. She saw what others (besides Ash) couldn't and I loved her for that. 
 Damn near everyone was trying to kill Zarek in this book. Artemis, the Squires, Thanatos. It was crazy. I was so glad Zarek hadn't been betrayed by his friend. Poor Ash. Stuck up there on Olympus with Artemis. I know he keeps saying the goddess has her own problems and she likely does, but man I hate that bitch. If Simi doesn't like her, she can't be very likable. I feel for Ash every time he has to deal with her. She wonders why he doesn't love her, it shouldn't be so hard for her to figure it out. But she is too selfish to realize all of the things she does wrong by him. 
 Finally we get to learn about Zarek and the crap he's had to deal with throughout both of his lives. When Valerius realized he and Zarek were brothers at the end of the last book, I wondered as he did if Zarek realized the same. Now we know that he did. And that while Valerius had tried to be kind to Zarek when they were children, it often only made things worse. We got to see why Zarek keeps so many people at arms length and why he has such a sharp tongue. It was interesting to see Astrid break through. I can't wait to see how he interacts with the other Dark-Hunters now that he has gotten some healing from her. Learning why he didn't have a Dark-Hunter tattoo was surely a shocker. 
 I was glad with the way things turned out for the most part. I just hate Ash having to deal with Artemis. I love learning little bits and pieces with him spread out through the books. I can't wait to get to his book.

Fact: I did not cry during TFIOS movie till the last ten minutes. Reason: I am about as sentimental as rock. 
 It was 1:30 in the am when I finished this book. My eyes were red and my nose was running. I have exams in two days and instead of reading at snail's pace I finished it off quickly and still suffer from a book hangover. 
 The characters are - what do I say - not fictional. You're one of them and their love is palapable. Taylor and Jonah has a zero soppy relationship, and the kind of love passed from a generation before her is inexplicable. 
 At first, I was thrown off by the infodump taking place. i had no idea what's going on, who is narrating and each page brought forth a dozen more characters. But I pursued and I thank myself. This book doesn't brief you about what has happened so far, just jump onto the train while it's running and go wherever it takes you.

I got the kindle version from Jillian, I have to say I was pretty speechless becuase I have never won anything from a favorite author. This last chapter in the series was more the I expected. I laughed, I cried, I even had to put it down and take a minute to gather my feelings. I have to say, I got a little worried when Keatyn way swaying g towards one life when I wanted her to choose another. But I had a feeling since the beginning she would choose the perfect man. Also what happened at the school, totally didn't think that would happen, then when they thought something happened to the guys and how the other guys did what they did......sorry no spoilers here so this is how its going to happen. Thank you Jillian for awesome adventure.

Where do I even start? I had so much fun reading this book. Probably one of the more enjoyable reads of my whole year. 
 First off, I loved Cath. Like... LOVED her. I wanted to put her in my pocket and carry her around and let her write fic all day. She was adorable and believably awkward/ self-doubting/ self-conscious without becoming irritating. Her narrative of her first few days of college felt so real that I wanted to cry (I DID cry when my mom dropped me off at college). 
 Second, I wanted to junk-punch her twin sister, Wren for most of the book. They started their fandom journey together and it was something the two of them shared in an intense way for many years. I get that Wren wanted to go away to college and try new things and become a new person. It's totally understandable, especially as an identical twin who's spent her life being part of a pair. But she didn't have to cut Cath out of her life so entirely while she explored her options and she REALLY didn't have to be mean about Cath's fandom stuff. I swear, when she was mocking Cath's fic, it physically hurt, like the worst kind of heartfail. There are some things that are just off limits. 
 That said, I suppose Wren redeemed herself by the end, but only just. She had a lot of bad behavior to make up for. I get why Cath just let her back in (they're twins... they just are ), but I kind of wish she'd snapped back at her a little more. 
 And then there's Levi. I can't remember the last time I read such a vividly-rendered, thoroughly engaging romantic lead. He was so real, so delightful... I felt like I was smiling irl every time he entered a scene, just like Cath. He was so wonderful, even when he was being a bone-headed dumb boy. 
 I loved this. I loved it because Rainbow Rowell has clearly done her time deep inside a fandom and knows our ways. It was wonderful to see fandom culture depicted realistically and lovingly. But I also just loved this book. This sweet, real heroine, her flawed family, her amazing boy.... 
 Sigh. I loved it. That is all.

Second time reading this book and, quite honestly, I found it better on the second go-round. Having originally come to this book from The Night Angel Trilogy, I was a little disappointed by this one and left irritated that I knew I'd be getting the second one when it came out. 
 Two years later, I decided to reread The Black Prism before getting a start on The Blinding Knife. I still remembered most of the plot, but I figured it wouldn't hurt to refresh my memory a bit. Knowing what was coming, I noticed a lot more of the little foreshadowing hints that I failed to pick up on the first time through. 
 There were some points that were as frustrating as I remember, however. Such as Kip and the continual reference to how he's so fat and out of shape and isn't it funny? 
 I get it. Kip's overweight. There doesn't need to be multiple references to it in every single one of his chapters. 
 Occasionally the Gavin/Dazen crossover makes things a little convoluted, particularly when he is referring to both of the brothers in the same paragraph. Thankfully this doesn't happen all that often, but the blurred line between the two of them can sometimes make it the whole thing a bit weird. He usually succeeds in making them differentiable, but sometimes it's just clunky. 
 Definitely would say that this benefitted from a second reading, though.

Why do I keep falling in love with Aussie books? 
 I have to live, knowing the sequels are out there, existing on the author side of the world, and I either have to wait a solid year or more, or shell out $20 shipping costs before I can read them. 
 But anyways. I loved this. Finally, a Sherlock adaption where the Sherlock character isn't a complete and utter asshole! Or, well, he's sometimes an asshole but at least he gets called out on it. 
 Again, this is one of those books where the characters are everything. Yeah, the plot is pretty solid too, but the main reason you read this is to experience these kids' lives and relationships and growth. It's fuckin great. Solid 4.5 (have I mentioned how much I hate that GR's rating system doesn't allow for half stars?).

Initial thoughts: How did I go from feeling lukewarm about Shadow and Bone to meh about Siege and Storm as well as Ruin and Rising to absolutely loving Crooked Kingdom? Leigh Bardugo's really grown as an author. The character development in Six of Crows duology was on point, as was the plot and plot progression. 
 I have to admit, I'm still not sold on the whole Ketterdam/Amsterdam and Ravka/Russia world building but in Crooked Kingdom there were less made up words that basically mangled Russian, Dutch and German. That helped me keep my mind in the story, and wow, did Crooked Kingdom serve! I loved the wit and the scheming as well as the complex relationships among the many characters.

I know that The Forgotten is really just filler, but I love it. A time parodox, an exotic locale, the struggle against nature itself - it was one of my favorites as a kid and holds up well. The whole plot is very fly-by-the-seat-of-your-pants, there's more humor than you'd expect, and you really get to see Jake struggle with the mantle of leadership more so than in most books; for once, to the point of real failure. It's fun, but also contemplative, which is what's so great about Animorphs.

The joy of having a six-year-old niece who loves to read (and be read to) is that when my sister-in-law finds a particularly cute book for her, I get to read it. This provides me with an excuse if I start to feel too juvenile for my own comfort. At any rate, "Tuesdays at the Castle" was one of those cute, light stories, somewhat in the same vein as Diana Wynne Jones' "Howl's Moving Castle". There were parts of the plot that seemed too simple, even if the story is geared toward young readers; but still, it was a fun read.

Was a little concerned about the length of this tome when it turned up on my doorstep (I have LOTS of review copies to read, this will certainly take longer than the others) but then I read the first chapter. 
 I like the way this guy writes. 
 And now I'm REALLY looking forward to getting to it properly!
I loved this Sookie book as much as the others. I'm going to be very sad to read the last one but am glad there is an after Sookie book :)
2 stars - Contemporary Romance

Lots of people have commented about the first half of this book being amazing and the second a bit of a let down. This almost put me off reading it but I'm so glad I read Ashes. The first part of the book is definitely more action packed, the main character is attacked by zombie like creatures and trying to find her way to somewhere safe. The second part slows down and allows the reader to get to know the character and sets the scene for what will hopefully be a trilogy. I can't wait for the next book and hopefully there will be more Tom.

Damn those blasted cliffhangers! I'm starting the next book RIGHT FREAKING NOW!!!! I NEED THIS 
 Annabeth + Percy REUNITE!!!! Piper and Jason!!!! I CAN'T EVEN AAAAAAAAAAAAA
I loved the book. Although a lot of bad things happen the end was sparkly, happy and amazing. Loved the atmosphere.

There are books that change your life...and I'm pretty sure this was one that has changed mine. Sometimes the changes are obvious and other people will notice them and other times they remain under the surface. I couldn't tell you what type of change has been made...but it's happened. This book was absolutely amazing, unlike Katherines I actually felt that it was going to be a great book from the first page.

Oh my God! What was that? Lord Henry Wotton, are you by any chance trying to brainwash me? Oscar Wilde, what have you done? 
 I started reading this book one week back, resolving on a twenty to thirty pages a day daily quota. Somewhere along the middle of the week I started ignoring Dorian Gray for my favorite jerk Sherlock Holmes. Then last night, I again plucked up the courage and to my complete surprise found myself unable to stop reading. Not something you expect from a Victorian novel. The story is absolutely brilliant. My goodness, how can anyone not like Oscar Wilde? Another entry in my all time favorite list!

Having read the whole series, I can say with certainty, this is my least favorite of all the books. It is so ooky. And what's worse - the ooky part was so vague I had to go back and reread to make sure I had gotten it right. 
 That was really the overwhelming piece of this book for me - even though it is not a big part of the book in terms of page count. 
 Clearly it didn't bother me enough to stop reading (as I said, I've read the rest of them) but it was a plot curve that really made this one drop in the ranks.

This is a dystopian novel set in the United States where everyone is required to take a test that places them in society. The novel switches point of views between Day and June. Day is an extremely notorious rebel who is the most wanted man in the country. June is a child prodigy who aced the societal placement test, and works for the government. When June's brother is shot allegedly by Day, June atttempts to apprehend Day herself. 
 I really loved this book, due to the genius both characters displayed. 
 I really the world building that occurred in this book, as it paints a really belieavable picture of the US. 
 The plot of the book is well developed, and really well written. 
 There is not a single thing I would change about this book!

This is not a great book filled with twists and turns, love and heartbreak. This isn't a glorious piece of literature. But once you pick up The Statistical Probability of Love at First Sight you won't be disappointed. 
 17 year old Hadley would rather be anywhere than where she is going, but she has no choice. However, what she considered to be a journey through Hell, only to have Hell as the destination turns out to be..not so bad. 
 It really is a simple story of boy-meets-girl, and in its simplicity lies its charm. While having romance as it's main themes, the book also focuses on various contexts like marriage, love and parental relationships - and it comes out strong on all fronts. 
 Well-written, humourous with plenty of light moments, as well as bittersweet parts, it is a light read for readers looking to take a break from the 'awesome' and the 'amazing'. I loved it!

"Summer is just a 3 month guilt trip" -Greg Heffley 
 A hard core gamer with no other interests, Greg Heffley's perfect summer would be spent playing video games with a bed sheet over his head. Unfortunately with his sports loving dad, crazy brothers, secret crush on Heather Hills, and squabbles with his best friend, Greg has a hard time achieving his "dream summer" although his real one doesn't turn out so bad.

My brother gave me this book for Christmas. 
 I'm hovering between giving this 3 or 3 1/2 stars. I will settle for the latter and round it up. This is the third Philip K. Dick book I've read (the others being VALIS which I disliked but maybe just didn't "get" and The Man in the High Castle which was alright) and this is probably my personal favorite. Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? has all of the multi-layered, complex, makes-you-think-about-the-nature-of-humanity sort of shit you expect from Philip K. Dick except the boiled-down story itself is rather conventionally straight-forward. I'm generally not a Philip K. Dick fan so I think that's a good thing.
This book was truly, strange and yet beautiful.

A fast read that explores faith, belief and how we can be cruel to each other just by the unknown. This was well written and surprisingly fast paced, despite being so long (close to 500 pages for a YA contemporary!), but I really enjoyed it.

Every time I pick up a book from this series I remember the first one and how good it was and how much they have gone down hill. This book is no exception. 
 For most of the book Ever is paranoid and woe is me, which after 300 pages is just too much. I just wanted to reach through the pages and shake her until she gets over herself and her situation. Yes, people won't always like you, it is not always your fault. Damen was so blah through out the book. 
 One of the only bright spots of the book was Haven, but she was so over the top that you could only take her in small doses. Roman is back and just as arrogant as ever, you just hope he gets his in the end. But when Ever discovers some secrets of his past you feel sorry for him and what happens to him. Jude seems to take a more center role and I am just not sure what to think of him, I think he has a hidden agenda. 
 It seems like what Damen struggled to keep a secret for so long is now becoming common knowledge as everybody and their brother is getting to know the whole secret or part of it. 
 With the ending and comments that people made it will be interesting to see what happens next.

This book was better than the first one! I actually cared about Mercy more. And, all in all, it delivered a pretty good urban fantasy story. 
 Adam claiming Mercy as his mate for pack politics? Great, if she would've kept going out with him past just a few dates. Now, the scene that got interrupted by his daughter.... That I wouldn't have minded reading a bit more about ;) Mercy talking to ghosts? That brought in some humor and a fun character. Mercy allowing Sam to kiss her? Twice?!!?!?! Gotta put an end to that. And wait... this is no longer a triangle? We don't need to add any more issues here, let's keep it simple! 
 Sam - He is still living with Mercy, he is growing on me, but more as a friend. I wasn't to thrilled with his original mentality of wanting Mercy because that was almost a sure ticket to getting kids. He is a good guy, and I admit he does love Mercy now, and genuinely cares for her, and I wish I could find a character that would suit him better. I was sad to read about his past history and his girlfriend losing his kid. 
 Adam - Where do I start? He is hot. He's all alpha, possessive, dominant, protective, and he should be more aggressive and forward with Mercy. Come on!!!!! 
 Stefan - What happens in this book threw me for a loop, specially at the end, once you read the book, or if you've read it, you'll know why. WHAT?!?!?!!? Anyway, he gets Mercy involved in all this vampire politics drama. I wonder if there really will be lasting effects... Vampire politics are a mess. 
 Warren - I was really sad about him getting injured. I'm glad to know he is more dominant than we thought, and that he gets back with Kyle in the end. 
 Mercy - I felt that she had more of a backbone in this story. She's growing, experiencing more things, and starting to feel more comfortable in what she can do. Just please give Adam a chance already! She played it smart, used the resources at her advantage, created a beneficial association with a cop that could help them in the future and at the end saved the day. She did good!

This is only my second foray into the Newsflesh world, but if this is any indication of how it's going to go, I better prepare myself for nightmares. 
 This novella is particularly interesting, since it takes place during the 2014 San Diego Comic-Con, the veritable mecca of of geekdom. I couldn't have picked a better location, as this whole series really has a focus on online media, blogging, etc. It just fits. 
 Right away, I was swept up with all the mentions of Firefly, Dr. Who, comic books, gloriously cheesy scifi tv! I was in heaven reading all the details. 
 As before, this novella really pays homage to media. The beginning of each chapter starts in interview format, and then goes into a timed countdown of the events of that day in 2014. Seeing the time slowly tick down obviously created a lot of tension, and the multiple POVs were definitely enjoyable. But somehow it just didn't work quite as well for me. Something about the flow, or the characters, were off. Whereas in "Countdown", I had an immediate connection to the entire cast of characters, I really didn't find myself becoming attached to anyone. Some of the writing felt a little forced (too many nerdy references mayhaps), but overall, it really didn't take too much away from my reading experience. I still thoroughly enjoyed it, and I felt it really added another layer to the world, seeing it up close and personal like this. It really is terrifying. 
 Overall, an enjoyable read, and well worth the couple of bucks. The fear is palpable and the tension stays strong the entire way through. 
 The author really knows how to use dogs for a good gut punch, though. *sadface*
I wanted to like this book because the main character had an alternative lifestyle, but I just couldn't get into it. I hope to try again in the future, but for now, this is a DNF
I have mixed feelings about this, but I'm glad to have read another classic. It was a bumpy ride for me, but one that I did enjoy at parts.

When I first opened the first page of the book I totally flipped out as you can see from my first status update. Seriously WTF! Natania...that bitch! I mean is Piper stupid? Does she have to sleep with the Sahar? Honestly? Couldn't she tuck it into some little hidey hole somewhere and be done with it? 
 Blah Natania was so bad for me I almost had to set this book aside because I just couldn't deal. Luckily though I got through it. 
 Now her father is not part of the Consul anymore, and she has no apprenticeship, Ash is back in the Overworld healing, Seiya and Lyre are captured.  Lots going on. Her father, man Piper's father is a piece of work. Seriously. A piece of work he is such an asshole to Piper and she doesn't ever contradict him or put him in his place, which honestly now that she is 18 needs to be done. He still thinks of her as this naive girl and while she still has some naive tendencies she's a lot more competent about the daemons that he is. And he treats her like shit. Drove me nuts. This was sort of explained away  he was poisoned by the Ra's  Yea such a cop out because he was still a dick before that. 
 Eventually Seiya and Lyre get found and Ash makes his way back to Piper....though nothing is hunky dory. Something though that bugs me is that Lyre expects Piper to tell him things but he has to keep is secrets. I suspect that Lyre was supposed to get his own series so we, the audience, would get to know him better, but who knows because that doesn't appear to be the case. 
 Overall the book we ok, there are some great moments, but there are also some no moments lol. Definitely enjoy the series but can't see how it all ties up in 1 book.

I'm so freaking excited to start this book! Reading the introduction only intensifies that feeling! 
 4.5 Bad Boy Bax Stars! 
 Welcome to The Point. 
 Wow. This book. What is it about "Bad Boys"? Especially bad boys with a heart? That is exactly what Shane 'Bax' Baxter is. Just released from prison after a 5 year sentence, he picks up his sweet as hell ride and heads straight for pussy. Not just any pussy, one he knows is guaranteed. Just after his post-coital bliss, he gets knocked around by Benny. Benny is Novak's, the bad, bad mans right hand man. They inform him that Race, his best friend is missing. They also inform him that Race has a sister and that they tried to get her to talk. 
 So next thing Bax does is go to interrogate this sister. This is where he meets Dovie, a plain Jane type of woman. But something about her drawls him to her. She brings out his protective side. This is where we get a glimpse into the man Shane, not Bax. And let me tell you, it is such a beautiful sight seeing the man behind the 'bad guy' label. He doesn't show that side to anyone but Dovie. 
 I really liked Dovie. She was EXACTLY what Bax needed in his life. She knew how to handle the bad guy while drawing out the good in him. 
 "You don't need anyone to show you how to be good, you're so much better when you're bad." 
 The story progresses with Bax and Dovie trying to get information on the where-abouts of Race. Bax needs to know what went down to put him in jail because things didn't add up to him. We meet several important side characters as well. Bax's half brother Titus is one of those characters. He is one you will love from the start, and love him even more throughout the book. 
 When confronted with all the bad that Bax has following him around Dovie had the best response. 
 " Some boys...they are just better when they're bad. Bax is one of them and I'm starting to think my brother might be one of them, too. I just have to be good enough for all of us to balance it out." 
 I obviously don't want to give away too much about the story so I'm telling you if you enjoy reading about men who are bad, with a touch of good, this is the book for you. If you like men who have a past and are trying to work through it the best they can, this is a story for you. If you love romance with a side of angst and drama, you will most definitely love this book. 
 I am a HUGE fan of Jay Crownover's work and will read anything that woman writes. I can't wait to see what she has in store for is with this series and with the Marked Men series. She can write the bad sexy men perfectly!

3.5/4 Stars 
 I would like to start off that I truly enjoyed and appreciated the story line and underlying theme in this story. Sometimes I get so frustrated with leading females in a romance because it seems they are so quick to change themselves, give in to a man's demand, not have enough self confidence, etc...the list could truly go on forever. 
 I applaud a story that shows you can be in love and still prioritize your wants/needs/dreams. I wish there were more strong willed heroines like this in contemporary romance!

3 stars is not the real rating: it stands for "I have NO IDEA how to rate this." More importantly, I don't need to rate it, it's a classic. My opinion has little relevance. So I will just list some bullet point thoughts, good and bad. SPOILERS. 
 -There are some beautiful and very thought-provoking moments scattered all throughout this book, but there are times where they do seem very scattered indeed. Excellent moments are usually the speeches and things like that, such as the Elder Zosima's homilies, Ivan's passionate diatribe on suffering and religion as spoken to Alyosha, Ivan's conversation with "the devil," the prosecutor's speech at Mitya's trial, and Grushenka's story about how "I gave an onion." All these scenes were very compelling. 
 -I don't know if it was the translation or if this is just Dostoyevsky, but the style could be really, really tedious at times. Likewise the story itself: I am not someone who needs a fast read. I like slow paces and thoughtful stories, but a hundred pages would go by and I'd find myself thinking "what happened here? Anything? Where on earth is any of this headed?" 
 -Also on the subject of style: while the speeches were often soaring, the actual prose was very, very dull. No description, no sense of place, and very rarely any striking turn of phrase. The emotions were conveyed with all fervor, and sometimes very powerfully...but not very beautifully, in the prose sense. 
 -I do like how each character is true to their virtues and, more commonly, their faults without any sudden unrealistic reversal of nature. Even Mitya, who seems to have some change of heart at the very end, after his trial, is still unwilling (unable, as he puts it) to bear consequences. He didn't kill his father, but he nearly killed Grigory, and so his final "nobility" while something...was not full-blooded. Grushenka and Katya remain teeth-bared towards one another. Ivan's religious struggles are not fully resolved and his attempt to do right was thwarted. Basically, nothing has a neat bow, and everything and everyone's a mixed bag. 
 -Alyosha was good-hearted but he also didn't really do anything except take the young crowd of boys and steer them right. He feared for those he loved, he helped them, he heard all their confessions and speeches, though I was deeply grateful for his goodness--it was a relief as compared to Mitya, Ivan, their father, Grushenka, Katya, or really anyone else except maybe Grigory. 
 -Ivan was the most interesting, which was why--despite it being intriguing that Dostoyevsky did it this way--I was most disappointed not to see anything about him resolved. Does he live? What about he and Katya? Most importantly, does he resolve his argument with God? Does he come to faith, or die in doubt? 
 -Smerdyakov: this too is very unresolved, in the story-sense. We can assume his motivation for murder, but only assume. We don't know. And we never really understand his despair, or why he kills himself. Is it to try and destroy Ivan too? Whereas everyone else's motives and thoughts are given lengthy explanation, Smerdyakov is left in the dark. His voice is not heard. Even Alyosha has nothing to say about or to Smerdyakov except that he was the murderer. I take it to understand we're meant to have compassion on Mitya in his almost-crime, but not on Smerdyakov in his actual crime. Why not? I mean, he was guilty, but why no exploration for him as for Mitya? Is it a class thing? He wasn't socially "important" enough? This bothered me. 
 -Perhaps because I'm more accustomed to British novels of this era and their sort of dry wit and primness, but everyone (except Alyosha) seemed WILDLY, impossibly dramatic. Always weeping and screaming and brimming over with emotion, and beating their chests and bowing to the ground. It's not that I disliked it, it was just really jarring. I don't know if this is a Dostoyevsky thing or a generally Russian thing, but though the pathos was frequently earnest, it was also often exhausting. This is often lampshaded within the text, where the narrator notes that people don't always mean the things they say in the passion of the moment, or where the prosecutor talks about the difference between feeling passionate and noble feelings, versus actually cultivating the character to back it up. 
 -On that token, there's a lot more up front acknowledgment of immorality in society. Grushenka is open known to be and referred to as a "kept woman." Katya's virtue is in question before the public during the trial, and Mitya and his father are both know to...well...basically womanize all over the place. Smerdyakov is a bastard by Mitya's father, and talk of drinking and carousing and dancing girls. This fascinates me because I feel like usually in novels from this era, all this stuff just 'isn't talked about among proper society.' 
 -I know very little about Russian culture past or present, so this was an introduction to pre-Soviet Russia and all sorts of things I just didn't know about, like how they kept referring to how the serfs were recently 'freed' and things like that. Also how deeply, deeply religious even the non-religious people are. It would seem, before the Communist era, Russian society was soaked in religion. This too was jarring, since I usually think of Russia in cold-war era atheistic terms. 
 -There is a lot of passion in this novel, not all of it comes to anything, but it's sometimes painfully realistic, and I just don't know what to make of any of it. I'm definitely glad I read it, but if asked whether I "liked" it or "enjoyed" it, I would not know how to answer. Had you asked me during my reading, I might have given a different answer a dozen times over depending on the day. Sometimes I was exasperated and couldn't wait for it to be over, other times I was mesmerized. Make of that what you will.

 Let me just start this review by saying that Jenn Bennett can do no wrong! Her Urban Fantasy series is among my top 5 in its genre, and now she's also landed a spot on my Paranormal Romance list with ROARING TWENTIES. The first installment introduced readers to bootlegging and speakeasies; now it's GRIM SHADOWS' turn to bring forgery and treasure hunting to life. Once again I loved absolutely everything about this book! Bennett's writing immediately sucks you right in, and then her characters and universe keep you hooked until the very last page. 
 I loved how different this novel was compared to BITTER SPIRITS; the 1920's feel remains at the forefront, and the story still revolves around the Magnusson family, but there were more paranormal elements in this installment and the plot focused on mystery rather than danger--although, there was a bit of the latter as well. I enjoyed experiencing the thrill of the hunt through both an archaeologist's POV, and that of an academic; putting the pieces of the djed amulet puzzle together alongside the protagonists was exciting, and uncovering the real truth behind it all was even more thrilling. Then of course there are the supernatural goodies like the Mori, fire giant, AND griffin--yes folks, this book has it all! 
 At first, I thought there was no way that the younger Magnusson brother was going to be able to compete with Winter, but of course leave it to Bennett to make me feel like a hussy! Lowe's a con man, a liar and a player so it's easy to discount him; however he's just so gosh darned charming with his sexy Swedish accent, way with words and handsome bod. It's hard to believe a single thing that comes out of this man's mouth, but he somehow manages to make deceit look hot. Hadley's his polar opposite with her funeral-like fashion sense, uptight personality and touching phobia. I liked how the author made her character professional yet racy at the same time; if Bacall's patrons only knew what she has on underneath her drab attire! I loved her insistence on being treated like a man, and her ability to control the Mori made her someone not to be underestimated. 
 It's hard to make a romance evolve from two strangers to happily-ever-after in one book, and have it be believable, but once again this author makes the feat look easy. I liked how Hadley and Lowe challenged each other on an intellectual level, and their opposing personalities made their dialogue incredibly entertaining to read. Bacall's fear of touch has resulted in a practically non-existent sex life, so when she finally unleashes her inner goddess the result is explosive! Slow burn romance, infectious chemistry, and squelching romp sessions--Jenn Bennett really can do it all! Her writing always packs one heck of a punch, whether we're talking action or passion, and a lot of the time the two go hand-in-hand anyway. 
 GRIM SHADOWS exceeded my expectations with more paranormal, more ROARING TWENTIES, and more romance; if I could live off Bennett's books and the hot Magnusson brothers, I would. 5+ stars.

I love it when you can tell that a book is going to be great right away. Such is the case here, with wonderful writing and a fresh approach. 
 Quinn Roberts has basically been in his bedroom for six months. When his sister and movie-making partner, Annabeth, is killed in a car accident, he has no idea who he is or what he's supposed to do with his life. Luckily, his best friend, Geoff, has had enough and rescues him from disappearing altogether. 
 He blames himself for Annabeth's death. She's been ignoring one of their film projects while she works on applications for college and getting ready for graduation. They fight about it, and that's the last time Quinn sees her. He won't even use his phone because he can't bear to see the last thing he texted to her. 
 The themes of redemption and forgiveness run rampant throughout the book. Not only does Quinn need to forgive himself, but Annabeth, too. It's about saying things out loud - sometimes we think that we are the only ones who see our faults, our problems, our secrets, when others are just waiting for us to reach out and speak first. Quinn's attraction to and pursuit of Amir is sweet and just what you'd think someone's first relationship would be like. 
 The movie references add a touch of realism to Quinn, as does the explanation about his writing style. Seemingly tough subjects are told in an honest but often amusing way. The characters and the relationships they have are, at the same time, simple and complex. And the more they reveal, the more real they get.

 I do not know what exactly my top ten favorite books are but this is definitely on the list. This was amazing. I got the ending I wanted except my only issue with this whole book is I wanted it to keep going, I wanted more because we got is so good I don't want it to end! But I think the reason there isn't more is that Mark has no reason to continue his log entries because he finally has other people around. I guess I might also have a minor issue with the fact that we don't see the crew back to earth. The many different points of view that the story was told from could have finished the journey without a log entry from Mark, and we know that Hermes isn't in tip top condition so I guess that we are just meant to assume they make it back but if we've learned anything from this book and space missions in general is that even the best laid plans aren't guaranteed. 
 I, of course, am not scientifically or mathematically minded so maybe not a single sentence of this entire book could have made a bit of sense but I don't care, maybe it's better that I don't know. I seem to want to talk about these characters as if they are real people and that this was a non-fiction story of survival and so that right there should tell you it was amazing, plus I listened to this on audiobook which made Marks log entries sound even more real. 
 As mentioned earlier, the book has many points of view. How exciting was it when Mindy Park realized Mark was still alive! At the beginning of this I thought for sure that Mark was going to die without anyone on earth ever knowing until the distant future when someone recovered his logs. Sometimes the book would have the voice of an unknown narrator stating facts that have occurred ie the HAB and airlock incident and marks rover crash in the soft sand, leaving the reader to not know if Mark was alive because it wasn't him talking about it yet. As long as the section of the book started with "log entry" we knew Mark was alive, unless of course he wasn't and this was a grand re-telling of events from someone in the far future who had indeed recovered those logs. It was a grand story, a great mystery, really addicting and I crave more books like this. 
 Another great thing that I've seen others say which I agree with is how funny this book is. You don't expect it from someone stranded on Mars but the character of Mark Watney is hilarious and manages to keep his spirits up through the whole ordeal. Don't see strength in characters like this very often! 
 Highly recommend this book to anyone!

I was quite surprised when I found myself loving this book because this is the kind of book I would never have envisioned myself loving. I can't put my finger on the exact reason why, but I have a strong feeling it's because I was expecting a supposed tear-jerker that would have me with more eye-rolls than tears. I wasn't expecting it to drench me with emotions. 
 This book lacks a solid plot but still managed to be engaging, which goes to show good storytelling. We meet eighteen-year-old Mia after an accident which kills her family. What more is that she finds herself facing her own gravely injured self and is for the time being, merely a ghost floating about. In the she has a decision to make, should she stay or should she leave? 
 The book is for the most part about her memories prior to the accident, the beautiful moments, the sad things, the people she loved and who she was. A few days ago, if you had asked me whether I would enjoy such a book I would have said no without much thought. 
 I don't think that simply talking about how the characters were great is going to do any justice to the story. So all I'm going to tell you is that they were indeed fantastic and realistic. 
 Music is a significant aspect of the novel, so if music is life to you, you'll enjoy this book a lot better. Mia is a cellist, her (supportive)parents were music freaks back in their days and her (lovable) boyfriend is in a band. Mia's parents were supportive and made a big impression on me. 
 All the characters made a big impression on me. Be it Mia's little brother or her best friend, Kim. That is what made the story even more heartbreaking - my undeniable connection to the characters. 
 This is the kind of book about life, death and the choices that will really have you thinking about your life and how amazing it is to be alive and loved. You know how sometimes you start crying, and you can't stop but something so good is happening and radiating happiness that you don't know whether to keep on crying or start smiling? And you just end up smiling between between the big fat tears? 
 This is that kind of emotional roller-coaster.

 I imagine this book may have some "fit" issues with different readers, but for me, a near 50 female married with children, it was perfect. First, I love the premise; vignettes from childhood to old age, each scene in a room; her childhood house, her college and first apartment, then her family home. We drop into her life at various consecutive points, and throughout observe the trajectory beginning with big ideals and ambitions and *spoiler:  gradually settling into a stereotypical housewife role. We see the closing in, as her dreams fall by the wayside, as she postpones forward movement for the current. We see the denial of self, but saddest is the lack of ability to commit to her choices; this is a woman who is filled with regret until the end.  
 The writing is so good. I loved the shift in pov, from first person to very distant 3rd person (and back). I loved the different symbols, mirrors, jewelry, teacups, etc. I loved the way the author explored different paths at the same time (such as the scene in chapter 35; the Bar, when two different scenes play out, one in the mirror and one in real life). It just really seemed to capture the aging process and how our lives narrow down as we make choices. The book is on the short side, but so much is here. Each chapter explored some specific idea or milestone, no words were wasted. Loved it.

 "I cannot tell you how thankful I am for our little infinity." UGH. I AM SO NOT FINE RIGHT NOW.

When I was first introduced to Isaiah in Pushing the Limits, I didn't have the best opinion of him. I liked him more than Beth but he seemed to be more into getting high than anything else. This book really dispels that myth and shows Isaiah's strengths and good qualities (he has also stopped using and was never really into partying). Like with Beth in Dare You To, Crash Into You gives a different view of Isaiah.

What makes this work however is the desire to see two broken people get a much deserved happy ending.  This is the one where we get all the answers. Vol. 10 is reserved for thematic and emotional cleanup, and Vol. 9 tells us the rest. Turns out Y is not the last man, he's one of two, and the other is Allison's father, Dr. Matsumori. He claims that it was his act of cloning Allison -- not himself -- that brought on the plague . . . and he's determined to finish the job. Both Matsumori and Toyota are taken care of in the end, but not before 355 is gravely injured. Allison's mother patches her up, but she won't be able to have any kids. This doesn't seem to be an issue until Allison points out that she's in love with Yorick, and has been for quite some time. But 355 keeps it to herself, and she and Yorick head to Paris to look for Beth, not knowing that Other Beth, Beth, Jr. (Yorick's daughter), and Hero are also headed there. Allison and Rose stay behind, as it's now Allison's duty to mankind to repopulate the Earth with Yorick clones until she can perfect the cure to the plague and bring back other men from the dead, clone-style. 
 I know a lot of people see these answers as a cop-out, but for me reading this series was never about finding an answer to what killed all the men. 
 We also get to catch up with some old faces in the two one-shots that close out the volume. The Obituarist brings us back to that supermodel that Yorick met all the way back in Unmanned, and Tragicomic catches us up on the Fish & Bicycle acting troupe who were putting on theater productions The Last Man, but now are focused on film. When that flops, they turn to comic books, and the series comes full circle as they endeavor to "create something new, something that challenges our audience at the same time it's helping them escape." They create The Last Woman.

 I always try to sum a book up in my review, but I am unable to do it with this book. I can only tell you about the beginning. So here goes: 
 Maya is a princess. She is one of many children born to a wife in the harem of the Raja of Bharata. She is cursed with the darkest horoscope. Since everyone knows a horoscope predicts the future, everyone is afraid of her. She is very much alone and her only joy is her baby sister Gauri. Since everyone stays away from Maya, she gets to run around and spy on the council and becomes her father's favorite. When her father deems the best way for Maya to be useful is to have her marry a prince to create an alliance for future wars, Maya does the only thing that she can for her father. Her wedding takes a complete wrong turn and Maya ends up being saved by the Raja of Akaran, Amar. He is madly in love with her and whisks her off to his kingdom... 
 Okay, that's it. That all the synopsis I can give you. That is really just the start of this story. There is so much more happening in this book. 
 The not so good: The romance fell flat for me. I wanted Amar and Maya to be on the same page in at least one scene. Amar seemed a very one dimensional character who existed only to love Maya. We don't get any of Amar's back story. He just appeared out of nowhere and swept Maya off her feet. He keeps secrets about her past from her. It leaves her hating and distrusting him so much. I mean, really, he should have known her reaction to the set up from their past shared experiences. 
 The good: I LOVED Maya! Her introduction was priceless. She is feisty and very much alone at first. Then she is swept away and adored. Then she is cast out and must prove herself. I really enjoyed learning about her. In a place where women end up one of many wives and living in harems, Maya's story really stands out. She will be remembered, even when she is forgotten (that makes a whole lot more sense if you have read the book). The best part is that her story is only one aspect to her, there is this whole destiny thing that makes her life with that bad horoscope seem like a bad dream. 
 I loved the blending of Indian culture with Greek mythology. This was so unique. Also, people subscribing to stars alignment when a child is born to predict that child's future was so barbaric. I love how those horoscopes were EVERYTHING when Maya was young and then later people didn't even care. That's how the world really is and I think it says a lot that the author made the people crazy like that. People are really crazy when it comes to a belief. There is a scene later where Maya uses belief to her advantage. 
 Also, there is a demon horse in this story named Kamala. Kamala pretty much stole the show in the second half of this book. She plays on words with Maya. Maya needs Kamala, but then... Gah! I can't say anymore. 
 This book spans years and still manages to tell a complete story. Also, I feel like the author answered a lot of questions in the writing. These myths and the rules brought up so many questions for me. How did that happen, why can't person just do this, what made this person so angry....the author read my mind and then inserted reason/backstory/explanation right where I needed it. 
 This story totally blew my mind. The language goes beyond being descriptive and is almost poetry. I could not only see the world through this language, but I could smell taste and feel it. This writing is in a class by itself. Really.

 A bunch of misfits banded together to create a better life for themselves. That is not an unknown concept in fiction - unless we talk about regency romance. Then it's the first time in the history of the genre, or at least the first I've read. 
 Being a poor relation of British aristocracy is not for the faint of heart. It takes a strong character to survive the bleak ordeal of hidden poverty. It often takes nimble fingers and a complete evisceration of one's pride and integrity, if one is determined to eat better for at least a few evenings a month. The alternative is to start working for your living, but the nobility in general abhorred such a solution. Still, that is what our heroes did to climb out of their pits of poverty. 
 I loved this humorous and poignant story. As a romance, it was clean and didn't follow the standard formula. Its protagonists were not standard either. 
 A seventy-year-old martinet of a lady and an impoverished old officer, an aged rogue with a penchant for thievery and a timid, colorless spinster, a fluffy-headed but pretty and kind widow and a young ravishing beauty - they are all poor relations, eking their miserable existence on the fringes of the pitiless high society. It takes guts for them all to admit their plight to each other. And then to try to improve their station in life by going into trade. 
 There is a lot of bitter-sweet humor in the story. The writing is solid, and the only flaw I could determine in this short book was too many POVs. 
 With so many characters to watch for, the main plotline is undetermined, sort of diluted. Was it a romance? I don't know. Was it a story of the clever poor tricking the fickle society? Perhaps. The protagonists were also unclear, as too little page space was dedicated to any of them. It seems a group story rather than a personal story. 
 Despite this one serious flaw, I enjoyed reading this book and I smiled all the time I read it. I will definitely read the next in this series of poor relations.
