In this science fiction book, scientists have performed an experimental brain operation on mice which augments intelligence. The white lab mouse, Algernon, is running through mazes at record speed. The mentally challenged Charlie, who does menial jobs at a bakery, is asked to be the first human to undergo the experimental surgery. He writes about his conversation with the neurosurgeon before the surgery: "And he said that meens im doing something grate for sience and Ill be famus and my name will go down in the books. I dont care so much about beeing famus. I just want to be smart like other pepul so I can have lots of friends who like me." 
 Charlie keeps a diary of his progress, and his spelling, grammar, word choice, and punctuation change as his intelligence increases. He undergoes emotional changes, and is able to see his childhood from a different view as his IQ zooms higher. He has flashbacks where he feels that the disabled Charlie is looking through a window at the new Charlie. Then the scientists notice changes in Algernon's behavior, and wonder what will happen to Charlie. 
 Daniel Keyes had a degree in psychology, had published science fiction stories, and had experience in teaching developmentally disabled adults when he wrote a short story called "Flowers for Algernon" in 1959. The story was expanded into a novel in 1966, and several movies have been based upon the book. The author shows a great understanding and compassion for developmentally disabled people who are often treated by other people in a superior, condescending manner, or made the butt of cruel jokes. There's a lot of food for thought in the pages of this book, so I can see why the story of Charlie and Algernon is so popular for classroom use.

This book follows part of her first year of high school as she attempts to navigate through her life in an attempt to build friendships with others, new skills, and understand what she truly believes about God.

 Because I've not read this for so long and have no desire to again I may be a bit rusty on some details. 
 My first issue with this is that most of the characters are simply not believable. I have never met anyone who speaks the way Hazel and Augustus do and frankly I'm glad of that. They don't sound like love sick teenagers, they sound like conceited, irritating ones. If I was to meet someone who speaks in the same way as Augustus, I would genuinely have trouble stopping myself from punching them. No 17 year old's speak like this for a very good reason. Also, Augustus' ridiculous cigarette metaphor really bothers me, even if anybody was so narcissistic, I highly doubt that another person would not only 'understand' it, but would think it was perfectly reasonable and even support it. Going into a shop to by them whilst he's in hospital! I am aware that he didn't smoke them but that is beyond the point. It was more important to both of them that he continued being a smart-arse than spending their short remainder of time together. 
 Hazel is another matter completely. The way she treats everybody around her is ridiculous. Her parents being worried about her and more than likely struggling to deal with the fact that their only child (as far as I remember) is dying, is enough for her to treat them like they were something disgusting on the bottom of her shoe. This really aggravates me. Yes, Hazel is in a situation that I, thankfully, can't imagine being in myself and it must be unbelievably difficult to cope with but that does not give ANYBODY the right to treat others like shit. She also consistently looks down on others. Sometimes because she perceives they are less intelligent than her. Sometimes because they are 'frankly not Augustinan'. Sometimes because they are an author who has their privacy invaded by two teenagers who think he owes them something (which he absolutely doesn't). The thing that bothers me most about Hazel's attitude is that the main 'moral' of this story is to live every day as if i might be your last and that even in spite of her awful prognosis and life expectancy, Hazel loves the things around her and lives a full life in the time she has. I don't believe that she does. Hazel loves Augustus and An Imperial Affliction, that is all. She demonstrates no love (or even respect) for her parents or her friends. 
 Isaac is my favourite character in this, he is the only one I believe in and the only one who demonstrates any form of real life feelings. The loss of his sight devastates him and, as far as I remember, he doesn't try to console himself with over the top metaphors, he allows his condition to ruin him for a while then picks himself back up. This is realistic. 
 The second issue I have with this is not the fault of the author but is an unfortunate truth. This is the single most wildly over rated piece of writing I have ever read. I am not exaggerating at all here. You only have to look at the reviews on this website to found literally thousands of people gushing about how this is perfect and the most profound piece of literature they have ever encountered. It simply isn't. There are some utterly beautiful pieces in this book but that is exactly the point. SOME. Almost all of these come from Isaac. However, most of the passages that are lauded over by people who love this book are over the top, pretentious metaphors. My thoughts are starts I can' fathom into constellations Erm, what? 
 There are some other issues I have with it, including the fact that Hazel's life only becomes bearable because an extremely attractive boy walks into it (and the reverse for Augustus). This is not a healthy concept for young people of either sex, there is a lot more to life than having a boy/girlfriend. 
 This is supposed to be realistic fiction and so much of what happens is completely unbelievable. There is no way that the charity involved would agree to send two terminally ill children half way across the world with no adult chaperone. It is unreasonable that Peter Van Houten would have been so kind to them, relatively speaking. These two pretentious teenagers turned up on his doorstep and he actually spoke to them. Obviously not in the way they wanted him to, but that is the point. They had no right to show up and even less of a right to question him about it then chastise him when he didn't have the answers. Frankly, Hazel and Augustus are both rude, arrogant and seem to think that the world owes them a favour. It doesn't! Yes, they are in an awful situation but it is nobody's fault. 
 I'm going to stop here because, if I don't, I will go on forever.

Shallow Anecdotes, not a Memoir 
 This is the story of 4 children who survived horrific abuse and neglect by their alcoholic father and out-to-lunch "artiste" mother, told by the second daughter. It's being marketed as a memoir, but if you're looking for another Angela's Ashes, or even Running with Scissors, this isn't it. The author appears to have learned nothing from her experience. She closes the book with her mother making happy toasts to the memory of the father, even as her younger sister (understandably) has taken off for California after being discharged from a mental hospital--after all, that sister had "never really applied herself." 
 There is no depth to this book--no mention of the mental anguish she might have felt when she escaped to New York and left her younger brother and sister in that environment, no mention of seeking help (Al-Anon, support groups, therapy, *something*) once she was in a position to make that happen, etc. This is a classic story of an alcoholic family, and the people play their roles admirably (The Hero, The Lost Child, The Scapegoat, etc). Too bad the author doesn't realize it. As I said, this isn't a memoir; it's a series of shallow, pseudofunny anecdotes. Not recommended.

 4**** 
 This is perhaps Dame Christie's ultimate achievement in mystery-writing. 
 Ten strangers are invited to a private island off the coast of England. On arrival they find that their mysterious host is not in attendance. Instead he has left a recording to be played after dinner, in which each is accused of having committed a murder in their past. Shortly after this revelation, one of them dies after drinking a whiskey laced with cyanide. The next morning another is found dead in bed. Clearly the murderer is on the island; a storm has made it impossible for a boat to arrive or depart. One by one the guests die - murdered in accordance with a child's nursery rhyme. Tension mounts as the ever smaller group of guests try to find their murderous host before they themselves are killed. 
 Talk about a locked-room scenario! The detectives try to puzzle it out in the Epilogue, without success. The murderer finally confesses in a missive delivered much after the fact. Somehow, I wish Christie has left that last chapter out. I kind of liked trying to guess. 
 Hugh Fraser does a fantastic job narrating the audio book. His pacing helps to build suspense, while keeping the story moving forward. His skill at voices and inflection helps to differentiate the characters.

I had heard about this novel's nasty teenage protagonist, Jorg, and bought the book because (as a writer myself) I was specifically interested in how a novelist could create any sympathy for an unpleasant protagonist; or, rather, whether they could succeed in this. 
 Well, the nastiest references to acts are near the start, when we casually discover that the protagonist raped, then burnt women alive. I almost put the book down at that point, but I wanted to know how, if at all, the writer would try and redeem Jorg. Well, he doesn't really. You can't. What happens is that so much occurs quickly that later events just swamp out the first few pages. Also, later explanations imply diminished responsibility for Jorg. None of that convinced me though. After finishing the novel I think it would have been better without those extra nasty references at the start. My dislike of the protagonist for that was never overcome, and the acts were beyond what was required to establish the antihero. I know that the author was partly inspired by A Clockwork Orange, but that doesn't mean that the worst parts needed to be emulated. 
 The rest of the book, if we ignore the unpleasant core character, is well written, well paced, always on the move, full of action and intrigue and duels of words. My biggest problem was not caring about the main characters. When you don't care if they live or die, and you're not given anyone good enough to root for, their causal deaths are just names dropping off a page. Attempts to redeem them later are paper thin. So Makin is a protective knight who risks his life to fulfil his role, and misses his wife and daughters? Square that with his actions at the start, slaughtering peasants and joking about the rape and murder of women. There's no consistency; it is not convincing; they're two separate characters with the same name. It's a shame because so much of the novel is excellent. I think the overt attempt to shock at the start (or to downplay the cruelty, which would be even more worrying) actually damages many of the later workings of the book. 
 I said the writing is good, though it is prone to cliche sometimes - I got tired of characters spitting on the ground to punctuate their sentences (it felt like it had to happen once per chapter). 
 Another mixed blessing is that the writer plays with setting in an interesting way; unfortunately I don't think it is fully successful, particularly in the twists of "ancient" language and the culture that survived. There are references to ancient authors; these tell us we are on Earth; an early paraphrase of The Wizard of Oz is a tip-off that we may not be in the past. Once we find out more it becomes doubtful that ancient authors and their comparably few works (almost lost to time now) would somehow survive where the absolute tsunami of modern culture in every format is completely lost. The reason this is so is for author expedience (so Lawrence can play the trick up his sleeve) for a twist that is then over quickly; it would have been better for the world-building if a more convincing survival had taken place. 
 I haven't read, seen, or played Game of Thrones, but it existed long before this book was written, and from the little I know of George Martin's work I imagine it was an influence on Lawrence. Even the phrase "game of thrones" is used twice in the novel. So if you like Martin's work, you may like this book (and its two sequels). 
 I enjoyed the adventure, and the way it was written: it passed the time. The bitter taste of the start was slightly milder by the end, though it didn't leave me wanting to read further books in the series. My reticence is furthered by the fact that each one is more expensive than the last - a publisher tactic that smacks of drug pushers who want to get you hooked and invested so they can charge more later. I got what I came for and am happy to say bye to the Prince of Thorns world and move on.

The third book in The Hunger Games series is called Mockingjay. I call it a wasted opportunity. This book is mostly set in District 13 and deals with the war effort and how the regime at the Capitol is taken down. So much could have been done in this book to make it a truly inspiring series. But everything is degraded down to action scenes, which were not even too compelling. 
 Katniss should have had more recognition and power in this book for the series to have truly worked. As it is, in spite of everything that she had done over the last two books, she was treated like a little child AGAIN. Considering how much I loved the feminist perspective in the first book, I just hated how the story deteriorates by making the heroine another pretty face to boost people's confidence. It was a pretty tame approach to take. 
 Another problem I have is with the love triangle. I was on team Peeta right from the beginning. The boy with the bread stole my heart but in the end, it looks like Katniss just picked him because he was around and Gale wasn't. If you are going to weave in a love triangle and build it up to such a crescendo of suspense, you owe it to the readers to resolve it properly. 
 This books plays around with characters and kills them off but we don't really get to know them. Prim's death was a waste. Right from the first book, I wanted to see more of Katniss' relationship with her sister. We are told that she is protective and she loves her, but we don't actually get to see it often. There was plenty of opportunity in this book to have developed that relationship but it simply does not happen. The same goes for Finnick. I could not even place the other people who died because I just was not paying attention to the action. 
 Which brings me to the unnecessary time and space devoted to mindless killing and butchering. In the first games, the action was all about survival and strategy and using your knowledge and strength. So it was interesting. In the second, it was about cooperation and pooling resources. It was repetitive but still not bad. This book was terrible because it was all about how to kill helpless people. Shoot here, shoot there, run up, run down, rest, clean wounds, shoot ... *yawns* I don't even care about the people who died because I never knew them. There simply was not the emotional connect that the first two books provided. 
 So many characters had so many stories to tell. Primrose. Finnick. President Snow. President Coin. The people from District 13 whose names I don't even remember because so little attention was given to them, yet we were supposed to mourn their deaths. I would have loved to know more about these people because they made the story, not Katniss. In this book, Katniss might have been the narrator but she was unimportant. I never got the sense that she was the actual heroine. But nothing was explained. This book also fell prey to the mistake so many authors make of drawing caricature undeveloped villains. I wish there was more of President Snow. I realise the author could not have dealt with each person's story in detail but if she wanted to make me care about their fates or make them believable, I need more context than just that the enemy smells of blood. (WTF, really!) 
 The resolution of the war also left me unconvinced. At this stage, it was difficult to relate to either side and at some points, it was even difficult to relate to Katniss. How exactly did they organise themselves in a democracy? Why have that conversation with Boggs about how important Katniss' support would be after the war to the elections, when they just send her home to breed? What happened to Coin's supporters? The end was too rushed and left me very unsatisfied. 
 That said, there were some brilliant moments in the book. I especially loved what happened to Peeta. I loved how Collins gave him a plot of his own and showed a different side to him. Though the beginning was slow, I enjoyed the first half of the book when people are trying to cope with the beginning of the revolution and trying to adjust to live in 13. I loved what Katniss did instead of killing President Snow, though by this time I was so thoroughly tired of the action that I was skimming and missed it completely! Then I got confused when she got arrested and had to go back to reread it. But that was a brilliant idea. 
 I read this book to get a sense of closure. Closure in the conviction of how the Hunger Games would never again take place. I did not get it. I would recommend this book just to finish the trilogy (since the second book leaves everything hanging), or just read the first book and be happy with it.

Okay, I read this quite a long time ago, but when I read it, I honestly had no idea about what to write for a review, besides, it's too short, and it's always really difficult for me to write reviews for short stories. 
 Well, anyway, this story starts telling us there's a plague spreading and a prince locks himself and some other people in a castle while everyone else is left outside to die. In there, he throws parties and whatnot. There's a particular one that is a masquerade party. Where the party took place are seven rooms painted all in different colors--one of them is black, but no one dares to enter it. 
 This is the point when things start to give you chills up your spine: Someone plays the brave and enters the room just to see something that was better lest unseen, and everyone is doomed for that reason. 
 My brother read this story last year in school, and this year, when I got Poe-maniac (Definition: A person who gets obsessed with no particular reason with either Poe as a person or his works), he told me that he had read this one and The Premature Burial (which, as all of Poe's stories, is really good, IMO) many, many times because he had liked them a lot. 
 Listen, my brother hates to read. In my family, I'm the only bookworm, so of course if my brother decides to read a book on his own, a once-in-a-lifetime kind of thing is happening. Now imagine if he re-read a book. That's something scary and never to be seen again! 
 You may have noted that I've rated all of Poe's stories 3+ stars. Well, that's because I simply love Poe. I love his voice in the books, the writing, the storylines, the messages he leaves with each story... everything. He's not what I call my "literary god," or my "life-changing" author, but I admire all his works all the same. 
 Needless to say, this is a must-read. I feel I've written more than what I should, given the fact that this is a short story, but that, I'm going to take the liberty of saying, is a good thing. 
 Do you like horror? Then this is just for you.

 A Little Something Different is, well... different. Different in the sense that, well, first off, the book isn't in the main characters POVs. Instead, it's set in 14 different viewpoints, ranging from Lea's roommate, Gabe's brother, the barista at the Starbucks they both frequent - even the squirrel that likes to scramble around their campus. 
 Inga is a creative writing professor and, every year, she picks two people in her class she decides will be cute together and does everything in her power to get them together. She specifically tailors her assignments in the class that you HAVE to work with someone, which usually ends up with her succeeding in her goals. 
 As the book progresses, you get to see how Gabe and Lea interact with one another through another person's eyes and how they are so obviously meant to be together. 
 Honestly... When I first started this book, I kinda hated it. I was doubtful that I would even finish this book. In the beginning, you can't wrap your head around such an odd book. 14 different view points? A professor who sets her eyes on her pupils in the beginning of the year, says "That's who I want to be together" and sets her sights to do so for the rest of the year? Random people getting involved in their lives? Hearing view points from a BENCH and a SQUIRREL?! 
 However, the more you push through, the more absorbed you become. Eventually, you forget how skeptical you once were because you can't help but root for these two and you get so emotionally invested (as you probably saw from my updates). 
 The best way I can really describe this book is that it's like a really cheesy rom-com tv series that you know isn't that great of a show, but it's still your guilty pleasure. 
 Honestly, I think if I read this at a different time, I wouldn't have given this a three star rating. While I found myself giggling at many parts, commenting out loud at others (yes, that actually happened), and really engaged in this book, there was a part of me that knew this book wasn't stellar. I'm sure if I read this during the summer or on another break (i.e., my mind isn't so scattered because of papers, group work and midterms), this book would probably have gotten a two or two and a half star rating. However, this book was definitely a great way to take a break from the stresses of school and just immerse yourself in a different world that was fun, cute and very unrealistic (in what world do university students have so much time that they're constantly going to parties and still getting As??? I've also never heard of students going out to eat so much. Additionally, having 14 different characters be SO engaged in your love life??? Yeah, definitely not realistic). 
 I know fiction books are called fiction for a reason, but bare with me. 
 One thing I definitely have to praise this book for is the different POVs. It was really cool seeing two people fall for one another, but not really being in their heads. A good point almost everyone made was that these two were so blinded by how much they liked the other, that they never realized how much the other liked them. A really good reminder to all that 1. Not everything is as it seems and 2. Sometimes, you need to take yourself OUT of yourself and try to think rationally and objectively. 
 All in all, it wasn't a bad book. I'm not sure I'd recommend it, but I think it's a nice book to read when you want to get away from your stressful days and just read a bunch of fluff. 
  
 Also, Gabe was SO cute whenever he spoke about Lea to anyone else. The hopeless romantic in me was forever squealing.

 Always Yours, Baby is the forth Baby Saga book by Airicka Phoenix. Each book can be read as standalones though, with interconnected characters. This is my first Airicka Phoenix book, but I will look for more from her in the future and I can't wait to go back and read the previous books in this series. 
 Damon Comb and Willa McClain have loved each other since they were kids, and have always been the best of friends. Though they do everything together, they have never risked their friendship by telling each other how they really feel. Though everyone knows but them, they are scared that opening up will destroy everything between them. Just when it appears that everything might finally be going their way, Damon's past threatens to ruin everything they are building. Can he find a way to make it go away while protecting Willa, or will they be over before they ever get a chance? 
 I really liked these two. They were so sweet it might be a little sickening if they weren't so adorable together. These two were literally everything to one another, how they were so blind to the love they each felt was beyond me. Damon was sweet and kind, protective and caring. He was always looking out for Willa, and I loved how great he was with her. Willa was a bit on the fragile side and was prone to letting her emotions get the best of her. But with Damon there for her she seemed to draw strength from him. I loved how supportive these two were of each other, and I couldn't get enough of them together. 
 Overall, this was a good story. It was very sweet for the first two thirds of the story with the last bit being a little more action packed. Things started to happen with Damon's past suddenly changing things for everyone, and I felt bad for the characters. I loved how determined they each were to protect one another, and you could really feel the love between them. This was a good quick and easy read with characters that truly loved one another. There was no cheating or love triangles, and I found it really refreshing that there was no one but each other for Damon and Willa. I would recommend this book and look forward to more from Airicka Phoenix in the future.

Of course everyone knows the story of the bullied girl who snaps after a cruel prank is played on her at her high school prom, but there were still quite a few surprises along the way for me. Some of the characters were a lot darker and deeper than presented in the movies, and some were only just glossed over. It was a lot more about the telekinesis and Carrie fantasizing about her revenge from the very start (I think her being a lot more timid and mousy all along makes the psychotic turn considerably more dramatic, by the way), and about the actual insanity and physical abuse of Margaret, all of which of course was quite disturbing. It was almost clinical in how some of the information was presented, and actually pretty convincing regarding the probability and cause of telekinesis. The back-and-forth between events and narrators basically as flashbacks and the investigation of the White Commission and subsequent interviews made for pretty compelling storytelling and some nice reveals. And amazingly it sent a terribly obvious message about not bullying that quiet, weird kid (or anyone, really) without being overt or heavy-handed, which is actually pretty impressive. I will say that it had some language and content that was a little much for me, which was annoying (it probably would have been five stars otherwise). I get that it's adult fiction, but they're still high school students and come on. 
 I've never read Stephen King, and this was a pretty good primer into his work (not that I'm dying to read more... it's not exactly my thing overall, especially more than the 200ish pages this was). I've always found this story fascinating, with its crazy combination of coming-of-age story/cautionary anti-bullying tale/psychological study/ultimate high school revenge fantasy, and the book only added to that by filling in the gaps with a lot of details. I think the movie(s) actually made some improvements to the story and characters, but the message was abundantly clear (BE NICE TO PEOPLE), and it was still interesting to get the full picture and to finally just dip my toes into bloody Stephen King. Yikes.

This wonderful tale makes for an absolutely chilling read, and for 80 pages, you're immersed in horror with valuable lessons attached. 
 In her short story, The Yellow Wall-Paper, Charlotte Perkins Gilman provides an incredible, semi-autobiographical tale of a woman slipping into the depths of madness. A nameless woman and her physician husband move into an old mansion as a form of treatment for her 'hysterical tendencies', and she soon descends into psychosis. The character becomes obsessed with the coloring and pattern of the wallpaper, and soon imagines that there are women creeping around behind it, believing that she is one of them. Over a few months we see in distressing detail how her failure to match her identity with the role of submissive wife that American society desired creates a descent from acuity to anguish. 
 In terms of feminism, the tale provides a clear damnation of the androcentric domination within medicine at the time. Gilman's attitudes are reflected in the character, as she craves to get out of the domestic sphere that is actually contributing to her insanity, not reducing it. This is a piece of work that is still incredibly relevant if we are to break down the walls that limit women all around the world, and we can only thank Charlotte Perkins Gilman for sowing that seed in the minds of many.

These are an ability that a select few have, they allow the person to change the colour of items, the shape of them, and also to make things grow, like a bud to a flower. These abilities are tested in the holding facilities and each girl has to successfully master one, before moving up to the next. If you're looking for something a tad different or unusual, this would definitely fit the bill. At times I wasn't sure whether I liked or hated this book, but in the end, it really stuck with me.

The story takes readers through the Spanish Flu epidemic and some of the anti-German sentiment on the homefront during WWI. The heroine, Ivy Rowan, is 25 and lives at home when the story opens. We learn that she has very recently recovered from influenza and when she discovers what her father and brother have done to a local German merchant, she leaves home in horror. 
 The rest of the novel focuses on Ivy's journey of self discovery. She moves out on her own, unusual for a young woman of that time, and in her own way, she seeks to make amends to the surviving brother of the German shop owner. Her observations of life make Ivy an intriguing character. The creepiness and the ambiguity of the world Ivy navigates also make for page-turning reading, as it can be hard at times to figure out exactly what is going on - and that's by design. 
 The romantic elements of the book left somewhat to be desired at times, but I did enjoy the overall story.

In Matched, we follow Cassia as she gets ready for her Matching ceremony where the Society will choose her perfect mate for her. All her life, the Society has made the best choices for her, what food she eats, what books she reads, what history she learns. But there is a problem with her Match that sends Cassia on a journey to learn the truth. I'm a big fan of the Matched books and can't wait to read Reached later this year. What I liked about Matched most was the romance between Cassia and Ky. It did seem at times that the dystopian element took a backseat to the romance in the book, but I didn't mind at all. Cassia was a great female lead and both Ky and Xander made great potential matches. The journey we take in learning about Ky, his past, and his possible future is very interesting. And the internal struggles Cassia has concerning her Society and the realities she begins to deal with are very intriguing. I liked Crossed as well, though it definitely has a much different feel. Crossed also brought us Ky's POV, which was a big bonus. And in Reached, we'll get to hear from Xander. Some might be turned off from Matched due to the high level of romance and the similarities of the society to The Giver, but if you like a good amount of romance in your dystopian novels, the Matched Trilogy is a good place for you to start. I gave Matched 4 stars.

 Where she finds things quickly hook up with their story. She's been sent into the thick of it. Her cousin Frances arrives, and they see what they can do.

The previous volume of Daredevil was critically lauded, and with good reason. Kevin Smith started the Marvel Knights: Daredevil run off with an interesting story, then we got David Mack's unique take on Daredevil and the introduction of Echo, then Brian Michael Bendis's fantastic run, Ed Brubaker's brilliant storytelling that took Bendis's work and kept the standard similarly high... then there was Andy Diggle and the Shadowland fiasco, then the putrid Reborn arc. Diggle's run was awful. Flat dialogue where before it sparkled, a big event story unsuited to the character... even Mr. Tan's awesome art couldn't save it. Then Reborn--the most hackneyed, rehashed, recycled, unimaginative, piece of shit story I can remember reading. A horrendous end to an otherwise fantastic volume. 
 So what next? What is Mark Waid to do with this shambles he has been handed? A legacy of amazing creative runs followed by a complete bollocking of a once amazing property? 
 He injects it with new life. 
 This is both a metaphor for the resulting work and an apt description of Waid's approach--in his own words he elected to "tweak the adventure to depression ratio", and decided to imbue Matt Murdock with a more swashbuckling presence, a lighter outlook on life, and grander adventures to pursue. Gone is the gloom that hung over DD like a heavy cloud. Replacing it are fun stories with a light touch and art that is fantastically inventive and unabashedly bright. Marcos Martin does the best work of his career here. If this doesn't make you a fan, then nothing will. 
 Overall this could have tanked. To take a dark character in a seedy part of the world and inject a bit of Errol Flynn derring-do? On paper it doesn't sound so good. But with assured confidence, great art, and stories that dash the reader's expectations, this is an exciting success, and a new chapter that refuses to try and recapture past glory, and boldly sets a new direction for the long-established character. Any complaints are minor, and don't affect enjoyment of the piece--the only one worth mentioning is that for long-time Daredevil readers it may feel quite jarring to encounter Matt Murdock's new lease on life (especially off the back of the Reborn arc), but if you can succumb to Waid's far-fetched emotional logic to explain said change, then you'll get the most out of the experience. 
 Mark Waid really is doing the best work of his career these days, as anyone who has read Irredeemable can attest. A good jumping on point for new readers.

I have to say, I've never really enjoyed the explicit nature of adult romance novels. I've always been much more attuned to the innocence and subtleties of YA fiction, and I've felt that constant explicit references to sex are only a ploy to distract a reader from poor writing, subpar character development, and a seriously lacking plot. 
 When I decided to read the Dark-Hunter series, I really had no idea what I was in for and after the first few chapters I almost gave up...ALMOST, but not quite. The fact is that regardless of the unexpected sex, I completely and unabashedly fell in love with Julian. While there were moments when I would have loved nothing more than to wring his neck, I have to admit that the softer and more damaged part of his character completely bewitched me. I found myself wanting nothing more than to reach out and wrap my arms around this man in an attempt to heal his pain. He wasn't "perfect" by a long shot...but some of the most worthy men I've ever encountered (both in reality and fiction) are those who are "perfectly flawed." In this respect, Julian doesn't disappoint. 
 I also found myself laughing out loud A LOT, which came as a sweet surprise considering I was expecting a very dark and brooding story. Kenyon's comic elements were placed perfectly, and she always seemed to know when a healthy dose of laughter was needed to lighten things up a bit. I also appreciate an author that can poke fun at her own writing (which Kenyon managed to do once or twice as well). 
 My biggest pet peeve with the series as a whole (which really I've only just begun to read) is the complexity of the reading order. The fact that there are so many 1/2 volumes that can only be found in anthologies or by downloading them online leaves a bitter taste, as does the fact that down the road the series will branch into TWO parallel series. The truth is that I'm lazy (and easily distracted) and would rather not have to utilize a roadmap in order to enjoy a story. But that's just me. 
 Overall, I am really enjoying the series as a whole. I'm five chapters into "Night Pleasures" (I skipped "Darkswan," but it really hasn't affected my understanding or enjoyment of the story), and so far I'm enjoying it IMMENSELY! However, I'll save that review for a later time. 
 Happy reading!!

I appreciate seeing all three characters dealing with their very complicated pasts, and enjoyed this novel's exploration of "ghosts," both as supernatural entities and as shadows of the past. Clearly I must also be a bad feminist, as I had a fair amount of difficulty making it through Roxane Gay's wildly popular essay collection. 
 Or perhaps it's not so much my inherent belief in women's equality as my inherent belief that essay collections should be read from front to back that's the problem. Feminist is divided into six sections - Me, Gender & Sexuality, Race & Entertainment, Politics, Gender & Race, and Back to Me - which offer an obvious and helpful structure to a reader not previously familiar with Gay's work, most of which has been published elsewhere before being collected here. We open with a "Hi, this is me!" before moving onto the subjects that most concern her and then circling back around to how the discussion of those subjects impacts her and her view of herself as a feminist. 
 Which would be great, except that the introductory essays are easily the weakest in the book, a slog only alleviated by "To Scratch, Claw, or Grope Clumsily or Frantically," a fantastic tale of Gay's love affair with Scrabble tournaments that's an unacknowledged but very obvious homage to David Foster Wallace. After that it's another eighty pages (filled with, God help me, literature reviews which are largely just synopses of the books discussed) before Gay finally, amazingly hits her stride and starts taking on pop culture (Chris Brown! Django Unchained! Fifty Shades of Grey!) in such a virtuoso fashion that you wonder what the hell her editor was thinking to backload all the awesome a full 120 pages into the book. (That's not my only question for the editor. There's at least two essays that should have swapped places due to a reference in the first that's much more impactful and meaningful if you've read the second.) 
 I'm completely onboard with Gay's view of feminism as something that's never 100% pure, but somehow I think her argument would be more compelling if it were more tightly packaged; cutting the excess third of this volume would have left it diamond hard, absolutely gorgeous, and cutting as hell. Unfortunately, bad editing undermines Bad Feminist and leaves it a mess from which you have to mine the gems.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Read the book before you read this because I'm going to spoil things. First off, let me say that it pains me to give this one star. Because the book, other than the bigggg problem I have with it, deserves five stars. It's fun, fast-paced, with fun characters who are well fleshed out (with one glaring exception), snappy dialogue, creative use of multiple types of media (social media, survey answers, chat, traditional prose, scene outlining), all in all a joy to read. Except for the ending. 
 Now, normally a shitty ending would only merit dropping a book to about three stars. But see, the ending in this case isn't just an ending, it's the premise that ties this book together. The whole concept of Wife22. The marriage survey she signs up to take, who sent it, and why. It starts the book off, and it ends the book, and therefore it is not just the end of the book: it IS the book. 
 So, what's the problem? Well, it's like this. We have Alice, a wife who is flawed, yes, but mostly charming and real. She's a failed playwright, a part-time drama teacher at an elementary school. She seems pretty normal to me. Other than her (understandable) angst over reaching the age (45) that her own mother died at. Her daughter (who she adores) doesn't seem to like her anymore. Her son may be gay and she's very supportive in trying to help him come out (even if he's not really gay, which he's not spilling one way or the other when we start). She has friends. She has support groups. And she has William. Her cipher of a husband. He doesn't really talk to her. He runs and likes to cook. He needs his space. And oh yeah, he acts badly at his advertising job and gets demoted from creative directive and then shitcanned. He basically comes off as a dick. While this is going on, Alice signs up to take a marriage survey, at the end of which she'll get $1,000. She gets assigned Researcher101 and is renamed Wife22 for anonymity's sake and is given many questions in random order. We don't see the questions, only the answers. And through the rather colorful scenes (playwright, see above) we get to see why she fell in love with William. 
 She and Researcher101 also begin to chat more than they should. By more than they should, I mean about 20 sentences, which is probably 18 more than she gets from her husband, so of course she falls for him. And he falls for her. She gives him tons of info about herself and about her feelings about William. Researcher101 gives her jack. 
 Have you figured it out yet? Cuz I did roughly 1/3 of the way in and was pissed off. William is Researcher101. But I thought there was still a way for Gideon to turn this around and give it some meat. If Researcher101 actually started sharing too, if William could use this proxy to actually COMMUNICATE and not just STEAL info from her, then it would be okay. 
 Uh no. 
 They almost have an affair. They don't cuz he doesn't show up for their first meeting at a coffee shop. Finally she figures out it's him. Her friends all think it's the most ROMANTIC THING EVUH!!! Angels sing. Roses rain down. Harps play. She realizes she loves him. Their marriage is saved. Oh and best of all, she gets him a great new job from the woman she stole him from when they first met--cuz that's the way the world works!! Wacky music plays. End montage with how things turn out a few years later with them and all the fun supporting characters. 
 Seriously????? Stop the romantic Rom-Com music and pull your heads out. In what world is this romantic? Her husband, in a unilateral move and a complete betrayal of trust, tricks her into telling him how she feels while sharing NOTHING of how he feels. She convinces herself that she loves him and he has to do NOTHING. No thing. No gesture. No apologies for being a whiny ass baby. He never knows she got him out of the job he found for himself (post it note ordering guy at a family run office supply store) for the VIP catering manager at a really big firm cuz, you know, she doesn't want to hurt his fragile pride and all that--plus again, guys don't have to DO ANYTHING to get what they want and need. I was simply appalled that with all these strong female characters in this book, this would be the ending we landed on. That this unilateral, betrayal of trust was going to be the ending of choice and deemed ROMANTIC. In my world, Alice told him to shove his fake research company where the sun don't shine and then broke it to him that she got him his cool new job, and he could use the big paycheck for her alimony and the child support. Buh bye.

John Ames is a 76-year-old preacher living on the dusty prairie in the town of Gilead, Iowa. He is nearing the end of this life, as he has been informed that his heart is slowly failing. So he sets out to write letters to his 7-year-old son of his history, his life, his hopes, his religious beliefs, his failings, for his son to read when he is a man. The letters, often meandering through a variety of topics, focus mostly on John's life with his preacher father and preacher grandfather, life in this small town, his two marriages, and mostly, on his own rumination on life and faith and light. 
 The back of this book states that this book is about "fathers and sons and the spiritual battles that still rage in America's heart". That captures the essence pretty truly. John Ames is somewhat of an optimist- looking for the best in people, hoping to forgive... finding immense beauty in the light that streams through the window. He is also a romantic, in some ways- wandering the town at night, sitting in the church as dawn arrives. His one failing is in his namesake- a boy that his best friend named John Ames in his honor. But the adult John Ames feels this as a failing- as his own wife and child died in childbirth. He cannot help but feel the lack in Jack (the younger John Ames) and focus on the most difficult of his Commandments- covetous toward thy neighbor. And when Jack proves to be a mischievous scoundrel, John Ames almost feels justification in his suspicion and unhappiness. But the narrative takes us down the path of reconciliation between the two. 
 This book has a grand plan, and it is executed well. But it feels slightly pompous to me, a little too self aware of it's proclamations of faith and understanding. This is why I gave it 4 stars. I'm not sure how it could have improved upon this point- it must certainly be difficult to "write from the pulpit" and not sound condescending, but all the same, it detracted from the book a bit for me. 
 As well as the times where my eyes slightly glazed over. I wanted to be able to put this book down and ponder the deeper meanings of some of the truly excellent points that John Ames brought up- but my mind would sort of go blank. I don't think I was meant for deep philosophical thought, haha. But I did enjoy the history of this book, the prose, the character of John Ames, and the imagery. It is a beautifully told story, even if I cannot truly appreciate the depth of it. 
 Here is a quote that describes the heart and purpose of the book pretty well: "I'm writing this in part to tell you that if you ever wonder what you've done in your life, and everyone does wonder sooner or later, you have been God's grace to me, a miracle, something more than a miracle. You may not remember me very well at all, and it may seem to you to be no great thing to have been the good child of an old man in a shabby little town you will no doubt leave behind. If only I had the words to tell you." 
 Did it deserve the Pulitzer? Eh. I don't really care about the Pulitzer. I've read several Pulitzer books that I thought were TERRIBLE, so I don't place much stock in the award. But do I think this was a good book? Yes. I do. It was sweet. 
 This book has been on my shelf for years. You know, I thought I'd already read it because it has a similar spine to a book that I know I'd read. It was only because I was looking for that other book that I pulled this one off the shelf and thought, "huh. Why doesn't this sound familiar?" So I'm glad I found a hidden treasure on my bookshelf. This is why I like to go to book sales- you bring home a bunch of books and then years later you find a treasure to enjoy. 
 I almost don't want to let this book go. I almost want to sit and ruminate on the nature of existence (and the question of why God can't "exist" because he is the creator of "existence" and therein lies a vocabulary problem, haha, according to Reverend Ames) and the beauty of the light, and write letters to my unborn children to tell them... anything. Something. 
 "A man can know his father, or his son, and there might still be nothing between them but loyalty and love and mutual incomprehension."

FULL REVIEW 
 If I'm being completely honest, this is the hardest review I've written to date. I won this book courtesy of Amy back in October and it's been sitting on my shelf staring at me ever since. I had every intention of picking it up and getting this bad boy reviewed by January 1, but everytime I reached for it the lump in my throat and throbbing in my stomach won out and I chose an easier read. I'm going to stop right here and preface two things: 1) If you are wanting to go into this book completely blind (though I'm not sure how you would if you've seen any marketing for it yet) then stop right here. I'm not going to spoil the read, but I will be delving into the content matter a bit and wanted to give fair warning. 2) If you have a rape trigger, I normally advise against reading rape-related material, but if you've ever been a victim of sexual assault I'd highly encourage you to read this. Hopefully it'll bring you some of the comfort you may never have received from your close ones at your lowest points. 
 "Violators cannot live with the truth; survivors cannot live without it." 
 - Chrystine Oksana 
 I'm sitting here with tears streaming down my face and snot pouring out my nose because I realized I've been searching for this book for the past decade; this coming October 20 will mark 10 years since the night I was raped. As difficult as it is to put those words to paper, it's in the hope that I can reach someone who is silently suffering from a similar situation that needs an anchor. My intention is not to make this review about my experience or go into intricate detail; however, I want to establish the foundation of why this book is so necessary for women like myself. The media for years has pummeled our society with the notion that rape is a rare occurrence and only is acknowledged in the most brutal of circumstances. While film and literature tend to portray rape as only happening at the hands of serial killers, kidnappers, and psychopaths, most women are actually assaulted by someone they know, not a stranger. I spent many years questioning the validity of my own assault because my attacker was a "good guy"; he had always been kind to people and never once given the impression he was a monster of this sort. This book addresses that more realistic and messy type of situation and helped ease some of the confusion I had struggled with for years. 
 Consent- it is the entire foundation for Hatvany's latest novel. I can already tell this book will ruffle some feathers and bring up all kinds of discussion and controversy amongst it's readers. The plot revolves around Amber and Tyler; Amber is the only "miracle" child of her over protective parents (I could easily relate to this being an only child myself and the product of 10 years of trying to conceive after being told having children might not happen for my parents). She's been shouldering the weight of feeling like she must succeed in everything to make up for the lack of other children her parents were unable have. Tyler moves in next door and becomes the older brother Amber never had; together they help each other through some extremely dark times, and although Tyler has always harbored feelings of more than friendship for Amber, she has never seen him as anything more than a brother. Enter here the controversy of consent. Without spoiling the read, we come to a point many years later that stops the reader in their tracks to consider their own belief on where consent lies. 
 All in all, this is the type of story that crosses genre barriers and holds us accountable for our views and how we treat victims. While this is a story about the attack and it's ripple effect of consequences, it's also a story of hope and redemption. Is it possible for someone to commit an unthinkable act and change? Can healing take place between two parties when this level of violation has occurred? I love how this book didn't make it easy for the reader; there are no clear cut answers or magical happy endings. The reality of the attack altering Amber's life forever is something all victims can relate to; while it is possible to work through the side effects (anxiety, depression, fear, and self-loathing) with therapy and sometimes medication, there's never a fix all cure that can take back that horrible event. This book did, however, present the right questions that we as a society need to consider as we continually see rape cases being paraded across the media in a trivial fashion. If you are looking for a book that will grab your heart and cause you to think about some really tough, but timely issues, I highly encourage you to pick up a copy of It Happens All the Time. Amy chose to limit the graphic violence and sexual scenes; the rape scene is really a very small portion but I believe this made the book all the more powerful and readable while being less showy for the shock value. This is a story that will stay with me for years to come; I'm so proud of the author for sharing via social media her own experience with being assaulted at a young age, her drive to help overcome the stigma surrounding rape, and encouraging the support of victims everywhere. 
 *Many thanks to the author and publisher for providing my copy and the platform so that I would have the ability to share my own experience.

Sometimes my husband likes to pick out books he thinks I will like, and the only problem is I've usually already read them! But when he pulled this one off the shelf and handed it to me to read the back, I was excited that he had found something I hadn't read yet, and I became rather intrigued by the premise. 
 Unfortunately, the book did not begin to live up to my expectations. The way in which the story was told, flipping back and forth between Grace's trial to the 21 days she and the shipwreck survivors spent in the lifeboat (39 in a boat meant to hold about 32, with little food or fresh water), made things rather confusing. I realize that Grace was meant to be an unreliable narrator, but I think more backstory describing her marriage to Henry and the cause of the shipwreck itself would have made the story stronger. I also get the sense that Grace was a rather manipulative person, so it's difficult to root for her in any way. 
 This book was far too introspective, focusing as it does on Grace's thoughts and opinions and motivations, as hazy as they can be at times. Getting into the mind of a shipwreck survivor would be fascinating, it's true, but there needs to be quite a bit of action as balance. It's also difficult to differentiate between some of the characters because few of them are fleshed out completely; they all seem to be rather two-dimensional and flat. 
 The Lifeboat is a fast read, I'll give it that, but now I'm grateful I checked this out of the library instead of spending money on it.

Nadia Turner, the protagonist of this debut novel, is haunted by the suicide of her mother. As a teenager, she acts out, and gets pregnant by the son of the local pastor and subsequently is haunted by the abortion her lover and his parents push on her. Her friend, the straight-laced Aubrey, lives with her sister and her sister's wife, having escaped from a sexually abusive boyfriend of her inattentive mother. 
 Does it sound excruciatingly Oprah-esque? There are touches of that, but the writing is good and the characterizations are mostly subtle. Besides the flawed and troubled mothers described in the story, the other "mothers" are a group of African American church ladies who act as a sort of Greek chorus commenting on the action in the book. I'm not sure those mothers added much to the work, but I may need another read-through before I decide. 
 I liked Nadia because of her prickly independence and in spite of some poor decisions. I was a little put off by the emphasis on her abortion remorse, because while I know that some women feel that way, I also know that many women don't, and the lie that women are psychologically harmed by abortion is used against us by anti-choice forces.

Paul Muad'Dib. Gurney Halleck. Thufir Hawat. Jessica. Leto. Irulan. Chani. Stilgard. Alia Atreides. Contest though you might, I submit that these could be the most solid foundation of characters in all of science fiction. 
 The plot of the novel centers around the interstellar maneuverings to exploit the desert planet Arrakis, home to a bountiful harvest of spice, or melange, which is costly beyond belief, and for which people will seem to do anything. The Duke Leto Atreides heads a House that is to move to and run the planet, until he is betrayed by another family, House Harkonnen. Thusly events are set in motion. The Harkonnen's motivations --and sources therein-- become increasingly clear as the novel moves on, and most protagonists roles end up metamorphosing entirely by the novel's final "chapters." There is a running theme of jihadist religion and cultish worship, and the natives of Dune (Arrakis), the Fremen, adhere to a cult of suicide and ritual violence that is disturbing in its parallels to modern counterparts and in their seeming equanimity with all of their faith's attendant bloodshed. Paul Atreides, it is no spoiler to say, inhabits a messianic character by novel's end, and events culminate in a fascinating meeting with a then mysterious character who has authored the small historical quotations and snippets that have preceded every chapter hitherto. 
 Much more subtle than most science fiction, "Dune" is one of the all-time greats, and, it will excite us to know, that a new film version is due out in the next year or two. Considering how mediocre previous TV and film versions have been, I am looking forward to material that begs to be on screen with the aid of modern technology. The biggest issue I foretell: who is going to play Alia?

Going into this, I thought the length was going to be a downfall. 500+ pages for a YA contemporary seemed like a recipe for boredom. To my surprise, I inhaled this book without even the slightest urge to skim.

Once again, however, the shadow of her father's political affairs disrupts her life, and not only has her recommendation letter to John Hopkins been withdrawn, she's forced to pick the bottom of the barrel job as a dog walker. 
 Andie is a serial dater. As someone who avoids an emotional connection, Andie isn't into long-term, committed relationships. Yet, here enters Clark, and his adorable Great Pyrenees, Bertie. With his adorkable fandom t-shirts, glasses, and oh! the fact that he's a successful fantasy writer, Clark is a bit of a dreamboat, let's be honest. Their relationship is sweet, beginning as an awkward admittance of feelings and graciously moving into something more. The thing is, though, I liked them, but I didn't love them. He's her unexpected everything, and I get that, but there's periodic encounters with her on-again-off-again fling, Topher, that I guiltily wanted more of. 
 As a YA contemporary, of course there's an underlying romance, but I felt more invested within the friendships. Toby, Brie, Palmer, and Tom were such a great group to read about. They torment each other in no other way than a loving friend should. Their text messages, filled with emojis, were the highlight of the chapters. 
 Andie's struggling relationship with her father was nice, too. He's not a perfect father, but he's not necessarily a bad one either. Their connection over the summer was incredibly genuine and heartwarming.

And with that, the Night Huntress Series come to a close. More with a whimper than with a bang. 
 In my thirty years on this earth, I'd already seen and done more than many people would in a lifetime, but I wouldn't have made it this far if not for love. That had been the solid ground beneath my feet when everything else around me had crumpled, and despite the danger and uncertainty of what lay ahead, I knew it would be again. 
 I'm going to be harsh, because I loved this series. The first two books are among my all-time favourites, with Cat and Bones being my favourite urban fantasy couple but also amazing, stubborn, and messy characters. All the previous entries in the series have been four and five stars. I love the humour, the paranormal aspects, and the fast paced action that has brought me excitement, despair, and happiness. This is maybe why I am so disappointed with this last book. 
 Firstly, it seemed to be rushed. They flew around the country and overseas, they stayed at different places, the met with different people (all who are known to the reader by now), and it all didn't seem to matter. Some seemed to be included just for the hell of it, because it was the last book, and there were a few leaps of faith in regards to where information was obtained from. It almost seemed like this was two books merged into one at some points. 
 When Cat was still human (well, half human really) it took her so long to be able to trust Bones, to admit that she loved him, and then it took another three books for her to decide that becoming a vampire wasn't really the worst thing in the world. But here, Cat develops a maternal instinct in two pages, and seems willing to do anything to save the life of this child who is her blood. After this revelation, I was expecting the pace to slow down some, as Cat realises what it may mean to be a mother, and how this would change her life, but she doesn't even have a conversation with Bones about it, seemingly alienating him from her feelings on the matter. 
 Suddenly, Bones and Cat doesn't seem to matter anymore. Towards the end he really seemed expendable, with Cat willing to die to protect her child and leave her husband to the ashes if that is what it took. I know characters grow and develop and whatever, and this book was kind of the entry point to the next stage in her life and gives her a good reason to depart from the world and isolate herself and the members of her close family, but it didn't ring true at all. Maybe if the reader got the time to know Katie, to see her and Cat together, perhaps then I could have grown to like their new situation. But we weren't given that time. 
 A few more issues: The fake out deaths were cheap, especially Bones since he had done this before, the brief trip to Romania was weird (even though this was likely to do with Vlad's own spin off series), Katie's discovery was too convenient, and Cat was a mega bitch to...well pretty much everyone who didn't agree with her. 
 This isn't the series that I loved so much, it wasn't even a shadow of itself, it was almost a completely different world. Even in the end, Cat and Bones didn't get any last moment together, something to show that they are going to try and make this family work. They just seemed so apart, like they were living in different worlds. It was sad to see them end up this way, and as they sailed into the distance, I found myself standing on the same shore as everyone else, waving goodbye to my friends but soon turning my back and not giving them a second thought.

I just finished reading Fellowship of the Ring, so I was quite glad to have this simplistic easy to read book to turn to. Eventually my relief wore off, and what I found was a completely unremarkable story. 
 I don't actually have a ton to say about this one, because there just isn't anything about it that captivates you, not even for a second. I nearly dnf'd from boredom, which probably would have been a good idea. 
 The story is set in Russia back in 1963. Through a series of events, our protagonist, Yulia, learns she is a psychic and ends up training to become a spy. There's also a meh love triangle and a bunch of other bland characters. 
 This story should have been fun and exciting, but the execution just wasn't good. We're thrown into the story and it took a few too many chapters for me to get my bearings. We then settle into a repetitive 'Yulia banters with other psychics while training her powers' plot line, which got pretty old. 
 Eventually Yulia went of some missions, but it was far from the badass spy action I'd been hoping for. In fact it was actually even less engaging that the beginning. 
 I would say this is one to skip. It's just not special or well written, so I wouldn't waste my time on it. I'll probably regret it, but I will read the last book just because I already own it.

This story was okay. My biggest complaint is that it felt rushed, not much happened for the first half, and the world lacked detail. I ended up skimming a lot, because so much of what went on during the early parts of the story felt unnecessary. It may have been a symptom of the length, which was too short to really support a decent subplot that I think it really could have used. Some of the details that were revealed through heavy telling (about the main character's wild tendencies, about the mountain city, about dragons, about the war, etc.) could have been better shown if there was space for supporting story lines. With subplots, the extraneous characters who were introduced could have had purpose, and there would have been greater opportunity to feel the developing relationships rather than being told it was happening. 
 This probably would have been a 2-star book, because unfulfilled potential tends to get under my skin worse than a genuinely bad book. However, this wasn't poorly written, and the core plot was fine, so I can't in good conscience rate it lower than 3 stars. Still, it could have been fleshed out into a much better book.

 "Be glad of your human heart, Feyre. Pity those who don't feel anything at all." 
 Where Feyre kills a wolf in the woods she's unaware of the consequences. Tamlin - a faerie - demands she give her life in exchange. She's forced to cross over the wall with her captor and live out her days in his manor. Feyre, however, feels less like a prisoner and soon discovers herself developing feelings for the handsome faerie. But a dangerous sickness plagues Tamlin and his land - if Feyre doesn't act fast not even the mortal world will be spared. 
 Despite being an entirely new series with no relation to Maas's other series Throne of Glass - this novel doesn't escape it's shadow entirely. Feyre in particular seems to have shades of Celaena all over her. They have some base differences (a love of painting vs. a love of music) but I didn't feel like I was meeting someone entirely new. 
 That being said the rest of the cast was fascinating. Tamlin and Lucien are fantastic together. Rhysand in particular is an interesting character, though it's a shame he didn't get more page time. Between Tamlin's sweetness, Lucien's wit and Rhysand's mystery there's a well rounded out male cast. Feyre's has sisters who are a little involved as well and Nesta in particular is a good female character. It would have been nice to see more female friendship bonds though. 
 Beyond the characters Maas has built a brilliant and interesting world. The faerie are all interesting, the different species really make the world colourful. It's interesting to see how they all react to a human. The courts are also fascinating - four seasonal, three time - although I would have preferred to see a little more of how the citizens of each court differ. It would have been nice if magic had been given a set of rules or more explanation but otherwise the world building was well executed. 
 There are several references to fairy tales. For the most part A Court of Thorns and Roses is a loose retelling of Beauty and the Beast - however, there are references to Cinderella and a few other stories if a reader is observant. Though these might not be intentionally they're fairly close to the original texts (ex. Cinderella/Feyre picking lentils out of ashes). Just little nods to older tales made the story charming. 
 Perhaps the most enjoyable part of the novel was the tasks and riddles that the reader gets to experience with Feyre. The tasks are certainly the most exciting parts of the story but the riddle is something else entirely. It's a joy to be given a riddle and then be allowed to work on the answer for several chapters before it's handed to you. 
 It's a good book - in fact I believer that A Court of Thorns and Roses has the potential to start a series even better than Throne of Glass.

 I'm not sure if I was aiming too low, if I'm just too old to read YA fiction now. But my reading tastes and abilities haven't really changed in the couple of years since I was smack bang in the middle of the target audience. 
 Overall, I wouldn't recommend. A good idea, but terribly executed!

I like Falling Kingdoms.

 Three kingdoms. Auranos, Paelsia, Limeros. Four POVs (at one time, five). Cleo, Jonas, Lucia and Magnus. It was hard to track everyone, to tell you the truth. Because just when I was getting comfortable with Magnus, the POV shifts to Lucia, or Cleo. Given that, I am not sure which of them I should give my support, so to speak. But Magnus is the most compelling among them. Intriguing, this prince was. =) 
 So maybe if you like A Game of Thrones, there is a possibility that Falling Kingdoms will appeal to you. The lack of regard to characters is a similarity. Why, you ask? See, the first character who was growing on me, while I'm still on the verge of attaching to him... he was murdered. After displaying himself as a formidable man to watch out for, he has to die suddenly. *grunts* I hate that author's trick. 
 Suffice it to say that I clung to Magnus to give me hope on this rather boring lament of Cleo and maybe Jonas, too. I couldn't care less what happened to them. So Magnus' character... his tortured soul was such a joy to watch. I have no qualms if he's good or bad. I just want Magnus to be this powerful, definitive, and convincing Blood Prince that everyone expects him to be. Bring it on, then. I'm sure Magnus will fit the role perfectly. *evil grin* 
 The few curveballs that made Falling Kingdoms a massive jolt to my system? I'm still deciding if I like them. I think I need to read Rebel Spring to say if this fantasy is worth investing my time and emotions to. I believe it can be better, so let's hope that it will be.

This book greatly frustrated me. It is one of a worrying trend of stories where the title refers to something that largely doesn't feature in the plot, so the blurb on the back cover is highly misleading. I think we should be allowed to get our money back on such books, on the grounds of them being mis-sold to us. 
 Set in the Victorian era, Faith is on the cusp of early womanhood. Her mother knows her place in society and plays the game well. Her father is a reverend and scientist with little respect for females. Faith wants to be a natural scientist, but she's trapped in a world of men who don't believe women are capable of intelligent thought. Darwin has recently published his 'On the Origin of Species' and religion is under scrutiny. Faith's father turns up mysteriously dead, and Faith goes on a mission to discover what happened. This involves learning all she can about a plant he kept hidden, which feeds off the lies we tell. When the lies take hold in society, the tree bears fruit. When you eat the fruit, you have a hallucinatory vision in which some truth is supposedly revealed to you 
 Such a great idea, right? Original and outlandish in all the right ways. The trouble is that even though we're told most of this on the back of the book, her father doesn't actually die until almost halfway through the novel. Before that, the book is largely boring nothing scenes only there to demonstrate how badly women were treated in that period. There is no discernible plot for almost 200 pages. It took me two months to read them. 
 When the tree finally appeared, the book was exciting and fascinating. I couldn't put it down. The characters seemed to change and gain life, whereas they had been cardboard cutouts before. I tried to forget the first half of the book had ever happened. The trouble is that in the end - well, I won't ruin the solution to the mystery, but suffice it to say that the ending focused again on feminism and the tree actually served no purpose. It didn't REALLY help Faith solve the mystery. The idea of lies didn't relate to the feminist messages that began and concluded the novel, which made it seem like the author had two distinct story ideas and didn't know how to mesh them together; it felt confused. 
 What's more disappointing is that the idea of the lie tree was wasted. If someone else used the idea again to write a really good story, it would be called a ripoff - but I still think someone should. To show you what I mean: there were so many good ideas in there that weren't followed through. You had a reverend struggling with his faith, a daughter NAMED Faith, who had a pet snake and spent all that time with a tree that dropped fruit that gave her knowledge. It was so clearly intended to be a Garden of Eden allusion. Near the end, one of the characters even said the tree was clearly the Tree of Knowledge. And you know what the conclusion to that was? Faith said, 'No, I don't think so. Because why would it be outside of Eden?' And then it was NEVER MENTIONED AGAIN. And if the tree wasn't meant to be biblical...what message is the author sending with a story about lies and deception giving you great insights and understanding? She also didn't really bother to explain where the tree came from, how it worked, why, etc. 
 It all smacked of a writer who didn't have it in her to think her ideas through fully. She could have written an incredible story about philosophy and faith and legends and beliefs, but instead she wrote a cheap modern mystery full of red herrings and lacking a clear solid plot. I also found all the feminism tired and outdated. No one in the modern world would relate to the concepts in this novel. If I wanted to read about historical attitudes to women, I would read either non-fiction or an actual Victorian novel. I think it was a huge mistake to make the whole focus of this novel be something so irrelevant to today's readers. 
 I give it three stars for the idea, and for some of the exceptionally clever, beautiful language - but overall, this book didn't work. I hear her other books are better. I'm not sure if I'll bother checking them out.

 I adore Alice in Wonderland retellings; it's always been one of my favorite stories. "Curioser and curioser." And I LOVED this book! The Collectors' Society was a wonderful and crazy twisted ride, perfect for the inspiration behind this novel. :) 
 Alice is crazy. Or so everyone says. Living in an insane asylum, Alice lives out her days taking pills and staring at ceilings. Until a stranger shows up, asking her to take a giant leap of trust and faith. Asking her to save the world she left behind and had made herself forget the last couple years. 
 Alice was such a strong character, a little crazy, a little tainted, a little cool on the outside. She's hiding a lot in that busy brain of hers, even when she becomes part of the society and the world as she knew it is turned upside down. It's a lot to take in, but I think she handled it really well. And she's clearly more than she seems at first. She may have seemed a little off, and she may be guarded about her past, but she's determined to do whatever is necessary for the people she loves. But she's not alone; she has the rest of the society. And Finn. 
 I loved the romance in this book! It's very slow-burning, and though they fell in love quickly (I'm pretty sure that whole line is a contradiction in and of itself), I believed it. I especially believed it when other characters show up and Alice's past starts to unravel. I was not as bothered by it as I thought I would be, because the way the author handled it was extremely well done. 
 There were plenty of other characters, though! And they all had their own personalities, and they all played huge roles in this story. They were all wonderfully developed. I loved the camaraderie that they shared with each other, and how they were such a close-knit group of people. You have to be, in a place like this. And you have to trust each other, although it took Alice a long time to learn that (understandably so). 
 Man, it's so hard for me to tell you about this book without giving anything away. There is just A LOT going on and you'll just have to experience it for yourself. Just know this: It's a retelling, so it's different from the Alice in Wonderland story you've heard, but the twists are awesome! I'm kind of dying for the sequel right now, especially after that ending. Not that it was a cliffhanger, but it just left me wanting MORE. 
 Out of the ones I've read, I think this is my favorite Alice in Wonderland retelling! It kept a lot of the same elements from the original and yet the author made it uniquely hers with the twists and plot that I can't tell you about. The Collectors' Society was a wonderful beginning to an intriguing new series!

 Characters

 Main Conflict

About half way through the book I felt a tension rose that necessarily wasn't there before. At times it was nice to feel America get tense and her boots shaken about the whole ordeal. And then the love triangle. Once in the book I counted a six page difference where she made up her mind on who she wanted to be with. This was more towards the book which ended up getting on my skin. I wished the characters could be more realistic or that America would get caught with Aspen already and leave the palace. 
 Author's Writing Style 
 *	I feel like the author's writing style is overall bland. I wished that it could become more poetic throughout the entire book. The only part where I think Cass as a writer took time is when she wrote what Maxon said and all his heartfelt lines. 
 Other Feelings 
 Love Triangles 
 *	Holy cow do I have a lot of feelings and emotions about this topic in general and in this story. After I finished a chapter about how America was head over heels in love for Maxon, not even a page later she would be back thinking or even hanging out with Aspen. Towards the end of the novel I see her pull away and make more of a decision of who chase after, which was nice to finally make more of a decision. But for goodness sake I can't stand the way Cass writes this love triangle. 
 Final Thoughts 
 *	After enduring and finishing this book I would have to rate this a 2.5/5 stars. Even though this book dragged on for forever and ever with the constant whining, I still somehow magically liked the ending and I how no clue as to why that would happen. I decided to rate this book a 2.5/5 stars. It would have been 3 stars but oh goodness America is to blame for that star rating with her love triangle of not making up her mind and acting like a two year going through their "terrible two stage". While Maxon on the other hand did everything right. He saw opportunity as America was being distant and he took full advantage for it! And Aspen... lets not even go there. What an irritating little shit head who just either needs to run away from the castle OR gets special treatment and magically gets killed off by one of the rebel groups. I don't know if I will be picking up the third book.
