As a whole, I've enjoyed The Underland Chronicles. However, I do find myself a little disappointed that almost every series or trilogy ends with a grand war. Or more specifically, a last book where a single war takes up the entire plot. Yes, it does make for compelling reading and I was engaged the whole time, but I feel like it's somehow . . . wrong (?) to need all this violence in order to craft intensity for the climax (i.e. the last book). It also seems like a Collins trademark now, her last books need to be ridiculously war-centered with way too much gore and killing. 
 This aspect certainly seemed overdone in Gregor and the Code of Claw. I couldn't tell you how much imagery included blood dripping, spurting, running down and mixing with someone else's blood, seeping, etc. Not to mention this is for a young audience. I feel in order to create this emotional and action-packed potency she needed to make everything as violent as possible, and it made me feel like she lost track of the children she was writing for. There was even a scene where a rat ripped the head off another. It just seemed like too much, like she's feeding the stereotype that children need action and violence to be entertained. There certainly was a lot of that here. 
 All that aside, though, it wasn't all bad. I enjoyed Lizzie's role, and the softer side of Ripred. I felt like the relationship between Luxa and Gregor became a bit planned and awkward (including making Luxa's role "smaller" because she needed to be protected all the time since she was a woman and beloved by the male protagonist, despite her skill). 
 But all in all this series has some beautiful moments and great story lines that I enjoyed.

I was excited to pick up the sequel, but unfortunately it just didn't do it for me. For one, it was very slow and not a lot happens. When things finally got interesting though, when The Program found them  I realize I was at the end of the book. I just wish we got more insight on The Program, and that we got to meet more patients and hear their stories-the ones whom The Program saved and the ones whom they destroyed. I always found the actual plot line more interesting than the characters, so the fact that The Treatment was more character driven made it less enjoyable for me. The ending was also very rushed, and I'm not sure how I really feel about it-it wasn't a horrible ending but it did feel abrupt.

"Shiver" by Maggie Stiefvater left me torn and undecided, and I am lost somewhere between adoration and disgust. 
 The book holds a certain tone of beautiful heart shattering melancholy, and it has a ghostly atmosphere of sadness and loss. The writing contains vivid imagery, and made me feel cold on a warm spring day. 
 The story is by no means a realistic account of true feelings, it is rather a lyrical tale of a poetical love. The dialogue isn't witty or even believable - but it is stunning. 
 On the other hand, there is almost no plot at all. The majority of the pages are "wasted" on sincere descriptions of a deep love, and when something dramatic actually is happening it seems misplaced and wrong. 
 Grace and Sam do not feel real; they're just pretty reflections of Stiefvater's artistic phrases. And their surroundings feel flat and tame; Stiefvater does not really describe anything else but Grace and Sam, their love, their heartache and the atmosphere in the woods. 
 I adore Stiefvater's writing, her compositions and her words, but I despise her simple story and her lack of characterization. Sam does not feel convincing. Grace is highly illogical. And their thoughts blend together in a hazy blur, so it's impossible to tell them apart. They do not have individual personalities, they only have each other and their mutual love.

7/10 
 A meandering trip though mountains and across deserts from China to Istanbul, and then into the war between Prussia and France. The summons to leave China is suspicious and never fully explained, the circumstances in Istanbul are suspicious but never fully explored, and the battles are messy, disorganized, and demoralizing defeats--that part is probably the most realistic. 
 Parts of the story should have been more detailed and explored with more depth; that lack of detail and depth weakens the overall book. And yet, Laurence and Temeraire continue to be wonderful and engaging characters, and some of the secondary characters, like Granby, Tharkay, Keynes, and even the Chinese cook, Gong Su, help fill out the story. There are only a few dragon characters with whom we spend any time--Lien and Arkady chief among them, with a cameo by Iskierka. 
 All in all, a weaker installment in the Temeraire series. I hope the subsequent books return to the tighter plotting and writing of first book in the series.

One of my reading objectives this year is to revisit some (as many as I can, really) of the Stephen King books that I read more than a decade ago, just as a way to reconnect with one of my favorite authors. I began with Gerald's Game, which I believe is one of King's most underrated works. The entire narrative is pervaded by a sense of desolation and desperation and is brilliantly crafted. The tension that he creates with such small details (a glass of water, for instance) is absolutely masterful. This book is graphic and gory and disturbing on a very visceral level, but for some reason, I love it. I think because, at its core, it's a very feminist work, which is completely unexpected.

I like the journey the characters go on to find or resolve the problem, yet I find the endings are always a bit of a let down or an anticlimax- I always feel a bit underwhelmed. These books are kind of like my 'break' books between others. I enjoy them for the easy read, a familiar pattern I can rely on and it's easy to slide back into these characters. So yeah, they are always a solid 3 star read for me, and I always fly through them and feel compelled enough to read the next one.

I found Uprooted a rather nice twist on Dante. The opening line of the Inferno goes something like "In the middle of my life, I found myself in a dark wood wandering/ for the straight way was lost." And boy, oh, boy, is that a dark wood in Agnieszka's valley. Terrifying and enchanting. I especially liked the source of its evil and how it related to the enchantment on the Dragon's castle. 
 Middle-aged grumpy Dragon subs for Dante and his Beatrice is Agnieszka, and she proves to be the active protagonist and a lot more interesting than Dante's muse. 
 I liked the book and thought it was well-written, but I could almost hear Novik's agent telling her to keep the story moving. Chapters end on cliff-hangers, which is not bad in itself, even if Dan Brown has overused it and given it a bad name. But there were a lot of times when I would have liked to dive deeper into the way magic worked and into the complicated relationship between the Dragon and Agnieszka instead of rushing off to the next crisis. The end result of this rushing was that the Dragon never became three-dimensional to me, though I thought he had a lot of potential to be a profoundly interesting character. 
 Ok, ok, I'm caviling. Honestly, once Prince Marek appeared on the scene and they went into the Wood to get the Queen, it moved along very well and I had trouble putting it down. 
 There was a discussion in the Science Fiction and Fantasy group about whether or not this is YA. There was some dislike of the sex scenes, which were few, IMHO, and well-written and certainly not too much for YA. My writers' group has a very talented writer of paranormal YA. She stops at the bedroom door, so to speak, but doesn't shy away from the fact that much of her audience is probably sexually active. Heck, I remember that many years ago, an elementary school librarian gave my nine year old daughter a book, Spider's Voice, which tells the story of Abelard and Heloise from the POV of a mute who is himself castrated, if I remember the story correctly. This necessitated some very delicate discussion when my daughter came asking about...um...er...what they did to Abelard. The book looked like a middle grade book, had a middle grade sort of cover, and without her questions I would never have known. So there you go. 
 Anyway, all that to say that Uprooted doesn't come close Lev Grossman's or GRR Martin's adult fantasies, which are full of sex. I wouldn't have hesitated to recommend this to my daughter in high school. It would have seemed tame to her, I'm sure.
Well, this book's majority wasn't my favorite but that ending made everything sooooo well worth!

Starship Troopers, when you boil it down is a military journal. It is an account of Rico's trials and tribulations as he climbs through the ranks in the Mobile Infantry. The characters are not overly well defined, the plot meanders and at times seems to have decided to not show up for a particular chapter, and yet, the story as a whole never once failed to keep me reading. 
 The settings and weapons are the most descript portions of the story and yet I never found myself asking Heinlein to get on with it. 
 I've read a few reviews of this novel myself and several of them have criticized the book for its lack of a romantic thread, but in my opinion, it doesn't need one. Heinlein made it clear that his protagonist was a man and that he not only noticed women but felt a strong desire to have them in his life - more so to remember what he was fighting for, but it is not as though the character completely ignored the female sex. 
 Two other criticisms claim the novel is militaristic, or that it has a fascist agenda. This novel is about a futuristic military power - of course it's going to be pro military - Heinlein was creating what he saw as a potential for a perfect society. In his opinion that meant a place where proven dedication to the greater good was the only means by which to gain citizenship - but it certainly didn't mean a lack of war. I can see where the fascist thoughts arise because the book is so militarily focused and if you really want to get into it, I'm sure there are dozens of forums out there that will gladly accommodate you. 
 Overall I enjoyed the novel immensely.

 In the end, when Elend is killed... it seemed really emotionless. I didn't care, and I should have. But something in the chapters beforehand made it so I didn't. He was dead and I was fine with it. I feel like main characters should do something to make me feel one way or another about their death. This fell short of the mark for me.

Williams never seizes to amaze me. I love every one of her books; this on is no exception. I was shocked by the turn of events though. And I'm having some thoughts on a bigger picture here...

Evie O'Neill is making the move from small-town Ohio to New York City. Her unusual gift (and her mouth) has forced her family to send her to live with her uncle until things blow over. Uncle Will runs The Museum of American Folklore, Superstition, and the Occult (or The Museum of the Creepy Crawlies as it's known around town), with the help of his assistant Jericho. As Evie begins her stay in 1920's NYC, she has dreams of fabulous parties and adventures to last a lifetime. What she doesn't count on is a supernatural stirring that is taking over the city. When a series of grusome murders seems tied to some sort of cult, Will is asked to help (and Evie, not to be left out, tags along). She soon realizes that the gift that got her exiled from Ohio could actually help catch a dangerous and evil murderer. 
 With an incredible cast of characters, The Diviners gives readers a mystery and so much more! 
 My Thoughts: 
 I read this book for book club, so if it wasn't for that I probably never would have picked it up. It's so far outside of my comfort zone that I just don't seeing it ever getting on my radar. I mean it's Historical Fiction AND Supernatural... two genres I generally never read. Maybe because this was so different from my usual, or maybe just because the writing was so awesome, I found myself loving it right away!! 
 I have never read a Libba Bray book before, but I can pretty much guarantee this won't be the last. I didn't read much of the synopsis before I started, so I went in pretty much blind. I read one page and I was like "oh this is in the 20's??" and I wanted to quit. There's just something about Historical Fiction that just turns me off. But I pushed through... oh woah, I am so glad I did. It got SO interesting and even though the book is huge (578 pages), I flew through them because I was hooked. 
 My favorite part of this book was all the characters. Normally a book with so many main and side characters would have me confused. Somehow that didn't happen at all here. Every character had a story and a purpose. And they were all so memorable. You have troublemaker Sam, flapper/Ziegfeld girl Theta, sensible Mabel, strong and silent Jericho, sensitive Memphis, thick-headed Isaiah, set-in-his-ways Will, blind homeless Bill, good guy Henry... and of course head-strong Evie and so many more. And I loved them all! (Ok Jericho was kind of a yawn for me, but still...) My favorite was Memphis, but I don't think I'm alone in this. Hello!! Smart, sensitive guy who writes poetry and can heal people?? What more do you want? Evie, however, was something else. I enjoyed having her as the main character, but it's hard not to have a love-hate feeling towards her. She was such a smart-ass!! Especially for the time period! But at the same time I respected her courage and related to her inability to hold her emotions in. Her immaturity could definitely turn some people off, but she had enough redeeming qualities that I think people will be able to like her eventually. 
 I could tell this novel was the product of a ton of research. The way the era and city was painstakingly described was definitely a high point of this book for me. The atmosphere totally captured my imagination and has me wanting to read more about the history of New York. Some of the dialogue seemed a little forced and irked me at times, but all the "and how"'s, "giggle water"'s, and "pos-i-tute-ly"'s had me grinning most of the time. 
 If I could point out an observation about this book it would be that it seemed very adult. It's not the subject-matter or anything like that, it's just.... something. A feeling that I have that it's written more for adults who read YA than it is teen readers. I could be totally off base, but even my book club mentioned it, so it's not just me who's feeling it. Maybe it's because most of the characters are either adults or teens who live adult lives or maybe it's just the vibe I got, but something about it gave me the teens-won't-like-this-as-much feeling. 
 Bottom line: I can't wait to read the sequel! I look forward to seeing if/when these Diviners team up to defeat evil!!! 
 OVERALL: WOW! Definitely a favorite for me. I never read Historical Fiction, but this one made me want to try out more of them. It's one part mystery, one part paranormal, and one part historical.... and all parts creepy and addicting! Definitely a recommended read from me.

I always appreciate a fantasy story that doesn't channel Tolkein too much. I was impressed too by how young the author is.

This was the first post of my weekly literature blog on tumblr. 
 I come from a country where fantasy is third class fiction. It's not really literature. It's regarded as cheap escapism. And yet I was drawn to it and thought that it had a potential to express what reality-based books fail to convey. Unfortunately, there are a lot of books in this genre that can't quite live up to literary standards. I was growing tired of the recurring, poorly executed themes, of the lack of authenticity. (Authenticity in fantasy? -Yes!) 
 With 'The Name of the Wind' Patrick Rothfuss has created a book that is an ode to life and that restored my faith in fantasy. It celebrates life in all its beauty - music, poetry, knowledge, the pleasure of crafting something with your own two hands, the complexity of human interaction, the delight of going off into the unknown, the fascination of different cultures and different ways of thinking - and for me, it includes in this beauty also the 'darker' aspects of loss, loneliness, not knowing how to pay your rent, let alone your university tuition fees next semester. Oh - and silence. And I don't even mean the silence in three parts, which commences and ends each of the books in the series. This is merely synonymous for a greater delight that I find in these books: yes, Kvothe, our young protagonist, is quite exceptional, constantly in trouble and stumbling through many extraordinary adventures, yet the Kingkiller Chronicle has what many other fantasy tomes are lacking: an appreciation of the small things and the quiet moments between the big bangs. 
 I doubt that I am truly able to bring across what I so love about Patrick Rothfuss' writing. I discovered him around the time when I started to come out of my shell, to change my guarded attitude to that of embracing the small beauties in life, of encountering people with a smile and an open heart, and of daring to take risks (such as going abroad), and I found a soulmate in these books. 
 Snuggle up in bed with a big pot of coffee or tea and a jar of biscuits beside you and enjoy!

But it's good to show that Katniss is affected by everything going on, all the death and realizing that Peeta is being tortured to break her. I felt helpless, so that's good writing, buck-os. 
 Plus, with Peeta gone, we get more Gale. She even tries to give it a go with him when Peeta comes back and she writes him off as insane, which was awesome--we needed that to realize that even if it wasn't his bomb in the end, they wouldn't have been happy. The scene where she fantasizes about what could have happened if she wasn't reaped was spot on. But those things did happen, and it changed her. Gale doesn't understand the changes it made in Katniss--she's seen so much destruction and it damages her, while Gale is almost immune to it. That's part of the reason why she needed to be with Peeta, imho. 
 There were a couple times I shed a few tears. My boyfriend kept looking at me funny, but whatever. Like when Katniss figured out why Snow had Peeta; Finnick (Sheesh that one was a surprise) dying even after he just got Annie!; and then Prim....ugh. My heart stopped. 
 That scene confused me. But I think that jumpy narration is perfect for the series, because it'd be pointless to show her watching people stampede in--and boring. So the exposition giving it away was nice. The shock she felt, the mental retreat, was spot on. I felt it with her. I mean, the entire revolution started when she volunteered to save Prim--and then for Coin, the president of the rebels, to kill her? I don't know how Katniss even recovered. 
 Ok, Katness now. I dig her. She's not perfect, in the slightest. She doesn't listen, she is indecisive, she doesn't really know herself (she's a teen--that's natural). I don't think she ever led on both Gale and Peeta, she just would need comfort which is totally understandable. And she wasn't with either of them, too. Actually, I saw her kissing Peeta more out of choice, while when she kissed Gale it was always to comfort him. It just wasn't as romantic on her side towards him, in my opinion. That "warm" feeling (haha) only arrived with Peeta, if I remember it right. 
 Ok, now the end..... How the hell she wrapped up the Peeta/Katniss relationship bothered me. There should have been more confrontation before suddenly the line, "we grew together." Uh...huh? That's not a good way to wrap up the romance, but I got it. Katniss was damaged, so was Peeta. They kind of had to re-learn how to function with each other. And I liked how a lot of what Peeta said in the first book was reiterated here, but his meaning more clear. That was perfect. I just wanted a little more grandiose when they finally got together. But I did like the last line of, "You love me. Real or not real?" Because it stays true to Katniss: she would never have admitted it without Peeta to push her. Gale and her would have been a little emotionless in that sense, because it was always Peeta who made that emotion come out. 
 I dunno. I loved it. I didn't want it to end but I couldn't put it down. Now I dunno what to read.

Faithful Place made all sorts of Ten Best lists in 2010, for novels in general, not just mystery. It's one of those mysteries in which the whodunit is subservient to the character development and the ambiance. It is set in contemporary Dublin, where narrator Frank Mackie is an undercover cop, estranged from his dysfunctional family for 20 years. He returns to his family and neighborhood when his former lover Rosie's suitcase and later her body shows up, 20 years after he assumed she ditched him on the night of their planned elopement. 
 This is a good read, very atmospheric, with Irish-tinged dialog so vivid you'll almost think you're listening to an audiobook! The reader's heart goes out to Frankie, so damaged by his upbringing amid poverty and alcoholism, and trying hard to be a good father to his own daughter. The resolution of the plot is not particularly surprising, but that is not particularly important, either.

This was a sad story. Period. There is no sugar coating to a book that revolves about the suicide of one girl, and the thirteen reasons that drove her to make that decision. It's a book that shows you the hard truth, that in a sensitive situation, almost anything could be the last straw, that one final nail that would seal the coffin. Some of the reasons that Hanna stated in her tale could have been ignored if there where just a singular event, like the ass grabbing thing that happened right at the beginning. It doesn't mean that it's not a sexual abuse, and it doesn't mean it's any less humiliating that anything else that happened to her, but if it was just that, just a single event, she could have made it pass that.  
 We listen to the tapes with Clay, and to be honest, I felt as sick as he did the more I advanced. Hannah tells her story in a very simple manner. She tells you exactly why it happened, because she has nothing to lose anymore. She knows she'll be dead soon, so why not bare it all? 
 It broke my heart to read all the reasons, to listen how with each day that passed she cracked even more, until she couldn't hold it together anymore. All the signs were there, but no one saw them because it was easier to ignore her than try to help. But I can't judge anyone about those 'obvious' signs, because sometimes it's not that obvious, and anyone that knows someone that killed themselves knows that. 
 She's been through a lot, and she gave up. And when she recorded her story, Hannah knew it was the end. That by the time anyone would hear it, she would be gone. And on the other side, we read Clay's reaction to her story. We read the horror and the pain, the emotions that took over him and made it nearly impossible for him to finish listening to her. And toward the end, it got harder for me to keep reading the book as well, because she was always so honest about what had happened to her, and it just broke my heart even more. 
 I feel like everyone should read this book, because it had such an important message and maybe it will help someone to stop a friend from taking their own life.

I'll admit I was a little disappointed when I started reading and it wasn't about David after his escape but holy wow am I glad I kept reading because this was even bloodier and gruesome than the first one and just wow. 
 Definitely liked Will's character more so this time around, but I think my favorite character was Gates. Gates and all of his craziness. He's possessive, obsessive, compulsive, and I just love his character so much. Not in the I'd-totally-like-to-meet-and-hang-out-with-them kind of way, because he is absolutely crazy and I don't want to get anywhere near that kind of crazy. But he still saved the kids in the school. I mean, he screwed up his initial escape plan, but in the end he helped them out. In a way. Even though he screwed that up too. His intentions are good, and that's what counts? 
 I love love LOVE Lucy's transformation. She joins the Sluts and learns to stick up and fight for herself and I just love it. I love the new Lucy. She has this new air of confidence to her that is just great and although the shit she had to go through to get there was hard to read, it was worth every bit of it and I really hope if the next book isn't about Will it's about Lucy. You go girl. 
 I thought the last one was gory, but wow this one was even worse/better. There were parts where I cringed, parts where I felt I needed to look away, but I loved every moment of it. It's one thing when a movie makes me cringe, but it's a whole other level when a book makes me cringe. You can't look away, you have to read it. Because if you don't, you'll miss something. And I just love that about books, and this one didn't disappoint.

I kept changing my mind about the rating, but I think three stars is what it deserves. This story has a lot of problems, and I don't think I can blame the translator this time. I think this all falls on Yoshimoto. 
 The Lake is about an artist named Chihiro who is assigned the job of painting a mural for a struggling school, but her integrity is challenged by the corporation funding her and that instills some personal drama. She's also just started a new relationship with the emotionally distant Nakajima, who she's been going all "Rear Window" on by spying on him across the street. But he's a brooding mess. Oh does he brood! Then he takes her to his "family" and broods some more. Then the book ends with this sort of revelation about why he broods & then I brooded about why I even liked the lady who wrote this. 
 This is Yoshimoto's longest book, but boy did it feel longer. I think she was attempting to write something more like a novel in length. What ends up happening is she circles around the same problems, in the same scene, over and over, until you want to puke. The summary of the book is also misleading, because the Japanese cult that "inspired" this tepid mess is mentioned in the last 30 or so pages and doesn't really deliver anything exciting. I know her books aren't meant to be exciting like that, but she relies too much on Nakajima's past without using it to her advantage. So he's angry because of this cult, which doesn't even get discussed properly, and we don't explore why or what specifically happened. It's all ambiguous, and the book should have explored Nakajima's past a lot more than it did, instead of hiding it like it was some great surprise. 
 The beginning and end of the book had a lot of promise, but the 80% that made up the middle just felt like filler. Despite some nice poetic phrases and descriptions, which is the only reason this book didn't get one star, I was bored. And I think the translator could have done a better job. Some of the prose came out staggered like this: 
 "I feel bad. This is why I feel bad. In conclusion, I feel bad." 
 I think it's safe to say she didn't intend it to sound like that, and it could've been consolidated. This happened in another recent book of hers I read, but the book didn't rely solely on her prose so I didn't mind it as much. So this is really a one star book, but because Yoshimoto can emote something in one sentence that some writers need pages to convey, I gave it three. I just wish the plot that inspired these prose was more fascinating.

I enjoyed this, despite all the "incredible coincidences" as the lawyer put it. There were one or two oversights that annoyed me,  such as the fact that Cathcart mentions the location of the gun in his letter and a few pages later they're speculating about whether or not he knew where it was. Granted the letter had just been read and introduced into evidence, but I'd think that's the sort of thing a decent lawyer would make a note of . I've always wondered how Lady Mary and Parker met, and while this doesn't really show much of the development of the relationship that is seen in later books, it is interesting to see the first steps.
This was surprisingly really good! It was a story that was very loosely Romeo and Juliet feeling. Loved the chemistry between Nicholas and Livvy. Looking forward to the rest of the series.

I find it a little strange that so many people have recently given this book one-star reviews--I actually found it to be decent writing. I suppose though, I've given plenty of non-stellar ratings where others have given heaps of praise. 
 I finished the book really quickly--it was one of those that I couldn't stop reading. I don't like books to waffle on--these days I have very little patience with super-long scene-setting--and this one didn't, though it still set the scene very well. The main character is a good character, and I think the author did a good job in doing a looking-down-from-heaven  perspective. She didn't sugarcoat what life would look like for Suzie's family, but didn't go the route of the classic angst. It encompassed a wide world view, something that was very interesting to me. 
 The only thing I perhaps wasn't super happy about was when Susie suddenly exchanged places with Ruth and then had sex with Ray.  I mean, I believe most books ask you to suspend belief, but that got a bit too much for me. It also seemed rather random. I understand that having sex is a big stage in life, but it wouldn't be the first thing I'd do whilst down on earth if I HAD managed to exchange places with someone.

It is fucking insane how good this book is. I liked Oryx and Crake but this one is so much better. Post/Pre Apocalyptic mayhem, an eco-cult that works words like 'australopithecine' into the hymns, wacky new technology that sounds fun/horrific, and much much more. This book has it all plus some strippers.

Of course I started reading this immediately today, I barely convinced myself to go to sleep last night after finishing the first book. 
 So, book two. My theory is confirmed! *fist pump* And I loved the story. Almost as much as the first, but not quiiiiite. 
 First, it took me awhile to get into it - I felt like Willa made some crap choices. Once the story got moving, those issues disappeared. But the slow start this time around was to blame on Willa being kind of unlikable instead of world-building. 
 Second, it's bordering on too much sexual tension - with 6 people constantly giving each other heated glances and almost kissing and dropping innuendos and and and I get it, man. They're all super horny for each other. Can we please get back to the god trying to turn you into a Jeffrey?! 
 Third, the wraith plot was just one thing too many. It felt completely unnecessary to the story and kinda ridiculous. I was confused as to where this was going the whole time I was reading it and then it was over, and it was such a non-starter I was like "Why did I just read that?" 
 There are a few other minor, but very spoilery, complaints that make me rate this 4 stars instead of 5. But I'm still shelving it on my favorites shelf. Again, I laughed out loud - painfully, actually. I have a twinge in my abs from laughing. I'm really looking forward to the next book. 
 Highly recommended.

I loved the beginning of this book, and the overall story, but the ending was a let down. It seemed a bit rushed and I was left a little confused. I still don't understand the physician and who he was or how exactly things ended with him. Overall a good read, but was hoping the ending was a little more clear and not so rushed. 3.5 stars!

 Pure was so much better than Half Blood. The plot twists in Pure had me seriously debating skipping class to keep reading, only to be responsible and just read the book on my iPhone during class instead. The character development is progressing along nicely and in a believable manner. While Alex is still irrational, she is starting to accept responsibility for her actions. Pure was devastatingly good and broke my heart numerous times, especially the stupid cliffhanger ending. My heart was protesting all the pain it had to deal with once I finished reading. 
 I am completely in love with Aiden and I want him for myself. It is so obvious that he is completely in love with Alex and just doesn't want to admit it because of the risks it poses for her. If you had any doubts about Aiden's feelings in Half Blood and Pure, his actions at the end of Pure will get rid of those doubts. It upsets me more than it should (being that this is a book) that Aiden and Alex are not allowed to be together (I mean, even both their names start with A *sigh*). The Breed Order is stupid, and that is the best word to describe it. If Aiden and Alex are not together at the conclusion of this series, I may not be able to function ever again. 
 While I know a lot of people love Seth, I just do not get it. Frankly, he annoys me to no end. I don't hate Seth, but I don't really like him either, at least not as a love interest, I like him as a character (if that makes any sense). I feel like their relationship is based too much on the need they have to be together rather than their actual feelings. 
 When I compare Aiden and Seth, I cannot help but think back to the Oracle's statements on love and need. Maybe it is just my biased opinion, but I cannot help but identify Aiden with love and Seth with need. Alex loves Aiden simply because of who he is. Alex needs Seth because he is the other Apollyon and they are fated to be a team (team not couple). I can never shake the quote "The first is always the most powerful.---Then there is need and fate. That is a different type. Need covers itself with love, but need... need is never love. Always beware of the one who needs you. There is always a want behind a need, you see.--- Sometimes you will mistake need for love. Be careful. The road with need is never a fair one, never a good one. Much like the road you must walk down. Beware of the one who needs." I feel like the Oracle was trying to warn Alex that choosing Seth was not the right choice, because it is clear he NEEDS her in order to become the God Killer, whereas Aiden just loves her for her without any of the Apollyon stuff. I also think that her and Aiden have a major role in the changing of the Breed Order. 
 Wow I kinda went on a rant there, I just have so many feelings when it comes to this book. I would most definitely recommend this book! If you haven't read it yet, go out right now and buy it, if you have- read it again because it is that good!
I really liked this story, but it just seemed too short! I wanted to read more! Luckily, I have the next book in the series, so I'm good to go. :)

great twist. unexpected plot.

Robin Sloan's so fun, so smart, tbh. This is a bit less exciting than Mr.Penumbra's, which read quickly and easily but also felt sort of urgent and relevant. This is mostly quirky fun and food history, both things I can definitely get behind.

The story continues right after the events of Alpha & Omega. Charles and Anna arrive at his home, their wolves mated but the humans not yet mated, and Anna is having problems adjusting to her new circumstances. A rogue werewolf has killed two people in the Cabinets, a harsh wild area north of the pack's area. Bran sends Charles and Anna out to draw the rogue out and deal with the problem. Charles is still wounded but healing. The time alone may just help this newly mated couple. One rogue werewolf...how hard could that be? Right? Mating bonds, a rogue werewolf, black magic, spirits, old wolves, new wolves, the Marrok, oh my! 
 When this series first debuted, I was not convinced it would be as good as I hoped. Where Mercy's books are told in the first person past tense, this one is told through two protagonists in third person past tense. My fears were unfounded and although I absolutely LOVE the Mercy Thompson series, I really enjoy the Alpha & Omega series too. Anna and Charles are so good together and they work through their problems. Charles is an old wolf who has shut himself off and doesn't let anyone too close because he may have to kill them later in his role as the Marrok's enforcer. He had all but given up on meeting his mate until Anna came along and bowled him over. Seeing the normally stoic Charles all aflutter is amusing and witnessing their mating bond and relationship settle in is heartwarming. 
 It was quite the romantic journey and I recommend this series.

Thoughtful, considered and worth the effort - just like Jace.

ALL ANIMALS ARE EQUAL. 
 BUT SOME ANIMALS ARE MORE EQUAL THAN OTHERS. 
 This must be the highest point of honesty that we can reach. Because it doesn't just apply to animals, it applies to humans as well. Better, if you want my opinion. 
 This is, if you have much imagination, a really scary book. Let's say, for the sake of argument, that hypothetically this could happen. I'd shit my pant. I've lived my whole life thinking that even though in an animal there is a soul, there is not enough intelligence to resemble what I, as a human being, can do. What if one day I find out that that's not the case? Huh?! I'd probably run for the hills and start living in a cave. 
 What George Orwell has a lot of is humor. His jokes wouldn't be funny in meaningless contexts, but in Animal Farm, everything he did had a purpose - that of showing us how not so different we are from them. For that, he used satire and a lot of figures of speech, and he managed to create a world we could believe in. 
 It's still scary, though.

This is a solid story by Sara B. Larson. 
 I enjoyed getting to know Alex/a, her brother, and her love interests. Everyone who know me knows I'm a sucker for cross-dressing/gender-bending stories where the female lead must dress as a male in order to fulfill her dream (fighter, join the army) or to keep her alive (escape from rape houses, as was in the case of Defy). 
 What makes me giddy is when the male lead learns of the deception. Did he always know? Was he fighting an attraction to a boy? All stories in this genre get an automatic comparison to "These Old Shades" by Georgette Heyer. Which, if I'm being honest, is one of the best girl-pretends-to-be-a-boy novels. Not many newer novels stack up against a Heyer novel. So I'll just move on. 
 I know many objected to the rape houses (reviewers) in Defy, and I wasn't a fan of them, either. Other than the plot catalyst to make Alexa become Marcel's "brother", the rape houses (aka Breeding Houses) really didn't add to the plot overall. Thankfully we only see inside the rape house once, but it is talked of a lot (men buttoning their breeches as they leave the rape house). It certainly leaves an impression... 
 I guess I just didn't see the point. It would take years for any children born of the breeding houses to become soldiers, or, if a female child, to be raised as "incubators" until their monthly courses came. So, for the sake of argument, it would take 13 years for this to take affect... 
 Eh, I could have done without all of that, and I would have rather seen a different reason for Alexa to become Alex. 
 There were a few times that I wanted to slap Alexa. When everyone knows her as Alex, she's a fucking badass. But when others realize/learn she's a female, she becomes...dunno...not a badass? I get it. The author needed us to see that, on the inside, Alexa is vulnerable and has no idea of how to be a female. But the essence that made her her shouldn't have changed all that much. 
 Between her two suitors, I'm team Rylan all the way. Sorry Princey-poo. I could have done without the love triangle, and the semi-insta-love between Alexa and Prince Damien. I'm still of the opinion that he's only using her. 
 Overall, parts dragged, parts were exciting, and the fighting was good, and I kept reading because I really wanted to know what happened next! For that, 3.5 stars. I'll pick up Ignite when it's in the 4.99 range. Right now, as I write this review, it's 9.99. A bit too high for my e-book buying range.

I became a vegetarian some four years ago after reading this book and it's been since then since I've read it. What I do want to say is that I often point to Foer's sympathetic understanding that food is communion, and that when you're denying that experience on a political (or perhaps nutritional) level, you're missing the cultural side. You miss out with, say, Grandma's dumplings, Grandma's cooking. And what about turkey on Thanksgiving? (Thank God for Morningstar) 
 I also can't resist the play on words on the title, as being eating animals that also eat animals. Now that's food for thought! 
 This is a book with a agenda, but what I appreciate about it is that, for the reasons above, it's realistic and honest. (If course, this is all from memory :p)

When I started reading Good, I thought it was just a typical student-teacher romance, but no, it isn't. Good is a realistic and very controversial book. 
 Cadence Miller grew up in a Christian family. Ten months ago, she was involved in a robbery, with other teenagers, while high in cocaine. This led her to ten months of juvenile detention. This changes everything for her when she came back to school. Almost everyone in school started bullying her. She also lost her friends and her parents' trust, 
 While cleaning the streets during detention, Cadence met Mark Connelly. When she came back to school, she discovered that he is her math teacher. They fell in love and entered in a secret relationship (which includes a sexual relationship). 
 Good also showed Cadence's point of view on Christianity, and how she interpreted the Word of God, and how she let it affect her decisions and her relationship with Mark who has different beliefs compared to hers. This also twisted her beliefs in some way. In some parts of the story, I saw that instead of her Christian beliefs affecting her relationship, it was her relationship that affected her beliefs.

When I started reading this book, I thought "ok, this is starting out like 3 other YA books that I've read". Teenage girl with a somewhat traumatic life, shipped off to another school where she meets a boy who has her mesmerized. Even though I was tempted to stop reading this, thinking this was going to be like the others, I'm glad I stuck with it. 
 Emma's living with her Aunt, after escaping a death at the hands of her drunken step father. She's enrolled it a very posh private school, where her aunt is on the board and her younger cousin is her only ally amongst the student body. When she meets Brendan Salinger, she doesn't expect her reaction. 
 "He turned and looks at me for a brief second - any my pulse sped. I didn't expect my response. I'd been around good looking guys before -- but this guy looked like a rock star. Long black lashes framed his green eyes - twinkling green eyes that locked with mine." 
 I like that Emma had issues fitting in at the new school. She didn't fit into any of the pre-established "cliques" and didn't really try, figuring out what the dynamics were at the school pretty quickly. She did manage to make friends with the "outcast" Angelique, when no one else would because she was a scholarship student. I also like the fact that even though Emma felt drawn to Brendan, she wasn't overly obsessive about him (which could have very easily happened). 
 Brendan was one of those male characters that we all wished we had as our first (and true) love in high school. Once he stopped running from what he was feeling, he was the boyfriend that made his girlfriend feel like a princess. He was protective, but not in the "I'm going to put you in a bubble" sense. Even when he knew that the two of them being together could be disastrous for Emma, he admitted he wasn't willing to let her go. 
 The story did have it's villans and they were spectacular in a high school kind of way. Kristin was the ultimate bitch and made sure to make Emma's life a living hell. How dare she snag the hot guy! And we can't forget about Anthony. He was evil, in every sense of the word. 
 Sprinkle in a little magic, some century old curses and plain old high school woes and you've got yourself quite an enjoyable read. I recommend this one.

4.5 STARS 
 "The orphaned daughter of a sorcerer and a half-demon, Savannah is a terrifyingly powerful young witch who has never been able to resist the chance to throw her magical weight around. But at twenty-one she knows she needs to grow up and prove to her guardians, Paige and Lucas, that she can be a responsible member of their supernatural detective agency. So she jumps at the chance to fly solo, investigating the mysterious deaths of three young women in a nearby factory town, as a favour to one of the agency's associates. At first glance, the murders look garden-variety human, but on closer inspection signs point to otherworldly stakes. 
 Soon Savannah is in over her head. She's run off the road and nearly killed, haunted by a mystery stalker and freaked out when the brother of one of the dead women is murdered when he tries to investigate the crime. To complicate things, something weird is happening to her powers. Pitted against shamans, demons, a voodoo-inflected cult and garden-variety goons, Savannah has to fight to ensure her first case isn't her last. And she also has to ask for help, perhaps the hardest lesson she's ever had to learn." (From Amazon) 
 I loved this novel right from the beginning. I enjoyed Savannah's fiestiness from her teens day but has a more mature outlook now that she is twenty-one. The mystery and suspense in this novel was great - both supernatural and non-supernatural. Cannot wait to read the final two books but will be sad when there is no more.
This was fun.

Hounded was awesome. It was full of action, humor, fantasy, and mythology that was insanely fun to read. I devoured it in a short amount of time, raving about it to others the entire time. It was such a cool mixture of old mythology and lore with modern times. Atticus, a 2100 year old Druid, had such a good grip on today's world. His sense of humor was awesome and his narration kept me turning the pages. 
 Hounded had all sorts of mythological elements. Atticus was a Druid, lived in a town with witches, had a Viking vampire for a lawyer, and was friendly with a werewolf pack. He was visited by the Morrigan, an old Celtic goddess (but the sort of goddess who would NOT appreciate being called old!) and just about every other legend, god, or creature existed in this world. Demons, faeries (the terrifying kind), even Mary. I loved how the author created such a universe. It never would have occurred to me to have a world where every religion was true to some degree. 
 Atticus definitely made the story. He could communicate with his Irish wolfhound, which was hilarious because his dog was awesome. He fit in with college kids, but his insight and narration had me cracking up. He made the best references ever. "These are not the Druids you're looking for" came out of his mouth at one point, which is basically awesome. As Atticus fought a powerful Celtic god, his dog was commenting on the action and made South Park references that had me laughing. 
 Overall, Hounded was one of the most fun books I've read all year. It's definitely a must read for any geek and any lover of a fun fantasy book.

Quick disclaimer: I only read the last 2 pages.

 "I need a SparkNotes interpretation of this" was the first thought that popped into my head when I finished page 232. 
 Initially, I thought this was going to be a light historical fiction novel set during the early years of World War II (but then again when is a book about WWII ever light?), but I'm quite surprised by how this read more like a fairy tale mixed with some magical realism. And strangely, as I was flipping through each page I had these sudden urges to recognize every rhetorical device and wanted to annotate the entire thing. Anna and the Swallow Man rekindled the literature student in me (in a pleasant way). 
 In Anna and the Swallow Man, readers meet young, precocious Anna. Her father is a linguistic professor and naturally he knows many languages. In fact, so many that Anna doesn't know what her father's native tongue is. She grows up not really knowing how to identify herself. All she has are the many ways to say Anna. Anja. Khannaleh. Anke. Anushka. Anouk. But then one day her father leaves her in the care of an old friend and he never returns. Soon after, with the war wearing down the civilians, the hospitality her father's friend once has dissipates and she finds herself at a level of despair and fear she's never anticipated to experience before. All changes when she meets the mysterious Swallow Man. Despite his intimidating looks, Anna grows attached to this tall and peculiar man because he's just like her and her father, one that is skilled in many tongues. They embark on a seemingly aimless journey and he teaches her his language, Road. A language that uses deceit for the purpose of protection and survival. 
 In a rapid riot of conflicting languages, she answered all his questions. 
 In Yiddish she said, "I am better now," and then in Russian, "I do not think my father will come back." In German she said, "I am myself," and then in Polish, "And now I am waiting for you." 
 Aside from the deep messages the story presents, the writing is probably my favorite part of this book. The prose was quite unusual but very beautiful. It was not easy to read at times since Savit really enjoys expressing things implicitly through riddles and a lot of uncommon rhetoric, but almost every detail seemed to serve a purpose in the story. Most of the book was told in thoughts and long paragraphs; there was very seldom any dialogue. But the lengthy passages were appropriate for a story like this. 
 Savit has a compelling voice and great flow in his writing, but the story did drag with the first third of the book, which is the only reason why I'm deducting half a star. Like the premise suggests this band of vagrants walk for several years with no apparent goal (or so readers thought initially; we later gain more insight behind everything). But as more is explained and a certain character is introduced it picks up and becomes rather fast paced. 
 As for why I think this made me jump back to my high school literature days was the usage of different perspectives between our two consistent characters, Anna and the Swallow Man. Each offers an important view for a certain type of reader. The non literature student/ya loving bookworm in me instantly felt connected to Anna's naivety, innocence, and her outlook of the consequences of war and her adventure with the Swallow Man. On the other hand, the adult and more experienced reader (and old literature student) in me could see both Anna's and the messages behind the Swallow Man's clever wit and insight. These two characters provided two very different perspectives, making this a read fit for readers of all ages. 
 All the characters were rather simply built but they possessed a depth behind their words and thoughts as the story progressed. It was hard to not grow attached to them. 
 And deep behind the story there's also some subtle, hidden messages about humanity's true nature. How the consequences of war can change someone so. Or motivate them to be who they are. There were lots of thought provoking concepts explored in this. 
 And why I began this review with my plea for a SparkNotes annotation of this story is because by the end there were still riddles and questions unanswered. The conclusion was cloaked in mysteriousness, and there was much left for the reader's interpretation. 
 Even so, there's no doubt that Savit is a marvelous story teller. Anna and the Swallow Man reminded me a mix between critically acclaimed works such as 
 The Glass Castle 
 , 
 The Boy in the Striped Pajamas 
 , and 
 Night 
 . This was magical realism at its finest. I highly recommend this fabulous debut.

She is dating Dante now and she is finding a lot of moral men to to take down. Her friends totally don't approve of Dante and I can totally see why she's upset about that because they gave her such a hard time about Seth and now they're saying that she is better than Dante and that she is she is good even though that she is a demon. She used to be such an optimist and seeemed to bring out the best in others and this is really hit her hard. I know that her and Seth are just one element to it because we saw even in her human life how she made the mistakes with her husband and she regretted it so badly and that she would sell her soul that he wouldn't be in pain. We've also learned some about her and a priest that she became friends with and then cared about and that didn't have a good ending. So hard just to see how life has handed her so much bad hand after bad hand pain on top of pain. 
 We do get to meet a lot of new characters since she has been sent to Canada. I'm unsure when she's up there because I miss Carter and Hugh and her other friends. there is of course more going on behind the scenes then she even knows about. the whole thing with Niphon in the last book is still in the back of her mind-- just wondering if there's something up with her contract because he came after her so hard. And now there's even more for her to worry about because she's right in the middle of another supernatural issue because she always seems to have trouble around her and she is always looking for a solution because that's the kind of person that she is. 
 When she loses her powers, I got to see a vulnerable side of Georgina, because she is suddenly afraid. She can't shape shift and she believes for a while that she can even die. In her depression, she was thinking that immortality was too long. That the all consuming pain she felt after losing Seth and realizing what she was missing being in a relationship. Being with Dante does make her more cynical and dark. But she feels that he understands, and in some ways, he does. But in others you can tell that she isn't as happy with him as she was with Seth. 
 There's a lot to put into words for this one and of course and I can't wait for the next one. I felt like there was a lot of character growth but Georgina of course is still really really struggling but not having sex in her life and having to watch him with Maddie. 
 I was pretty surprised that one of the characters who came on the scene in order to help solve the whole issue with Jerome as well as the Immortals in kind of a stasis not having their powers. It definitely adds a new dynamic to Georgina's living situation as well as adding more depth to the plot 
 In some ways I got to see a few ways the story line with Georgina and Seth might end up playing out. I got some scenes that I've been hoping for four blocks but it also brought around as much negative as positive in ways that Georgina really never even imagined. Of course I kept in mind the visions that Nick gave her in the last book and I kept my fingers crossed because I knew some of the things that she have longed for in her very long immortal life. 
 I kept getting more reinforcement in this one that Georgina is really a problem solver and a go getter. Where a bunch of people will tell her not to get involved or tells her they can't help. if she sees a problem in front of her she is going to want to do everything she can to solve it. This is one of the things that help make these books so fast paced. one of the ways I can describe it is she is like a house from the TV program house where if there was medical puzzle he would do anything and everything to get the answer and she's the same way. 
 This one ended much like the other ones in the series where the big plot lines from this one are tied up pretty well. and then we are given a new problem to work over in our minds as to how in the world everything is going to be handled in the next book and how miss mead is going to get us there. 
 I am lucky in that I am reading this after all the books in the series are released and I have a nice little hole in my reading schedule where I can binge on these and I'm going to start the next one as we speak 
 Bottom Line: Great book in this addictive series.

 I received this book for free from the publisher in exchange for an honest review. This in no way affected my opinion of the book, or the content of my review. 
 How do I even begin to talk about this book? It was so incredibly weird and it had all the makings of a book that would go totally wrong, but somehow, for me it went right. The writing was beautiful and poetic, the story was full of mystery and dark romances and Greek mythology references that kept me wanting more at every turn. It was one of those books that don't quite have a solid conclusion, and it was frustrating but at the same time it was satisfying. If that makes any sense. 
 Anyway, first let me try to summarize what the story is about. This is the third book in a series, but I have not read the first two books and I do not think that is required, since each of the books is based on a different set of characters. They are different generations of a family that is deeply affected by forces of magic that are hard to explain. This book follows Tally (and she is the daughter of one of the main characters from the first book), a girl who wants to be an astronomer and after her eighteenth birthday goes on a quest back to the home hometown of the mother who abandoned her to discover her origins. 
 There she discovers a town that is deep in mystery and magic, a man who may or may not be her father who is trying to forget the past, and a girl who may or may not be a monster, who helps Tally discover her own self. 
 That's a good as I can summarize it anyway. Among the things that I loved about this book were: the beautiful writing, the flow of the prose, which kept me reading on and on. The way the author wasn't afraid to experiment. As readers we tend to seek concrete answers to everything in a story, but that's not always what happens in life, or in art. Even or main character, who sees herself as a scientist, starts out wanting everything to be rational, and comes to realize that not everything in life can be explained. I do feel like I was able to connect to Tally, even if the other characters were a bit outside of my understanding. 
 I also loved the diversity of the characters: most o them are non-white, non-convetional, there is a transgender character and the main character is bisexual (among others). So if that's something you're looking for, there you go. 
 All that being said, I do think that if the story had been more clear or had it been broken down into a couple more chapters (the whole things is just huge chunks of text with almost no break, seriously) it would appeal to more readers. I would recommend it, but take it with a grain of salt if that's the kind of thing you don't like. This book worked for me, but it really isn't for everyone. 
 I'm not sure I'm that interested in reading the previous books, though maybe they would shed some more light into the overall story arc (anyone who has read them, please let me know).

Found picks up right where Lost left off. Maria and Owen are happy together and they seem to have settled into the relationship. In Lost, Maria was the broken one, who needed Owen to help her heal, they had both gone through tragic experiences that had shaped them into the people they were. 
 Having Owen in her life has changed Maria, where she was once fragile and weary of everyone, she now feels safe and accepted with Owen by her side. 
 But unfortunately Owen's life begins to unravel or rather catch up with him. He gets terrible news from home, and begins to blame himself for what happened. It doesn't help that it seems everyone is against him. Not knowing how to react to the situation he pushes Maria away, a decision he immediately regrets. 
 Maria is not willing to let Owen retreat into himself, she's there for him every step of the way. Helping him when he has to make the most difficult decision he's ever made in his entire life. Even when this is all over it seems Owens pain is still not over, his dream, his education might be at risk. 
 Owen goes on a downward spiral, his thoughts are in a dark place. He sabotages his relationship with Maria and she's not there to help him when he needs her most. But she ultimately pulls him out of it and they both realise how much they need each other. 
 This was a great ending to the series (at least I think it's the end), I'm glad it wasn't dragged out. Found is a story about loss, pain and healing and I like reading books like this even though it doesn't always seem like I do. I got really attached to the characters. It was great to see how Maria had blossomed into a stronger person, she was always there for Owen when he needed her. 
 I really felt like this was Owen's book, and Lost was more Maria's book, although both books were written in dual POV's. The letter at the end was a great a touch, I have to say this was a very satisfying read. Thank you to the author for allowing me to read and review this story.

Okay okay okay. When I first read this book, I loved it. I thought it was the best in the series (my bad, cycle), and that Paolini was truly visionary. 
 What the hell was I on?! 
 All the praise I had for this book has evaporated. It was a whole lotta bor.ing. My God, could it have been drawn on any longer? On average, there was like one page of plot for every seven pages of filler. Paolini tried to trick his reader's into being excited by throwing in random-ass action scenes. "Well, since the Varden is just sitting around and Eragan is having repetitive philosophical conversations, lets have Roran bash 200 heads in. And describe every single one!" Dear Lord, Paolini was trying to write this book in real time or something. I DO NOT NEED TO KNOW WHAT ERAGON HAD FOR BREAKFAST. I DO NOT NEED TO KNOW EVERY STEP IN MAKING A MYSTICAL SWORD. I DO NOT NEED ENDLESS DESCRIPTIONS OF PLACES WE HAVE ALREADY BEEN. 
 90% of this book was filler. And if you already know the 10% of plot beforehand, Brisingr is pretty much a snoozefest. But I guess I understand Paolini's reason for creating this brick though. It's clear he loves his world. Hey, it probably comforted him when he was busy not getting laid in high school. He just wants to share every bit of it, meanwhile showing off his developing writing skills. But it's important to know as a writer that details you find interesting might not be so for the readers. Sometimes, you just have to stick with the story, and suck it up. There's world building and there's being excessive. 
 I re-read Brisingr in preparation for Inheritance, which I have been waiting for a loooong time. But since I enjoyed Brisingr when it was fresh, chances are good I will enjoy Inheritance. I hope so, as it appears Paolini has saved all the plot for the last book.

I'm not sure where to start with this book. I loved it, but at the same time, I really don't like the reason for it. 
 Cancer and terminal illness is a loaded topic for me, not least of all because I was diagnosed with non-Hodgkins lymphoma when I was 19 years old. 
 It's old news and I'm fine now, but I'm sharing this information because obviously, the experience has influenced my response towards this book. 
 I was never terminal, nor was there any uncertainty about whether I would survive at all. My story is definitely very different from the story John Green has written, but I can relate to an extent, and I would like to speak from my own personal experience. 
 One part of the book which particularly rankles with me, is Chapter Eight, when the group of Hazel's doctors were talking about Hazel's response to the drug Phalanxifor. Dr. Simon in particular, was terribly callous and pessimistic, dismissing Hazel's positive response towards the drug. 
 It galls me because it was the kind of dismissive treatment I received in the hands of my oncologist back then, and I think it's a testament to John Green's writing that he manages to portray all the disinterested doctors in the world through the embodiment of Dr. Simon, and better yet, with just that one word that Dr. Simon says at the end of his sentence; "yet". 
 I know not all doctors are like that, Dr. Maria, in the book, was kind, and I appreciate doctors like her. 
 Cancer perks are funny things, and I love how Hazel and Augustus deal with it in the book. On the one hand, it's nice that you get away with things a healthy person wouldn't, on the other hand, you hate that you're only getting these perks because of pity. 
 When I was diagnosed, I didn't tell everyone, not even some of my close friends knew and some of them not until years later. I didn't like being defined by cancer. I didn't like that people made a big deal out of it when they found out about it. 
 One minute they treated me like they would anyone else, the next, they'd fall all over themselves trying to do stuff for me and make me comfortable. Which only made me uncomfortable, of course. 
 One person actually tried to make me cry over it. Which I didn't because I was over it, and she was like, "But you're so young, it's such a pity, oh you poor thing you. How could you not cry over it? It's safe to cry in front on my shoulder." And I still didn't and I told her I was fine, really, and I didn't need to cry, and she went, "Oh, you don't have to be strong. I'm totally here for you." Blah, blah, blah... 
 *cue eyes rolling* 
 I digress, but you get the picture. Cancer survivors don't really like being treated differently. Well, at least I don't, and I totally relate with all the instances throughout the book of how Hazel and Augustus were treated differently, how they felt about it, and how they sometimes took advantage of it. It was funny, annoying, and bittersweet too. 
 The thing is, even though this is a book about cancer and dying, I often felt that it's so much deeper than that. It's about life. 
 Take the metaphor of Augustus putting the killing thing in his mouth but not giving it the power to kill him, ie. cigarette but not lighting it. It resonated with me, and I think it applies to all the other killing things in the world. They have no power except what we give them. Ever. 
 I also love how Hazel's favorite (fictional) book, An Imperial Affliction, ended abruptly in the middle of a sentence. The fact is that in real life, things often end abruptly, and there's no closure to be found. Though having said that, I have found that often without closure, we speculate and in effect, write our own stories of what might have been, which can sometimes be a beautiful thing. 
 There's also the whole glass half-full or half-empty thing, on the first paragraph of Chapter Twenty-Two, about how the room was "two-thirds full but felt one-third empty." I really felt the importance of perception within that observation and how it can make all the difference. 
 Most of all, I felt Augustus' fear of oblivion, of having lived for nothing, the belief that "if you don't live a life in service of a greater good, you've gotta at least die a death in service of a greater good". 
 I've definitely wondered what my own contribution to the greater good is at many points of my life. You don't have to be dying to wonder what you're living for. 
 Even now, I still ask myself this, and I wonder if I've done anything that have made a difference in making the world a better place. I think we all search for that; the affirmation that we are good people, that we deserve our place in this world. 
 I have so much respect for John Green for writing what must have been a difficult book to write, and to write it so well and with so much truth and sensitivity. This may be a book about cancer and dying, but it's also about life and living. The whole mess. 
 It's intense and difficult to read emotionally, but so beautiful and so worth the read.

 Synopsis: 
 The last year of high school, somewhere in America. A girl meets a boy. She is called Echo, he is called Noah. Both have serious family issues but of different kind. He falls for her because she smells like cinnamon rolls. She falls for him because he is a very handsome, bad-boy stoner with...er... issues. And a six-pack stomach. The crazy attraction between them refuses to go away although their friends are not impressed. Will they stay together?  You bet  
 My impressions: 
 I rarely read YA novels nowadays. Why? The moment I start them the plot seems so strangely familiar, too familiar - after a page or two I am pretty sure I've read it before. Like one hundred times before. It holds no appeal because there are no real surprises or twists I wouldn't have predicted. Not nice or even downright boring. Pushing the Limits wasn't an exception to the rule. 
 Echo, is a high school student who went from a popular girl with a jock boyfriend to a gossiped-about outsider with "freaky" scars on her arms during one month. Noah is a boy who has lost his parents in a fire and cannot visit his younger brothers so he is revolting against the school rules and any rules at all. Both are attracted to each other because they are in fact very similar in their rejection of ugly reality. You don't have to be a genius to assume they will be an item at one point against all odds - especially that she is a very attractive girl and he is a very handsome young man. The main problem is not "what" but "how" and "when". 
 And here I wasn't impressed - the execution simply didn't work for me. It felt too overwrought, too obvious, too overwhelmingly angsty and dramatic to make me really engaged with the story. Almost spurious. While I was able to feel for both Echo and Noah occasionally, I didn't really connect with them. 
 The book is narrated by both of the main characters. First annoying feature: Noah's and Echo's voices were quite similar, very surprisingly so. The only thing really differentiating them: Noah's dialogue was peppered with profanities. Well, perhaps it's just me but personally I found Noah's chapters also the silliest of all. He thought like a girl - I mean no teenage boy would speak/think like that. His repeated use of expressions like "siren", "angel", "nymph" and "seductress" produced more snort-laughs than swoons from me and the constant reminder of how Echo smelled (cinnamon rolls) made me only annoyingly hungry (where's the nearest bakery, pronto?) but honestly, do tell me, do you know any REAL GIRL who smells like that without using any kind of perfume? 
 There are also many kinds of cliche secondary characters which have been featured in really EVERY SINGLE ONE high school YA novel I've read so far: a douche bag hunky boyfriend (Luke), a false female friend who is also a bit of a meanie (Grace), a bunch of evil gossipers, Noah's 'bad company' consisting of heavily tattooed, marijuana-smoking misfits who, of course, still have a single saving grace or two...I wasn't able to find even one inch of originality here. 
 Final verdict: 
 A decent story but also an instantly forgettable one. It was short and relatively readable but also nothing that can persuade me to read YA novels more often.

So. 
 Yeah. 
 How to talk about this book? It's a little bit of crazy, a lot of WTF and a whole bunch of confusion is probably the most accurate way I can begin. Basically, Annihilation is the journey of the unnamed biologist who is part of the twelfth expedition to Area X - an isolated, mysterious area that Southern Reach (which I understand to be some type of government agency) sends expeditions to on a regular basis to learn its secrets. In theory this all sounds pretty straightforward, but reading it is anything but. 
 The narrator isn't named, but her life is so consumed by her job, that it doesn't feel particularly strange not to know her name. However, there is a lot of information about her life before the expedition, her relationship with her husband, her fascination with other worlds around her, and some rather candid introspection into her own character. She's particularly comfortable with herself, which is rather refreshing for a main character. 
 And then there's the crazy, WTF and confusion. At first introduction, Area X seems quite straightforward, but quickly escalates into some seriously weird stuff. I've always struggled with the super-strange in fiction, but I really enjoyed what Vandermeer does with Annihilation - it's all a bit strange and I won't even pretend that I understood, nor spent large chunks of time trying to decipher exactly what was going on, but nevertheless I found it strangely addictive. 
 I have absolutely no clue who I'd recommend this book to, because really it's quite hard for me to put it in a nice little box and say 'yes, this person would LOVE it' or 'this person would HATE it'. It's one of those books that's very hard to predict who it would appeal to, and why. And I'm keeping this all rather short and quite generic, but I was totally sucked in...even whilst I was scratching my head and trying to figure out exactly what was happening.

Why I picked it up: I needed a religious fiction for my reading challenge and a friend recommended this one. She said the main character reminded her of how I might have been at that age. 
 When Addy learns that she was chosen by her principal to represent her school in a reality TV program to win a date to prom with the president's son, she is not pleased. Addy does not want the spotlight. She is happy with her quiet life and just wants to get good grades so she can go to an Ivy League college. The producer of the show thinks Addy is trying to steal the spotlight from the girls he wants to win because their families have paid him money. Addy doesn't like being on the show, but she is convinced God has her there for a reason. And the president's son is even better looking in person... 
 It was okay. Addy did remind me of myself as a teen, though without the God Having a Plan For Me in my case. There was a little too much "God put me here for a reason" for my taste, but as Christian fiction goes, it did not rub me the wrong way too much. I did like that Addy wasn't perfect and her role models also were not perfect. In that vein, I really liked the journal entries from her mother's journals from her missionary time that showed that she really doubted some of the things she was doing. Not all Christian fiction is willing to include doubts. I found it frustrating yet realistic that when Addy was kind to one of the other contestants, many of them thought she had ulterior motives. I loved Addy's roommate Kara. Jonathan was a little too good to be true, but so are many fictitious teenage boys. 
 Genre Bingo: Religious Fiction

Most books I never really feel inclined to give a review on but having just finished this book I feel the need to express my thoughts on it. 
 I absolutely adored this story for several reasons. 
 The first and foremost was how downright creepy it was. The strange mother-daughter relationship that was almost passed down through generation and the eerie similarities between those relationships. The teeth in the dollhouse was probably the largest creep-factor though (same with the carpet made of hair) and I love how the author hints at these subtly throughout the book with Amma's mention of how she likes the ivory floors and how it's a shame they don't make them anymore, and how Lily's hair reminds her of the carpet in Camille's old room. 
 I also liked how it was a book about a self-harmer but the emphasis wasn't necessarily on the self-harm or hospital visits and the like. It's refreshing to hear a story of someone who's done these things in the past but still struggles with them in the present - resisting the urge while trying to live a normal life. It pissed me off that the cop decided he wanted nothing to do with her after seeing her scars, but sadly that's something that does happen and it makes the story that much better that Camille didn't have the perfect fairy tale ending with the guy (who actually seemed to be quite an ass hole throughout the whole story and not just at that part). 
 The relationship between Camille, Curry, and Eileen was parental and was made obvious in the beginning of the story but I think that it was at least some what of a happy ending that she has two people in her life substituting for the mother and father she never had. The bond between her and John through similar struggles and the desire to punish themselves is true to real life: sometimes people that have both gone through tough things can find comfort in each other (in other ways than sex, of course). 
 Finally, I loved the plot twists. From a little bit before half-way through (a little bit before Camille starts to suspect her mother) it was obvious that Adora was being set up in the story as the perpetrator of the crimes although it wasn't necessarily known to the characters at the time. This solution seemed to simple to me, however, and my brain would jump from Amma to Adora to even Adora's mother at one point (perhaps she wasn't really dead?) but that was only in passing. To have it turn out to be Adora and Amma, who was under the sick influence of her mother was an interesting end although it was not entirely surprising (the dollhouse thing was a surprise though, and so was the fact that John had suspected Amma). 
 Overall I thoroughly enjoyed the story and towards the end it kept me reading on until I was finished.
