So after reading boatloads of raving reviews, I guess I was expecting to be blown away. That's not to say I didn't enjoy it, after about halfway through, I couldn't put it down. 
 My biggest complaint is the excessive use of '!' everywhere. It was practically every other sentence - especially in any action scene. I'm sorry but I would rather have descriptive action that builds excitement and tension, not have it slapped in my face telling me that it's exciting. It comes across as you're telling me something instead of showing me and it's rather frustrating. 
 There were also quite a few grammatical errors but I could get past it. Sometimes. 
 A few moments are pretty strange...this story is told from swapping POV from the two main love interests - Lily and Tharin. I mean reading Tharin's POV describing his brother making out with someone is weird. Very weird. Shouldn't he look away instead of explaining how intimate their kiss was. It's strange. If I saw my sibling doing that, I would look away...privacy much? Awkward more like. 
 Anyway I think that the story/world is fascinating. The idea behind their magic types and how it works, I love it. Each character had their own unique abilities and strengths (and it's sort of how I told them apart). The portals, demons, magic, weapons...it's all a fun ride. I can't wait to see more of it in the following books. 
 Lily is stubborn - to the point of annoyance every now and then but I suppose that she can't be perfect. The whole romantic drama seems a bit forced, since Tharin feels the need to NOT tell Lily he broke things off with whats-her-face for some unknown reason? Why. She's clearly bothered about it....why not tell her what she wants to know. Of course just for teen angst that I can't say I'm looking forward to in the next book which from the summary will be a lot more prominent. I'm oh so excited. 
 The journey so far has been interesting with plenty of action and good development. I have enjoyed Tolan and Tharin, as well as Lily and Julia. I also liked the bits of Phoris we saw - his magic is intriguing to me. I'm excited to see more of the magical possibilities in the following two books. 
 I also hope we'll see some legit romance. (I want some passion~!) Though Tolan and Julia were pretty amusing before they got all cute and sappy :D 
 The pacing was pretty good, a bit slow but pulled me along and the writing style was very easy to read. 
 Anyway I'm ready to see what's in store next. I'm rooting for the current couples.

 Overall, this book was an exciting blend of fighting, politics, and magic. I was drawn into the fantasy world of the Season and Rhythm kingdoms and finished the book with a strong desire to learn more about the kingdoms and magic we hadn't been directly introduced to. I enjoyed the fighting scenes and especially loved the relationships between the eight Winterians who had been separated from their home nation. Meira was a strong-willed, capable protagonist but she was never reduced to a mere "badass heroine" trope. I felt for Meira and her sense of disjointedness--she has spent her entire life fighting to get back to a homeland she has never known. 
 My only complaint is that this book didn't feel very cohesive. I listened to the audiobook of Snow Like Ashes, so I am unaware if this book was divided into parts. However, while listening, it seemed like there were three distinct sections of the plot. I would be listening to the book, thinking I had a relatively clear idea of where the plot was headed, and then Raash would change it up and the characters would be in an entirely new setting with seemingly different priorities. These include the nomadic section, when I thought the novel would be about the Winterians travelling about searching for the second half of the locket, the Autumn section, where all of a sudden a love interest was thrown in and Meira became a political pawn, and then the prisoner section where Meira discovers her real destiny.  I think with different pacing of events, these sections would have felt less like their own separate novellas and more like a single story. I am highly anticipating the release of the sequel.

 This version of Hansel & Gretel by Neil Gaiman has to be one of my favorites. I loved that it stays close to the original Grimm version and preserves the chilling details... 
 "Today, when the oven is hot enough, we will roast your brother," said the old woman. "But do not be sad. I will give you his bones to chew, little one." 
 What I cherish most about this edition are the illustrations. There's no color in any of the pictures by Lorenzo Mattotti as they're simply black and white. What's interesting is how certain details in the written story are left out, but then you find them sketched in the pictures. For example, the mother is originally with the father as they lead the children into the dark forest and also with the original tale there's a duck that helps them reach safety by swimming them across the river. There's no mention of it, but you will find it in the illustrations. 
 In the back of the book there are a few pages that cover the history of the tale and where it originated. It also covers some other fairy tales that are similar to "Hansel & Gretel" including "Hop-o'-My-Thumb" and "Nennillo and Nennella." 
 Overall, I really liked this edition. I felt that it might be sort of drab when I saw that it was all in black and white, but there's a lot more to see in the illustrations if you just take the time to pay attention. 
 4****

I've finally done it, everybody. I've finally found a Milan book that I absolutely love. I've only read two of her books before this one and they were always simply okay to me but Milan's magnificent writing and layered characters had me wanting to keep trying with her stories until I found the right one. And I finally did. 
 There is simply so much to love about this story. I love the feminist message that these books give in such a time when women were not allowed to be seen as intelligent or independent. Violet was such an endearing character as well, I almost instantly felt for her and her passion for what she did was inspiring. Even more so was Sebastian's constant full support of her. I think that made me love their romance more then anything else. 
 I feel like this story is a prime example of what most relationships should be like and what we should be expecting out of our love stories. It was so full of respect and support. Sebastian never crossed any lines with Violet and he always made sure that she was okay and comfortable with whatever he was doing. People who say constant reassurance isn't sexy need to read this one because I was swooning with how deeply Sebastian cared about Violet's well being. 
 Sebastian was definitely a favorite book hero of mine, possibly ever. His love and admiration in Violet was heart wrenching and on top of that he was such a charming and lovable guy, almost impossible not to adore. There was no need for anything heavy or overly sexual when reading about how in love with Violet that Sebastian was. That alone had my heart racing, especially when everything he loved about her was who she was as a person and not anything as superficial as her appearance. 
 This story has immediately become a favorite of mine and restored my faith in the historical romance genre and I now cannot wait to finish the rest of this series, as well as Milan's other works.

This book started really nicely. A classic coming-of-age book, with a solid, balanced dose of brothers-in-arms drama, combat, politics, and magic. I also liked the non-linear storytelling, and how different plots slowly connected and joined. It also radiated that nostalgic honesty you get in good literary works. 
 However, the second half, or rather, the last quarter of the book felt a bit forced. I was under the impression that the author got tired, and then he started dropping heavy Scooby Doo clues that do not align with the simmering tension he built up to this point. The romance with Sherin also feels weird. Combat scenes were rushed and not immersive enough, and when it came to the siege toward the end, there was so much potential in creating a daring, life threatening scenario, but instead, it's resolved in an almost effortless way, as if the author was distracted while writing, and couldn't really bother with the emotional engagement piece. 
 Another problem is that Vaelin feels like an old git, and he has the wisdom and bearing of a 40-year old veteran, not an orphan kid with daddy issues. All that said, this is still a well paced book, with good, down-to-earth characters, good story, and you don't feel like you're reading a wannabe HBO script. I'm looking forward to the second book. From what the little spiders whispered in my ear, it is supposed to be better, more composed, polishing these rough little edges from the first volume. 
 Now, after a long time, the limerick pimp striketh again: 
 In Vaelin's mind there was a song, 
 It would tell right from wrong 
 For Nurse Sherin, 
 With love and carin', 
 Al Sorna bought a medieval thong. 
 Withhold your judgment! 
 You will figure out after you read the book.

Received a copy of the title in exchange for an honest review. 
 Reviews are all about the honest one so I'm going to be super candid right here, right now: 
 When the arc for TALON popped up on my Kindle, I inwardly groaned. Without looking at the title, without looking at the author, the cover itself told me it was part of the ASHES & EMBERS series and while I liked the three previous books, and I rated them as such... it wasn't necessarily a series that I was going to be all about following each new release. {Granted, if you didn't have any feels for Vandal at the beginning of his book, you and I can't be friends}. 
 So I went into TALON with a bit of a chip on my shoulder -- reading a book that I didn't really want to read, all because I'm a series lover and signed up for this series before even knowing Carian Cole's writing style. 
 Depressed yet? 
 Let's cut to the chase then, why don't we. 
 BEST. 
 BOOK. 
 In the series. 
 Favorite book I read last week. 
 I was totally engrossed in this story -- I didn't want to put it down, and I found myself re-reading scenes because I loved them so much. I loved bad boy Talon and his desire to settle down but wasn't because of the... selection, I suppose. I loved that he kinda sorta believed in this concept his mother was shooting him. And I really loved that he was so disappointed in the result of his questionnaire. 
 While Asia may not have been what he wanted on paper, she was so, so good for him. 
 "...give it time. Relationships take work. You don't just add water and stir." --Dad 
 These two -- their chemistry was off the walls. I absolutely adored them. I loved as these two slowly tolerated one another; I loved watching them pick out their house and watching as Talon fully accepted and supported the parts of Asia she swore no one understood. I most loved whenever he thought of her or spoke of her as 'his wife', even early on. I found that very telling for his character, as it was thought as an endearment rather than a fact. 
 I loved how these two loved one another. The way they met may have been super-unconventional; the fact they had to stay married for the length of this study certainly put forth the thought that marriage is work -- that you will fall in and out of love with your spouse and you have to always work for it, definitely was showcased. The very vows that are spoken are fully looked at and worked on in Talon and Asia's story, too. 
 I loved Asia's growing relationship with the members of Talon's family, but most notably, Evie. I really loved the connection Talon and Lukas had, as well as Asher's acceptance of Asia -- right from the beginning, to the parts where Talon questions things. 
 See? Lots of love. So glad I signed up for the series, because I wouldn't have gotten to Talon's story, and like I said, his was definitely the favorite for me -- and with it... I'm now in that "following the series for each new release" boat. 
 Speaking of future releases... so many questions where Asher is concerned, in this head of mine. I'm curious if we'll get to see more of this brother. Oh, and all because Rayne put the thought in my head, I'd really love seeing Talon and Asia in a birthing room. Thanks for the idea, Rayne.

uh oh, I'm in the outlier club again. 
 The author is a man writing under a pseudonym. Apparently he fell in the love with slasher movies and decided to write a book about the final girl trope: the last girl standing after a madman goes on a killing rampage. 
 All the elements are there for a slasher flick. Was this supposed to be a spoof? Things just don't add up or make sense, stretching believability. Perhaps this would make a better movie than book? 
 - a character had a hacksaw sever an artery and she not only didn't die, she went on to kill the perp. Nope, medically impossible. 
 - The author does get kudos for surprising me. There were red herrings galore but then the actual ending surprised me, and not in a good way. Is a twist a twist if it's just pulled out of the air? 
 - The prose is often awkward with an abundance of nonsensical similes - one of my pet peeves! Here are some examples 
 "....I want to shake Sam so hard that the truth finally dislodges and plunks to the ground like the acorns dropping all around us" 
 "....my stomach feels as squeezed dry as an empty water bottle" 
 - "I feel as if I'm strapped to a bottle rocket, hurling through the ozone, streaking sparks until we both explode." 
 "....as if my insides have been scraped out by the ice cream scoop I use to drop batter into muffin tins" 
 "....the frigid grip of fear subsides. Taking its place is the hot burn of despair. Trapped between cold and heat, I act accordingly, melting into a puddle on the kitchen floor." 
 Too many implausible things happening: 
  
 - no one mistakes a white bloodstained dress for a red one. NO ONE! 
 -Saks doesn't have security cameras? They just traipse around stealing stuff? 
 -At the cabin Quincy had sex with a stranger after turning Craig away because she wanted her first time to be special? Please, that would never happen IRL! 
 - and what's with Quincy beating up a man, sending him into a coma? The forays into Central Park made no sense. And her rages? All to throw us off the scent but red herrings need to subtle or at least make SOME sense. 
 -Coop's declaration of love (rolling my eyes here) - a WTF moment! And he's the killer at the cabin...for such a stupid, stupid reason?! 
 -The cops wouldn't still be in contact and have a personal relationship with a victim after 10 years, and this happened not just once with Coop and Quincy but also with Lisa and Nancy, the policewoman? (more eye-rolling) 
 I could go on but I'll stop here.... 
  
 Sure, some of these are nitpicky but when they start to pile on top of one another they begin to matter. 
 Recommended for those who want a quick read and can suspend disbelief and enjoy the book for what it is.

Now going into one of Ms. Flinn's modern adaptations of fairy tales, I don't have expectations of high brow thinking or wonderfully tight plots. This book had neither, but it didn't bother me in the least. Sometimes you really just want to read something fun and quick, something that will make you happy when you're done without challenging your brain. That is exactly what A Kiss in Time was. It was fun, entertaining, and fulfilling. 
 A Kiss in Time follows Princess Talia of Euphrasia and slacker Jack of Miami as they meet, argue, travel, and eventually fall in love. Talia is your "Sleeping Beauty", blessed with grace, beauty, and intelligence. But she is also cursed. At her christening, an angry witch declared Talia would prick her finger on a spindle and die. Another fairy at the event prevented Talia's death, but she must fall into a deep sleep along with the rest of her kingdom, with a hedge growing to prevent outsiders from finding the castle until her true love can come and wake her up with true love's kiss. 
 Talia grows up spoiled and angry because she can't leave her castle or do much of anything. In her impertinence, she ends up pricking her finger just as the witch said, and her kingdom is left sleeping for 300 years until Jack comes and wakes her up. He's then left to help her adjust to a new time and escape her fuming father. 
 It seems at first the two are meant to be at odds, but somehow Jack makes Talia less of a brat and Talia makes Jack care about things other than partying (and his awful ex). 
 As I said before, I enjoyed a simple, light read for the summer. I also enjoyed the back-and-forth from Jack and Talia, and the split narration. Sometimes it gets boring hearing from only one character for an entire book, but I liked hearing each of their opinions on the events. Overall, not life-changing, but certainly worth a read if you like retold fairy tales and fun!

The start of The Beekeeper's Apprentice put me in mind of some of the later entries in Elizabeth Peters' Amelia Peabody series. A tongue-in-cheek author's note describes how King came upon this manuscript, and scoffs at the idea that even such an imagination as hers could have come up with "the farfetched idea of Sherlock Holmes taking on a smart-mouthed, half-American, fifteen-year-old sidekick." 
 The smart-mouthed, half-American fifteen-year-old in question is Mary Russell. Mary's parents have died recently in America, and she's come to live with an aunt in the Sussex Downs. The aunt is mostly interested in the money that comes with Mary's large inheritance, so the girl spends most of her time wandering the Downs, her nose in a book. Her nose is in a book when she literally walks into Sherlock Holmes. 
 It's 1915 and Holmes has retired to the country, leaving behind the (somewhat exaggerated) exploits narrated in very popular books by his friend, Dr. Watson. He's sinking into depression, spending all his time on his beekeeping. All that changes the day when Mary Russell walks over him as he's lying on the ground, observing bees. Her brilliant deductions show him that she's in possession of a brain at least as good as his. Before he knows it, he's taken her under his wing and is teaching her all he knows. 
 Many years ago, I read and enjoyed A Letter of Mary, which is the third book in this series. Normally, I'd have gone straight to the beginning of the series, but when I found out Mary is 15 at the start of The Beekeeper's Apprentice, that really put me off. See, Mary and Holmes are a married couple in A Letter of Mary, so I knew there would be a romantic relationship. And even though I loved their relationship in that book and thought that, in spite of a really large age difference, there was a wonderful equality in it, the idea of a 15-year-old girl and a man in his 50s kind of skeeves me out. 
 Well, I needn't have worried. King develops the relationship between Russell and Holmes slowly and carefully, and over several years. Initially, it's a relationship with no sexual component whatever. You realise these two come to care for each other, but the romantic element comes late. Even better, I didn't get the feeling that Holmes was moulding Russell's mind, Pygmalion-style. He does teach her a lot, but doesn't change who she is. Even from the start, their relationship felt more like one between partners than one between student and teacher. So, I'm happy to say, no creepiness there at all. 
 Something else that might have been a pitfall is that King, obviously, is taking someone else's character and continuing the story. As someone who has read and enjoyed all the original stories, I was curious to see whether I'd recognise her Sherlock Holmes as the same man Conan Doyle created. I haven't had the best of experiences with tricks like that (see Jill Paton Walsh's A Presumption of Death). And again, King cleared the hurdle with room to spare. This was Sherlock Holmes. In fact (dare I say it?) it was a Sherlock Holmes who was the same man, but with even more depths. Watson was also Watson with depth, and the same goes for Mrs. Hudson. 
 And as for Mary Russell, she is a wonderful creation. She's a highly intelligent and logical, almost cold young woman. I loved it that King didn't feel she had to soften her or make her behave in irrational ways to make her more acceptable as a heroine. It's made very clear that Russell has feelings and cares about (some) people, but she does so in her own way, without sentiment of mawkishness. The exact thing can be said about Holmes, and I found myself convinced they were soulmates. It's a relationship that's about the meeting of two like minds, and though the bodies they're in are attracted to each other, that's not as important. 
 The structure of the plot is quite interesting. At first, it sort of echoes how most of Sherlock Holmes' appearances take place in short stories. Mary learns the detective trade through different unconnected cases. At least, it seems that they're all unconnected to anything. But then a villain shows up who clearly has an axe to grind against Holmes, and some of that might have to be reconsidered. All these are interesting cases, peopled by interesting characters, and provide opportunities for some of those excellent, satisfying deductions one associates with a Sherlock Holmes mystery. 
 I also thought the writing was excellent. I started listening to this one after the hugely unsatisfying and frustrating The Silent Touch of Shadows. I'd been forcing myself to keep listening, until I got pissed off and just deleted it. And then I started The Beekeeper's Apprentice and felt the difference immediately. King is an elegant writer, and an author who trusts her readers' intelligence, and therefore doesn't feel the need to spell everything out. You have to pay attention, but it's most definitely worth it.

It's so refreshing to read a fantasy world that does not feel derivative and which is so carefully worked out: we get so many details about how every aspect of the world works, though Samatar never info-dumps or gives away too much: but she makes her world feel solid and completely believable. I love her descriptive language, especially of the cities: their magical quality reminds me of Italo's Calvino's "Invisible Cities". I also admire the inter-textuality of the book: it's a story about reading, and there are many stories within the text. I especially admire her story of Jissavet, the girl with the wasting disease who is so desperate to make her voice heard, and I think Somatar makes a wonderful point about the value of every life.

 Lincoln works for a newspaper in their IT department. He makes sure that the emails being sent and websites being browsed are appropriate. There are many flagged words, and when said words become flagged the email that they are a part of is sent to Lincoln where he reads through it, and, if necessary, sends a warning email. He soon starts getting emails from Jennifer and Beth, two women who consistently use their work email for private conversations. He finds himself slowly (and inconveniently) falling in love with Beth. 
 SPOILERSSSSSSSSSSSSSSS DISCUSSION!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! 
 Okay, so I just want to say that Jennifer and Beth are HILARIOUS!!! Like, OH MY GOODNESS SO FUNNY!!!! This book took me twice as long as a book of its size normally would because I would reread sentences over and over again and giggle to myself. Yes, that's what this book reduced me to. They were just great. The thing about humor when it's as amazing as it is here is that I can't really write paragraphs about it, but I can't mention anything else without it being brought up. Like, it just permeates the entire book and there's really no scenes that don't have some sarcasm and humor thrown in. It was just great. 
 I really liked Jennifer and Beth's friendship. I liked that they were in different places in life but still managed to connect on a very deep level. I like that they could depend on each other when they felt necessary but could also put their own feelings aside when the other needed a moment about her. I liked that they were best friends, but not obsessive and unhealthily attached best friends. I liked that they were always teasing each other. I liked that there was a great degree of mutual respect between them, and while they would offer advice they would wait for it to be asked for. I liked that they told each other pretty much everything. I just loved their friendship and I think that, to be completely honest, its the relationship that has the most page time. Like, their friendship is a hugely key part of the whole thing, and I like that. 
 Doris was awesome and I absolutely loved her friendship with Lincoln. Great. I also loved that she went ahead and befriended his mom too, and when they see each other she's like, "Oh you look so great." That was hilarious. 
 The emails were honestly the best part of the book for me. I liked Lincoln and all, I really did, but I could've just read a book about their emails and I would have been so happy. They're great! And the ones about My Cute Guy... oh so funny. And cute. And amazing. 
 I liked that Lincoln was this very relatable character. He's stuck in the in between, he's stuck between kid and adult and school and work and comfort and new experiences. That's a very normal place to be, I think, when one's 25-ish and I liked that we saw him move from the in-between and go more self-assured. He was very relatable, but not as interesting (to me, at least) as beth and Jennifer were. 
 Okay, so Sam kind of appears out of no where at the DVD rental place or whatever and is acting like they're BFFs and she didn't cheat on him for months. Like, NO SAM!! I was so worried, he'd just started making progress and then BAM! Crazy cheating lady comes back! I would've preferred a little closure on that whole thing, but I also know it probably would have made me want to throw things so maybe it's a good thing that wasn't included. 
 I liked that Jennifer was struggling with having kids and stuff. I think that's something that most people who want to have kids struggle with, and I think that it can often be brushed over. I also like that it's the man in the relationship who really wants the kid and the woman who's not sure, since it typically seems to be the other way around. I just liked that element of Jennifer's character a lot and I really liked the layer that it brought to the story as a whole. 
 There is only one real thing keeping this book from five stars for me, and that's the ending. Now, a couple of things about the ending: a) it felt really rushed to me and like we didn't get the time that we needed to understand this new relationship and how it came about and why it's important etc. etc. b) We didn't have enough pages to experience more in-person cuteness, which I was really looking for! Finally, c) I don't like the implication that true love means that you're always happy to be with the other person and never need space and stuff. Like, the book ends on them talking about how they love each other always and will never need space or whatever, and for many people (including myself) I don't think that's possible. Now, I'm not saying it's cool to be Chris, because that's not an okay relationship from where I stand, but I can love you to the moon and back but still not want to be around you 24/7. That doesn't make my love any less real, it just makes it different, and that felt like a really glossed over and just... not good ending.

 ! ---After how much I enjoyed reading On Dublin Street by young author Samantha Young, I absolutely had to get my hands on Down London Road, the sequel to the On Dublin Street series. I was a bit disappointed to hear that it wouldn't be about Joss and Braden anymore, but their story was told and would somehow live on in that new story, featuring Johanna (Jo) Walker and Cameron McCabe. 
 Jo is actually Joss' colleague, and bartenders with her at Club 39. From what On Dublin Street suggested, Joss is always on the lookout for "sugar daddies", as Joss likes to call them, who would be kind enough to treat her well and cater for Jo's family. Needless to say that the impress you could have of her in that first part of the series was not the most postive. But Down London Road will lead you to the deeper meaning of her actions. It turns out that she dropped out of school at 16 in order to take care of her younger brother Cole, since her mother - sick, alcoholic and agressive - couldn't deal with it anymore. Jo has always been deprived of parental love, and the least thing she wants is to have Cole grow up like this, so she acts like the perfect mother to him. 
 Actually, her looking for a sugar daddy is more selfless than you could think since she endures it all for him. However, with Malcolm, there hopefully might be more to it. That's what she thought until she met Cameron, who does nothing else than say out loud what most people think of Jo: that she is a selfish whore, only after Malcolm's money. They met at an art showing and the tension was undeniably there between the two of them. Usually, Jo doesn't care about people's opinion, but when Cameron, this self-assured, tattoed and undeniably hot guy, confronts her with that, she feels hurt even though she tries to hide it 
 Call it a coincidence, but little time later, Cameron moves into the flat right below Jo's. Inevitably, and very much to Jo's dislike, he finds out about the harsh reality that's weighing upon her and sees her in a different light. That's when the attraction they have for each other really starts to burst. Could she make such a selfish decision and leave Malcolm for someone like Cameron? What would happen to her family? 
 Again, Samantha Young wrote a great piece of romance, mixed with the harsh reality of what some people have to go through at time. Just like the first book was about the loss of loved ones, this book is about the harsh condition on being alone and doing anything it takes to care for your family. We all like a bit of fairy-tale romance now and then, but sometimes, reading something like Down London Road makes stories even more realistic and even more intense, since there's a glimpse of hope that there's a happily ever after "for the fucked-up crowd" (and I quote Crossfire Series author Sylvia Day). And this time it's not about child-abuse, but about something more common (and more than you'd like), which is alcohol-abuse. 
 Again, Samantha Young made this read very enjoyable and down-to-earth, yet heartfelt and packed with emotions. It's a beautiful story she's telling, suspenseful and sizzling. And again, the evolution made by the main character - Jo becoming more open and realizing she should step in for herself too - was really well laid out. I also liked that the characters from On Dublin Street also played an important part, and that their story was somehow continued. 
 I look forward to reading the other Novellas, and will definitely find a place for Samantha Young in my top-5 favorite author ranking.

Ashamed. That's how I feel right now. Only after I've finished the book "A Canticle for Leibowitz" I find out that it has been considered a masterpiece for over 50 years, being awarded the Hugo in 1961. It is also the only novel published by the author. And, oh boy, there's so much inside. If I have any presumptions on my knowledge over science fiction and fantasy works, I should have known better. 
 I feel there's a big gap between the old, classic science fiction works and the more recent publications. The classics have a stark innocence in terms of quality of writing. Characters are so thin you can see right through them. Dialogs are so poor that they seem more like a history class than a conversation between people. In contrast, there was a richness of ideas and reflections about the world, the human condition, the impact of progress on human society, and so forth, which would blow up the mind of the readers. And these ideas, these discussions, would make these works last for decades, being fresh every time you read them. More recent writers have "learned how to write", and can tell a story that will glue you to the book up until the end. Those great ideas, however, were forgotten, or in the best scenarios, had to share its space with complicated plots and deep characters, leaving less room for them to flourish. This is nothing new, and it is the basic difference between Star Trek and Star Wars. The cool thing about this book is that "A Canticle for Leibowitz" has that richness of the classics, but it is able to tell compelling stories, with characters one can empathize with. 
 Walter Miller Jr fought in the World War II, and at that time he was part of the bomber crew that participated in the destruction of Mount Cassino. The monastery at the top of Mount Cassino had lasted for over 14 centuries, and it had been a place where knowledge was greatly valued. A place where monks spent centuries losing their eyesight on candlelight while producing copies of works they believed should be preserved. Oh, it had its share of destruction way before World War II, and it was rebuild afterwards, but the themes of the Abbey as a bastion for lost knowledge became the inspiration for the book. 
 A Canticle of Leibowitz tells the story of mankind for about two millennia after a nuclear holocaust. Leibowitz would have been a technician who survived the holocaust, and realized the importance to try to preserve our accumulated knowledge for the future, since most of the remaining survivors of initial fight blamed science, and those who manipulated it, for the destruction of the world. He became a priest, and established a religious community that would try to preserve as much as possible. He eventually became a martyr, when the mob capture him. But his community maintained his purpose, and centuries later he'd be raised by the Catholic Church to the status of Saint Leibowitz. 
 The book is split into three novellas, each one hundreds of years apart. The first one is set on the 26th century, when a young and clumsy novice of the Leibowitz order accidentally stumbles on a fallout shelter, full of relics that might help support the cause of the sanctification of Leibowitz. The second is set on the 32nd century, where scholars learn about the hidden texts at the abbey which might represent a jump in human knowledge. And the final act is the 38th century, where the order of Leibowitz begin their preparations to fulfill their duty again, when faced by mankind threatening to annihilate itself again on another nuclear war. 
 Several themes are discussed throughout the book. The author clearly had faith on the Catholic Church, or at least on its resilience, being able to survive even a nuclear war. There are discussions about the "burden" of knowledge and the freedom of ignorance; about the misuse of science, and if there's an ethical responsibility over those that research science, if it has a potential for doing evil; about how individuals can be wise, but masses always tend to act stupid; about the conflict of scientific thought versus the religious philosophy. And more, way more. There's a slight tendency to protect religious belief, even though it reflects on some if its flaws. 
 This was one of the first works on post-apocalyptic scenarios, and probably the first one to get a large audience. This has one additional benefit - classic science fiction work tends to feel terribly dated. After all, it is guessing work to depict how the world will look like in 50, 100 or 1000 years from now. However, in a post-apocalyptic scenario the author has the benefit of looking backwards - for instance, the first novella looks very much like it is set in the Medieval Dark Ages. The only way it feels dated is because nowadays we believe that mankind will destroy itself an environmental catastrophe, or (given by the amount of works produced in the genre) by zombie outbreak. 
 As I said in the beginning, I bare my shame to you, for not knowing more about this book before reading it. And I beg you to find room in your shelf to read it sometime in the future, if you have any interest in the science fiction genre at all.

2013 will be a science-fiction year for me, that's for sure! I have no idea why I gave up reading SF, but I am rediscovering the pleasure for this genre. Oh, my, I have a lot to catch up with the classics! 
 The Demolished Man is one of these SF classics and I enjoyed it quite a lot. It is like a detective novel, only that the events take place in the future, when mankind is divided in Normal people and Telepaths. The latter are capable of reading minds and they have various degrees of skillfulness: the most gifted ones, of which there are only a few, can read the innermost thoughts and even things that are buried deep in the subconscious. That is why, for more than 70 years, it has become impossible to commit a planned murder. 
 The idea behind this novel reminded me of The Minority Report, but I found out that The Demolished Man was first at the party! 
 Ben Reich, the rich owner of a huge company, is haunted in his dreams by a nightmarish appearance, the Man with No Face. He is convinced that this is a personification of his rival, D'Courtney, so he decides to murder him. He will have to make a perfect plan and avoid being caught by the Telepaths. I won't tell anything about what is happening, you'll have to read the book to see if he succeeds or not! 
 The crime is investigated by Lincoln Powell, the Police prefect, who is a gifted Telepath. Yet, he can't rely only on reading Ben Reich's mind, because this is not admitted as solid evidence by the Court. He has to provide motif, opportunity and murder weapon in order to get Reich convicted. And this is not the only problem, because he will eventually figure out who is the Man with No Face and will discover that the mankind is in great danger. 
 The title refers to the process of Demolition that a person who has committed crime is subjected to, but don't think you've got the meaning of it, because you are in for a surprise at the end! 
 There was something I didn't enjoy, though: some dialogues were too superficial and cheap, not suited for a novel that is otherwise very smart and imaginative!

Elise wants to be normal. She wants friends. She doesn't need to be popular, she just wants the average sleepovers, parties, have-a-place-to-sit-in-the-cafeteria high school experience. But when you've always been the outsider--the one with the big ideas, the one who doesn't even understand why the other kids act and talk and dress the way they do--it's really hard to fit in. Things are looking pretty bleak when Elise accidentally stumbles into a dance club downtown and meets the DJ. With her typical big-project flair, Elise decides to learn everything about becoming a DJ. Through her passion for music she starts to understand the people she meets in the club, and to discover the difference between surface friendship and true acceptance. 
 Elise is a highly relatable character, even if I did want to shake some sense into her at frequent intervals. This is a great book for any musically-inclined readers out there (I learned a lot about DJing from this book), though I would really recommend this to any realistic fiction readers.

The perfect man. A gentleman. He's a lawyer who has never lost a case, defending women in domestic abuse cases. He's charismatic, charming, handsome. He wants to look after you. The perfect man. You will no longer have to work. He wants to give you a house for a wedding present. He promises to look after Millie when she can no longer board at school. The perfect man. How can you refuse. 
 On your honeymoon in Thailand, you discover you should have refused. When you get home, things get worse. You no longer have control of your life. No money. No passport. No phone. No way out of your own room, much less your new home, and no one to tell. Above all, you have to protect Millie. So you play the perfect hostess, the perfect wife, and you plan.

While I have fallen in love with various aspects of the Guardian series, there have been two dominant threads plucked in the background, piquing my curiosity and humming along behind the humor, the violence, and the happily-ever-afters of every other book. This ever building anticipation culminates in GUARDIAN DEMON, and Brook makes this last book more than worth the wait. Engrossing action, off the charts romance, GUARDIAN DEMON is one of the most satisfying series finales I've ever read. 
 Part of this satisfaction is derived from the build up. Brook has crafted a long, sweet road to this final conflict. The battle with Lucifer has always been on an epic scale, spanning millennia and every possible attack from crafty betrayals to full frontal force. This book brings all of those different political fronts to a head, and the lynchpin is once again Michael. Leader of the Guardians, the Alpha hero to end all Alpha heroes, and by this point in the story, battered, broken, and barely hanging on. Michael's vulnerabilities make it believable once the inscrutable, all-powerful shield comes down, when we get to see the raging mass of power and emotion underneath his holy warrior shell. But this chink in his armor does not make him any less alien. Rather, Brook does a fantastic job imagining how the love affair of an immortal, magical being might progress. And the sex scenes, oh my sweet heavens the sex scenes. As interesting as Michael's emotional landscape may be, I must admit even that was overpowered by the reality of a shape-shifting, super-sonic teleporter in bed. For the first time in a thousand years. Michael is everything I could have hoped for, everything I was anticipating, and once I got a taste of him I couldn't get enough. 
 In fact, my only complaint about this book could be that I was so engrossed in the romance I often lost patience with the "battle for the fate of the world" side of the plot. The action was very well paced, and gave Taylor and Michael's romance both a believable foundation and room to breath, but every time the hero and heroine left the page (or paid attention to anyone other than each other), I was just biding my time, waiting for our smoldering hero to come back. Brook made me laugh out loud, fan myself, devour GUARDIAN DEMON in one sitting, and then wish there were more... It's always hard to say goodbye to a series, but it's also hard to imagine any Guardians book could ever be better than this one.

When I requested One True Loves I decided not to read the blurb. I knew TJR writes a good story and I wanted to be surprised. You can understand my shocked face when in the first few paragraphs she says something like: I was with my fiancee when my husband called." Of course, I reread this sentence a couple of times until I realized there were no mistakes. I thought to myself: TJR sure can grab a reader's attention from the get-go. What follows was a story of loss and rebirth. It was a love triangle with features of Cast Away. I was thinking that Jesse probably was feeling like Tom Hanks when he comes back to land to find out his woman is with another man. 
 I love how involved I became with these characters and their back stories. I could divide the story into three parts: Emma with Jesse, Emma with Sam and then Emma, Sam, and Jesse together. I was torn between both guys. They truly were nice guys who loved her and they were perfect for her during a certain time in her life. I did have a favorite and I was hoping he was the last man standing. 
 Emma was a good character too. She spent the first few decades of her life trying to move away from her family and her town. When she loses Jesse, she finds comfort returning to her family and their bookstore. Her character evolves and she discovers she can be happy again. Meeting Sam again confirms it. But, when Jesse is back in her life, she has no idea whom her true love is. It's a road to self-discovering. 
 My only complaint with this book is that I felt like their conflict was solved to easily and Emma kept on going back and forth between both guys. Overall, it was a good book!

Contrary to the opinion of my YA reading son, I enjoyed this sequel to the original DIVERGENT better than its predecessor. There was a lot of action, perhaps too much action, but I liked the way the puzzle of this "faction" society became what it is was laid out, and the race to find out what the big secret and also to find out what lay beyond not only the factions but further away as well became something that grabbed me and compelled me to continue reading till I reached the end. 
 And I found myself satisfied with the conclusion to this book and I find myself looking forward to the October release of the third book in the series, which will presumably answer all the questions that remain. Compared to the MAZE RUNNER, I think I enjoyed these two books better. I liked the characters a lot more and I found the background to be more interesting than what I have learned of that other dystopia. I was also pleased to note that I could actually detect certain themes being worked out here - themes of selflessness vs selfishness, of action vs contemplation, of courage vs impetuousness. I think that my children will perhaps be induced to think about some of these important ideas, and that's one of the marks of a really good book for me.

After I watched new Gilmore Girls episodes, I just had to read Lauren Graham's book Someday, Someday, Maybe. This book is just as entertaining and witty and brilliant as Lauren/Loralai is. 
 It's a story about young actress who has promised herself that she will be a real actress within three years and if not she'll go back home. She does not want to be that actress who works odd waitressing jobs for ever, waiting to her start role to find her. But there is just six months till her deadline and she still has not done much. 
 She works as a waitress, goes to acting studio, there is a big show coming in studio, where all the agents will we in audience. Franny thinks her part of the show was really bad, but still she has two callback from two agency. The first one is safe and relaxed but the second one is fast and scary, and all of the sudden she has auditions and small "laughing girl" part and an actor from her acting studio is interested about her. 
 When all this exiting rush slows down, Franny realizes that the deadline is even more closer, but even if she has an agent, she still does not have a real acting job and she has lost her waitressing job and her boyfriend makes strange propositions and .... 
 The deadline is over and Franny must decide whether she'll go back to home, or to hope, that the things that at first seamed not so right might be the best things ever. And that might be true about many things. 
 The story is funny and sweet and it makes you think. 
 And there is one thing I would like to share with you: 
 FASTER- don't talk down to the audience, take us for a spin, don't spell everything out for us, we're as smart as you - assume we can keep up; 
 FUNNIER - entertain us, help us see how ridiculous and beautiful life can be, give us a reason to feel better about out flaws; 
 LOUDER - deliver the story in the appropriate size, DON'T be indulgent or keep it to yourself, be generous - you're there to reach US.

I have been reading the Dark-Hunter series since its first publication years ago. I thought he was a misunderstood character, but had no idea just how misunderstood he was in actuality. This is a true story of don't judge a book by its cover or through your own preconceived notions. All is not what it seems and especially when colored by Acheron who was going through his own personal crap being shoved on him. Both Acheron and Styxx were both involved with their own tortuous live that they could not see past their own hurt. 
 Kenyon did an excellent job of showing both sides of the story. We are familiar with the story, but that was from Acheron's perspective. I loved Rhyssa in Acheron, but did not like her in this book. In addition, it showed the reader how fallible even a god can be in his own ideas and beliefs.

 It has been 23 books and years later since Kenyon began her series. Honestly, some of the books have been somewhat of the same thing and not as gripping for me as a reader.  Things I didn't like: Finnick's death. (Jacking up the body count, anyone?) Prim's death - even though I understand the why. That it drove a wedge between Gale and Katniss. Katniss giving up in the end and wanting to kill herself. The entire storyline with Peeta. I was fine with the torture. I expected it. But I hated the hijacking and how it altered him and his fundamental characteristics. I also wanted more explanation on his eventual healing - I feel like we missed something in the time Katniss sat in her dirty clothes in her home in the Victor's Village. The whole notion of another Hunger Games. Did these people learn nothing? 
 There's more in both columns, I know. I thought the love triangle was handled much much better in this book, but I still wasn't a fan of it. I will always like the idea of Gale/Katniss, but I never felt as if they were suited for one another. I wish we had seen him and Katniss on better terms in the end. I hate the idea that we never saw him again. And I didn't feel like we needed the epilogue. 
 I seem like I hated the book, but actually I really really enjoyed it. I laughed, and discovered an epic love for Finnick Odair. EPIC love. I cried more times than I can count. The book was very bittersweet for me in a lot of ways and also very moving. I like that everything wasn't happy and shiny in the end, but I feel like Suzanne Collins rushed toward the ending a little too quickly. Things that should have been elaborated on weren't.

I came away from this book so impressed. When I first picked it up a really liked Addie's voice and the set up for her world. She lives in a secret compound in the middle of Texas made up of paranormal people who all have special mind gifts. Major government agencies are aware of them and some of the paranormal people have even lived successful lives out the outside as famous entrepreneurs and inventors. Addie's gift is "divergence" she can search two potential outcomes and decide which path she would like to take. 
 When Addie's parents get divorced she needs to decide which of them she will live with, her mother, who will be staying at the compound or her father, who will be leaving to live among the "norms." At first I thought this was a terrible thing for her parents to do to her, but she later explains they only did it because of her special ability. The majority of the book is told in alternating chapters between the two choices. 
 In the beginning I worried that the alternating chapters would be confusing, but they weren't at all. I actually really appreciated the way it was told. If "norm" Addie was going to a football game on a Friday night then "compound" Addie was also doing that. I really appreciated the acknowledgement and mirroring that took place between the two situations. 
 There is quite a bit of suspense in this book and I thought it was handled really well. There's a drug-dealer who's after Addie's best friend's dad who Addie's dad is trying to help catch in both scenarios. In the compound world there's the attractive football player who's taken a sudden interest in Addie and her rebellion against her mother. In the norm world there's the cute boy Trevor (who I loved!) has an evil girlfriend and who's haunted by an injury that Addie's old world might have something to do with. 
 Rather than having these connections and kind of crazy scenarios feel contrived they felt so real and I immediately related to Addie. West's writing and the world she created were both very strong and believable. As the story goes on it becomes more and more clear what an impossible decision Addie has to make. 
 My only criticism of this book is that I didn't feel like I ever really got to know Addie. Did she get good grades? Did she have friends besides Leila? What was her childhood like? What does she want to be when she grows up? I never really got a feel for her beyond the immediacy of the story, which was ok because I really liked her in the story, but I still wish I knew more about her. I also thought Addie's gift should have a name other than "divergence." I know Veronica Roth doesn't own the word divergent, but still, I think that series is what comes to the minds of book people when they hear that word. 
 The end of this book was so heartbreaking. I was worried because I know there's a sequel and I kept wondering where West was going to leave the story. But I have to say that I thought she ended it in a pretty perfect spot. There are a still questions and things I very much want to have happen, but there's no huge suspenseful cliffhanger. 
 Bottom Line: This is a book I really enjoyed and I would recommend it without hesitation. Kasie West created an interesting and believable world with characters that are extremely relatable. Even though this ends with a cliffhanger it's not overly dramatic. I just hope the next book will be as satisfying!

False silver coins are showing up in town, and Beka's own friends are getting in trouble over them. Then a riot ensues over the raising prices of bread. Beka, a first-year Dog that is once more partnerless, is sent with Goodwin to Port Caynn to dig deeper into the surge of counterfeits. But the local Dogs aren't at all worried about the problem, and Beka's managed to offend the ruling Rogue. Together with the scent hound Achoo, Beka starts digging deep enough to uncover some truly nasty secrets. 
 This is a tad long, but the tension manages to stay strong throughout. The various clues about the counterfeiting ring surface slowly, and Beka's got to play the part of stupid visitor (a role that does not suit her at all). It's interesting to see how local corruption in the Dogs (the police force) feeds the greater corruption in the city, and how Beka functions when friends and allies are few and far between. It's also interesting to see all the various discussions around counterfeiting, and how it debases the currency, and how that ripples out to broader impacts. And of course, this is a strong cop story, with plenty of scuffles with Rats and an unflinching look at some of the uglier sides of the Dogs. 
 I wasn't as keen on the romance. Beka's lived a rough enough life that she should've realized she was being played, and it's kind of annoying how willing she is to bed someone she's known for about two days simply because she's got a pregnancy charm (what about diseases? or better yet, the fact that he's still technically a SUSPECT?). So it was hard to read the romantic sections without skimming because the only reason she falls for him is that he's good-looking and persistent about flirting with her. 
 The other thing I wasn't keen on is how much page time is devoted to glorifying Okha/"Amber" as a woman in a man's body and how beautiful that is (and the homosexual relationship is also portrayed as good, although that one is more just there, whereas the prose specifically takes time out to highlight Okha and his particular deviancy). I do not believe "feelings" define gender, because this makes as much sense as me saying I'm really a purple six-legged pony from Jupiter because I know it in my heart. (Bonus: since there's no evidence no one can prove you wrong, and you're just branded a hater for not going along with it.) 
 Anyway, I do enjoy them for the cop stories, and for a look at Tortall from a different angle. Magic certainly comes into play, but for the most part this is hardboiled detective work (and in this instance, a couple of scent-hound tracking sprees). If the rest of it doesn't bother you, then go ahead and read it. I rate this book Recommended.

I received this book in exchange for an honest review from netgalley. 
 So...where to begin? I really hate giving a negative review; I know Ms. Aster has probably poured her heart and soul into this book, and anything bad that is said about it would be akin to telling a mother her child is a spoiled brat. But, there...I've said it. This book left me feeling unfulfilled. I really, really wanted to <3 <3 <3 it. I read the entire book, because I hoped to find a turning point where I said, "ok...NOW it's found the groove..." but no such time came. The amount of name-dropping bothered me. I don't profess to be a big-time city-dweller. However, just because I don't live in the Almighty NYC (that's 
 New York City 
 for all you fellow rural-dwellers out there) doesn't mean I need to have things spelled out for me over and over and over again. Ms. Aster repeatedly mentions the same brands, and almost always puts a name in front of an item. I don't need to know the name of a facial cream to understand that Taddy is wealthy. I felt like this book could have been a fun read- one I would have perhaps even re-read- and lured me into the rest of the series. Instead, it came across as a Sex In The City wannabe crossed with a bad copy of The Devil Wears Prada. I wasn't buying the Mormon assistant who had no trouble getting fake boobs and watching a porn star do the nasty  but was still ridiculously stupid. Just because someone is religious, doesn't mean they've never watched TV, read a book, or HEARD PEOPLE TALKING AROUND THEM. I really have issues when characters act like they've been living in a hole in the ground circa 1932. Unless, of course, the character is a time-traveller. 
 As for Taddy, I went back and forth between thinking she deserves to be a bitch because her family sucks, to thinking she is a self-righteous a-hole that should be a little more thankful for how her life is turning out. Yes, she is a hard-worker. Yes, she treats her friends better than they treat her (although I've only heard her side- maybe this isn't really the case). I still felt myself cringing inside every time she complained about how much it was costing her to help someone, or telling Jesus he owes her for what she did, or mentioning a brand name yet again. I pay attention when I read; I don't need to be told that the lip gloss is from Baden Cosmetics 3,800 times. 
 Some things didn't hold true for me, such as an incident with Rielle and Warner. I don't think he would've been so slow to handle things, and that felt contrived. Also, the way she talks about her life-long friends makes me think she's shallow and feels like she's doing them a favor by talking to them. 
 My final issue is two-fold. Some of the phrases felt like they should have been left in the 80s. Back when people said things that NO ONE looked cool saying. I felt like the author was trying too hard to be cool, pretentious, and over-the-top. And seriously, if I had read the term "Manhattanite" one more time, I would've thrown my Kindle through the window. I GET IT. Manhattan rocks. Every other place in the world sucks. I might have to go dig my own hole to live in since I am not a fierce, awesome, taxi-cab-calling, Judith Leiber clutch-holding Manhattanite. Or, I could revel in the fact that even though I live in a small town, I could rock a Judith Leiber clutch- if I was so inclined. ;)

On one such night, he finds that someone has stolen his copy of Tamerlane, a rare collection of short stories written by Poe and valued at approximately $400,000. Shortly after, he finds that someone has left a baby in his bookstore, seemingly with the understanding that he will raise the child. 
 And thus begins the gradual melting of A.J.'s heart. And yours, too, most likely. The Storied Life of A.J. Fikry is not what I expected - it was so much more. It's incredibly well-developed, with beautiful characters and an engaging plot. It has twists that you'll probably see coming, but that doesn't ruin anything.  I adored this book and read it from the second I got home from work until I had to go to bed, only to repeat again the next day. Highly recommended for any book lovers, and anyone who enjoys a good story.

 "The Program controls the media, James. They control everything." 
 I would have liked to see a little more world building, especially revolving around The Program. They just seemed like this big faceless enemy without any solidity. I'm not sure it would be feasible in real life. 
 All in all, I love the concept of this duology - the fact that suicide is an epidemic to be treated is fascinating and brilliant!

The Air Awakens books are so packed full of actions and emotions, Water's Wrath was no exception. I breezed through this book. I tried to go slow- bracing myself for overwhelming feels and trying to savour every moment but it proved to be difficult. Elise's words carried me deep into the world and kept me wrapped inside the story. 
 I can't say too much about the story without giving away major spoilers but just know, s*** goes down! There's a bit of a lull at first where we learn about court life and such but none of it was dull. I especially enjoyed the moments where Vhalla trained (with) the soldiers. It was therapeutic to have everyone happily laughing together. Even if we all knew it couldn't last. I can't say I was surprised by the betrayal because the suspicion never left me. I was guarded but I appreciate the lead ups to the reveal. It was dramatic, logical and very well-done. 
 The war in the North is at an end but Vhalla's personal battles are far from over. She faces new challenges and is once again tested. Emotional boundaries are pushed to their limits. I absolutely love Vhalla's character arc, she is nothing but strong and resilient. A fighter. Even in her new state I have no doubt Vhalla will prevail because she's not just the demure librarian at the beginning of Air Awakens anymore. She's so much more. 
 In Water's Wrath we finally find out what has Aldrik so tortured. Our moody prince has been carrying a big secret. Guilt has been eating away at him since a young age. It's a relieve when he finally shares it (with Vhalla). Our prince has become much more level-headed in this installment. Perhaps because of his time away from Vhalla? He was careful to keep up appearances, make better decisions and even show sentiments, dare I say, affection towards his brother. No matter the past, Aldrik is a worthy leader well on his way to become a formidable ruler. 
 Vhalla and Aldrik parted ways at the end of Earth's End and I've been holding my breath for the moment they reunite. Elise did not disappoint me. The tension and longing's still there but they establish a peace (no matter how fragile). I'm loving how mature the two of them are in Water's Wrath. They toed a dangerous line but both understood the risks and rewards should things fail or succeed. Vhalla and Aldrik are the ultimate power couple no matter what so this second (third? fourth?) chance better come to fruition.  
 In true Elise Kova fashion, there's a heartbreaking event. The type that just hurts like someone ripped out all of your inside. Sorry that almost sounds too graphic but that's how I felt. I refuse to believe it. There has to be more to it because this event almost seems meaningless to me. It felt like a filler storyline. Why did it have to happen? Please let it be more than that!

It's kind of hard to come up with new ways to say that these books are terrible, because they are for the most part all terrible in the same way. Like the other books in the series, Breaking Dawn suffers from being overwritten - there are just far too many words used in the service of almost nothing happening. And so many things are unnecessarily said multiple times - if everything were said only once, I would imagine the book would be about 400 pages shorter. (Seriously - there's no need at all for this "story" to be 700+ pages; did Stephanie Meyers get paid by the word?) 
 What makes Breaking Dawn special in the pantheon of the Eclipse saga is that there is a good long section told from Jacob's perspective. Which is awesome, if you've ever wanted to get a story from the perspective of the angry, violent and possessive not-really-an-ex-boyfriend-because-they-never-actually-dated-so-let's-just-call-him-an-asshole. Bella's perspective was nothing earth-shattering, and was frequently frustrating because she just sucks so bad, but, and when I say this you must understand that I hate all of these characters, Jacob is just the most terrible character to come down the literary pike since I-don't-know-when. At least of those who are supposed to be likable. So some 300 pages of his petulant whining is a uniquely unpleasant experience. 
 One other random thing that bothers me mightily about Breaking Dawn (other than how very irritating I find it that Bella calls her parents by their first names), and the Eclipse saga in general, is that it seems like there are no drawbacks to being a vampire - they can walk in the day, there's no loss of strength due to not drinking from people, and Bella herself doesn't even experience the usual newborn vampire discomforts, nor does she have to lose her relationship with her father. Which isn't right - there should be definite repercussions to choosing never to grow, to change, to develop as a person. Choosing one's own path is a popular theme in YA literature, but it's strange and unsettling to see a series that celebrates dropping out of life altogether.

My feelings for this book are so divided. Part of me loved the mystery and was HOOKED by the whole premise of rich boys who might get away with murder. But the other part of me thought this book was a little draggy and Kate got a little too "Junior Detective" at times. 
 Basically, it was FIRST HALF = LOVED!! Second half = EHHHH. 
 I'll explain. At first it was super interesting that Kate was hiding that she was texting with Grant for weeks before he died. She was supposed to meet up with him on the night he died, but there was a misunderstanding and she didn't go to the party he invited her to. She was majorly struggling with guilt because she never let him explain himself and now he'll never be able to. Also, I was FEELING the mystery. I was thinking "how in the hell would you figure out which one did it without a confession?" I was completely fascinated and wanted to read this book straight through. 
 But THEN.... well there was this big twist and OMG I LOVED IT. I didn't see it coming at all and I kind of wish it was saved for the end of the book. Because the book immediately went into a downward spiral from there. It became draggy-- the main character just going over and over and over information that we already knew. It became unbelievable-- would a high school student be asked to do all the things Kate was being asked to do?? Wouldn't they have law students to do it at least?? Then Kate became annoyingly Ms. Nancy Drew. She was always trying to be Jr. Detective, but she took it to a whole new level towards the end of the book and I just wasn't feeling it. 
 There's a romance in this book and I did like it. I thought it was cute and I know that it wouldn't have happened without the twist--- but I would have been okay with that. It was a sweet romance, but it didn't make the book what it was. The book was exciting because of the whodunit element. 
 OVERALL: I loved parts of this book as much as my favorite books of the year-- but I equally didn't love parts of this book as much as books that I've DNF'd. It's a weird duality, but I think I would recommend it. There was enough of the ADDICTING parts to override the DRAGGY-NESS.

Both the story and the style of writing was a tad too simplistic for my liking (this is my personal opinion), the antagonist and his motives were (again, my personal opinion), borderline tedious and uninspiring, the protagonist a mix between "alright" at best and self-absorbed and annoying at worst and I found that there were a few things, in need of an explanation, left unexplained.

Fighting to Forgive is book 2 in a series. The series centers around a group of professional MMA fighters. This book is the story of Blake "The Snake" Daniels. He had a very big role in book 1 so we go into this book knowing a lot about him. He is a 6'2" ex-Marine Jiu-Jitsu black belt and received his nickname because of his submissions. 
 Blake had a troubled childhood. His father, a General in the Marines, was mentally abusive to him, his mother and his brother. Blake chose to draw his father's wrath to protect the other members of his family until being sent away to military school. After finally getting out from under his father, he is making his own way in the world of professional fighting and is known as one of the biggest playboys ever, usually taking home 2 or 3 girls together. He is all about the jokes, never being serious except in the ring. He's the group's comedian and sex god, often combining for a lewd sense of humor and behavior. About the only rule he follows outside of the ring is never sleep with a woman who has kids. 
 "Well, fuck me." Literally. "What's a girl like you doing in a dirty mind like mine?" 
 When she was 16, Layla woke up after a party beside a guy realizing she had lost her virginity and later finding out she was pregnant. They married, and he has made her life hell for years. Her own daughter is now 16, and Layla is finally got the nerve up to leave her husband and make a better life for her and her daughter. She gets a job working as an assistant to the guy in charge at a UFL Training Center. 
 That's the backdrop. Then of course, the shit hits the fan. 
 Si vis pacem, para bellum. 
 If you want peace, prepare for war. 
 I love this series. Everyone who knows me knows I love my fighters. The author seems to really know the subject matter so of course that makes the storyline more appealing and flow more smoothly. Also, the plots are pretty unique. A lot of the books I read are interesting, but the story seems recycled. So far, I have been surprised when certain things happened; I didn't already have it all figured out. I really liked both of the books currently out in the series, but this one was my favorite. I love Blake. What a man he turned out to be! Swoon. 
 "I want them. They're mine."

 Hidden is a difficult book to rate. It's the first installment in the Avena series, so I expected a large amount of world building, character development, and buildup. I had high expectations because I have read other works by this author. However, Hidden was excruciatingly slow, the plot didn't get going until the middle of the book. 
 That being said, I did enjoy Ebony's character because she is a tough girl who has been sheltered all her life, and all she wants is to enjoy being a teenager. She was stifled by her parents, and understandably upset by the secrets they kept. Still this story felt incredibly juvenile in the beginning when Ebony throws fits because she isn't getting her way. The book started off slow in character development, I felt it was more like one action sequence after another, and didn't allow us to learn about who Ebony was. We only got to see Ebony at her worst, and I wanted to know why I should care about this seemingly selfish child. I did enjoy it more when the plot began to move. Marianne Curley does do a fantastic job of creating a fascinating mythology, and that's what I appreciate most from this novel. 
 I loved the idea that there were 4 different realms: Earth, Skade, Avena, and Peridis. Earth is the mortal realm, Skade is the equivalent of hell, Avena is where angels live, and Peridis is essentially heaven for mortals. This was all very fascinating especially where a fallen angel is the king of Skade. Prince Luca was an angel of Avena, until he decided he wanted to be the ruler but ended up exiled to Skade. He was interesting because you could tell he didn't have good intentions, but he still drew you in. 
 Jordan was by far the most interesting character. He was entertaining and heartfelt, and he'd lived a hard life, which really made me connect with him. Jordan had the most depth than any other character within the novel. His dad is in prison for life, and his mom overdosed and died when he was seven. Jordan was creating a life for himself until a tragic accident happens. As a result, Jordan is ostracized and nearly dies a year later. 
 Thane, is the angel that has been sent to Earth to find a missing angel, and he saves Jordan's life because of a connection between Jordan and this mysterious angel. Thane was a hard character for me to get into because he alternates between being a funny and confident guy, to waffling over how to approach Ebony and get her to listen to him. He also seems to have secrets although it's clear he cares about Ebony, and what's to keep her safe. 
 One of the parts that I had trouble connecting with was the love triangle. When Jordan and Ebony meet for the first time, it is an instant love connection. She stumbles into him at a club and he catches her and then they're instantly in love. A few chapters later, Thane and Ebony meet, and they lock eyes across a crowded parking lot then they're also in love. It creates an awkward love triangle, because there is no history, nor any build up of emotion; in just an instant, they love each other. I'm not sure how any of them can be as they haven't spent any time together. I do hope that there is more character development in the future. The only character that I feel like I know is Jordan, but I would also like to get to know Ebony and Thane. What are her likes and dislikes, and what does Thane enjoy? 
 Once I had read halfway through the novel, I did really begin to get into the story, especially once the other angels show up, and the plot progressed at a much better pace. My favorite scene is when Jordan finally points out that while Ebony may have free will, if someone is coercing her into making a decision then how could it really be a free choice. I liked that observation, and I enjoyed that Thane had acknowledged Jordan was correct. By the end of Hidden, I did feel like the plot had progressed and I was starting to get a feel for the characters, but I definitely had quite a few questions left unanswered. 
 I feel that although Hidden has a slow start, there's great potential for this to become an incredible series. I will definitely be keeping my eye out for the next installment, and I look forward to learning more about the characters.

I am a fan of this series and enjoyed reading this very much. I really like Claire's inner monologue, and appreciate that we can see the characters' motivations. The plot lagged for me in this one, though. I found myself reading through and wondering when something was going to happen other than the battle. The Grey-Beauchamp-Fergus intrigue was a fairly pivotal plot point, but felt kind of weak to me. I could have used some more attention to that. Also, I'm really not sure why Roger and Buck ran off to 200 years ago seemingly at the drop of a hat. I realize that happened at the end of the last book, but I don't think I understood that they'd actually done it until this one. It just seems so rash.  
 Although this one fell a little short for me, I'm still in until the end. It's worth saying that the end of this book could have functioned as the end of the series quite nicely.

Well, one thing's for sure. You definitely get your money's worth with this book! Boy, was it LONG and it's only $2.99! And boy, oh boy... did it mess with my friggin head! Seriously, wtf was that and how did the author get me rooting for a complete and utter asshole throughout the whole book? Okay, I lied. There was a short period where I found myself thinking that Dawson Bade, was just what our broken h, Morgan, needed. But, that didn't last very long! I quickly started questioning what the hell was wrong with him that he actually put up with so much shit for so long! But mostly, this book made me question what was wrong with me, that I actually wanted to see "the misogynistic evil [thank you, India Lee! (: ] that's Drew Kelley get his HEA. Mind you, I was still rooting for him even after I'd already acknowledged that his reasons for treating Morgan the way that he did, just didn't cut it! See, it doesn't make any sense to you either, does it? Yep, every bit of my common sense was screaming for me to hope Morgan ended up with the 'normal' guy, but where would the fun be in that? Well, that's my story and I'm sticking to it, because I still have no idea why I loved that ass Drew! 
 Maybe this can help you somewhat understand what this book was like... towards the beginning I couldn't help but draw comparisons to the movie SLEEPING WITH THE ENEMY and the CONSEQUENCES Series. Yeah, it was drama filled and just a smidge disturbing. Well, maybe more than a smidge, but for some reason, I enjoy reading that sort of thing. Yeah, you can all psycho analyze me later, back to the book. 
 Morgan went through so many horrific things in her life that I couldn't help but feel for her. For the longest time, the poor thing couldn't catch a flipping break. Then all of a sudden, things started falling into place and I truly thought she was afraid to make any decisions because she honestly didn't know how. She was programmed. Then, I became proud of the strong independent woman she blossomed into, only to once again fall back into the pattern of not being able to make up her freaking mind - it went on for so long that at one point I wanted to scream at my Kindle. Seriously, if there's one thing I can't stand, it's when I have to read chapter after chapter of a heroine not being able to choose between two men. I could understand it more so in Morgan's case and I truly respected the way that she handled it with Drew, but with Dawson, ehhh... not so much. 
 I found myself either loving or hating the characters, which shows that the author did her job. Without question, I hated Derik the most and absolutely loved the free spirited Starlight. 
 Oh, and I loved the Warning at the beginning of the blurb! It made me want to read this all that much more! 
 " Warning! This is not your everyday fall in love romance. This book contains disturbing situations, strong language, graphic, sexual content, some forced, some not. If it's your happily ever after love story that you are looking for, you should probably move on. If you are up for the ride, stick around and it may just turn into a love story after all." 
 Loved it! And I highly recommend it! Just keep in mind, this is not for everyone... Also, plan accordingly, because it's definitely NOT a quick read.
