I was given this book as part of my HSC reading criteria, as a supplementary text. This meant that while I should read it, I didn't have to. So of course I didn't touch the book until I returned it. 
 But at the beginning of my first year at University one of the lecturers recommended the book as a 'must be read at least once in everyone's life' kind of book. Also a few users on Booklr and BookTube recommended it as one of their favourites. So I thought okay, I might read this book now, and bought a copy. 
 I'm sorry to all the people who love this book, I can see the potential, but I just do not love this book at all. It was long and over written, as is the case with many older books, and the themes were interesting but ultimately not set out in a way that allowed me to remain focused on this book for more than an hour or so at a time. 
 It was a book that made the reader think but one that also requires quite a lot of mental focus to read accurately. It did bring up interesting and relevant points about society but I am not the type to read books that take up quite so much thought process. I enjoy reading books that make the reader question things, such as the make up of society and the class rankings, but I prefer to do so with books that I find myself able to absorb. I was not able to get lost in this book. I constantly had to force myself to continue reading and I wish it was different, but this book was not one that I connected with. 
 That isn't to say it isn't a wonderful, insightful book. If I had been a more politically or legal minded person I am sure this book would be a favourite. 
 As it is I prefer books that allow an escape from reality, not books that shine spotlights on it.

Hannah and Matt meet online in a writers community of sorts. They co-write a story together and their relationship is supposed to be totally professional and anonymous. They know each other as Night Owl and Little Bird only and want it to stay that way. Until one night Matt asks what Hannah is wearing....and an unexpected, intense chemistry sparks between them. 
 The Night Owl was something very different and something very similar at the same time. The difference to other books was that the storyline was totally original. I doubt there is a book around that has similar plot. The similarity was the characters - secretive, hot, sexy man and an innocent but willing woman. 
 I was deeply hooked from the moment I switched on my Kindle. My God, I couldn't put the book down for a second before I had read 39% of the story. And believe me, I would have kept going if I hadn't already made plans for the evening and wasn't running late as it was. 
 The relationship between Hannah and Matt is intense. He has a Fifty Shades of Grey vibe to himself - he is bossy, arrogant, crazy sexy, a little broken and paranoid, says exactly what comes into his mind and makes Hannah and ME blush in embarrassment. The man talks dirty. B-I-G T-I-M-E. 
 The book was definitely one of the best I've read all year (and that would be close to 100 books so far). The book had graphic sex scenes, but it was also very much more. I can't go to specifics because that would only lead to spoilers, but the book had a depth to it way beyond hot sex scenes. When I reached the end - and the epilogue in particular, I gasped out loud and shouted "No way!". Got up from the sofa and paced around the living room holding my head. Lol! Honest to God, that is what I did. And my husband looked at me like I had lost my mind. So it's probably needless to add that the book ends in a cliffhanger, but regardless of that is a book worth reading right now! 
 5+ stars

We put our lives in other people's hands, and for the most part, they looked at us blankly and said, What lives? What hands? 
 I didn't know, when I randomly picked this up off the library shelf, that this book is based loosely on That Kiss, from 2010. I remember that, I remember my heart exploding with love for the two of them. So, reading the inside book blurb, I got very happy. 
 And then I opened the book and read the first couple of pages. And may or may not have shaken my fist at the sky and muttered, "Damn you, Levithan." 
 This book overflows with beautiful words. Sentences and paragraphs that I want to eat, they are such delicacies. Three separate tales, all woven together by narrators using the threads of history. A sad, glorious history that makes the modern day stories all the more sweet, all the more sad, all the more fun. 
 I expected to cry, but was doing just fun until the last maybe 10 pages. 
 I hate you, David Levithan. I hate you so much. 
 I love all of these characters. These are not the stories of Matty and Bobby. Cooper is not Tyler Clementi. But they are close enough to cause tears and joy and again, hating David Levithan for the destruction of my tear ducts. 
 Short, and beautiful, and powerful.

Actual rating: 2.5 
 I was prepared to write a lengthy review, but now that I've finished the book and had time to think on it, I've come to the conclusion that I just physically and mentally can't. Not for any discernible reason I can attest to, either, but I'm left feeling a bit depressed and disappointed. 
 This was not the book the blurb makes it out to be, and because of that, I was both pleasantly surprised, and sorely frustrated. The cover art and synopsis associated are misleading. This started off making me feel a bit uneasy, as I guessed the intention was: a young man working at a video store in the late 1990's receives a few complaints about odd and slightly disturbing images being spliced onto their rented VHS tapes. First, I must say the nostalgia hit me terribly here. Blockbuster and video rental stores were like a second home to me growing up, so the idea that this novel centered around one was exciting. What I came to find out, however, was that... it wasn't. The story grew, in a quite disjointed manner, into one of broken families, growing up, dealing with grief- and all swirling around these weird video tapes. 
 There's really not much I care to say. 
 It just left me feeling sad and nostalgic and underwhelmed just like life.

This is my third time reading this story and I still love it so very much. 
 This is the most perfect christmas book out there - from the few I've read that is. I absolutely adore everything about it. THere's things to be learned for both children and adults. 
 'For it is good to be children sometimes, and never better than at Christmas.' 
 The thing I like the most about this book though, is the writing. It's so beautiful. I cannot even begin to express my love for Dickens' writing style. It's so unique and very easy to read. I found myself reading some sentences over and over again just for the beauty of it. 
 'Why show me this, if I am past all hope!' 
 I like Tiny Tim and Marley, but best of all is Scrooge. Yeah, I know, no surprise there. I especially like the scene with the turkey and also the last scene with Bob. Those two scenes describe in a beautiful way what Christmas is about. 
 'I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year. I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future. The Spirits of all Three shall strive within me. I will not shut out the lessons that they teach.'

A lovely book about a young girl's childhood in Vietnam, and her struggle to adjust to a new life in America. It's written in simple, spare verse that captures the strong feelings and attachments of a child. It's told however with an adult's retrospection and understanding, making it all the more heartbreaking. According to wikipedia, Thanhha Lai intially set out to write a book for adults that was "third-person omniscient, spanning 4000 years of Vietnamese history." Thank God she wrote this book for children instead. 
 I would recommend if you liked "Persepolis".

 The only bad thing about this books was what exactly happened to Audrey that she was left the school? What did Tasha, Izzy and the others do to her? 
 I would highly recommend this book!

Requested from netgalley in exchange for a fair review. 
 'Scuse me, can someone let the author know this is not how this book was supposed to end? Because she is confused and that is not how you end this story goddamit?! 
 ::ahem:: 
 I knew going in that this wouldn't be a feel good kind of book. I was prepared for that, it's a horrifying thought, a family consisting of a mother and daughter constantly on the run from an abusive man. Then suddenly the floor is yanked out from underneath the daughter when her mother goes missing. 
 I should've known it was going to be rough when Peaches got abandoned in the first five pages. You just don't abandon a cat, you know. It's not very nice. Especially an indoors only cat, it's cruel and made me very cranky right out of the gate. 
 I realize this was a very short book, but I feel like we didn't get nearly enough storyline out before the great chase. The end of the book, with apologies and making it right, would've been a lot more powerful if we hadn't only had maybe two scenes involving Imogen, and one scene with Precious. And for all of Jermaine's bad boy status/mistreatment at the hands of students and faculty alike, again, maybe two examples. Makes for telling rather than showing. 
 We had a villain on the part of the teacher, Ms. Barnes, but we never really had any motive on her part. Sure, some teachers just really despise their profession, but the scene in detention, where she purposefully messes with Edie about whatever life she left behind in Canada, made absolutely no sense without some exposition behind it. 
 I really did think she would end up finding her mother. Despite it all, I didn't think her mother was really dead. So even though I hadn't quite gotten emotionally involved here, I was caught up in the suspense of wanting to know what happened to her, and there was a lump in my heart when we found out. 
 I was annoyed at the jail scene. We'd gotten to a part in the book where Edie genuinely was finding her own inner strength, which is lovely and all. But the strength she used against her father felt fake, and forced. His anger and irrationality back at her also felt forced. 
 Not all abusers are alike, but the majority know how to hold composure in front of others. And I don't see someone who held a facade for that long, who worked with the police department, letting the mask fall away quite that easily. Fake, and forced.  
 A good story, but it probably needed to be longer in order for me to become invested in any of these characters fully. Disappointing, but not terribly so.

Stolen There are so many 5 star ratings for Stolen that I'm almost hesitant to write my less than enthusiastic response. The writing was lovely, the characters were dimensional, but I did not connect with them emotionally like this book seemed to require in order to fully enjoy this. The one thing that definitely comes across in Stolen is the emptiness and the hopelessness that Gemma was feeling. It was easy to understand how confused she must have been, yearning for human contact yet not being able to fully trust that he wouldn't cut her into pieces and feed her to his camel. The camel, by the way, was my favorite character in Stolen. I did like that the kidnapper was not shown as some tyrannical monster but that the reader was able to somehow sympathize with his motivations even while knowing his actions were unforgivable.Mostly I just thought that it would be horrible to be kidnapped to such a barren landscape with no books, internet, or anything to distract from the kidnapper who keeps weeping at me. The kidnapper's emotional vulnerability was a bit much and annoyed me almost as much as the slow pace of the story. I was partly offended on Gemma's behalf and partly amused when she would try to escape and Ty (weepy kidnapper) would sigh in boredom and act like "Really Gemma? Again? Can you leave a good trail this time for when I have to rescue you....again." And he would just let her go without much protest knowing she wasn't getting anywhere. I will say that Gemma was not completely docile, nor did she quietly come to terms with her fate. The Stockholm Syndrome aspect of Stolen was definitely well done and quite believable. I can see why so many people loved this story and I wish I could have liked it more. Ultimately, it was like the barren landscape it described, it's beauty was only visible to those who were meant to be there. As I said though, I really did like that camel!!

Seeing Mila 2.0 on my Netgalley dashboard was a nice surprise that came during a couple of rough days last month. To be honest, I went into this book half-afraid. I had huge expectations from Mila 2.0, but I didn't really like the prequel novella. I'm glad to report, my expectations were met, in some aspects also exceeded. 
 Mila is an android that more than one group of evil guys would love to get their hands on. But Mila is more than just a cutting-edge piece of technology; there is more humanity in her than her creators could ever assume. The chase starts around chapters two or three, with barely a moment's respite for the rest of the book. Debra Driza doesn't shy away from the painful, the ugly and the tragic, and I think that might be my favorite part of the book. Also, the novel moves at a great pace and there's a nice rhythm to the writing. The android and the human parts of Mila mesh well; she might desperately wish to forget that she has wires and tubes running through her body, but when circumstances demand, she learns how to utilize her android gigs to protect the ones she loves. 
 On the cons side, there was a point where I started feeling that Mila was getting whiny. The whole ordeal with Hunter was also weird; he is a nice guy, but the sort of guy that I instantly assumed had something to hide. And despite his niceness, I don't think the short encounters between Mila and Hunter warrant that sort of trust. Too strong, too fast, almost insta-love, and as always I have my reservations about that. 
 If you are looking for a kick-ass, action-packed YA novel, you cannot afford to miss Mila 2.0.

 I really really enjoyed this book. I didn't love it but it was still oh so good and oh so addicting. (It would be a 4.5 rating if we did half stars) I would like to thank Shane from Itching to Read for allowing me to be part of the blog tour and also, HarperTeen and Ingrid Paulson for sending us an e-arc to read and review. 
 Absolutely, hands down, the best thing about this book is a guy named Tucker 'Tuck' Holloway. Oh my... *fans self* He is absolutely perfect. To be honest, he reminds me a lot of Puck from the Iron Fey series, personality wise. Which is an amazing thing because Puck happens to be my favorite fictional character so it's a great comparison. He's not as much of a jokester but man, he slings smartass comments every opportunity he gets. 
 I love the relationship between Ellie and her older, extremely protective brother, Graham. I love when older brothers are protective of their younger sisters, it's such an awe factor. However, sometimes they do go too far and hover worse than a parent may. Graham definitely takes his protectiveness too far a few times but Ellie really loves him and really looks up to him. She wants to protect him the same way he's done for her their entire life. Especially when her world starts changing the moment she steps foot in her grandmothers small town in Norway. The townspeople are not very welcoming and extremely rude to her for what she thinks is absolutely no reason at all. They blame her grandmother for something and decide to take it out on Ellie, as well. 
 Valkyrie's are real and they're about to invade Ellie's life in more ways than one. What she thought was just a summer away at her grandmother's place turns out to be so much more. Her world is about to be turned inside out and every other way possible. 
 The story was interesting enough, especially with the mythology mixed in to it. (Actually, it plays a big role) But what really grabbed my attention were the characters and their relationships, especially. In the beginning, I thought there was going to be a love triangle and I am so relieved to see that it's not at all what she was doing. The growth of Ellie's relationship with Tuck was perfect, realistic and just...amazing. The way the insulted each other all the time was highly entertaining, as well. They've always just meshed so well together it's totally like these two personalities were made for each other. 
 I definitely recommend checking this book out. It entertains, it's got lots of action, amazing character bonding going on and just a real enjoyment to read.

In some ways, this is your basic urban fantasy; we have a young female protagonist (Ivy Granger) with a supernatural talent (psychometry) working as an independent contractor (private investigator), and a world where various supernatural beings exist unbeknownst to the general population. As it turns out during Ivy's investigation there is a threat to the community that must be dealt with, and Ivy happens to be in the center of things. 
 Contrary to what the cover suggests, Ivy does not wear spike-heeled latex fetishwear and flash her panties in murky dungeons. For most of the time, there is no romance element, although one suddenly appears in the final chapters from a (to me, at least) unexpected quarter. 
 I spotted a few silly copyediting mistakes like using diffuse instead of defuse, waste instead of waist (although waist was also spelled correctly several times in the same paragraph), and phase instead of faze, but they were rare.

Entertaining and difficult to take a break from for sure. I would have appreciated a little more subtlety in the struggle of "good vs evil" here, but maybe I am being a touch too harsh for a book series that originally held the first title in it as Men Who Hate Women. I think at one point when they introduced the Blonde Giant, I had to come to terms with the fact that I am actually reading a drier pulp fiction, and didn't have any real problem with some of the sillier things after this realization because of it. I could have done with a little less on the sections detailing Lisbeth's every home purchase, but even the delivery of this kind of information seemed to at least add to the mood of what was going on in the story with an odd sort of urgency that paralleled her situation. 
 Gets a touch preachy, although I am very happy to see that the author was interested in discussing the subject of institutionalized misogyny at all, and I am sure that many people feel that touching the subject at all would make you "preachy" rather than shoving it under the rug (like, yanno, the rest of society does.) In interest of full disclosure, I am utterly thrilled to see inequality between genders and sexual orientations spoken of in terms that are realistic, especially from a thriller, as it is so common that most of these more sensational stories end in wilting into a pistol-toting Marlowe's world-weary arms, and Lisbeth's agency comes as a welcome breath of fresh air to me. At many points she seemed a little superpowered, but I think the part of me that wanted to see a female character as beefed-up as the scores of male ones in the genre overrode my odd feelings on it. 
 I took a lot of enjoyment from Mimi's character being explored further, as well as Berger's, as it seemed to give the overall relationships of the story more depth and interest. Mimi in particular provided one of my favorite parts of the book with her questioning, as I for one can speak to the experience detailed here of certain types of men being threatened, angered, or intimidated by my orientation and trying to either taunt, belittle, or otherwise approach me with aggression. I find it delightful that many of our most ambitious, effective characters in this installment are the women, and it is through a variety of qualities and skills that they are able to reclaim power: Lisbeth through wits, speed, and violence; Mimi through humor, martial arts skill, and firm resolve; and Berger through her ambition, emotional intelligence, and self-motivation. 
 I still need to think more clearly about some aspects of the story (some really hamfisted lines in this one I need to recall), but definitely worth continuing.

Let's get things straight: even though the blurb promises superheros, it really leans more to the paranormal factor of things. True, there are superheroes, but not in the traditional sense. It was as if I was reading City of Bones with the added bonus of superheroes, if you understand my meaning. It also reminded me of Hex Hall, with its sharp snarky atmosphere and wit. 
 OK, the snark isn't as sharp as Hex Hall, but still... 
 Audrey was possibly the strongest point in the whole novel. She was a solid narrator, and acted as a normal teen should. She's funny and logical, and she accepts that she can't be fearless. That she does get scared from time-to-time. 
 That's actually what a lot of authors forget in this age of teens-saving-the-world. These guys are between the ages of fifteen and seventeen, and you expect them to save the world and not be scared? 
 Leon was also another strong point. He was warm hearted, thoughtful, cute and a pleasure to get to know. It's been a while since I've read about a protective-type guy who isn't overly protective in a way that he controls everything the heroine does, whoever she meets or whatever she says. 
 You know the guys. 
 However, the romance was horribly paced. Even though I liked the guy, there wasn't much romance development. As in, the romance came out of nowhere! 
 Then we move on to Audrey's mother. 
 As cool as a breeze, as feisty as a lion, and will do anything in the name of protecting her daughter, Morning Star is truly the best mother to feature in YA fiction. 
 And do you know what? It just shows you that most of the parents in YA fiction truly don't give a damn about their kids. They let them off doing whatever, whenever, and they don't care. They don't mind, and they leave them at it without asking too many questions. Maybe this is a turning point - maybe authors are starting to cop-on to themselves and realize that parents would actually take a bullet for these kinds (well... some of them, anyway...). 
 The writing was quite vague when describing a few key world-building concepts, Audrey's Knowing abilities, and with describing action sense (the few that are there) and the monsters. I still have no idea what the demons look like. Also, Bethany Frenette tries to write beautifully, but it doesn't work. Instead, she tries too hard and it ends up being funny or weird. 
 Now, we move on to the plot, and world-building. 
 There is nothing new here. 
 The concepts were - like I've said before - very much like the City of Bones, except with superheroes. Again, the concepts are also very vague, and quite confusing. I still don't understand why the 'Kin' are saying their protecting the city. There clearly just looking out for themselves, since the demons aren't interested in humans. There only intent are killing off members of the Kin. 
 Or, at least, that's what I gather. 
 Never the less, Dark Star might not be the best book I've ever read, but it was still an enjoyable read with some great characters.

Ruh roh, I'm going against all of my friends' reviews here, but I didn't think this book was that bad. Yes, I was angry a few times and wanted Jessie to move away from Justice because he was being a hypocrite, BUT... 
 *ducks for cover* I kind of understood why Justice thought he couldn't be with Jessie. He has proved himself to be a guy who thinks of every angle before he makes a move. He understood the huge ramifications that their relationship could have with both the New Species and the humans - along with the danger to Jessie herself. 
 I also understood Jessie's point of view. She thought she would be okay with a casual relationship with him, but then realized she was selling herself short by allowing him to keep her on the "down low". When she found out that she was living in a house that he was reserving for his future mate - a New Species mate, she decided that she didn't want to be his dirty little secret anymore. I thought that was a better decision than being his fuck-buddy. 
 Now, as penance for my unpopular opinion, I shall hang my head in shame.

There isn't much to say about this awful time that has not already been said. This book details the author's time in a concentration camp with his father; I have read other Holocaust books and each one adds something different to my understanding of this horrific time. I like the author's revelations of his inner struggles with his belief in God to his feelings about wanting to take his father's rations when his father was on the brink of death.

I knew I was gonna love it I mean four hot brothers? Umm, yes please! 
 Storm is that it's unlike anything I've ever read. Okay partly since I have read Carrier of the Mark. But in this book, there's four hot brothers who can control the elements. Michael with Earth, the twins Gabriel and Nick with fire and air, and then there's Chris with water. Storm is told in dual POVs. Chris and Becca. Becca is first introduced when she saved Chris from a fight. Later on the guys who beat up Chris thinks that Becca is somehow involved with them -even though she's not ... yet. 
 I loved the whole concept Brigid Kemmerer had with the whole elements. There's many people who falls in this circle of the elements but not on the points where they can actually hardcore control it -except for the Merrick brothers of course. And if they do lie on a point, there's these people called The Guides who kill the pure elements but not the fifths who can basically control every element. 
 When there's five guys and one girl in this book there has to be some teasing and drama going around. Right after Becca takes Chris home, Michael, the oldest brother, goes all overprotecting which kinda made him annoying to me. I loved the twins so much! Gabriel has this snarky, sarcastic attitude that I just love and the things he say is hilarious. Nick is the opposite of Gabriel. He's kind, quiet, and the brother who keeps everything balanced and peace. Other than the brothers there's this new kid named Hunter who I DID NOT like at all. I'm not gonna go in depth of that since that's like a whole lot of spoilers. 
 Since this is dual points of views, we get to see how the guy and girl feels. Its clearly obvious that they both like each other so happy relationship right? Wrong. There is a love triangle in this book. Half of the story is Chris ans Becca helping each other out, Chris trying to avoid Becca, they're just friends, and Hunter. Yes Hunter is the other part in this love triangle. Relationship wise, there was barely and chemistry between them but I hope to see some development in Spark. 
 Overall, a fast paced book full of supernatural aspects. I recommend you all read this and I cannot wait to read the sequel with my favorite brother Gabriel in it!

This was really weird. I don't really know how to review it. The first book in the quartette was easy enough to read. The writing of Orson Scott Card is really "beautiful" but he finds some way to twist his ability to write well, into a means of promoting really horrible ideas. So I'm a bit mixed. The writing is something I just get into, but what he's really saying just is hard as can be to read, especially if you ignore the writing.

We Are the Ants by Shaun David Hutchinson is easily summarized by stating that this is a book about grief. Our first person narrator, Henry, is a teen who is abducted by aliens, these aliens show him the end of the world on January 29th and also give him the power to stop it. These same events are correlating with Henry having quite an awful time, even by adult standards. Henry's boyfriend killed himself a few months ago without a note, leaving Henry with a horrible deep depression. This book is his journey as he tries to handle his grief and the things he has no control over. On top of that, his home life is stressful but above all, he is the victim of one of the worst bullying I've read in YA. I mean, cops have to get involved type of bullying. I want to mention this because this book is filled with triggers; suicide, rape, verbal abuse, physical abuse, humiliation and severe bullying. 
 Overall - this book is utterly beautiful. This is one book I want to give to all teens because I can imagine it speaks to them on a level that deeply impacts them, it's relatable. Henry is very relatable for teens and anyone who is in deep depression. Hutchinson has a great way with language and he weaves scientific fact as metaphors in an elegant manner. I took a mean pink highlighter to this book and I don't regret it. I did find some parts of it a little repetitive but I imagine that was because it was meant to reiterate certain points but as an adult reader it felt a little on the nose at times but that was so minimal it's almost not worth mentioning. I will say, if you go in expecting a lot of sci-fi you will not find that here, this is purely a YA contemporary and in my SPOILER section I will discuss in depth. 
 SPOILERS!! 
 * 
 * 
 * 
 I want to touch briefly on my final thoughts that will reveal plot points so please don't read if you don't want to be spoiled. 
 I don't think there were ever aliens, I think Hutchinson craftily used aliens and the end of the world as beautiful symbolism to Henry's inherit alienation from everyone around him and his own desire to end 'his world' because of his inability to cope with his grief and Jesse's death. I think Henry suffered two great loses - the first was his father, as he states in the book, his father leaving and his first 'abduction' happen around the same time. His second loss, Jesse's death, brings about the end of the world choices. Both the abductions and the end of the world are a manifestation of Henry's internal struggle. He blacks out for days, he has hallucinations - I'm not a psychologist but anyone can see he is experiencing displacement, severe mental trauma and deep depression. Henry is an unreliable narrator but done in the most excellent of ways and I give Hutchinson 100% props for crafting such an impeccable story. 
 Now, despite giving this book 5 stars (well deserved) I don't think this is a favorite of mine. Despite connecting deeply with certain phrases and quotes, I was alien to Henry and his world. I can appreciate it as an observer but it didn't stir emotions in me like other books have. That is of personal nature, it's got to do with me being 36 and seeing things differently than Henry who is a sad boy who I deeply sympathize with rather than identify with. Also, despite his romance with Diego being lovely and sweet it didn't make me gush like it probably did for others but I think this is because Hutchinson did a great job of portraying teen romance which I see with a critical eye. My personal favorite character was Charlie - his character development was amazing as was how Hutchinson wrote him. 
 Overall? GO READ THIS BOOK.

It seems that I couldn't completely get rid of my issue with the series. Iain Banks' prose, or more particularly his dialogue, just makes me happy. Forgive a lengthy quote, but this right here is what I enjoy in a Banks book. The protagonist and narrator, Ken, doing what he does best - going off on one:* 
 "Faith is fine for poetry, for images and metaphors and art and for telling us who we are, who we've been. But when faith tries to describe the world, describe the universe, it just plain gets it wrong. Which wouldn't matter if it admitted it was wrong, but it can't, because all it's got is its unwavering certainty in its own infallibility; the rest is smoke and mirrors, and admitting imperfection brings the whole lot tumbling down. There are no crystal spheres, and the planets are not the result of some sky god's wet dream. If that is supposed to be taken literally, then it's a lie, plain and simple. If it's a metaphor, then it has bugger all to do with the way things really work. Reason works, the scientific method works. Technology works." 
 Ah, I feel like creating a meme and sending it winging its merry way around t'interweb. 
 But there's more to the book than polemic. There's Banks' brilliant ear for dialogue and accent. There's a slow build of character and situation, nudging all the players into just the right arrangement, and then - blamm! Or perhaps, splat? All hell breaks loose for the exhilerating final act. 
 The panicking, expletive-ridden stream of consciousness narrative puts you right into the situation, complete with mortal terror, appalling hangover and catastrophically loose bowels. 
 The ludicrously, farcically extended house-breaking scene probably shouldn't work; it's just far too silly for a book like this! Isn't it? But somehow it does work, and it's heart-in-the-mouth, page-turning stuff; one minute snorting with laughter at the idiotic farce; the next minute feeling a queasy sense of horror - because this is Iain Banks, and I've read his books before. There's no guarantee Ken's going to make it out alive... 
 I can't remember when I stopped avidly reading all of Iain Banks' books, or why. Possibly cuz I struggled with The Algebraist. But Dead Air has reminded me how much I enjoy his writing. Everything after Whit has just made it onto my reading pile. 
 * I was going to change that to 'shooting his mouth off' because more people will understand that phrase. But taking a leaf from Banks' book, I'll use my own colloquialisms and force people to understand instead of pandering to a global, generic culture!

JM Coetzee writes allegories. His books always work on at least two levels. So while the plot of this book is that a professor fucks his student and is disgraced for it, that's not what it's about. 
 It's about post apartheid South Africa, Coetzee's home country. Whites, in charge for so long, lose power. Blacks, furious, punish them. People struggle to find a way forward. Out of it all, inevitably, a biracial baby is born.  Coetzee (rhymes with "book see") uses rape as a metaphor, which seems to be a thing for him. Tony D'Souza calls Disgrace "the definitive work on South Africa's present state." 
 Coetzee writes exact books. He knows what he's doing. He has a point, and every sentence aims at the point. His work is powerful but manicured. There are no unruly digressions. They are strict. And nasty, too: violence and rape are Coetzee's recurring themes. Coetzee seems to have more sympathy for women than for men. His protagonist here, ex-Professor Lurie, is awful. His daughter Lucy is sympathetic and complicated, the soul of the book. "You behave as if everything I do is part of the story of your life," she tells him. 
 You are the main character, I am a minor character who doesn't make an appearance until halfway through. Well, contrary to what you think, people are not divided into major and minor. I am not minor. I have a life of my own, just as important to me as yours is to you, and in my life I am the one who makes the decisions. 
 There's some metafiction here, as there always is in Coetzee. He knows what he's doing with this plot. "Half of literature is about it," he points out. "Young women struggling to escape from under the weight of old men." The book is about the struggle, not the weight.

I love Jane Eyre. It is one of my favorite classics so I approached this book with some reserve, especially since I did not like Pride and Prejudice and Zombies and was unable to finish that particular classic mashup. There is a huge difference between Jane Slayre and Pride and Prejudice and Zombies however. It is obvious from the first page that the author has much respect for the original work. The addition of vampyres, werewolves, and zombies is cleverly and rather tastefully done. Most of the book retains the feel of Jane Eyre so I felt like I was rereading the original much of the time. Jane Eyre is a grave book and does not have much humor in it but I found the humor sprinkled throughout Jane Slayre to be refreshing in instances like Jane wondering if perhaps Blanche Ingram is a vampyre. The main characters retain their essence and much of the dialogue is the same so I was able to enjoy the interactions between Jane and Mr. Rochester. In the original, Bertha Mason is merely mad. Here she is also a werewolf, which explains further Mr. Rochester's treatment of her and her strange behavior. I loved that the Reeds were vampyres. I thought they were horrible people in the original so I thought this suited them perfectly. 
 There were some things that I did not enjoy-particularly the zombies at Lowood and the treatment of Helen Burns. In the original, Helen is a close friend of Jane and very important to her. In Jane Slayre, I didn't feel that Jane was as close to Helen and I didn't like Helen's fate in the novel. Most of the time however, I was able to enjoy the changes to the story but there were a few times that I did want to go pick up Jane Eyre instead. My favorite parts of the novel were at Thornfield Hall and I thought the author did a fantastic job with it, particularly Jane and Rochester's relationship. 
 Overall I thought this was a tastefully and respectfully written mashup with some great humorous moments mixed in with a good story. I love Jane Eyre but I enjoyed Jane Slayre as well and it made me want to reread the original Bronte novel. There have been a number of mashup novels since the publication of Pride and Prejudice and Zombies but this one would be a cut above the rest. I would recommend this to fans of that new genre as well as to those who enjoy satirical writing. Be sure to check out the reader's guide in the back as well. The discussion questions will have you howling! If the idea of messing with the story of Jane Eyre sounds sacrilegious to you, you may want to skip Jane Slayre but I think it is an excellent retelling which might inspire new fans to seek out the classic.

This is another mean girl falls from grace book I just had to read. There was just something about how little I knew about this book that intrigued me, so I decided why not and picked it up on a whim. And let me tell you, Rose Whitfield is fucking awesome. 
 I just finished reading Ruthless by Carolyn Lee Adams and Rose reminds me a lot of Ruth. Both are strong, fierce, and, for lack of a better term, ruthless. But, where as Ruth was cold and calculating, Rose was a lot more energetic and fun. 
 Torched is essentially about a high school mean girl who's framed for arson after her boyfriend's family boat catches fire. Everyone turns against her, convinced she did it. Rose has to then clear her name with her partner in crime Paxton. 
 What makes this book so different from others of its kind is both Rose's character and just how Colt takes on the theme of forgiveness. Let's talk about Rose first, because this girl is awesome. 
 What sets Rose apart from a lot of other characters in this type of book is that Rose truly is sorry for what she's done. Over the course of the novel, she learns that her actions had consequences and rather than try and shove the blame on someone else, she takes full responsibility for her actions. There's a scene where Rose asks Paxton if her being framed is some sort of retribution for all the pranks she's pulled. It is one of the most emotional scenes in the entire book because not only does Rose own up the fact she's done wrong, she truly believes she needs to make up for it, even though the after effects weren't her intention. 
 Rose is proof that teens are perfectly capable to taking responsibility for their actions. She doesn't try to blame her actions on her friends or her war with Paxton. No, she says "This is my fault. I'm sorry and how can I make up for it?" And that, leads us to the central theme in this book. 
 An apology doesn't solve everything. 
 Plain and simple. You can't say "I'm sorry", whether you mean it or not, and expect everything to work out and for everyone to forgive you. Almost everyone turns on Rose, her friends, parents, ect., because they truly believe she set the fire. Alinda, Rose's best friend, feeds her the dogs, demanding she apologize and makes Rose's life insufferable when Rose doesn't bow to her will. 
 But, when Alinda finally comes around and realizes Rose was telling the truth, she apologizes to her and wants things to go back to normal. And guess what? Rose doesn't forgive her. They don't go back to normal, because they can't. Alinda left Rose without listening to her side of the story and that's something Rose just can't forgive. She realizes Alinda wasn't the friend she thought she was and can never go back to who they were before. 
 The same goes for her boyfriend, who lies put Rose in even more trouble. He still cared about Rose, and for most of the book he was the reason she wanted to clear her name, but once all the lies came to the surface, it became obvious that Rose and Ryan wouldn't be the same. 
 In the end, that's what sets this book apart from so many others. Forgiveness has to be earned, no matter your history. You can't expect betrayal to be forgiven nor can you expect everything to wrap up nicely. Rose's story is about coming to terms that everything has repercussions and forgiveness is not easily awarded or taken.

Well, I'm due for a book hangover, and I think I finally found my hangover-worthy book. The 5th Wave was enthralling, addicting and so very, very hard to put down. Yancey has a unique concept that was executed very well; I was a little lost in some of the description of the camps and tech, probably in part because it's science fiction and partly because I read it so darn fast. But the set up was flawless, the first 70 or so pages setting up the invasion as it was and the invasion as it is in the present. I thought I wouldn't like the multiple perspectives, but I loved it; it was done very well. Jumping between two totally different characters and experiences (survival alone versus survival in a refugee/boot camp) showed the depth of the post-invasion world that Yancey created. 
 My only disappointment is that I felt that there is a total set up toward the end of the book for a love triangle opportunity here, a ridiculous YA trope. Whether or not this comes to pass will definitely affect my enjoyment of the second book in this series, because love triangles are the worst in books like this; I want action and plot and excitement, not ooey-gooey feelings crap. 
 I am eager to start loaning my copy of this book to my friends. I just hope they devour it as quickly as I do, because I need someone to talk about this book with! This one is going to stick in my mind for a while, and I'm not sure I have anything else on my shelf that will capture my imagination the way that The 5th Wave has. Cue the book hangover.

My third time reading Vampire Academy and finally the time to review it(don't expect much. You know I'm not one for detailed and eloquent reviews). 
 At this point since there is a Vampire Academy movie I would normally use some gifs from it. But this time I won't. The VA movie was a disgrace to the book and I'm trying my best to forget it exists. 
 Lissa is the last of the Dragomir bloodline, one of the 12 royal houses of the Moroi. Rose is a dhampir, best friends with Lissa since childood and Lissa's future guardian. Two years ago Lissa and Rose escaped the Vampire Academy to save Lissa from an unknown threat and have been in hiding since then. They have a special bond between them that allows Rose to know what Lissa is feeling and makes Rose the one person capable to help Lissa. Their luck has run out though and the Academy's guardians are here to take them back. Now Lissa and Rose have to confront not only the unknown threat but Lissa's mental instability and a school full of teachers and students who want to know why they ran. 
 Rose in Vampire Academy is still a very immature girl. She is only 17 so that is understandable but this doesn't excuse everything. In the beginning of the book she is reckless, slutty and completely uncaring about other people(except maybe Liss). She is back at school and she is determined to win the "party girl" status back. She thinks she is always right. I think what annoyed me most from Rose in this book was the bitchy way she tried to separate Liss from Christian. Luckily by the end of the book she is much more mature and less reckless, I particularly like her determination to help her friend. Not that she comes all the way but she has 5 more books to develop. 
 Lissa in Vampire Acady is a very sweet but unstable girl. She has powers that no one else seems to have except an old teacher who went crazy. She fights her inner demons, the attacks from Mia(a Moroi girl from school) and the unknown enemy who has made bold moves since her return to the Academy. What we see of Lissa in this book makes her seem very compassionate and nice. 
 Dimitri is a God. Or at least he should have been since he is the best guardian in the school and the one who found the girls and now has to train Rose. He is determined, focused, caring and very protective. I have little to add to him since he is one of the best heroes I've ever come acroos in YA Paranormal.(Btw I know the photo doesn't look like a 23 year old but I never could imagine Dimitri so young. He is way too mature and serious.) I DO NOT approve of his romance with Rose. First of all they don' fit, he is way too mature to fall for such an immature girl, and secondly she is 7 years her senior and her teacher. 
 Christian is a little psycho and he wears it well. I love Christian(in this and the next books). He is probably my favorite character in the series. He is a little dark, kind of emo, kind of tortured, completely an outcast. He is also the only one who can calm Lissa almost as much as Rose.(And she definitely doesn't deserve him.) 
 I like all the secondary characters in this book(and series in general). Richelle Mead does a great work in creating her world and her characters. I admit that by the end of the series I have many ups and downs but the first book is one of my favorite in the series despite Rose's behaviour.

When he gets bigger, he is sent to live on her uncle's farm, where he is set to be killed in the winter. Wilbur's best friend, Charlotte the spider comes to his rescue this time but spinning words into her web to attract attention and make the people realize what a great pig he is. 
 It's funny to me that all that attention is directed to the pig and not to the incredible spider who weaves those magical words, as Mrs. Zuckerman is quick to point out.

This book was everything and nothing I was expecting it to be!

It feels like Burton began the book with this story in mind and as she continued to write forgot what it was she was supposed to be talking about and so began a new story and then was reminded right at the end of her original plot and lazily bought it all together. 
 I'm not normally a fan of books set from years ago, but the plot of this mysterious miniaturist intrigued me. As I went through I began to realise this story line was being forgotten and thought that maybe I would begin to grow bored of the story however I was extremely mistaken. I was so involved in the characters lives that I almost forgot about the miniaturist myself! 
 Burton pulls at heart strings with her characters and I can admit I did have a little cry to myself over this book. I fell in love Johannes, he was a good man who was trying his best to keep his unconventional family going and he did not deserve the fate that was brought to him.

Really enjoyed the second volume of Buffy S8! It kind of went off in different directions before bringing us back to the main plot line, but I guess that's what you get when you switch a tv show into comic form.

 I love that they are having writers from the show write the scripts, because it really reads just like an episode of the show would. Because of this, the characters really do come to life (the great art doesn't hurt either).

It was fun to go back to her high school days to a time when the storylines were less complicated and before the show's formula changed. Back to when we were dealing with more of a "monster of the week with a big bad through the season" formula. 
 Anyway, I will definitely continue to make my way through these volumes. So glad the show lives on through these comics!

Brilliant, absolutely brilliant. There is so much going on in this story I was never bored. Sinclair has a sadness to him that the heroine sees when he doesn't think anyone is looking. Bertie (Roberta) has a desire to live a life free of the darkness of the poverty and danger of her cockney upbringing. She is a delight always seeing wonder and possibilities. Bertie is an unforgettable character. Ian even allows her to touch him. Speaking of Ian, he makes a cameo helping to shed light on anonymous notes being sent to Sinclair regarding his deceased wife. Slightly Scandalous is the third book in the Bedwyn Saga, following a large aristocratic family in the early 19th Century. It was not until after I finished this audiobook that I realized that the heroine was actually introduced in a prequel to the series, which I did not know about. I wish I would have read A Summer to Remember first, as that story is such a huge part of Freya Bedwyn's history. 
 Freya Bedwyn is the eldest female of the Bedwyn clan, and I was first introduced to her in Slightly Wicked, where she struck up a friendship with Ranulf's wife, Judith. In that book, Freya seemed to be fearless, indomitable, and searching for excitement to break up the tedium of her life. In Slightly Scandalous, Freya was at turns priggish and reckless. Sometimes she was so uptight, I couldn't stand her. Other times, Freya was a delight as she thumbed her nose at hostile acquaintances. But one thing I couldn't get over with her character was how often she resulted to using her fists. She punched our hero several times (or tried to). While I could forgive her the first two times due to the circumstances... at other times she was resulting to violence in anger. I wasn't down with that. 
 Joshua Moore, Marquess of Hallmere was a wonderful hero. After unexpectedly inheriting his title from an uncle, Joshua finds himself at the center of marriage schemes left and right. I enjoyed watching him thwart other's plans with regard to his matrimonial future. Joshua also had a wonderfully flirty personality. He didn't take anything overly serious, and he did a good job at riling up our heroine (and earning a few punches to the nose for it). Aside from his looks and personality, Joshua had suppressed vulnerability that made him relatable and tugged the reader's heart strings enough to establish a character connection. 
 The romance between these two started as a lark. Joshua needed someone to stave off his marriage-minded and scheming aunt, and Freya was seeking a distraction from heartache. I did feel bad for Freya and her feelings regarding Kit and Lauren... but I was missing the backstory from the earlier book that I should have read. It is clear that the situation made Freya somewhat jaded, and she was not looking for romance. She looks for every reason to not love Joshua, and she jumps to many conclusions very quickly (and sometimes ended up looking foolish for it). I enjoyed the banter and interactions for the most part, as long as Freya wasn't being punchy. 
 As usual, the Bedwyn family bands together when needed and I enjoyed seeing them come (en masse) to Joshua's aid in this story. Wolfric, the Duke, is being humanized bit by bit with each situation... and I can't wait until I get to his own tale of love. I have a feeling his future wife is going to be a most improper female.

 I read this for the first time almost four years ago. It was only a few months after it came out, before it was truly well known. And I loved it. It was a perfect combination of badass characters, elegantly crafted dialogue and plot, and creative magic. And thankfully, it held up during this reread. It may be a simple fantasy novel that isn't meant to change my life or view on the world, but it's perfect for what it is: a character driven fantasy series beginner. 
 I love this book, I really do. However. It feels so much like a standalone novel. It has such a wrapped up, specific plot. So going forward, it kind of has to start from scratch. And in my memory, Crown of Midnight feels like a different story. I wish there was better transition between the beginning and the rest of the series. 
 Celaena Sardothien is a grade-A badass. That's just a fact. If you think differently get the hell out. Okay, no, not really, please come back. But seriously, she's such a powerful, unique, intuitive character and I wish I was like her. She's such a strong example for young women. I mean, yeah, she's an assassin which isn't the best career choice, but her character and independence are #goals for women--and general humans--everywhere. In this first book, we learn so much about what is inside of her head, rather than her past or her future. But it's a wonderful starting off point. 
 Chaol Westfall, you beautiful, brooding bastard. In all honesty, we learn very little about Chaol in this book. But what we do learn we want more of. He's hard, kind, determined, powerful, dark, judgmental. He has a true power struggle in this novel; at the beginning, he believes that people that do good things are good and people that do bad things are bad. It isn't until he meets Celaena that he learns that things are not that black and white. And though he is a man of few words and few chapters from his perspective, we know that he can be so much more. 
 Dorian Havilliard...I have no words. Like, I love Celaena and Chaol, but there is something about this complicated Crown Prince that keeps my attention like no other. I love being in his mind, as well as watching him through Celaena's eyes. His mannerisms, his personality, his spirit, are so infallible. He's not God or anything, but he can do no wrong in my mind. Hopefully I don't end up eating those words. 
 People may scream at me for this, but in this book (and a little in the second too--don't kill me!) Celaena and Dorian are my ship. And rereading this, it reminded me how prominent they are. Of course there are the underlining, less obvious feelings Celaena has for Chaol, but her attraction to Dorian is spoken first, more often, and is actually acted upon. I mean--DAMN! Those kisses they share are passionate and powerful and so honest. Swoon. So yeah. I'll take the lighthearted Prince vs. the Brooding Guard any day. 
 I really enjoy Sarah J. Maas's writing. It's simple, but has a lot of depth if you are paying close attention or want to look for it. And every once in a while she throws in these powerful scenes or conversations or quotes and it makes me pause and think. I love that. She also writes some really hilarious exchanges that just have me laughing awkwardly in public like a fool. 
 I am eager as hell to plow through Crown of Midnight so I can finally start reading the books I haven't read yet. I have this fear that people reading this that have read the others are just straight up laughing in my face because of what's to come. But I'm really finally ready to have my own opinion of the whole series instead of being on the outside of the chaos.

So after For Real, this one was a bit of a letdown. 
 Not because it wasn't an enjoyable read--it was--but because it simply didn't touch me quite as deeply as the former. 
 Waiting for the Flood is a quiet story with lots of introspection, single 1st person POV of Edwin. Which fits, since Edwin is an introspective guy, to a point where he's so focused on his inner goings-on that he almost forgets there's still a whole world outside his own head. Used to being disregarded from an early age--a "seen, not heard" child-- he trapped himself in his Snow White's coffin of consternation and hurt over being abandoned, for completely elusive reasons, by his long-time boyfriend. Actually, I found Edwin a bit hard to like with his--let's call a spade a spade--endless self-pity. 
 But inescapably, persistently and relentless like the flood he's waiting for, life invades his solitude in the person of a big, red-haired bear of a man named Adam. Edwin can't escape any of them, and he deals with both the same way: first fighting them--a bit halfhearted at first, and with a kind of awkward ardor later--then coming to terms with them and eventually, daring to enjoy them with all his heart. I loved how this book was something of a parable, how Edwin's (and Adam's, really) philosophical sophism fed my little inner geek.  Adam and Edwin's first flirt was a conversation about game theory of all things. If that isn't geeky, I don't know what is.  The writing turned a bit wordy at times, but never to the point of boring; I think Edwin's narrative voice mirrored his character (AND the changes he went through) perfectly. I liked following his musings from "oh poor me" to "bring it, life, I'm ready", and I'm really, really in awe of writing skills that can achieve this. 
 Despite what I said first, I recommend this book for its smart writing and my quiet enjoyment of Edwin's slow awakening. Just don't expect an emotional impact like with "For Real", this one is a whole'nother animal (or pair of wellies, if you want.) 
 Oh, and Edwin's elderly lady neighbor, Mrs Peaberry? She was a lovely breath of fresh air, literally, first blowing a bit of spicy scent over the barren plains of Edwin's daily routine and later on making delicious little waves in the oncoming deluge.

This book is a well written and researched, and convincingly argued, attempt to answer the question of why different people with strong moral grounding and a real desire to do the right thing can disagree so fundamentally on what that "right thing" is. 
 Written IMO for people like me - those of us who are WEIRD - Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich (relatively anyway) and Democratic - who think that if we just explain things clearly enough anyone with good intentions can be won over. Haidt sets out to elucidate why that is not the case. 
 There are a lot of very detailed reviews of this book. Many far more analytical and complete than mine. 
 I felt that there were two main points: first that there's more to morality than care/harm and fairness/cheating which are the prime directives of the WEIRD ethos. Other factors which carry lower weight for me (like loyalty/betrayal) may be considered more vital than fairness, for example, in some world-views. This is why my appalled reaction to sending a whistle-blower to prison and not persecuting the wrongdoers he exposed, isn't equally shared by those who are appalled by his disloyalty. The author also posits authority/subversion and sanctity/degradation as additional foundations for moral judgments that weigh heavily in some people's moral frameworks. 
 The second point is that logic, reason and rational thought are not the prime drivers of moral decision making. In fact, we are much less likely to have our moral judgments changed by reasoning than by emotions. This is why propaganda works better in many ways than science for forming opinions. We all look for evidence and opinions that confirm what we believe, not contradict it. We close our ears to evidence which works against us, and are past masters at rationalizing, selective analysis, seeking out the positive, and using any hint of ambiguity to confirm our biases. (I know I do this too, and I put an awareness of the value of negative data into a novel.) 
 This is pretty depressing reading for those of us who are of a scientific bent, who want to think that if you just explain with charts and diagrams and statistics, people will see your point. It does explain how one wave of the flag can seem to wipe out a dozen images of dead foreigners, if loyalty and authority place higher than some abstract of care/harm in someone's moral framework. 
 In fact, we do respond to evidence and logic but (unfortunately for our planet) very slowly and often behind the curve of needed change. Just IMO, of course. I guess I'm WEIRD all right.

 The thing is I never know if steam punk exists in the modern realm with an inspiration to the past or if its something completely different. So I'm guessing its both since the world building in this novel is impeccable. The setting is fully fleshed out and completely detailed. I loved the intricate descriptions of some of the inner workings of the gizmos and gadgets that appeared in the story. Adrienne thoroughly did her research and she did it well. Her scenes open up just like a movie creates the feeling of a time period, but what is great in the setting, lacks in other areas. The key driver for most books is plot. There wasn't a story that kept me from turning the pages. I had to stop and pick it up again and that is always a big sign that I won't end up liking the book in the end. I tend to get hooked into books very easily but if by the first 50-150 pages I'm bored, then I can automatically assume there's nothing worthwhile. I'm glad I kept going because the story does pick up in the end, and it turned out to be one heck of an adventure. 
 Characters

 Pacing 
 Slow..Very slow to pick up in the beginning, but the end makes up for a great climatic ending. 
 Cover & Design 
 Gorgeous. Love what the models are wearing and how they have such a strong pose. Also kudos for featuring an Asian on the cover! (Not very many now-a-days) 
 Plot 
 A murder mystery that is quite similar to the TV show Charlie's Angels where females kick butt and solve crimes. 
 Read it for all its steam-punk goodness and the incredibly rich character development!

I think Jhumpa Lahiri's talents tend to shine most clearly in short stories. There she's forced into letting her characters have strong emotions, and clear character arcs. All of her longer works (which is what this is) are a bit like white noise to me. That's not entirely bad. White noise is soothing, calming. Never objectionable to me. This oddly serene tone works for some novels. 
 But it's a problem when you're telling a story such as this one, I think. The Lowland spans some 60 odd years, and deals with some incredibly emotionally charged, frequently painful events. A lot of said events are conveyed to us after the fact, as the characters ruminate on them. This isn't a bad thing, necessarily. However, here's where the white noise comes into play, again. Everything is conveyed with the exact some emotional affect. Executions and suicide attempts are conveyed with the same low key melancholy afforded to jet lag or mildly awkward dinner parties. There's absolutely no sense of urgency, and so every time a character makes a life-altering decision it all feels so artificial. There were a couple times when the melancholy could have been broken up by happier things; I wanted to see Subhash adjusting to a relationship where he felt loved by his equal. Most of his life he was at a distance from his peers, so it would have been fascinating to see the early parts of his relationship with Elise, to get a sense of how it differs from Gauri or Holly. It would have been nice to see the early weeks of Bela caring for a newborn. What would it be like for her to be grounded in way she hadn't been since she was 12? What new insights would she have about her mother after experiencing love for her daughter? Yes, these are happy events, but the mere fact of them being happy doesn't mean you somehow learn less about the characters!  
 In the end we are told so many things. There are truly beautiful descriptions of landscapes, and, every so often, character interactions. I remember reading this back in high school and man was it bad. Like really bad. And yet for some reason I avoided reviewing this book. I think part of it was because I had a huge headache by the time I was done with it that I wanted nothing to do with it after.

 I honestly don't know what to say about this that hasn't already been said. Bottom line:

 One of my main problems with this book, like everyone else who hates this book, is Patch's behavior towards Nora. Yeah, I know, Nora's an idiot but still . . . 
 No matter how stupid she is, she doesn't deserve to be humiliated, belittled, harassed, stalked, or threatened by Patch. I don't know how anybody could be attracted to this guy. I don't. Every scene he was in, I just found myself terrified of this guy. It also doesn't help the fact that he actually wants to kill Nora. 
 Reading in Nora's perspective, I understand her fear of Patch but I'm also confused by her attraction towards him. While she's suspicious of Patch trying to kill her (and pretending he has nothing to do with it) she is also having this mentality of Patch never lifting a finger on her. But what's also is confusing is her persistence of thinking that 'he could never hurt her' but then she wants nothing to do with him after he makes fun of her in class and eventually chases her around her car. 
 HUH? 
 So get this. The teacher and the rest of her biology class watch as Patch is harassing Nora and laugh along with him. Naturally, she is uncomfortable and requests that she be moved. But then her teacher, which I still can't believed that something like this happened, assigns her as Patch's tutor. 
 Fucking what? 
 Are you serious? You know what, I'm not surprised anymore. At first, I was confused on why Nora had conflicting feelings for Patch. But now that I think about it, how can you blame the poor girl? After trying to separate herself from him and telling the teacher and her friend that she doesn't like him and he makes her uncomfortable they push them closer together. No wonder her feelings are all over the place. You know, how can I argue against that? 
 How did behavior like this become so acceptable that we just encourage it and brush it off like it is no big deal? 
 How sad is it for most teenage girls to find this rapist killer hot and romantic that as the rest of the books are being read, Nora is actually encouraged by readers to be with this kind of guy in the end? 
 I know I'm suppose to hate Nora for being just a weak and stupid character. But honestly, I just feel so bad for her for having to put up with all this crap from the other side characters. I know what it's like to be told to 'deal with it'. I know what it's like being told that I'm 'overreacting'. I know what it's like being told to 'suck it up'. 
 And yet we have the same people scratching their heads wondering why some women don't just leave their abusive partner. Gee, what a world we live in.

"Let me tell you something straight off. This is a love story, but not like any you've ever heard. The boy and the girl are far from innocent. Dear lives are lost. And good doesn't win." 
 This is more like 3.5 stars; though it is a beautifully written book I thought it lagged a bit at times. Let me say right off that if you're a purist you should save yourself the fury and skip this one. Anderson takes the tale of the boy who wouldn't grow up that we all know and turns it on its head, twisting it to fit the story she wants to tell. Normally this would bother me, but she did it so poignantly that I found it hard to mind too much. It was almost like reading something completely separate from Peter Pan which just happened to have a similar setting and a few like-named characters. 
 In Anderson's Neverland, at some point in your life a significant event stops you from outwardly aging. Peter is sixteen and Tiger Lily is a natural fifteen when the two meet and fall into a tentative first love. Tinker Bell (who wasn't always called Tinker Bell and doesn't belong to Peter) follows Tiger Lily, reading her thoughts and those of the people around her, giving an omniscient style to what would ordinarily be a first-person narrative. For much of the book we read Tinker Bell's observations of Peter and Tiger Lily's young love, watching them run wild through Neverland together while Tiger Lily tries to balance the responsibilities she has to her people with what she really wants. 
 My biggest beef with this retelling (besides Whitey sticking his nose where it doesn't belong and ruining everything, that is) is the depiction of Wendy. The Disney Wendy is a bit too girly for my liking but Anderson's Wendy takes the cake. This Wendy is so innocent she can imagine no harm coming to her, yet she knows exactly how to flirt and get Peter and the Lost Boys under her spell. She tilts her head charmingly when she listens to Peter talk; she laughs at everything the boys say even if it isn't funny; she is just so scared of everything and so delighted when the boys beat her at games. You big strong man, you! She isn't exactly mean and catty, but you get the impression that is only because she doesn't think she needs to be: Like the Mounties, Wendy always gets her man. 
 To further illustrate the differences between the Wendy bird and Tiger Lily, when the two first meet Wendy is described as wearing a dress the color of calla lilies. So you have this: 
 ...versus this: 
 Tiger Lily is color and life, a walking Impressionist painting; Wendy is a blank canvas onto which I can only imagine someone painting a bland watercolor of a loaf of white bread. Everything about her makes me want to shove her in a muddy puddle and give her a noogie to muss up her hair. 
 But in spite/because of this, Tiger Lily is in turns beautiful and heartbreaking. It is a story about love, loyalty, loss, betrayal, and being different. It is a story of how our lives sometimes turn out nothing like we'd expected, how sometimes the ending we get may not be the one we would have chosen. We can always look back on the road not taken and see how we could've been happy someplace else, with someone else... and alongside that longing, that ache for what might've been, we can still find happiness where we are.

As the first grandchild of Harris Sinclair, Cadence has a lot to gain. The Sinclairs are east-coast old money whose family came to the U. S. on the Mayflower. Harris owns a small island, Beechwood, where the family gathers each summer. 
 Two of the most important summers at Beechwood are when the Sinclair cousins--Cadence, Johnny and Mirren--are eight and when they are fifteen. At eight, they meet Gat, the nephew of the (Indian) boyfriend of one of Harris's daughters. Gat immediately becomes one of the group, one of the Liars. But his presence creates some ethnic tension. Harris doesn't like that one of his daughters (Carrie) has brought Indians into the perfectly tall and perfectly blonde family. 
 Gat returns each summer and is a great friend of Johnny's. During the Liars' fifteenth summer, Gat and Cadence fall in love. That much Cadence can remember, but little else. She was in an accident and hurt her head. She ends up with amnesia and horrifying migraine headaches for which she must take strong painkillers. Due to her accident, she is kept from returning to Beechwood for her sixteenth summer. During her seventeenth, she goes back and tries to recall all that happened. 
 With her memory loss, headaches and medicated state, Cadence is a very unreliable narrator. However, she sees her family as a sort of King Lear story--the bullying granddad with his three daughters who argue about money and inheritance. She also thinks a lot about various fairy tales and how the characters in those tales fare against magic and fate. All of her musings are interesting and pull the reader into her drama, as does her love for Gat and for her cousins. Yet because Cadence is such an unreliable narrator, the reader is in for a crazy ride and some serious shocks about what happened during "summer 15." 
 High school housekeeping: If you aren't used to reading a book with an unreliable narrator, We Were Liars is a great place to start. This novel is wildly popular with professional reviewers. For my own part, I ended with a sense of "No fair!" because it felt like the author had cheated a bit in laying out the story for me, the reader, unreliable narrator or not. But this really is a compelling story. I recommend it to all teens and particularly lovers of mysteries and family dysfunction.

 In contrast to Joe Abercrombie's other books, Half A King has been marketed as YA and fills an intermediate role of not quite fitting into either YA or fantasy for adults. That's by no means a bad thing and I'd recommend it to adults and mature teenagers alike. And just look at that gorgeous cover! Isn't it simply incredible? One more reason to get it. 
 Prince Yarvi, disabled young man in a world where war and violence rules, cannot hold a shield with his crippled hand. His only asset is his razor-sharp mind, but that doesn't command the respect a well-build fighter would get in this world. When he has to ascend the throne gears are set into motion and he's swept up in an adventure that demands everything he can give and more. Sold as a slave and chained to an oar, how can someone as weak as him survive the ordeal? And how can he reclaim his stolen throne, even though he'd never wanted it in the first place? 
 This is a tale as expertly written as Joe's other books and as enjoyable. I wouldn't call it great, but it's a good story nonetheless, with memorable characters and powerful adversaries to beat. The journey at the side of Yarvi, seeing him struggle because of his crippled hand but using his mind to overcome every stone in the road, no matter how big, fills an afternoon with an entertaining tale. It's a short book because the about 350 pages are easy to read with a great flow that simply carries you with it without any effort of your own. 
 It suffers a bit from predictability and one big revelation can be seen from miles away. As you can already understand it before you're half-way into the book, it lacks surprise when it's revealed at the very end, and as such lacks impact. Another smaller, quieter one took me by surprise as I only noticed it right before its disclosure. This second mystery fit the intelligent Yarvi much more and shines a very interesting light on the whole story. 
 The setting has a very viking-esque vibe with shoulder-man standing besides their brothers and protecting them with their shields. The Shattered Sea plays a major role too, for war and commerce. Slaves are used abundantly too, taken for example in raids and used as oarsmen in horrible conditions, chained to their benches and beaten relentlessly. 
 [...] 
 Concluding: What I can say without doubt is that I'm very interesting in what Yarvi will do in the future. I want to know what he'll do, how he'll overcome whatever is thrown into his way. It's not Abercrombie's best book, but still better than a lot of other fantasy stories. As the first book in a series it manages to invest the reader in the characters and the plot and make them want to read on.

My Cousin Rachel: Or, Hi, It's Me, the Irrational, Unstable Man-Child 
 How many times in one novel can one say "My Cousin Rachel?" Because never would I have thought I'd hear the title of a book so many times before. That being said, Daphne du Maurier manages to weave a meticulously intriguing tale as told by an unreliable, irritating man-child named Philip Ashley. 
 Philip Ashley was raised by his uncle in a household devoid of women. So when his uncle meets and suddenly married a woman named Rachel in Italy, the now "master" of the house Philip must "deal" with this woman. We only get the story from Philip's point of view so everything is skewed in an obnoxiously one-sided way. We will never really know if Rachel is "evil" or just a woman trying to get by in a man's world. It's up to the reader to decide.  
 For me, I "side" with Rachel because putting up the insanity and misogyny that is Philip Ashley wore me out. But I can't commend author, Daphne du Maurier, enough for masterfully creating a twisted tale of suspense.

LOVED The Interestings so I wanted to try another Meg Wolizer book. Similar to The Interestings, this book is filled with relateable, realistic characters whose stories I thoroughly enjoyed reading. However, the stories were too single-faceted to really get a broad character picture the way that I have gotten in her other books. 
 The basic premise of this book is that when the new drama teacher at a local high school puts on a production of Lysistrata, Aristophanes's Greek comedy about women who intend to stop the Peloponnesian war by refusing to sleep with the men, all of the women in the town suddenly lose interest in sex. 
 There are essentially two parts to this book. The first is a brief look into the lives of many of the women in the town, all at different stages in their lives (from high school students, to new mothers, to older women) and the look at what sex means in the current stages of their lives. This part I found to be a very interesting study on female sexuality throughout a lifetime. 
 The second part of the book describes the mysticality of the "spell" that overcomes these women. It's constantly described as a "chill" that comes over the women. These intense descriptions do NOTHING for me and almost ruin the book. Not to mention the ending, where we find out that the drama teacher has been casting the spell on purpose all over New Jersey to "revitalize" peoples' sex lives??? I'm all for mystic powers, but for one person to reveal them in the last 10 pages of the book just seems terrible. This caused me to drop a whole star from my review. 
 There are some other interesting parts, and some storylines that are not totally wrapped up (is Eli going to come back from MI to be with Willa??). But for the most part, the various women's stories are not interesting enough to need clean, tidy endings.  
 Furthermore this book features the use of teenagers talking online using speak like "ru there" which is my biggest pet peeve in books because teenagers have not done that in real life since 2004.
