Somewhere in the middle of the book it hit me that this is going to be a love-story. And not just a love story, but a teenage love-story. While I can appreciate a well-written romance now and again, I absolutely refuse to recognize it as a plot. Star-crossed lovers striving to overcome various obstacles in order to be together is not enough. Something must be happening aside from that. 
 To be fair, Suzanne Collins does try to set this something going - alternative future (not a very pleasant one, mind you), the Hunger Games as some sort of gladiator matches/survivor TV-show - but the fact that any significant changes in the main heroine aren't caused by the situation she is in kind of eradicates author's attempt on the plot. 
 It annoyed me to no end how much time Katniss, the main heroine, spends being confused about her love life. You'd bet boys wouldn't be the first of your worries when a dozen people are eager to chop you in a half. Although, thinking back, I realize to my mounting horror that there really weren't too many things I preoccupied myself with aside from, well, boys. Not that my life has ever been at any serious peril - I have, at least, this one excuse. 
 And then there is this whole "I'm so undeserving" crap. Katniss is a smart, charming, beautiful, brave, kind young woman who has no clue how truly awesome she is. I knew there was a reason I disliked The Ugly Duckling. Humbleness can be cute but to a point. After that point it just makes you look stupid and/or fake. 
 What saved the book for me, however, was an extremely well-done first person narration. Despite being tied to only one character's point of view, Suzanne Collins manages to give us a rather whole picture of The Hunger Games's world. Katniss, when she is not torn between her love interests and not caught in a net of self-depreciation, is a pleasant and observant story-teller. She is honest and genuine. There is non of this "I ran my dainty fingers through my shiny black as a loveliest summer night tresses and averted my emerald-green dastardly beautiful eyes" nonsense. Seriously, if I start referring to my hair as sun-kissed honey-colored locks, you have my permission to shoot me on the spot. 
 I also surprised myself by disliking Peeta (love interest #1) who I am obviously supposed to like. I wonder if there would be some basis for this aversion in the second book.

 It can take years to mold a dream. It takes only a fraction of a second for it to be shattered. 
 The Kiss of Deception focuses heavily on romance and very little on fantasy. The main character, Lia, makes a lot of bad choices and the love triangle between the three POV characters takes centre stage, leaving everything else behind. The world-building is shallow and vague, the action mostly takes place off-screen, and nothing of interest happens until the last 3/4 of the book. 
 Mary E. Pearson does create one good mystery, though. The real identity of the Prince and the Assassin is an intriguing thread to follow, and the execution is done well. The twist is a bright light in this novel, and it does bring a little excitement to an otherwise boring story. 
 The book starts with Lia running away from an arranged marriage and settling down in a little village, hoping to start a new life away from duty and tradition. And that is where she stays for most of the story, which impacts the world-building in a negative way. Especially when it becoming clear that staying there is a very bad idea after a few things happen. 
 That makes Lia as a main character very difficult to like. It seems as if she has no common sense, and purposefully ignores all indications that she might be found out/is in danger. Her attention is firmly placed on her two love interests and, you guessed it, kissing. 
 And that is the main focus of the novel for about 300 pages. Lia in this village, Lia with the boys, Lia doing very little to move the plot forward and make it engaging. In between that, there is very little character development. The writing also doesn't help much, being chunky at times and moving quickly over action scenes -- or just telling us they happened off-screen. 
 The last 100 pages or so do improve, though. It takes a long time, but things do start happening. The plot progresses and develops towards something that is not only romance-focused, and gives us a little tiny bit of information that expands the world-building and explains a little about the world Lia lives in. 
 In the end, The Kiss of Deception is a disappointment. There isn't a balance between the romance and the fantasy, the characters aren't developed, and the first half of the story is slow and boring. I'm sure YA fans who like love triangles and don't mind vague world-building will have fun with this, but sadly this book wasn't for me. I will read the second installment though, as I've already purchased the book.

Look at Froi fine ass on that cover. God I love these books. Melina Marchetta is everything. 
 The events of Froi of the Exiles takes place three years after the end of Finnikin of the Rock. Lumatere is still working hard trying to rebuild their kingdom. Froi has been training with the Kings Guard as well as taking lessons with the Priest King, learning the languages of all the other kingdoms in the same way Finnikin once had. Queen Isaboe is ruling her kingdom with her heart, doing whatever she feels is right for her people, all while raising her and Finnikins first born and still trying to make time for her king. The focus is to rebuild Lumatere, but when an opportunity to kill the king of Charyn, whom everyone believes was responsible for the Days of the Unspeakable and the curse on Lumatere, presents itself, Froi is sent into the kingdom to do just that. 
 The world building and character development in these books are absolutely phenomenal. I found it much easier to get through this book because I was already familiar with the characters and some of the kingdoms and it was just good to get a better look at some of the other characters who played major roles in Finnikin of the Rock. Especially Froi. 
 Froi is approaching the age of 18 and in the three years that he's been in Lumatere, many things about him has changed. He can now read and write, fight with the best of them, and he no longer goes around spitting on people. Not without effort, but progress is progress. While he's on his mission to kill the king of Charyn he meets the princess of the kingdom, Quintana and of course that throws his whole mission out of wack. 
 Quintana is a bit mad. As in she's completely crazy. She has three different personalities and they each present themselves at different times throughout the book. See, Lumatere wasn't the only kingdom that was cursed. Charyn has been cursed for 18 years and in order for Quintana to survive the consequences of that curse, she created different identities in order to cope and survive. 
 I loved Froi and Quinitanas relationship and interactions. Its a bit more of that slow burn kind of love that I loved about Finnikin and Isaboe's relationship in the first book. They have a similar kind of rawness and savagery that helps them bond even though Froi is put off and confused by her in the beginning. The tension between them is perfect. There's not so much of a will they won't they situation...More of a HOW and WHEN will they, situation. 
 Froi spends months in Charyn meeting new people, finding out the history of Charyn and its people, discovering things about his own past, getting to know Quintana and trying to figure out how to get to and kill the king. 
 What I loved most about this book was how the events in the first book had a big affect on what went on in this book. You can tell while reading that Melina really thought out every single detail of the books before she started putting pen to pad. There were just things that happened that just could not be improvised. The writing was so beautiful as well. Melina has a way of saying so much and getting so much detail across using as few words as possible. Her writing is almost poetic. 
 One issue I did have with the second installment of this trilogy, was that it was kind of easy for me to predict what was going to happen for most of the book. There were little hints about certain things that didn't make the plot obvious...but when you read these kinds of books frequently, it gets easier and easier to spot the twists and surprises. So certain things would be said, and I would kind of instantly know how the next few pages or chapters were going to play out. 
 I've left ALOT of my thoughts for this book out of my review for two reasons. One being its the second book so...spoilers. And the other reason is because a lot of what goes on in Froi of the Exiles is either a major plot point, or plays a large part in the major plot points. 
 This trilogy is definitely worth reading though. I love it so much. I love the fierce friendship and loyalty that the characters have for one another. The sense of pride and honor the men and women walk around with. The short but super sweet showings of affection between the couples. Its just really easy to fall in love with this world and its characters and just want more and more. As soon as I was about 15 pages from being finished and realized there was no way ANYTHING was going to be resolved, I put the book down and paid 3.99 for the third book to be shipped here in one day. I'm playing NO games. I NEED to know whats going to happen.

First of all, this book wasn't as depressing as her previous book "All The Bright Places", and I am VERY happy about that. Like her previous book, this one is also told in two point of views. 
 I know this book had some criticism before being released, about the blurb. Yes, the book refers to a girl (Libby Strout) as "America's Fattest Teen", but this goes beyond a girl being fat. This is a book where a girl discovers her worth, and learns who she is beyond hurtful titles. This girl is both shy and wild! I don't know how... but she can go from keeping quiet about the bullies, to punching a boy in 3 seconds. (Girl, just be wild! Defend your honor!) 
 We also have Jack Masselin; who has Prosopagnosia, meaning he cannot recognize faces. The real problem here is that instead of letting people know about his disability, he has kept it a secret. He cannot recognize faces and he doesn't let people know! Instead, he goes through life trying his hardest at recognizing people by certain "markers". (I was a bit frustrated with this because... HOW COULD YOU NOT TELL THIS KIND OF INFORMATION TO ANYONE? NOT EVEN YOUR PARENTS?!) 
 Not so fun fact: Jack once screamed that a strange woman (his mom) was kidnapping him, because she got a haircut and he couldn't recognize her anymore. 
 He plays the cool guy at school, and hangs with jack-asses (which technically turns him into one) because they are easy to recognize. 
 The only reason I'm not giving this book 5 stars, is because the reasons why they seem to fall in love, are not convincing enough for me. The development of this relationship wasn't deep enough for me. Not to mention, the back and forth Jake has with his popular and hot evil girlfriend (who may I add, is a constant bully to Libby because of her weight) is annoying. Did we really need the evil popular girlfriend cliche? 
 When I was writing the previous paragraph, I almost thought of dropping the rating. But I didn't, because I other than this, I enjoyed the book VERY much. I loved how Libby grew to accept and love herself. At the beginning of the book, Libby seemed to be finding her worth by finding a guy who would love her... by the end of it, she finds her worth without needing a guy (but of course, she still cares for him). I wish I could say the same thing about Jake's growth, but honestly, I don't think he did as much as Libby. He accepts his disability, but I didn't see much beyond that. 
 I'm going to take a minute to talk about Jack's little brother... that kid is AMAZING AND HE NEEDS TO BE BLESSED! This kid destroys stereotypes and I'm sure he got bullied a lot, but he's so adorable and innocent. He's my favorite character, even though he's not out a lot. I LOVE YOU DUSTY! 
 As usual, with all of my reviews, I'm sharing my favorite quote from the book, and OH MY GOD... this quote is just perfect! (Also, it's something Jack says to Dusty aka. my favorite character.) 
 "People are shitty for a lot of reasons. Sometimes they're just shitty people. Sometimes people have been shitty to them and, even though they don't realize it, they take that shitty upbringing and go out into the world and treat others the same way. Sometimes they're shitty because they're afraid. Sometimes they choose to be shitty to others before others can be shitty to them. So it's like self-defensive shittiness." 
 I'm adding a second quote from this book, because the author brought up something really important and real. Jack is a black character, and this is something his mother tells him after he gets into trouble... 
 "You may not see yourself as black, and you may not think people see you as black, but it's a fact that our society treats kids of color more severely than others." 
 I'm not sure why she would think Jack doesn't see himself a black, but she does bring up a good point. PoC have an additional pressure in life, they can't screw up because they will be judged harder. 
 Even though this book is written by a white author, we can see diversity portrayed as a black boy with a disability and an overweight girl. At the end of the book, the author explains what kind of research she did regarding Prosopagnosia, and I must say... I'm impressed.

June is destined to be an elite soldier for The Republic. Day is a wanted outlaw living underground, whose family thinks he is dead. In Day and June, Lu creates characters that at first seem so opposite that they are each other's antitheses. Strange twists of events bring them closer and closer to each other. 
 In this bleak future, The Republic occupies territory containing the cities of Los Angeles and Las Vegas, and is always at war against the colonies to the east (Texas?). Citizens of the republic all take The Trial when they are 10 years old. The results of The Trial determine each citizen's place in the republic. June is a prodigy with the only perfect score she has ever heard of. Her destiny is sealed as an elite soldier in the republic Army. Day failed The Trial. He was taken to a "work camp" and experimented on, before he was left for dead with the other corpses. 
 June's family is wealthy. They have always been vaccinated against the plague, and her older brother is already climbing the ranks of the republic. Day's family has always struggled to get by in the poor lake district, barely able to afford food. When his little brother tests positive for the plague at the age of 9, there is little hope. The plague patrol officers will take him away and he will surely die, unless Day can find some way to steal or buy a "cure" from one of the hospitals for the wealthy or on the black market. His mother does not know he is alive and watching over them. 
 As Day and June's paths cross, they discover that they are more similar than opposite in spite of all of their differences in background and station. Will they live their seemingly destined roles of hunter (June) and hunted (Day)? Or will they question this destiny laid out by the republic? 
 I would recommend this book to anyone who liked The Hunger Games or Divergent, or The Maze Runner. I am going to finish the series when I have time.

 The story is told from Jocelyn Butler's POV. Joss is in her early twenties. She moved to Edinburgh, Scotland, her mother's homeland, after suffering the horrible tragedy of losing her entire family to a car accident, when she was only a freshman in high school. This loss was followed up by the loss of her best friend Dru, a year later. Joss had a lot of trouble coping with all of the tragedy in her life, and made some bad choices in her attempts to bury the pain. Wanting to finally put her past behind her, she decided to move to Scotland permanently, entering into university there. 
 Joss finished her education, and was starting a new career as a writer, when her whole world on anonymity started falling apart... and it all started on her way to Dublin Street, where is was to meet a potential new roommate. Forced to share a cab with a stranger... this is where she meets "The Suit." Just recalling the scene, makes me want to pick up the book and read it again!!! There was instant physical attraction, arrogant comments and sexual banter right from the beginning! 
 Shortly after, Joss meets her new room mate Ellie, a sweet, pretty young blonde who she develops an instant connection with. Just what she was trying to avoid...connections. It won't be long before she is drawn completely into Ellie's life and family, especially her half-brother Braden, who was no other than "The Suit." 
 Here's where I melt into a complete pile of goo!!! Braden Carmichael is a gorgeous 30 year old businessman, who has become quite successful in the development business he inherited from his father. He is the quintessential alpha male, arrogant, and funny with enough sex appeal to render any woman completely dumbstruck with desire. His deep brogue and tan muscular bod just a precursor to the totally hot forcefulness of his manner. He exudes self-confidence, and his instant attraction to Joss is so sweet. And his caveman possessiveness adorable!! I just went into a romantic fog, that didn't let up!!! 
 This book had it all!!! I mean, some incredibly STEAMY HOT SEX!!! Angina causing sexual tension, some really sexy and playful scenes, some REALLY FUNNY moments, some tense and troubled situations as well as some tears, as Joss starts to deal with her issues and her grief. There is also EXTREME frustration, where Joss falls into an unrelenting STUPIDNESS that made me want to slap her silly. 
 I loved reading this, seeing Joss slowly become involved in Ellie and Braden's lives, her developing attachment to their family and friends, and seeing her face the grief that she'd been hiding from for 8 years!!!! 
 Beautiful 5 star story!!! Samantha Young... I love your style!!!! I hope you keep writing more like this!!!!! And Thanks for Braden, he will share top honors in my favorite Alpha Male characters of all time!!!!

I would say, though, that it's time for Ruth to lose the duck. It was funny for a while but now it's just tiresome. Not Penny's best book, but well worth reading.

Warning: LONG fan-girly, gushing OMG review ahead.....every now and again they happen for me. I try to save that for my reading journal but I just can't with certain books. 
 Let's just put this out there right now - I was hella excited about Lola and the Boy Next Door but I was a bit scared to actually read it because I loved Anna and the French Kiss something fierce. I kept thinking that, while there is a good chance I'll really enjoy Lola, I'm never going to feel the same way about it that I did with Anna. It would be like the replacement goldfish that your parents try to convince you is just as great as the one you had to flush down the toilet. It's not the goldfish's fault...but it's just not the same as the one you really loved. 
 The verdict? I'm going to boldly say that I loved Lola from my head down to my toes....I actually think I liked it even better than Anna. I can't believe I'm saying it but it's true. Stephanie Perkins brought the awesomeness and somehow created a story that could top Anna and the French Kiss for me -- the amazing characters, the romance, a compelling storyline, the great setting. It's all there. While the romantic city of Paris really propelled the story of Anna and St. Clair for me in ATFK, Lola truly is the shining star in Perkin's second novel. 
 Lola is just one of those unforgettable characters. I instantly connected with her -- she's different and I can appreciate that as someone who has always used clothing as a way to set myself apart...especially in high school. It was something I could control amidst the chaos that was my life. I can't say my wardrobe was even a fraction like hers but I still understand her mentality. I can truly say I felt like I was reading the character of Lola as a little sister. I was protective of her, I wanted to hug it out with her during both crappy moments and awesome moments and I just wanted to tell her what an amazing girl she was. 
 Ok...I'll address the big fat elephant on the blog. The Boy! I know...you want to know if the boy is as wonderful and amazing and swoonworthy as St. Clair. Yes, ladies. Eat your heart out. For those of you who loathed St. Clair (yes there are people out there that do -- one of my fave ppl of all time and I had a friendly banter about St. Clair at BEA when she revealed this to me), you will be so thrilled about the new crush that Perkins has handed to you on a silver platter. There are seriously not enough "nice guys" in YA lit...but Cricket is leading the army against all those douchenuggets that seem to be in the "in" thing. I want to see more guys that are super nice, but not pushovers, and actually have a personality. He was sweet and sensitive and honestly the type of guy I love and I truly felt as though he complemented Lola so well. The thing I loved most about him (aside from his adoration of Lola) was how he was SUCH a real teen boy to me. Sometimes I find that most of the guys I read are always written so much more eloquently and more mature than teen boys actually are. They always seem to take on these hot, underwear model characteristics and always are suave and dashing. But Cricket was just so real. He's got quirky hobbies and interests and, hell, he's got his awkward, stupid boy moments. So refreshing. I love me some Cricket. 
 All of the secondary characters really felt so lively and real to me -- Lola's parents were incredibly supportive and definitely NOT absent. I really liked Max in the beginning and even though my love for him fizzled...he still felt very real. I LOVED how Perkins incorporated Anna and St. Clair into the novel without making them centerstage. PERFECT roles for them and I was ecstatic to see what had become of them. 
 I don't want to give away ANYTHING about this book but I honestly loved the whole story, the romance, the tension that was present in different threads of the story, and the ending! I felt myself charmed by San Fransisco and swept up in Lola's life. Anna's story was somewhat dreamy and escapist for me but Lola's story felt so realistic to me and I really appreciated that. Lola persevered through a lot in the story and I really believed in her progress and the path that Perkins lead her on. Lola was not overwrought with emotion and drama but perfectly captures the complicated nature of love and relationships with family and friends. It also shows the joys that come with the pain, awkward moments and general confusion of being a teen. I love that about this book -- it captures the teen voice in a genuine way with out being too "OMG this is a teen book" that actually doesn't accomplish the teen voice...like when your mom or dad tries to act really hip and up on the lingo. 
 I typically don't make bold statements like this but I'm going to because I feel so strongly after reading Lola: Stephanie Perkins is on auto-buy for me now. If she writes it, I'm going to beat down doors to get it. If I were my 13 year old self, I'd be bedazzling shirts proclaiming the awesomeness that is Stephanie Perkins and making a shrine in my room dedicated to her. Um yeah, I totally did that for certain boy bands back in the 90's. 
 Stephanie Perkins, after two novels, has become my go-to for wonderfully written contemporary YA with swoonworthy romances and unforgettable characters. She infuses so many quirky elements into her books and the little details are so wonderful. Lola is certainly no exception -- from an awesome reference to one of my favorite bands (Phoenix!) to having an incredibly cute dog named Heavens to Betsy..I just found myself smiling at the smallest details and it added SO MUCH to my overall enjoyment of the story. Perkins rights the perfect contemporary novel for me. It isn't so distorted of a reality that it too far-fetched for me but it has just enough drama that keeps you reading....because, let's be honest, if realistic novels were TOO realistic we'd be bored and feel like we were reading about our own lives. She writes things I felt as a teen and still feel now at 25. And oh my gosh, PLEASE PLEASE read the acknowledgments at the end of the book to her husband. SO CUTE. I had to read it out loud to my boyfriend because I just was so moved by it...and then I proceeded to gush about it on Twitter.

This is a mixture between something by Michael Crichton, Resident Evil, I am Legend(the movie) and The Walking Dead. Sounds awesome, I know.... 
 Pros: 
 1. Pre-Apocalypse and Post-Apocalypse (they don't show the actual apocalypse tho) 
 2. Vampires (a plausible scientific way for them to come about) 
 3. Bad-ass female lead (booya!) 
 4. Make that 2: The little girl was bad-ass too. In a different way. 
 5. Survival 
 6. At least 3 decent major action scenes ( The facility is overrun (Chrichton moment right there), the Las Vegas debacle (can you say "BOOM"), the events that led up to the train chase  ) 
 7. People die 
 8. I enjoyed that it was sort of PG13. (Little cussing, sex was dealt with off stage and some of the darker material were handled really well) 
 Cons: 
 1. It is WAY too long! It could have been half as long and would not have lost anything in the way of important story points. 
 2. Very poorly paced. Who edited this? Can someone shoot him, please? 
 3. The author skips over exciting scenes only to summarize it later. For the life of me I can't figure out whyyyyyyy he would meander so with unnecessary detail and then when something happens he skips over it. 
 4. The dialogue isn't always great. 
 5. The characters aren't well developed. After 5 days, I still don't feel like I know Peter, the main character. 
 6. So much pointless detail 
 7. The love stories? I didn't feel any of it. 
 8. Way too long! 
 A tiresome, tedious read. If they make it into a movie, I'd rather recommend that. Movies have a way of stripping the source material - in this case, that would be ok. 
 This book would have been AWESOME if it had been shorter. 
 I'd rate it: 4/5 For the bits I enjoyed. 
 And I'd rate it: 1/5 For making me read through all the crap to get to the good parts. 
 /endrant

The Walled city is considered a young adult book, but it certainly didn't feel that way. There was tons of violence, rape/prostitution and drugs, enough that I consider this book to be a very adult book. I started this book not knowing anything about it other than reading the interesting description here on Goodreads. I was hooked right from the beginning, learning the how the walled city worked and meeting the three main characters. I really enjoyed the character of Jin Ling the best, she was so determined to save her sister and be tough, that it was hard not to like her. Dai and Mei Yee were good characters too, but I liked Jin Ling's viewpoint the most. Chma was even well thought out as a character even though he was a cat. 
 The world of the Walled City was very well described, you could see the dingy, dirty streets filled with trash, broken glass and street kids. Even the desperation of the people that lived there was felt while reading this book. The writing overall was very good, everything was described really well, the characters were great, they felt like real people to me and I really wanted them to escape the walled city for somewhere better. 
 There wasn't anything that stands out as needing to be fixed about this book. There were no serious plot holes or writing errors. It was interesting, had good characters and an exciting plot. Overall, I am giving the book 4 out of 5 stars.

I read this because of a Tor.com post in honor of the author, Alfred Bester. The post says that the book is about how someone would commit a crime in a world full of telepaths, which sounded really interesting, and it was. The story starts out with the antihero, a man who wants to commit a crime -- premeditated murder -- and then goes back and forth between him and his nemesis, an "esper" (telepath) police detective. 
 Even though we get the criminal's perspective, this still manages to be a mystery novel -- parts of what happened and why aren't revealed until the end, although Bester drops some pretty good clues for the reader. 
 It's also really, really good as science fiction. The Tor.com post refers to the "totally detailed and convincing way in which society is changed by one science fiction element" (the espers). I really, really enjoyed how Bester worked this out -- for example, the way in which the antihero, who owns a major company, avoids telepathic espionage when communicating with another corporate executive. But there's more to the worldbuilding that doesn't need to be tied to a single explanation. The story happens mostly in New York City a couple of centuries from now, and Bester played with a lot of ideas for technological and cultural change. Humanity has expanded through the solar system, a secondary character lives in a building damaged in a very interesting way by World War who-knows-what-number, and people are still inventing slightly new ways to pretend to be witty at parties. 
 With scifi of this era (okay, most scifi) I'm annoyed that authors can imagine amazing new technology better than they can imagine changes in society. This book is no exception. I enjoyed a couple of the female characters, but they're all more sexualized than the male characters. I was disgusted by the way Bester writes about a blind character. And this is one of those books where it's safe to assume that everyone is white unless stated otherwise. A black character briefly appears in a way that I think deliberately suggests that the reader should be more sympathetic to the Esper Guild's eugenics plan -- they require all members to marry other espers, but (the narrative seems to suggest) at least it's not racist, because the Guild is happy to accept black members. 
 Still, the worldbuilding is really good. I would love to read more stories in this universe -- maybe some that aren't centered around powerful white men.

I really enjoyed this latest installment with the exception that I didn't remember the previous book and didn't remember the characters or the story. I had to go back and read reviews about book 1 to figure it out. Otherwise it was a fun adventure, once again.

I discovered this book by chance, drawn to it by its title and I'm glad I decided to give it a shot, because it was truly amazing. Miss Taylor's writing is heartbreakingly beautiful -no, seriously, it tears the soul apart to read her descriptions of Prague and Loramendi and Brimstone's shop and, most of all, the protagonists' emotions. Karou and Akiva are both great heroes, fleshed out and believable, as are the secondary characters. The plot, though simple in its core, is intricately crafted and with such imagination that it manages to give new breath to an old story. Short version: I absolutely loved it!
This is the second book I read from Paulo Coelho, and was a special one. I learned some lessons from it and recommend it to all of you.

As soon as I learned The Lotus Palace was a historical romance/mystery set in Ancient China, with actual Chinese people as main characters, I knew I HAD to read it. When you have read as much historical romance as I have, you don't find many new things. Even with the known trope - rich playboy falls for servant girl - I found the culture and setting so different that half the time I didn't know how characters would react to things. It made for a fascinating read. 
 The Pingkang Li is the City's pleasure quarter, full of beautiful, educated, sophisticated courtesans who compose poetry, act as hostesses in events and generally trade wits with scholars. It wasn't clear to me if selling their bodies was part of the bargain, but it seemed they had the liberty of choosing their own lovers. Yue-ying, our heroine, is the servant of a famous courtesan in the Lotus Palace. She's practical, hard working, tough and has a port-wine stain that mars her face. Bai Huang, the hero, is a rich, charming, extremely attractive, good for nothing scholar who has been "courting" Yue-ying's mistress for a while. But everything is not as it seems with Bai Huang - he's been exaggerating his reputation as a fool to spy for his father, who's a powerful government official. For a while, he's been noticing Yue-ying because she feels real to him as compared to the illusions of the Pingkang Li. 
 Yue-ying's past was horrific. I won't go into details because I don't want to give spoilers but although she doesn't dwell in the past, it's clear that it damaged her deeply. Bai Huang, for his part, hasn't had as charmed a life as you would expect, but it's mostly of his own doing. When he meets Yue-ying, he's desperately trying to redeem himself in the eyes of his father, who he disappointed terribly. 
 It takes a long time for Yue-ying to give in to the advances of Bai Huang. Practical creature that she is, she suspects his motives and it's not taken by his pretty face. She can't believe that a man like him - who could have any woman he wanted - would be interested in her, with her marked face, her situation in life and her past. But Huang crumbles her defenses slowly, with his love and persistence. Their relationship is not only about the physical but it's about trust and understanding. I was very touched when Huang acknowledged: 
 He had never trusted anyone else with the worst parts of himself. 
 The mystery was just somewhat disjointed with clues all over the place. Half the time I thought they were chasing red herrings and I didn't even recognize the murderer when he was unveiled. Definitely not the stronger part of the story. 
 I was fascinated by the cultural aspects of the book. I know next to nothing about Ancient China so I loved the descriptions of places, clothes, customs, etc. It amazed me how concerned people were with each other's privacy, to the point that they wouldn't share important thoughts or feelings because "you don't talk about those things." I was surprised by the way the final hurdle between Bai Huang and Yue-ying was overcome and it was only possible due to the differences in culture. 
 I'm definitely reading the next book - Constable Wu and Mingyu sound like a very intriguing couple. If you are looking for a different read, this book will definitely be for you!

This is the first in a trilogy of books that has been recommended to me many times over the years. But since I refuse to consider a series until it is "complete" (well, setting A Game of Thrones aside, *sigh*), this one didn't make it to my TBR list until 2013, and then a short delay until it was actually started... yes, 2.5 years is short, I still haven't started the Harry Potter series though I own all the books! 
 Anyway, the recommenders are correct! At least based on this initial book, this is a series I'll greatly enjoy. I do feel like Atwood's prose style is unnecessarily verbose for this type of tale, but it was explained by Snowman repeatedly reminding us that he is a "word person" and not a "numbers person" like his friends. He studied literature, he wrote for a living. So I suppose it is ok that his journal reads more like a literature masterpiece than notes jotted down as he tries to survive. Sort of. 
 I like the world that Atwood created - the genetically enhanced creatures (I want a pet rakunk!), the created disease that wipes out humanity as we know it (probably? maybe? the ending of this book hints otherwise...) , the differences in living conditions between the cities and suburbs, the pills and medications that the people took. It is interesting that although she was very creative and forward thinking with the biological technology, Atwood wasn't particularly inventive with the electronic types - computers, email, television, phones, all seem to work exactly like they would have in the late 1990s when this book was published. But maybe electronics is an area she just doesn't know enough about to be able to speculate. 
 I was surprised by the revelation of Oryx and Crake's current whereabouts, although I suppose I shouldn't have been. Of the two, I really liked and related to Crake (yes, despite his obvious issues), but I didn't care for Oryx at all. Crake's thinking and acting was very logical and we could follow his train of thought and why he did and said certain things (though his conclusions were problematic, sure, but this isn't the first story that works its way to this conclusion... 2001: A Space Odyssey anyone?). He was a bit of a jerk at times, but he was a likeable jerk if you ask me, and he meant well, I think. Whereas Oryx... she remains a mystery. Her motives are very much hidden from us, and sometimes her behaviors seem to contradict themselves. I still wonder if she knew what was going on when she went out to get the pizza. And if she really was as surprised as she acted to Jimmy about the ... origin of the disease. Manhattan project, or two-faced bitch? Hard to say. And I think the way this story has gone so far, it will be difficult to get any kind of back story or into her head. She will forever remain a mystery. 
 To be honest, she didn't play as much of a role as I expected given that she's a title character, aside from being a love interest. Maybe a better title for this book is Snowman and Crake (or Jimmy and Crake?). Hm. 
 Anyway, I'm looking forward to the second book, which I've barely begun so far. I'll be interested to see where this story goes, what happens to Snowman, and whether the Crakers will turn out the way that Crake intended...

American Gods is not a perfect book, but it is a great book. It is an Epic in the same vein as Beowulf and The Iliad, with a huge cast of characters, a slow build to multiple climaxes, and multiple interweaving plot threads all connected by one unknowing protagonist, who has no idea what is in store for him or the pivotal role he will play in the events ahead. There are some slow sections that are almost boring, but the rapid pace towards the end of the novel compensates for it. The conclusion is mostly satisfactory. I would have liked to have seen more of what happened in Lakeside. And now that I've finished this, I can finally go back and read "Monarch of the Glen" in Fragile Things. Very excited to hear that an HBO series and possible sequel (in addition to Anansi Boys) may be on the way.

Another enjoyable tale about Harry the wizard in modern-day Chicago. This one involved werewolves, and lots of them. Like any good suspense novel it keeps you guessing. Harry continuously gets put through the wringer, and the imagined physical and emotional pain left me cringing. 
 I'm definitely getting into this series - it's very fun and explores the possibilities of magic in our own universe. My biggest complaint is that I get through them so quickly!

This is a sweet, sexy, flail-inducing read! I've been on a bit of a sports kick lately and was very happy to see that Jen Frederick had written her very own hot athlete for me to get to know. And, right from the first page, Knox won my heart. Not only is he a fantastic athlete with the sexy swagger you expect, but he's also very focused on his future...so focused in fact that he's still a virgin. Yup...you read that right!! Knox has no intention of letting a girl get in the way of his path to the NFL and he works hard to ensure that his dreams will come true. But, then along comes Ellie and he's absolutely thrown for a loop. 
 From the start, he knows that she'll change his future and his outlook on his path. He knows that she's meant for him and that he'll do what it takes to have her in his life. And, for some unknown reason, I was able to overlook the insta-love on his part. I think it was because Ellie made him work for it and therefore provided the needed time for him to be sure of his feelings...or maybe it was just because it's interesting to see such intense feelings from a guy in a book. Either way, my heart melted as Knox began his pursuit of Ellie. 
 These two characters were fantastic and their chemistry was explosive. Ms. Frederick has a knack for writing characters that you would like to have as friends in real life and these two are no exception. Both Knox and Ellie were strong characters who knew what they wanted. Ellie has some family issues that she has to deal with and that forms the basis for the angst in this story. It's a very unique situation that makes this sports-themed book different from any I've read in the past. Her loyalty to her brother, even though it poses a danger for her, is great. And speaking of her brother, I also loved the secondary characters in this story and am hoping that there are more books to come in the future. Dear Ms. Frederick...please consider this a plea for books for Jack, Ty, Hammer, Ace...oh, heck...just write a book for every single one of those football hotties!! 
 So...if your looking for a fun read with sexy athletes, hot chemistry, wonderful writing and a unique storyline, look no further! Enjoy!!

Well written and interesting, a book that can be loved easily. I gave it three stars out of five just because of one reason; I couldn't stand the rollercoaster of emotions that it gave me. All the feels were crushing on me and it was tiring. The characters were confused and they managed to confuse me as well but it was annoying. The book was all about the two main leads, rejecting and hurting each other all over again and again and again. At some point I had enough, wondering who really does that in real life so it had me questioning about whether the book is realistic or not. I don't know... I mean the happy end could have had happened earlier but the author kept dragging it and trying to bring more obstacles. I don't know how to express it since I am not fluent in English but I hope you get what I am trying to say. 
 Other than that, it's a book you can read if you don't have anything better to do and if you can enjoy that kind of plot.

I was seriously surprised by how much I liked this book. From the cover, it just didn't seem like something I would pick up on my own, but I read a lot of good reviews, so that got me interested. I actually didn't have any idea what it was about when I started it. So, it was exciting to figure out what was going on with Helen right along with her. Of course if I had paid attention to anything, like the cover, or her name, or the names of the new family that moved into town, it would have been obvious (but, I was apparently not in a thinking mood). 
 I will say, right off the bat, this book has a LOT of similarities to Twilight. A LOT. Normally, when I reading things like, "This book will appeal to fans of The Twilight Saga" it makes me want to vomit, but in this case, it's really true. I also usually get annoyed with books that have so many similarities, but in this case, I didn't. Even though there were many parallels, this book was just written well. Josephine Angelini wrote Starcrossed similar enough to Twilight that you will love it, and different enough from Twilight that you won't hate it. Does that make sense. I guess what I'm trying to say is that if you loved Twilight, you will like this one too, but if you hated Twilight, you might find that you still like Starcrossed. The biggest reason that's true, is Helen. Helen is no Bella. 
 Helen is a fantastic heroine. I loved that even though she had an enormous amount of power at her disposal, she would do anything to keep from hurting people. While it might have been easy for her to use her "brawn," she preferred to use her brains instead. She was kind, but she was no doormat. She was inexperienced, but she could still kick butt when she needed to. She didn't need rescuing, she would do the rescuing herself. 
 Then there was the Delos family. I loved them all. The romantic tension between Helen and Lucas was intense!! I absolutely ate it up, and wanted to pull my hair out at the same time. Talk about frustrating!!! But in a good way. And did anyone else end up crushing on Hector? I love him! 
 The storyline is fantastic. I love Greek Mythology, so I loved rehashing all the old myths, but I also really enjoyed the "true and untold" stories that Josephine makes up. She takes all the stories we're familiar with, and adds her own little twist to them. It does end in somewhat of a cliffhanger. I was really hoping it wasn't a series....I've seriously had enough of series, but it is. It will definitely be one that I stick with, though, and those are getting few and far between! 
 I think that if the Percy Jackson series and the Twilight series had a baby, Starcrossed would be that child. I really liked this book. I think you will like it too! Try it on audio! 
 Andye

The ghost hunting gig gets much darker for Cass in this sequel to Anna Dressed in Blood. Cass just isn't satisfied with the way things ended with Anna. Is it because he can't let her go that she is haunting him? Can Cass find a way to put her to rest? Can he bring her back to him? Although Cass is still the snarky teen we love, his funny, smart-ass comments are fewer and farther between this time around. Things are just too serious for joking around. The horrific images are even stronger in this one - the Suicide Forest is not something I'll soon forget. A perfect read for this time of year (Halloween)!

When she sees a vision of her father dead and a man, Rook Mcqueen, with her fathers blood on him, she knows he must be the killer and must find him first before he can get to her father. So she heads to Cornerstone, and some truths become unraveled and she learns that he isn't her fathers killer. As they join forces to find out what is really going on, they find answers to questions that only lead to more questions, as they search for the real truth, a powerful desire builds between Brynn and Rook, and soon Rook will have to decide what is more important his status as Alpha of the pack, or Brynn as his mate... 
 After reading a review and recommendation from a friend, I began to see that I really needed to pick this one up. So I did, and I was so stunned by how well I enjoyed this one. I wasn't sure how I would, considering this is a new author for me, but Black Rook was tantalizing and intense and packed with everything I expect in a steamy shifter romance and then some. This isn't just a shifter romance, it does have some additions paranormal elements mixed in there, and it really adds some dramatic flair to the plot. The author does a stunning job of describing the world she has created, and the way that she stuns us with the creative scenes and the in depth characters. 
 The story begins with a misunderstanding, and what a misunderstanding, the heroine here well she has courage...willing to die to save the father that has never cared much for her. I loved her tenacity and courage, she has that inner strength that you can't help but admire. She has 'balls" that is for sure, she surely knows how to carry how a task that she puts her mind to. You see how she grows in this story, and I loved seeing her change into a woman of sacrifice and doing what is right even if its hurts the ones you love. Rook, is not the first child, but because he is a black wolf, he can be alpha if he desires. He has worked hard, to prove himself to be the obvious choice. He knows that he would be a leader and a good one. But when Brynn lands in his lap, his priorities change, one to where pursuing her earnestly with honest intent is more important than being the alpha. Their relationship from working together, turns into a slow courtship. They have sparks from the beginning, but not just physically, the author does a wonderful job in creating a bond between them that goes deeper than sex. (Although those parts were pretty sexy and fun), but we also see the development of their relationship, emotionally. 
 This first book in the series, sets the stage for the rest of the series, where we find out that there are some villains, that are dangerous, and it will take a miracle for them to come out alive. I so enjoyed the action, the suspense, the sensuality, the focus on their intimate relationship, and the bond between the brothers, and the way that this story was written was sexy, sensual and stunning in detail. A must read for paranormal romance lovers!!!

This is Book 2 in the Tanglewood series, but it can stand alone and it's definitely worth reading, as it's a very happy book. I love the Regency period and often wonder what it would really be like to live back then. Of course, it would probably be better if I had a title than if I had to be a servant. Cora is caught between the two worlds. Her parents almost force their way into society and in an effort to secure their position, they decide to marry her off to a most detestable man. So she runs away and becomes a servant--a housekeeper, to be exact. What would I do if I were in her shoes? I honestly don't know, but it would sure be miserable to be stuck with someone you can't stand. She knows what she wants and won't let anything stand in her way of obtaining it. 
 There's something about Cora, whether it's her teasing nature or sunny disposition, that draws those around her close. Her humor diffuses tense situations and breaks down barriers. Jonathan is considered to be somewhat of a tyrant, but Cora captivates him from first sight. I love the way they balance each other, especially when Cora is able to worm her way in and cause changes around the whole place. I love their relationship so much! I love the little misunderstandings and the slight groveling to resolve the situation. There are some shimmery sparks from the start and it's fun to see what happens, especially with the few little twists. 
 These are characters who are fun, interesting, and easy to adore in a beautiful country setting. I can't wait to get another story in the series!

 This was an intriguing read, not going to lie. 
 For a New Adult title, it was certainly different, but in a good way. We have two characters who are trying to figure out life, all while walking down the paths their parents paved for them. 
 Max is the heir to White Lace Productions, an adult films production company. His father is the owner and his late mother was a star -- and due to this, Max has had his share of side-eyed looks through the years. Then we also have a certain Miss Everly, the daughter of lawyers, who is finishing up law school herself. Her late grandmother, however, could see that Everly had other passions in life and before she passed, left Everly with a short bucket list of things to do before she graduated. 
 She has less than a semester to complete this list. 
 Her roommates, both escorts, meet with Max about a casting role at a local cafe that Everly studies at, and it's there that they first meet. 
 She is everything Max doesn't go for. She is girl-next-door, who could probably pull off the naughty librarian scene, but he really isn't getting those vibes from her. She's innocent, ambitious, and stuck her nose up at his profession. The thing is, though? 
 He hasn't reacted to a female the way he does Everly in a long time. 
 When he first approaches Everly, she figures he's just being nice. When he offers to help her with her bucket list, she pretty much just rolls her eyes and goes with it -- this good looking guy would never actually want to be with her, right? When sex gets put on the table (because of course it was going to get there, right?), Everly's biggest fear is that she's not adventurous enough; why would the heir of a porn company want silly, little, missionary style her? 
 I really enjoyed these two characters and watching them figure out how to actually go for what they wanted in life. It was interesting to see Max hold back when it came to a girl. I have to say, though, I had a hard time imagining the twenty-three year old Max and his friend, Ben, in the porn world (at least in the award winning porn world); I felt they were more true to their characters when hanging out with the group at a bonfire. 
 Everly and Max have issues -- neither puts 'relationship' on their agreement and therefore don't actually talk about things. They pretty much roll with the punches and when things get tough, they take their toys and go back home. 
 When it's simple and easy, you can tell that these two could have something great. They test one another's boundaries (in a good way) and start to learn to go after what they truly want out of life. 
 I want to see more of Max and Everly, that's for sure. As this series is title "White Lace", I can only imagine that Ben will have one of the next titles, and I have to say, I'm certainly curious about this videographer who isn't afraid to get a little hands on... (...who's also a damn good friend for Max and has decent family advice. Wonder how the man who doesn't believe in soulmates will take falling in love?).

It seems like Goodreads has, for the most part, overlooked this title, which is a very, very sad thing. Andrew Smith has done something truly amazing here with Winger and it's a bit sad when you see how few people have read this book. 
 I originally only picked Winger up because of my beloved Andrew Smith, but I was a bit apprehensive because well, the last two Smith books I've read were dark, depressing, and violent and I really couldn't see him write a contemporary book. 
 But the moment I started reading, I realised that I had made a huge mistake and that Winger was definitely as good, if not better, than the Marbury Lens series. 
 Winger follows the story of Ryan Dean West 'Winger' as he traverses high school as a fourteen year old junior. He recently landed himself in the Opportunity Hall of his boarding school, where they keep all the school's worst cases, after stealing his teacher's phone. And of course, he manages to get put in the room with his arch-enemy, Chas Becker. 
 Ryan Dean's voice is one of those rare ones that are very unique. It was a voice that made it extremely hard to drop the book even for a few minutes, and to quote Cecil Baldwin, 'and I fell in love instantly'. I knew from very early on that Winger was not going to be a book I'd forget anytime soon. 
 As a character, Ryan Dean West was easily one of the most relatable characters that I've ever 'met', yet also one of the most average characters out there. He wasn't special, not really - not in the way that most YA characters are. Ryan Dean was a very normal character, and I think that contributed much to his appeal because much of popular YA has the main character special somehow, whether they be vampires or the next Katniss Everdeen. 
 Smith's writing was absolutely superb. He manages to trap the essence of a young fourteen year old boy, with all its ups and downs, amazingly well. He takes you on an amazing ride that will make you laugh and fall deeper and deeper in love with the characters and the school and the book, but by the end, all the book's hidden severity comes at you like a wrecking ball and you're left gasping for air by the end. 
 Under all of Winger's hilarity and romance is a very deep story which I'm going to try and lightly step around because the last thing I want to do is spoil the discovery for you. If you want to know more about it, I've put it under a spoiler tag. For most of the book, the subject of 'titles and labels' is briefly danced upon. It's talked about at times, but more often than not, only really there if you look for it. There are some quotes that really shout it out to you but chances are, you'll be more focussed on the humour of said quote than the severity and meaning. 
 "And then it's always that one word that makes you so different and puts you outside the overlap of everyone else; and that word is so fucking big and loud, it's the only thing anyone ever hears when your name is spoken. 
 And whenever that happens to us, all the other words that make us the same disappear in it's shadow." 
 Certain things happen at the end and it kinda comes at you in a rush because for most of the book, it's been pretty light. Sure, shitty things happened but it was never really... bad, you know? There weren't any moments that made you wonder if there was more to the book but there were moments that were shocking, to say the least. 
 But at the end, suddenly everything hits you. I spent the last few pages in utter shell shock because the humour that had hidden everything before suddenly fell away and what I had was an utterly heartbreaking book.  
 One more aspect worth mentioning is the absolutely fantastic artwork. Sam Bosma's art is just brilliant, oh ym god, just look at it! The art adds another beautiful layer to the book. 
 In all, Winger is a book that I don't think I'll ever forget. I recommend it to everyone!

I love this series. I love the way Gail Carriger writes. I love her humor. I love her characters. I love her quirky imagination. And I really want to lie to you all and tell y'all that I loved this book.... 
 But I can't. 
 If we were sitting around a parlor in Victorian England sipping some earl grey, in a lace trimmed visiting gown, with my best kid skin gloves and ringlets I would be forced to submit to my best manners and in accordance with polite society gush over the entire book with alacrity. 
 But we are not. 
 I am just unsure what went wrong here. I enjoy this series for the humor, the outlandish plots, and the fire between Alexia and Conall. This book did have humor - just not as much as previous books or as expected. The plot was outlandish - but overly so and not believable enough. And the fire between Alexia and Conall was tempered by marriage and Conall always trying to appease Alexia. 
 I get the feeling that this book was set up more as a filler type novel, but to me you really only get those types of books in series that do not have definite ends, where as the 5th book in this series is supposed to be the final. So then I though maybe it read like a filler book because it was meant to build up to the last novel and that it was going to be a whopper! Only the 5th book takes place 2 or 3 years later, so that doesn't make sense either. 
 The reason this book felt like such a filler novel was because the plot supposedly revolved around a assassination plot against the Queen of England except for most of the book no one was ever really doing anything about it!! It felt like most everyone's efforts were given to the relationships between secondary characters and the minutia of manners when a pregnant woman is involved. 
 And what was going on with all the secondary characters in this book??? All the old characters seem cast off and forgotten to be replaced by new ones. Where was Ivy in this book?? She barely gets any time and the little she has is weak. It was not necessary for her to go to Scotland, but its as if Carriger couldn't figure out where to stick her so she just came up with this flimsy idea as a way to put her in the story anywhere. Akledama got a bit more screen time because of the issues concerning Alexia's child I guess, but he seemed less important this book. Also I keep hoping we will get to see more of Floote in these novels but every time I am disappointed. Even Genevieve seemed less important and that is ironic considering her role in the book. She hardly has any face time until the last 50 pages. I get where she was during all that time, but she still could have been included more. Instead we got all this information about Biffy. So much so he felt like a main character for a while there. (In the 5th book there are even whole sections written from his POV!) 
 And the whole thing with Lyall...just pissed me off! I thought he was the definition of kindness, understanding, and politeness. Instead he has shown himself to be conniving, manipulative, and uncaring. Yes his concern was for his pack, but he also showed no concern for others feelings. He allows Conall to believe that his old pack were murderers, or at least attempted murderers, even though he knows how much it pains Conall because he is too much of a coward to confess his actions to his alpha and seek understanding and forgiveness. Since when has Lyall become a coward? Seriously, I was so completely let down by him. And what's more - all that stuff between Lyall and Alexia's father - that was a pretty weak and unbelievable tie in. I didn't think it added to either of their characters. There just had to have been a better way to do that. Basically Lyall went from one of my favorite characters to one of my hated ones. I could have forgiven his actions if he would have been honest about them to Conall, but instead Lyall allows his Alpha to suffer with the thoughts that his old pack was inherently bad and that as alpha that was his fault.  
 And OMG, WTH??? Alexia spends the ENTIRE FREAKING BOOK 8 months pregnant but the model on the cover is not preggers?! It's like urban fantasy covers with kickass heroines sporting knifes on the cover but you everyday normal girl as the main character (I'm looking at you Mind Games) 
 I just expected more. 
 I am starting book 5 so all I can hope is that it is amazing and the whole series ends with a bang!

What do you think your last day on earth will be like? Will you have any regrets at the moment you realize your end is certain? Sam's last day starts about as normal as it gets. She goes to school, hangs out with her friends, heads out to a party. Then, on the way home, the car she's riding in crashes and Sam dies. And wakes up again in her bed at the beginning of the same day. We never really find out exactly why Sam keeps coming back, but she finally figures out that she's got to change something about that day or she will be doomed to continue repeating. This book sucks you in right away and never lets go. The reader will sympathize with Sam and hate her at the same time. She's not always the nicest person and doesn't always make the best choices, but at least she is able to learn and put things in perspective. As she goes through each day over and over, she attempts to get to the bottom of who exactly needs saving and how that can happen. 
 I was afraid this was going to be a bit cheesy or overwrought, but such was not the case. Oliver's writing is solid; her characters very realistic and the situations will seem familiar to any American teenager. It's no wonder this book made many librarian's top ten lists of 2010. I felt like it actually lived up to most of the hype.

Thoughts on the Overall Book: I picked this book up expecting something akin to I Hunt Killers and...didn't really get that. The synopsis of this book fails to mention the supernatural element so that was a little jarring. Once I got past that though, I was able to enjoy the book more. 
 Cover--Yea or Nay: It's kind of bland, but I do like it, I think it works for the kind of book this is. 
 Characters: John Wayne Carver...I'm still a little unsure how I really feel about him. While I was able to sympathize and even relate to Jazz Dent in I Hunt Killers I'm not sure I was totally able to do that with John who is definitely more of a psychopath and rather frightening. Maybe I liked him because of that? I enjoyed reading about him and from his point of view too. It was an interesting perspective to have and I totally applaud the author for being able to get into that character--and just for going there in the first place. I know how scary that can be as an author. So I don't know that I can say I really liked him, but I did like reading about him. It was interesting reading about the other characters from his point of view too. I actually liked his friend Max and Brooke as well. I sort of felt sorry for his mom, but at the same time, I think she could have done more to understand his condition and not just either freak out or pretend nothing is wrong, but I guess that's just human nature. Mr. Crowley was an interesting character. I'm going to admit, I was a little disappointed after finding out that he was a demon and not a serial killer. it just made him less scary in my opinion. He wasn't really malicious, he had to kill people and being a supernatural creature makes it less scary because you already expect him to be bad or at least be capable of it. To quote Dean Winchester: "Demons I get, people are crazy." So yeah, the final part where he was chasing John and his mom was creepy, but apart from that, there really wasn't anything particularly frightening about this book and it lessened the cool psychological to psychical chase that I love in serial killer stories. The profiling is the fun part. Demons don't need profiling.  
 The Romance: None. I don't even think I'm going to call a budding romance between John and Brooke yet. 
 Writing Style: I did love the writing style. As I said before I always applaud authors for going out of their normal comfort zones (or at least I hope they are) and writing characters who go beyond reluctant or anti-heroes to maybe even past dark hero status. To put yourself in the head of a potential serial killer is a feat of skill, especially if you can make it sound accurate which Dan Wells does. And the fact that it's in first person makes it even better, and makes the reader experience some uncomfortable moments. 
 Accuracy/ Believability: Despite the supernatural element, the psychological depictions of John's character are spot on, and I really appreciate the research the author must have had to do into psychological disorders and serial killers. 
 Problems/What bothered me: As I mentioned before, my only complaint was that I thought demons were more boring than serial killers. I know there's something wrong with me... 
 Conclusion: 4 stars. I do look forward to continuing this series. Now that I know what I'm getting into, I think I'll be able to pick up the next book with fresh eyes and enjoy it more without the jarring realization that it's supernatural. 
 Recommended Audience: Girl or guy read, 17 and up. Fans of I Hunt Killers, who would like to see it crossed with Supernatural would like this. And for the record, it's actually less gritty than I Hunt Killers as well. Even though I think this is classed as 'adult' I would say, at least the first book, reads like YA.

In Chinese culture, it's believed that the seventh lunar month (the seventh month in the Chinese calendar) is when the gates of hell open and the dead can come back to the world. It's a month where the smell of incense is thick (and the haze makes it worse). If you're not a fan of all this smoke and ashes, you may wish for the Japanese Obon, which is similar but only lasts for about a week. At any rate, it's the seventh month now, and I decided to read The Ghost Bride. 
 Anyway, The Ghost Bride is a fantasy novel set in Malacca, back when it was still a British colony. Li Lan is the beautiful protagonist, and the story starts when her father asks her if she'd like to be the bride in a ghost marriage. 
 Her family's quite poor, but the groom's side is rich, so if she marries him, she'll live in comfort. But the prospective groom visits her in her dreams (bad decision on her part) and he is so repulsive of course she won't want to marry him. Instead, she prefers his cousin, who was originally her intended. 
 And because the story is complicated, this isn't even the main plot. 
 The bulk of the book features Li Lan after she accidentally left her body and meets Er Lang. He enlists her help in finding out information from her prospective ghost groom, and we get to see what the spirit world is like. 
 While it's quite complicated to follow, I didn't have any problems with the plot, probably because I have years of Chinese dramas behind me. I thought it was pretty well-paced, and I never grew bored with the story. 
 I really liked the descriptiveness, although it went a bit overboard sometimes. Although I could believe the idea that Li Lan didn't really know about the spirits because of her father being a strict Confucianist, I didn't get why she had to explain every single little bit of life, including translating the word 'baju' into English. I can only assume it's for the ang moh's, or perhaps the author is illustrating the hold our ex-colonial masters still have on us. 
 Oh, and even though relationships (and romance) is one of the pillars of this book, I wasn't annoyed by it at all, which is a first for me. I mean, there are three guys that Li Lan gets involved in and they are: 
 - the Ghost Groom: Odious so whatever 
 - Tian Bai (Ghost Groom's cousin): Li Lan gets a crush on him because who wouldn't when their intended is so repulsive 
 - Er Lang: the mysterious dude that helps Li Lan. They bicker a lot, but I genuinely like how their relationship develops. 
 So to me, it's not a love rectangle because two of the three guys aren't even serious candidates. Which really helps because I am not a fan of love triangles or shapes of any kind. 
 If you're looking for a lyrical, absorbing fantasy book set close to home, you should definitely pick this up.

 To honor this book I'm starting off this review with my very first haiku. Do I think I will ever master the poetic talents of our main hero Apollo? No, there aren't many as sure of their own talents as our main man, even if they don't have said talents. Not to say Apollo doesn't have a way with words. He really, really does. Because with The Dark Prophecy, the second book in The Trials of Apollo series, Rick Riordan knocks it out of the park. 
 Something about the way he writes Apollo is just so lovable. You can't help but smile at his woe and flair for the dramatics. While he may have turned into a mere mortal there is no lack of showmanship. Setting this from his POV saves the book on its own. But in the second book of this new Percy Jackson spin-off series it feels like the pace picks up compared to the first one. Loveable characters return and do not outshine the new ones. The only one that outshines them all is Apollo, but it doesn't matter because he's just so fun and charming. 
 Apollo is a little different from his other series in the sense that if you take away his point of view there's not much left. He keeps this thing afloat even more than Percy Jackson did. All of the new chracters have played a part before in the vast history of this Greek God and it's pure delight to see Riordan's take on it. This is a coming of age story, not of a teenager, but of a God that learns what it's like to be a man. And he continues to do so with the most flair I've ever read about. 
 If I were to rate this book on plotdevices and craftsmanship I would probably rate it 3 stars. You may want to prepare yourself for what I am about to say, but I managed to catch a mistake that Riordan made. It's bound to happen with so many books he's written, but it bothered me nonetheless. It's a really minor thing where he wants to make one of those "heh, look at those millenials" kind of reference, but it felt really out of place. Apollo complains about the younger demi gods being on social media on their phones. Yes, their smart phones. It's implied in earlier books that demi gods aren't supposed to carry around smart phones because it's like a magnet for monsters. This is a pet peeve for me, because to be honest I've never gotten the we need to keep social media and technology out of fantasy books so it can stay more magical argument, 
 which is probably what writers like Rick Riordan and J.K Rowling are doing.  
 Even though this book didn't have a chapter that stood out for me (like others did) and a few pet peeves my enjoyment rating went through the roof. Unlike Magnus the jokes hit the mark right from the start, maybe because Apollo is more charming. Like all the other Percy Jackson books this is one rollercoaster of fun and silliness that never seems to stop, but it's the small, endearing, heroic and touching moments where Apollo truly shines. Some may feel overdone, but that fits his character. 
 I love these books as much as I do Harry Potter (but with better spin-offs). So naturally I've spend some time thinking what camp half blood cabin I would be in. If I could choose, I'd definately pick Apollo's.

I liked The Haunting of Hill House. It was a little slow to start, but Eleanor's odd characteristics intrigued me, and since I knew we were leading up to a haunted house, I was willing to stick it out. The house itself was great-- I loved Jackson's descriptions of the rooms and the disorienting nature of its odd angles, much like the "House of Mystery" at the "Oregon Vortex" which I visited this summer. There were a few scenes that truly gave me the shivers, such as part V, chapter 4, which ends with Eleanor waking up from a dream (?) to wonder whose hand she'd been holding if it was not Theodora's (creepy!) and I enjoyed viewing Eleanor's descent into crazy-town from her own POV. In general, the book satisfied as a classic horror story. 
 The biggest problem that I had with it was what it left out. My favorite character, by far, was Mrs. Dudley. I absolutely loved her robotic role in the house, including her strict schedule of food and of course her dire warnings that she always leaves before dark and will be much too far away to help you if you scream in the night. I kept waiting for the big reveal about the Dudleys-- they were under the house's spell or they were evil or they were dead-- but it never came. In fact, their role in the story began to fade by the end. When the insufferable Mrs. Montague arrives, there is no mention at all of her being warned away at the gate by Mr. Dudley. And then there was that strange scene on page 211 where Eleanor eavesdrops on a conversation between Mrs. Dudley and Mrs. Montague and, for the first and only time in the novel, Mrs. Dudley sounds like a normal person. I am ashamed to admit it, but I didn't understand that part. I couldn't tell if it was showing a side of Mrs. Dudley that they had not seen before or if it was a false observation made by Eleanor in an altered state. (I would welcome some enlightenment on this from others.) 
 So, while the ending satisfied me in terms of the main characters, I closed the book feeling very dissatisfied about the Dudleys. I think they deserve more, maybe even their own novel. Maybe someday I'll write it.

 The great think about Curious Incident isn't that it is a mystery story about a boy with Asperger's Syndrome, it's that Mark Haddon does such a great job of reinventing the mystery formula. Let's face it, the Sherlock Holmes stories (which play a pretty prominent role in the novel's construction) are the benchmark by which a lot of detective narratives are mentioned. But they're pretty formulaic, especially in terms of character: Sherlock Holmes is a genius and Watson is a sidekick; Sherlock Holmes is a thinking machine and Watson takes dictation; Sherlock Holmes knows your darkest secrets from looking at your shoes and Watson can't even remember where he was wounded (his arm? His leg?). Doyle needed that structure--he had to have a straight man for his great detective; one who could palm the ace so that the readers could enjoy the pleasure of being told how the crime was committed (as opposed to the pleasure of figuring it out for themselves). After all, Watson always knows the who, what, where, and when, but he's very careful to keep it hidden from the reader by reporting himself as a (let's be honest) bumbling. Who else but a John (or was it James?) H. Watson would be willing to represent himself as perpetually awestruck? 
 Even though Holmes and Watson perpetually haunt Curious Incident, their roles have been radically rewritten. There's no need for a crime-fighting duo here (a puzzle master and his biographer, the brain and the brawn, or the machine and the lover). Christopher fulfills both those positions and in doing so, repeatedly hides the "whodunit" not from the reader, but from himself. It is this recurring dramatic irony--the reader watching Christopher struggle in coming to grips with the fact that deductive logic alone is not enough in crime solving--that makes the book effective in so many ways. For starters, Haddon is engaging with precisely those qualities that made Sherlock Holmes a literary celebrity. If Holmes truly is a thinking machine, how effective can he really be? When taken to the extreme, isn't Holmes simply Christopher? Or, alternatively, Christopher is what Holmes would be if he were removed from a fictional world in which people can be read like texts, soil can be identified on sight, and monographs can be produced on 140 varieties of tobacco ash. Christopher's world, in other words, simply doesn't measure up to the categories Holmes produces for people. After all, what is a detective to do when deductive analysis cannot filter out motivations for utterly irrational behavior?

 Science fiction? A retelling of one of my favorite fairytales from when I was young? And an illness sweeping the world, seemingly without a cure? Oh goodness, that sounds like the trifecta when it comes to books tailored to me. But that's just the plot. Marissa Meyer topped all that off with characters and dialogue and wicked awesome writing to make this easily one of my favorite reads for the year. 
 Cinder is a story about so much set to the backdrop of Cinderella. Yes, it's a Cinderella story, but it's so unique and well written that it feels more like a new story, rather than a retelling. The writing that Meyer put to the pages really made the difference between a retelling and a complete and utter re-imagining. I was absolutely blown away by the details and vivid descriptions. I saw New Beijing and everything Cinder encountered in my mind's eye, making it that much more of a rich reading experience. 
 This story was completely addictive, fast-paced, high-intensity and non-stop. From the very beginning, Meyer hits you in the forehead with a proverbial brick, demanding the reader to wake up and pay attention. The world(-and-moon)-building is absolute genius, the characters were all full to the brim with life and personality and the dialogue, both external and internal, was saturated with equal parts hilarity, calamity and individuality. Cinder is a whole new world (couldn't help but stuff in a tiny Disney reference), and Meyer does an excellent job of describing the science fiction elements. But it's done so in a way that was more show, rather than tell. 
 My only teensy complaint that prevents me from sending my rating over that coveted five+ mark is that the big reveal moment was incredibly predictable. I called it very early on in the book. I will say that several of the twists (and there are lots) were unexpected but the one that was meant to be a major wow moment was lackluster. 
 To say that I enjoyed Cinder is an understatement. I found the ending to be a great opening for the next books of this series without the heart-wrenching cliffhanger. Speaking of the next books, I cannot wait to get my hands on them. And if you've not picked up this book yet, I strongly urge you to do so. Story lovers worldwide will appreciate Cinder.
