Like the humanity it portrays Cormac McCarthy's prose in 'The Road' is pared down to it's core, teeth bared with a vicious depiction of humanity. His words are careful and full, hinting at far more then they ever reveal. Anonymous disasters past and present hound the unnamed narrator and his son as they journey along the deserted highways of America, past the last dregs of a society long drained of its humanity. Mad Max without the hero, apocalypse without the bang, a study of character in the face of nothing. 
 These features make the book as sparse and barren as the landscape it's describing. I found it difficult to become invested in the fate of characters who were having trouble investing in themselves. The progress is hazy, and the victories hollow, like shells of people traveling forward due to a lack of friction rather then any particular drive. Hopelessness in all it's glory. 
 The book ends on an up, a minor victory, which is slightly disconcerting. It seems contrary to the world being created, the used up nature of everything else encountered, too hopeful and incongruous. Like a felt tail pinned to a picture of a donkey, it may fit but it doesn't really belong. Death was expected, inevitable, required, but the hope seems like a prayer in a book that long ago declared god dead, a turning on itself to find something that it didn't bother to construct. I enjoyed the text, found things worth pondering, loved the descriptions, but I do not think it's untouchable. It's too inhuman to love as a piece of sentimental literature, but too hopeful to realize genuine despondancy.

Defending Jacob isn't my normal kind of book. It's a crime thriller, and I just don't often get around to that genre. I picked it up for my mom, and I'm not even sure why I started reading it, but a day after finishing (to say something about it, I finished it in one day in three giant chunks) I'm still thinking about it. 
 Andrew Barber is the First Assistant DA in his upper class, educated, small-town, good place to grow up in, community. The murder of a 14 year old boy rocks the town, and Andy, knowing this will be a high-profile case, decides to take it on. He is then called off the case when the primary suspect emerges: his own 14 year old son Jacob. Soon, everything Andy knows about his son is called into question, except that for Andy, Jacob is forever innocent. 
 A majority of Defending Jacob is good. Jacob isn't the sweet Boy Scout type (a fact Andy only begins to understand). He owns a knife, his internet posts are suspicious, accounts from his friends show him to be moody, mean sometimes, mysterious, and with a definite grudge against the deceased boy. This is a smart choice on Landy's side--for one, the reader doesn't automatically side with Jacob. This isn't a clear cut trial. Just as soon as Jacob may seem innocent, something else emerges that makes you question everything. Secondly, while Jacob's flaws are exposed to the reader and Andy, Andy's steadfast belief in his son is only more highlighted. Andy is not a naive man, but he is a father who loves his son and may have a giant blind spot where Jacob is concerned. 
 Because Landay's spent time in the legal field, the courtroom scenes are written well. I found myself able to see the courtroom and the trial as it unfolded. Done less effectively for me is the talk about genetics and how it plays into the defense/prosecution. The prosecuting attorney is portrayed as the villain, and because this is in Andy's point of view I get it, but he seems a bit too 'mustache twirling' for my liking. 
 Keep reading until the end. Just when you thought you knew how it will go, it'll throw you.

 If I'm going to actually jump into the second one this month, I should attempt to write my review for this one. Otherwise, I'll just muddle them together. 
 I've only read one other Keri Arthur book, but she has a tendency to shove everything and the kitchen sink into a story and make it work. This book is no different. It's one part paranormal romance, one part urban fantasy, one part science fiction, and one part dystopia. It should basically be a mess, but this book is anything but that. 
 Tig is a dechet, a lab-grown super-soldier made to fight in a war years earlier. She lives in the bones of her old bunker, everyone else eradicated by the shifters during the war. The bunker is full of ghosts that she can talk to, children ghosts that follow her around. Despite being a hermit, she's thrown into the middle of a plot where people are stealing children and, as a big ol' softie, she risks life and limb to try and save them. That and people threaten her ghosts, which isn't cool. 
 Teaming up with shifters who are wary of her existence and her nature, she uses all her powers to find out who's behind the kidnappings. Along the way she meets up with an old lover, and they pick up their fling where they left off. She's also quite smitten with the shifter she regularly runs missions with, but he's not at all trustworthy of her. 
 The vampires in this series are pretty gross, and I thank the author for going that direction with them. They swarm and become insubstantial. They devour and smell bad. Honestly, they were pretty terrifying. 
 I picked this book up and I didn't set it down. I loved every minute of it and I can't wait to pick up the next installment. I especially loved the little children ghosts. They were unsettlingly cute, and helped get Tig out of a few tough scrapes. 
 Tig's background is intense and Keri Arthur does a great job explaining it in bits and pieces without the entire history being an infodump or slog. I appreciate that. Not many authors can throw such a mishmash of things together and keep the plot moving at such a pace. 
 There is one thing that threw me out of the narrative for awhile. Tig's old romantic partner was a special breed of assassin called the, and I'm not making this up, Blue Steel Project. 
 Oops. I dunno if Keri Arthur just never saw Zoolander or if she did and was doing a subtle nod at it, but a salamander-humanoid assassin, Blue Steel class? I died a little on the inside. I had to take like a thirty minute break and yet I still somehow finished the book in a day. 
 Anyway, great book. Great characters. Would recommend. Now it's time for me to go start the second and hope upon hope it doesn't suffer from second book syndrome.

This seems like a good candidate for so many of my usual tags--horror, fantasy, specfic... Wright's book is chock-full of minute detail, including some details so bizarre that they're hard to process. In some ways Scientology is very like any other cult (pardon me, "new religious movement.") It has leaders who enjoy exceptional wealth while the majority of its members labor in penury. It isolates its members from their families and friends, and seeks to control their financial, personal, social, and psychological lives. It's said to hold some of its members in physical gaol, where they're subject to physical and mental abuse as well as near-starvation conditions. This is all pretty familiar stuff from Jim Jones, Waco, the Rajneeshi, and a ton of other coercive spiritual movements. 
 But Scientology is especially interesting in its symbiotic relationship with Hollywood and the cult of celebrity. When you think about it, the star factory is an ideal partner for a fringe religion. It's the locus of fabulous riches, insecure and idealistic personalities, fast deals, and constantly shifting norms. What does any cult need to thrive? People, preferably wealthy and impressionable. What do aspiring film stars need? Connections, relationships, a way in. Scientology took advantage of this opportunity early on, and positioned itself as a leg up for actors, directors, writers, and others trying to break into a very tough business. It's not hard to see why so many people, caught up in the ego-slamming whirlwind of Hollywood, would be grateful to clamber aboard the good ship L. Ron Hubbard. And it's not hard to see what Scientology gains from charging people thousands of dollars for auditing and courses, or from associating itself with influential, popular, high-access people like Tom Cruise and John Travolta. 
 Still, it can be a little tough to live in the Scientology mindset for the four hundred fifty-odd pages of this book. My hat is off to Wright. By the time I was finished reading about the constant bullying, paranoia, psychopathy, abuse, delusion, and greed of the Scientology set, I was feeling pretty sick. I admire him for taking on the topic, not only because it's so glum but because Scientology is famous for mercilessly persecuting its critics, in ways both legal and illegal. 
 And I admire him even more for coming to the conclusion that many if not most people don't join Scientology because they're dumb or greedy. Most join because they believe it holds the key to making the world a better place. They're idealistic and they have good intentions--they buy into the rhetoric telling them that if they can go clear, they won't just better their own lives, they'll improve the world as a whole. It's hard not to get a little more depressed at the thought of just how wrong they are.

 This 4th book of the Chaos series by Kristen Ashley made me feel so many emotions I am not even sure where to begin. The story of High and Millie made me smile, broke my heart, made me cry and then made me smile again. The roller coaster that was this book kept me reading until I could barely keep my eyes open and then when I finished it I was devastated that it was over. 
 As in all of Kristen Ashley stories her male protagonists are yummy in all of their alpha bad*ss ways. Logan "High" Judd was no different. He was the sweet and cocky young guy in love starting his life with his brothers in the Chaos motorcycle club. Then he was the angry, once spurned, never-to-be-hurt again bad*ss biker who lived his life for himself and his club, but never again for a woman. His hurt was palpable even after all of the years that had passed. 
 Millie Cross was so heartbreakingly loyal she made you feel like a lesser person just by reading about the sacrifices she made. She loved High and would do anything for him, including giving him up for his own good. She lives life in the shadow of the one that she once had. All of this for a man that once loved her and now hates her more than he has ever hated anything. 
 Millie and High was a couple that I wanted to see together more than any other couple I have ever read. I wanted so badly, no I needed them to have a happy ending. I felt their pain so acutely it was like I was actually living it.
